stories.Headline: Senator Chris Van Hollen endorses a bipartisan Senate select committee on artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen endorsed a proposed bipartisan Senate select committee on artificial intelligence on November 20, 2026. This endorsement occurred as Congress weighs how to oversee the technology and as Democrats prepare to take control in January 2027. Van Hollen is competing with Senator Chuck Schumer for the Senate majority leader job following a Democratic midterm victory. He released a plan for tackling AI risks amid increased concerns about cybersecurity and the possibility of superintelligence. The senator argues that the American people should decide how AI is developed and governed rather than tech leaders.

The proposal is tracked as S. Res. 918, which was introduced by Senator Ruben Gallego on September 29, 2026. This resolution would establish the select committee and specify its investigative powers, including the potential for subpoena authority. A companion measure, the AI Systems Transparency Act, S. 5471, was introduced between September 23 and 24, 2026. This act would require disclosures about how AI models are structured and would be overseen by the new committee.

Van Hollen also suggests banning recursive self-improvement in AI systems to prevent agents from evading human controls. Senator Van Hollen said the Senate moves like a glacier compared to the rushing stream of AI risks. He believes the Senate needs to be equal to the AI age and mount an ambitious, sustained response. Van Hollen called for independent third-party evaluations of leading AI models and said companies should bear responsibility for harms. He also wants to re-establish the Congressional Office of Technology Assessment to operate independently of the executive branch.

His plan includes moving bipartisan legislation concerning AI safety, affordability, and national security through the Senate. Supporters argue a dedicated committee would provide sharper oversight, focused resources, and the power to compel testimony and documents. Senators John Hickenlooper, Ben Ray Luján, and Ruben Gallego have voiced support for the proposed select committee. Hickenlooper sent a letter advocating for AI oversight on November 19, 2026, which Van Hollen later posted on X. AI companies could be affected by mandatory outside testing and liability for the risks their products create.

Van Hollen also wants to protect workers from paying higher electric bills for data centers built by corporations. Congressional AI oversight has so far been spread across existing committees that have other priorities and different focuses. Senator Chuck Schumer has previously supported the CHIPS and Science Act and the 2024 AI roadmap from Insight Forums. Schumer has called on the administration to brief Senators on frontier AI testing and protecting against AI-enabled cyber threats.

Van Hollen has pushed the White House for tougher guardrails with China and demanded transparency from the Federal Aviation Administration. He also introduced the Ready to Work Act in September to provide job opportunities for long-term unemployed workers. The Senate is set to vote on the new majority leader on December 1, requiring a simple majority. It remains unresolved whether S. Res.

918 or the AI Systems Transparency Act will receive a vote before 2028. The new Senate majority must decide if it will embrace mandatory outside testing of leading AI models. These decisions will determine whether the resulting oversight of the AI sector becomes binding or remains merely advisory. The articles leave open whether Van Hollen or Schumer will ultimately secure the Senate majority leader position.

stories.Headline: Malaysia proposes AI Governance Bill to mandate incident reporting for high-risk systems
stories.Summary:
Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo announced on November 24, 2026, that Malaysia is considering new regulations for artificial intelligence. The government plans to introduce the AI Governance Bill to create a formal incident reporting mechanism. This new system will allow the government to analyze emerging risks and strengthen existing safeguards. These measures are specifically designed to address high-risk applications that could cause emotional dependence in children. The proposed legislation requires mandatory crisis protocols and response mechanisms for high-risk AI companions and chatbots.

These measures will be determined by risk patterns that the government identifies through sectoral monitoring. Mental health issues will be handled through the Health Ministry’s HEAL 1555 helpline for those in need. Social protection matters will be referred to the Talian Kasih 15999 service to ensure proper support. Minister Gobind Singh Deo explained that the government is also developing the Malaysia AI Safety Institute under AI Malaysia.

This institute will focus on the research, testing, and assessment of AI risks to establish safety standards. He stated that responsibility for harmful AI content would depend on the roles of application developers and platform providers. Both parties could be held jointly liable for the harmful content generated by their systems. The Minister noted that platforms like TikTok and ChatGPT are already subject to regulation by the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission.

This commission has the authority to investigate harmful content and can impose restrictions when necessary. Gobind provided these details while responding to questions in the Dewan Rakyat regarding legal liability for AI developers. The government aims to balance innovation with the protection of vulnerable users through these new laws. More to follow.

stories.Headline: New York Assembly investigates AI impacts in K-12 classrooms ahead of Dec 1 hearing
stories.Summary:
The New York State Assembly is investigating the impacts artificial intelligence is having in K-12 classrooms, Spectrum News reported on Nov. 24, 2026. A hearing is set for Dec. 1, 2026, where lawmakers will hear testimony from educational leaders. The hearing is being held so lawmakers can seek a better understanding of how AI can impact students in the classroom, in libraries, and at home. The Assembly's Dec. 1 hearing is scheduled for 10 a.m. The New York State United Teachers Union is preparing to testify in front of the Assembly Standing Committees on Education, Libraries and Education Technology, and Science and Technology.

NYSUT has taken the position that children pre-K through second grade should not have access to AI. From the third through eighth grades, it believes students should learn AI literacy, and only in high school should students be allowed to use AI with adult supervision. NYSUT is also calling on tech companies to protect students' privacy and that any AI programs be tested before they're deployed in classrooms. Democratic Assemblymember Robert Carroll is chair of the Committee on Libraries and Education Technology. Carroll says New York state has 750 school districts, which means it is the Wild West, and sometimes schools in the same district do totally different things.

Melinda Person, president of the New York State United Teachers Union, said children only get one childhood and should not spend it participating in some experiment that Silicon Valley is running. Person said every decision about every product that goes onto a Chromebook in a school, or that kids get access to via their school technology, should be a really intentional conversation deliberated with educators and parents at the table. She said it should not be a decision being made by tech companies. Carroll said what New York should not have, and the state is rare in this, is that it too often allows for complete local control.

Carroll is hoping for a more mainstreamed approach when it comes to AI. Last legislative session, Carroll introduced a bill that prohibits the use of most artificial intelligence in classrooms prior to high school. It was referred to the Assembly Committee on Education, and he says he intends to reintroduce it this upcoming session. Carroll says the one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI in New York City schools for grades K-8 is based on his proposal.

Student-facing generative AI refers to AI tools including chat and tutoring bots and writing assistants. Carroll said he sits on the AI task force in schools of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and in many ways the mayor's moratorium models his bill. Carroll said there is a basic moratorium for kids K-8, and then there are exemptions inside high school where they delineate specific programs that can be used. Carroll said New York state is rare in too often allowing complete local control.

Person said decisions should not be made by tech companies. NYSUT is calling for any AI programs to be tested before they are deployed in classrooms. The hearing will hear testimony from educational leaders. More to follow.

stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms said it would suspend its planned Class C share issuance while it faces shareholder litigation challenging its proposed recapitalization, delaying a financing initiative intended to support artificial intelligence investments. The corporation agreed not to issue the shares during pretrial and trial procedures in Delaware's Court of Chancery. The suit targets Meta's proposal to issue a new class of nonvoting Class C common shares in January 2027. The plan would effectively be a two-for-one stock split, giving Meta more leeway to fund acquisitions and keep personnel while preserving CEO Mark Zuckerberg's voting authority. The suspension also affects Meta's planned $60 billion at-the-market stock offering program, which was not slated to start until the Class C shares began trading.

The delay comes as Meta continues to make large investments in advanced semiconductor chips and data center infrastructure to compete with artificial intelligence startups like Open AI and Anthropic. The litigation creates uncertainty in the timing of Meta's anticipated equity fundraising and capital allocation strategy. The company has also been growing its consumer AI application business as competition heats up across the tech industry. Shareholders will be watching the shareholder lawsuit, with the trial due to begin April 19, 2027.

stories.Headline: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signs a five-year ban on selling AI chatbot toys to children
stories.Summary:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a five-year ban on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026, on the manufacturing, distribution and sale of toys that use artificial intelligence chatbots in New York state. The law covers talking stuffed animals, robots and dolls marketed to children 12 and under, and it applies to both online and brick-and-mortar retailers. Hochul signed the bill at Grandma's Place Harlem, ahead of the major holiday shopping rush. The ban runs through 2031, according to the legislation.

The law will not take effect until 90 days after signing, which is after this holiday season. Violating the ban can lead to civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day. Because the law is not yet in force, Hochul urged parents to take notice as they shop for gifts. She said toys out there can be harmful to children, saying harmful things, planting ideas and using explicit talk that parents would never want a child to hear.

Hochul said parents should pay attention because children hear this from a toy they trust and put in front of them. Assemb. Rebecca Kassay, a Democrat from Port Jefferson who sponsored the bill in the Assembly, said consumer protections, especially those that protect youth, must keep up with rapidly evolving technologies. A report published earlier this month from the U.S. Public Interest Research Group found some chatbot toys marketed to children talked about sexually explicit topics, told kids where to likely find matches in the home and acted upset when a child had to leave. Some toys could record a child's voice or scan their face, and the toys had no or little parental controls, with safety limits weakening the longer children spoke with a toy.

The bill is the latest in a series of laws Hochul has signed related to the expansion of artificial intelligence. In October she signed a law banning companies from offering certain unsafe chatbot features to children, including features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage children in sexually explicit conversations. On Tuesday Hochul signaled the state would go further in seeking to limit possible dangers from the most advanced artificial intelligence models. Hochul said in her State of the State address in January she will lay out new safety standards, including putting independent experts inside artificial intelligence companies to ensure they follow the rules and insisting humans remain in control of the technology.

stories.Headline: OpenClaw launches ShellBench to test AI models on complex enterprise tasks
stories.Summary:
OpenClaw launched an AI performance benchmark called ShellBench on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. The organization worked with industry players including Hugging Face, Nvidia, Red Hat, Google, and Amazon. They also partnered with Parsewave and UC Berkeley to create this new testing tool. The benchmark compares various AI models to see how they handle complex queries. It aims to replicate complicated tasks that a typical enterprise would perform.

ShellBench tests 13 models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, DeepSeek, MoonShot, and Nvidia. These models are tested across five harnesses named Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, and Pi. The benchmark uses 100 real world tasks involving emails, calendar exports, spreadsheets, receipts, and PDFs. Roughly 20 tasks are public, while 80 tasks remain private to avoid benchmark contamination. The number of tracked models will double to 26 by next week.

Vincent Koc, the chief architect, said the focus was on everyday use for enterprises. He stated that most businesses cannot replicate the speed and scale of ShellBench. Louka Ewington-Pitsos said the division of public and private elements in the benchmark is complicated. He explained that private tasks prevent data leaks from the internet into model training data. OpenClaw argues that this benchmark is more realistic than other existing AI performance benchmarks.

Thomas Randall said ShellBench offers little direct use for organizations buying AI from large vendors. Brian Levine noted that reproducibility is essential and questioned if others can check the work. Ishraq Khan said the leaderboard will become outdated, but the evaluation methodology has longer life. Jason Andersen claimed the benchmark is interesting because it decouples the harness from the model. Frank Dickson said the researchers deserve credit for the high bar of rigor they set.

The benchmark tests models in messy environments rather than the clean settings of other benchmarks. It evaluates if agents can keep track of information while performing multi-step jobs across systems. The tool measures how agents fail, such as stalling or confidently doing the wrong thing. It looks at whether models are consistent when the same task is run three times. The system evaluates both open source and proprietary models and their corresponding agent harnesses.

The benchmark found a median gap of 45.7 points between the best and worst models. Top models like GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 hit only a 60 percent completion rate. The results show that 51 percent of failures were related to omitting important information. OpenClaw will soon expand the number of models it tracks to a total of 26. The articles leave open how useful the results will be for most enterprise buyers.

stories.Summary:
Eight Mile Style, the co-publisher for Eminem, amended its copyright lawsuit against the AI music generator Suno on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The publisher added 108 more AI tracks that it alleges infringe on the rapper's catalog to the original legal filing. This updated complaint was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California thirteen days after the first suit. The filing maintains a claim for damages totaling just over 47.7 million US dollars across three separate legal claims. It also accuses the AI firm of misappropriating the voice and likeness of the rapper, though no separate claim exists.

The lawsuit covers 269 compositions, with new examples affecting 26 songs including Stan, Mockingbird, Without Me, and the hit Lose Yourself. The publisher seeks 40.35 million dollars for copyright infringement, 6.725 million dollars for stripping credits, and 672,500 dollars for bypassing controls. The filing claims that Suno used copyrighted lyrics and musical elements, often verbatim, in the voice of the famous rapper. Eight Mile Style and Martin Affiliated are the plaintiffs, while the rapper himself is not a party to the case. The publisher wants the court to impound or destroy all unauthorized copies, including those in model weights and server infrastructure.

The publisher characterized prior denials from the AI firm as false and claimed the company willfully violated the United States Copyright Act. They stated that Suno wanted the rapper because he is the ninth best-selling artist of all time according to Chart Masters. A spokesperson for Suno previously said the service exists to help people create original music and prohibits unauthorized use of work. The company claimed it does not allow prompts for specific artists and works with third parties to screen audio and lyrics. Suno also asserted in a different motion that its outputs do not replicate the auditory characteristics of any real artist's voice.

The amended complaint responds to statements Suno made to press outlets and in a motion filed in a Boston federal court. This other case involves a proposed class action from Jason Isbell and three other musicians who are also suing the firm. The publisher believes the 108 new examples are just the tip of the iceberg regarding the company's infringing AI outputs. Other music rights holders are also suing, including Universal Music Group and Sony Music, over the use of recordings in training. Elvis Presley Enterprises is suing under the Tennessee ELVIS Act, which covers a person's voice and likeness rights specifically.

The original complaint alleged that Suno copied songs from lyrics and streaming platforms without permission to train its generative AI models. It cited a specific track titled Lose Yourself By Eminem that allegedly copies the lyrics of the original song verbatim. The publisher also has a copyright case against Meta covering 243 compositions, though a Michigan judge limited that case in June. The amended complaint mentions a June funding round where Suno raised over 400 million dollars at a 5.4 billion dollar valuation. Warner Music Group settled with the AI firm in November 2025 and signed a licensing deal with the company.

The legal team for the plaintiffs, led by Richard S. Busch, has also filed suits for Reservoir, Gerencia 360, and Round Hill Music. The court must now decide if the infringement was willful, which determines if the per-song damage cap is 150,000 or 30,000 dollars. The publisher is seeking a court order that would bar the AI firm from further infringing on its copyrighted songs. The articles leave open whether the court will grant the request to destroy the AI model weights and internal repositories. The allegations regarding the misappropriation of voice and likeness have not yet been tested in a court of law.

stories.Headline: Appeals court revives Trump bid to move hush-money case to federal court
stories.Summary:
A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit revived a bid by President Trump on Monday, November 23, 2026. This legal move allows him to try once more to transfer his Manhattan hush-money case from state to federal court. The panel consisted of Judges Raymond Lohier, José Cabranes, and John Walker, who issued a brief order regarding the matter. This decision follows a May 2024 conviction where Trump was found guilty on 34 counts of falsifying business records. He had previously been sentenced to an unconditional discharge for these specific crimes.

The appellate court ruled that Judge Alvin Hellerstein erred by treating removal as categorically unavailable after a conviction had occurred. The panel also found that the previous judge was wrong to decide that Trump lacked good cause to seek removal again. Because Judge Hellerstein died in October, a new judge in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York must now decide the issue. The panel ordered that this new judge provide a prompt ruling on whether the case should be moved.

Additionally, the court paused Trump's separate appeal in the New York state Appellate Division to preserve the status quo. The panel's decision reverses a denial issued by Judge Hellerstein in August, which followed earlier denials in 2023 and September 2024. Robert Giuffra of Sullivan & Cromwell, acting as Trump's lawyer, argued that the case belongs in federal court due to presidential evidentiary immunity. This argument relies on the legal standards established in the case of Trump v.

United States. A spokeswoman for Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg declined to provide a comment on the ruling. The New York Times reported that if Trump wins removal, he could ask the federal court to throw out the verdict. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google limits AI search in schools as students keep using AI tools at home
stories.Summary:
Google announced changes to how AI tools and Search behave on K-12 student accounts in early November 2026. These changes sparked fresh debates over what school districts should allow or block for their students. Some districts imposed strict limits or moratoriums while others tried to define where search ends and generative AI begins. These policies aim to restrict AI search inside school buildings and on school-issued devices or campus networks. However, these bans do not stop students from using AI tools at home on personal phones and laptops.

The changes affect K-12 student accounts and involve Google Search and AI tools used in classrooms. Some Google workers urged the company to let schools use search without AI features on November 20. Students can still access AI at home on family laptops, home tablets, and personal phones after the dismissal bell. This creates a split screen where students face filtered tools at school but use chatbots for summaries at home. These home tools can provide a three-bullet summary in two seconds for students to paste into worksheets.

Sebastian Chen says treating school policy like a force field around a teenager's brain is wishful thinking. He claims that prohibiting a tool at school does not teach skepticism and turns software into contraband. Chen argues that teachers lose visibility into how students use AI when the tools are banned on campus. He suggests that students will not admit to using inaccurate AI summaries if the tools are forbidden. He believes that wrestling with ideas is how students build mental muscles instead of using instant answer machines.

A letter to the editor claims that preventing AI use at school is doing something without accomplishing anything. This writer argues that students will still use AI at home and avoid engaging in true learning. Researchers Heather L. Schwartz and Melissa Kay Diliberti found rising AI homework use in a March 2026 report. Their RAND American Youth Panel report found that roughly 60 percent of surveyed youth expressed concern about AI. These students worry that using AI for school-related work can harm their own critical thinking skills.

A 2026 systematic review in the Journal of Information Technology Education Research looked at AI and critical thinking. Researcher Storrøsæter and colleagues found potential upsides when tools act as support for youth and children. They warned that treating AI as a shortcut to ready-made answers increases the risk of shallower thinking. The researchers also pointed out major gaps in long-term evidence regarding the use of AI by youth. This background shows that AI search has become tightly tangled with AI assistants and summaries for students.

Next, parents can ask to see rough notes, outlines, or search history alongside any finished student assignment. They can also play spot-the-flaw by looking for missing nuance or mistakes in an AI summary together. Another suggestion is a first-try rule where students write three bullet points before they look anything up. Adults can talk openly about shortcuts and ask when AI helps learning versus just finishing faster. The articles leave open whether Google workers will successfully get the company to remove AI from search.

stories.Headline: Illinois Supreme Court appoints 18 members to a standing committee on artificial intelligence in courts
stories.Summary:
The Illinois Supreme Court announced the creation of the Supreme Court Committee on Artificial Intelligence. This new standing committee was established to study the safe and effective use of AI. The court created this group to examine how technology can be used within the judicial system. It will focus on streamlining court processes and administration while preserving fairness and judicial independence. The committee will submit regular reports and recommendations to the Illinois Supreme Court.

The committee consists of 18 members appointed by the court for three year terms. The Hon. Jeffrey A. Goffinet serves as Chairperson, and the Hon. Sara D. Smith is vice chairperson. Members with terms ending December 31, 2027, include Joel B. Bruckman, Megan E. Goldish, George T. Pappas, Oliver Roberts, and Judge Smith. Those with terms ending December 31, 2028, are Sarah R. Duffy, Matthew Prochaska, Ashish S. Prasad, Dev Thain, Thaddeus L. Wilson, and Judge Goffinet. Members with terms ending December 31, 2029, are Judy L. Cates, John Connor, Jennifer A. Mao-Jones, Samuel Oh, Nichole C. Patton, and Mark Palmer.

The Illinois Supreme Court is responsible for appointing the members of this new standing committee. The court charged the group with evaluating risks related to data privacy, confidentiality, and cybersecurity. They also tasked the committee with ensuring compliance with court records and creating ethical standards. The group will recommend specific governance measures, oversight, and training for the use of AI. The Administrative Office of the Illinois Courts will provide the necessary administrative support to the committee.

The committee will affect the judicial system by creating safeguards for the use of AI. It will examine how to improve court administration without compromising accuracy or judicial independence. Members will evaluate how to protect data privacy and maintain confidentiality within the court system. The group will also look at ways to ensure that AI use remains ethical. These efforts aim to balance technological efficiency with the need for fair judicial processes.

The court created this committee after the Illinois Supreme Court AI Task Force conducted previous work. Judge Goffinet previously served as a co-chair for that specific task force before this appointment. The new committee is a standing body, which differs from the temporary nature of a task force. It was established to provide ongoing study of artificial intelligence within the state courts. This move follows a need to address the evolving risks of emerging technology.

The committee will continue to study AI and provide regular reports to the Supreme Court. It will develop recommendations for training and governance to manage the risks of new technology. The group will work to establish long term ethical standards for the Illinois judicial system. The articles do not state when the first official report will be submitted to the court. They also leave open which specific AI tools the committee will recommend for court use.

stories.Headline: Avanade's Ben Beath says firms must redesign work to gain 200% to 300% from AI
stories.Summary:
Ben Beath discussed how to create value from artificial intelligence during a video interview with ISMG. This conversation took place on November 24, 2026, at the Microsoft Ignite 2026 event. Beath serves as the chief AI officer for the company known as Avanade. He explained that organizations must redesign business processes to maximize the return on their AI investments. He argued against simply layering new technology onto existing work patterns to achieve better results.

The AI Reality Report from Avanade found that only 18% of global organizations fundamentally reshaped their AI usage. However, 75% of these organizations claim they are doing better with AI than they actually are. Layering AI onto existing processes yields about 30% productivity gains according to the data provided by Beath. Building AI into the business can yield 200% to 300% through new revenue opportunities for the company. This approach requires alignment and a specific perspective on both governance and security for the enterprise.

Ben Beath is responsible for scaling AI adoption and integrating agentic systems into various enterprise operations. He stated that rethinking how a business operates is hard work for any organization to undertake. Beath believes that velocity is the right way to think about AI adoption rather than focusing on speed. He noted that human oversight must evolve as AI agents gain authority to make decisions of consequence. He also explained how Avanade uses Agent 365 to help employees build more intelligent AI agents.

The reports indicate that many global organizations are affected by what Beath calls the AI reality gap. These companies claim higher success rates with AI than their actual process redesigns would suggest. C-suite leaders are the primary group Beath works with to scale these complex AI adoption strategies. The data shows a significant difference in value between simple layering and full business reinvention for firms. Most organizations are currently failing to fundamentally reshape how their teams use these new artificial intelligence tools.

Beath has more than 20 years of experience in digital transformation and innovation for various businesses. His professional expertise includes enterprise AI strategy as well as generative AI and machine learning technologies. He previously co-founded the digital agency Loud & Clear along with PlayHQ Sports and FanHub Media. He was also a co-founder of the company called Sidekicker before his current role at Avanade. These experiences inform his view that business reinvention is necessary for achieving high returns on AI.

The next step for organizations is to move beyond simple productivity gains toward new revenue opportunities. Companies must decide if they will continue layering AI or commit to the hard work of redesigning. The articles leave open how exactly human oversight should evolve as agents gain more decision making authority. It remains unclear how many organizations will close the AI reality gap in the coming years. The text does not specify the exact timeline for achieving these 300% gains in revenue.

stories.Headline: North Carolina treasurer Brad Briner says state's $250 million Anthropic stake is now worth $950 million
stories.Summary:
North Carolina invested $250 million in the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, State Treasurer Brad Briner said, and that figure was worth $950 million after the company went public last week. Briner said the state found Anthropic's Series G round, raised in March of this year, extremely compelling when the company was worth $380 billion. The investment is emblematic of a broader shift of strategy since Briner took office in January 2025, which has seen a more aggressive approach in investing. Briner said North Carolina had long run a roughly 45% equity and 55% cash and debt portfolio. The state's investment grew to $950 million after Anthropic's public debut, the articles reported.

Briner said the average pension fund in the country runs 70% stocks and 30% bonds, so much higher risk than North Carolina's. He said the state has changed that fundamentally and is now roughly 65% stocks and equities and other things like that, 35% debt and cash. Briner said the state delivered a 13% rate of return in its first full fiscal year, which is double of what it is trying to do at 6.5 percent. Other notable investments include Andruil, Revolut, Databricks, and Bending Spoons. Briner said the state cannot sell its entire Anthropic position at once because there are 23 different expiration dates governing when shares can be sold.

Briner said the goal is very clear to get to 100% funding and to reinstate cost-of-living adjustments on a permanent basis for state employees. He said the state will get a little bit in a couple weeks and then unlock slowly thereafter. Briner said the state will begin selling that stock through its investment manager when it can, and it is a lot for the state in a single position. He said the state wants to take some of those profits in reinvestment of other things. Briner said the state's retirees haven't had a cost-of-living adjustment in nine years.

Wendell Powell, President of the State Employees Association of North Carolina, said if the state makes $700 million in gains, that will definitely go a long way toward helping retirees get a COLA and putting money into the benefit package so employees can get raises in the upcoming year. Powell is a Correctional Captain at Harnett Correctional Institution. Powell said stronger pension performance could also help the state attract workers by giving employees confidence that their retirement benefits will be available. He said people want to make sure there is money there so they say they want to come to North Carolina and get into its pension system and work for the state because they know they have a defined benefit waiting. Powell said he is hopeful the General Assembly, whose new session will begin in January, will utilize the additional funds.

Powell said the association is happy that the Treasurer is finding ways to enhance the pot, making the pot bigger so the legislature can have tools and revenue streams to pull from to take care of state workers. The performance is especially noteworthy to public sector employees and retirees. The articles said Anthropic's IPO made major headlines last week, and in the case of North Carolina, major money. The articles were reported by Michael Perchick and published Monday, November 23, 2026 at 11:11 PM. The articles were datelined Raleigh, N.C.

The state will take a piecemeal approach to selling its Anthropic shares, with a little bit coming in a couple weeks and unlocking slowly thereafter. Powell said he is hopeful the General Assembly will utilize the additional funds when its new session begins in January. The articles leave open how much the state will ultimately realize from the position and what the General Assembly will do with the funds. The articles leave open whether retirees will receive a cost-of-living adjustment and whether employees will get raises in the upcoming year. The articles leave open what the state will reinvest the profits in.

stories.Headline: Nvidia uses parallel processing and CUDA software to dominate the AI chip market
stories.Summary:
Nvidia created graphics processing units that placed the company at the center of the current artificial intelligence boom. These chips evolved from simple add-on cards for video games into powerful tools for generative artificial intelligence. The company dominated the graphics chip market during the late 1990s and the 2000s. A research breakthrough and a global race to build larger models helped Nvidia become a dominant supplier. These developments occurred as the US and China competed for leadership in the field of artificial intelligence.

The chips use a parallel execution model to perform over a quadrillion mathematical operations every single second. In 2007, Nvidia released Compute Unified Device Architecture, known as CUDA, based on tools from Stanford University. The AlexNet neural network used two Nvidia GPUs to win the ImageNet challenge in 2012. Google researchers introduced the transformer design in 2017, which became the foundation for many generative AI systems. These chips are fabricated largely by the Taiwanese company Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., which is called TSMC.

Jeffrey Young, a principal research scientist at Georgia Institute of Technology, explains why these GPUs are so important. He states that GPUs are ideal for AI because training neural networks requires multiplying enormous grids of numbers. Young notes that software made GPUs useful beyond graphics, allowing scientists to run general purpose programs. He explains that Nvidia was positioned to benefit because it spent years building the CUDA software environment. The author describes how the company now earns record profits by selling chips and software to others.

Companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, and xAI are building large data centers using these high-end GPUs. Chinese firms including DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Baidu are also focused on training next-generation foundation models with this hardware. These models, such as Gemini, Claude Fable, and GPT Astra, can reason and write software code. Competitors like AMD and Google, which makes tensor processing units, have built strong alternatives to Nvidia chips. The US government has debated restricting advanced chip sales to China following a scandal involving Jensen Huang.

GPUs began as modestly priced cards for video rendering and were sidekicks to central processing units, or CPUs. While CPUs handle a few complicated tasks, GPUs perform many simpler mathematical operations in parallel. Nvidia redesigned its hardware to include specialized matrix multiplication math and larger amounts of fast memory. The Trump administration tightened export controls for advanced GPUs after Huang was linked to an alleged Chinese spy. This boom relies on the ability of neural networks to identify objects and translate between languages.

Leading AI companies continue to compete to build more capable models, which will likely keep chip demand growing. However, the boom faces limits because AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity for their operations. Memory chip shortages have also strained supplies, affecting everything from smartphones to gaming graphics cards. Startups and cloud companies are promising to run artificial intelligence more cheaply and with less power. It remains an open question if Nvidia's hardware and software advantages can hold off these various challengers.

stories.Headline: Sierra Leone children share AI concerns at Freetown policy dialogue
stories.Summary:
Children in Sierra Leone shared their experiences and concerns about artificial intelligence during a national policy dialogue. This event took place in Freetown on November 23, 2026, to commemorate World Children's Day. Government partners and young participants gathered to discuss child rights in the digital era. The dialogue focused on how the youngest users are already utilizing new technology. These contributions will now feed into a global UNICEF initiative regarding children's rights and AI.

The dialogue was held at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Freetown on November 23, 2026. It involved children aged 10 to 17 from various backgrounds across the entire country. The event will help strengthen the Data Protection and Right to Access Information Bill. It also informs the National AI Readiness Assessment to guide the national AI policy and strategy. These efforts aim to protect personal data and ensure the best interests of the child.

Mariko Kagoshima of UNICEF said AI is already part of the present for children in Sierra Leone. She stated that responsibility for AI lies with Parliament, Government, and technology and telecommunications companies. Minister Chernor Bah said children must be involved in shaping policies, not just in conversations. Minister Isata Mahoi reaffirmed the government commitment to stronger online child protection and personal information safeguards. Minister Kenyeh Barlay stressed integrating children's rights into national development planning and digital investments.

Children expressed worries about misinformation, privacy, cyberbullying, harmful content, and an over-dependence on these new tools. They called for safe and fair access to AI instead of blanket bans on the technology. Twelve-year-old Halimatu said children must have a voice because today's decisions shape their future opportunities. Aissatou Diallo of the World Bank Group said children need AI taught in schools and affordable tools. Seraphine Wakana of the United Nations reaffirmed support for an inclusive and rights-based digital future.

The dialogue was organized by UNICEF and the ministries of Information and Civic Education and Gender and Children's Affairs. It also included the Ministry of Communication, Technology and Innovation as a partner in the event. The process built upon a national consultation with children who had varying levels of AI experience. A national pledge on child online protection was presented last week in Manila at a global conference. UNICEF has worked for children globally for 80 years and in Sierra Leone for over four decades.

Children's recommendations will now help build accountability, participation, and inclusion into the National AI Readiness Assessment. AI could potentially be used to simplify laws and translate policies between English and Krio. The dialogue does not establish new binding regulations but provides policymakers with direct accounts from young users. Future goals include reducing inequalities in access for girls, children with disabilities, and those in underserved communities. The articles leave open how the government will specifically implement these recommendations into binding law.

stories.Headline: Dell raises fiscal 2027 revenue forecast to 202 billion dollars on record AI server orders
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies increased its annual revenue outlook by 10 billion dollars on November 24 due to surging demand for artificial intelligence servers. The company reported record orders for these systems and raised its financial expectations for the third time this year. This latest adjustment follows previous increases in the revenue forecast that occurred during May and September. The strong performance was driven by a massive increase in orders for infrastructure and AI technology.

The updated revenue forecast for fiscal 2027, which spans from February this year through January next year, is now 202 billion dollars. This new figure is an increase from the previous estimate of 192 billion dollars and exceeds the market consensus of 194.5 billion dollars. Dell also raised its adjusted earnings-per-share forecast to 29.68 dollars from an earlier estimate of 25.50 dollars. Specifically, the revenue forecast for AI servers rose to 78 billion dollars from 74 billion dollars.

Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke stated that the company booked 60.2 billion dollars in orders during the third quarter alone. He noted that the AI backlog has reached an all-time high of 132.3 billion dollars as demand spreads worldwide. Clarke explained that the Infrastructure Solutions Group now drives most of the growth and profit for the business. He added that the company expects both revenue and profit for the fourth quarter to beat market estimates.

The third quarter, which covered August through October, saw revenue reach a record 54.94 billion dollars with adjusted earnings-per-share of 9.45 dollars. Revenue for the Infrastructure Solutions Group nearly tripled from the previous year to reach 41.97 billion dollars. Dell also approved an additional 25 billion dollars in share buybacks following these strong financial results. The company is currently working to transform itself into a full-scale information technology infrastructure company.

stories.Headline: FCA sets out agentic AI expectations for financial firms and their senior managers
stories.Summary:
On 24 November 2026 the Financial Conduct Authority published a new webpage, Our approach to Agentic AI, setting out more specific expectations for those looking to develop and deploy products in the financial services sector. The FCA said some of these products may require FCA regulation at launch or evolve in a way that makes regulation apply. The webpage follows a statement that the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum recently published setting out its views on firms developing and deploying personal AI agents. The FCA said firms across financial services are moving from experimentation to deployment of AI agents. The FCA said it is engaging with firms looking to offer personal AI agent products to UK consumers.

The FCA said it will provide regular updates on the webpage to support the development and roll out of agentic products at pace. The update for 24 November 2026 states that the FCA expects AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers, bolstered with effective operational safeguards. The FCA said that where a regulated firm develops or deploys agentic AI or relies on a third-party provider, responsibility for complying with regulatory obligations remains with the firm and senior managers within the firm. The FCA said it expects firms to demonstrate that they understand the systems they use, the degree of autonomy those systems have, the risks they create and the controls necessary to manage those risks in real time and in stress situations. The FCA said senior managers are responsible for any AI models deployed within the area of the business they are responsible for, whether developed in house or by a third party.

The FCA said senior managers need to take reasonable steps to understand the risks arising from AI, provide effective oversight, challenge deployment and make sure governance, controls and escalation arrangements are appropriate for the risks. The FCA said a technology provider or social media platform considering launching an agentic product in the UK needs to consider whether it is carrying out activities regulated by the FCA. The FCA said that just because a business describes itself as a technology provider does not mean it does not need to be authorised by the FCA to provide financial services in the UK, and that this boundary is set by Parliament. The FCA said it has powers to intervene if it believes regulated financial services are being offered without its authorisation and will not hesitate to use them if necessary. The FCA said it intends to facilitate cross-industry engagement through the launch of a dedicated Agentic Policy Sprint for firms, policymakers and tech providers to collaborate and unlock innovation in a safe and responsible way.

Matthew Gregory, partner at global law firm Norton Rose Fulbright, said many financial services firms are now facing increased interaction with clients' agents as well as deploying AI systems themselves in connection with the provision of regulated products and services to clients. Gregory said the FCA has provided a timely reminder of its requirements with the publication of the new webpage. Gregory said the regulator notes that these products can blur the line between regulated and unregulated activity, and between the protections consumers receive for their finances and their data. Gregory said that under the Consumer Duty firms must avoid causing foreseeable harm, make sure consumers get the information they need and support customers in pursuing their financial objectives, which makes the conduct risks of autonomous agents a frontline concern for client outcomes. Gregory said governance is another key area, with responsibility for meeting regulatory obligations staying with the firm and its senior managers, including where a firm relies on a third-party provider.

Gregory said the FCA's October 2026 publication, AI in financial services: good practice and areas for improvement, reinforces this and calls for governance that covers the full AI lifecycle, ongoing monitoring, meaningful human oversight and a clear risk appetite. Gregory said firms should therefore avoid a piecemeal approach and adopt a coordinated, firm-wide strategy for agentic AI. The FCA said its AI Lab provides a range of services to support firms develop and test new agentic services and products. The FCA said it and other regulators welcome early engagement and provide services to support those looking to innovate so they are clear on what regulatory requirements may apply and to test products. The FCA said companies developing or deploying agentic AI products can engage with it through its innovation services and pre-application support service.

The FCA said AI is redefining financial services and that, deployed well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth. The FCA said AI agents can widen access to financial tools and information and be part of new products that offer significant consumer benefit and convenience. The FCA said these products can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive in relation to their finances and data. The FCA said that as AI becomes capable of moving beyond providing information to initiating transactions, moving money, arranging borrowing or making investment decisions, all at speed and scale, firms must understand which activities require authorisation and where regulatory requirements may apply. The FCA said firms must be mindful of the operational resilience of their platforms and their commercial partners.

The FCA said it will assess the services firms provide through agentic products, including how they develop over time, to ensure they keep to regulatory requirements. The FCA said firms should also consider how they will respond when customers use AI agents to interact with them, including how they establish that they are dealing with an agent, what consents are in place, what an AI agent is allowed to do, and how customers can get support if something goes wrong. The FCA said this also includes information provided to consumers through agentic chatbots or where agents are used to help resolve complaints. The FCA said firms should consider their systems and controls, any liabilities that may arise from accepting instructions and whether it is appropriate to accept payments instructed by an AI agent, or from a digital wallet controlled by an AI agent. The FCA said consumers should make sure they understand how a tool works and what protections, if any, they might have if something goes wrong before using it and allowing it to make transactions for them.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO to revive AI stocks after Donald Trump pushes for reinstatement
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang returned to his role as the chief executive officer of Nvidia on Monday, 23 November 2026. He had previously resigned from the position after leading the company for more than 33 years. His departure occurred 11 days before his return following reports of an affair with a customer. This customer was suspected of being a Chinese spy, and he had a second affair with a subordinate.

The return of the chief executive officer caused Nvidia shares to soar 31.5 percent on 23 November 2026. This surge restored nearly US$1 trillion in value and marked the biggest daily rise for the company in 23 years. The Nasdaq 100 climbed more than 6 percent, while the MSCI Asia-Pacific index rose 4.6 percent. Taiwanese shares shot up 9.1 percent, and the South Korean KOSPI surged 6.5 percent. Japan's Nikkei jumped as much as 5 percent after traders returned from a local holiday.

US President Donald Trump used the power of the Oval Office to push for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang. He stated on social media that the United States needed Nvidia to ensure the prosperity of the American economy. Trump claimed that Nvidia needed Huang to ensure the success and prosperity of the company. He rose to the defense of the leader to end a market rout. The president has previously reported holding millions of dollars in investments within the company.

Charu Chanana of Saxo said the return removes an important source of uncertainty and restores strategic continuity at Nvidia. She noted that it reduces immediate risks to the technology road map and the supply chain. Investors in AI stocks were affected as the relief rally revived the trade and eased growth concerns. The rebound lifted bets for Fed tightening, pushing the US dollar and Treasury yields higher. Chinese shares saw only small gains due to concerns over tighter US chip export curbs.

Huang had been removed from his role after scandals involving a suspected spy and a subordinate. Nvidia is described as a pre-eminent chipmaker and a key financier for technological development in the AI ecosystem. The company uses powerful semiconductors and deep pockets to backstop a wave of coming AI investment. The AI ecosystem relies on Nvidia for supplying chips and bankrolling the industry's massive buildout. The return of the leader followed a whirlwind week that whipped markets and tore through the ecosystem.

Investors will now focus on the PCE Index data on 25 November 2026 before the final Fed meeting. An investigation into the conduct of the chief executive officer is still ongoing at this time. Questions remain about corporate governance, boardroom independence, and the power of founder-CEOs within the company. It is unclear if the relief rally can become a sustainable recovery for the AI industry. Unanswered questions remain regarding the sustainability of hyperscaler spending and the returns on AI investment.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act mandates rights impact assessments for high-risk deployers as US divergence threatens global standards
stories.Summary:
A legal and governance study published in Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance examined how algorithmic technologies across corporate value chains are forcing a transition from fragmented compliance to unified governance models. The study was published on November 25, 2026, and was reported by Bioengineer.org. It examines the European Union’s regulatory framework, anchored by the mandatory Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment introduced under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. The study demonstrates that this framework establishes a mechanism that embeds binding human rights accountability into commercial deployment decisions. It also addresses the Council of Europe’s voluntary Human Rights, Democracy, and Rule of Law Impact Assessment methodology.

The study states that the European Union enacted Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, known as the Artificial Intelligence Act. Under Articles 8 and 9, upstream technology providers bear legal responsibility for mitigating technical risks through continuous risk management systems. Article 27 establishes distinct obligations for downstream deployers, addressing the operational deployment phase where developers no longer exercise direct operational control. Under Recital 96, the requirement to conduct a formal Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment was introduced to safeguard protected rights in core economic and public sectors. The final text of Article 27 confines mandatory compliance to public bodies, private entities providing public services, and commercial operators deploying high-risk systems for credit scoring, creditworthiness evaluations, or risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance.

The study identifies the Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment as an innovative governance tool that enforces an anticipatory, by-design approach to system deployment. It states that the regulation compels private corporations to internalize the societal costs and externalized harms of digital technologies. The authors observe that while core elements of fundamental rights cannot be infringed, non-core interferences require robust justification demonstrating proportionality and the absence of less intrusive operational alternatives. They note that many deploying organizations, particularly small and medium enterprises across distributed value chains, lack the interdisciplinary expertise required to analyze machine learning architectures, identify vulnerable demographic cohorts, and execute culturally nuanced stakeholder engagement. The study emphasizes that the voluntary Council of Europe methodology functions synergistically with the EU AI Act, allowing multinational corporations to apply consistent rights-based practices.

The study states that the potential for these complementary European assessment frameworks to establish unified global standards is increasingly threatened by deep regulatory divergence with the United States. It says that market-driven United States policies explicitly counter multilateral rights-based standards. The study explains that applying the doctrine of horizontal effect, or Drittwirkung, to contemporary artificial intelligence introduces unprecedented legal complexities that traditional bilateral frameworks cannot address. It states that modern artificial intelligence systems operate through dispersed value chains that distribute operational responsibilities across software developers, commercial deployers, and third-party data suppliers. The study notes that algorithmic systems exhibit high degrees of opacity, automated adaptability, and systemic bias, and that their downstream consequences affect individuals through complex automated workflows that deployers themselves may not fully comprehend.

The study states that corporate human rights compliance historically relied primarily on voluntary corporate social responsibility initiatives and ethical business norms that lacked formal enforcement mechanisms. It says that the 2011 United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and its three pillars of state duty to protect, corporate responsibility to respect, and access to remedy remained limited by their voluntary nature whenever commercial profit margins conflicted with rights safeguarding. The study states that civil litigation under the United States Alien Tort Claims Act faced severe judicial restrictions regarding extraterritorial jurisdiction and corporate liability. It notes that European jurisdictions enacted targeted due diligence legislation such as France’s Loi de Vigilance and Germany’s Supply Chain Due Diligence Act, which primarily focused on formal enterprise risk management and shareholder interests rather than systematically mitigating algorithmic harms. The study states that the Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment represents an institutional evolution of the Data Protection Impact Assessment mandated under Article 35 of the General Data Protection Regulation.

The study states that the European Parliament originally sought to mandate assessments across all high-risk systems, while the final text narrowed the assessment’s mandatory scope. It describes the Council of Europe’s voluntary framework as offering an algorithm-neutral, multi-step governance architecture developed by the Ad Hoc Committee on Artificial Intelligence. The study states that this framework encompasses four interconnected procedural stages: Context-Based Risk Analysis, Stakeholder Engagement Process, Risk and Impact Assessment, and Mitigation Planning. It says that each consecutive phase is documented within a centralized Project Summary Report, creating institutional transparency and establishing empirical records for continuous lifecycle oversight. The study states that the voluntary methodology’s triage phase informs organizational determinations regarding whether operational benefits justify identified risks, while mitigation planning formulates targeted risk-treatment strategies and establishes accessible grievance remedies.

stories.Headline: Nestlé opens Swiss deep tech center to test AI and robotics across its food brands
stories.Summary:
Nestlé opened a deep tech center in Orbe, Switzerland last week, the company said, to develop, test and scale advanced technologies across its portfolio of frozen pizza, chocolate chips and coffee. The world’s largest food company said the center will help it develop and test ideas faster, maintain consistent quality and improve efficiency. Nestlé is leveraging artificial intelligence, sensors and robotics to boost growth across its sprawling portfolio, according to Food Dive. The Lean Cuisine and Hot Pockets manufacturer said it will use AI, sensors and rapid prototyping to develop and test ideas faster. Sensors and robotics will handle routine or physically demanding tasks and help maintain consistent product quality and improve efficiency, Nestlé said.

The center will handle consumer experiences, research and development and manufacturing, Nestlé said, and will help create more personalized experiences. Those experiences range from customized coffee menus to insights that help pet owners support their pets’ health and nutrition, according to the company. The center will help Nestlé draw on consumer insights, accelerate innovation, maintain quality and run more efficient operations, according to the company. Nestlé said real internal growth, which measures volume, rose 1.8% in North America in its third quarter compared to a 0.6% decline in the prior three months. In the U.S., Nestlé’s biggest market, food and snacks delivered strong growth, led by an improvement in confectionery and in frozen brands like Stouffer’s and DiGiorno that resulted in market share gains, according to the company.

Philipp Navratil, Nestlé’s CEO, said in a statement that innovation at Nestlé starts with the consumer and that for the company technology is an enabler. Navratil said technology helps Nestlé understand consumers better, deliver superior quality, drive smart innovation and run more efficient operations. He said this ultimately supports the company’s growth. Navratil also said Nestlé is still struggling with Gerber and its nutrition unit, which he said underperformed. The company said the snacking giant’s brand is growing 2.5 times faster than the cookie category and is benefiting from consumer demand for high-end treats.

Food Dive reported that CPG companies have turned to advanced technology to help them improve efficiency and more quickly respond to changing consumer demand for healthier offerings. AI and other technologies have proven especially valuable as consumers cut back on spending due to inflation, putting pressure on food volumes, according to the report. International Supermarket News reported that Nestlé is stepping up its investment in advanced manufacturing technology as artificial intelligence, robotics and data-driven production become increasingly important to the global food industry. The publication reported that the initiative reflects a wider shift among major food producers towards factories that can respond more intelligently to changing ingredients, production requirements and consumer demand. The publication reported that the development comes as food manufacturers face pressure from higher operating costs, supply-chain uncertainty and changing consumer expectations.

International Supermarket News reported that one of the biggest challenges in food manufacturing is managing natural variations in raw materials, because milk, coffee, cocoa and other agricultural ingredients do not always behave in exactly the same way. Temperature, quality and composition can influence production, creating challenges for consistency and efficiency, the publication reported. Nestlé’s research is exploring how artificial intelligence, sensors and robotics could help manufacturing systems respond to these variations, according to the publication. Instead of relying entirely on fixed production settings, intelligent systems could use real-time information to adjust processes and improve operational control, the publication reported. The publication reported that better monitoring and more responsive production could help reduce waste, improve quality management and make factories more adaptable.

International Supermarket News reported that moving from research to large-scale industrial application will require substantial investment, and that manufacturers must demonstrate that advanced systems can deliver reliable results, integrate with existing equipment and generate measurable financial returns. The publication reported that for retailers the implications could eventually reach beyond the factory gates, and that more flexible production may help suppliers respond faster to changing demand, improve product availability and manage manufacturing costs. The publication reported that Nestlé’s initiative highlights an important question for the industry about whether the next generation of food manufacturing will be defined as much by artificial intelligence and robotics as by traditional production expertise. Food Dive reported that the center will help Nestlé draw on consumer insights, accelerate innovation, maintain quality and run more efficient operations. The company said the center will help create more personalized experiences, from customized coffee menus to insights that help pet owners support their pets’ health and nutrition.

stories.Headline: Indian AI companies raise 1.6 billion dollars in first nine months of 2026
stories.Summary:
Indian AI companies raised 1.6 billion dollars in equity funding during the first nine months of 2026. This total represents a 96 percent increase compared to the same period in 2025. The funding occurred between January and September of 2026. Data intelligence platform Tracxn provided these figures in a recent report. This amount is the highest nine-month total recorded by the report since 2019.

The funding total was 1.6 billion dollars, which is 162 percent above the 616 million dollars raised in 2024. Mumbai became the largest recipient of AI funding, raising 765 million dollars for a 48 percent share. Bengaluru raised 711 million dollars, which was a 44 percent share of the total. Neysa in Mumbai raised 600 million dollars in February, while Sarvam in Bengaluru raised 255 million dollars in June. Sarvam raised another 90.4 million dollars in August, and Yotta raised 150 million dollars in July.

Tracxn reported that a small number of large deals drove the surge in funding. The platform stated that around 90 percent of the total capital was raised in just 10 rounds. Tracxn noted that the number of deals fell from 149 in 2025 to 87 in 2026. The report indicated that the average deal size more than tripled to 18.5 million dollars. This increase was up from an average of 5.5 million dollars a year earlier.

Fortune India noted that a handful of deals drove the surge, showing a concentration of capital. Seed-stage founders are affected as they compete for a thinner slice of investor attention. Early-stage and late-stage funding rose by 191 percent and 4 percent, but seed-stage funding fell by 42 percent. This suggests investors favor companies with more mature technology and business models. India accounted for 0.4 percent of global AI money, trailing countries like the US, China, and the UK.

The 2024 base of 616 million dollars was the lowest of the three periods in the report. Funding in the first nine months of 2025 was 822 million dollars. Mumbai's funding was only 15.7 million dollars, a 2 percent share, in the first nine months of 2025. The report tracks equity funding only, excluding debt, grants, and compute credits. India is ranked ninth among countries in terms of AI funding raised during this period.

The reports leave open how much funding went to applications versus infrastructure. They do not disclose the specific investors or individual deal sizes for all rounds. It remains unclear if the funding is driven by infrastructure, enterprise traction, or scarcity. Future durability depends on whether customers renew contracts or compute demand continues. The data does not specify which firms drove the jump beyond the largest named rounds.

stories.Headline: David Tepper exits AMD and Broadcom stakes to increase investment in SpaceX
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom led chip stocks lower on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, as the artificial intelligence trade came under renewed pressure. Nvidia stock retreated 6 percent on that day, giving back some of a 31 percent surge from the prior session. Peers AMD and Broadcom also declined from a rebound on Monday, while other AI trade stocks retreated. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and ASML fell more than 3 percent each, and Arm Holdings was down 8 percent. Memory chipmakers Micron Technology and SK Hynix dropped roughly 10 percent, giving back some of their double-digit gains from Monday.

The decline followed the decision by the board of the AI chip giant Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as the company CEO. Storage and memory players Sandisk, Seagate, and Western Digital all fell, while neocloud providers CoreWeave and Nebius also saw their stocks retreat. Billionaire David Tepper and his fund Appaloosa Management exited all 197,500 AMD shares and all 150,000 Broadcom shares in the third quarter. Tepper increased his stake in Space Exploration Technologies by 1,626 percent, ending the third quarter with over 3.8 million shares. This stake was worth 557 million dollars, or about 7.4 percent of the reported portfolio, at the end of the third quarter.

David Tepper has been a successful hedge fund manager for over three decades and founded Appaloosa Management after leaving Goldman Sachs in 1993. Tepper may have sold his AI chip stocks to take profits because he believed the AI trade needed to catch its breath. Elon Musk, the founder and CEO of SpaceX, said the company had 1.7 gigawatts of compute provided by data centers. Musk stated he is highly confident the company can bring another 10 gigawatts of compute online by the end of 2027. He also suggested that the company could potentially bring as much as 20 gigawatts of compute online by that same date.

Investors in the AI trade were affected as they questioned potential returns from AI capital investment during a rough third quarter. The MSCI World Semiconductor Index fell about 13 percent in July, which was its worst month since the year 2022. Wall Street analysts project that SpaceX will grow revenue to about 181 billion dollars in 2027, up from 49 billion this year. These analysts project 4.21 dollars in adjusted earnings per share for 2027, implying the stock trades at over 44 times earnings. Market participants may not fully buy into these projections because achieving them will require significant capital expenditures and negative free cash flow.

The background includes AMD reporting strong second-quarter results on August 4, with revenue up 50 percent and data center sales more than doubling. Despite this, the AMD stock fell sharply after the report due to lofty market expectations and a lack of margin expansion. Broadcom reported on September 2 that AI semiconductor revenue rocketed 221 percent higher to 16.7 billion dollars, but guidance landed below consensus. Rising interest rates may have added pressure to the market, as higher yields often hit highly valued growth stocks the hardest. SpaceX went public in June at 135 dollars per share, which was the largest initial public offering at that time.

SpaceX currently offers a low earth orbit satellite internet service called Starlink, which had over 13.6 million paying subscribers in the third quarter. The company also has an AI division with multiple data centers, the social platform X, and a planned future Terafab facility. The articles leave open whether the market will fully believe the ambitious compute goals set by Elon Musk for the year 2027. It remains unclear if the AI trade will recover or if valuations will continue to leave little room for error for chip companies. The reports do not state if other large funds will follow David Tepper in exiting their positions in AMD and Broadcom.

stories.Headline: Z.ai launches GLM-5.4 loop transformer model to save memory by rerunning layers
stories.Summary:
Z.ai launched the GLM-5.4 AI model on November 23, 2026, as a loop transformer. This new system reruns specific layers to increase depth without adding more unique weights. The company describes the model as having roughly 750 billion parameters in total. It uses a mixture-of-experts design with 40 billion active parameters per token. This architecture allows the model to perform more work per token during inference.

The model uses a 26-layer prelude, looped layers 27-54, and a 24-layer coda. These 78 stored layers result in 106 layer passes because 28 layers run twice. This design saves weight memory but not compute, adding about 36 percent more passes. Hosting falls under China's National Intelligence Law, specifically Article 7, in the city of Beijing. The system is available in Z.ai Chat, the ZCode tool, and for GLM Coding Plan subscribers.

Z.ai claims that looping adds depth and provides meaningful gains for about 10 percent extra training compute. They reported that AIME25 rose from 19.2 to 30.4 in a 30-billion-parameter ablation test. GPQA-Diamond increased from 47.6 to 56.3, and AA-LCR rose from 40.3 to 47.7 in the same test. The company says per-token gates and a shared KV cache keep the second pass stable. Z.ai also states that the model reuses sparse-attention maps and fuses core operations.

Wccftech reports that the model can reach speeds of up to 200 tokens per second. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology measured the previous GLM-5.3 model as four months behind. This independent assessment by CAISI on September 17, 2026, focused specifically on cyber-capability benchmarks. Safety researchers warn that reasoning inside hidden loops is harder for humans and monitors to follow. Users are affected by the lack of independent evaluations for the 750-billion-parameter version.

Z.ai continued training the GLM-5 base rather than starting from scratch to avoid performance trails. The company previously released GLM-5.3 weights about two weeks after its launch on August 14. A US counterintelligence bulletin notes that China's 2017 Cybersecurity Law requires certain data to be localized. The 2021 Data Security Law sorts data into tiers based on its importance to state security. The Commerce Department added Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology to the Entity List in January 2025.

API access will follow a safety evaluation, and open weights will follow safety hardening. Z.ai has not provided a specific release date for the API or the weights. The official GLM-5 repository currently lists GLM-5.3 as the newest model and omits GLM-5.4. It remains open whether the gains from the small ablation test will scale to the full model. No independent reports have yet measured if looping closed the gap with the US frontier.
