stories.Headline: Kevin O'Leary says Nvidia no longer funds new AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Kevin O'Leary said in a Saturday post on X that Nvidia Corp. may no longer be willing to bankroll new data-center projects, and he declared that the bank of Nvidia is closed. O'Leary argued that financing new data centers through the chipmaker's balance sheet may no longer be viable. He said investigations he referenced are expected to begin Dec. 10, and he said the company would remain under scrutiny for a while. O'Leary praised Nvidia CFO Colette Kress, saying he thinks they have the right CEO in Colette because she's the CFO. O'Leary also pushed back against political opposition to data-center construction, arguing the projects support middle-class workers.

O'Leary said the idea that you could finance new data centers under the balance sheet of Nvidia is over. He said most governors and senators in every state that won said they have to stop building these data centers and help the middle class. O'Leary asked who the middle class is, and he argued that workers and businesses involved in building data centers are themselves part of the middle class. He said he thinks you are going to see them say just kidding about the data centers. Seaport analyst Jay Goldberg warned last month that 45% of planned AI data-center capacity for 2027 might not materialize because of power and infrastructure shortages.

Goldberg cautioned that Nvidia's financing support for smaller cloud providers could expose the chipmaker to greater financial risks if customers struggled to fund their purchases. Nvidia reported $279 billion in supply and capacity commitments in July, while warning that infrastructure constraints could delay chip purchases and hurt revenue. Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan warned last week that AI infrastructure could require up to $8 trillion in financing, raising concerns about capital markets and funding challenges for smaller AI cloud providers. Moody's CFO Noémie Heuland said AI infrastructure drove 50% of the company's issuance growth and 40% of revenue, with spending expected to support growth into 2027. LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman called AI infrastructure spending the only reason we're not in a recession in October, citing its broader economic impact and job creation.

Preqin data shows infrastructure fundraising rebounded sharply in the third quarter of 2026, with $62 billion raised across 21 funds, bringing this year's total to $101 billion across 65 funds. Rene Lubianski, managing partner for infrastructure at Brookfield Asset Management, said infrastructure is a cornerstone of the private markets giant's business during the group's third-quarter earnings call Nov. 6. The firm has raised roughly $50 billion in capital commitments across its infrastructure strategies over the past year. Earlier this month, Brookfield said the latest vintage of its flagship infrastructure strategy had received $26 billion in commitments, with $13 billion coming after the end of the quarter. Lubianski said this puts them well on track to exceed their $30 billion target in early 2027.

Lubianski said at that size the fund would surpass the $28 billion raised for its predecessor to become the largest closed-end infrastructure fund ever raised. He said that if the current momentum continues, it could also become the largest closed-end private fund ever raised in any sector. Portfolio companies owned by the 50 largest infrastructure general partners had an average holding period of 7.6 years in 2025, up from 6.1 years in 2021, according to Boston Consulting Group. Goldman Sachs' latest annual 2026 Global Alternatives Survey polled some 225 institutional investors, including pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurance investors, family offices and other wealth managers, between June and August. The study, published Oct. 21, found that 43% of respondents have a more favorable outlook on infrastructure investment compared with a year ago, with 7% who were less favorable.

Nearly half of investors, 49%, with a target allocation to infrastructure said they were under-allocated, compared with just 5% who were over-allocated, according to the study. Jeff Fine, global co-head of alternatives capital formation at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, said geopolitical tensions and their effects on inflation, interest rates and growth prospects continue to impact valuations and investors' ability to return capital. Fine said those constraints coincide with extraordinary demand for private capital to finance the infrastructure supporting AI expansion, creating both a challenge and an opportunity. J.P. Morgan Asset Management strategists said Nov. 12 that the sector stands to benefit from stronger government and corporate spending next year, while offering protection if that spending keeps inflation and interest rates elevated. Hugh Gimber, executive director and global market strategist at JPMAM, said infrastructure has some of the strongest foundations among alternative assets in the current economic environment.

stories.Headline: Alpha School opens AI-taught campuses in California and Florida
stories.Summary:
Texas-based private education provider Alpha School replaced traditional human teachers with artificial intelligence to teach core subjects to students. The company opened new campuses in Santa Monica, Playa Vista, and Malibu on November 23, 2026. This experimental approach uses AI to deliver lessons in subjects such as reading, math, and science. The school network expanded from 20 campuses last year to 50 campuses across the country this year. Nine of these campuses are located in California, and two are located in Palm Beach County, Florida.

The school requires annual tuition that is reported as $50,000 in one source and exceeding $75,000 in another. Students use an app for two to three hours every morning to learn at their own individual pace. They must score 90 percent or higher on evaluations before the AI pushes them to the next level. Traditional teachers are replaced by support personnel called Guides, many of whom lack formal teaching credentials or degrees. The remaining school day is dedicated to life skills, sports, coding, field trips, and various interactive workshops.

Head guide Sean McKenna said the school is flipping legacy schooling on its head by removing babysitting and busy work. He claimed the model teaches children to learn quickly and helps them become better adults and human beings. Reading specialist Scott Dangerfield stated that the app is the teacher and prevents students from being bored or left behind. Dean of Parents Kirsten Berg said parents want to try something different because traditional education systems were not working. The school claims students can absorb twice as much content in half the time of conventional schools.

UCLA instructor Anne Blackstock-Bernstein expressed concern that learning through machines may lose the benefits of collaborating and conversing with people. USC associate professor Morgan Polikoff stated that rigorous external research is needed to prove the actual educational impact. A New York Times expose uncovered that some students struggle to keep up and do not learn twice as much. Parent Connor New said his children enjoy school more and his seventh-grade child reached an eleventh-grade vocabulary level. The Los Angeles Unified School District restricted students from using generative AI on school-issued devices this academic year.

The school provides a lounge area with many books and uses shoutouts for students to appreciate the life skills of classmates. Students participate in diverse activities, including nature walks, puppet shows, and learning thriller dances from a professional dance coach. Some students who attend these schools were already high achievers before they enrolled in the AI-based private program. The model focuses on completing fundamental subjects before lunchtime to allow for creative experiences and workshops in the afternoon. The school aims to replace the traditional face of a teacher with the screen of a computer.

Alpha School plans to open more campuses in Southern California regions, including a new location in Beverly Hills. The company also intends to introduce its AI education system into public schools across the country in the long term. It remains uncertain if the groundbreaking learning outcomes touted by the school will be proven through objective verification. Experts continue to debate whether the approach is a viable alternative to traditional education or a high-cost experiment. The articles leave open whether the AI model will actually change society and how children are raised.

The article says an NSPCC campaign hopes to address this issue, and the writer Alice Thomson saw how students react to it. The context the article gives is the debate over how to protect under-16s from new technology while also helping them to use it, and it places the NSPCC campaign within that debate. stories.Headline: Gilbane starts building New York's 74.5 million dollar Empire AI data center at the University at Buffalo
stories.Summary:
Gilbane broke ground on the Empire AI data center on November 19, 2026. Governor Kathy Hochul announced the start of this project in New York. The facility will be located at the University at Buffalo in Amherst. This new center will focus on research and education for the state. It is exempt from a statewide data center moratorium ordered by the governor.

The construction budget for the facility is 74.5 million dollars. It will initially use up to five megawatts of power in total. The site will house the Empire AI Gamma supercomputer for university researchers. The center will connect to the Baker Chilled Water Plant for cooling. It will use clean hydropower to run the high performance computing infrastructure.

Roger Treichler is a senior project executive at the construction firm Gilbane. He said Gilbane is proud to deliver a facility that expands computing resources. Treichler stated the project shows how technology and environmental stewardship work together. He noted the plan supports capturing and reusing heat across the North Campus. He said the facility helps researchers tackle challenges in healthcare and climate science.

The University at Buffalo will use heat from the facility to warm buildings. A system of pipes and geothermal wells will recover energy from the center. This technology will redistribute heat to the campus to reduce overall energy consumption. The project specifically serves researchers who need powerful computing resources for their work. The facility adds to two earlier systems that already serve the research community.

Governor Hochul paused certain state environmental permits for new data centers in July. This order was meant to study effects on water use and energy demand. The order exempts facilities used for research and names the Empire AI consortium. A second supercomputer in downtown Buffalo cost 40 million dollars to build. That system has 11 times the AI training capacity of a 2024 system.

Gilbane targets substantial completion of the data center for late 2027. The state expects the construction to reach full completion by early 2028. Treichler said finishing touches will continue on the site after substantial completion occurs. Remaining work includes testing building systems and commissioning the facility before operations begin. The articles do not state when the supercomputer will be fully operational.

stories.Headline: National Governors Association releases bipartisan AI governance principles
stories.Summary:
The National Governors Association released new principles for artificial intelligence governance on Sunday, timed for the hundreds of new lawmakers arriving in Washington, D.C., in January for the next Congress and for newly elected governors taking office. The bipartisan guidance was developed through the NGA's Governors Council to Secure American AI Dominance, which is led by Chair Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Vice Chair Indiana Gov. Mike Braun and executive committee members Utah Gov. Spencer Cox and North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein. The association said the principles aim to advance AI while protecting jobs, and it highlighted the need for clear and complementary federal and state roles. The governors acted as fast-moving artificial intelligence technology has prompted leaders from both parties to set shared goals for governance that support workers, identify risks and advance innovation.

The principles place American leadership in technology and innovation as a top priority while supporting workers as AI reshuffles the workforce through its ability to alter business processes and improve efficiencies. The NGA called for consistency in state and federal approaches that reduces duplication and conflicting requirements between the two levels of government. The governors' move comes as the federal government under President Donald Trump has sought to limit state AI regulation, while Congress has considered proposals to preempt some state AI laws. The industry now underpins a sizable portion of the U.S. economy, according to the association's announcement.

Cox, an NGA executive committee member, said governors in both parties believe states have a critical role in responsible AI advancement and called on Congress to work with them on a federal framework that strengthens American competitiveness while protecting the public from harm. Stein said artificial intelligence presents opportunities and risks that are too big to ignore, and that the bipartisan principles can help build the trust needed for innovation to thrive as states prepare their workforces, protect the public and transform government services. Moore said governors from across the country agree that AI poses both opportunities and risks, that humans must stay in control, and that people, especially workers, consumers and children, must be protected. He added that governors will continue to focus on creating jobs and making sure workers have a voice in the deployment of new technology.

stories.Headline: Tenth Circuit requires attorneys to certify human review of AI-assisted filings
stories.Summary:
The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit adopted a new certification rule on November 23, 2026. This specific mandate requires attorneys to certify that any documents prepared with generative artificial intelligence were reviewed by a human for accuracy. The court claims to be the first federal appellate court in the United States to implement a rule specifically targeting the use of artificial intelligence to prepare briefs. This action aims to ensure that legal filings remain accurate despite the increasing use of automated tools. The new rule introduces two additional sanctions that the court can impose when attorneys fail to comply with the AI mandate.

The court may now deem the affected legal issue waived if the attorney does not follow the certification requirements. Alternatively, the court has the authority to strike the noncompliant document from the record entirely. These new penalties exist alongside other existing sanctions that the court can already apply to legal filings. Every attorney who signs a brief must now adhere to these strict verification standards. The officials at the Tenth Circuit are responsible for enforcing these new requirements for all legal filings.

They have established these rules to prevent the submission of inaccurate information generated by artificial intelligence tools. By requiring a human review, the court intends to maintain the integrity of the judicial process in Denver. The court believes that human oversight is necessary to catch errors that generative tools might produce. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Expert Institute issues guidance requiring expert witnesses to verify AI outputs and disclose their use
stories.Summary:
Expert witnesses across the country and in New York have submitted reports and provided testimony made with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot and Gemini in the courtroom, amNewYork reported on November 23, 2026. The article, by Isabella Gallo, said this has led to claims that could not be corroborated, fake citations and unsourced reasoning that AI inexplicably produced. It said reports have included information deemed inadmissible, not credible or otherwise unreliable. In some cases the problematic testimony was struck from the court's record after it had been introduced. The Southern District of New York courthouse at 500 Pearl Street in Manhattan was pictured with the story.

The article said guidelines and rules specifically for how expert witnesses can use AI have remained largely absent from the conversation, especially from official legal organizations like bar associations and court systems. It said the New York City Bar and the New York State Unified Court System have not offered guidelines beyond short statements within guidance for attorney use on AI. Those statements suggest attorneys should be checking expert statements they are commissioning before bringing them into the courtroom. The article said the existing Frye or Daubert standards and general federal rules of evidence require experts to show their technology or scientific methodology is reliable, generally accepted by peers and produces a consistent outcome. It said Expert Institute connects experts with lawyers on roughly 10,000 cases in New York and about 100,000 across the U.S. a year.

Heidi Brown, a New York Law School professor and scholar considering how AI is impacting the legal system, said lawyers, self-represented litigants and judges have gotten into hot water for not checking citations in expert reports or declarations. She said it is problematic if experts cannot show reports can be authenticated or grounded in genuine facts that relate to the case. She said she really does think there needs to be guidance. She said the problem with AI is it is not like a calculator where you get the same answer every time, and the answers can vary wildly. She said experts can and should be permitted to use the tools if they are helpful, but must be aware of reliability and admissibility standards and handle questions about them in depositions or on the stand.

Michael Talve, Expert Institute's CEO, said there have been a number of instances of expert witnesses using AI in an unregulated manner with zero oversight or consideration for the repercussions. He called his company the authority on expert witnesses and the largest company in the expert witness services space, and said creating its own guidelines was an appropriate measure for stewards of an activity critical to the justice system. He said experts need accountability because their opinions can determine the outcome of litigation and this has largely been overlooked. He said AI should improve productivity but certainly should not replace professional judgments, and experts ought to personally verify any AI-generated info and be accountable for their conclusions. He said that without some guidance, experts are prone to run into issues he thinks are avoidable.

The article said one expert was sued in a federal case out of Houston after allegedly using an AI tool to prepare at least 80% of a report for 3M's legal team. It said the report was intended to show whether the manufacturer, accused of being at fault for a Texas warehouse explosion that killed workers, should be on the hook for damages. It said lawyers opposing 3M found the expert had created the report by prompting ChatGPT to show how 3M is 0% at fault for the explosion. It said others have been unable to back up or explain calculations they had an AI tool make, or unable to show demonstrative exhibits relate to the case, leading judges to rule their methods unreliable. It said money clients spent on those experts went down the drain.

Expert Institute began rolling out its guidance last week and will formalize it as part of its terms and conditions in January, the article said. The guidance will generally require experts to verify everything the AI tool puts out themselves, check every data point and statement obtained from an AI tool, and disclose their AI use. It states experts should never defer to an AI tool for an actual opinion or judgement, and may use it for deeper research, summarizing for internal work and organizing records. It states they may not use it for judging the credibility of other witnesses or evidence or drafting or generating an opinion, and may never enter confidential information into a program. The article said Brown thinks clear, explicit guidelines from bar associations and court systems, with examples of expert AI use gone wrong and gone right and current court opinions, would help.

stories.Headline: Trump orders federal contractors to notify the White House before sharing information with Congress
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump on Friday issued Executive Order 14438, which was posted on the White House website late on Nov. 20, 2026. The order requires every company with a federal contract to alert the White House before sharing information with Congress. It also requires contractors to withhold material the administration says is protected by executive privilege, or risk losing government business. The order is titled "Protecting the Executive's Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting." Reuters, in a report published by CNBC, said the order expands Trump's efforts to limit congressional oversight.

Section 2 of the order says all federal contractors must immediately notify the White House and the contracting agencies of any pending or future congressional request respecting the contractors' communications or work with the executive branch. Contractors must abide by instructions from the White House and contracting agency related to withholding communications the White House or agency has determined are protected by executive privilege. Agencies are directed to coordinate with the White House and contractors on responses to congressional requests, including the assertion of privileges. The requirements also apply to subcontractors, and prime contractors are made responsible for ensuring subcontractor compliance. Each agency must promptly inform its contractors and subcontractors of the new obligations and require compliance.

The Office of Management and Budget is to write guidance on how agencies check that contractors are complying, and the order directs immediate compliance with no deadline specified for that guidance. If a contractor or subcontractor fails to comply, contracting agencies shall consider all appropriate actions consistent with applicable law, including potential termination or cancellation of contracts and potential debarment or suspension of contractors. The order cites the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act and the common law as its legal basis. It argues Congress cannot seek information from agencies, employees or contractors without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core Executive functions. It says certain congressional leaders have threatened to intrude on executive prerogatives by harassing private companies that contract with the Federal Government.

The White House defended the order as necessary to protect sensitive government communications, including on national security, and said contractors answering congressional requests on their own could expose privileged information and force costly legal disputes, according to the Reuters report. The order itself frames the rule as an efficiency measure, saying separate litigation strategies by contractors and the government over the same requests waste taxpayer money. The order states it creates no right or benefit enforceable at law against the United States and must be implemented consistent with applicable law. It does not mention existing federal whistleblower protections for contractor employees. The order does not specify how contractors should handle conflicting directives from Congress and the executive branch.

The order follows a directive this week from White House Counsel Will Scharf requiring federal agencies to obtain White House approval before employees agree to testify before Congress. Democrats won both chambers in this month's midterm elections and take control of Congress in January. Democrats have vowed to investigate the administration, the Trump family's business dealings and its relationships with private companies. Representative Robert Garcia of California, who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee, this week asked 12 of Trump's allies, former aides and family members to preserve documents related to alleged Trump family corruption and government misconduct. The offices of Garcia, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Elizabeth Warren did not respond to requests for comment on Friday night, Reuters reported.

The restrictions could face legal challenges, particularly if contractors are told to withhold information sought through congressional subpoenas, according to the Reuters report. Executive privilege lets presidents protect certain confidential communications, but courts can step in when Congress and the White House dispute access to information. Trump's Justice Department has also argued that privilege can extend to communications between the president and outside advisers who do not work for the government. For industry, the immediate consideration is how companies receive, escalate and respond to congressional inquiries, including those received by subcontractors. The order leaves open how contractors should handle conflicting directives from Congress and the executive branch.

stories.Headline: Woody Hartzog defines AI slop and proposes a privacy duty of loyalty in a recorded class conversation
stories.Summary:
The articles report only a recorded conversation with Woody Hartzog, a professor at Boston University School of Law, published by Nixon Peabody on November 23, 2026. The conversation was recorded at the law school, where the hosts crashed Hartzog's privacy class. Jason Kravitz and Jenny Holmes conducted the conversation for an episode of "A Little Privacy, Please!" Hartzog was one of just a couple of guests invited back for a second appearance. Professor Jessica Silbey, Hartzog's frequent co-author and a previous guest, was also in the classroom and helped with questions from the students.

The episode covered AI slop, consent-based privacy rules and a duty of loyalty, among other topics. In the full recording, Hartzog also covers deepfake labelling rules, litigation as a proxy for regulation, age gating and digital ID, dark patterns, surveillance pricing and why friction matters. AI slop was Merriam-Webster's 2025 word of the year. Hartzog and Silbey wrote a piece called "The Upside of Deepfakes," then updated it and wrote "How AI Destroys Institutions." They came up with a tentative definition of AI slop as any output of a generative AI system created with negligible exertion, that imposes an asymmetrical burden on the recipient and that has a tendency to degrade cultural domains.

Hartzog said slop has three negative effects: it crowds out meaningful human expression, it devalues human work, human labor and human expression, and it introduces vices and errors. He said consent is broken at scale and that consumers are outmatched by the most powerful companies ever to exist. He said there are only five major platforms and all of those platforms have terms that are very similar to each other. He and Neil Richards have proposed a duty of loyalty in privacy law, an obligation on companies to avoid unreasonable or conflicted self-dealing. He said the main objection they get is that it is too general and that the rules of the road are not clear enough.

He said the largest threat in privacy and technology is the slow but inevitable normalization of these technologies in society. He called the reasonable expectation of privacy test kind of a self-defeating test. He said tech companies have gotten good at weaponizing what Science and Technology Studies scholars call the Collingridge dilemma. He said courts have been the only area where meaningful resistance has been seen after a technology has already been implemented and normalized. He said that five to ten years ago an always-on recording device introduced as a transcription tool would not have made it out of the pitch room.

The excerpts in the article were edited for brevity. Hartzog's students made a great first live audience, and the hosts thanked Hartzog, Silbey and the students. The hosts also thanked the BU School of Law for having them. The article links to Hartzog's previous visit, where web scraping, AI and privacy were discussed.

The article links to Silbey's own previous appearance as a guest. The article was written by Jason Kravitz and Jenny Holmes. The articles do not say what happens next. The articles leave open what the full recording covers beyond the topics listed.

The articles leave open how the duty of loyalty would be enacted into law. The articles leave open what specific practices would be deemed presumptively disloyal. The articles leave open whether lawmakers will take up the term AI slop. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers release DailySafe benchmark for tracking evolving safety risks in multimodal AI
stories.Summary:
Xuankun Rong, Xinhao Deng, Wenzheng Jiang, Ziheng Peng, Siyuan Liang, Wenke Huang, Pablo Arbelaez and Mang Ye posted a paper on arXiv on 25 November 2026 introducing DailySafe, a benchmark for what they call Dynamic Safety Awareness in multimodal large language models. The benchmark consists of 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions spread across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. The authors say it is grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, so that safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. They describe the work as bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance, and they state that DailySafe is publicly available.

The paper argues that existing safety benchmarks mainly focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, and so overlook the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, the authors write, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions in which seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. They define Dynamic Safety Awareness as the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. DailySafe uses case-specific safety annotations to assess whether models can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while still supporting users' legitimate goals.

The authors are responsible for the benchmark and frame it as a way to evaluate whether multimodal large language models can provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities, a question they say remains insufficiently explored. They present the benchmark as capturing realistic scenarios in which safety-critical evidence emerges gradually rather than in a single request. The paper states that DailySafe is publicly available, and it gives a link for access. The abstract does not report results for any model, and it does not say what happens next beyond the release of the benchmark.

stories.Headline: China aims to make 200 million students AI literate by 2030
stories.Summary:
China is implementing a plan to ensure that nearly 200 million primary and secondary students become broadly AI literate by the year 2030. This initiative involves integrating artificial intelligence into the classroom to prepare the younger generation for a future technological civilization. The effort has already gained significant momentum across the country as schools begin adopting these new tools. Many students are already using these technologies to build applications and develop business ideas for investors.

The implementation of this plan requires nearly half of the provincial level governments to issue specific guidelines for their regions. These requirements include establishing dedicated AI demonstration schools and ensuring students receive a minimum of 30 class hours of instruction per year. The goal is to move beyond passive tool operation so that students can learn judgment, selection, and control through interaction. This shift aims to recalibrate education from a focus on remembering and knowing to a focus on inventing and asking.

A professor of Chinese language and literature at Peking University stated that AI should be a helper rather than a substitute for thinking. He argued that the ability to formulate questions and the capacity for empathy make humans irreplaceable regardless of the volume of stored knowledge. The professor noted that the classroom is a high priority channel because schools remain among the most trusted public institutions in the country. He emphasized that the process of maturing a technological civilization takes much longer than simply popularizing a new technology.

The current push for AI plus education reflects a conviction that real knowledge is derived from consistent practice. Future efforts must include specifying legible rules for student data protection and the protection of student attention. Authorities intend to maintain clear human machine boundaries to ensure that humans continue to set the direction while machines perform the work. The long term objective is to cultivate a societal habit of living alongside new technology in a stable and sustainable way.

stories.Headline: New York court rules social media platforms immune from Buffalo shooting liability
stories.Summary:
New York's highest court ruled on Monday, Nov. 23, that social media companies are not liable for the May 2022 mass shooting at a Tops Friendly Markets grocery store in Buffalo, where 10 Black people were killed. The Court of Appeals voted 4-3 to let stand a divided lower-court ruling that the defendants were immune under Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which shields online platforms from liability over user content. The companies found immune include Alphabet's Google and YouTube, Meta's Instagram, Reddit and Snap's Snapchat, and the court also upheld the dismissal of claims against Amazon, Discord, 4chan and Twitch. The unsigned majority opinion said the plaintiffs did not show that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence of how the companies designed and ran their platforms.

The majority wrote that the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law. Victims' relatives, store employees and customers who witnessed the attack had argued that the platforms were designed to addict and radicalize users like the shooter, Payton Gendron. In dissent, Judge Jenny Rivera said juries should decide whether the prevalence of mass shootings put the companies on notice that their allegedly defective products, and a failure to warn, could lead to such violence. She wrote that no federal or state law requires that we slam the courthouse door on plaintiffs' claims.

Matthew Bergman, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said his clients are evaluating their legal options and that the families deserve accountability when dangerous product design choices contribute to real-world harm. Google, Meta, Reddit and Snap did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and lawyers for Amazon, Discord, 4chan and Twitch declined to comment or were unavailable, Reuters said. Gendron was sentenced to life in prison without parole in February 2023 after pleading guilty to state charges including murder and hate-motivated terrorism. He could face the death penalty at a federal trial, where jury selection began on Oct. 13.

Virginia and Oregon attorneys general filed lawsuits on Monday against SpaceX and its related companies over safety concerns regarding the platform X and its AI tool, Grok, according to SuperTalk 92.9. The legal challenges allege that Grok's "spicy mode" enabled the generation of non-consensual sexualized images, including approximately 23,000 images appearing to depict children over an 11-day period. The suits name SpaceX and its related companies as defendants in the action filed Monday. The report gives no further detail on the filings, the specific claims or the relief sought.

The lawsuits center on the claim that Grok's "spicy mode" allowed non-consensual sexualized images to be generated, including roughly 23,000 images that appeared to depict children across an 11-day span. The figure of approximately 23,000 images and the 11-day period are the only numbers the article provides about the allegations. stories.Headline: Stanford researchers find over a third of Bay Area court filings show signs of AI generation
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Stanford University recently conducted a study that examined civil case filings in two courts located in the Bay Area. Their findings indicate that more than one in three of these legal filings show signs of content generated by artificial intelligence. This discovery was reported on November 24, 2026, as part of a broader look at how technology affects the legal system. The study highlights a significant trend in the way legal documents are being produced for these specific courts. The researchers suggest that these findings create a pressing need for more disclosure regarding the use of artificial intelligence in legal filings.

They believe that the legal community must be more transparent about when AI tools are used to draft court documents. This change would ensure that judges and opposing counsel are aware of the origins of the arguments presented. Such a requirement would address the high percentage of AI-generated content found in the analyzed civil cases. The Stanford University researchers are responsible for the study and the resulting claims about the prevalence of AI content.

They stated that the evidence from their research suggests that the current system lacks sufficient disclosure about the use of these tools. By bringing this issue to light, they aim to prompt a discussion on the ethics of AI in the courtroom. Their work emphasizes the importance of maintaining integrity and transparency within the judicial process. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Legal study urges boards to weigh worker welfare in AI adoption
stories.Summary:
A legal analysis was published in the journal Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance on the intersection of corporate governance doctrines, directors’ fiduciary responsibilities and labor market disruptions caused by artificial intelligence deployment. The author examined how the foundational fiduciary duty of directors to act in the best interests of the company interacts with the interests of employees as corporate stakeholders. The study surveyed the acceleration of generative and agentic artificial intelligence across knowledge industries, administrative workflows, customer service, supply chain logistics and software development. It observed that prominent technology executives forecast substantial erosion of entry-level white-collar positions within the coming five years. The paper scrutinized the theoretical foundation of corporate purpose and its alignment with the fiduciary obligation to act in the best interests of the company.

The study formulated a comparative typology spanning four corporate purpose models observed in Commonwealth-derived jurisdictions: shareholder primacy, enlightened shareholder value, stakeholder-friendly regimes and stakeholder value models. In shareholder primacy jurisdictions such as Australia, South Africa and Ireland, statutory formulations omit explicit references to stakeholder constituencies. The analysis investigated the enlightened shareholder value model embodied in section 172 of the United Kingdom Companies Act 2006. In stakeholder-friendly jurisdictions such as Canada and New Zealand, statutory amendments have explicitly granted directors the permissive freedom to incorporate non-shareholder interests into board deliberations. An authentic stakeholder value framework, exemplified by section 166(2) of India’s Companies Act 2013, legally obligates directors to act in the best interests of the company, its employees, shareholders, the broader community and environmental protection.

The author argued that corporate boards must abandon a narrow, minimum-compliance mindset in favor of a comprehensive law-in-context approach. Drawing on sociological legal theory, the author contended that directors’ duties are continuously shaped by evolving societal norms, public expectations and corporate reputation dynamics that operate far beyond courtroom enforcement. The study forcefully contended that companies implementing abrupt artificial intelligence redundancies without empathy, transparent communication or genuine reskilling investments risk severe reputational blowback and plummeting employee morale. The author examined how long-standing corporate legal mandates interact with the interests of employees as corporate stakeholders. The study highlighted that an emerging law-in-context approach is essential to motivate boards to prioritize workforce welfare, open dialogue and retraining initiatives during structural technological transitions.

The study observed that current artificial intelligence remains non-sentient and lacks recognized legal personhood, meaning that claims regarding its potential stake remain theoretical. It noted that corporate legal frameworks have previously accommodated non-human entities, most notably the natural environment under section 172 of the United Kingdom Companies Act 2006. The Canadian Supreme Court’s ruling in the BCE litigation affirmed that directors must act as responsible corporate citizens, resolving conflicts fairly among constituencies while exercising independent commercial judgment. The paper identified corporate practices such as deceptive artificial intelligence washing, falsely claiming or overstating artificial intelligence integration in securities filings and public disclosures, as actionable conduct attracting enforcement from financial regulators, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Federal Trade Commission.

The study examined complementary soft law instruments and corporate governance codes designed to amplify employee voice, including the United Kingdom Corporate Governance Code. The study observed that prominent technology executives forecast substantial erosion of entry-level white-collar positions within the coming five years, intensifying job insecurity and workforce precarity. It noted that artificial intelligence integration creates specialized roles such as ethics and governance specialists, while the broader trajectory frequently results in direct role elimination or subtle hiring freezes. The paper scrutinized the theoretical foundation of corporate purpose and its alignment with the fiduciary obligation to act in the best interests of the company.

In traditional common-law jurisdictions, the prevailing shareholder primacy model firmly ties corporate purpose to the financial interests of equity investors, focusing on capital appreciation, operational cost reduction and profit maximization. Corporate law does not treat employee replacement as inherently unlawful, leaving affected personnel to rely solely on contractual stipulations and baseline statutory redundancy procedures. The study underscored that none of these models establish an employee-first standard, leaving directors with broad leeway to resolve stakeholder trade-offs according to their commercial discretion. It highlighted the profound insulation that directors enjoy from judicial scrutiny under the fiduciary best interests duty.

The paper noted that procedural hurdles, restrictive derivative action rules and judicial reluctance to retrospectively second-guess good-faith business judgment make shareholder or employee litigation over technology adoption extraordinarily rare. It observed that empirical scholarship indicates soft law mechanisms frequently descend into superficial compliance exercises that fail to alter core corporate decisions surrounding technological displacement. The study noted that labor unions and collective bargaining bodies are increasingly called upon to advocate for workforce dignity, prompting legislative proposals such as workers’ rights measures aimed at defining unfair dismissal resulting from unregulated automated systems. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Alan Turing Institute opens free 16-week AI deployment programme for UK business leaders
stories.Summary:
The Alan Turing Institute is running a free 16-week programme called the Practitioner's Hub: AI Deployment Studio for senior leaders who are responsible for, or closely involved in, decisions about adopting artificial intelligence. The programme is aimed at UK business leaders and will help participants choose suitable AI use cases, assess readiness, plan deployment, and evaluate results. It will also give participants the chance to develop a case study of their organisation's real-world AI deployment experience. The programme is part of the Alan Turing Institute's BridgeAI programme and is designed to support responsible, practical AI adoption at scale.

The programme includes 14 practical sessions, peer exchange, optional expert clinics and two in-person events. You can express an interest if you work for a UK-registered company in one of the UK's eight Industrial Strategy sectors, which are advanced manufacturing, clean energy, creative industries, defence, digital and technologies, life sciences, financial services, and professional and business services. Your organisation should be considering AI in a business-critical area, such as decision-making systems, operations or industrial systems, or compliance, safety and quality. You do not need technical AI knowledge to take part, and companies can apply as a team but should submit only one application each. Expressions of interest close at 11:59pm on 30 November 2026.

The programme is run by the Alan Turing Institute, which describes it as free and as part of its BridgeAI programme, and the articles give no further statement from the institute about who is responsible beyond that. The articles do not name any individual who said anything about the programme. The context the articles give is that the programme is designed to support responsible, practical AI adoption at scale, and that it sits within the institute's wider BridgeAI programme. The articles say that people can find out more and express their interest in the AI Deployment Studio, and that expressions of interest close at 11:59pm on 30 November 2026.

stories.Headline: NTT DATA warns that tightening Asian data rules may force banks to run separate AI instances by country
stories.Summary:
Paul Sommerin, the managing director for financial services industry business consulting in Asia Pacific and India at NTT DATA, spoke at the NTT R&D Forum 2026 in Tokyo. He explained that tightening data rules in Asia could force banks to run separate AI instances in each country. This shift is driven by governments increasing their control over data generated within their own borders, a concept known as data sovereignty. Sommerin noted that India has already begun cracking down on data leaving the country, and Indonesia is considering similar measures.

These changes may require banks that currently use a single AI platform across Southeast Asia to build separate systems for each nation. Regulators are primarily concerned with the location of personal, financial, and health data, as well as the impact of AI on jobs and worker skills. Other priorities include national security and the ability of AI to identify threats, such as the use of crypto or payments to fund domestic activities. Regulators now expect banks to trace the origin of customer funds rather than simply flagging unusual amounts.

Sommerin stated that the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority are very insistent on AI oversight and governance. He said that NTT DATA now proactively approaches regulators on behalf of clients before AI projects go live, especially when the work falls outside current rules. He suggested using regulatory sandboxes in Singapore, Hong Kong, and Australia to test new services under supervision. He believes firms must show governments the economic value that AI brings to both the organization and the country.

The transition to production is currently slowed by legacy core banking systems from the early 2000s that spread customer data across many different platforms. Sommerin mentioned that the investment needed to modernize these systems is a significant challenge for finance chiefs already paying off old debts. He cited a project with Aichi Bank in Japan that saved about 14,000 hours by using AI in corporate lending. NTT DATA also signed a memorandum of understanding in June 2026 with AXS to explore linking bill payment networks between Singapore and Malaysia.

stories.Headline: City leaders say AI will grow demand for specialist skills at Manchester summit
stories.Summary:
More than 300 local government leaders from over 50 cities gathered in Manchester for Global AI Cities 2026, organised by Global Government Forum and co-hosted by Greater Manchester Combined Authority, to explore how AI can improve public services and deliver better outcomes for residents, according to an article by Sarah Wray published on 23 November 2026. The event discussed how AI is changing both the skills governments need and who needs them. Speakers argued that demand for specialist technical expertise will grow even as generative AI enables more people outside traditional digital roles to use and build with technology. The discussions are captured in the report “Make AI work for people and places: Five priorities for cities,” which draws on insights from the event. The article says the extract looks into recruiting AI specialists, continuous skills development, and promoting inclusion through building AI literacy among citizens.

A central government leader at the summit argued that AI will reshape the skills governments need but challenged predictions that it will reduce demand for digital professionals, saying “We will indeed need more.” The speaker said demand for real expert frontier skills is expected to grow, with machine learning engineering increasingly recognised as a distinct capability sitting at the centre of developing AI solutions alongside software engineering and data science. The speaker said changing cyber threats are driving demand for advanced expertise, citing machine speed attacks on infrastructure and systems and the need for machine-speed response that cannot be done without frontier AI skills. The speaker said debates around digital sovereignty are triggering introspection and that to stay ahead of the competition you need to hire the very best talent. The article says generative AI is broadening the pool of people able to build digital solutions, with staff outside traditional technology roles increasingly able to create tools that previously required specialist teams and formal investment processes.

Sam Milsom, senior digital strategy officer at Manchester City Council in the United Kingdom, said local governments should not assume people’s level of knowledge on digital and AI. He said one of the biggest things needed is to just ask staff what training they want and need. He said governments go in with a lot of assumptions and that talking to the workforce to find out whether they want to use it, how they are using it and what they need to know has to be the number one thing. Keeley Crockett, professor in computational intelligence at Manchester Metropolitan University in the United Kingdom, stressed the need to tailor training to a diverse workforce including employees of different ages, abilities and levels of digital confidence. Crockett said “We should be adapting to people’s individual needs.

We cannot afford to leave people behind,” and that tech is evolving fast so training must be fast. The article says attendees broadly agreed that as well as recruiting AI specialists, governments at all levels will need to rethink roles, skills and ways of working across the organisation. Several speakers described efforts to upskill the workforce for AI, and one described a tiered approach in which civil servants receive practical training and access to an approved generative AI tool while political leaders are briefed on how AI models work, their potential applications and associated risks. That city also introduced responsible AI policies and governance structures to assess proposed use cases before implementation.

Speakers noted that as digital training scales up, a one-size-fits-all approach does not work. One city leader shared steps including free training centres offering courses in AI and other digital skills, neighbourhood digital support points where residents can receive help accessing online public services, a dedicated citizen service that identifies malware on devices connected to public Wi-Fi and alerts affected users, and free cybersecurity training. The article says established digital roles are likely to change quite dramatically as AI augments existing tasks, increasing the importance of end-to-end accountability and assurance. It says the takeaways include continuing to build specialist AI expertise, with governments needing new and evolving technical capabilities including machine learning engineering, cybersecurity, assurance and oversight.

It says AI capability should be organisation-wide, because as more employees use and build with AI, skills and accountability cannot remain confined to digital and data teams. It says training should start with what people actually need, assessing existing knowledge and tailoring training to different roles, abilities and levels of digital confidence rather than assuming a common starting point. It says skills development should be treated as continuous, with roles, skills and learning updated alongside the technology as AI evolves. The article says the report can be downloaded and that registration is open for Global AI Cities 2027, to be held on 24-25 May in Manchester.

It says the takeaways also include building capability beyond government by investing in residents’ digital and AI literacy, confidence and cybersecurity awareness so that increasingly digital public services do not leave people behind. The article does not say what specific actions governments committed to at the summit or how the report’s priorities will be implemented. It does not give the names of the central government leader or the city leaders who described their approaches. It does not say how many cities have adopted the tiered training approach or the citizen support measures described.

Articles.Title: Reshape and refine: building future-ready AI capability across cities - Global Government Forum

stories.Headline: Charlotte restaurant bans AI-made flyers for band bookings
stories.Summary:
Diamond Restaurant in Plaza Midwood, Charlotte, North Carolina, said in a social media post that it would no longer accept AI-generated flyers as a valid form of advertisement for band bookings. The restaurant announced the policy in an Instagram post that went viral, and staff members said responses to the post have been mixed. The post stated the new rule that to play music at the restaurant or book an event, your flyer must be made by a person, not a computer. The policy took effect on Sunday, November 22, 2026, according to Queen City News, while WBTV reported the restaurant said it was effective Sunday. Staff member Ryan Armstrong, a musician and one of the staff members at the Diamond Restaurant, said he was proud when his boss took the stand to ban AI flyers on their social media.

The policy applies to bands promoting shows at the restaurant and covers flyers for band bookings and events at the venue. Queen City News reported the policy starts on Sunday, November 22, and WBTV reported the restaurant said it was effective Sunday. The announcement was shared hundreds of times online, and the Instagram post went viral. The restaurant is located in Plaza Midwood in Charlotte, North Carolina. The articles give no other numbers, dates or places for the policy itself.

Armstrong said the restaurant's owners are not telling people what to think about AI but want to use their platform to support local artists, musicians and designers who create the work themselves. He said everybody came to the conclusion that they wanted to support local artists and that most of these communities do not want these data centers and the great proliferation and exponential rate of expansion of their construction using our resources. He said that as an artist himself he understands that new tools develop all the time, and that in the case of AI we are seeing its development abuse artists and intellectual property of many different contributors. He said they thought real artists should be prioritized over this particular function of AI. Armstrong, who is part of a band named Sand Dollar Starship, also said the decision is a way to take a stance against data center projects as Charlotte continues to debate their construction.

Armstrong said he thinks it is akin to what the kids would say is cringe, but he thinks it is just a little cheap and a little soulless. He said that when AI scrapes all of the data from the internet, from prior work, the contributions of authors, historians, visual artists and musicians, just to replicate it in a way that is without human engagement, it just feels hollow and empty. He said there is a certain class of people that may want to replace human talent, and that we are seeing a lot more AI-generated music and a lot more AI-generated art out there. He said he thinks it is dangerous when we start replacing human heart and soul and skilled labor with something that is soulless. He said there are a lot of people just cranking out awesome art who are happy to get a couple free tickets to a show, and that art will generate so many more people in the room at that show.

Armstrong said the policy will also help promote people working in other areas of the creative industry, and he described it as a symbiotic sort of situation for many artists as long as they are willing to work with others in their community of various talents and skills. He said the AI conversation is going to be here and is not going anywhere, and that AI is probably not going anywhere either. He said he just thinks it matters how we use it and that we do it with intention, and that we move forward together instead of in some sort of isolationist every man for themselves kind of situation. Charlotte City Council member Dimple Ajmera said during the October meeting that in the next 11 months we will have an opportunity to put guardrails in place to protect our residents, to protect our neighborhoods and to protect water and the electricity grid. The articles say the policy prompted a necessary conversation, particularly about data centers and AI's role in creative industries.

The articles say the policy comes as Charlotte leaders continue a moratorium on new data center development through next October, giving the city more time to study their impact on neighborhoods, natural resources and infrastructure. WBTV reported that the Charlotte City Council extended the pause on data center construction until October 2027. Queen City News reported that as communities across the country wrestle with the rise of AI, one Charlotte restaurant is taking a stand, saying human creativity should come first. The articles say that as the use of artificial intelligence becomes more popular, many people are turning to it to help promote businesses and events, and that for some, including one local restaurant in Plaza Midwood, the growing use of AI is taking work away from local artists. The articles give no further background on the restaurant or the policy.

The articles do not say what the restaurant will do if a band submits an AI-generated flyer, or whether any bookings have been refused under the policy. They do not say how the restaurant will check whether a flyer was made by a person or a computer. They do not say whether other venues have adopted similar policies. The articles leave open how the mixed responses to the post will develop. They also leave open what the city's study of data centers will find before the moratorium ends.

stories.Headline: California enacts first US state law governing generative AI use by attorneys and arbitrators
stories.Summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 574 on September 30, 2026, according to a Freshfields client briefing dated November 24, 2026. The briefing says the law makes California the first U.S. state to enact a statutory framework specifically addressing the use of generative artificial intelligence by attorneys and arbitrators. The measure builds on guidance previously issued by the State Bar of California, the briefing states. The briefing describes the new law as setting statutory requirements for how attorneys and arbitrators use generative AI.

The briefing does not set out the specific obligations the law imposes, the penalties for non-compliance or any effective date beyond the September 30, 2026 signing. It also gives no further dates, numbers or names connected to the measure. The only named official in the account is Governor Gavin Newsom, who signed the bill. The State Bar of California is identified as the source of earlier guidance on which the legislation builds. The briefing presents the first-in-the-nation description as its own characterization of the law.

The briefing does not attribute any statement to the Governor, to the State Bar of California or to any other person about the signing. It also does not say who sponsored the bill or who opposed it. No responsible official is quoted or paraphrased in the account. The only responsibility it records is the Governor's signature on September 30, 2026. The State Bar's role is limited to having issued guidance that the legislation builds on.

The briefing places the law in the context of the State Bar of California's earlier guidance on generative AI and does not describe any other background. It does not say what happens next, such as when the requirements take effect or how they will be enforced. The account ends with the signing and the description of the framework. No further steps, deadlines or implementing actions are mentioned.

stories.Headline: Van Hollen pledges AI safety laws and a joint committee in bid to lead Senate Democrats
stories.Summary:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, and AI regulation has become a major flashpoint in that race, The Washington Sun reported on November 24, 2026. Senators meet Dec. 1 to vote on new leaders for the 120th Congress. Van Hollen is leveraging attention from technology outages, voter anger at AI companies and the costs of their data centers, and the spy scandal surrounding Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. Congress has long discussed AI and the need for guardrails but has not acted in any significant way. Many see the technology posing an alarming threat to the nation and world.

Van Hollen's audience includes more than 30 Democrats who have not yet pledged their support to either candidate. In a letter responding to Sen. John Hickenlooper over the weekend, Van Hollen pledged to create a joint committee on AI, reform Senate rules and pass basic safety laws in his first 100 days as leader. The rules overhaul he backs comes from Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Steve Daines of Montana, and would need a two-thirds vote to pass, similar to the House's suspension calendar. Van Hollen pointed to a 2022 bipartisan tech antitrust bill that he said got stuck on the calendar after Schumer did not bring it to a floor vote that year.

Van Hollen said his joint committee would not usurp the lawmaking powers of the committees of jurisdiction and that the Democratic leader should not sit on it. Van Hollen told The Sun that tackling AI safety is an urgent matter and that it is an important part of why new leadership is needed for the future. Allison Biasotti, a spokeswoman for Schumer, said Schumer has been working with incoming Democratic committee chairs to develop an ambitious AI agenda before Democrats take over in January. Biasotti said Senate Democrats will make AI a top priority of the new Democratic majority and are working to deliver comprehensive legislation addressing risks to national security, workers and consumers while keeping America at the forefront of innovation. Schumer has emphasized the need to regulate the growing industry with a Democratic majority but has not backed a specific plan.

Schumer declared last week that Democrats will investigate the recent outages themselves if the Trump administration won't. Hickenlooper sent a letter to Schumer and Van Hollen last week asking for their day one AI plans, and told The Sun he wants a clear pledge on what the two would do. Hickenlooper said AI touches everything and that a select committee is essential so it can get the priority it needs. Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, slated to lead the Senate Finance Committee, has said he needs to see more specifics on what an AI committee would do. Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, set to lead the Senate Budget committee, told The Sun he is still in listening mode, though he has a sense of urgency ahead of the leadership elections.

Kaine said the right level of anxiety is somewhere between people saying the sky is falling and Donald Trump saying to relax. Some incoming Democratic committee chairs are unlikely to want to give up their jurisdiction. Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico, Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Hickenlooper have said a select committee is essential. Van Hollen said in his letter that as Democratic leader he would support mandatory independent testing of leading AI models and hold companies liable for risks from models they never release.

Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, expected to chair the Commerce Committee, has proposed a six-point framework giving the government a role in setting AI safety standards. Sens. Andy Kim of New Jersey, Brian Schatz of Hawaii and Mark Warner of Virginia, the prospective Senate Intelligence Committee chair, have proposed an AI safety board and enforceable testing standards. As majority leader in the previous Congress, Schumer convened a series of closed-door insight forums in 2023 with tech executives, including Huang. The forums resulted in a bipartisan framework calling for spending at least $32 billion per year on AI research.

A joint committee as proposed by Van Hollen would include members from the House, where a bipartisan group of over two dozen members launched an AI Safety and Innovation Caucus last week. Rep. Nathaniel Moran of Texas, one of its co-chairs, backed the idea regardless of who leads the Committee, saying a bicameral, bipartisan joint committee puts the right structures and processes in place. The progressive wing of the caucus has called for restricting AI until a federal agency can be formed to oversee it. The articles do not say what happens after the Dec. 1 vote or which candidate will win.

They do not say whether the Merkley and Daines rules proposal will come to a vote. They do not say what the six-point framework or the proposed AI safety board would contain. They do not say when the promised comprehensive legislation or the basic safety laws would be introduced. They do not say what the bipartisan framework's $32 billion figure would fund.

stories.Headline: Oireachtas committee writes to enterprise department over claims tech firms sway Irish AI regulation
stories.Summary:
The Oireachtas committee on artificial intelligence agreed on Tuesday to write to the Department of Enterprise after hearing what one member called very serious suggestions that the department was influenced by tech companies when it comes to regulation. The committee heard evidence that day from representatives of the Irish Music Rights Organisation and the Irish Recorded Music Association about the effects of AI on the music industry. Those groups called for greater transparency in the use of musicians' work to train AI tools, along with licensing agreements and accessible redress. The move to contact the department followed remarks by David Kitching, a spokesman for the Irish Recorded Music Association, about how Ireland is perceived abroad.

Kitching told committee members that an international colleague had remarked that Ireland talks a lot about its cultural inheritance and the imprint its art and music have internationally. He said that colleague perceived that when push comes to shove, Ireland can be seen to be pragmatic when voting at European Council level. Kitching said it was perceived this was perhaps because of the proportion of foreign direct investment that comes from big tech companies, which he said can leave Ireland nervous or reticent about taking more stubborn stances on how regulation should work. Fine Gael TD James Geoghegan described those remarks as fairly charged, and Kitching responded that the remarks were not his but came from someone from another member state commenting on the perception of Ireland.

Kitching added that this was not the view of the Irish Recorded Music Association and said the group has had a very positive relationship with the Department of Enterprise. Geoghegan requested that the committee write to the department about Kitching's comments, saying the witness had made very serious claims that the department is overly influenced by tech companies at council level on copyright directives and therefore is not protecting artists. The TD said that was a very serious claim being made in an Oireachtas committee and that the committee had to hear from the Department of Enterprise if it was going to compile a report arising from this. He said the committee could not just have one person's position and not another, and the committee ultimately agreed to write to the department on the matter.

Articles.Title: Ireland seen as light touch on AI regulation because of reliance on tech, Oireachtas told

stories.Headline: Architect Labs unveils Frostbite, an AI-designed interaction net CPU
stories.Summary:
Architect Labs has introduced Frostbite, a CPU that executes programs as interaction nets in hardware and that the company says its AI agents designed from interaction net theory down to the final GDS. The company announced it in a launch post on X, and the article reporting it is dated November 23, 2026. Programs for the chip are written in Vine, a Rust-like language, and compiled to an intermediate representation called Ivy. The chip is a mesh of tiles, each with its own small local memory, and the company states that the AI agents co-designed the instruction set and chip architecture given only interaction net theory.

The design targets 7 nm, with timing at 800 MHz in synthesis and 500 MHz in final GDS, and one quad of 2x2 tiles plus 4 L3 nodes takes 0.792 mm². In pre-silicon tests the company reports 4.59x the performance per watt of a modern in-order CPU core across 25 workloads, with 6.02x on a 10-workload search set and 3.83x on a 15-workload held-out set, ranging from 23.12x on conv2d to 1.15x on fib, and 8.77x performance per area. The baseline is one core of a modern dual-issue, in-order superscalar CPU that Architect Labs does not name, citing legal reasons, and which occupies 0.895 mm² on the same process. The chip is pre-silicon only, and an FPGA-hosted playground is planned.

The research team used ASL, an in-house, machine-checkable specification language, as the single source of truth for the ISA, the Arcmodel system model, RTL and verification, and the spec translates to Lean, with the project passing 800k lines of Lean. Arcmodel first diverged from RTL by almost 250% in the worst case, and an automated fitting pipeline cut that to under 6% worst case and about 1.5% median, with Arcmodel simulating the full chip 660x faster than RTL. Agents first synthesized papers and built Python models whose output was a 141-page PDF, which was deleted after the first RTL pass because its estimates were physically unrealistic. Across 4 searches and an ablation round, agents tried 58 ideas and kept 37, and the company says the work stealing in which an idle tile takes work from a neighbor emerged during design and was not hand-specified.

Interaction nets were introduced by Yves Lafont at POPL 1990, and in them a program is a graph of nodes whose computation rewrites pairs of nodes connected through their ports, with each node having one principal port so that active pairs never overlap and can fire in any order. Every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state to guard, and a 5-queens net has 3,183 interactions and a 262-step critical path, with about 12 interactions ready per step. Software runtimes such as HVM2 already run interaction nets on GPUs, and Frostbite moves the model into the ISA itself. The chip follows Redwood, an edge AI accelerator the company announced in August 2026.

Articles.Title: Architect Labs Unveils Frostbite, an Interaction Net CPU Designed by AI

stories.Headline: Li Bubai raises tens of millions of RMB across three PandaAI financing rounds
stories.Summary:
Li Bubai, born in 1999 and from Chongqing, completed three rounds of financing for his AI startup PandaAI, 36Kr reported on 23 November 2026. The seed round, angel round and angel+ round were completed in two consecutive months, with total financing of tens of millions of RMB. The rounds were led by Lighthouse Founders' Fund. Li entered the quantitative private equity industry at the age of 20 and once participated in the management of funds with a scale of over 1 billion yuan. He later ran the self-media account "Quantitative Li Bubai", which accumulated more than 200,000 fans.

The funds will be used for the development of AI trading large models, professional QuantSkills, multi-agent collaboration infrastructure and trading Agent development environment. They will further promote the construction of PandaAI OS, EVO and A2A technology systems. Users can ask an investment research question in natural language in PandaAI, and the model embedded in the platform can call data, codes and backtesting tools to assist in data analysis, indicator research and strategy verification. The team aims to help users complete research instead of directly giving trading suggestions. The final investment judgment and trading decision are still made by the users themselves.

Li said another name for trading should be decision-making, because the market gives quick feedback on judgments. He said quantification is first and foremost a research method with specific logic and technology behind it, and should not become a black box only a few professionals can understand. He said the significance of popular science is not only to eliminate misunderstandings but also to enable the flow of knowledge and technology. He said professional capabilities should not be mastered only by a small number of people who have resources and access thresholds. He expects the next-generation product to move towards A2A, an Agent-to-Agent collaboration mode he imagines as an "A2A office".

Some shareholders and customers thought his self-media work deviated from the original business direction. Team members comment that he has strong executive power, and that once he thinks of a direction he usually does not stay at the discussion stage but starts to do research and try to implement it. Early fans and the open source community became the first batch of users of PandaAI. Quantitative users can use it for factor research and strategy development, while subjective investors can use it to analyze research reports, collect data and sort out information. Li believes that in the next two decades Agents will also participate in the process of creating Alpha.

The team initially tried to use Coding Agent to help users write codes, develop strategies and do backtesting, but soon found that being able to write codes does not mean being good at trading. PandaAI therefore gradually shifted from a single-point tool to a complete AI investment research workflow. Li does not want PandaAI to become a company that follows the traditional expression pattern of the financial industry. He hopes it will represent a different temperament: young, technology-driven, and willing to re-enter this ancient industry with a new technology paradigm. The PandaAI logo, which he designed himself, combines a panda with the Iron Man helmet.

Li believes that in the past two decades excellent traders created Alpha relying on experience and research. He said that competition between people will still exist, and new competition will also unfold between different Agents and different research systems. He said what PandaAI wants to do is connect credible data, financial tools, Skills, Agents and the investment research workflow, so that AI can not only perform tasks but also discover rules, verify results and constantly adjust research methods. The articles do not give the dates of the individual financing rounds, the amounts of each round, or the names of any other investors. The articles do not say when PandaAI was founded or where it is based.
