stories.Headline: Polar and Crusoe plan 40MW Norway AI facility for late 2027
stories.Summary:
Polar Data Centers announced on October 21, 2026 that it is expanding its partnership with Crusoe with a new facility, DRA02, at its Tørdal campus in Norway. The announcement said DRA01, Polar's facility in Tørdal, is now live and providing 12MW of IT capacity. DRA01 is powered by 100% hydroelectric energy and supports Crusoe Cloud, Crusoe's AI cloud platform and AI services. Polar and Crusoe first announced their partnership around DRA01 in June 2025. The press release was issued from London, United Kingdom, through EINPresswire.com.

DRA02 is expected to go live in late 2027 and plans to deliver an additional 40MW of critical, liquid-cooled IT capacity. The new facility is also powered by hydroelectric power. Crusoe plans to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 at DRA02 to support the next phase of its AI cloud expansion in Norway. DRA01 combines modular infrastructure, advanced cooling technology, and resilient electrical systems designed around the requirements of the latest GPU deployments. DRA01 was recognised as "Most Successfully Delivered Data Centre" at the Data Centre World Awards 2026.

Andy Hayes, CEO of Polar, said the company's ambition has always been to help customers develop the future of AI, and called the Crusoe relationship a great example of that in action. He said Polar has successfully delivered DRA01, Crusoe is live and operating in Norway, and the companies are now moving forward together with the next phase. Hayes said the expansion into DRA02 demonstrates the strength of the collaboration and the confidence that comes from successful delivery. He said it is about much more than bringing capacity online, and about creating the infrastructure, operational performance, and customer relationships that enable customers to continue scaling. Cully Cavness, Crusoe's Co-founder, President and Chief Strategy Officer, said the expansion with Polar in Norway lets Crusoe serve some of the world's most innovative companies with reliable access to Crusoe Cloud's AI cloud services.

Cavness said what makes Tørdal stand out is that it runs on 100% renewable hydroelectric power, which he said aligns with Crusoe's value of bending the arc of energy towards sustainability. He said Polar has been a solid partner to help Crusoe scale its presence in Europe. The move from initial deployment into stable operations represents an important milestone for the partnership, according to the announcement. The companies said the milestone demonstrates their ability to deliver and operate infrastructure for the world's most demanding AI workloads.

The expansion significantly increases the scale available to support Crusoe Cloud's continued growth in Europe and beyond, the announcement said. The announcement described Polar as a European developer and operator of AI-ready data center infrastructure. It described Crusoe as the AI factory company. Polar said it is building a growing European platform of AI-ready infrastructure, combining renewable power, resilient design, high-density cooling capability, and a customer-led approach to development and operations.

Crusoe said it provides a reliable, scalable, cost-effective, energy-first solution for AI infrastructure, harnessing large-scale energy sources, building AI-optimized data centers, and delivering a powerful AI cloud platform. The announcement said the expansion reflects Polar's approach to developing long-term customer partnerships by delivering initial capacity successfully, operating it reliably, and creating a platform that can scale as customers' requirements grow. The announcement said the move into DRA02 takes the relationship to its next stage and supports Polar's wider vision to accelerate AI infrastructure. It said Polar aims to create the infrastructure platform customers need to develop the future of AI.

The articles did not state the cost of DRA02 or the terms of the agreement between Polar and Crusoe. The articles did not state how much capacity Crusoe plans to use at DRA02 beyond the 40MW planned for the facility. The articles did not state when construction of DRA02 began or whether it has started. The articles did not state how many NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems Crusoe plans to deploy at DRA02.

stories.Headline: Tidal bans fully AI-generated tracks and will remove over 29 million songs starting December 9
stories.Summary:
The music streaming service Tidal announced on Tuesday that it will ban and remove millions of songs created entirely by artificial intelligence. This decision follows a massive surge in submissions where over 43 percent of tracks uploaded in the last 90 days were AI generated. The company intends to stop the flood of low quality content that is currently inundating its digital platform. This aggressive move aims to protect the visibility of human musicians against a tide of automated audio.

The removal process will begin on December 9 and is expected to delete more than 29 million songs by the end of the year. Under these new rules, the platform will reject between 80,000 and 85,000 tracks every single day. Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering tracks that are 100 percent AI generated based on their metadata. While fully automated songs are banned, the service will still accept music that was created with AI assistance.

Robert Anderson, who leads Tidal Music, stated on X that previous efforts to demonetize AI tracks in June were not enough of a deterrent. He explained that the sheer scale of these uploads means authentic artists are getting buried under a mountain of synthetic content. The company noted that 27 million tracks, or 6.3 percent of its library, are fully AI generated. They further observed that 96 percent of those specific automated tracks have received no streams at all.

Tidal claims to be one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music in such an outright manner. Other services like Deezer are introducing filters, while Spotify and YouTube Music have chosen to label the content instead of removing it. The company believes that drastic action is necessary to maintain the authenticity of the music discovery experience for its subscribers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming

stories.headline_source: Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming

stories.Headline: Congressional Research Service urges Congress to evaluate defense against agentic AI cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
A new report from the Congressional Research Service warns that agentic artificial intelligence could automate complex cyberattacks that usually require entire teams of hackers. The document highlights a mid-September 2025 operation that Anthropic attributed to a Chinese state-sponsored group known as GTG-1002. This specific group allegedly automated between 80 percent and 90 percent of a campaign that targeted approximately 30 different organizations. Some researchers have since questioned whether this particular attack was actually as autonomous or successful as the initial reports claimed.

The report suggests that Congress should evaluate if the Department of Defense is appropriately postured to detect and respond to these autonomous threats. It notes that the Cybersecurity and Information Systems Information Analysis Center has found no official government policies specifically addressing agentic AI yet. Under Section 1535 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, which became Public Law 119-60 on December 18, 2025, the Secretary of Defense must establish an AI Futures Steering Committee by April 1. Additionally, the report questions if voluntary partnerships with the Department of Commerce Center for AI Standards and Innovation should be made mandatory.

The Congressional Research Service describes agentic AI as systems that can pursue specific goals while requiring very limited human supervision. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency claims that its AI Cyber Challenge showed AI agents can fix open-source vulnerabilities faster than human teams. This capability could potentially support a strategy of AI-on-AI defense to counter the speed and scale of autonomous attacks. The AI Futures Steering Committee is expected to deliver its official findings to congressional defense committees by January 31, 2027.

Congress may use these upcoming findings to determine the necessary authorizations, appropriations, and general oversight for Department of Defense agentic AI programs. Lawmakers are also considering the reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, which was part of Public Law 114-113. This specific information-sharing law is currently set to expire on December 11 under an amendment found in Section 2011 of Public Law 119-103. These legislative steps aim to address the evolving capabilities of militaries exploring autonomous decision-making and operations.

Articles.Title: Agentic AI Cyberattacks Raise Questions for Congress on Defense

stories.headline_source: Agentic AI Cyberattacks Raise Questions for Congress on Defense

stories.Headline: TGood and LG enter the power resources market to meet AI computing demands
stories.Summary:
TGood and LG have rushed to enter the power resources market during a scramble driven by artificial intelligence. This race for electricity occurred as computing power demand surged, redrawing cost accounts for energy storage and gas-fired power. The scramble extended to gas fields, where advanced gas power has taken 69 percent of the market share. These events were highlighted during a Grid Revaluation Special Summit held on November 19. The summit gathered North American power traders, researchers, and gas-fired power operators to discuss shifting computing power loads.

The U.S. Department of Energy issued a 5.1 billion dollar loan to Alliant Energy last month for gas storage and power. This funding is earmarked for building 1.6 million kilowatts of new gas-fired power capacity in the United States. TGood signed a centralized procurement contract for power cabins at computing power centers worth 250 million yuan. Vertech, a subsidiary of LG Energy Solution, plans for North American production capacity to reach 70 GWh by next year. LG Energy Solution also reported backlogged energy storage orders reaching 160 GWh by the end of the third quarter.

U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said that gas storage facilities function as warehouses for buying gas when prices are low. Tristan Doherty of Vertech stated that idle grid capacity can meet the pulse load of data centers. TGood claims its computing-power-power island solution reduces the construction cycle by about 70 percent compared with civil engineering. LG Energy Solution was selected for the NVIDIA DSX Ready energy storage partner list, which includes only three companies worldwide. These leaders suggest that batteries are now part of computing power infrastructure rather than just backup power supplies.

Residents in Lowell, Massachusetts, sued the state environmental protection department over the expansion of diesel generators at a data center. These residents have seen electricity tariffs rise by more than 50 percent due to the competition for power. Fifteen U.S. states are considering pausing new data center approvals to manage the growing power gap. The National Data Administration noted that China's computing power scale has reached 3.1 million PFLOPS, ranking second globally. The National Energy Administration estimates China's computing power electricity consumption will reach 800 billion kilowatt-hours by 2030.

BloombergNEF projects that new natural gas consumption from U.S. data centers will reach 15 billion cubic feet per day by 2035. This increment exceeds the total national gas consumption of any country except China, Russia, Iran, and the United States. Massachusetts released a regulatory framework in June requiring data centers to provide their own clean power and cover grid costs. Projects with peak power consumption exceeding 25,000 kilowatts must now obtain community approval before applying for official permits. New York State also released an advanced nuclear power master plan targeting 5 million kilowatts of new capacity.

Small modular reactors remain on the drawing board, with Amazon and Meta investing in X-energy and TerraPower respectively. TGood has expanded overseas with computing power center projects in Thailand and Malaysia during the third quarter. The company's total winning bids for overseas business have exceeded 1.3 billion yuan. Financial statements have yet to reflect performance, as TGood recorded a net operating cash flow of negative 188 million yuan. The articles leave open how the real cost impact will unfold as the real bill is yet to come.

Articles.Title: TGood & LG Enter Market Amid AI-Driven Power Resources Scramble: Advanced Gas Power Holds 69% Market Share, Real Cost Impact Yet Unfolds - 36Kr

stories.headline_source: TGood & LG Enter Market Amid AI-Driven Power Resources Scramble: Advanced Gas Power Holds 69% Market Share, Real Cost Impact Yet Unfolds

stories.Headline: HCLTech and Cohere partner to deliver sovereign AI in Canada and Germany
stories.Summary:
HCLTech and Cohere announced on 17 November 2026, in a release dated from Noida, a partnership to design and deliver what they call sovereign AI solutions to enterprises and public administrations. Under the agreement, HCLTech becomes one of Cohere's preferred global systems integrators in two countries, Canada and Germany. The release presents Canada and Germany as priority markets for HCLTech and says sovereignty is shaping AI adoption by businesses and governments there. The agreement combines Cohere's platform and models, including North, its agent platform, with the integrator's professional services.

Initial developments will target insurance, financial services and industry, with the release citing claims processing that takes jurisdiction into account, secure analysis of sensitive financial data and faster access to technical documentation as examples. Solutions will be installed in the environment chosen by each client to meet data residency, security and regulatory requirements, and Cohere's presentation lists public or private clouds, on-premises installations and fully air-gapped environments as possibilities. Only one certification is cited, ISO 42001, the international standard for AI management systems, which both companies hold. Nothing in the release indicates exclusivity, and the release does not say which entity contracts or where the teams operating the systems are based. France remains outside the announced scope, and the two companies say only that they want to extend the partnership to the rest of the world, with no timeline.

Phil Blunsom, Cohere's chief technology officer, said organisations should not have to choose between the benefits of AI and control of their data, according to the release. Vijay Guntur, his counterpart at HCLTech, and Dave Chopra, who heads the Indian group's Canadian operations, are also quoted, and the only country manager to speak is Canada's. As of 19 November, Cohere's press room did not mention the agreement. HCLTech reports more than 230,000 employees in over 60 countries and USD 14.8 billion in revenue for the twelve months ended September 2026, and its German headquarters is in Frankfurt/Eschborn.

The release mentions none of Cohere's other German elements: its merger with Aleph Alpha, its latest funding round led by the Schwarz Group and its offering on the STACKIT cloud. The Aleph Alpha merger, announced in April, produced a definitive agreement on 16 September, and the combined entity will operate under the Cohere name with headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, keeping the Heidelberg office as a research centre and employing more than 1,000 people. The merger had not been declared closed as of 19 November, and Cohere and Aleph Alpha were expecting in September to close it before the end of 2026, within six weeks of that date. Each partner has other alliances: Cohere announced a global alliance with PwC on 5 October and a partnership with OpenText on 16 September, while HCLTech concluded a Global Premier partnership with Anthropic on 12 October.

Articles.Title: Cohere leans on HCLTech for sovereign AI in Germany - ActuIA

stories.headline_source: Cohere leans on HCLTech for sovereign AI in Germany

stories.Headline: Germany plans to coordinate EU AI Act market surveillance through its Federal Network Agency
stories.Summary:
The article says that in 2026 the EU AI Act in Germany is an operational matter, not a policy debate for later, and that Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is being phased in across the Union. It says duties for prohibited practices, high-risk systems and general-purpose AI models are arriving on staggered timelines. It says that in 2026 national enforcement structures, market surveillance and data protection scrutiny begin to take shape in Germany. It says the guide was written by Global Advisory Experts and published on November 25, 2026. It says the guide covers conformity assessment, technical documentation and an investigation playbook designed for German conditions.

The article says the Act is the first broad, cross-sector law on artificial intelligence anywhere in the world, a claim it attributes to no one else. It says the Act takes a risk-based approach, so the greater a system's potential to harm health, safety or fundamental rights, the heavier the duties. It says that because the Act is a regulation it applies directly in every Member State, so German businesses do not need to wait for a national transposition statute. It says the core obligations come straight from the EU text and are supplemented by national enforcement and designation measures. It says prohibited practices and AI literacy duties applied in the first phase, general-purpose AI transparency and documentation duties follow, and high-risk requirements apply later.

The article says each Member State must designate competent authorities for market surveillance and for notifying bodies. It says Germany's federal structure and its group of technically capable regulators suggest enforcement will involve several bodies working together rather than one super-regulator. It says national planning has identified the Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur) as the intended central coordination point for market surveillance, and that the final designation should be verified against official German government sources. It says the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy publishes German policy and implementation material and is a key reference for national strategy. It says the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) issues guidance on measures relevant to the security of AI systems, and its standards are likely to influence how conformity is assessed in practice.

The article says the Regulation creates EU-level governance, including the European Artificial Intelligence Office within the Commission and the European Artificial Intelligence Board, to promote consistent application, while day-to-day enforcement stays with national authorities. It says a compliance position accepted in one Member State is not automatically shielded from scrutiny elsewhere, and guidance or decisions from other national authorities can shape the German approach. It says industry observers expect German market surveillance bodies to draw on established product-safety enforcement techniques, since much of the high-risk regime rests on the EU's existing product legislation. It says the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI) and the state data protection authorities provide the enforcement strength on the data side. It says coordination between AI Act surveillance and GDPR enforcement is expected to define the German landscape, and a single system can face scrutiny under two regimes at once.

The article says likely triggers for regulatory action include market surveillance inspections started by the authority, whether routine or intelligence-led. It says complaints from users, competitors, consumer bodies or affected individuals are a trigger. It says data protection referrals, where an AI system's handling of personal data raises GDPR issues that overlap with AI Act duties, are a trigger. It says incident reports from post-market monitoring, including serious incidents that providers must report, are a trigger. It says the Act sorts systems into prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk and minimal-risk tiers, and that misclassification is itself an enforcement risk.

The article says high-risk systems include many used in critical infrastructure, employment, essential services and safety components of regulated products. It says technical documentation for high-risk systems must cover the system description and intended purpose, design and development choices, data governance and the datasets used for training, validation and testing. It says the documentation must cover risk management records, human oversight measures, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity metrics, and a post-market monitoring plan with records showing it operates. It says providers of high-risk systems must run a post-market monitoring system and report serious incidents to the relevant authority. It says many high-risk systems can rely on an internal conformity assessment by the provider, while others, particularly systems covered by existing product-safety legislation that involves notified bodies, need a third-party conformity assessment body.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Krishnamoorthi urges government observers inside AI companies and pre-release testing of advanced models
stories.Summary:
Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi called for government observers inside AI companies and independent tests of the most advanced models before release. He made the case in an October 26 roundtable published by Princeton Alumni Weekly on November 24. The roundtable took place over Zoom and was moderated by PAW senior writer Mark F. Bernstein. Alongside Krishnamoorthi were Princeton computer scientist Edward Felten, political scientist Julia Morse and author and columnist Virginia Postrel. PAW edited the conversation for concision and clarity.

Krishnamoorthi urged third-party inspection and validation of the most advanced AI models before they become publicly available. He also urged embedding government employees at AI companies to observe development, drawing on banks being required to stress-test internal controls. He distinguished updating existing rules, as for road safety and financial-market security, from writing an overarching AI law. He said the details of general AI regulation become very fuzzy and called for caution. He also called for treaties requiring human control of AI, arguing that autonomous weapons make those agreements urgent.

Morse, an associate professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, said mandatory evaluations may be necessary because they cost money and companies could put them off. She compared the idea to banks' required monitoring for money laundering, saying banks must monitor activity even when screening transactions is not in their commercial interest. She rejected treating AI as just another technology, pointing to its dual-use character, its spread across the economy and its rapid development. She argued that warnings from knowledgeable researchers warranted action, even though no policy could eliminate risk completely. Postrel pushed back on treating researchers' warnings as reliable forecasts, saying technical expertise does not necessarily make someone good at predicting what risks will materialize.

Postrel argued for identifying a specific concern before choosing a remedy, which might not involve regulation. In her view, lab researchers can inhabit a bubble that magnifies their sense of the technology's importance. She invoked early internet debates as a warning that today's feared problems may not be tomorrow's actual ones. Felten shifted the focus to human operators, saying AI could help attackers find security weaknesses but could also help defenders locate and fix them, with the outcome of that contest unclear. For international threats, he pointed to deterrence and military capabilities rather than regulation alone.

The discussion produced no shared prescription. The central constraint is still how to target oversight without treating every AI use, or every catastrophe warning, the same way. Their differences concerned both the nature of the danger and which institutions should respond. Krishnamoorthi drew a line between updating rules for specific areas and passing one broad AI law. Morse argued that AI's rapid development and potential for both helpful and harmful uses justify acting amid uncertainty.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: South Korea study group meets Wednesday to discuss revising AI Basic Act and extending enforcement pause
stories.Summary:
South Korea's AI Basic Act study group and the National AI Strategy Committee are scheduled to hold a joint on-site meeting on Wednesday, Nov. 25, at the Seoul office of GIST in Jung-gu, Digital Daily reported Tuesday. The session is meant to gather views on revising the law and on adding further grace periods before enforcement begins. No decision has been announced, and the report gives no start time. The Ministry of Science and ICT set a pause of at least one year when the Act took effect on Jan. 22, 2026. The pause cannot end before Jan. 22, 2027, about two months from now.

The Act's enforcement ladder runs from a fact-finding investigation to a corrective order and only then to a fine. MSIT has described the pause as covering fact-finding investigations, corrective orders and fines. The fine cap is 30 million won, about $22,500, a figure Cooley says applies to failing to notify users that AI is in use, failing to designate a local representative and ignoring a corrective order. Draft rules allow machine-readable watermarks users cannot see, paired with at least one visible or audible notice that content was AI-generated. Digital Daily counted 19 amendment bills filed within about six months of the Act taking effect.

Lee Sang-yong, a professor at Konkuk University Law School and chair of the study group, is scheduled to give a progress report, according to Digital Daily. Sangchul Park, a professor at Seoul National University Law School, is scheduled to present key discussion points. In July 2025, Digital Daily reported Park's view that subordinate rules alone would not be enough and that a Japan-style overhaul deserved study. Lee presented on revising the Act at the Kim & Chang AI Law and Policy Forum seminar on Sept. 4, 2026. Law Times' account of that seminar did not report a stated position on a grace period.

At the September 2025 MSIT briefing, industry was reported to be asking for three years at least. In April 2025, Democratic Party lawmaker Hwang Jung-ah introduced a bill to postpone enforcement of key provisions by three years. A Startup Alliance survey found that 98 percent of 101 startups did not feel ready for compliance, according to the Stimson Center. The National Human Rights Commission raised concerns about postponement in a September 2025 letter, and a joint civil-society comment followed days later. In an Oct. 1, 2025 submission, the Institute for Digital Rights and allied groups argued that a fine grace period would effectively suspend regulation of minimal duties such as prior notice and designating a domestic agent.

Korea's Act was modeled on the EU's AI Act, and the EU has already moved its calendar. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, was published in the Official Journal on July 24 and entered into force July 27. Stand-alone high-risk systems, such as those used in education and employment, now face obligations from Dec. 2, 2027, and high-risk AI embedded in regulated products moves to Aug. 2, 2028, a deferral of about 16 months for the first group. Brussels moved its deadlines by statute, while Korea's pause is an administrative policy. A compliance guide describes the pause as ministry policy rather than statute, a third-party reading rather than a statutory finding.

Neither MSIT nor the committee has announced an extension, and published policy trackers list no extension notice or fixed end date. Nothing public says whether an extension would cover all provisions, only some, or specific sectors, and Digital Daily reports the topic of amendments but no specific proposals. The meeting's outcome and any readout are unknown. For operators, the practical reading is that Jan. 22, 2027 is the earliest possible start of enforcement, not a fixed one. The labeling and notice duties apply now regardless of when investigators begin to use them.

stories.Headline: China names 34 flagship smart factories to expand AI use into consumer goods sectors
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology named 34 facilities as flagship smart factories on Thursday, November 23, 2026. This latest group of recognized sites includes manufacturers of electronics, alcohol, and clothing, showing a shift away from heavy industry. One of these highlighted facilities is operated by the Jiangsu-based HLA Group, where artificial intelligence helps coordinate production. These systems work alongside human operators to turn consumer preference insights into specific design ideas.

The program was launched in 2024 to upgrade supply chains through the use of artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies. It requires factories to integrate smart systems that can analyze market trends and streamline the manufacturing process. By recognizing these 34 facilities, the government aims to encourage the adoption of high-tech tools across various consumer goods sectors. This transition allows manufacturers to better understand what customers want before a product ever reaches a retail shop.

The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology is responsible for identifying these flagship factories and overseeing the broader technological upgrade. Officials stated that the goal of the initiative is to modernize the way goods are produced and distributed throughout the country. They believe that integrating AI into the manufacturing sector will create more efficient supply chains for a wide range of products. The government intends to continue promoting these advanced systems to ensure that Chinese industry remains competitive.

stories.Headline: New Zealand Commerce Commission issues AI guidance for businesses
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Commission of New Zealand released new guidance for businesses on November 18, 2026, regarding the use of artificial intelligence. This regulatory framework helps companies understand how existing consumer protection and competition laws apply to their modern technological tools. The commission issued these instructions because businesses are increasingly using AI to conduct transactions, engage with consumers, and support commercial decision-making. These guidelines aim to clarify the legal landscape as AI continues to change the way various businesses operate. The new guidance specifically explains how the Commerce Act 1986 and the Fair Trading Act 1986 apply to AI systems.

It highlights potential legal risks and provides practical steps that companies can take to manage those risks effectively. The framework requires that businesses remain fully accountable for all outcomes, regardless of whether decisions are made by people or algorithms. Companies must ensure that the information they provide is accurate and that all consumers are treated fairly. Deputy Chair Anne Callinan stated that using artificial intelligence does not shift the legal accountability or responsibility of a business.

She explained that the commission is not focusing on regulating the technology itself, but rather its impact on markets and competition. Callinan urged boards and senior leaders to treat AI as a governance issue that requires constant monitoring. She emphasized that leaders must ensure sufficient safeguards are in place to oversee how the technology influences corporate decisions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Automakers integrate agentic AI into production and development by 2026
stories.Summary:
Automotive manufacturers and suppliers integrated agentic artificial intelligence into their core production and development infrastructure by the year 2026. These companies moved from using bounded pilot projects to deploying autonomous systems that make decisions previously reserved for humans. AI now inspects welds, schedules production, monitors equipment for failure, and writes vehicle code. These systems also talk to drivers from the dashboard and assess every resistance spot weld in real time. AI agents now inspect finished vehicles and enhance both drivability and safety.

GM uses AI and simulation to shorten vehicle development to roughly two years and reduce physical testing. BMW integrates intelligent systems at nearly every production stage and plans to extend agentic AI into vehicle development. Horse Powertrain launched the kAIros initiative to pair an AI Factory with digital twins for autonomous decision-making. This kAIros initiative targets a 50 percent reduction in time-to-market for the company. The Commerce Department's Connected Vehicle Rule prohibits covered software linked to Russia or China starting with model year 2027.

Foley and Lardner stated that automotive companies must now navigate product liability, negligence, and warranty risks. They said that companies should establish clear accountability and maintain an inventory of every AI system in use. The firm recommended that manufacturers maintain human oversight and test systems in digital twin environments before production deployment. They suggested that companies strengthen vendor contractual protections and continuously monitor AI performance for drift. They also advised preserving records to allow AI-driven decisions to be reconstructed for legal reasons.

The EU AI Act and various US state laws affect companies by classifying AI systems by their risk level. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has proposed rules addressing design requirements for automated driving systems and certain ADAS-equipped vehicles. Tier 1 suppliers are affected because flawed signals from AI demand-forecasting agents can cause minimum-volume disputes and OEM penalties. Third-party AI vendors create risks because they often update models and change data sources without providing notice. These legal and operational exposures impact any manufacturer or supplier deploying autonomous AI agents.

The articles state that AI has matured from experimental tools into autonomous, production-scale systems across the automotive industry. This shift includes software-defined vehicles, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and warranty and quality analytics. Development pipelines for advanced driver-assistance systems and automated driving systems also utilize these matured AI capabilities. Earlier AI systems only made recommendations for humans, but the newest agentic systems act on their own. This transition from advisory tools to autonomous agents creates new legal and operational risks for the industry.

Companies must now build governance programs to adapt to a patchwork of overlapping and shifting global obligations. They need to define when human approval is required before an agent acts and maintain manual fallback plans. The Commerce Department's Connected Vehicle Rule also prohibits covered hardware linked to Russia or China starting with model year 2030. The articles leave open how specific liability will be allocated between vendors and deployers when autonomous agents fail. It remains unclear how companies will successfully reconstruct every AI-driven decision to demonstrate reasonable care in court.

stories.Headline: Senate passes bill limiting environmental reviews to speed energy projects
stories.Summary:
The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, S.5653, on Nov. 19, 2026, by a 62-33 vote, with 14 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent joining most Republicans. Thirty Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent voted against the bill. The bill's sponsors are Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Republican Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance vouched for the legislation in a Nov. 20 news conference. The bill must win approval in the House to advance, and the House could amend it, which would require the Senate to approve the new text. The bill would limit the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act. The Natural Resources Defense Council's analysis concluded that under the bill a court "can never invalidate a permit" based on a violation of the National Environmental Policy Act or the National Historic Preservation Act. The bill would cut the time to build a major new transmission line from 10-plus years to five or six.

About 2,000 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are waiting to connect to the grid, and 85 percent of that capacity is solar, wind, or storage. The bill requires data centers to pay for their impact on electricity supply rather than shifting those costs to ratepayers. Juniper Katz, a University of Massachusetts-Amherst assistant professor of public policy, said there are priorities both sides want and the bill "is not perfect." Geoffrey Henderson, a University of Michigan assistant professor of environmental policy and planning, said it is reasonable to be concerned that development of each kind of project Ruffalo mentioned could be facilitated by the bill. Henderson also said the bill's impacts are highly uncertain, depending on political, market, geopolitical and legal outcomes.

The NRDC analysis said that if the Trump administration issued a blanket grant of all permits for oil and gas infrastructure without any environmental review, the bill provides no clear mechanism for a future administration to revoke those permits. Ruffalo's representative did not respond to an inquiry for the article. Mark Ruffalo said in a Nov. 18 video viewed 22 million times that the bill would fast-track AI data centers, pipelines, mines, power plants and ICE camps while sacrificing clean water, tribal rights, public lands and endangered species. Groups supporting the bill include the Solar Energy Industries Association, the AFL-CIO, the American Petroleum Institute and the Edison Electric Institute.

Groups opposing it include the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Climate Justice Alliance, a range of tribal organizations, the NAACP and the American Civil Liberties Union. Opponents say their concerns about ICE facilities stem from the use of the National Environmental Policy Act to oppose ICE facilities in court in Maryland, Arizona and Florida. Ezra Klein, a New York Times columnist considered left of center, said he was "unnerved" by conflicting interpretations of certain provisions but still supported the bill. The bill grew out of concerns from both fossil fuel backers and renewable energy supporters that opponents could stymie projects for years in the courts.

Supporters said growing energy demand and rising electricity prices meant a failure to build new infrastructure would consign the United States to a spiral of insufficient energy supplies and higher costs. Critics say the bill effectively guts tools to prevent local governments, citizens, Native American tribes and other local interests from blocking harms caused by such projects. Critics also say the Trump administration, which refuses to acknowledge the possibility of emissions-driven climate change, could wield the law to advance fossil fuel projects over renewable energy infrastructure. The NRDC analysis devotes almost 1,000 words to describing what it considers the bill's positive features, including improving electric capacity by increasing how much power existing transmission lines can carry and enabling construction of new lines.

The bill's fate in the House is uncertain, and the potential for updated language and the difficulty of predicting how courts would interpret its provisions make it difficult to know whether Ruffalo's scenario will come to pass. The bill could also boost non-energy projects that have faced long-running challenges in the courts, including rail and transit, affordable housing and broadband access, Klein wrote. The bill does not directly address ICE detention facilities. The articles leave open whether the House will amend the bill and whether the Senate would then approve new text.

stories.Headline: A Munich court holds AI model creators directly liable for memorized copyrighted works
stories.Summary:
The rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence and large language models has created unprecedented structural challenges to the foundational doctrines of copyright law across the European Union, according to a legal analysis published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance. The analysis examines friction points between the European legal acquis, specifically Directive 2019/790 on copyright in the Digital Single Market and Regulation 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act. It traces the allocation of liability across an interdependent lifecycle and finds that a settled European legal framework governing infringement remains years away. That leaves a persistent deficit of legal certainty for actors in data gathering, model deployment and downstream application development. The analysis was reported by Bioengineer.org on 23 November 2026.

The analysis divides the generative artificial intelligence value chain into three sequential yet interdependent phases: data ingestion and training, model storage and dissemination, and downstream output. During training, developers harvest literary works, artistic images, music, films and press publications, and the central question is whether computing model weights is an actionable reproduction under Article 2 of the InfoSoc Directive 2001/29/EC or an extraction under the sui generis database right. Article 3 of the Digital Single Market Directive provides a mandatory, non-waivable text and data mining exception for scientific research by research organizations and cultural heritage institutions on lawfully accessible works. Article 4 permits commercial text and data mining by any entity but is conditional on rightsholders not having opted out through machine-readable reservations or other appropriate mechanisms. Article 53(1)(c) of the Artificial Intelligence Act mandates that general-purpose model providers implement internal copyright compliance policies to respect reservations.

The analysis holds that the prevailing view in European legal scholarship is that training inherently involves acts of reproduction, aligning with Court of Justice of the European Union jurisprudence recognizing broad protections for permanent and temporary reproductions incorporating an author's intellectual creation. It notes that advocates of the non-copying thesis maintain that training merely extracts non-copyrightable statistical regularities into mathematical matrices rather than storing expressive works. The analysis states that the operational feasibility of opt-out reservations remains highly controversial when scraping occurs at web scale. It observes that Recital 105 of the Artificial Intelligence Act and the 2025 Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI Models suggest training falls under the mining provisions. It adds that several scholars and recent judicial opinions argue text and data mining was intended solely for analytical extraction of semantic information rather than the assembly of generative engines competing directly with expressive originals.

The analysis cites the landmark November 2025 ruling by the Regional Court of Munich in GEMA v. OpenAI, which addressed allegations that language models infringed copyright in song lyrics. The court defined memorization as a condition where a model retains training materials so that identical reproductions can be generated in response to targeted user prompts. It ruled that memorization constitutes a complete implementation of the work within the model, taking reproduction beyond the legitimate analytical scope of the text and data mining exception, and placed direct liability on the model creator rather than the user.

The analysis states that European infringement analysis under the Court of Justice's Mio/Konektra ruling requires protected elements to remain recognizable as the author's own intellectual creation. It notes that primary liability at the output boundary will in many practical scenarios naturally attach to the end user who prompts the system and downloads, commercializes or publicly communicates the generated asset. The analysis states that the operational opacity of deep neural networks establishes a profound epistemic barrier for both rightsholders and developers. It says the internal parameters of complex language models are not directly interpretable in a manner disclosing whether, or to what extent, individual protected works have been copied, memorized or transformed within mathematical weight matrices.

It observes that rightsholders struggle to demonstrate actionable copying while developers face symmetrical difficulties proving the absence of reproduction or the applicability of legal defenses. It adds that evidentiary standards and the allocation of burdens of proof have become fiercely contested terrain where statutory transparency duties under the Artificial Intelligence Act may prove insufficient to detect infringement. It notes that European copyright infringement has historically operated primarily under standards of strict liability, while certain aspects of infringement assessments require findings of volition or direct control poorly suited to autonomous or semiautonomous probabilistic engines. The analysis states that disentangling independent user liability from primary or secondary developer liability demands significant recalibration of doctrines governing inducement, accessory participation and contributory infringement across multiple commercial layers.

It notes that courts scrutinize a provider's degree of architectural control, actual or constructive knowledge of recurring violations, and implementation of technical safeguards such as output filters, prompt moderation classifiers and forensic watermarking. It adds that the absence of effective filtering tools where infringing outputs recur predictably can expose providers to negligence findings. It observes that the applicability of pastiche to synthetic imitations of artistic style remains heavily contested, since copyright safeguards concrete original expressions rather than broad, abstract stylistic conventions. It notes that complex doctrinal questions arise when users generate similar works unintentionally without prior knowledge of the training data, challenging traditional concepts of independent creation.

stories.Headline: NTT uses AI to find software vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them
stories.Summary:
NTT Group detected and blocked seven times as many cyberattacks in October as in the same month a year earlier, according to President and CEO Akira Shimada, who spoke at the NTT R&D Forum 2026 in Tokyo. The Japanese telecommunications group is now using artificial intelligence to find vulnerabilities in software before attackers do. Shimada said there had been 20 confirmed or potential customer data leak incidents since September involving NTT Group and its vendors. He said attacks are increasingly targeting consumer websites, online stores and official apps on a large scale, and that leaks through vendors and supply chains are becoming more visible. The effort requires NTT to examine source code and internal design with multiple frontier AI models for white-box testing, and the group supports customer vulnerability assessments from identification to prioritisation and fixing.

To protect sensitive data such as source code, NTT is developing AI-based methods that run in on-premises IT environments, using open-weight models whose trained parameters are public so organisations can run them on their own systems. NTT says its current AI approach achieves 70 to 80 per cent of frontier AI performance in vulnerability discovery. For older systems, industrial equipment and internet of things devices that cannot run endpoint detection and response software, NTT uses the network as a sensor to identify and block threats from network traffic. Shimada said attacks are becoming faster, with exploitation attempts sometimes detected before a vulnerability is publicly disclosed, citing a PHP vulnerability where attempts were detected days before its October disclosure and spread globally within 24 hours. He said AI makes it easier to find and analyse vulnerabilities, potentially leading to more such attacks, and that attacks are also more complex, with multiple minor weaknesses combining to create system access.

He said targets are widening to include industrial equipment and operational technology, such as an October attack on supermarket refrigeration equipment in Europe. NTT has shifted its defence from perimeter security to zero trust and now incorporates AI-powered defence for proactive vulnerability discovery. The articles say reported data exposure at Japanese companies reached 376.21 million records by October 2026, compared with 49.53 million for all of 2025, citing MM Research Institute. NTT says basic security practices such as applying updates and removing unused accounts remain essential.

stories.Summary:
Microsoft Copilot AI predicted a historic Hyperliquid rally in an article by Ahmed Barakat published on cryptonews.com on November 24, 2026. The article said the Copilot outlook points to a potential move by early 2027 that could significantly outperform other digital assets. It said the thesis hinges on traditional finance institutions and regulated derivatives exchanges adopting Hyperliquid's technology and liquidity as an on-chain venue. It said that venue would serve high-performance perpetual futures and institutional-grade derivatives trading. The article said HYPE's daily drop of -1.5% made the bullish prediction seem more hopeful than realistic.

It said price continues to hold above key intermediate support while facing resistance around $75 to $80. It said a sustained breakout above $100 to $120 would confirm intermediate strength and open the path toward significant new price discovery. It said Copilot's scenario put HYPE at $450 to $800, with a stretch target of $1,200 or more, by January 1, 2027.

The article attributed the prediction to Microsoft Copilot AI and to Bill Gates in its headline. It said the catalyst would require extraordinary coordination between traditional finance institutions and the Hyperliquid ecosystem that is currently highly unlikely. It said this remains pure speculation and entertainment, not a realistic base-case outlook. It said momentum indicators currently sit in neutral territory with substantial room to run into the extreme overbought levels typical of parabolic advances. It said clearing prior highs would likely trigger powerful measured-move extensions and multi-cycle Fibonacci projections from the longer-term base.

The article said the outlook points to a potential move that could significantly outperform other digital assets. It said increased professional and institutional activity could make HYPE a key part of the infrastructure powering the next generation of decentralized and hybrid derivatives markets. It said the article was fact checked by the CryptoNews Editorial Team. It said crypto is a high-risk asset class and the article does not constitute investment advice. It said readers could lose all of their capital.

stories.Headline: Brazil's Congress advances a dedicated AI bill as ANPD enforces LGPD duties on automated decisions
stories.Summary:
Brazil's Congress has advanced a dedicated artificial intelligence bill, Projeto de Lei nº 2.338/2023, and the Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados keeps refining its expectations for automated decision-making under the Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados. The ANPD interprets and enforces the LGPD through guidance, normative acts and public consultations, and supervises automated decision-making and large-scale processing. The ANPD has published analyses on AI and data protection and is widely expected to hold a central supervisory role under any future AI framework. ANEEL regulates electricity and sets expectations on operational safety, service continuity, technical standards and incident reporting. ANATEL covers telecommunications and network infrastructure, including connectivity, certification and communications for connected charging networks.

As of early 2026, no single comprehensive AI statute is in force in Brazil, although the dedicated bill is moving through the legislature. The LGPD, Law No. 13.709/2018, applies whenever an AI system processes personal data, and it gives individuals the right to ask for a review of decisions taken solely through automated processing that affect their interests. The LGPD limits processing to what is necessary for a specified, legitimate purpose, and it requires a data protection impact assessment, a relatório de impacto à proteção de dados pessoais, where processing is large-scale, involves sensitive data or creates material risk. The LGPD's rules on international transfers apply where AI vendors host infrastructure or training environments outside Brazil. The Ministério da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação leads the Brazilian AI strategy, which is not binding in itself.

André Fortes Carvalho & Furtado Advogados, listed as a Gold featured expert on the matter, is the guide's named adviser for Brazil. The guide says AI used for grid optimisation, load forecasting, EV charging routing and predictive maintenance is exactly the kind of system regulators are most likely to treat as high-risk. It says such systems affect safety and continuity of supply and rely on large volumes of personal and operational data. It says a compliant AI deployment has to satisfy LGPD and ANPD duties and ANEEL and ANATEL duties together. It says AI does not create a separate data-protection regime but makes existing duties heavier.

The guide says operators using AI today include grid optimisation and load forecasting, charging optimisation and routing, predictive maintenance, and dynamic pricing and demand response. It says smart-meter readings, EV user accounts, charging session records, roaming identifiers and predictive-maintenance logs frequently contain personal data. It says a charging operator sits under two sector regimes plus the LGPD, and the three should be run as one coordinated programme. It says regulators dealing with critical infrastructure expect operators to show that systems fail safely, that humans oversee consequential decisions, and that fallback arrangements keep service running. It says a model failure in grid balancing or charging allocation can threaten supply continuity and public safety.

The guide says the LGPD sets out lawful bases for processing, the rights of data subjects and an accountability principle that obliges operators to prove compliance. It says properly anonymised data sits outside the statute, but anonymisation must be robust and not reasonably reversible, and pseudonymised or re-identifiable data is still personal data. It says an operator that decides the purposes of processing is the controller and carries primary accountability, while a vendor that only processes data on the operator's instructions is a processor, an operador. It says ANEEL's existing obligations should be assumed to extend to AI-driven decisions. It says ANATEL's remit covers network aspects, equipment certification (homologation) and communications requirements.

The guide sets out a 90/180/360 day action plan and a twelve-point checklist. It says operators should appoint a data protection officer (encarregado) or equivalent and name an accountable executive for each high-risk AI system. It says a cross-functional AI governance committee should keep an inventory of AI systems, classify them by risk and approve deployments before go-live. It says governance should state explicitly who can override or suspend an AI system in an emergency. It says operators should test for accuracy and bias before deployment and set automated alerts for when a model drifts outside acceptable limits.

stories.Headline: Fujitsu launches a vulnerability assessment service with OpenAI to verify exploitable flaws
stories.Summary:
Fujitsu Limited announced on November 25, 2026 that it has expanded its collaboration with OpenAI and joined the Daybreak Defense Network, OpenAI's cyber defense partner program. The announcement came from Kawasaki, Japan, according to JCN Newswire. As its first offering through the program, Fujitsu launched a vulnerability assessment service on November 25, 2026. The service combines OpenAI Daybreak's cyber defense capabilities with Fujitsu's proprietary vulnerability assessment system. It provides end-to-end support, from vulnerability discovery and exploitability verification to remediation guidance and post-remediation retesting.

The service combines dynamic testing of running systems with static source code analysis within the scope authorized by the customer. Reports include the summary and cause of discovered vulnerabilities, the specific location in the source code, Proof of Concept Code to reproduce the vulnerability, and proposed remediation methods. After customers implement fixes, Fujitsu retests to check whether those fixes are effective under the conditions of the assessment. If remediation is found to be insufficient, Fujitsu reports the findings and supports the review of additional countermeasures. Fujitsu will offer the service to customers in Japan and overseas.

Shuda Shinichiro, Global CEO and Senior Managing Partner of Uvance Wayfinders at Fujitsu, said AI continues to advance and cyberattacks are becoming increasingly sophisticated, with attackers analyzing systems at the code level. He said simply using AI to detect large numbers of potential vulnerabilities is not enough, and what matters is verifying whether vulnerabilities can actually be exploited. He said Fujitsu is pleased to expand its collaboration with OpenAI into cybersecurity and introduce the new service. He said bringing together advanced AI technologies and the expertise of Fujitsu's cybersecurity specialists will help customers strengthen their cyber defenses. He said Fujitsu will contribute to a safer and more secure digital society.

Dino Mizushima, Head of GTM Partnerships at OpenAI Japan, said the Daybreak Defense Network aims to bring frontier AI into companies' day-to-day cyber defense work. He said Fujitsu's experience building and operating enterprise systems is an important part of this effort. He said Fujitsu's security specialists play a key role by reviewing the results of AI-assisted assessments. He said validating vulnerabilities from an attacker's perspective helps customers determine which risks to address first based on exploitability and potential impact. He said that together with Fujitsu, OpenAI will help more companies in Japan turn those findings into concrete steps.

In May 2026, Fujitsu began collaboration with OpenAI, combining OpenAI's advanced AI technology with Fujitsu's knowledge of system construction and operation. Fujitsu said the cybersecurity landscape is undergoing significant change amid advancing generative AI and AI agent technologies and their expanding corporate use. Fujitsu said companies face challenges in securing highly skilled human resources to quickly discover and address vulnerabilities and in managing growing volumes of diagnosis and response operations. In 2026, Uvance Wayfinders' Security Consulting, led by Takeshi Sato, conducted red team tests for approximately 30 organizations and successfully penetrated all of them. In internal verification before the launch, Fujitsu discovered new vulnerabilities that were difficult to detect with conventional methods, even for expert teams, and confirmed they could be practically exploited in a real environment.

Going forward, Fujitsu will utilize OpenAI Daybreak's cyber defense capabilities across various areas of cybersecurity beyond vulnerability assessment to further expand its cybersecurity services. Fujitsu will leverage its own AI technologies, including the enterprise-grade generative AI "Takane" and the AI platform "Fujitsu Kozuchi," alongside its system construction and operation expertise. Fujitsu said it will support customers in a wide range of challenges, including advancement of the Software Development Life Cycle and system renewals such as modernization and migration. The articles do not say how many customers have adopted the service or what it costs. The articles do not give a date for further service expansions.

stories.Headline: Hassan plans hearings and legislation to require AI safeguards against terrorist planning
stories.Summary:
U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan is set to become New Hampshire's senior senator in January and to chair the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, which oversees the Department of Homeland Security and guides policy on cybersecurity and artificial intelligence regulation. She recently directed the Government Accountability Office, the congressional watchdog, to study whether common artificial intelligence models such as ChatGPT can be used to plan terrorist attacks on the United States. The report found that the tools can easily plan out violent attacks, which prompted Hassan to call for more investigation and regulation. Hassan discussed artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and her plans for the next legislative session with Morning Edition host Rick Ganley.

Hassan said she wants to hold hearings with experts to learn about the vulnerabilities of artificial intelligence systems and to investigate the cause of major technology outages around the country. She wants to implement legislation that regulates artificial intelligence, including prohibiting tech companies from releasing new models without proving they have safeguards to stop them from being used to plan violence or terrorist attacks on the United States. The GAO study found that users can easily bypass safeguards on artificial intelligence models within about 12 hours and come out with detailed instructions to conduct a terrorist attack. Hassan said the results were not surprising but were deeply concerning, and the models provide instructions on how to build a weapon and offer advice on what events to target, when to attack and how to avoid law enforcement.

Hassan said she wants to ensure that artificial intelligence companies report attempts to dangerously manipulate the technology to law enforcement and to explore defenses against potential attacks, such as a defensive model or other tools. She said she wants to work with other committees in Congress that oversee artificial intelligence safety and to introduce a comprehensive package of legislation quickly, and to work with private companies to balance regulation and market competition. She said the Senate should thoroughly investigate the cause of outages at major technology companies and government systems in recent weeks. She said the administration should take artificial intelligence more seriously as a threat to national security.

stories.Headline: China-nexus actor uses AI agents to breach East Asian universities via zero-day flaw
stories.Summary:
A China-nexus actor used AI agents to breach universities across East Asia outside mainland China. The attacks began on September 8 and lasted for approximately 48 hours. The actor used the Cairn penetration testing tool to conduct these operations. These agents exploited a zero-day flaw in an open source medical imaging application. The goal given to the agents was to obtain shell access.

The agents mapped API endpoints and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They used path traversal to write files and execute a Python reverse shell payload. This process took about 11 minutes from mapping the API to gaining root access. One failed operation lasted 16 hours and involved 148 actions against a Redis instance. Another six hour operation tested 30,000 credential combinations against a university GPU server.

CJ Moses is the chief information security officer of Amazon Web Services. He wrote a report published on Friday by Amazon Threat Intelligence. Moses stated that agentic offensive operations are already happening. He noted that the agents adapted for nearly a full day without human direction. He advised that defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable.

Cris Thomas is a security advocate at Semgrep and a former hacker. He said AI agents change the economics of vulnerability discovery without skilled humans. Ross Filipek is the chief information security officer at Corsica Technologies. He recommended that organizations maintain an inventory of exposed assets and restrict application access. These attacks affected universities in East Asia that ran exposed open source software.

Cairn is an open source, AI-based penetration testing tool used by threat actors. Other China-linked actors used Cairn to breach 10 organizations to steal secrets. These actors also used Cairn to automate an attack spree against high-profile websites. A similar tool called Artex is also used to facilitate and automate cyberattacks. The agents in this case researched public university presences to assemble usernames.

Defenders should monitor for suspicious uploads, unexpected file writes, and unusual process execution. Thomas suggests that security fundamentals must now work at machine speed with automated detection. Filipek advises that teams should analyze server logs to spot unusual patterns of activity. Organizations should decide in advance who has authority to isolate a server after hours. The articles do not state if the zero-day flaw was patched.

stories.Headline: Dutch hospitals must inventory and classify AI systems in 2026 to meet EU AI Act duties
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Global Advisory Experts on November 24, 2026, is a guide for Dutch hospitals and clinics on the EU AI Act, and it states that the Regulation attaches binding duties to Dutch care providers as its requirements phase in. The guide says 2026 is the year for hospitals to get organised, and it addresses hospital boards, compliance officers, chief information officers, chief medical information officers and quality and safety managers. It states that the AI Act, the Medical Device Regulation, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation, the General Data Protection Regulation and Dutch healthcare law each place their own demands on the same tool. The article says the guide explains what applies, when it applies, and how it sits alongside existing medical device and data protection rules. It states that generic policies will not cover that, and it presents itself as a jurisdiction-specific roadmap.

The article states that the AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and applies directly in every EU Member State, including the Netherlands, without national transposition. It says Dutch hospitals are caught as deployers of AI systems and, in some cases, as providers where they build or substantially modify tools in-house. It states that AI that is, or is a safety component of, a medical device under the MDR or IVDR is generally classed as high-risk, which brings the strictest obligations. It says the Regulation entered into force on 1 August 2024, that prohibitions on unacceptable-risk practices and the general provisions applied from early 2025, and that obligations for general-purpose AI models followed later in 2025. The article states that high-risk systems that are, or are safety components of, products covered by EU harmonisation legislation such as the MDR and IVDR have the longest transitional period, running to around mid-2027.

The article states that the AI Act forms part of the European Commission's wider European approach to artificial intelligence, and that Member States must still designate national competent authorities to supervise and enforce it. It says a hospital is usually a deployer of systems bought from vendors, and that if it develops a tool internally, puts a system on the market under its own name, or substantially modifies a third-party system, it may become a provider. It states that providers of high-risk AI carry the full weight of conformity assessment, technical documentation and post-market monitoring, while deployers have a narrower but still significant set of duties covering human oversight, monitoring of operation and use in line with the instructions. It says the five priority actions for 2026 are to inventory every AI system in use, classify each against the high-risk criteria, assign governance responsibilities, align supplier contracts with AI Act duties, and put human oversight and post-market monitoring procedures in place. The article states that transitional arrangements are detailed and system-specific, so the dates for each tool should be checked against the current text of the Regulation.

The article states that the MDR is Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and the IVDR is Regulation (EU) 2017/746, and that the AI Act adds AI-specific obligations on top, including data governance, transparency, human oversight and post-market monitoring of AI performance. It says the Regulation tries to avoid duplicated burdens by allowing AI Act requirements to be built into the existing medical device conformity assessment where possible, so one process can address both. It states that almost all clinical AI processes health data, which the GDPR treats as a special category of personal data with enhanced protection, and that hospitals need a valid legal basis for processing, data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing, and a clear approach to the rules on automated decision-making where AI outputs materially affect patients. It says the Dutch Data Protection Authority enforces the GDPR and issues guidance on AI and health data, and that the AI Act's data governance rules and the GDPR are distinct but reinforce each other. The article states that Dutch sector law sits over the EU regimes and names the Wet kwal, Wkkgz and WGBO.

The article states that the difficulty is that several regimes apply at once, and that the AI Act does not replace the MDR, IVDR or GDPR but sits on top of them. It says governance is not optional, and that human oversight, risk management, technical documentation and post-market monitoring all need named owners, standard operating procedures and board-level reporting. It states that the first route to high-risk status captures most clinical AI, and that if a tool is software qualifying as a medical device under the MDR or a diagnostic device under the IVDR, and that device needs notified-body involvement, the associated AI is treated as high-risk. It says the European Commission's medical devices portal and Medical Device Coordination Group guidance help establish when software is a medical device at all, and that the European Data Protection Board gives guidance on how the GDPR intersects with AI. The article states that Dutch government guidance on AI policy gives national context for how the EU obligations fit the domestic landscape.

The article states that for planning purposes 2026 should be treated as the year to complete internal readiness, so that systems, documentation and oversight processes already work when the high-risk obligations apply in full. It says procurement and IT roadmaps will need AI Act milestones next to existing MDR compliance schedules, and that classifying systems, rewriting contracts and building governance takes real time. It states that each system must be assessed on its own intended purpose and device class, and that borderline cases should go to qualified regulatory advisors. It says the determination should be recorded for every system and that it must be able to be defended. The article states that the window during 2026 is finite, and it leaves open the detailed transitional dates for each tool, which it says must be checked against the current text of the Regulation.

stories.Headline: Van Epps introduces bill to set safeguards for agentic AI in federal civilian networks

Representative Matt Van Epps said he has introduced the AI INSIGHT Act, a bill aimed at creating safeguards for the use of agentic AI systems in federal civilian networks, according to a press release posted on November 24, 2026. The stated goals of the measure are to help agencies identify AI agents on their networks, limit access to what tasks require, monitor activity, and suspend or revoke access when needed. Under the proposal, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency would offer guidance and technical assistance as part of the framework for securing AI agents. Van Epps said the bill is meant to let agencies use AI while reducing security risks, according to the release. Van Epps is the representative who introduced the bill, and the release presents the stated goals and the role for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency as his proposal.

He said the measure would help agencies identify AI agents on their networks, limit access to what tasks require, monitor activity, and suspend or revoke access when needed. stories.Headline: OpenAI publishes a preprint claiming to prove the matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 9/4
stories.Summary:
OpenAI published a preprint on November 25, 2026, that it says proves the matrix multiplication exponent, written ω, is exactly 9/4, according to a post by Deedy on X. The post says the preprint runs 111 pages and addresses a problem that is 57 years old. Deedy writes that the problem ranks 31st on ProofAtlas’s list of the top 500 open problems in mathematics and is arguably second only to P versus NP in algorithms. The question at issue is how many steps it takes to multiply two n by n matrices, where the schoolbook method takes n cubed and the true cost is n to the power ω.

The post traces the history of bounds on ω, starting with Strassen in 1969, who beat 3 for the first time with 2.807. Schönhage reached 2.522 in 1981, and Coppersmith and Winograd reached 2.376 in 1990, according to the post. It says 36 years passed from 1990 to August 2026 to shave off 0.005, bringing the figure to 2.3712. The post states that in November 2026 OpenAI proved the upper and lower bound is 2.25, and it links to a GitHub page and to ProofAtlas rankings.

The post presents the result as OpenAI’s claim, and it does not name the authors of the preprint or describe the proof itself. Deedy, the account that posted the summary, says it is wild to see things taught in university change before our eyes. A reply from the account Somi says exactly 9/4 is a clean answer after decades of shaving off decimals. The articles give no statement from OpenAI beyond the linked preprint and no independent verification of the claimed proof.

The articles do not say how the result would be checked, who would review the 111-page preprint, or when any verification might come. They give no reaction from mathematicians or from anyone outside the accounts quoted above. They also do not say what the claimed exact value of 9/4 would change in practice beyond the stated cost of matrix multiplication. More to follow.

stories.Headline: UK regulators examine how AI tools affect real money and customers, putting BILL Holdings in focus
stories.Summary:
UK regulators turned a spotlight on AI agents and old rulebooks on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. This regulatory focus examines how tools like Meta's Muse might touch real money and real customers. Bailey Pemberton reported that this tension between automation and accountability creates friction for regulated financial services. These shifting guardrails could put the stock of BILL Holdings in focus for investors. The situation creates potential openings for those watching companies that operate within these regulated environments.

BILL Holdings runs a regulated financial operations platform for small and midsize businesses in a compliance heavy setting. The company handles accounts payable, receivable, payments, and spend management for its clients. It generates about US$1.7b from software and programming and has a market value near US$5.3b. The company uses AI driven underwriting for invoice financing to move money and prove controls. This specific AI process grew volume and revenue about 30% year over year in FY26.

A bullish analyst narrative on Simply Wall St claims this position could do more than cut admin. The analyst argues that network level data helped more than halve expected loss rates for invoice financing. This performance could support a future step up in financing revenue for the company. Such growth might lead to a materially higher contribution to net margins and earnings. The analyst believes AI driven financing could accelerate earnings for the business.

The report asks what happens if a single assumption about disciplined customers under tighter AI risk controls shifts. Such a shift in assumptions could change the margin expectations for the company. The articles suggest that these shifting guardrails could expose hidden fragilities within the business. Investors are watching how the tension between automation and accountability affects regulated financial services. The focus remains on whether the company can keep auditors comfortable while using AI.

The background provided shows that BILL Holdings sits on the fault line between payments plumbing and compliance. The company provides a way for midsize firms to move money while maintaining necessary controls. This operational role is critical because the financial services sector is heavily regulated by government authorities. The current market value of the company reflects its position in the compliance technology sector. AI is being integrated into these existing financial workflows to improve efficiency.

The articles leave open whether tighter AI risk controls will shift the current margin expectations. It remains unclear if AI driven financing will accelerate earnings or expose hidden fragilities. The future impact of UK regulators on tools like Meta's Muse is not yet determined. Investors must consider if the current bullish narrative on Simply Wall St will hold true. The long term effect of these shifting guardrails on the stock is not specified.
