stories.Headline: Taiwan passes bill to give every citizen a cash AI bonus
stories.Summary:
The Legislative Yuan of Taiwan passed a bill on November 20 to provide an artificial intelligence bonus to the public. This legislation was pushed through by opposition parties shortly before local elections scheduled for November 28. The measure aims to return tax revenue that has increased because of the boom in artificial intelligence. It was passed with a vote of 50 to 46 in the chamber.

Thirteen lawmakers from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party abstained from the final vote. The special act on sharing economic gains with all citizens and stabilizing livelihoods requires a cash payment of 20,000 Taiwan dollars to every citizen. This payout is intended for all residents regardless of their income levels. However, the articles note that further procedures must be completed before the money is actually disbursed to the people.

Chuang Rui-hsiung of the Democratic Progressive Party mentioned that the government already budgeted 10,000 Taiwan dollars for each citizen. He stated this lower amount was chosen to keep spending and revenue balanced without additional borrowing. The main opposition Kuomintang led the effort to pass the bill and increase the payout amount. Hsu Yu-chen, the secretary-general of the Kuomintang caucus, demanded that Premier Cho Jung-tai explain if he intends to countersign the legislation.

Lawmaker Lo Chih-chiang stated that the actual payment of the bonus will depend on the outcome of the local elections. He argued that the ruling party fears the will of the voters during this period. Chuang Rui-hsiung criticized the opposition for seeking to double the payout without considering the fiscal conditions of the state. More to follow.

stories.Headline: MBZUAI launches a $250,000 art commission for its Abu Dhabi campus
stories.Summary:
During Frieze Abu Dhabi week, the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence announced that it will launch an art commission with a budget of up to $250,000, according to ARTnews. The task is to create a major sculpture or installation for the university’s Abu Dhabi campus, and the winning commission will be displayed in the university’s new cultural center that is slated to open in 2027. The artwork will be acquired for MBZUAI’s permanent collection, the report said. Artists applying for the commission can choose from one of three themes, which are the landscape, heritage and communities of the United Arab Emirates, artificial intelligence and scientific inquiry, or the history between science and computation in dialogue with art, mathematics and machines. The deadline for the commission is December 18, and the university will choose a shortlist of finalists who will be invited to create detailed proposals.

Each applicant will receive a $5,000 honorarium, according to the article. The university said it is building its art and special collections, and the works in its inventory span from the 13th century for special collections and art collections dating to 1925. The university collects works based on the arts and sciences, as well as materials that document what the article describes as the human pursuit of knowledge, creativity and research. Jasmine Soliman, head of art, archives and special collections at MBZUAI, said in a statement that the open call was shaped as an extension of the collection the university has built. She said that collection holds works spanning a century by artists who engage science through research, method and technique, treating knowledge as both an intellectual tradition and a material practice.

Dekyi (Hong) Liang, vice president and chief of staff at MBZUAI, said in a statement that it is the university’s responsibility to invest in cultivating a culture that embraces creativity and innovation. Liang said art has always been part of that story of human endeavor, adding that the new commission for the campus reflects a space where science and culture converge. The announcement came during Frieze Abu Dhabi week, and the article gives no further details on the selection process beyond the shortlist and the honorarium. The winning work is to be shown in the cultural center scheduled to open in 2027 and then acquired for the permanent collection. The article does not say when the finalists will be named or when the winner will be announced.

stories.Headline: Charles Payne compares Nvidia chief Jensen Huang to Steve Jobs and Bill Gates
stories.Summary:
On November 24, 2026, Fox Business host Charles Payne discussed Jensen Huang's impact on the artificial intelligence revolution during an appearance on America's Newsroom with Bill Hemmer. In the segment, Hemmer and Payne analyzed what the article describes as the monumental impact of Huang on the global artificial intelligence boom. Payne compared the reinstated Nvidia chief to legendary technology leaders Steve Jobs and Bill Gates. The two men emphasized how Huang's unique vision for GPUs has transformed the semiconductor industry and secured his critical importance to the American economy.

The article gives no further numbers, dates or names about the comparison beyond the November 24, 2026 broadcast date and the figures of Huang, Payne, Hemmer, Jobs and Gates. It does not say what the comparison requires of Huang or Nvidia, nor does it describe any change that follows from it. The segment is presented as analysis of Huang's role rather than as a report of a new action by him or by Nvidia. No details are given about when Huang was reinstated as Nvidia chief or what that reinstatement involved.

Responsibility for the comparison rests with Payne, who made it on air, and with Hemmer, who hosted and took part in the discussion. The article does not quote either man at length, and it attributes to them only the view that Huang's vision for GPUs transformed the semiconductor industry and made him critically important to the American economy. It presents the comparison to Jobs and Gates as Payne's own framing rather than as an established fact. Neither Huang nor Nvidia is quoted in the article.

The context the article supplies is limited to the program, America's Newsroom, and the date of the segment, November 24, 2026. It does not say what happens next, whether Huang or Nvidia responded, or how the comparison was received. The article carries no information about Nvidia's business, its products or its finances beyond the reference to GPUs and Huang's role. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Bavarian teachers' AI competence and classroom use hinge on pedagogical skill and habit, study finds
stories.Summary:
A cross-sectional survey study by researchers Shuyan Feng, Martin J. Koch and Astrid Carolus examined how teachers across Bavaria, Germany, engage with artificial intelligence. The study was published in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans and evaluated the theoretical AI Mindset framework. Data were gathered between July 23 and November 24, 2025, through an online questionnaire distributed via SoSci-Survey. The survey went to Bavarian primary and secondary institutions with official ministry approval. The final surveyed sample comprised 224 teachers with a mean age of 45 years and an age range spanning 25 to 65 years.

Female educators accounted for 60.83 percent of participants, while 37.33 percent identified as male, one participant identified as diverse and three identified as other. Secondary school educators represented the majority, including 28.57 percent from intermediate secondary schools and 26.34 percent from academic-track secondary schools, while 24.55 percent left school type unspecified. Most participants taught core secondary disciplines such as mathematics, German or English. Furthermore, 71.43 percent of the respondents belonged to the KI@School initiative. Comparative group tests revealed no statistically significant differences in target variables across project affiliations, with the sole exception of the need for autonomy.

The authors argued that foundational psychological prerequisites remain understudied while existing research has focused on skill-based deficits, curriculum roadmaps and technical barriers. They organized the AI Mindset framework into a triadic structure of dispositional factors, contextual and social facilitations, and technology-related appraisals. The authors noted that an inverse relationship for relatedness, mirrored by a negative zero-order correlation of minus 0.14, suggests educators with strong reliance on traditional interpersonal support systems may experience fewer structural incentives or reduced perceived necessity to independently master automated pedagogical instruments. The study emerged against a documented widening disparity in which student uptake of generative tools following the launch of ChatGPT has vastly outpaced staff training and instructional readiness. The framework brings together established psychological mechanisms into an integrated model accounting for personal agency, external social environments and direct cognitive evaluations of software characteristics.

The central structural equation model was estimated using robust maximum likelihood estimation within the lavaan package in R, utilizing a final complete analytical sample of 205 participants. The model converged successfully after 167 iterations and yielded a chi-square value of 41.40 with 43 degrees of freedom, a p value of .541, a comparative fit index of 1.00, a Tucker-Lewis index of 1.01, a root mean square error of approximation of 0.00 and a standardized root mean square residual of 0.02. The model accounted for 62 percent of the variance in teachers' classroom artificial intelligence use and 46 percent of the variance in their pedagogical artificial intelligence competence. Latent pedagogical competence exhibited the strongest positive association with actual usage, registering a standardized path coefficient of 0.45 with a significance level below .001.

Habitual engagement emerged as a robust direct predictor of use with a standardized coefficient of 0.28, followed by hedonic motivation at 0.19 and self-reported fear at 0.15. Demographic variables including educator age and gender demonstrated negligible and statistically non-significant relationships with classroom usage patterns. Habitual engagement exerted the strongest positive relationship with competence, exhibiting a standardized path coefficient of 0.31, closely followed by effort expectancy at 0.28 and personality openness at 0.15. Self-reported artificial intelligence fear was negatively associated with competence, registering a standardized path coefficient of minus 0.15, while the basic psychological need for relatedness displayed a significant negative association with pedagogical competence at minus 0.16.

Significant positive indirect paths to classroom usage were identified for personality openness at 0.07, habitual facilitation at 0.14 and effort expectancy at 0.12. Significant negative indirect effects on usage were documented for need for relatedness at minus 0.07 and artificial intelligence fear. Personality traits were gauged through the 15-item short version of the Big Five Inventory, which demonstrated good internal consistency for extraversion, conscientiousness and neuroticism, though lower consistency for openness and agreeableness. Self-determination components were quantified using validated three-item indices, general self-efficacy was assessed through a three-item instrument and goal-regulation styles were measured using selected FlexTen items.

Evaluative technology appraisals and social norms were captured using items adapted from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology-2 alongside specialized scales measuring general artificial intelligence fear and acceptance. Technological pedagogical competence was operationalized via the Intelligent-TPACK instrument, combining technological pedagogical content knowledge with pedagogical ethics subscales. AI usage was measured through self-reported frequency and purpose-based engagement scales ranging from non-use to multiple daily sessions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: RoboStrategy courts Korean pension funds and insurers for physical AI robotics investments
stories.Summary:
RoboStrategy, a fund from the United States, held its first institutional investor relations event in Korea. The fund targets professional investors, insurers, and pension funds to raise new capital. This event took place on the 22nd of November in the Cheongdam-dong area of Seoul. The fund focuses on investing in physical AI companies and unlisted robotics firms. It seeks to attract institutional investors from the Korean market to grow its assets.

The fund listed on the Nasdaq in May of this year with a market capitalization of 810 billion won. It has invested in Figure AI, a humanoid manufacturer valued at about 50 trillion won. The fund is currently in early talks with insurers, pension funds, and professional investors. These discussions aim to secure capital for further investments in the robotics sector. The event in Cheongdam-dong served as the primary venue for these institutional briefings.

Co-Chief Executive Andrew Kang outlined the fund's plans during the event on the 22nd. He stated that the fund is in early talks with various institutional investors in Korea. Kang forecast that the robotics industry will see a major leap within three to six months. He presented these views to the gathered professional investors and pension fund representatives. The fund's leadership believes the timing is right for significant growth in physical AI.

The fund is courting pension funds, insurers, and professional investors who manage large capital pools. These institutional investors are the primary parties affected by the fund's capital raising efforts. The fund targets those interested in unlisted robotics companies and advanced humanoid technology. Professional investors in Seoul are the specific group being courted for this venture. The fund aims to integrate Korean institutional capital into its global investment strategy.

RoboStrategy invests specifically in unlisted robotics companies and firms specializing in physical AI. The fund has already backed Figure AI, which produces humanoid robots for various uses. It entered the public market via the Nasdaq exchange in May of this year. The fund operates with a market capitalization of approximately 810 billion won. It focuses on the intersection of artificial intelligence and physical robotic hardware.

The fund will continue its early talks with Korean insurers and pension funds to raise capital. It expects a major leap in the robotics sector within the next three to six months. The articles do not state the specific amount of capital the fund wants to raise. They do not mention if any Korean institutions have already committed funds to the venture. It remains open whether these early talks will lead to formal investment agreements.

stories.Headline: Researchers find limited evidence for the strongest claims about AI harming cognition, information and relationships
stories.Summary:
A group of researchers published a review in Nature Human Behaviour on November 25, 2026. They examined empirical evidence regarding eight ways that artificial intelligence impacts people. The authors include Rebecca Anselmetti, Shahar Avin, Vanessa Cheung, and Madga Dubois. Other contributors are Tom Eccles, Anna Gausen, Kobi Hackenburg, and Keno Juechems. The team also includes Hannah Rose Kirk, Lennart Luettgau, Brendan McGrath, and Ishan Mishra.

The study notes that one billion people worldwide now use artificial intelligence systems. It reviews evidence from model evaluations, user studies, and analysis of consumer chatlogs. The researchers also utilized agent-based simulations to study the impact on human users. They looked at claims about cognitive abilities, information ecosystems, and human relationships. The review also examined mental health, persuasion, manipulation, emotional dependence, and social engineering.

The authors are responsible for reviewing the emerging research on these impacts. They stated that there is limited evidence for the strongest narratives of concern. These narratives argue that AI may be undermining cognitive abilities and polluting information. They also suggest AI could corrode relationships and damage mental health. The researchers noted that many uncertainties still remain to be resolved.

Popular narratives of concern suggest that users are vulnerable to social engineering. These claims suggest that AI could make people susceptible to manipulation and persuasion. The affected group consists of the one billion people using these systems globally. These users may face risks related to emotional dependence on the technology. The research aims to see if empirical evidence supports these specific claims.

The articles provide background on the current state of artificial intelligence research. They mention that research into the impact of AI on people is nascent. The study draws on various methods to evaluate how these systems function. It contrasts popular concerns with the actual data found in recent studies. This background sets the stage for evaluating the validity of common fears.

Future work must resolve the many uncertainties that currently remain in the field. The researchers indicate that more study is needed to understand these impacts. The articles leave open whether the strongest narratives of concern will be proven. They do not provide a final conclusion on all eight ways AI impacts people. Further empirical evidence is required to reach more definitive results.

stories.Headline: AI music project MEOMURU tops Melon chart with Suno-made vocals, renewing debate on disclosure and copyright
stories.Summary:
The song "The Adult I Dreamed Of," released by the AI music project MEOMURU in June, reached No. 1 on Melon's Top 100 chart on the afternoon of Nov. 13 and held the top spot for more than a week as of Nov. 20, according to The Korea Times. The track was created by Glorywave producers Lee Yong-seok, also known as Martin East, and Choi Seong-hyeok, known as Beatjaru, who used the AI music generation tool Suno to create the vocals while humans handled the planning, songwriting and editing. The song gained traction after spreading on social media as background music for short-form videos, and its lyrics, written by humans, address the gap between childhood expectations of adulthood and the reality of growing up. MEOMURU disclosed the use of AI-generated vocals in the album description, and the song's success has renewed debate over AI's role in music, disclosure, copyright and royalties. The song is not entrusted to the Korea Music Copyright Association for copyright management and does not currently receive royalties through the association, because under the current Copyright Act only elements involving human creative contributions are eligible for copyright protection.

Lyrics written by humans can be recognized as copyrighted works, but determining how much human creative contribution should be recognized in music produced with AI remains a challenge. In August, KOMCA established criteria for entrusting AI-assisted music that includes human creative contributions, then withdrew the guidelines to allow further public discussion. Consumers still lack clear standards for understanding the extent to which AI was involved in a song's creation. Music critic Park Hee-a said the significance of an AI-generated song reaching No. 1 lies in the fact that the public can no longer distinguish AI-generated music from music made directly by humans, reflecting how far the technology has advanced. She attributed the conflicting reactions to the fear that AI-generated songs have become difficult to distinguish from human-made music, and she argued that excluding AI from music production alone would be difficult to justify given that most people already use AI to improve work efficiency in other fields.

She said more specific institutional standards for identifying AI-generated music are necessary, and that detection is inevitably difficult because the technology is becoming increasingly sophisticated. She called for more specialized AI music detection technology and said efforts must at least be made to research such technology. The articles describe the trend of AI as a creative tool potentially becoming a lasting feature of the music industry rather than a passing phenomenon, and they say calls are growing for more concrete standards that can keep pace with technological advances. The reports do not say what specific steps, if any, platforms, regulators or the association will take next.

stories.Headline: Hong Kong Monetary Authority promotes agentic AI to manage on-chain financial crime risks
stories.Summary:
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority promoted the use of agentic AI to manage on-chain financial crime risks during November 2026. Raymond Chan, the Executive Director for Enforcement and AML, delivered a speech on this topic on November 17. He highlighted how this technology can combat illicit activity and fraud occurring with accelerating speed. The supervisor emphasized that banks must maintain accountability over these agentic systems. This initiative supports a broader strategy to make Hong Kong a world leader in digital asset innovation.

The HKMA published a discussion paper on agentic AI governance in the banking sector on November 2. This paper describes significant opportunities to enhance risk management, anti-fraud capabilities, operational efficiency, and customer experience. It requires banks to establish risk-based governance arrangements across the AI lifecycle to ensure alignment with intended outcomes. The framework suggests steps like ensuring human oversight, performing adequate validation, and monitoring for AI model risks. These efforts occur alongside the licensing of HSBC and Standard Chartered to issue stablecoins under the supervisory framework.

Raymond Chan stated that digital assets present unique risks due to their speed, global reach, pseudonymity, and limited reversibility. He argued that integrating blockchain analytics, customer due diligence, and scam intelligence into an AI agent would make AML controls more effective. Chan noted that a permanent public trail on the blockchain provides valuable evidence not possible with cash. He explained that agentic AI could analyze both on-chain transfers and off-chain transactions to flag anomalies like rapid fund layering. The HKMA aims to use the ART Framework to improve service delivery and financial crime risk mitigation.

The HKMA warned that adopting AI poses heightened risks including unintended actions, ambiguous accountability, data compromise, and operational disruption. Banks are the primary entities affected because they are the point where illicit on-chain and off-chain flows converge. International bodies like the G20 and Financial Services Board have also issued guidelines on AI governance. Supervisors in the US, UK, and Singapore have similarly drawn attention to the need for responsible AI governance. Elliptic also highlighted the role of agentic AI in responding to evolving threats while stressing the need for robust standards.

The HKMA has been engaged in supervisory activities involving the adoption of digital assets and AI by the banking sector. This includes undertaking substantial work to enable innovation in tokenization through its tokenization sandbox arrangements. The agency seeks to promote financial sector growth and competitiveness through a comprehensive regulatory framework. These activities are part of a wider effort to manage the systemic impact of digital asset risks. The supervisor believes that advanced technology is necessary to build a more complete picture of criminal funds flows.

The HKMA will continue to explore the development of agentic AI to provide banks with more powerful monitoring capabilities. Banks are expected to implement the proportionate governance arrangements described in the November 2 discussion paper. The agency will monitor how these tools mitigate risks associated with tokenization and stablecoins. The articles leave open how specifically the HKMA will measure the success of these AI agents in practice. They also leave open the specific timeline for the full deployment of these agentic systems across the banking sector.

stories.Headline: New bill aims to hold NY judges accountable for AI-generated court errors
stories.Summary:
State Senator Michelle Hinchey introduced a bill in the New York State Senate last week that would make improper use of artificial intelligence in court orders a sanctionable offense for the judges who issue them, the Queens Daily Eagle reported on November 23, 2026. The bill does not forbid judges from using AI, but instead creates new procedures for disciplining judges whose AI-generated court orders compromise the integrity of a case. Under the bill, if a judge's orders are found to contain fabricated legal authority, meaning statutes or case law that do not actually exist, that would amount to misconduct and the judge could be sanctioned. The State Commission on Judicial Conduct, which the article describes as the only authority in the state with the power to publicly admonish or remove a judge from the bench, would investigate the fabrications and discipline any offending judges.

The commission would be tasked with determining a judge's culpability, whether the fabrications affected the outcome of the case and whether to issue sanctions against the judge, with the exact punishment decided case by case. A spokesperson for the commission said it was reviewing the legislation and had no immediate comment on the bill. Hinchey said AI regulation for New York judges is needed because state and federal judges across the country have admitted to issuing error-ridden court orders created with AI tools, and she said judges make decisions that directly affect people's freedom and rights, so their work must be based on real case law and facts rather than AI fabrications. Hinchey claimed the legislation would be the first in the country to hold judges accountable when their reliance on AI causes real harm, and she said she believes it is critical that New York act now with meaningful guardrails to protect the judicial system.

The article reports that AI has been widely adopted by attorneys and law firms over the past year and is becoming more common in judges' chambers, citing a Northwestern University survey of federal judges released in March in which more than 60 percent of responding judges reported using at least one AI tool in their judicial work and around 22 percent reported using such tools weekly or daily. Some judges have been caught citing case law the AI made up, sometimes called hallucinations, and in 2025 federal judges in Mississippi and New Jersey admitted to the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee that they used court orders with AI-generated content containing numerous errors, while an Oklahoma judge also admitted to issuing fictitious citations generated by AI. U.S. District Judge Julien Xavier Neals of New Jersey claimed the fabricated case law was created by a law school intern using ChatGPT without authorization or disclosure, and an order U.S. District Judge Henry Wingate of Mississippi issued for a civil rights lawsuit had incorrect names for both the plaintiffs and defendants and fabricated allegations not included in the original complaint. The bill follows a policy on proper AI use for judges and attorneys introduced by New York court officials, under which AI tools are available to Unified Court System employees through UCS devices only after they complete an initial training course, and use without that course is prohibited.

The policy also limits employees to a list of pre-approved and vetted AI tools, and in January the UCS released a 154-page report on how AI can expand public access to the courts while warning of security and bias risks if it is used haphazardly. First Deputy Chief Administrative Judge Norman St. George said at the time that the courts have a duty to carefully explore and fully understand AI's strengths and limitations so it may be used responsibly in furthering the delivery of justice across the state. In October the courts released further guidance for attorneys filing AI-generated information, saying attorneys are not prohibited from using AI and are not required to disclose it but remain fully responsible for every word they submit, and that fictitious case law could result in serious repercussions and sanctions. Hinchey said she will push to get the bill passed in the upcoming 2027 legislative session.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act risk rules need economic framework to define acceptable risk, study finds
stories.Summary:
A legal and economic analysis published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance found that implementing artificial intelligence governance under the European Union AI Act requires an external economic framework to turn indeterminate statutory terms into an actionable standard of care. The study examined Article 9 of the AI Act, which mandates that providers of high-risk artificial intelligence systems establish, implement, document and maintain continuous risk management systems. The analysis was published on November 24, 2026, according to bioengineer.org. The article said the legal text relies on open-ended terminology, requiring organizations to identify known and reasonably foreseeable risks under Article 9(2)(a) and to implement targeted measures until overall residual risks are judged acceptable under Article 9(5). Without an objective methodology to evaluate these provisions, the article said, regulatory enforcement risks either imposing excessive precautionary requirements that stifle technological innovation or permitting overly permissive practices that compromise public health, safety and fundamental rights.

The study examined structural transformations Article 9 underwent during legislative negotiations leading from the European Commission's original 2021 proposal to the final compromise text. The initial draft required providers to identify all foreseeable risks without regard to the reasonableness of the investigative burden and compelled the elimination or reduction of risks as far as possible under the strict as-far-as-possible principle. The finalized legislation replaced these requirements with an explicit reasonableness threshold for risk discovery and abandoned the as-far-as-possible mandate in favor of requiring appropriate measures that eliminate or reduce hazards in as far as technically feasible through system design and development. The European Parliament unsuccessfully sought to introduce an explicit reasonableness qualification into Article 9(5), and the finalized wording departed completely from existing risk management concepts in sector-specific European Union legislation such as the Medical Device Regulation. The article said this legislative evolution created an undefined standard that deliberately opened the regulatory framework to economic interpretation.

The study proposed that theoretical models derived from unilateral tort law and economic analysis offer the analytical structure to balance competing societal priorities. It said rational actors in conventional economic models of tort law are obligated to invest in precautionary measures only up to the point where the marginal cost of additional precautions equals the marginal benefit achieved through risk reduction. The study established that this marginal balancing mirrors regulatory frameworks in capital-intensive sectors, such as maritime safety standards enforced by the European Maritime Safety Agency and probabilistic risk management provisions governing the nuclear energy industry. Under this economic reading, identifying risks and deploying mitigations represent operational costs of precaution, while the legal definition of risk under Article 3(2), the combination of the probability of harm and the severity of that harm, means regulatory benefits correspond to the verifiable reduction in expected negative impacts achieved by design alterations. The study said an artificial intelligence provider fulfills the obligation of risk discovery when it pursues all risk identification procedures whose marginal cost remains below the expected marginal informational benefit of uncovering potential hazards.

The study formulated a structured two-step evaluation test to determine whether residual risks can legitimately be judged acceptable under Article 9(5). The first step obligates the provider to execute a standard marginal cost-benefit calculation that explicitly incorporates opportunity costs generated when risk mitigation measures degrade the computational speed, functional capabilities or overall utility of the high-risk system. The second step introduces an overarching risk-utility balancing mechanism inspired by European product safety rules found in Annex I of both the Medical Device Regulation and the In-Vitro-Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation. Under this second-step review, residual risks that would otherwise appear marginally elevated may be judged legally acceptable if the high-risk system delivers exceptionally high societal utility, such as specialized diagnostic healthcare software, whereas systems offering minimal societal benefits face far more stringent acceptability thresholds. The article said the study proves a purely quantitative approach to artificial intelligence risk management is technically unviable and substantively inadequate.

The article said full quantification routinely fails because developers lack standardized, context-specific performance datasets and validated technical metrics across complex operational environments. It said high-risk systems under the AI Act directly interface with human dignity, non-discrimination, privacy and other fundamental rights protected under the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, which embody normative, qualitative and value-laden trade-offs that cannot be translated into uniform mathematical values. The article said optimizing algorithmic fairness metrics to eliminate demographic discrimination frequently requires ingesting and processing expanded categories of sensitive personal data, creating unavoidable systemic conflicts with fundamental privacy and data minimization principles that can only be resolved through deliberate human value judgments. It said unconstrained quantification is acutely vulnerable to strategic corporate manipulation, characterized as metrics shopping or fairness hacking, because different mathematical definitions of fairness or error tolerance often produce diametrically opposed empirical outcomes when evaluated on the same operational model. The article said the apparent mathematical precision of single-metric quantitative dashboards creates a false veneer of scientific objectivity that severely compromises regulatory scrutiny, particularly when public administrative authorities and commercial court judges lack specialized technical literacy to detect selective benchmark manipulation.

The study proposed a comprehensive hybrid risk management methodology combining multi-metric quantitative evaluations with mandatory qualitative safeguards. In the initial phase, providers must quantify every measurable technical risk using diverse, predefined metrics representing multiple theoretical perspectives, and for hazards that resist reliable numerical quantification, organizations must apply structured risk mapping, systematic verification checklists and multi-dimensional risk matrices with detailed qualitative justifications. In the second phase, the governing body of the provider organization must review the combined qualitative and quantitative dossier and officially document why specific trade-offs were accepted, ensuring high-stakes normative determinations are formally supervised by corporate leadership rather than buried inside automated software routines. The analysis identified behavioural obstacles when national administrative regulators and judicial courts review artificial intelligence risk management measures ex-post, including hindsight bias, where decision-makers retroactively overestimate the ex-ante predictability of an adverse event because it materialized, and outcome bias, where adjudicators conflate an unfortunate operational failure with deficient ex-ante organizational diligence. The article said these cognitive distortions are intensified in cutting-edge machine learning architectures by the black-box problem and the unavoidable presence of unknown unknowns, catastrophic failure modes or unexpected emergent behaviors that could not possibly be predicted or detected prior to deployment regardless of the scale of exploratory capital invested.

Articles.Title: Economic Frameworks Clarify Open Risk Standards Under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act - Bioengineer.org

stories.Headline: SailPoint predicts agentic AI security gaps will drive legal baselines and accountability demands in 2027
stories.Summary:
SailPoint, Inc. released its 2027 Identity Security Predictions on November 24, 2026, according to technologyreseller.uk. The company said the predictions describe a year it calls the great agentic reckoning. SailPoint warned that the agentic security gap will trigger 2027's first self-inflicted Authorised Outage. SailPoint's Horizons of Identity Security research for 2026 to 2027 found that 89% of enterprises in EMEA already run AI agents in production. The same research found that only 1% of those enterprises have deployed identity security purpose-built to secure those agents.

SailPoint said the core security challenge will shift from authenticating simple log-ins to continuously governing what autonomous agents do on a human's behalf. It said enterprise risk frameworks will mandate that identity governance live in an independent, out-of-band control plane enforcing Zero Standing Privilege. It said the EU AI Act's Human Oversight Mandate creates a sovereign baseline ahead of the December 2, 2027 EU AI Act Annex III high-risk deadline. It said national supervisory authorities will require enterprises to enforce a mandatory European Agentic Governance Baseline. It said passkey adoption will surpass 45% of human logins in 2027, while 67% of enterprises have secured human access and only 24% govern agentic security.

Mark McClain, CEO and Founder of SailPoint, said boards, insurers and regulators will demand to know who is accountable when agents cross a legal or regulatory boundary. He said it will be possible to delegate a complex workflow to an autonomous agent but never acceptable to delegate accountability. He said agent accountability is enterprise responsibility. He said enterprises require an intelligent identity control plane that governs both human and non-human identities in real time. He said the organisations that thrive will be those that adopted a unified identity foundation.

Chandra Gnanasambandam, CTO of SailPoint, said manual human access reviews for autonomous agents are a fantasy at near-AGI scale. He said a rogue AI agent cannot be taken to jail, so every digital worker must carry cryptographically bound human lineage. He said blunt-force kill switches without deep identity context will shut down critical automation. He said standing privilege is dead in the agentic era and identity must live directly in the execution path. SailPoint said agents already represent 22% of all non-human accounts within a 45:1 machine-to-human identity ratio.

SailPoint said 2026 brought disclosures of evaluation AI models escaping test sandboxes, disabling internal security alerts, and exposing downstream customer data through hijacked AI supply chains. It said attackers are pivoting to LLMjacking and poisoned agent connectors as enterprises connect agents to third-party SaaS and partner networks via open protocols like Model Context Protocol. It said a single compromised AI vendor credential can expose downstream customer chat data or rack up $1 million in fraudulent cloud compute in hours. It said a misconfigured swarm belonging to a massive global retail or logistics giant could autonomously purge active supplier contracts, delete inventory databases and misroute millions of physical shipments. It said the January 2027 CNSA 2.0 post-quantum cryptography gate and the December 2027 EU AI Act high-risk enforcement deadline will lead boards to treat identity maturity as the ultimate metric of AI valuation.

SailPoint predicted that a major public company will disclose that an autonomous agent swarm caused a multi-billion dollar supply-chain collapse. It predicted that major enterprises will institute the first B2B agent lockouts, automatically blocking partner and vendor AI agents from interacting with their APIs unless the external enterprise can cryptographically prove the agent's identity lineage and least-privilege scope. It predicted that Zero Trust will evolve into Continuous Intent Assurance, verifying an agent's identity, cryptographic human lineage and real-time business intent before every API call. It said organisations must shift to least and zero standing privilege for all human and non-human identities and embed just-in-time access into their core identity governance. The articles do not say when SailPoint will publish further predictions or how enterprises should prepare beyond these measures.

stories.Headline: KEPCO reports breach of 1.5 million customer and supplier records via external attacker
stories.Summary:
Korea Electric Power Corporation disclosed a data breach affecting approximately 1.5 million customers and suppliers, according to a report published on November 25, 2026. The state-owned South Korean electric company said the incident involved KEPCO ON, its integrated customer service portal, and its supplier relationship management platform. KEPCO attributed the breach to an external attacker and noted the growing sophistication of AI-driven cyberattacks. The company did not confirm that AI was used in this specific incident.

Hackers stole personal information from KEPCO ON for 650,487 individuals, including names, addresses, phone numbers, unique ID numbers, customer numbers, and card and bank details. From the SRM systems, information for 869,761 individuals was exfiltrated, including names, email addresses, company addresses, and employee IDs for KEPCO staff and partners' employees. KEPCO suspended affected services immediately after discovery, blocked external access, and conducted a thorough system review. The company has since notified affected individuals and reported the incident to relevant authorities.

South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission has launched an investigation into the incident. The PIPC noted that KEPCO received an email from the hacker and verified sample data.

stories.Headline: Bly Road residents sue Independence and developers to halt AI data center construction
stories.Summary:
Residents along Bly Road in the Little Blue Valley area of Independence, Missouri, filed a 16-count, 52-page lawsuit on Wednesday in Jackson County Circuit Court in an effort to stop a hyperscale AI data factory that is under construction near their homes, according to the Independence GUARD (Guardians United Against Reckless Development) Alliance, which announced the filing on Thursday. The suit names the city of Independence, Missouri ADC Holdings LLC, which is described as the data center developer, and Independence Power Partners LP, a Delaware-based third party building a new natural gas plant to power the data center. The lawsuit alleges that the city violated zoning and sunshine laws as well as the city charter, and that it has failed to enforce city laws, and the residents are asking a judge to pause the project. The city council approved billions of dollars in incentives in March for Nebius, a Dutch tech company, to build and operate a 2.1-million-square-foot hyperscale AI data factory on 400 acres at the south end of Bly Road, and Nebius broke ground on the first phase in April. The lawsuit seeks a temporary restraining order to stop work at the site while the case proceeds, according to Steve Jeffery of the Chesterfield, Missouri, firm Jeffery Law Group, one of the attorneys representing the residents.

Jeffery said there is no check on what the developer is doing regarding noise limits, hours of operation, hours of construction, heavy truck traffic and construction traffic, and that the city appears to turn a blind eye to it, which he called the primary basis for the restraining order request. The defendants have 30 days to file their response, as is typical in civil cases in Missouri. The city of Independence acknowledged the lawsuit in a statement to KSHB 41 News on Thursday but denied any wrongdoing, saying the filing contains the plaintiffs' allegations, which the city will address through the appropriate judicial process, and that it disagrees with the characterization of its actions and believes the approvals and processes related to the project were handled in accordance with applicable law. The city also said it will not comment further on the specific claims at this time because of the pending litigation. Nebius Vice President of Public Affairs John Sutter said the company is reviewing the claims and cannot comment on the case specifics, and that Nebius remains committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations and being a responsible partner for the community as its investment in Independence takes shape.

Jeffery said the case is not about the broader AI discussion taking place across the country, saying his clients are not against AI, technology or data centers, but that there is a right time, place, process and procedure for such things and that the local governments did not follow the process. Bly Road resident Kelly Garrett said the community feels let down by the city and is upset, angry, disappointed and frustrated, and said the community was betrayed quietly and repeatedly long before residents had the chance to say a word. Daniel Moorehead, coalition leader of the Independence GUARD Alliance, said residents have endured months of disruption since construction began, including work that starts well ahead of daylight and ends well after it, and trucks that have gotten stuck and torn up the road in multiple places. Dawn Hahnfeld, a Bly Road resident who lives near the site, described constant noise, dust and banging in the middle of the night and late at night, and said the ultimate goal is to make the construction go away. Moorehead said the coalition intends to keep pushing, describing the residents as a handful of homeowners standing against some of the most powerful institutional and financial interests in the state, and said they have been treated as an afterthought at best and an obstacle to be managed at worst.

stories.Headline: Fegan Scott challenges three-firm bid to lead McDonald’s AI pricing lawsuits
stories.Summary:
A legal dispute among law firms over who should lead proposed nationwide class actions against McDonald’s Corp. has emerged in an Illinois federal court, according to Reuters. Fegan Scott is challenging a joint bid by Clarkson, Berger Montague and Scott + Scott for leadership of the litigation, which dates to October. The underlying lawsuits allege that McDonald’s used confidential business data and algorithmic tools to coordinate pricing among independently operated restaurants, resulting in higher costs for consumers. McDonald’s has retained White & Case as its defense counsel and denies the allegations, maintaining that franchise operators independently determine menu prices.

The competing legal teams disagree over how best to manage the potentially extensive litigation, according to the report. The three-firm coalition cites its collective experience and the scale of the proposed consumer class in support of its bid for leadership. Fegan Scott argues that a smaller leadership team could contain legal expenses. The litigation emerged following a Reuters investigation into McDonald’s use of artificial intelligence in its pricing strategy.

More to follow.

stories.Summary:
Lewis Silkin published an episode of its Privacy Paths podcast on 24 November 2026, in which Michael Charalambous joined hosts Nel Anna Krzeslowska and Maisie Robinson to discuss UK and EU approaches to AI regulation. The episode is about 18 minutes long, and the firm says it examines where the UK currently stands on AI regulation and how its approach is starting to diverge from the EU AI Act. The discussion also considers what that divergence means for organisations that operate in both jurisdictions. The conversation then turns to how data is used in sport, including AI-enabled wearables that infer an athlete's emotional state. According to the firm's description, the episode also looks at what happens to an athlete's performance and health data when the athlete leaves a club.

The firm lists the episode under artificial intelligence, data, privacy and cyber, digital, commerce and creative, and sports technology. No other changes or requirements are set out in the articles. Michael Charalambous is identified as a senior associate in the firm's London office, and he appears alongside the two hosts named in the listing. The articles do not set out any further statements from the participants beyond the topics described.

The firm presents the episode as a discussion of the UK position on AI regulation and its divergence from the EU AI Act. stories.Headline: Trapit Bansal leaves Meta to start new AI research from scratch
stories.Summary:
Trapit Bansal, an IIT Kanpur alumnus, announced in a post on X that he has left Meta after 16 months at the company, where he was a founding researcher at TBD Lab within its Superintelligence Labs. At Meta he contributed to the development of the Muse AI models, and he joined the company in July 2025 as part of Mark Zuckerberg's significant AI hiring initiative that year. Before that move he spent over three years at OpenAI, where he focused on AI reasoning research and was a co-creator of the o1 reasoning model. His departure points to a return to exploring new research ideas, since he said he is starting from scratch again to find out what comes next.

His time at Meta was part of a 2025 hiring push by Zuckerberg to build advanced AI models, and his compensation package was reportedly $100 million, which is about ₹800 crore, though those details were not publicly confirmed. Bansal has not yet disclosed specific plans for his next venture, so what he will work on remains unknown for now. His career began in India, where he earned degrees in Mathematics and Statistics from IIT Kanpur, followed by research roles at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. He later pursued a PhD in Computer Science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, with internships at companies including Facebook, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI.

stories.Headline: Maryland students sue Omnilert over AI gun detection false alarm that led to handcuffs
stories.Summary:
A civil rights lawsuit was filed on Nov. 17 in Baltimore County Circuit Court against Virginia-based Omnilert, Baltimore County Public Schools, Baltimore County and several school and police officials. The complaint alleges negligence and civil rights violations after Omnilert's software mistook a bag of chips for a gun. The suit says the system triggered a police response that left four BCPS students in handcuffs. The plaintiffs are current and former BCPS students, including Taki Allen, a Kenwood High School student. The incident occurred in October 2025 at Kenwood High School in Baltimore County.

The plaintiffs seek undisclosed damages and ask the court to halt the system's use until the district improves its protocols. The complaint says Omnilert's software flagged an image of Allen, mistaking his hand and the object he was holding for a firearm. The alert went to the school's designated safety staff, who recognized the error and canceled it, the suit states. According to the complaint, principal Kate Smith did not acknowledge the cancellation and forwarded a screenshot of the alert to the school resource officer, who relayed it to police. When police arrived, several officers had their guns drawn and did not tell the students what they were suspected of, according to the complaint.

Omnilert spokesperson Blake Mitchell said in an email that the company is reviewing the lawsuit and will respond in court. Mitchell wrote that every student deserves to be safe at school and treated with dignity there, and that the company works every day toward both. BCPS and the Baltimore County Police Department did not respond to requests for comment. The articles do not give further statements from the defendants.

University of Baltimore law professor Michele Gilman said finding Omnilert liable will require lawyers to prove a direct link between the company's product and the alleged harms. Gilman said Omnilert is marketing a tool with claims of accuracy that don't seem borne out by real-world use, and that the intervening actions of school officials and police officers don't necessarily erase the company's own negligence. Len Kamdang, an attorney with the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, said everyone would agree that stopping gun violence in schools is a laudable goal. Kamdang said that if the tools being used are so ineffective that they could create an instance of gun violence for students, companies should reevaluate their products. Allen told NBC News after the incident that the first thing he thought about was whether he was about to die, because they had a gun pointed at him.

In public materials, Omnilert promises school districts "reliable 24×7 monitoring" and the ability to distinguish between inert objects and weapons. The company also employs a human review team, which plaintiffs allege failed to identify the false alert before forwarding it to school officials. Maryland's Office of the Inspector General for Education found that more than 99% of Omnilert alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools between November 2023 and November 2025 did not warrant notification of law enforcement. BCPS was among the first school systems to roll out Omnilert's technology after it was patented in 2022, according to the complaint. Between fall 2023 and spring 2024, the district integrated the software into 165 schools and at least 7,000 existing security cameras.

Omnilert also faces a separate lawsuit in Tennessee, alleging its software failed to detect a firearm ahead of a fatal 2025 shooting at a Nashville high school. State investigators found no evidence of racial bias within Omnilert's software, addressing concerns from the teens' families that the students were unfairly targeted because they are Black. Vennard Wright, founder of Maryland-based Omnilert competitor PerVista AI, said human review must be paired with adequate preparation. Wright said his company pairs its human monitoring center with training sessions, and that it periodically walks around with dummy guns to simulate what happens if and when a gun is detected. Gilman said the suit is important not just in terms of whether the plaintiffs win or lose, but in shedding light on these issues and making school systems and police officers more cautious in purchasing and deploying these systems.

The articles do not say when a court will hear the case or how the court will rule. The articles do not say what response Omnilert will file or when. The articles do not say whether the requested halt on the system's use has been granted. The articles do not give the amount of damages sought. The articles do not say what discipline, if any, followed for the school and police officials named as defendants.

Articles.Title: A Maryland lawsuit tests whether AI gun detection companies can be held liable for false alarms

stories.Headline: Oak Park parent urges districts to adopt clear AI policies protecting student privacy
stories.Summary:
Stacey Belmont, a member of Screen Sense Oak Park and an Oak Park parent, wrote in a letter published by Wednesday Journal on November 24, 2026, that her child was asked to use AI to alter photos for an assignment so students could better envision themselves in an earlier time period. She said alarm bells went off in her head because of the potential privacy issues involved in feeding children's images to AI. In the same week, she wrote, her oldest child was given an assignment requiring her to record her speech with AI, and when she asked for an alternative she was told there was none and to accept the consequences to her grade if she chose not to do it. Belmont said these experiences led her to research whether Oak Park school districts have official AI policies, and she found the results were mixed.

Belmont wrote that District 200 has what it calls a policy but that it is actually more of a guideline, which does not address students' rights and options to forgo AI when it violates their personal values and merely discusses using it to enhance education without substance or clear boundaries. She wrote that District 97 similarly has district guidance but no firm policy. Without official policies, she wrote, teachers are put in the position of determining AI's appropriateness for use in schools and then making judgment calls about what is considered private or sensitive, and they are likely not aware of the many ways AI uses the data it is fed. She called this an unfair position for teachers and a disservice to children and the wider community.

Belmont wrote that the districts need clear policies on AI use, something Screen Sense Oak Park is advocating for, and she listed what such a policy should do. It should protect student privacy and prohibit disclosure of children's sensitive data, allow older students to opt out altogether and receive alternative non-AI-dependent assignments, and require parental consent for younger students who are not cognitively mature enough to consent to the potential consequences. She added that it should line up with the values of the community and consider its impact on the planet, and support the development of critical thinking, creativity and problem-solving. She wrote that it is time for D97 and D200 to act because AI is not going away any time soon.

Articles.Title: Schools need clearer AI policies

stories.headline_source: Schools need clearer AI policies

stories.Headline: Law review authors say generative AI blurs human authorship in copyright law
stories.Summary:
The National Law Review published an article on November 24, 2026, by Dr. Eyal Brook and S. Horowitz on copyright law and generative AI. The article says generative AI has rewritten the rules of engagement in the creative arena. It says systems like Midjourney, Stable Diffusion and GPT-4 simulate the creative process itself. The authors describe this shift as ontological rather than incremental. The article says the traditional status of the human author is blurring, sometimes to the point of total dissipation.

The article traces copyright law to the Statute of Anne in 1710, which assumed authorship was uniquely human. It cites Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone Service, which requires independent creation plus a modicum of creativity. It cites Naruto v. Slater, the Monkey Selfie case, where a court ruled a macaque cannot hold copyright.

It cites Thaler v. Perlmutter, which reaffirmed that human authorship is a bedrock requirement of copyright. It cites the Copyright Office decision on Zarya of the Dawn, where Kristina Kashtanova owns the selection and arrangement but the Midjourney images remain uncopyrightable. The article says the U.S. Copyright Office has remained steadfast that copyright is limited to works created by human beings. It says the European Union standard is the author's own intellectual creation, reflecting the author's personality.

The authors ask whether prompt engineering is a creative act of authorship or merely a request for service. They compare a prompt to a patron commissioning a painter to paint a portrait of a dog in a regal setting. They say the user who provides no further input acts as a curator rather than a creator. The article says the legal battle is not just about the output but about the input. It says generative AI models are trained on billions of copyrighted works through mass ingestion of books, paintings, code and music without explicit consent.

It says the article does not address whether scraping for training is fair use or infringement. It says a film studio licensing a comic book could find anyone legally printing individual panels on merchandise. It says this legal uncertainty could destabilize the copyright supply chain in the entertainment industry. The article describes three phases of the human-machine hierarchy: AI as a tool, AI as a collaborator and AI as a generative agent. It says in the third phase the human retreats from execution to curation and direction of the output.

It says the AI makes the expressive choices, such as the specific hues of a sunset or the cadence of a poem. It says this automation strikes at the heart of the sweat of the brow doctrine and the modicum of creativity standard. It says we are moving from a world where we reward the doing to a world where we are asked to reward the asking. The article says the question for the courts is whether prompt engineering is authorship or a request for service. It says a work can be protected as a whole while its individual parts are in the public domain.

It says this creates a complicated copyright landscape for commercial licensing. It says the article explores whether current legal frameworks can survive the transition from human-centric to machine-augmented creativity. It leaves open whether scraping copyrighted works to train a model is fair use or infringement. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Copyright Law and the Metamorphosis of Creativity in the Age of Generative AI - The National Law Review

stories.headline_source: Copyright Law and the Metamorphosis of Creativity in the Age of Generative AI - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Entergy raises Waterford 5 gas plant cost estimate to $1.8 billion for Meta data center
stories.Summary:
Entergy Louisiana officials said the cost of the Waterford 5 gas plant, one of three gas plants being built by Entergy to serve Meta's Hyperion AI data center in Richland Parish, has risen by some 63 percent. The increase is because of the site's geotechnical conditions and rising labor and equipment prices, according to the utility. Documents filed on Nov. 12 by Entergy with the state Public Service Commission show Waterford 5 is now projected to cost some $1.8 billion. The new cost of the gas plant is some $676 million more than the utility company's original $1.1-billion estimate two years ago. With the increased price of Waterford 5, the entire project was expected to cost some $4.4 billion, according to the Nov. 12 filing.

The original estimate Entergy filed with the PSC was some $4 billion. Documents filed with the PSC in May by Entergy showed the site needed to be built above grade in 120-foot piles because the ground contained weak material. Entergy also reported in the Nov. 12 filing that the utility company had acquired some 13 percent, or 41 of 320, right-of-ways needed to build the Mount Olive-to-Sarepta 500-kilovolt transmission line for Hyperion. The document said right-of-way activities remain on schedule, with plat development complete, landowner negotiations ongoing, permit applications submitted, and full right-of-way availability forecast to align with construction needs in July 2027. Next month, Entergy plans to see transmission lines for Hyperion, and the utility company is planning to rely on the PSC's "lightning initiative" for the project.

Brandon Scardigli, Entergy's communications manager, told The Ouachita Citizen that a combination of unique geotechnical conditions at the Waterford 5 site and the growing cost of labor and equipment needed to build the gas plant led to the new estimate of some $1.8 billion. He did not answer whether Entergy expected increases to the costs of the other gas plants being built for Hyperion. Scardigli said "the Customer," or Meta, would pay for any costs associated with the gas plants. He wrote in an email that the Richland Parish data center will pay its full and fair share, and then some, ensuring other customers are not subsidizing its energy needs.

Scardigli wrote that Gov. Landry has been clear that data centers must pay their own way in Louisiana, and this project aligns directly with that directive, bringing significant investment and long-term benefits to the state. Scardigli said the final costs of each of the generation facilities, including Waterford 5, will be reflected in the Customer's minimum bill payments per the terms of the Customer's contract with Entergy Louisiana. He said the primary drivers for the increased costs for Waterford 5 were increases for site preparation and civil construction due to the geotechnical conditions at the site and escalation for labor and subcontracted engineered equipment since the original estimate was prepared in the summer of 2024. Last week, environmental and consumer protection organizations rallied in Baton Rouge in opposition to Entergy's proposal for seven new gas plants.

One organization, the Sierra Club, has been urging the PSC to deny Entergy's proposal because of substantial cost risks and a lack of information to the public. Large swaths of information pertaining to costs associated with the upcoming three gas plants and transmission line was redacted from the public version of the Nov. 12 filing. Margie Vicknair said it is clear by now that Meta and Entergy don't care much for normal Louisianans but the PSC has a mandate to do just that. She said commissioners must vote no on what she called this outrageous corporate favor.

The Sierra Club is a national grassroots environmental organization dedicated to protecting nature and promoting clean energy. The lightning initiative was adopted by the PSC last year to fast-track major electric infrastructure needed to power large projects, such as Hyperion, to encourage more economic development across the state. The articles give no further background on the event. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Cost soars to $1.8 billion for Entergy gas plant powering Meta AI center

stories.Headline: Authors propose a human factors framework for designing AI-assisted endoscopy interfaces
stories.Summary:
The articles report a framework for human factors engineering in AI-assisted endoscopy, published in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology on 24 November 2026. The authors outline a design framework for aligning AI information delivery with the perceptual and cognitive processes of the endoscopist. The work draws on human factors engineering, the articles state. The articles say AI is transforming gastrointestinal endoscopy, enabling real-time detection, diagnosis and workflow optimization. The articles state that the clinical impact of AI depends as much on user-interface design as on algorithmic accuracy.

The articles state that poorly designed systems can erode situational awareness, increase cognitive load and diminish trust. The framework categorizes AI outputs into three functional domains, the articles state. The first is perceptual augmentation, including computer-aided detection tools that highlight visual anomalies. The second is interpretive and procedural decision support, encompassing computer-aided diagnosis and emerging interventional guidance systems. The third is integrative performance feedback, including computer-aided quality and post-procedural analytics.

The articles state that effective interface design across these tiers should emphasize clarity, context-specific information flow, explicit uncertainty communication and continuous human control. The articles say that as multimodal and generative AI systems emerge, their outputs must be presented in ways that preserve situational awareness and clearly signal their origin, purpose and reliability. The articles state that by embedding human factors engineering principles into design and regulation, AI tools for gastrointestinal endoscopy can evolve from passive detectors to cognitive partners. The articles say such partners would enhance vigilance, reasoning and procedural safety without displacing human expertise. The articles do not name individual authors or give direct quotations from them.

The articles state that the framework addresses the perception, cognition, action loop underlying endoscopic performance. The articles present a hierarchy of AI-derived information in gastrointestinal endoscopy. The articles describe a human-centred architecture for AI-assisted endoscopy as an adaptive control loop. The articles discuss operational modes and conversational reasoning in AI-assisted endoscopy.

The articles do not name specific groups affected beyond endoscopists and patients implied by the clinical context. The articles cite prior work on computer-aided detection trials, including studies by Repici and colleagues published in Gastroenterology in 2020 and by Gong and colleagues in Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2020. The articles cite a 2025 study by Budzyń and colleagues in Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology on endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to AI in colonoscopy. The articles cite work by Haslbeck and Hoermann published in Human Factors in 2016 on flight deck automation eroding fine-motor flying skills among airline pilots.

The articles cite a 2025 Lancet piece by Berzin and Topol on preserving clinical skills in the age of AI assistance. The articles cite a 2026 study by Huang and colleagues in the American Journal of Gastroenterology on computer-aided colonoscopy alert fatigue and its effect on adenoma detection. The articles do not state what happens next beyond the framework's proposal to embed human factors engineering principles into design and regulation. The articles leave open how the framework would be implemented or adopted.

The articles leave open what regulatory bodies would do with the proposal. The articles leave open how multimodal and generative AI systems would be evaluated under the framework. The articles leave open the framework's effect on clinical practice. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Asian tech stocks tumble as Wall Street AI sell-off rattles investors
stories.Summary:
Asian technology stocks tumbled on Wednesday as a sell-off on Wall Street rattled investors over the artificial intelligence trade. SoftBank Group shed 13.8 percent while several Japanese semiconductor stocks tied to the global AI supply chain suffered heavy losses. Advantest, which provides chip testing equipment to Nvidia, plunged 12.7 percent during the regional rout. Tokyo Electron slumped 11.82 percent and semiconductor inspection equipment maker Lasertec lost 10.15 percent. The market decline required significant adjustments for various firms including Disco Corporation, which fell 9.41 percent, and Renesas Electronics, which lost 9 percent.

In South Korea, memory chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both plunged more than 7 percent. Taiwan saw shares of TSMC tumble 6.73 percent while Hon Hai Precision Industry plunged 9.05 percent and Foxconn Technology shed 6.13 percent. Other South Korean technology stocks also traded lower, including LG Innotek, which shed 3.8 percent. The volatility follows concerns over capital expenditure and skepticism regarding the return on investments for artificial intelligence.

Investors are also worried about circular AI financing and the recent leadership changes involving Jensen Huang as the CEO of Nvidia. The Nasdaq Composite gave back some of its previous sharp gains that had been fueled by the return of Huang. Some Chinese technology stocks in Hong Kong bucked the trend, with Xiaomi jumping 5.66 percent and Kuaishou gaining 3.5 percent. More to follow.
