stories.Headline: Property lawyers name faster AI adoption by rival firms as their biggest competitive threat
stories.Summary:
Live polling at October’s Digital Conveyancing Summit found that 43 per cent of respondents named rival firms adopting artificial intelligence faster as the biggest threat to their commercial success, rather than AI replacing them. The findings came from a panel hosted by property data specialist Search Acumen before an audience of around 500 property lawyers, with senior figures from JLL, the Urban Land Institute and law firm Freeths taking part. Financial Times property correspondent Julie Steinberg moderated the discussion, which examined where commercial property law is heading over the next five years. The article says buying another AI subscription is unlikely to be the answer, and that the number of actual poll respondents was not disclosed.

Search Acumen managing director Andrew Lloyd argued that real estate’s fundamental problem is not AI but data, because vast quantities of valuable property information remain locked in separate systems and create duplicated work, unnecessary costs and missed opportunities. He said combining ownership records, geographical information, flood risks and climate resilience data could transform property due diligence and investment advice, and that advantage will increasingly belong to firms combining their own knowledge with wider industry datasets. The article lists five points for property lawyers: AI is becoming core infrastructure, firms should collect and organise data now and review confidentiality agreements, data retention policies and permissions, more complex public-private transactions are expected in housing, energy and infrastructure, climate data will increasingly influence transactions, and relationships still matter. It says the intellectual capital inside law firms could become one of their most valuable commercial assets, provided they can use it without compromising client confidentiality.

JLL technology executive Will Cohen said fewer than 40 per cent of organisations beginning to pilot AI had formal training or governance processes in place, a figure the article says was separately reported. Freeths’ chief knowledge and innovation officer Nick Pryor emphasised the importance of human judgment, data protection and making AI central to legal practice. The article says the competitive advantage will not necessarily go to the firm with the most expensive AI platform but to the firm that knows what to do with its information. It does not say what happens next beyond the five-year outlook the panel examined.

Articles.Title: Property Law’s New Competitive Threat Isn’t AI. It’s the Firm Down the Road

stories.headline_source: Property Law’s New Competitive Threat Isn’t AI. It’s the Firm Down the Road

stories.Headline: Oracle says it has full funding for its OpenAI infrastructure contract as shares fall 8.6%
stories.Summary:
Oracle shares fell 8.6% on Friday and closed at €92.06, according to ad-hoc-news.de, as a broad retreat from artificial-intelligence stocks gathered pace. The article, citing the Associated Press, said the trigger was the post-debut slide in Anthropic's stock, which turned a sector-wide spotlight on what the AI buildout actually costs the companies financing it. Anthropic listed on 19 November at an issue price of $83 per share, and as the session wore on investors began questioning whether the enormous sums being poured into artificial intelligence could be justified. The selling spread well beyond individual names, with the S&P 500 shedding 3.7% and the Nasdaq giving up 5.3%, the AP reported.

For Oracle, the selloff lands at an awkward moment, and Reuters noted that investors had been taking a closer look at the capital Oracle needs to expand its AI data centres and at its exposure to OpenAI. The company moved on Friday to draw a line under the financing side of that debate, saying that after its most recent capital raise in November the full funding for its infrastructure contract with OpenAI is in place. That package includes supplier financing, and Oracle stressed that delivering on the contract does not depend on further talks with those suppliers. On the ground, the Abilene site is nearly complete, and all permits are in hand for Shackelford, according to the article.

What the financing announcement does not settle is when the buildout starts returning more cash than it consumes, and Oracle reiterated that it expects positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028 while targeting more than $30 billion for fiscal 2029. The first figure marks the intended swing into the black, and the second shows the scale of surplus Oracle believes it can generate the year after, though both remain forecasts rather than results already booked. One data point predates the turmoil: on 10 November, Bernstein reaffirmed its outperform rating and its $325 price target on Oracle, a call made before Friday's rout. For investors weighing the stock now, the article says the pivotal issue is the handover from a debt- and supplier-financed expansion to genuine positive free cash flow, since capital requirements determine what Oracle must lay out to build while free cash flow reveals what is left once the investment is done.

Articles.Title: Oracle's AI Bill Is Paid; The Payback Is Still Three Years Out

stories.headline_source: Oracle's AI Bill Is Paid; The Payback Is Still Three Years Out

stories.Headline: Sproxil signs pharmacy council deal to deploy AI for online drug regulation in Nigeria
stories.Summary:
Sproxil, a health technology company, signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Pharmacy Council of Nigeria to deploy artificial intelligence in strengthening pharmacy regulation, sanitizing online drug sales and safeguarding patients nationwide, according to an announcement reported on Monday, November 23, 2026. The agreement was disclosed in Lagos following a workshop on artificial intelligence and pharmacy regulation, where Sproxil Chief Executive Officer Dr. Ashifi Gogo explained the partnership's structure and aims. Gogo said the collaboration is designed to make regulatory oversight more efficient and to extend the council's enforcement reach into Nigeria's rapidly growing digital pharmacy ecosystem. He noted that Sproxil has operated in Nigeria for over 16 years, primarily alongside pharmaceutical manufacturers and private sector players, and began expanding into public-sector healthcare channels roughly five years ago.

A central pillar of the collaboration is integrating online pharmacy transactions into the National Electronic Pharmacy platform, which the partners say will ensure digital drug dispensaries meet the same strict regulatory standards as traditional brick-and-mortar pharmacies. Gogo called for shared accountability across the digital ecosystem, saying social media networks such as X and LinkedIn must localize their posting pathways to automatically block drug listings that violate Nigerian laws before they go live. For illegal listings that slip through, he said Sproxil's agentic AI systems will continuously scan digital spaces, detect non-compliant vendors, capture digital enforcement evidence and transmit actionable intelligence directly to the council before fake or substandard drugs reach patients. Gogo also revealed that the company's state-level field teams recently conducted a nationwide health survey of over 80,000 Nigerians, covering 98 per cent of the country's 774 Local Government Areas.

Gogo said Sproxil is investing in Nigerian-designed and Nigerian-made hardware using 3D printing, additive manufacturing and local electrical and mechanical engineering to prevent anti-counterfeiting measures from driving up the retail cost of medicines. For pharmaceutical firms unable to invest in heavy serialization machinery, he said Sproxil offers unique code printing on empty packaging within a sanitized, Good Manufacturing Practice-certified facility. He also highlighted Aisha, the company's AI-powered health assistant, which he said has processed patient queries across more than 90 countries in multiple languages via diaspora and referral networks. To keep the service free for everyday patients despite rising business messaging fees on WhatsApp, Gogo said users are directed after a few initial interactions via a link to the Aisha Progressive Web App, which eliminates per-message costs while supporting richer medical content.

Gogo noted that Sproxil aligns its interventions with Nigeria's National Strategic Health Development Plan rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all model, recognizing that healthcare challenges vary significantly across states like Lagos, Niger, Bauchi and Rivers. On malaria control, he disclosed that new federal government initiatives are underway and expected to be unveiled in the coming months, which will expand access to locally manufactured malaria test kits paired with Sproxil's AI. He said the pairing will enable community pharmacists to capture, verify and report diagnostic results seamlessly. The article also states that Sproxil is currently raising $2 million in venture capital to further localize and scale Aisha across Africa and international markets.

stories.Headline: Premium Times publisher Dapo Olorunyomi urges AI regulation and fair publisher compensation at Africa media conference
stories.Summary:
Dapo Olorunyomi, the Publisher of PREMIUM TIMES, called for responsible regulation of artificial intelligence and fair compensation for publishers during the fourth Media and Development Conference, which began on Monday, 23 November 2026, according to the report. He said reliable information is a public good that must be protected through regulation, public investment and accountability from technology companies. The three-day conference brings together journalists, policymakers, researchers, technology companies, civil society leaders and development institutions from across Africa. This year's edition is themed "Media, Technology and the Future of Democratic Societies." Mr Olorunyomi said a handful of global technology companies now wield enormous influence over how hundreds of millions of Africans discover, consume and evaluate information, and that their decisions on algorithms, content moderation, recommendation systems and platform policies could determine the political visibility of information and the economic survival of media organisations.

He urged technology companies to be transparent about how their algorithms rank and amplify information, particularly during elections and other periods of heightened political sensitivity. He also called for meaningful investment in local-language content moderation so that speakers of Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba, Wolof, Twi and other African languages are adequately represented in systems increasingly shaping their lives. He advocated fair compensation arrangements for publishers whose journalism generates value for digital platforms and informs the development of artificial intelligence models, including large language models. He said technology companies that benefit from information produced by news organisations must recognise publishers' contributions and establish fair arrangements for using their work, and he stressed the need to protect the value of journalism and ensure that technology serves the profession rather than dictates its direction.

He cautioned against portraying technology as an inherent threat to journalism, arguing that the problem lies in the concentration of technological power without transparency, democratic oversight and equitable arrangements for sharing the value created. He said African journalists had demonstrated the benefits of technology through data journalism, satellite imagery, open-source intelligence, mobile reporting and collaborative fact-checking initiatives, which have helped expose patterns of public expenditure, document conflicts and human rights abuses, reach underserved communities and strengthen collaboration among newsrooms. He said the same companies have designed their algorithms to increasingly reward outrage over accuracy, virality over verification and engagement over the public interest, and he described information integrity as a public good that cannot survive on goodwill alone. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers find gaps in EU rules for AI medical device software
stories.Summary:
A policy review published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence on November 23, 2026, examined regulatory pathways and operational challenges for artificial intelligence medical device software across the European Union. Researchers from the National Center for Artificial Intelligence and Innovative Technologies for Health at the Istituto Superiore di Sanità in Rome, Italy, conducted the review. The study details critical gaps in European rules governing AI medical device software. It was published by bioengineer.org on November 23, 2026. The review addresses the intersection of medical device regulations and the Artificial Intelligence Act.

Medical device software in the European Union is governed by Regulation (EU) 2017/745, known as the MDR, and Regulation (EU) 2017/746, known as the IVDR. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act or AIA, adds a horizontal framework applying to AI systems across multiple economic sectors. Under MDR Recital 19 and IVDR Recital 17, software is a medical device in its own right when the manufacturer explicitly intends it for specific medical objectives. MDCG 2019-11 Rev. 1 states that qualification criteria remain unchanged whether software uses conventional deterministic rules or AI and machine learning.

Under MDR Annex VIII Rule 11, software informing clinical decisions is Class IIa, escalates to Class IIb if decisions could cause serious deterioration or surgical intervention, and reaches Class III if decisions may result in death or irreversible deterioration. AI systems in MDR classes IIa, IIb, or III, or IVDR classes B, C, or D, automatically trigger high-risk classification under AIA Article 6. AIA Article 60, as updated by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital AI Omnibus, allows real-world testing outside regulatory sandboxes for high-risk Annex I systems. AIA Article 43 permits Notified Bodies designated under the MDR or IVDR to assess compliance against AIA Section 2 requirements. Annex XIV of the Digital AI Omnibus defines notification codes and categories of AI systems for designation applications under Article 30.

The authors identify overlapping yet non-identical quality management and post-market surveillance obligations as a major friction point. They note that joint guidance MDCG 2025-6 acknowledges the dual burden without giving concrete procedural instructions for integrating both compliance architectures into unified documentation. They describe a surveillance gap in which MDR Class I software remains subject to device surveillance but falls outside AIA post-market monitoring. They state that AIA Article 3(49)(c) defines serious incidents to include disruption of critical infrastructure, breaches of fundamental rights, and environmental or property damage, beyond the MDR and IVDR vigilance threshold of death or severe health impairment. They conclude that targeted, synchronized guidance from the European Commission, the Medical Device Coordination Group, and the Artificial Intelligence Board is urgently required.

The authors say this guidance is needed to establish legal certainty, relieve cumulative compliance burdens, and ensure safe and rapid delivery of innovative clinical AI tools to patients. They state that assessing data computing, algorithmic transparency, and data governance demands specialized technical competencies far exceeding traditional medical software auditing. They note that Annex XIV does not specify how Notified Bodies must objectively demonstrate specialized competence. They write that the absence of aligned guidelines leaves unclear how real-world learning should be validated against traditional clinical evidence standards. Manufacturers face the practical challenge of managing cumulative obligations or maintaining parallel technical documentation streams, and hospitals deploying third-party algorithmic software become both medical users under the MDR and AI deployers under AIA Article 26.

The review states that in-house software developed and used exclusively within health institutions is exempt from third-party conformity assessment under MDR Article 5(5). It says such software avoids high-risk AIA classification under Article 6 while remaining bound by horizontal prohibitions, human oversight, and data governance rules. It notes that the AIA defines providers and deployers, whereas medical regulations define manufacturers and users. It states that increasing fine-tuning of large general-purpose AI models for clinical decision-support raises unresolved legal questions about whether foundation systems are governed as medical software, under systemic-risk rules for general models, or both. It says non-high-risk systems carry no incident reporting obligations under the AIA even if the identical malfunction triggers mandatory vigilance reporting under medical device legislation.

The review states that the AIA establishes no ongoing market surveillance or incident reporting obligations for non-high-risk AI systems. It says MDR Class I manufacturers must produce periodic post-market surveillance reports, and equivalent duties apply to IVDR Class A and Class B devices. It notes that current joint guidance from the Medical Device Coordination Group and the Artificial Intelligence Board acknowledges the dual burden without concrete procedural instructions. It states that AIA Article 73 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to report serious incidents to designated national market surveillance authorities. It says the expanded incident definition creates legal ambiguity about which events trigger reporting, which authority must be alerted, and whether single events require simultaneous notifications under separate timelines.

The authors conclude that synchronized guidance from the European Commission, the Medical Device Coordination Group, and the Artificial Intelligence Board is urgently required. The review leaves open how Notified Bodies must objectively demonstrate specialized competence under Annex XIV. It leaves open how real-world learning by adaptive AI models should be validated against traditional clinical evidence standards. It leaves open whether general-purpose foundation models fine-tuned for clinical decision-support are governed as medical software, under systemic-risk rules, or both. It leaves open how manufacturers can integrate both compliance architectures into a unified documentation framework.

stories.Headline: Baker McKenzie innovation chief predicts legal AI provider shakeout and billable hour rethink
stories.Summary:
Ben Allgrove, Baker McKenzie's global chief innovation officer, said in an interview with Lawyers Weekly that artificial intelligence has become a commercial issue for law firms rather than merely a technology decision, and he predicted a shakeout among legal technology providers. He said the legal profession had spent the past few years debating which AI tools to buy, and that this debate is rapidly becoming out of date. He argued that the implications reach well beyond document drafting and legal research, extending to law firm pricing, profitability, recruitment and the services clients will actually pay for. He also raised the question of the billable hour, given that clients can now do much of the work junior lawyers were once paid to perform.

Allgrove said Baker McKenzie has completed a substantial investment in AI-related talent and training and is now turning its attention to three main areas: improving legal services while managing risk, changing pricing arrangements, and understanding the costs of AI usage. He believes firms must share some of the efficiency gains with clients while demonstrating greater value, which he described as a big deal for firms built around billing lawyer time. He suggested that the firms that succeed will be those that use AI to improve legal outcomes, not simply to reduce the time spent producing them. On the technology market, he said it is already crowded, with too many providers offering similar solutions, often relying on the same underlying AI models, and he expects consolidation or failures as competition intensifies. He does not expect one platform to dominate every legal task, and he said Baker McKenzie's experience suggests complex matters can require three or four different AI tools.

Allgrove acknowledged the challenge AI poses to the training of junior lawyers, saying that future lawyers will still need legal knowledge, sound judgment and analytical skills but must also understand how to use AI to improve their work. The article said AI is increasingly capable of handling the routine contract reviews, due diligence and discovery work that juniors would normally do, and that removing the drudgery also removes the training opportunities those tasks provide. It said the profession therefore faces a new problem of how to produce experienced lawyers when the traditional apprenticeship tasks are disappearing. The article's central message from Baker McKenzie is that AI will change how legal services are delivered, even in complex litigation, major transactions and high-value advisory work, and that competitive advantage will not necessarily belong to the firm with the largest technology budget but to firms that combine excellent lawyers, better services and pricing models clients regard as fair.

stories.Headline: Lee Ju-hee introduces bills requiring AI smart glasses to include recording indicators and user notices
stories.Summary:
Lee Ju-hee, a lawmaker from the Democratic Party on the National Assembly's Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee, introduced two revision bills on the 23rd to require built-in recording indicators and user notices for AI smart glasses and other wearable cameras. The bills would amend the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection and the Personal Information Protection Act. The proposals would set manufacturing and import standards that link recording and indicator functions and require technical measures to prevent the indicators from being disabled. They would also ban making or distributing items designed to neutralise the indicators and expand notice obligations to individual users. The revision to the Information and Communications Network Act would require manufacturers and importers of wearable video recording devices, including smart glasses, to install recording indicator functions.

It would also require technical measures to link recording and indicator functions and to prevent arbitrary disabling or interference with their operation. The bill would ban the manufacture, import, sale and distribution of goods or programmes made to neutralise recording indicator functions. Sellers would have to explain how the indicator works and inform buyers about possible punishment or sanctions for filming others. The revision to the Personal Information Protection Act would expand the duty to notify that filming is taking place to individual users, requiring anyone filming a person or related objects with wearable devices such as glasses or watches to give notice through light, sound or signage regardless of whether the filming is for work. Violations would be subject to an administrative fine of up to 10 million won.

Lee said anyone must be able to know on the spot that they are being filmed and refuse if they do not want it. She said she would establish standards to protect privacy from the filming stage so that people do not end up discovering their appearance filmed by smart glasses online after the fact. The articles say smart glasses have recently sparked controversy over illegal filming without consent. In July, a man in South Korea came under police investigation on allegations that he secretly filmed his dating partner while covering the recording indicator light on AI smart glasses and posted the video on social media. The Personal Information Protection Commission pointed out on the 9th that smart glasses resemble ordinary glasses, making it difficult for people nearby to notice whether recording is taking place, and that users can hide filming by covering indicator devices.

Current law has no standards requiring smart glasses to include recording indicators at the manufacturing or import stage or to prevent the indicators from being disabled at will. Under the Personal Information Protection Act, obligations to display and notify that filming is taking place for portable video information processing devices are limited to filming for work purposes and do not cover individuals' private filming. This month, ahead of the College Scholastic Ability Test, concerns were raised about potential cheating using AI smart glasses, highlighting the need to control entry to test sites and secure detection technology. The articles do not say what happens next with the bills.

stories.Headline: Perplexity counsel says AI will not replace lawyers but will cut their administrative burden
stories.Summary:
On November 24, 2026, Proskauer Rose LLP published an episode of its AI Decoded series, a discussion between partner Oliver Howley and Nathan Barksdale, General Counsel and Vice President of Operations at Perplexity. The episode examined the role of human judgment in legal work, the future of the legal profession, and what is next for Perplexity. Howley is listed as a related professional and the London office as a related office. The two spoke about how lawyers use AI tools and about the opportunities AI creates for the profession. The episode was published on the Proskauer website.

Howley said there is a concern among certain people that AI in legal work removes true human judgment and risk analysis, to the detriment of clients and lawyers. Barksdale said AI and Perplexity is a tool that lawyers and humans use, and that they use their judgment to determine the outcome and how they use the information going forward. He called it a common misconception that these tools will replace all of the work, and said that is impossible. He said AI will find the middle point, and that a party wanting an edge needs humans to intervene and understand the variables of the company and its objective. Howley said there will always be a role, especially in Big Law and in-house teams, for a lawyer to make the ultimate judgment call and manage the room with the EQ and IQ to do a deal that satisfies the business.

Barksdale said AI solves the blank page problem, but does not solve reviewing every single word in detail and ensuring it aligns with the end goal. Howley said he would put in a precedent, describe what he wants, and the Computer for Counsel drafting tool produces a first draft for his review or an associate's review. Barksdale said AI is not going to replace lawyers, but will replace a lot of the administrative burden lawyers do day to day. He said it will make lawyers faster and more efficient and give access to information without going to three parties and waiting for others to finish their part. He said the idea that AI will reduce overhead for companies on outside counsel spend is absolutely incorrect, because there will be more demands on outside counsel as lawyers get more time back for more issues and more work.

Barksdale said the 14 hours a day spent on billable hours becomes the same 14 hours across many different matters and complex tasks, or the administrative side is removed so lawyers use judgment and expertise on more tasks the client wants. Howley said he uses Computer for all his matter openings, feeding in information about a new client so the fields are prepopulated and sent to his assistant, which has made her life and his life a lot easier. He said opening a new matter previously took an hour. Barksdale said a midnight deadline to file a brief spent checking page and word requirements and cutting a sentence in half is not an efficient use of time. Howley said his partner Colin, an antitrust lawyer, wrote a brief over a weekend under a word limit and used the tool to cut it back and make it pithy while keeping the substantive arguments, saving many hours.

Barksdale said it is like having a summer associate that is half the cost. Howley described an internal project reimagine function that automated the end to end process for private fundraising using technology and AI, removing administrative steps so associates can work on multiple fundraisings, service clients, meet them and do business development. He said the technology lets the firm do the work faster, more efficiently, more quickly and, he said, more cheaply. Barksdale said junior lawyers, aspiring lawyers and law students will practice entirely differently from how he and Howley practiced over the past 20 years. He said Perplexity brought in its first legal intern this summer, a first-year law student whose sole task was to figure out how the company and team can utilize AI better, and he called it probably one of the single most successful things the team did this summer.

Barksdale said the intern will take what he learned in-house to his second-year summer at a firm, and that classes and junior associate classes three or four years from now will practice wildly differently. Howley asked about the future for Perplexity, mentioning a potential IPO and the products Comet, Computer and Computer for Counsel. Barksdale said Perplexity has traditionally been at the top of the AI stack and is seen as the application layer, but develops every single layer. He said Perplexity recently announced Space, a sandbox layer where people can test workflows in a contained environment before release. He said Perplexity is next venturing into hybrid inference and hybrid AI, with products shortly for NVIDIA, Intel and Apple to meet better cost, security and speed.

Howley explained hybrid AI as having certain processes and models running on-device and calling out to the cloud when necessary. Barksdale said local AI allows much faster processing and speeds and more security assurances for customers concerned with the cloud environment, where only information absolutely necessary and at the customer's direction goes to the cloud or downstream sub-processors. He said this should help with costs and token usage because it will be local and contained. Howley said there is tension between sandboxed or air-gapped security solutions where nothing leaves the environment and the most powerful models hosted elsewhere, and asked how Perplexity bridges that gap. Barksdale said every business will be unique in how it wants its AI infrastructure set up, and more variety will be better for all industries and businesses.

Barksdale said AI is meant to be tailored and tweaked for every single customer and user, and that where SaaS was one-size-fits-all, AI is wholly unique to every individual. Howley closed by thanking Barksdale for joining. The episode was published as part of the AI Decoded series, and the page invites readers to view the rest of the episodes and subscribe to Proskauer's publications. The articles give no further steps beyond the products Barksdale said are coming shortly for NVIDIA, Intel and Apple. The articles leave open the timing of those products and where the potential IPO will go.

stories.Headline: Anthropic launches Enterprise Frontier Safeguards to detect harmful AI activity with zero data retention
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched a public beta of Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, a capability that lets organizations detect potentially harmful AI activity across multiple interactions while keeping zero data retention, the company said on November 25, 2026. The system uses automated safety systems to analyze conversations stored in customer-controlled cloud environments and to flag suspicious behavior for security teams to investigate. Anthropic said the tool addresses a gap in legacy zero data retention safeguards, which screen individual requests for signs of misuse even though sophisticated attacks can span several interactions that each look harmless alone. The company pointed to its September threat intelligence report, which documented an operation targeting roughly 50 organizations in which an AI agent delegated attack tasks to other agents and kept stolen credentials between sessions.

When the system detects a potential threat, it creates a Safety Case that security teams can retrieve from their cloud storage or access through an API, and cases can be integrated into security information and event management systems. Anthropic said the cases contain neither prompts nor responses, and the monitoring can help identify both deliberate misuse and AI agents acting beyond their users' intentions, such as exploiting software vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access to internal databases or external systems. Organizations store AI inputs and outputs in their own cloud environments, and according to Anthropic neither the company nor its cloud partners retain copies once the information has been transferred to customer-controlled storage. Customers configure access policies and audit logging and encrypt safety data with their own keys, while provider-side access to conversation content is restricted to automated safety monitoring systems, and Anthropic said neither its personnel nor cloud provider personnel can review it and the information is not used to train models or classifiers.

Omar Santos, a Distinguished Engineer at Cisco, said customers can keep sensitive data in their own environments protected with their own encryption keys while still preserving the specialized safety mechanisms frontier capabilities require, and he called that balance critical to broader adoption of advanced AI in security-sensitive organizations like Cisco. EFS is available through the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock and Claude on Google Cloud, and for Amazon Bedrock and Google-managed deployments the respective cloud provider operates the safeguards with the entire data flow remaining within its environment. Support for Microsoft Foundry is coming soon, and depending on the deployment customers can use Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage and are responsible for the associated storage and usage costs. Anthropic said eligible organizations will receive instructions on how to get started.

stories.Headline: Intuit study finds AI adoption makes employers more attractive to junior accountants
stories.Summary:
Research commissioned by Intuit, and published on 25 November 2026, found that employers showing off their AI capabilities while recruiting are more likely to attract entry-level accounting candidates. The study, commissioned by Intuit QuickBooks, surveyed 1,003 people in the UK aged 18 to 24 between 1 June and 11 June 2026. It reported that 89% of candidates want embedded AI tools, structured training and modern career pathways from the start of their employment. Respondents also considered conversational AI tools built into financial software very useful for data analysis, reporting, research, brainstorming, summarising insights and automating workflows.

The findings put candidate confidence at a high level, with 91% believing AI technology will lift their career prospects and feeling prepared for roles where it plays a central part. A total of 68% believe their skills will lead to faster career progression, while 35% expect to move into higher-value advisory positions earlier in their careers. Preparation varied across the group, with 47% naming self-directed learning as their main preparation for AI, 32% citing university education and 20% pointing to work experience. On training, 46% of candidates expect regular workplace training and 36% anticipate ongoing training throughout their careers.

The research also flagged a possible disconnect between candidate confidence and readiness for risk, since automating traditional junior tasks could leave graduates without the practical experience needed to underpin sound professional judgement. Intuit sorted future accountants into four personas, the largest being highly engaged users who favour strong governance at 34%, followed by cautious adopters who seek oversight at 26%. Confident users who tend to underestimate potential risks made up 23%, and the remaining 16% were uncertain about the technology and its implications. Overall, 88% of respondents said a firm's AI adoption makes it more attractive.

The study was commissioned by Intuit QuickBooks, which published the findings on 25 November 2026. It covered 1,003 UK respondents aged 18 to 24, surveyed between 1 June and 11 June 2026. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Hochul signs New York law banning internet-connected AI chatbot toys for five years
stories.Summary:
New York will ban internet-connected AI chatbot toys for five years starting 90 days after Governor Kathy Hochul signed S.9408A on November 24, 2026. The signing announcement prohibits manufacturing, distribution, and sale of dolls, stuffed animals, and robots that use the internet to hold conversational AI with children. Attorney General Letitia James may fine violators up to $15,000 per day. The law does not take effect before the 2026 holiday season, and Hochul used the signing to warn parents while shelves still hold chatbot products. S.9408A/A.11144B creates a five-year moratorium rather than a permanent ban.

The moratorium covers toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots that use the internet, such as always-on cloud models in plush form factors, not offline speech chips with fixed scripts. It covers manufacturing, distribution, and sale in New York, so companies assembling outside the state still cannot distribute into New York retail once it is effective. The effective date is about 90 days after signing, late February 2027 unless guidance shifts. The release cites findings including sexually explicit conversations, instructions to find matches inside a family home, emotional upset when a child stops talking, and parental controls that weaken as sessions lengthen. The release does not name the watchdog behind those described failures.

Sponsors Senator Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Rebecca Kassay say the pause buys time to study developmental impacts and write durable rules for biometric collection, open-ended dialog, and manipulation risks. Hochul said parents should not worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could manipulate feelings or risk privacy. James said her office will enforce and will not let children's health become collateral damage of big tech. Gounardes said the rush to sell AI toys is profits before kids' safety and the pause enables study then smart protections. Kassay said toys can mimic human relationships while collecting sensitive data without guardrails, hence the moratorium to assess emerging tech.

Common Sense Media and Mothers Against Media Addiction praised the moratorium but urge traditional toys this season because the ban is not yet legally active. Common Sense Media's CEO urges traditional toys and human engagement this season. The release says Gounardes and Kassay championed the bill with near-unanimous Senate and Assembly support. The release says the governor cites New York's number one national ranking after laws like the SAFE for Kids Act, Child Data Protection Act, Distraction Free Learning phone rules, and the RAISE Act on frontier-model transparency. The release tells caregivers to look past packaging for AI companion labels, data collection, and open-ended chat.

In October 2026 Hochul signed AI Companion rules blocking chatbot features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm, or engage minors in sexually explicit talk. The release says the toy moratorium extends that logic into hardware, since a microphone in a teddy bear is still a companion surface. The release says New York already banned unsafe AI companion features for minors and AI-generated CSAM and tightened school phone rules. The release says the toy ban adds physical devices to a portfolio that includes Safe by Design, Social Media Warning Labels, and Teen Mental Health First Aid funding. The release says New York already restricts phones in schools and funds Teen Mental Health First Aid.

The release says five years is long enough that federal rules may preempt parts of the moratorium, and it advises tracking National Governors Association governor frontier-AI letters for overlapping state-federal fights. It advises monitoring CPSC and FTC AI rulemakings alongside New York. It says retailers operating nationally should not assume New York-only SKUs are enough if drop-ship or marketplace listings still reach New York addresses. It advises documenting data deletion flows if toys record biometrics and pulling New York-bound inventory before the effective date. It says the post summarizes the November 24, 2026 governor signing release and is not legal advice, and it directs readers to the enrolled bill text on the New York State Senate site for definitions, exemptions, and exact effective language.

stories.Headline: Taiwan passes law to return AI industry tax revenue to citizens
stories.Summary:
The Taiwan Legislative Court passed a special ordinance on the twentieth of November to return tax revenue from the artificial intelligence industry boom to the people. This legislation, which is referred to as the AI Bonus Act, was pushed through by the main opposition People's Party. The bill passed with a narrow margin of fifty votes in favor and forty six votes against. This move aims to share the economic performance of the AI market to help stabilize the livelihoods of citizens.

The plan requires paying twenty thousand dollars per person to all citizens regardless of their age, income, or regional restrictions. This amount is significantly higher than the ten thousand dollars per person that the ruling Democratic Progressive Party already included in the budget for next year. The ruling party has expressed official opposition to the bill because of the current financial conditions of the state. The National Party has claimed that the results of upcoming local elections will determine if these bonuses are actually paid.

The ruling and opposition parties are currently fighting over the specific scale of the tax refunds ahead of the local elections. Members of the National Party appealed for public support by linking the bonus payments to the election outcomes. The Democratic Progressive Party argues that increasing the payment beyond their budget plan is difficult to achieve. Because the two sides are in sharp confrontation, the process to determine the final payment size will likely take time.

Taiwan has a history of providing cash and consumption coupons to the public to respond to economic downturns or shrinking consumption. During the global financial crisis in the late two thousands, the government distributed consumption coupons worth three thousand six hundred Taiwan dollars per person. In the early twenty twenties, the state paid coupons worth three thousand and five thousand Taiwan dollars during an infectious disease spread. Last year, the government handed out ten thousand dollars per person to alleviate economic shocks caused by mutual tariffs with the United States.

stories.Headline: Italy’s data regulator signals closer AI transparency checks from 2026
stories.Summary:
From 2026, Italian supervisory authorities including the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali are signalling closer scrutiny of how companies document, publish and prove the behaviour of their AI systems, according to Global Advisory Experts on November 24, 2026. The guide addresses businesses that build, sell or use artificial intelligence in Italy. It says AI Act transparency in Italy is no longer a topic for the legal team alone. The scrutiny comes on top of what the General Data Protection Regulation already demands. The guide sets out a step-by-step approach to assembling a package to put in front of a regulator.

The EU Artificial Intelligence Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. In Italy the AI Act is being put into effect through national legislation that designates the competent national authorities, while the Garante remains the data protection authority. GDPR Article 13 and Article 14 require that people are told about processing, Article 30 requires records of processing activities, and Article 35 requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment where processing is likely to create high risk for individuals. High-risk examples listed include employment and worker management, access to essential services, creditworthiness assessment, education, law enforcement and critical infrastructure. Biometric data used to identify a person uniquely is a special category of personal data under Article 9.

Responsibility is shared, the guide says. Providers, those who build a system or place it on the market, carry the main technical documentation and conformity burden. Deployers, those who use a system, carry duties around the context of use, following instructions and informing users. Under the GDPR the controller and any processors need clearly allocated roles recorded in data processing agreements. The guide says an accountable owner should be named for each set of documents before any drafting begins.

The guide says the high-risk threshold is wider than many businesses expect. Small and medium-sized enterprises should not assume they are exempt, and a business deploying a third-party high-risk system still carries deployer duties and GDPR controller duties for any personal data involved. The guide says a regulator is very often asked first to see the AI system register. It says the first things to show a regulator are the system register, the current DPIA, the model card and the model change log.

The guide says the AI Act sets up a risk-based regime, with the heaviest documentation and transparency duties falling on high-risk systems and on systems that interact directly with people. It says the AI Act does not displace the GDPR but sits alongside it, so one inspection can touch AI Act technical documentation and GDPR accountability evidence at the same time. It says prohibited practices are banned outright, and that deployers of high-risk systems must be able to show they use the system in line with the provider's instructions. It says the AI Act includes proportionality measures and simplified routes meant to ease the load on smaller providers, which change how documentation is produced, not whether transparency and safety duties apply. It says training data provenance is increasingly scrutinised in 2026.

The guide recommends running the steps broadly in order, though several can overlap, and says a timeline table after the steps gives realistic durations for a system of middling complexity. It recommends a tabletop exercise in which compliance, legal and an executive sponsor answer a simulated regulatory request under time pressure. It says such exercises reliably expose gaps, such as a missing DPIA signature or an out-of-date register, while there is still time to fix them. It says a strong package depends as much on organisation as on content, and that an inspector forms an early impression from how quickly a document can be found. The article ends mid-sentence, at the words "Adopt a stable, numbe".

stories.Headline: New York governor Kathy Hochul signs a five-year ban on AI-enabled toys
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill on Tuesday that bans the sale, distribution and manufacture of AI-enabled toys in the state for five years, announcing the measure from a toy store in Harlem. The ban is set to begin in mid-February and applies to anyone statewide, with violations carrying a fine of $15,000 per day. Hochul said the products are harmful to children and described the move as a warning that some toys out there could hurt kids. She said that when tech companies and unregulated AI pose a threat to children and babies, she is going to have something to say about it. The toys covered by the ban are often stuffed animals integrated with chatbots that children can talk or text with, and the articles describe tests in which some of them went rogue when led into certain conversations.

NBC News testers watched one toy describe gang-rape and historical execution methods in graphic detail, while another tested by Common Sense Media was found encouraging kids to jump from roofs and windows. That same testing found the toys urging users as young as 5 to believe the chatbot was as real as their human friends. The ban bars businesses from selling, distributing or manufacturing the techie toys to anyone statewide, and the $15,000 per-day fine applies to violations. Hochul was joined by State Senator Andrew Gounardes, a Brooklyn Democrat who authored the ban bill and evoked the menacing Talky Tina doll from the 1962 "Twilight Zone" episode. Gounardes said that what the show's writer and host Rod Serling warned of in 1963 is actually here, pointing to the headlines appearing day after day.

He asked who knows what these chatbots are saying, what data they are collecting on children and what they are doing with it. He said kids deserve a real childhood, real toys and real connections, and the ability to play with their friends in the streets and at home. Hochul declined to expand on how AI toys would be handled after the ban but suggested she would speak on wider AI regulatory plans at her January state of the state address. The articles describe the ban as the latest cautionary measure she has taken against AI in New York, noting that she banned data center construction for one year in July, a move that frustrated tech proponents but satisfied AI-skeptical citizens. The articles do not say what happens to AI toys already owned by families or what steps would follow once the five-year period ends.

stories.Headline: Uganda applies existing data, cyber and finance laws to AI under guide
stories.Summary:
Uganda has no dedicated artificial intelligence statute, and the country's existing laws already set rules for how AI may be built, trained and deployed, according to a guide published on November 23, 2026 by Global Advisory Experts. The guide says the Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019, the Computer Misuse Act, 2011 (as amended), rules from the Uganda Communications Commission and prudential expectations from the Bank of Uganda are the main building blocks. It states that businesses using automated systems to score customers, route network traffic or rank content are already subject to artificial intelligence regulation in Uganda. The guide was last updated in September 2026 and is aimed at founders, executives, compliance leads and product and risk teams at banks, telecoms operators and digital platforms doing business in Uganda. Brian Kalule of AF Mpanga Advocates is listed as the featured expert on the matter.

The Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019 and the Data Protection and Privacy Regulations, 2021 require processing to be lawful, fair and transparent, limited to a stated purpose, minimised, accurate and secure, the guide states. The Personal Data Protection Office, established under NITA-U, is the supervisory authority, and the guide says a lawful basis must exist before personal data is used to train or run a model. The Computer Misuse Act, 2011, as amended in 2022, criminalises unauthorised access to computer systems, unauthorised interception and interference with data or systems, according to the guide. The Uganda Communications Commission was established under the Uganda Communications Act, 2013, and the Bank of Uganda oversees financial-sector innovation under the National Payment Systems Act, 2020 and the Financial Institutions Act, 2004 (as amended). The guide says the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance steers digital strategy and emerging technology policy.

The guide states that the board or senior management should accept ultimate accountability for AI, and each material model should have a named owner for its whole lifecycle. It says a workable structure includes an AI or model risk policy, a register of the AI systems in use, approval gates before deployment and periodic reviews. The guide states that a data protection impact assessment is the central compliance document for AI that processes personal data at scale or makes automated decisions about people, and should be completed before deployment. It says people affected by AI should be told in plain terms that automated processing is taking place and given meaningful information about its logic and consequences. The guide states that the Bank of Uganda expects banks to manage operational risk, control outsourcing, protect consumers and maintain sound governance.

The guide says three areas carry the most immediate enforcement risk: unlawful or opaque use of personal data in AI systems, weak governance and model oversight in supervised financial services, and platform failures in content moderation and consumer protection. It states that businesses treating AI as an unregulated frontier risk administrative penalties, criminal liability under cybercrime provisions and reputational damage. The guide says the sensible response for 2026 is to formalise AI governance, give the board clear accountability, complete data protection impact assessments, tighten supplier contracts and build an incident playbook tied to each regulator's reporting timeline. It states that operators must reconcile automated network optimisation, traffic classification, content filtering and recommendation engines with consumer privacy duties and licence conditions. The guide says the lack of a separate set of UCC AI guidelines changes nothing because existing licensing and content rules already apply to algorithmic systems.

The guide states that the country has no dedicated AI statute yet, and that data protection law, computer misuse provisions, telecoms licensing and financial-sector supervision already set the rules. It says the current position should be thought of as existing law applied to new technology. The guide states that policy statements from NITA-U and the Ministry of ICT are not always directly enforceable but indicate where binding rules are heading. It says regulators increasingly cite those policy statements when interpreting existing obligations. The guide states that following these sources helps businesses anticipate the next phase of technology law in Uganda.

The guide states that regulated firms should track Bank of Uganda releases continuously and feed new instruments into their model risk framework without delay. It says any circular or guidance on automated decisioning, model governance or fintech operational risk becomes a mandatory reference point. The guide states that where a model makes or materially influences an outcome for an individual, such as a credit score, a fraud flag or a demoted post, good practice is to explain the basis for the outcome and offer human review and redress. It says gaining unauthorised access to third-party systems to harvest data can create criminal exposure. The guide states that if an AI-related security incident occurs, a business may need to involve cybercrime enforcement authorities in addition to making civil breach notifications.

stories.Headline: LexisNexis finds 20% of law firms rely heavily on a few partners for revenue as AI reshapes how expertise is shared
stories.Summary:
LexisNexis published research on 23 November 2026, based on a survey of more than 500 private practice lawyers across the UK and Ireland, which found that 20% of firms are either completely or heavily reliant on a handful of individuals for revenue. The research was presented in an article by a Legal Futures associate, and it describes the traditional rainmaker model, in which a successful partner builds the client relationship, wins the work and becomes closely associated with the revenue that follows. The article says that model is not going away, because legal services are still built on relationships and clients still want advisers they trust, but it argues the model is beginning to shift. The research also found that 65% of lawyers now use AI for legal research, while more than half use it for document analysis, knowledge management and client drafting. The article says the old model concentrates value around the individual partner, including the relationship, the matter history and the commercial context, which can be powerful but also creates risk, since the impact of a partner leaving can reach well beyond the loss of a senior lawyer.

The emerging model it describes is more distributed, still recognising the importance of the partner but placing more weight on the firm's wider platform, including deeper teams, shared knowledge, consistent delivery and technology-enabled ways of working. The article says AI makes it easier for firms to capture expertise, reuse knowledge and deliver work more consistently across teams, which challenges the assumption that much of the value sits in one person's head. It says personal expertise does not become less important, but that it can be turned into a stronger institutional asset. The article says clients increasingly expect the wider firm to deliver consistently, efficiently and transparently, with depth behind the relationship, continuity if people move on, and outcomes that can be explained to the business. It says that if AI can support faster research, document review and drafting, firms will need to show more clearly what clients are paying for, and that the answer will increasingly sit in judgement, quality, speed, commercial insight and confidence in the right result.

The article says the rainmaker is unlikely to disappear, but the role may become less about individual ownership and more about building trust that can scale. It says the most valuable partners will still win work and build relationships, but will also help develop teams, share knowledge and create client relationships strong enough to outlast any one person. The article frames the question for law firm leaders as a practical one: how much of a firm's value sits with individual rainmakers, and how much has been built into the platform around them. It does not say what firms or regulators will do next, and it gives no further dates or figures beyond those above.

stories.Headline: Nexent Capital launches $1 billion fund for quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy
stories.Summary:
Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited announced on 25 November 2026 the launch of Nexent Capital ADGM Fund I, a closed-end fund targeting US$1 billion in capital commitments with a hard cap of US$1.6 billion. The fund is dedicated to quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy investment, and it will deploy capital across five complementary strategies. Those strategies are infrastructure private equity in AI and data-center assets, private credit and structured capital, special-situations M&A, growth equity and PIPEs, and liquid public equity exposure within the AI and data-center value chain. The fund is structured as an ADGM-domiciled Qualified Investor Fund as the master fund, with a GIFT City-based IFSCA-regulated Alternative Investment Fund acting as its feeder. Nexent Capital ADGM Limited is being established as the fund's licensed ADGM Fund Manager.

The fund has an anchor commitment of US$20 million from the Tyagi family office and line of sight to an identified pipeline of quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy projects across North America and India. That pipeline includes data-center and power assets sponsored by affiliates of the Nexent Capital and Tryfacta platform, and the fund's minimum investment is US$500,000. Nexent Capital IFSC is working with a large Abu Dhabi-based fund administrator that globally manages over $3.4 trillion in assets, and it is progressing formal engagement of legal counsel and an auditor as part of its path to FSRA authorisation and first close. The fund is targeting a first close within approximately six months of FSRA authorisation, with a final close targeted six months thereafter, and it is preparing for FSRA authorisation.

Adesh Tyagi, Managing Partner of Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited, said AI is being built on a foundation of physical infrastructure, namely power, land and compute, that most capital is not positioned to finance at the scale or speed the moment demands. He said the fund, with its GIFT City feeder, is designed to meet that gap directly and to give institutional and family-office investors a disciplined way to back the infrastructure and energy assets underpinning the next decade of AI growth. Abhimanyu Tyagi, Director of Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited, said the pipeline is not theoretical but is built on relationships and projects the platform has been developing for years, from data-center conversions to gigawatt-scale energy campuses. He said that gives investors in the fund a head start that most new vehicles in the space simply do not have.

The launch comes as global investors increasingly look to deploy capital into the physical infrastructure underpinning AI growth, including power generation, data centers and advanced energy systems. It also comes as GIFT City and the Abu Dhabi Global Market continue to develop as complementary gateways for structuring cross-border alternative investment vehicles.

stories.Headline: Brookfield agrees $1.7 billion deal to buy PGP Glass from Blackstone and plans AI-led efficiency push
stories.Summary:
Brookfield, a global investment firm, agreed to acquire the speciality glass packaging manufacturer PGP Glass from Blackstone in a deal valued at $1.7 billion, according to Reuters, and the agreement was announced on Monday, November 23, 2026. Brookfield will acquire PGP through its flagship private equity strategy, and the investment will involve Brookfield Capital Partners and affiliate Brookfield Business Corporation. The transaction requires regulatory and government approvals, with completion expected during the first quarter of 2027. The deal marks a major investment in India's premium glass packaging industry, and it will transfer PGP Glass between two major global investment firms.

PGP Glass manufactures premium packaging for cosmetics, perfumes, pharmaceuticals and speciality food and beverages, and the company serves leading international brands across more than 70 countries. It operates three manufacturing facilities across India and Sri Lanka, and its services include product design, mould-making, speciality glass manufacturing and decoration. The company also maintains an extensive global logistics and warehousing network, and its integrated operations enable customers to access multiple packaging services through a single manufacturer. Brookfield sees considerable growth opportunities as global demand for premium glass packaging increases, and it plans to strengthen existing customer relationships while entering new international markets. Targeted investments in manufacturing capacity will support the company's expansion plans.

Artificial intelligence will play an important role in Brookfield's strategy for PGP Glass, and the investment firm intends to improve production efficiency through AI-driven operational changes covering sales planning, manufacturing operations and quality control. Aditya Joshi, Brookfield's private equity head for Asia Pacific and the Middle East, said that as demand for high-quality packaging continues to increase worldwide, Brookfield brings the scale and operating expertise to accelerate PGP's growth through an AI-led transformation program. Blackstone's Amit Dalmia praised PGP's operating performance and sustainability achievements under its ownership, saying the management team under Vijay Shah delivered outstanding operating performance, outpaced its peers and demonstrated leadership in sustainability. Shah welcomed Brookfield as the company's next investment partner, highlighting its international presence and experience managing businesses across economic cycles, and he acknowledged Blackstone's contribution towards PGP's manufacturing expansion and operational improvements.

The acquisition comes amid changing conditions in the global glass packaging industry, where European and North American manufacturers face rising costs and reductions in production capacity. These pressures could create opportunities for efficient manufacturers such as PGP Glass, and premium glass packaging also benefits from established demand and limited substitution risks. Brookfield manages assets exceeding $1 trillion across infrastructure, energy, private equity, real estate and credit, while Blackstone manages nearly $1.4 trillion across its global investment businesses. Brookfield will focus on international expansion, manufacturing improvements and technology-driven growth following the transaction.

stories.Headline: Anthropic rolls out beta install as app feature turning Claude artifacts into desktop apps
stories.Summary:
Anthropic said on November 24, 2026 that it had begun rolling out an “Install as app” feature in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows, letting people turn Claude artifacts into desktop apps. The company said an installed artifact gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. Anthropic said users can share the app with others, and that it needs the user’s permission before it can interact with the computer. The company said users choose how much to allow. Anthropic described the feature in a product update dated November 24, 2026, with a reading time of four minutes.

Anthropic said each installed app can use Claude and the user’s connectors, and updates automatically when the underlying artifact is edited. It said requests the app makes to Claude count toward the plan’s usage limits. Anthropic said installed apps can send notifications or add items to the menu bar or system tray. It said users choose permissions for each app, and that Team and Enterprise admins can turn app permissions and full access on or off for their organization. Anthropic said the feature is rolling out in beta on all plans, that HIPAA-ready organizations and hybrid deployments cannot use it, and that it is on by default for Team with full access off.

Anthropic said that on Enterprise the feature is off until an owner turns it on. It said users need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app, and that some artifacts cannot be installed, including Claude Docs, Slides and Sheets. Anthropic said users should describe their app to Claude, try it as an artifact, then click “Install as app,” and that they do not have to package or sign it. It said the app uses the Claude account, so there is no API key or separate login. Anthropic said users should update Claude for Mac or Windows, open an artifact, and choose “Install as app” from the Share menu.

Anthropic said installed apps can only do by default what they would be able to do in a browser. It said apps can ask to use common features Claude can tightly control, such as creating always-on-top windows, listening for global shortcuts or sending notifications. Anthropic said apps can ask for full computer access to run programs and read, change or delete files without asking each time. It said a user’s permission covers only the current version of the app, so Claude asks again after every update, even the user’s own edits. Anthropic said that if part of an app comes from another website, that part can change without Claude asking again.

Anthropic said users can give full access only to apps they made or, on Team and Enterprise, apps made by people in their organization. It said Anthropic does not review apps before installation, so users should give full access only to apps they trust. Anthropic said artifacts started as a work output to share, like a chart or a webpage, and that people now use them as tools for everyday work, such as a meeting prep page that pulls from calendar and email or a tracker for orders that need to ship that day. It said that if you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention. Anthropic listed demo apps including Linnet, a full layered image editor, and Phosphor, a file manager.

Anthropic also listed Sift, which sets up folder rules and uses Claude to keep things organized, Tern, a terminal with Claude to help and explain, and Vitals, a menu bar and tray app for peeking at the computer’s performance. It said more demo apps made by one of its engineers could be seen at a linked page. Anthropic said the feature simplifies building and maintaining apps for both knowledge workers and developers. It said the rollout is in beta on all plans. Anthropic did not say when the beta would end or when the feature would reach general availability.

stories.Headline: Bill Ackman says AI fears hit only a small slice of S&P Global as ratings drive real risk
stories.Summary:
Bill Ackman said AI fears hit a single-digit slice of S&P Global, and the rest of the company drives its earnings, according to remarks relayed on the We Study Billionaires podcast. The comments were reported by TIKR.com in an article last updated on Nov 23, 2026, written by Roxanna Maglangit and reviewed by Michael Douglass. S&P Global lost about $40 billion of market value in about 10 days this year, as AI-agent fears also hit FactSet and MSCI. In the first week of February, Anthropic released a set of plugins for its Claude assistant, and the market reaction was to sell every company that makes money selling information to professionals. S&P Global's 2026 guidance then came in light, and Bill Ackman's Pershing Square had disclosed a new stake in S&P Global over the summer.

Capital IQ clients pay by the seat, and an AI agent that does the clicking and the reading could make the seat unnecessary. Daniel Mahncke estimates that Capital IQ subscriptions bring in something like 6% of company revenue and even less of profit, roughly $900 million against fiscal 2025's $15.3 billion of total revenue. The Market Intelligence division that includes Capital IQ still grew revenue 7% in the third quarter, and FactSet grew its organic annual subscription value 7.0% in the fiscal year ended Aug. 31. S&P Dow Jones Indices grew revenue 20% to $554 million in the third quarter, driven mainly by asset-linked fees on higher assets under management. MSCI's Index segment revenue rose 18.1% in the third quarter, and consensus has normalized EPS rising from $17.95 this year to $22.77 in fiscal 2028, or about 13% a year.

Ackman argues investors fixated on threats to a single-digit slice of the company and lost sight of the fact that future earnings growth will be driven almost entirely by the benchmark business. O'Malley relayed that case on the show and said he thinks Ackman is mostly right. O'Malley was blunt about the ratings risk, saying that if it becomes clear AI was a bubble and it has popped, there will be a drought in debt issuance. Mahncke noted that the hyperscalers issued something like $240 billion of debt in the first nine months of this year, which is more than S&P had assumed for the entire year. The article's author wrote that Ackman has the AI story right and that the risk worth pricing in is a down cycle in ratings once AI borrowing slows.

S&P Global's ratings revenue grew 11% over those nine months, to $3.91 billion, and Moody's investment-grade ratings revenue jumped 18% in the third quarter on tech borrowers, including AI-related and hyperscaler financing. Moody's total ratings revenue slipped 1%, and the article says the ratings business is riding a wave of AI debt. TIKR tracks 23 analysts on S&P Global, and more than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. FactSet was called almost entirely an interface by Mahncke, and the article says it is far more exposed than S&P Global. The article says that if the company most exposed to this threat is still growing, a 6% slice won't sink S&P Global.

Even after a rebound from its June low, S&P Global trades at 23x forward earnings, well below its five-year average of 28x. It bottomed at 20x in late June, the cheapest it has been in five years. The article says the discount, at five turns below its average multiple, more than covers the ratings cycle risk. The article states that the market is pricing the wrong fear and that Ackman has the AI story right. The article says the real AI exposure is in ratings, where S&P Global gets paid when companies borrow, and right now the biggest borrowers are building data centers.

The next test comes in early February with fourth-quarter results and 2027 guidance. Guidance that keeps EPS on track for the $20.16 consensus would back Ackman's case, while a ratings outlook that leans even harder on hyperscaler deals would mean the cycle risk is growing. The article leaves open what S&P Global stock is actually worth, offering a TIKR valuation model that starts from Wall Street consensus estimates or adjusted inputs. The article's disclaimer states that its content is not intended as investment or financial advice and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any stocks. The disclaimer adds that the analysis might not include recent company news or important updates and that TIKR has no position in any of the stocks mentioned.

stories.Headline: Clients blindly trusting AI legal advice increase pressure and emotional labor for lawyers
stories.Summary:
Lawyer Huang Qin passed away after collapsing during a communication with a client. This event occurred on November 13, when Hubei Maple Leaf Law Firm released her obituary. The 48-year-old lawyer died following continuous high-pressure overwork and extreme exhaustion. She was handling a case for a legal aid recipient named Duan. The collapse happened after she told the client that his lack of trust broke her heart.

Duan insisted for three to four months that Huang Qin follow AI legal advice. This pestering delayed the case and included calls and texts at 9 p.m. Other lawyers, like Lin Liming from Beijing Yingke (Dongguan) Law Firm, noticed this trend since 2025. Lin Liming handled a divorce case where a party doubted a judge's property decision. This party relied on AI, which wrongly claimed the judge's decision was incorrect.

Lin Liming stated that incomplete case descriptions lead AI to provide wrong answers. He noted that AI often fabricates false laws and cases through hallucinations. Lawyer Xie He from Guangzhou Luoya Law Firm said AI caters to users. She claimed AI-generated documents can be unprofessional, emotional, and irrelevant to the case. Xie He warned that lawyers bear the liability for faults, not the AI.

Clients who blindly trust AI are driving lawyers to experience extreme mental exhaustion. These parties use AI to question the competence and professionalism of their lawyers. This behavior affects the judicial resource allocation of court mediation and trial systems. Legal aid recipients are often affected, as they may distrust randomly assigned free lawyers. Some clients miss first instance opportunities by following AI instead of hiring lawyers.

The articles state that AI can create information illusions for those lacking professional knowledge. Many people now use social media tutorials to learn about suing with AI. Legal aid lawyers are often young professionals who join the pool for experience. Article 46 of the Legal Aid Law forbids refusing or delaying legal aid services. This law applies to the random assignments handled by the judicial bureau.

Lawyers now face higher communication costs and more emotional labor due to AI. Some lawyers choose to compromise with clients, while others take a stronger attitude. It remains unclear if technology increases the burden or brings new opportunities. The articles leave open whether this trust crisis will permanently change the agency relationship. They do not state if new regulations will limit AI use in courts.
