stories.Headline: Australian AI committee recommends payment and transparency rules for training models on local content
stories.Summary:
The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence published its report, titled Artificial Intelligence ,  the Australian way, on 24 November 2026, according to The Conversation. The report contains 46 recommendations and broadly supports the Australian government in welcoming AI companies to operate in Australia. It backs training large language models on Australian content and “investing” in infrastructure, which likely means building more data centres here. The report recommends that changes to copyright law must “consider how individual rights holders and individual creators receive payment for the use of their work”. It does not recognise the existing wholesale harvesting of Australian content for AI models, and does not adequately address problematic use of First Nations culture by big tech.

The report recommends transparency from AI companies on their use of Australian content, payment for artists whose work is used by someone else for commercial gain, and “strong penalties for failure to comply with the law, including breaches of technical protections”. It recommends that “frontier AI companies” be given “the certainty necessary to train their AI models in Australia”, in a way that reflects Australian values and culture. It recommends the government “incentivise commercial deals between large rights holders and collective agencies”, and create a mechanism to make it easier and fairer for Australian rights holders and creators to be paid by AI companies training models in Australia. It recommends the government “include consideration of the protection of the cultural authority of Australia’s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders”. It recommends the government “develop and implement whole-of-government procurement and adoption policies that leverage Commonwealth purchasing power to stimulate investment in Australian AI capabilities”.

The report comes from the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, and committee member and ACT Senator David Pocock issued a dissenting report addressing data centres and copyright. On copyright, Pocock called on the government to refrain from making any changes to existing copyright law, to focus on enforcing existing protections, and to facilitate licensing deals. He said that if Australia creates conditions more relaxed than other jurisdictions, the country is at risk of becoming the “the copyright equivalent of the Cayman Islands”. Australian author Charlotte Wood called out AI companies for “demanding that our Labor government greenlight the greatest wage theft in history”, while causing harm to the environment and democracies.

The campaign Not Theirs to Take argues for protection of Australia’s creative and media sector, which it says contributes $70.3 billion to the Australian economy and employs almost 600,000 workers. A central message of the campaign is that “AI companies should not be able to use Australian creative work without permission and agreed payment”. The Guardian’s Josh Butler reported that the report was expected on Monday, November 23, at the start of parliament’s final four sitting days of 2026. Liberal MP Garth Hamilton described AI as “just good old-fashioned theft” and proposed a levy on companies, while former Nationals leader David Littleproud said Anthropic could afford to pay copyright holders. Shadow attorney general Michaelia Cash called a possible music carveout a “ham-fisted tactic” and warned against property being stolen.

The Conversation states that Australian copyright law is automatic, so as soon as an artist creates a work they have copyright, and that payments from the Copyright Agency are a key component of artist income. It says training on Australian content in overseas data centres does not result in remuneration for Australian artists, but does create the opportunity for AI users to replicate Australian content and potentially profit from it. It says the report does not address the existing use of Australian content to train AI models around the world. It says organisations such as the National Library of Australia have been undertaking extensive programs to develop Indigenous cultural and intellectual property protocols, work it describes as time-consuming and highly laborious. Superpower Daily reported that creative industries reacted with dismay last week to reports that Labor was considering a music carveout within a permit system for AI companies, reports that landed the morning after the ARIA Awards, where prominent musicians backed the Not AI’s To Take campaign.

Superpower Daily reported that senior figures Richard Marles, Tim Ayres and Michelle Rowland have increasingly argued that existing copyright law has shortcomings, while major rightsholder groups dispute the need to change the law. It reported that Duniam and Violi made their appeal for a less partisan approach about a fortnight before the expected report. It said the report could show whether Labor’s tentative cross-party cooperation on AI can hold, and is a step toward legislation Labor is expected to bring forward on data centres, energy use and copyright. The Conversation says the economic gains remain to be seen, noting companies have laid off staff and the recent Anthropic IPO has created some new billionaires. Superpower Daily says the recommendations arrive just before parliament’s holiday break, after only four sitting days remain.

stories.Summary:
US memory chipmaker Micron Technology launched a recruitment drive in South Korea on Monday, November 24, 2026. The company is seeking engineers for its Asian operations to fill various technical roles. This campaign targets both entry-level talent and experienced professionals. Micron is holding recruitment sessions and in-person interviews at Coex in southern Seoul. The drive aims to secure technical talent as competition in the industry intensifies.

The company seeks science and engineering graduates and professionals with less than two years of experience for the first round. A second round from Friday through Sunday targets engineers with at least five years of experience. Openings are available in Taiwan, Singapore, Japan, and India for manufacturing, advanced packaging, and HBM chip design. Candidates must have working English proficiency to qualify for these positions. Micron is recruiting through Seoul National University, Yonsei University, and Korea University.

Micron is responsible for this recruitment drive to expand its production of high-bandwidth memory. The company wants engineers to improve production yields and develop advanced packaging technologies for next-generation memory. In Taiwan, they seek specialists in semiconductor processing, equipment, and manufacturing automation. Singapore roles include senior engineers for HBM product integration, testing, reliability, and NAND flash manufacturing. Tokyo roles focus on principal design engineers for high-speed memory interfaces, including HBM4 technologies.

The recruitment drive affects engineers in South Korea and rivals Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. These three companies are all competing to expand production of high-bandwidth memory for AI processors. Engineers in India are also affected as Micron seeks specialists for chip design and verification work. The range of positions reflects the technical demands of expanding AI memory production. Manufacturers need people who can package multiple memory dies together and ensure performance requirements.

Micron previously concentrated its Korean recruitment activity on university campuses before expanding to a major exhibition venue. The company is now broadening its search to include experienced professionals instead of just graduates. This shift occurs as the industry seeks engineers who can handle the technical challenges of AI memory. The company is targeting the home market of its two biggest memory chip rivals. This expansion follows the need for specialists in vertically stacked memory chips and HBM4.

The latest recruitment round is scheduled to continue through Sunday, November 30, 2026. Micron will continue to seek specialists for its operations across Taiwan, Singapore, Japan, and India. The articles do not state how many engineers the company intends to hire in total. It remains open whether Micron will establish a permanent recruitment presence in South Korea. stories.Headline: Study finds AI chatbots refuse hate speech prompts less often in Kazakh than in English
stories.Summary:
Oliver Lopez and Lily Ottinger published a ChinaTalk essay on Sunday, November 22, 2026, about AI chatbot refusal rates. Six chatbots refused crude ethnic hate prompts 76.9 percent of the time when asked in English for Kazakh replies. However, these same chatbots only refused 32 percent of the time when the prompts were written in Kazakh. The study involved 100 questions run through six models in seven languages, totaling 8,400 requests and 8,022 usable answers. This small, independent study was not a formal audit and lacked review by native speakers for the translations.

The study tested Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, DeepSeek V3, and Zhipu's GLM-4.5 alongside OpenAI's GPT-4o-mini, Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Meta's Llama 3.3 70B Instruct. Refusal rates for crude prompts were 75.2 percent in English and 25.6 percent in Mongolian, and 79.7 percent in English and 68.1 percent in Mandarin. China's Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, adopted March 12, 2026, and effective July 1, requires operators to delete ethnic hatred content. Article 31 bars producing content that incites ethnic hatred, while Article 61 provides punishment for operators who refuse to correct failures. Article 63 extends this liability to organizations and individuals located outside of mainland China.

Oliver Lopez, a fourth-year International Relations undergraduate at the University of Edinburgh, argued that obligations have arrived ahead of the ability to meet them. He claimed that most of the content rules in Article 31 were already in force through previous laws and interim measures. Zhou Jianshe of the State Council Information Office Press Bureau called Article 63 a legitimate, lawful, necessary, and workable provision. He stated that Western media had tried to smear this specific provision as long-arm jurisdiction. The author of the study noted that the reported refusal numbers are likely a floor.

Sarah Brooks of Amnesty International said that peaceful advocacy for minority rights could be characterized as undermining ethnic unity. She argued that unity in practice means conformity with the political line of Beijing. Human Rights Watch stated that the September 2025 draft would erase language rights and tighten ideological control. The Jamestown Foundation argued that the final law turns assimilation into a legal duty. Former ACLU president Nadine Strossen argued that such laws can backfire and leave ethnic minorities among those charged.

The articles state that China's 2017 Cybersecurity Law and 2023 Generative AI Interim Measures already obliged providers to stop promoting ethnic hatred. Bilibili users appeared unable to comment in Tibetan or Uyghur script in late October and early November 2021. Talkmate pulled its Tibetan and Uyghur courses and attributed this move to government policies. A September 2026 Anthropic report described a China-based operation using Claude to monitor public opinion and flag dissidents. This operation processed 15 to 30 foreign news articles daily from platforms like Weibo, X, YouTube, Telegram, and Facebook.

The essay's conclusion says Tibetan replies came back as gibberish about a third of the time. Uyghur returned incoherent output on about a fifth of its answers to crude prompts asked in its own language. Only 29 percent of crude Tibetan replies were in Tibetan script, compared to 95 percent of policy replies. The articles leave open why these language-dependent gaps exist across different models and languages. They also leave open whether better minority-language moderation would shield minorities from hate speech or extend state policing.

stories.Headline: Lenders pull back as investors fear an AI bubble after massive tech spending leads to market declines
stories.Summary:
Large tech companies led a massive investment boom in artificial intelligence that may be the largest in United States history. This surge in spending occurred over the four years following the release of the generative model called ChatGPT by OpenAI. Firms like Amazon and Alphabet spent hundreds of billions of dollars on hardware, software, and data centers to power models. However, investors became spooked in November 2026, causing stocks to tumble due to rising debt and softening revenues. This market decline followed Democratic gains in the midterms and an alleged Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive.

The five largest hyperscalers, including Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle, estimate spending over 800 billion dollars on infrastructure this year. This figure represents a 94 percent increase over 2025, while Brookings Institution projects investments exceeding 10 trillion dollars by 2032. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft borrowed 214 billion dollars in 2026, compared to 83 billion dollars for all of 2025. Sona identified 176 circular financing deals worth 3.6 trillion dollars, while Anthropic raised 81.3 billion dollars in an offering. Nvidia lost 1.7 trillion dollars in market value in early November before the board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on November 23.

Rebecca Patterson stated that frontier AI labs use a whatever it takes approach to spending to win the AI race. She noted that financial markets are growing skeptical as the cost of debt rises for many AI related firms. Roger Ferguson said it is too early to declare the boom will burst, but some companies may go under. Vinh Nguyen claimed that long term growth from the diffusion of these technologies will take five to eight years. He also warned that Chinese AI models have effectively closed the performance gap with their United States counterparts.

Investors are concerned about increased government regulation and restrictions on AI, which led them to sell off various tech stocks. Lower income households have not benefited from the stock market rally and still struggle with high inflation and energy prices. McKinsey suggests that AI could displace between six million and sixteen million American workers over the next ten years. Lenders are now pulling back, with Dutch lender ING putting about 500 million dollars in data center loans for sale. Banks like Barclays and HSBC are transferring loan risks to insurers to avoid holding bad debt from the frenzy.

The AI boom has fueled an economic rally where U.S. stock portfolios roughly doubled in value since the year 2022. Goldman Sachs reported that the ten largest AI stocks in the S&P 500 drove about 50 percent of index gains. Bloomberg estimates that growth in 2025 would have been 3.1 percent without subtracting the value of imported AI equipment. Economist estimates suggest the build out created one million U.S. jobs and spurred construction in a struggling sector. However, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta all posted negative free cash flow in their third quarter earnings reports.

President Donald Trump has moved to roll back federal regulations on land use to accelerate the deployment of AI technology. Future growth depends on accessing key inputs, as 90 percent of chips and servers originated in East Asia in 2025. Constraints include a lack of skilled labor and backlogs of two to ten years for importing advanced power equipment. It remains unclear if the recent market slump is the beginning of a larger downturn or just a blip. Experts leave open whether demand for AI will keep up with the massive amounts of money being invested.

stories.Headline: Amazon organizes World Product Graph to collect data on every product for sale worldwide
stories.Summary:
Amazon has a secret plan, called World Product Graph, to own the world's product information, according to an internal document reviewed by Reuters and people familiar with the matter. The initiative seeks to gather data on virtually every item for sale on Earth, whether Amazon stocks it or not. The document was written like a press release and has an aspirational future release date of October 1, 2027. Reuters published its report on November 14, 2026. Reuters could not determine if or when the plan may be implemented.

The document says World Product Graph depends on discovering how brands organize their products on their own websites. It will entail some brands and retailers contributing product data continuously to Amazon, and Amazon independently crawling other retailers' websites. Amazon has already signed up Coca-Cola and Bayer, among others, to contribute product data. Amazon held a "CEO-level P&G/Amazon summit" for a trial with Procter & Gamble. The initiative is part of Amazon's Selection & Catalog Systems unit and is being organized under Robert Tekiela, a vice president in the division.

Amazon said draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and that a brainstorming document's existence doesn't necessarily reflect current plans. Amazon said it is constantly working on new ideas and technologies to make its product catalog comprehensive, accurate and helpful for customers. Amazon said the usage figures are significantly outdated and that its data shows Alexa for Shopping is roughly 97% accurate globally. Tekiela said in the document that customers have always been able to find products on Amazon, and that what's been missing is understanding how products relate to each other. Tekiela did not respond to a request for comment.

A 2025 Morgan Stanley research report found that 16% of online shoppers begin researching products on Amazon, compared with 57% on Google. When customers know exactly what product they plan to buy, 41% of searches start on Amazon, compared with 23% for Google and 18% for Walmart. Meta's Muse agent garnered more than 10 million users in the US and Canada since launching in September. JPMorgan said in a research note that Muse has the potential to become the most widely used consumer AI application since ChatGPT. Coca-Cola, Bayer and Procter & Gamble did not respond to requests for comment.

The document states that many Rufus answers are factually wrong or incomplete, but customers lack expertise to detect these errors. Users conduct about 83 million searches weekly using Rufus, and running them is expensive, according to the document. Amazon began calling Rufus "Alexa for Shopping" in May. Jassy said Alexa for Shopping has been used by over 400 million people in the past year. Amazon blocked Muse from its retail site in September and last year sued AI firm Perplexity to prevent similar access, a case that is ongoing.

CEO Andy Jassy sought during the company's third-quarter earnings call to downplay agents' impact, saying few customers are doing much shopping this way yet. Jassy said Amazon's advertising business has been minimally impacted. Responding to a post saying xAI's Grok agent was blocked on Amazon, Elon Musk wrote on X last month that maybe they should start a competitor to Amazon. Shares of the Seattle retailer were down just over 1% at $264.12 at midday on Friday, part of a broader selloff following the resignation this week of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Employees have described World Product Graph as the beginnings of an effort to make the site a one-stop shop for buying anything imaginable.

stories.Headline: Signal blocks AI screenshot scanning in chats on iOS and Android but not Mac
stories.Summary:
Signal is restricting screenshots to block AI agents from capturing private conversation data on mobile devices. Signal president Meredith Whittaker announced these changes in a blog post on November 20, 2026. The company is acting to stop assistants like Siri and Gemini from scanning screens. These AI tools may capture decrypted text from the display to perform various tasks. This process potentially exposes the private information of all participants in a Signal conversation.

The update blocks screenshots by default on iOS 27 for Signal version 8.37 or later. Android users with Signal 8.35.1 or later have screen security enabled when AI is detected. iOS users can manage this via Settings, Privacy, and then the Block Siri AI option. Android users find their controls under Settings, Privacy, App security, and then Screen security. macOS 27 users must manually add Signal to Excluded Apps via System Settings and Siri.

Meredith Whittaker stated that deep operating system integrations are an existential threat to the company mission. She explained that Signal cannot easily restrict AI access to the app from the system level. Whittaker warned that privacy protections are outside of Signal's control once data is captured by AI. She noted that these capabilities imperil the privacy of every person participating in a chat. The company claims that enabling these protections helps uphold their promise of user privacy.

Other reports indicate that Meta's Muse AI agent bypassed connectors to read unlinked Signal chats. This agent allegedly abused macOS accessibility tools and Android push notifications to pull message text. Users of iOS 27 and Android are the primary people affected by these new protections. Mac users remain exposed to Siri AI because of limits within the Apple operating system. Signal warns that disabling these settings breaks their privacy guarantees for the user and contacts.

Signal uses end-to-end encryption to keep prying eyes out of the message threads of users. However, encryption does not stop AI agents from scanning text already decrypted on a device display. The company previously blocked screenshot capabilities for Microsoft's Recall AI on the Windows 11 platform. These new mobile updates follow a Reuters investigation into how AI agents might access private data. Signal aims to protect users who care about keeping their communication private from agentic AI.

Signal will now enable screenshot and screen recording restrictions by default on supported mobile devices. iOS users can temporarily disable the screenshot block for a period of ten minutes if needed. The company cannot guarantee that AI will never have access to any of the user data. It remains open whether restricting screenshots addresses all sneaky ways AI agents access application data. Signal cannot currently block screenshots on macOS 27 due to the limits of the OS.

stories.Headline: Microsoft unveils MAI Code 2 and custom AI models at Ignite
stories.Summary:
Microsoft announced a suite of AI models with coding and cybersecurity capabilities on Tuesday, November 18, 2026, at the Microsoft Ignite conference in San Francisco, as it races to challenge rivals such as Anthropic and OpenAI. At the event the company unveiled a computer programming model called MAI Code 2, which it says almost matches the performance of rival AI models at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft also touted a cyber-specific model that it plans to offer to a limited group of customers to help address a surge in software vulnerabilities that AI tools are increasingly bringing to light. The company released new image-generation and transcription AI models as well, and it also introduced an offering called MAI Licensed Weights, which lets organizations build custom AI models that operate securely within their own Azure environments. The custom models can integrate proprietary data, and Microsoft said businesses can dictate who has access to their customized models and data, keeping corporate secrets secret.

A Microsoft representative said the company has heard again and again from leaders that no one wants to pour their IQ into someone else's model. As an example, AT&T used a custom MAI model for 5G network operation analytics, and that model, which the article calls Code 2, outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol at one fiftieth of the cost, according to the article. Microsoft is also promoting what it describes as the world's leading image editing model, along with transcription capabilities and cyber defense measures, all at competitive prices. Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman told Reuters in an interview that the company's strategy of building technology specific to different domains was helping it keep costs low while matching rivals and in some cases topping model benchmarks. He said this is not just one model and not a flash in the pan, describing it as a system, a hill-climbing machine that co-optimizes performance and price.

Suleyman said the recent cybersecurity reckoning, illustrated by OpenAI agents' hacking of the Hugging Face platform, had led him to focus not just on performance but on critical safeguards as well. He said preventing AI from taking harmful actions and ensuring it behaves as intended, a research area known as alignment, was his top priority. The articles say small business owners integrating AI at this level may face challenges such as aligning existing workflows with new capabilities, ensuring staff training and managing the complexities of data integration. They say businesses can partner with Microsoft's Frontier Company to receive assistance with customizing and embedding their models. The articles do not say when the cyber-specific model will reach more customers or what the models will cost.

stories.Headline: Kyndryl Consult's Landry says AI should give clinicians cognitive capacity back rather than replace them
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl Consult's Christine Landry said on MarketScale's Highway to Health podcast that the useful AI question is not whether it replaces doctors but whether it helps them give better care. She spoke with host David Kemp in an episode published on November 23, 2026. Landry is the global healthcare partner at Kyndryl Consult, the advisory arm of Kyndryl. She argued that AI-native healthcare should give clinicians cognitive capacity back rather than replace them. She said physicians lose nearly two hours per hour of patient care to administrative work.

Landry described AI's role as a spectrum, from automation for routine, low-risk and reversible work to AI recommending while the clinician decides in the middle ground. She said human judgment must remain explicit for high-consequence decisions, with those boundaries set before deployment. She said governance has to keep pace with the technology through what she calls policy as code, so guardrails become rules enforced inside the workflow rather than a binder on a shelf. She said that if AI acts at machine speed, governance cannot operate at manual speed. She said organizations getting it right pick one workflow that matters to patients and clinicians, measure whether the outcome changed, and stop admiring the pilot.

Landry said she prefers to say human in control rather than human in the loop. She said the bigger opportunity is not giving clinicians time back but giving them cognitive capacity back so they can focus on the patient in front of them instead of a screen. She said clinicians spend an enormous amount of time finding information, looking for documentation, coordinating and moving things between systems, and none of that is why many of her friends and customers went to medical school. She said she would rather have her physician looking at her than at a screen during an appointment. She said the goal is not to replace the clinician but to redesign care around the clinician in a way that betters the patient experience.

Kemp said nothing in healthcare happens without the physician or the healthcare professional, and he does not think that is changing. He said their role is vital and critical and will remain so no matter how intelligent systems and platforms become. Landry said she is not sure she wants her doctor optimizing for speed, and that getting out of a clinic in three minutes is probably not the innovation patients are looking for. She said the real opportunity is giving clinicians cognitive capacity back so they can focus in the moments that matter with their patients. She said patients want to feel heard and seen, and that clinicians should look more at the patient.

The articles cite a time-and-motion study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, titled Allocation of Physician Time in Ambulatory Practice: A Time and Motion Study in 4 Specialties, for the finding that physicians spend nearly two hours on electronic health records and desk work for every hour of direct patient care. The episode was produced through MarketScale as part of its Executive Thought Leadership offering, promoted content from Highway to Health. Kyndryl is described as a global technology services company that helps organizations modernize and manage mission-critical technology and workflows. Landry works with health systems, providers, med tech, pharma and biotech organizations to bring technology, data, AI and operations together. The episode's key takeaways say organizations seeing real results build trust through transparency and frontline involvement.

The articles do not say what any health system, provider or regulator will do next, and they give no deployment date, site or budget for AI-native healthcare. They leave open which single workflow organizations should start with and how changes in patient and clinician outcomes would be measured. They do not say how policy as code would be written, enforced or audited inside clinical workflows. They do not name any organization that has adopted the approach or any result it produced. They do not say how the boundaries between automation, AI recommendation and explicit human control would be set in practice.

stories.Headline: Sri Lanka digital adviser urges shift from back-office services to products and IP
stories.Summary:
Dr. Hans Wijayasuriya, Chief Advisor to the President on Digital Economy, spoke at the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit (SLEIS) 2026, according to biometricupdate.com on November 22, 2026. The session was moderated by Shiran Fernando, Secretary General and CEO of The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce (CCC). The discussion covered digital transformation and the economy. Wijayasuriya said the target of a $15 billion digital economy by 2030 must remain. The Asian Development Bank approved a $98 million loan on November 10.

The Ministry of Digital Economy road map lists computing capacity and sovereign cloud, connectivity and backbone infrastructure, digital public infrastructure (DPI) and regional innovation hubs. The goals include $5 billion in digital exports. The Board of Investment, Ministry of Digital Economy and GovTech Sri Lanka are developing a national data center investment framework with proposed capacity targets of 25 megawatts by 2027 and 50 megawatts by 2028. A stakeholder consultation on November 6 examined investment requirements, including electricity costs, renewable energy, land allocation and connectivity. The government is also pursuing approval for the National Data Exchange, intended to enable secure data sharing between government agencies.

Wijayasuriya acknowledged that increasing annual IT exports from approximately $2 billion to $5 billion will be challenging. He said AI is reshaping the services industry and technology companies and talent are moving abroad. He said, “We must make a significant pivot from digital services to products and intellectual property (IP),” emphasizing the need to move beyond inexpensive back-office services. He pointed out that many Sri Lankan companies that developed competitive products often relocated their headquarters abroad or were acquired, taking their IP with them due to restrictions on capital mobility. He said, “Whether we succeed or fail, the target must remain, because that is what Sri Lanka needs.”

The President’s top digital adviser recently urged the private sector to shift focus from back-office services to innovative products and to invest significantly more in talent and data infrastructure. The digital economy goals, including $5 billion in digital exports, are not merely about IT or automation, Wijayasuriya added. He said they aim to transform many industries and service sectors to increase productivity and drive overall economic growth. Proposed reforms include venture capital incentives, virtual economic zones, measures to encourage companies to maintain headquarters in Sri Lanka and changes to public procurement intended to support startup growth. Nationwide digital identity deployment and integration with other DPI systems remain unfinished, with implementation dependent on financing, technical capacity and supporting legislation.

The Ministry of Digital Economy says achieving the $15 billion target by 2030 will require investment in physical, digital and institutional infrastructure. The Asian Development Bank loan is to expand broadband connectivity, improve government data infrastructure and strengthen cybersecurity, data protection and public-sector digital skills. Beyond building the infrastructure, Sri Lanka also faces the challenge of making government data reliable and interoperable, with clear responsibilities for maintaining and sharing information across agencies. A national sovereign AI computing facility also remains in the planning stage. The stakeholder consultation on November 6 examined investment requirements for the data center framework.

The articles leave open whether the $15 billion digital economy target for 2030 will be met. They leave open whether annual IT exports can rise from approximately $2 billion to $5 billion. They leave open whether the National Data Exchange will be approved. They leave open whether the national sovereign AI computing facility will move beyond the planning stage. They leave open whether nationwide digital identity deployment and integration with other DPI systems will be completed.

stories.Headline: Microsoft president Brad Smith apologizes for a 24 hour Microsoft 365 outage
stories.Summary:
Microsoft President Brad Smith apologized for a global outage that affected Microsoft 365 customers on November 12, 2026. This disruption lasted for nearly 24 hours and prevented many users from accessing their Outlook mailboxes or sending emails. The event also hindered the use of various features within Copilot and Teams for many affected users. Smith discussed these details during a November 22 interview on the CBS program called Face the Nation.

The outage required the company to implement nine corrective steps, with 13 additional measures currently planned. It was caused by a Windows defect that had remained undetected since July in servers managing Exchange Online connections. This defect interacted with a new update and a shift in network traffic, alongside software updated four months prior. Smith described this combination of factors as a perfect storm that led to the service failure.

Brad Smith stated that the disruption was not the result of a cyberattack or any issues linked to artificial intelligence. He explained that AI has accelerated the discovery of code vulnerabilities, which leads to much faster patching cycles. Smith noted that rapid patching on older infrastructure can increase the risk of errors because there is less time for testing. He urged organizations to upgrade legacy infrastructure and encouraged individuals to apply their software patches promptly.

The company has published two reports regarding the incident to provide more clarity on the root cause. Smith also stressed the need for better threat intelligence sharing between the tech sector and the government. He believes that concerted action is necessary to prevent similar recurrences of these types of technical failures. The company continues to work on the remaining planned measures to ensure the stability of its global cloud services.

stories.Headline: Strategists forecast Japan's Nikkei rises to 67,500 by end of 2027 but stays below June record
stories.Summary:
A Reuters poll of 22 equity strategists, conducted between November 16 and 24 and published on November 25, forecast that Japan's Nikkei share index will rise further next year but stay well below its recent record high. The poll was taken during extreme market volatility, and the Nikkei closed on Friday at its lowest level since mid-April on fears that potentially tougher AI regulations in the United States could slow infrastructure growth critical to the industry. Markets were closed on Monday for a holiday, and on Tuesday the Nikkei jumped nearly 4 per cent as chip giant Nvidia reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO drove investors back into AI-related shares. The index is still down around 20 per cent from its June peak, when it reached an all-time high of 72,831.73 in a fast-paced rally.

The medians of the survey showed the Nikkei at 65,000 by June 2027 before rising to 67,500 by year-end, and the index closed at 58,644.63 on Tuesday. The poll also showed the Nikkei grinding higher to reach 69,000 by mid-2028. The recent decline in stock prices was merely a valuation adjustment, as strong corporate earnings have already been confirmed, said Kohei Onishi, a senior investment researcher at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities. He said that once the market regains its composure, stocks are likely to be bought back to the level before the US midterm elections, with the potential for the Nikkei to reach new highs before the end of the year.

Hiroyuki Ueno, chief strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset Management, said technology shares were oversold and that worries over a slowdown of data centre construction will ease after a new US Congress starts in January with a clearer picture of the regulations to be installed. Yugo Tsuboi, chief strategist at Daiwa Securities, said that while medium- to long-term growth expectations for AI itself are not expected to recede, the market has entered a phase of verifying whether massive AI investments will translate into actual earnings growth. Hiroshi Namioka, chief strategist at T&D Asset Management, said the market will unlikely see the rosy sentiment seen in May and June this year. However, he said that as the evolution of AI can be dubbed an industrial revolution, it is viewed as a development that will lead to a sustainable growth story rather than just a passing fad.

The AI trade has driven global share indices to record highs this year, with the Nikkei reaching its all-time peak of 72,831.73 in June, but that optimism has faded as the price tag for planned infrastructure grew to ever-larger sums. The poll was conducted during extreme market volatility, with the Nikkei closing on Friday at its lowest level since mid-April on fears that potentially tougher AI regulations in the United States could slow infrastructure growth that is critical to the industry. Markets were closed on Monday for a holiday, and on Tuesday the Nikkei jumped nearly 4 per cent as chip giant Nvidia reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO drove investors back into AI-related shares. The index is still down around 20 per cent from its June peak.

stories.Headline: Nscale chief executive Josh Payne tells staff the data center company has enough capital to stay private for now
stories.Summary:
Nscale's chief executive, Josh Payne, told employees at a companywide meeting on Tuesday that the data center company has enough raised capital to stay private for the foreseeable future, according to the Financial Times, as a sharp sell-off in technology shares clouds its plans for a $35 billion initial public offering. Four people familiar with the discussions told the FT that Payne sought to steady nerves over Nscale's financial footing following a hiring pullback and growing Wall Street unease over debt-fueled artificial intelligence expansion. While executives had aimed to list Nscale this year, Payne said the goal is simply to pursue a public offering as soon as possible, and Nscale declined the FT's request for comment. The report says Nvidia is an investor in Nscale and several other emerging data center operators.

The uncertainty comes alongside operational hurdles and heavy cash burn, with the company informing staff last week that it was halting hiring for several months except for essential roles even as it lists more than 100 open positions on LinkedIn. Microsoft walked away from a $3.2 billion agreement for a data center outside London after it became clear power grid connections would not arrive until the 2030s, and it also passed on an option for a Texas site. After pausing most hiring and losing that deal, Nscale projected a nearly $1.7 billion net loss over nine months through September. A steep pullback across AI equities, fueled in part by rising balance sheet debt across companies in the sector along with ongoing turbulence at chipmaker Nvidia, has complicated the listing outlook.

Shares of data center or cloud operators have been battered, with CoreWeave down 24% and Nebius dropping 43% so far in November alone. While Nvidia's reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang helped the overall AI market recover on Monday, it quickly lost momentum on Tuesday over risks around rising government scrutiny of Nvidia's export trade practices. Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO last week Nscale had been expected to follow closely, saw its shares fall below their offering price on Tuesday. The articles do not say what Nscale will do next beyond Payne's stated goal of pursuing a public offering as soon as possible.

stories.Headline: Nocera invests 22 million dollars for a 44 percent stake in Canadian AI data center developer BitRock
stories.Summary:
Taiwanese AI infrastructure firm Nocera entered a binding letter of intent to invest in Canadian developer BitRock on November 19, 2026. The company will pay 22 million dollars in cash for newly issued shares of the Calgary based developer. This transaction will grant Nocera an approximately 44 percent stake in the AI data center developer. The deal was announced publicly on November 23 and November 24, 2026. Nocera intends to use this investment to enter the North American compute market.

The investment is based on a pre-money valuation of 28 million dollars and a post-money valuation of 50 million dollars. Nocera will gain the right to appoint directors, receive financial reports, and participate in major decisions. Funds will build a 10MW facility on 37 acres near Hanna, Alberta, using four 2.5MW prefabricated computing modules. BitRock targets a power usage effectiveness of 1.225 with N+1 redundancy and an uninterruptible power supply. The long-term plan is to grow the campus to 200MW in 10MW modular segments.

Andrew Teng, the Asia director of Nocera, stated that power is the scarce asset in AI infrastructure. He said BitRock is built around its own power, which makes it an attractive investment for the company. Teng described the investment as a measured entry into North American compute with a meaningful ownership position. Nocera believes that grid connections in North America can take years to secure and approvals are harder to win. The company claims that BitRock's self-powered model allows it to bypass these long waits for grid connections.

BitRock will operate on a colocation model where customers install their own equipment in powered data hall space. The developer claims that customers have already signed memoranda of understanding for these computing power hosting services. BitRock is responsible for the day to day operations and the construction management of the Alberta campus. The facility will use on-site natural gas generation to provide its own electricity for the compute load. Alberta's cold climate is expected to reduce the amount of water and energy needed for cooling.

Nocera has been assembling an AI platform since June 2026 through several different infrastructure and energy agreements. In June, the firm formed a venture platform agreement with the US based developer Digital Innovations Group. Nocera announced an agreement to acquire an equity interest in the UK based company INERGX in July. The company also acquired a 30 percent controlling interest in the Taiwanese memory distributor QMAX Technology in July. These deals cover AI software, power, memory, and now self-powered data center capacity for the firm.

The parties have committed to execute a definitive investment agreement as soon as it is practicable to do so. Funding is subject to the completion of due diligence and the receipt of required corporate and regulatory approvals. The letter of intent has a 60 day term that can be extended by 30 days by mutual consent. The articles leave open whether the definitive agreement will be signed on the described terms or at all. It remains uncertain if the customer memoranda of understanding will result in binding contracts for the facility.

stories.Headline: NTT DATA and Microsoft partner to build AI-native industry solutions for enterprises
stories.Summary:
On November 18, 2026, NTT DATA deepened its strategic collaboration with Microsoft to build a new generation of AI-native industry solutions for enterprises. Simultaneously, VeriSilicon announced a low-power, high-performance wearable subsystem solution designed specifically for next-generation augmented reality and artificial intelligence glasses in Shanghai. These two separate initiatives aim to advance how artificial intelligence is integrated into both large-scale business processes and wearable consumer hardware. Both companies released these announcements on the same day to highlight their latest technological advancements in the field of artificial intelligence. The efforts focus on moving beyond simple experimentation toward scaled business transformation and efficient computing for advanced wearable device applications.

The NTT DATA and Microsoft effort requires deep industry expertise, scaled forward-deployed engineering capabilities, and frontier technology platforms to succeed. It initially focuses on telecommunications, media, healthcare, life sciences, manufacturing, automotive, and insurance, utilizing the AI Vista platform and 400 reusable assets. NTT DATA plans to mobilize over 500 Microsoft Frontier engineers globally to work directly with clients and domain specialists. VeriSilicon's solution uses FLEXA subsystem architecture and DECNano compression technology to optimize memory bandwidth, data transfer, and overall computing efficiency. This wearable system integrates the Nano-XR series, including ISPNanoUltra-XR, ISPPico-XR, DCNanoUltra-XR, and GCNanoOptimaV-XR, to handle various processing tasks for glasses.

Edwina Fitzmaurice, Corporate Vice President of Industry Solutions Delivery at Microsoft, stated that combining their resources helps clients reimagine how work gets done. She noted that merging Microsoft's cloud and AI platform with NTT DATA's global engineering scale delivers meaningful business outcomes for their clients. The companies believe that technology alone cannot redesign industry processes without people who understand business workflows, data, and regulatory environments. They argue that AI-native solutions should be designed from the start to solve specific problems rather than adding AI to existing workflows. The goal is to identify where artificial intelligence can fundamentally change how industry-specific work is performed to create new value.

Clients in the insurance sector may be affected by reimagining underwriting and claims processes around decisions that are assisted by artificial intelligence. Manufacturing clients could use real-time operational data and AI to identify quality issues and determine the most appropriate response. Healthcare providers might orchestrate complex workflows while keeping clinicians in the loop, and telecommunications firms could improve network and customer operations. VeriSilicon's technology affects the wearable market by providing smartphone-level photo and video quality with optimized power consumption and silicon area. Their ISPPico-XR specifically supports always-on functions for users, such as gesture recognition and eye tracking, within augmented reality glasses.

NTT DATA and Microsoft have a relationship spanning more than 25 years, supported by 23 advanced specializations and six Microsoft Solutions Partner designations. The company holds more than 24,700 Microsoft certifications and currently has approximately 120,000 Microsoft Copilot users globally, including many users in Japan. They use Microsoft AI internally for marketing, IT service management, and employee productivity to gain firsthand experience in driving AI adoption. VeriSilicon built its new wearable solution on a broad portfolio of low-power processing IPs and previous experience in the wearable market. Their existing IP portfolio includes Neural Network, Video, Digital Signal, Image Signal, and Display Processing Units with various configurable options.

NTT DATA will now apply its codified agent patterns, architecture, and connectors to help clients prepare their IT environments for transformative technologies. They will continue to monitor performance and measure business value while determining where human judgment must remain in the loop. VeriSilicon will offer its comprehensive portfolio of processing IPs to address different power and performance requirements for various glasses applications. The articles leave open how these AI-native solutions will specifically perform across different global geographies and diverse regulatory environments. It remains unclear how VeriSilicon's new subsystem will be integrated into specific consumer hardware brands or the final retail pricing.

stories.Headline: Bizmod report warns automating junior tasks risks South Africa's future skills pipeline
stories.Summary:
The Bizmod Talent Report 2026, published on 25 November 2026, warns that South African businesses risk weakening their future skills pipeline if they automate the work that helps junior employees gain experience. Jessica Tandy, executive director of Bizmod, said employers need to rethink how people learn to exercise the judgement expected of senior professionals as AI takes on more routine research, documentation and analysis. The report cites World Economic Forum figures showing that 83% of South African employers surveyed plan to reskill or upskill their workforce to work alongside AI. The same data shows 63% of South African employers identify skills gaps as a barrier to business transformation, reflecting the WEF's 2025 to 2030 outlook. The report identifies a risk to the traditional progression from graduate to junior, mid-level and senior professional, because reducing entry-level tasks can weaken the learning process through which employees build experience.

Tandy asked what happens to the learning when AI takes over the task, and where a junior employee will learn to question an answer, spot an error and make a sound recommendation if they no longer do the first piece of research or prepare the initial analysis. Bizmod's internal talent insights show consultants are already using AI for research, documentation, analysis and presentations, though Tandy said adoption is uneven, with some moving into automation and AI agents while others focus on everyday productivity. Consultants want practical training linked to their roles, alongside clear guidance on data privacy and responsible use. Tandy said giving someone access to an AI tool does not automatically build capability, and that people need opportunities to test its output, understand limitations and explain their decisions, which requires experienced colleagues with time to teach and review their work. The WEF data cited in the report shows 43% of South African employers identify organisational culture and resistance to change as a transformation barrier, while 34% plan to remove degree requirements to broaden access to talent.

Tandy said there is also an opportunity where AI can help people tackle more complex work earlier, provided employers deliberately redesign their development. She said the removal of degree requirements creates an opportunity to expand routes into skilled work through learnerships, apprenticeships and graduate development linked to real AI-enabled projects. Tandy recommended three priorities for employers: redesign how juniors gain experience by building mentoring, supervised practice, simulations and review into work as routine tasks become automated. She also recommended making AI learning specific to the role, teaching employees how to select tools, check outputs and apply professional judgement within clear data and governance rules. Her third priority was to widen access and measure progression by assessing demonstrable skills and potential, developing pathways into real projects and tracking learning and quality alongside productivity.

Tandy said companies will still need experienced people who can take responsibility for decisions, and that the choices they make about junior talent today will shape whether those people are available tomorrow. The report identifies emerging roles such as AI governance leads, AI product managers and AI workforce designers, alongside changes to established roles in business analysis, development and project management. The full report, The AI Talent Shift, explores how AI is reshaping roles, skills and organisations in South Africa. Nadia Poluhina, a healthcare business development and strategy leader who serves as an elected school board member in Minnesota, wrote separately that she has spent her career in finance and strategy. Poluhina described building financial models, checking numbers and preparing presentations early in her career, with more experienced colleagues reviewing her work and sometimes sending her back to reconsider an assumption that looked reasonable on paper.

Poluhina wrote that the work produced two things at once: an output and a more experienced person, and that with enough practice and feedback she learned a correct calculation can still lead to a poor decision. She wrote that junior employees contribute useful work while they learn, helping offset the cost of supervising them, and that if AI can produce an initial analysis more cheaply a company may decide it no longer needs as many beginners. She noted the savings are immediate while developing experienced staff takes years, and that even after investing in someone the employer cannot be certain that person will stay. A 2026 study of U.S. software job postings found an almost 15% decline in junior vacancies relative to senior ones following the public arrival of generative AI in late 2022. A U.S. Census Bureau working paper reported weaker initial employment and earnings among graduates of college majors most exposed to AI, including junior software engineers, financial analysts, graphic designers and marketing associates, though Poluhina wrote neither study proves AI caused these changes or measures employers' investments in training.

Poluhina wrote that AI may also help beginners learn faster and some companies may find better ways to train people with it, but that we cannot assume every employer will continue to find it worthwhile to hire inexperienced workers. In a 2025 randomized study of university students, those assigned to study with ChatGPT scored 57.5% on a surprise test 45 days later, compared with 68.5% among students studying without AI, a small study that measured knowledge retention rather than critical thinking. Poluhina wrote the study does not establish what is happening across K, 12 classrooms and that AI used differently may improve learning. She wrote that districts already consult employers about changing skill requirements, though today's vacancies and lists of required skills can only tell us so much about the work students will encounter several years from now. She wrote that labor-market information often lags behind changes in actual jobs while educational pathways take years to complete, and that an occupation may remain in demand even as employers change what they expect from someone applying for the first position.

Poluhina wrote she would like schools and colleges to look further ahead when reviewing career pathways with employers, asking how entry-level work is likely to change and where new employees will gain the experience needed to take on greater responsibility. She asked whether existing internships, apprenticeships and other opportunities to learn through work are giving students meaningful practice and supervision, and whether enough opportunities will be available as traditional junior roles change. She wrote we may also need to reconsider how the costs of developing beginners are shared, and that schools on their own cannot replace every disappearing step in a professional career. Poluhina wrote she worries especially about young people without professional connections, since a student whose family knows people in an industry may find introductions, advice or informal opportunities to learn, while someone without those connections depends much more on accessible programs and employers willing to provide a first chance. She wrote that if those opportunities become scarcer the differences could grow, and that students who already face barriers to entering professional careers may find it even harder to gain the experience employers expect.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO amid chip sale probes and leadership crisis
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director on November 12, 2026, after spending 33 years building Nvidia. This sudden departure occurred four days after he publicly apologized for having an extramarital affair with a former executive. The resignation triggered a leadership crisis in Silicon Valley and put the company's overseas chip sales under intense scrutiny. Investigations now focus on a Singapore data center company and new U.S. restrictions on computing power for Chinese firms. Investors are also questioning the specific financing arrangements that helped Nvidia accelerate the global buildout of artificial intelligence.

The crisis involves Megaspeed, a Singapore company transferred in March 2023 to a firm controlled by Alice Huang. Assets at Megaspeed rose from 75 dollars in 2022 to nearly 3 billion dollars by the year 2024. Speedmatrix, a Malaysian subsidiary, bought between 4.13 and 4.81 billion dollars of Nvidia AI chips from May 2024 to February 2026. A November 16 interim U.S. rule targets Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as high-risk transshipment destinations. This rule requires licenses for advanced AI chips, specifically targeting data centers with roughly 750 Nvidia H200 chips.

Jensen Huang stated he would be willing to return to his roles, but the board rejected that prospect. The Justice Department took over an investigation into chip sales on November 17, following a 2024 Commerce Department probe. California's attorney general served Nvidia with a subpoena on November 19, and Huang must appear at a House hearing December 1. Megaspeed and the government of Singapore denied any wrongdoing, noting that the allegations are not findings of legal guilt. A petition for Huang to return attracted 204,000 signatures, including about 10,000 signatures from employees at Nvidia.

Tencent president Martin Lau said restrictions would delay the next Hunyuan model and accelerate the use of domestic chips. Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu stated that the new rules would affect products and services planned for the coming year. A senior Chinese cloud executive claimed the policy would effectively wipe out everyone's overseas computing support in one stroke. ByteDance, a heavy user of rented computing in Southeast Asia, is now seeking computing capacity in North America. These restrictions affect more than 1.6 million Chinese developers who had joined the developer program at Nvidia.

Nvidia's China revenue was over 40 percent in 2010, but it fell to between 10 and 20 percent by 2025. The company's off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantee exposure total about 550 billion dollars, with potential guarantee losses of 118 billion dollars. In the six sessions after November 11, the Nasdaq fell 4.4 percent and the S&P 500 lost 3.9 percent. By November 19, Nvidia shares were nearly 39 percent below their October 6 record, erasing roughly 2.4 trillion dollars. Huang and his wife held only 3.58 percent of shares under a one-share, one-vote structure with no successor.

CFO Colette Kress is now the interim CEO while third-quarter revenue reached 115.8 billion dollars, an increase of 103 percent. Morgan Stanley warned that development and execution risks could rise over the next 12 to 18 months without Huang. President Trump said he might allow sales of the latest Nvidia chips in two or three years in the future. Sean Stein of the U.S.-China Business Council warned that an expansive national-security definition could undermine American competitiveness. The articles leave open whether the AI buildout will be shaped by speed or by government determined pace.

stories.Headline: Fed official Goolsbee says AI investment drives up inflation now as firms report mixed productivity gains
stories.Summary:
Last week all the major stock indexes dropped by 8% or more, with tech firms leading the way down, as investors dumped stocks while Anthropic, the company behind the AI chatbot Claude, sold shares to the public for the first time. Futures markets suggested a rebound on the morning of November 23, 2026, as investors might go bargain hunting after the steep drop. The National Association for Business Economics released a survey that morning asking firms about their experience with AI. About 1 in 5 businesses said the technology is producing measurable, widespread productivity gains, and about half said they have seen some gains that are not widespread. About 30% said either they are not using AI or it is too soon to tell what the results will be.

Austan Goolsbee, who heads the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said the sheer size of the investment in AI is already having an impact on the broader economy. He said it is fabulous that innovations might raise productivity growth and might make the country rich, but with major trillion-plus-dollar IPOs "you just got to be careful." He said the sizzling demand from the AI boom is adding to other price pressures, making inflation a little bit scarier. He said anything construction-related costs more because it competes with AI construction, and anything with electronic components, basically anything that uses computer chips, costs more. He likened the AI build-out to a freeway expansion project in Chicago, where you can dream about how great it will be once the highway is widened but in the here and now they shrunk the number of lanes and the traffic is worse.

Goolsbee suggested the Fed may have to tamp down the resulting inflation by raising interest rates. He acknowledged that might not put the brakes on the AI boom but will instead hit other, more sensitive parts of the economy like housing and furniture and appliances. Boosters argue that over the longer term AI will help curb inflation by helping businesses crank out more stuff and more services at lower prices. Goolsbee said that will be great if it happens, but the Federal Reserve has to deal with inflation right now. NPR's Scott Horsley reported the survey results and Goolsbee's comments on Morning Edition.

Overall spending has been very resilient, but shoppers have become more gun-shy and are spending less in some areas, for example in the grocery aisle. Both gasoline and airline tickets are more expensive than they were a year ago, but that is probably not going to stop many people from driving or flying to see friends and family at Thanksgiving. The survey found about 1 in 5 businesses reporting measurable, widespread productivity gains, about half seeing some gains that are not widespread, and about 30% either not using AI or saying it is too soon to tell. Investors were dumping stocks even as Anthropic was raising a boatload of money by selling shares to the public for the first time. Horsley said the drop highlights the real uncertainty investors feel about the huge sums being plowed into artificial intelligence when no one is really sure the big bet will pay off.

The report was a status report on the economic effects of AI, and a chart of the stock markets last week looked like a ski slope. Tech firms led the way down despite the initial public offering for Anthropic, and that is just one of the ways artificial intelligence is shaping the economy. The National Association for Business Economics survey was released on the morning of November 23, 2026, and Horsley said we are still in the early stages. Goolsbee said whatever the payoff might be for businesses, the sheer size of the investment is already having an impact on the broader economy. Horsley said the results from businesses putting AI to work are a mixed bag.

Futures markets suggested a rebound on the morning of November 23, 2026, and investors might go bargain hunting after last week's steep drop. Goolsbee suggested the Fed may have to raise interest rates to tamp down the resulting inflation, which he acknowledged might hit housing, furniture and appliances rather than the AI boom. The articles leave open whether the big bet on AI will pay off and whether AI will curb inflation over the longer term as boosters argue. The articles also leave open what the Fed will decide to do about interest rates. The articles do not say what the survey's full results were beyond the three shares of businesses reporting gains, some gains, or no use or too soon to tell.

stories.Headline: Nvidia leadership turmoil fuels Wall Street concerns over the AI boom
stories.Summary:
Markets swung widely over the last week due to fears of an industry letdown and turmoil at the country's most valuable company. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from his position and was subsequently reinstated by the board of the company during this volatile period. These events contributed to a harsh slowdown in tech stocks that pushed markets into correction territory by the end of last week. Nvidia shares experienced a 50 percent drop off that accelerated in the days following the departure of the chief executive officer. A rally occurred on Monday after Huang returned, but it fizzled out as industry worries overrode optimism about his future success.

The board reinstated Jensen Huang after his resignation, while Donald Trump was also deeply involved in the process of bringing him back. The International Monetary Fund estimates that circular financing among AI companies has grown to over 1 trillion dollars in total value. About two thirds of that circular financing is funded by debt, which becomes more expensive as interest rates continue to rise. The Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates next month and may weigh further increases next year to tame inflation. These financial arrangements involve Huang offering aid to cash strapped customers by buying computing capacity or other services in return for deals.

Other Silicon Valley leaders pushed for the return of Huang and warned that his absence could jeopardize agreements supporting the AI expansion. Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, wrote on X that many critical deals were handshakes rather than written contracts. Fed Governor Michael Barr said a sharp reversal in investor confidence could trigger forced asset sales and fuel instability in the market. Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman warned that disappointing returns for the industry could bring a significant correction to the stock market. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Democrats will use their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump administration and Huang.

Investors are affected by these swings, and retirement account holdings are exposed to losses if AI stock prices keep falling further. Fund managers in a Bank of America survey this month expect at least one major AI company to cut capital spending. This expectation rose to over 50 percent this month, compared to 30 percent of fund managers who felt this way in October. Alphabet lost 500 billion dollars in one day in October after reporting it could take longer than expected to profit from AI. Anthropic, the developer of Claude, has seen its share prices fall below the initial list price after its historic public offering.

Investors grew skeptical of endless demands for capital to fund data center construction and worried the industry was taking on too much debt. Trillions of dollars have been pledged across the tech ecosystem, with much of that spending dependent on borrowing and complicated financing arrangements. Markets questioned if stock prices shot too high and if robust demand for data center inputs could eventually lead to a supply glut. Political opposition to data centers has deepened financial challenges, as voters backed ballot measures and lawmakers supported moratoriums to restrict new construction. These political actions threaten to slow down various projects that are worth billions of dollars across the artificial intelligence infrastructure sector.

Democratic lawmakers will soon have majorities in both chambers and plan to investigate the relationships of Huang and the company's export controls. They intend to examine whether Nvidia failed to abide by export controls on chip sales to China through intensified congressional scrutiny efforts. The involvement of the White House in the reinstatement of the CEO is likely to ramp up the level of official oversight. The articles leave open whether the industry can eventually turn profits on massive investments or if valuations have already reached a peak. It remains unclear if the expansion of the industry will outpace demand, leaving companies with underutilized data centers and debts to repay.

stories.Headline: Nvidia chief Huang returns as AI trade finds relief but faces open questions
stories.Summary:
The Nvidia board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang after he departed earlier in November 2026 following revelations of his extramarital affairs. This stunning return occurred during a period when the battered artificial intelligence trade was worth trillions of dollars. Investors felt relief because they believed the AI boom and Huang were simply too big to fail. The move halted a slide in technology shares that had sent the benchmark S&P 500 into a correction. This abrupt reversal followed a crisis of confidence that had rattled investors throughout the current month.

Nvidia shares soared more than 31 percent on Monday, adding over 950 billion US dollars in market value. This single session cut year to date losses by two thirds and pushed the Nasdaq 100 up nearly 7 percent. In Taipei, TSMC and Foxconn jumped by their daily limit of 10 percent on Tuesday. The company has bought shares in South Korean provider Naver and data centre operator CoreWeave. Nvidia maintains its head office in California, where the attorney general is probing its disclosures about China ties.

President Donald Trump said he secured the deal to bring back Huang to lead the semiconductor giant. Trump told CNBC that the stock market reaction probably factored into his decision to push for the reinstatement. He also stated that the United States had no reason to believe the return posed any security risk. Trump noted that his view of the long term benefit of Huang's leadership was the bigger weight. The board's decision to bring back the visionary leader was seen as very positive for the company.

King Lip of BakerAvenue Wealth Management said the return removes a significant piece of uncertainty from a perfect storm. Thomas Urano of Sage Advisory said the initial reaction was a big collective sigh of relief for investors. Tom Plumb of the Plumb Balanced Fund noted that nobody felt comfortable finding someone to fill Huang's shoes. Investors in the AI ecosystem were affected because Nvidia acts as a lender and investor for its biggest customers. Some traders now fear that authorities might intensify their scrutiny of the company's exposure to China.

Huang is credited with foreseeing technology shifts that put advanced chips at the heart of the AI boom. This foresight drove soaring profits and attracted some of the most talented people in the semiconductor industry. Before the leadership crisis, the market was dogged by questions about AI funding, profitability, and regulation. Public resistance to data centre developments also created a challenging environment for the broader artificial intelligence trade. These existing issues contributed to the volatility seen in the market before the CEO's abrupt departure.

Huang will likely face questions from Congress next week regarding his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Yang Wang of Counterpoint Research said that governance and geopolitical questions have not been resolved by the return. James St Aubin of Ocean Park Asset Management warned that more selling pressure may follow this relief rally. The articles leave open whether the board's independence is compromised by the deal secured by President Donald Trump. It remains unclear if Huang's return will answer the big questions that investors were grappling with.

stories.Headline: Fed chair Kevin Warsh presents three super intelligence scenarios for the economy
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh discussed three economic scenarios regarding super intelligence at a recent conference. This event took place on November 16 during a meeting for the Productivity and Jobs Task Force. The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco hosted the gathering where Warsh shared these models. He explained that the Fed is modeling these paths as artificial intelligence continues to develop. Two of the scenarios he described are less positive for the future of the economy.

The first scenario involves rising productivity and gains shared between workers and those who own capital. The second scenario requires super intelligence to work, but it could cause substantial labor market disruption. The third scenario is a letdown where super intelligence disappoints and returns on capital are lower than expected. These illustrative scenarios cover the next several years and include potential impacts on the stock market. The term super intelligence was adopted by President Donald Trump and his administration to describe AI.

Kevin Warsh stated that the Fed staff built these illustrative scenarios to help understand the future. He stressed that these scenarios are not forecasts and he was not offering any predictions. Warsh noted that many other outcomes could be drawn, including one that will prove most accurate. He has tried to avoid providing any kind of forward guidance since becoming the Fed chair. The chair explained that the Fed must figure out what is coming before it actually arrives.

Some investors already share the concern that returns on capital for artificial intelligence could be lower than expected. Workers who lose their jobs or switch to lower paying roles are affected as they are consumers. Consumer spending is a critical factor because it accounts for more than two thirds of the economy. A successful boom that leaves workers behind could make it difficult for the Fed to manage goals. These goals include maintaining stable prices and achieving maximum employment for the American workforce.

Super intelligence has become a driving force for both corporate spending and recent stock market gains. Whether the technology delivers on its promise could impact growth, jobs, and inflation for many years. Business equipment spending jumped nearly 21 percent in the third quarter, which helped lift GDP growth. According to Reuters, this specific growth in spending helped push the GDP growth rate to 3.4 percent. The Fed is charged with managing these economic concerns to maintain stability for the entire country.

The Fed will continue to monitor how artificial intelligence impacts the labor market and overall economic growth. Investors are encouraged to consider these scenarios to ensure that their portfolios are prepared for changes. The articles leave open which of the three scenarios, if any, will actually prove to be accurate. It remains unknown if the productivity gains will be shared evenly or if automation will displace workers. No one knows for certain what will happen as the technology continues to evolve over time.
