stories.Headline: AI builder Will Thomas sees his model beat him in Fantasy Premier League
stories.Summary:
Will Thomas has played Fantasy Premier League for over 15 years, and last season the AI he built finished above him for the first time. He told Reuters it was a bit of a surreal moment and that he thought he was being beaten by his own creation. Thomas is an Englishman and the CEO and founder of Scoreline.ai, which delivers subscriber-based content including data, insight and analytics for fantasy sports players. Among its products is Fantasy Football Hub, which has around 60,000 paying subscribers and focuses on FPL, the official fantasy competition of the English Premier League. FPL offers match tickets and replica kits as prizes and had over 13 million registered teams in the 2025-26 season.

Scoreline.ai's purpose-built model finished in the top 0.5 per cent of those teams, ranking 67,829th in the world. A Reuters analysis of nine FPL teams, seven of which were run on the directions of AI chatbots, showed the chatbot teams scored an average of 499 points in the first eight gameweeks of the 2026-27 FPL season. The chatbot teams were operated by Scout Digital, a sports marketing firm that gives each separate chatbot the same instructions every week and, in most cases, has a staff member log in to carry out its decisions. Their performances were in line with the average human benchmark of 502, but about 75 points below the average of the top 1,000 human players. Scout Digital said newer versions of each AI model are used as they are released.

Thomas said there are still human managers beating the model, but it is getting harder to do, and he has a PhD in team leadership at the University of Sussex. Scout Digital managing director Mike Lewis said that so far they are two seasons in and the improvement they have seen is huge. Lewis said that in 2025-26 Scout Statto comfortably won, and that this season is looking neck and neck. Daniel Groos, head of AI at Groos Analytics, who built the open-source forecasting model OpenFPL, said the hardest question remains whether a player will even be in action on any particular gameweek and not dropped, rested or injured. Jonas Sand Labakk, the 2023-24 FPL champion, told Reuters that where you need human input is the expected minutes for players, because rotation, injuries and managerial choices are where he thinks the models miss the most.

Groos added that overall machines have an advantage because humans tend to be influenced by a spectacular performance, media narratives or a favourite player. The chatbot teams make about as few transfers as the best human managers, and the gap in transfer volume is small. The chatbot teams' captain picks trail those of the top 1,000 human players, and they also leave more points on the bench than the typical manager. The top 1,000 do not play against the grain, owning more popular players than the average manager, not fewer, which undercuts the idea that beating the field takes contrarian bets. Thomas also argues that the machines are weakest at the start of a season, when new managers and players give the models little data, and that fans of specific teams may have a slight insight advantage.

However, the early numbers do not clearly show that. The chatbot teams Reuters analysed were level with the official average in gameweek 1 of this season, pulled ahead in gameweek 2, and had dipped just below it by gameweek 8. According to industry research, Thomas is one of around 245 million people who play fantasy sports, where players take the role of manager or coach and build a virtual team made up of athletes whose real-life performances earn them points. As a control, Scout Digital also has a team titled Scout Statto, which is managed by the firm's co-founder Simon Gold and run without the use of AI tools. Beginning this season, FPL features its own conversational AI assistant titled FPL Companion.

While some predict a future where fantasy sports become a battleground purely for competing versions of AI, Groos does not expect the human element to disappear completely. Groos said the winning formula may turn out to be neither human intuition nor AI-based insights, but a combination of both. Labakk echoed that, adding that he thinks the best possible way is an engaged manager with the models rather than an AI with the models. Marcus Adebayo, 34, a software project manager from South London, uses Gemini by letting it do the structural heavy lifting but picks the team himself. Adebayo said treating it as a co-pilot works brilliantly, provided you are honest enough to admit that when the plane hits turbulence, it is usually because you grabbed the controls.

stories.Headline: Brands use AI pricing tools to cut Black Friday discounts and protect margins
stories.Summary:
Consumer brands are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence to help set prices, hoping to reduce discounts and protect profit margins, according to interviews with five firms that provide AI tools to brands and retailers. That could mean shallower bargains for inflation-weary US shoppers this holiday season, starting with Black Friday, an event synonymous with discounts. Brands from Gap to Under Armour are using AI tools to manage inventory levels, recommend retail prices and figure out when and how steeply to discount products. Often, the tools conclude that companies can reduce discounts without dampening demand, the AI pricing firms told Reuters. Software from retail decision-making company Impact Analytics, which counts Gap as a client, generally shows that brands need fewer promotions for less time on fewer products, chief executive officer Prashant Agrawal said.

Tools from AI pricing firm Kapnova advised a billion-dollar beauty brand to reduce its 2026 Black Friday discount on a skincare product to 30% from an initially planned 40%, CEO James Sun said, declining to name the client due to confidentiality. Tools from AI software company First Insight, whose customers include Under Armour and value chain Family Dollar, recently suggested that one brand scale back a buy-one-get-one promotion from 50% to 40% off, founder Greg Petro said, also declining to name the client. Holiday sales are set to rise 4.2% versus 2025 to just over US$1 trillion, National Retail Federation estimates show, though the bump would be largely attributable to an inflation rate currently at 3.7%. A Gap spokesperson said the brand uses Impact Analytics to make more informed markdown decisions based on demand and inventory signals, while Under Armour and Family Dollar use First Insight to decide what to charge for a product and to estimate how price changes will affect sales, the retail technology company said. Sun of Kapnova conceded that the practice is controversial, saying consumers want discounts but retailers are getting smarter and smarter with AI.

AI-driven planning platform Anaplan said LVMH-owned Tiffany, Dolce & Gabbana and Kering's Yves Saint Laurent use its software for pricing, and more than a dozen brands approached by Reuters, including those five, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The technology is not completely new, but it has become more sophisticated over the past two years at predicting demand for products at specific prices, and adoption is ramping up, experts and industry executives say. A 2025 survey by consultancy Simon-Kucher showed that a third of companies now use AI pricing for demand forecasting and 28% for real-time price optimisation, said Martin Crepy, the firm's global head of consumer. Predictive algorithms typically stop short of pricing items differently for individual customers, a controversial practice that retailers like Walmart and Target have said they do not engage in and that several states have taken steps to curb, but tools that allow retailers to quickly change prices, often called dynamic pricing, sit one layer removed from personalised pricing, according to former McKinsey consultant and e-commerce executive Sofia Serra, who said regulation is still evolving.

stories.Headline: DesignVerse finds AI coding tools without company context cost thousands of engineering hours
stories.Summary:
DesignVerse published its AI Coding Drift Report on 24 November 2026, examining 15 private enterprise codebases in sectors including aviation, banking and defense, each a complex legacy system between 15 and 20 years old containing more than one million lines of code. The research found that businesses using AI coding tools without knowledge of their existing systems and technical standards spend thousands of engineering hours correcting and rebuilding AI-written code. In one enterprise case, a year's work on a single product required an estimated 9,600 engineering hours without an enterprise context layer, a figure the report says fell to 4,000 hours, a 58% reduction, once such a layer was introduced. The 5,600 hours freed were valued at around $882,000, which the report describes as engineering capacity equivalent to about three engineers that could be redirected to other work rather than a direct reduction in staffing costs. The report also compared two unmanaged AI coding agents with DesignVerse's context-engineered system, which gives AI access to company knowledge, existing code, software architecture and technical requirements before it begins work.

The context-engineered system used the organization's own internal software components rather than inventing them or substituting public alternatives 92% of the time, compared with 55% to 59% for the unmanaged agents. The report introduces an Engineering AI Drift Index, which measures how much information an AI coding agent must read before producing code that can be accepted into existing systems, and across the examined codebases agents working without a dedicated context layer read a median of ten tokens for every token of accepted code, a ratio that reached 150 to one in a separate measurement on one client's legacy system. The report likens the problem to a skilled new hire with no handover, noting that an AI agent does the same on every task and forgets what it learned between sessions. Andrei Manolache, CEO and co-founder of DesignVerse, said businesses are investing heavily in AI coding tools because they expect to develop software faster and at lower cost, but there is a hidden bill many are not measuring in the time engineers spend checking, correcting and rebuilding code that does not fit their existing systems. He said companies paying for AI to write code only to pay engineers to fix it afterwards need to ask serious questions about the return on that investment, and that the next challenge for enterprise AI is not simply generating more code but generating code that fits the business.

He said an AI coding tool needs to understand the systems it works with, the company's architecture, its technical standards and the rules it must follow, and that without that context businesses risk creating more work for their engineers rather than less. The report sets out five recommendations, including building a persistent context layer of existing code, architecture, standards and project knowledge, giving AI tools access only to information relevant to each task, enforcing technical standards as code is generated, maintaining an audit trail of which company information and standards were used, and giving a named individual responsibility for keeping the context layer accurate and up to date. The full report, including its method, scoring rubric and limitations, is available online, and it sets out a two-week evaluation any engineering team can run on its own codebase. Businesses can also estimate the potential cost of engineering rework using DesignVerse's Cost of Drift Calculator.

stories.Headline: Leibenluft and Sperling propose five policy planks to prepare US workers for AI job dislocation
stories.Summary:
Jacob Leibenluft and Gene Sperling wrote a report on November 23, 2026, regarding artificial intelligence. They proposed five policy planks to prepare the United States workforce for potential job dislocation. The authors argue that policymakers must begin these preparations now despite an uncertain outlook. These measures aim to support economic dignity for workers during a potential transition. The report suggests that the United States currently lacks the basic infrastructure to support these workers.

The plan requires universal job search assistance and universal income support for all displaced workers. It proposes expanded, progressive wage insurance and the use of automatic scaling-up strategies for labor challenges. The authors suggest supporting redeployment and shorter workweeks without pay reductions to discourage unnecessary layoffs. One proposal includes a universal worker adjustment assistance program providing up to 104 weeks of unemployment payments. These policies would be funded by better taxing corporate profits and capital.

Leibenluft and Sperling stated that the United States lags behind peer nations in providing transition infrastructure. They argued that policymakers should reject training nihilism and invest in successful workforce development strategies. The authors claimed that universal eligibility is the best roadmap forward for assisting displaced workers. They noted that any transition agenda is only one element of a broader policy response. They stated that no adjustment policies can succeed without a commitment to creating good jobs.

The authors noted that many workers already feel anxiety regarding the impact of artificial intelligence. They argued that the gains of productivity growth should be more equitably shared among workers. The report suggests that the lack of good jobs would limit the benefits of training. The authors believe that these policies would also help workers who lose jobs for other reasons. They claimed that previous economic disruptions would have been handled better with these robust measures.

The report notes that economists suggest scenarios ranging from minor transitions to the dislocation of tens of millions. It mentions that past trade assistance programs failed because they required complex adjudication processes for workers. The authors cite a period in the early 2000s when two million workers were dislocated by imports. They noted that Trade Adjustment Assistance then provided training to fewer than 50,000 workers per year. This background serves as a warning against targeting only those who prove AI caused loss.

The authors state that the federal and state governments should start this work immediately. They argue that the approach will require ongoing refinement and experimentation as AI impacts become clearer. The report leaves open the specific details of how to create new jobs if AI causes net losses. It does not specify the exact tax rates needed to fund these proposed worker supports. The authors acknowledge that full answers to the effects of AI on jobs remain unclear.

stories.Headline: Colorado hearing officer dismisses Kipp complaint over Independence Institute AI video
stories.Summary:
A hearing officer in the Colorado secretary of state's office dismissed a complaint last week regarding an AI-generated political video. State Senator Cathy Kipp filed the complaint, alleging that the video violated state laws against unlabeled deepfake political content. The hearing officer, Macon Cowles, issued his decision on November 19 to dismiss the case against the video. The video was produced by the right-leaning Independence Institute to criticize a specific ballot measure before the election. This legal dispute centered on whether the AI-generated content required a specific disclosure under current Colorado state law.

The 2024 law requires a disclosure when generative artificial intelligence depicts a political candidate close to an election date. The video criticized Proposition NN before the November 3 election, a measure sponsored by Kipp and referred by the Legislature. Proposition NN passed with over 57 percent of the vote to let the state retain more revenue for education. The AI-generated video showed Kipp as a grocery store cashier who refused to give a customer their change. While the video had a closing line stating it was AI-generated, it lacked the text required by law.

Hearing officer Macon Cowles stated that the law applies to content that falsely appears to be authentic and truthful. He determined the video was parody and satire, which he wrote are protected by the First Amendment of the Constitution. Cowles wrote that no reasonable viewer would believe Kipp agreed to play a cashier who keeps a customer's money. He noted that Kipp is a public figure and this AI criticism is akin to a political newspaper cartoon. The Independence Institute conceded the video was not true but asserted that no viewer would consider it true.

Independence Institute CEO Jon Caldara said they were grateful the officer saw the video as a joke with a point. Caldara stated that nobody believed Kipp moonlights at a checkout counter and that voters deserved to hear their argument. Senator Cathy Kipp expressed disappointment that the complaint was dismissed in a text message sent to the Colorado Newsline. Kipp stated it was important for the Legislature to find out how the law they passed would be interpreted. She argued that laws must keep up as AI-generated imagery and deepfakes become increasingly prevalent and harmful.

The law at the center of this case was passed by Colorado lawmakers in 2024 to regulate campaign materials. The Independence Institute used the video to illustrate what they believed Proposition NN would do with taxpayer money. The video portrayed Kipp stealing grocery change to give to children for their education, which the institute admitted was false. Critics had already raised free speech concerns about the disclosure requirements of the law after it took effect in 2024. The hearing officer concluded that reasonable viewers would not believe the events in the video actually happened.

The decision made by Macon Cowles is subject to review by the deputy secretary of state before it becomes final. The articles do not state when the deputy secretary of state will complete this review or what the result will be. There is no information regarding whether Senator Kipp intends to appeal the decision or take further legal action. The text does not mention if the Independence Institute plans to release similar AI-generated videos for future elections. It remains open whether the Legislature will amend the 2024 law based on this specific legal interpretation.

Musk told his staff that failing to compete makes renting out compute more profitable. He shared data in a group chat with hundreds of engineers to show the lag. He called such waste a betrayal of the team while the company fails to compete.

The affected parties include the engineers at the SpaceX artificial intelligence unit and the investors. SpaceX is now a public company and faces pressure to show that it can profit. This puts Musk in a position where he rents power to companies he is chasing. Anthropic is described as one of the biggest competitors and biggest customers for Elon Musk. The tension highlights a central conflict in the artificial intelligence push led by Elon Musk.

Musk started the company xAI one year after the 2022 release of the chatbot called ChatGPT. He has spent billions of dollars on data centers to catch up with his rivals. The New York Times viewed communications where Musk changed a group chat name in August. That specific name was Sell compute because we can't compete to reflect the current situation. These actions show the struggle to balance immediate revenue with long term product development goals.

SpaceX will continue to manage the use of its graphics processing units for training systems. The company must decide whether to prioritize internal AI development or external leasing for profit. In August, Elon Musk changed the name of an engineers' group chat with hundreds of SpaceX employees to "Sell compute because we can't compete," according to a New York Times report published on Monday, November 23, 2026. In the same chat, the SpaceX CEO warned that anyone wasting GPUs on what he called bulls,  while the company was failing to compete would be asked to leave immediately, a step he described as a betrayal of the team. SpaceX had rapidly built data centers, including its Colossus facility in Memphis, Tennessee, to scale up its own AI business, but the company is now leasing compute to its rivals instead.

The report said SpaceX's AI unit now accounts for more than half of the rocket company's revenue through leasing agreements with other AI companies. Anthropic became SpaceX's biggest customer in October, surpassing the U.S. government, and is now paying an estimated $3.1 billion per month according to its prospectus, while Google is reportedly paying $800 million. The Times reported that xAI, which merged with SpaceX earlier this year, used less than half the capacity of its Colossus data center last year, citing internal documents. As income from leasing compute soared, SpaceX quietly shifted resources from several AI projects, including an AI companion feature, and laid off 60 employees working on Grok Imagine, an image and video generator, which The Information first reported the previous week.

The Times also reported that SpaceX shifted money away from the company's Digital Optimus project with Tesla, which was training AI models to do white collar work by first teaching them how to play video games. After Anthropic went public the previous week with a record-breaking initial public offering, both Musk and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made comments indicating their deal will likely continue in the near future. Asked on CNBC whether Anthropic planned to scale back its spending with Musk's company, Amodei said you can't be sure what you're going to do in the future, but that Anthropic was finding the compute to be high quality and enjoying working with SpaceX. Musk, speaking at the DealBook Summit the previous week, said he thought it was unlikely the company would stop leasing compute, and said Anthropic had told him its highest probability outcome was that it would like an incremental 10 gigawatts of compute from SpaceX, which he called a big number.

stories.Headline: HPE shares fall as rising AI server costs shrink margins despite strong revenue forecast
stories.Summary:
Shares of Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell about 16 per cent on Tuesday, November 24, as investors focused on the company's shrinking margins amid soaring costs, even though strong AI demand boosted its full-year revenue outlook. The stock had more than doubled this year through Monday's close, but it was set to lose about $10 billion in market value if the losses held. On Monday, HPE had soared more than 17 per cent as an Nvidia-fueled rally lifted AI stocks. The drop came as the company's upbeat forecast was overshadowed by concerns about profitability in its AI business.

HPE forecast an adjusted operating margin for the fiscal year ending October 2027 of between 14 per cent and 15 per cent, down from 15.1 per cent in fiscal 2026. At its Cloud and AI unit, which includes servers and storage and is a key growth driver, HPE expects an annual fiscal margin of about 14 per cent, down from 15.2 per cent in the previous fiscal year. Robust demand for AI servers helped drive a 50 per cent jump in HPE's fourth-quarter revenue to $14.55 billion, topping estimates. The company now expects fiscal 2027 revenue growth between 27 per cent and 35 per cent, up from its earlier forecast of 13 per cent to 17 per cent.

HPE finance chief Marie Myers said on an earnings call that costs were rising faster than pricing and that margins would take a hit in the second half of the year as the company ships more AI servers. Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B Riley Wealth, said that when input costs go up and not enough is passed along, margins have to take a hit, and that this clearly showed. He added that this raises concerns that pricing tailwinds are beginning to fade, and that supply shortages expected through 2028 will take a bite out of margins. Bob O'Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research, said the market seems acutely sensitive to any potential changes in profit margins at tech companies these days, and that HPE's solid numbers and robust forecast certainly did not seem to justify the market's reaction that day.

stories.Headline: US chip restrictions on Chinese AI labs threaten S&P 500 valuations
stories.Summary:
The United States government recently closed a long-standing loophole that previously allowed Chinese artificial intelligence labs to gain remote access to advanced American chips sold overseas. This policy shift occurred around November 2026 and has already caused the Hang Seng Tech Index to tumble 13 percent over two weeks. The e-commerce giant Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. suffered significantly because it rented compute from Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based operator. This specific operator is currently at the center of an alleged espionage scandal involving the chipmaker Nvidia Corp.

These restrictions may force the S&P 500 to retreat to about 5,600, which would represent a 19 percent decline. Such a drop could happen if consensus earnings estimates return to their 30-year trend and the price-to-earnings ratio falls to a long-term average of 17 times. The situation is complicated by the fact that semiconductors are expected to deliver more than half of S&P 500 earnings growth next year. Nvidia, the largest earnings contributor to the index, is still expected to generate 73 percent revenue growth over the next fiscal year.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc. warned that a return to normal corporate profits could deliver a double blow of weaker earnings and lower valuations. The US Securities and Exchange Commission is also investigating the accounting practices of Nvidia following a policy change in October 2025. This change involved reporting revenue based on customer headquarters rather than billing locations, which affected about 22 percent of sales billed through Singapore. Analysts worry that if the $104 billion billed through Singapore represented Chinese demand, a sizable chunk of revenue could disappear.

National security hawks in Washington are continuing to squeeze China despite the potential for significant economic damage to American firms. The global artificial intelligence value chain is so deeply integrated that it is almost impossible to diversify these risks away. Other industrial companies like Caterpillar Inc. and GE Vernova Inc. may see their orders diminish if capital investments in this sector slow down. The US will likely have to pay a hefty price for these actions as the trade becomes more pervasive.

stories.Headline: US Energy Department leads project to test fuel cell power systems for AI data centers
stories.Summary:
A three-year project led by the U.S. Department of Energy will examine how fuel cells, energy storage and power electronics can work together to meet the rapidly changing electricity demands of artificial intelligence data centers. The project, called StabilityMax, is led by the DOE's National Laboratory of the Rockies, with participation from Argonne National Laboratory and FuelCell Energy. The effort will develop and validate testing and modeling frameworks to evaluate integrated power system architectures under operating conditions designed to reflect the fluctuating loads of modern data centers. As AI workloads expand, data centers are placing increasing demands on electricity infrastructure, and their power consumption can change rapidly as computing activity shifts, creating challenges for maintaining reliable power and managing impacts on the utility grid.

Under the project, FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Connecticut that will serve as a national laboratory-supported testbed for evaluating integrated power systems. The National Laboratory of the Rockies will develop data center load profiles and simulation models to replicate the dynamic electricity requirements of AI computing infrastructure. Researchers will use the models and test facility to examine how fuel cells can operate alongside energy storage, advanced controls and power electronics to respond to changing loads. Argonne National Laboratory will contribute techno-economic and lifecycle analyses to evaluate potential deployment approaches.

The research will focus in part on the ability of fuel cell systems located alongside data centers to respond to power fluctuations while limiting impacts on the utility grid and other electricity customers. StabilityMax is part of the National Laboratory of the Rockies' broader work to develop modeling tools, planning platforms and testing environments for the growing energy requirements of AI-enabled digital infrastructure. The project also builds on FuelCell Energy's work with technology partners on integrated power architectures for data centers. Earlier this year, the company announced a collaboration with Siemens to advance a layered approach that combines multiple power technologies operating across different timescales.

stories.Headline: Study argues workplace democracy resolves corporate AI ethics better than public inclusion agendas
stories.Summary:
A philosophical investigation published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance on November 25, 2026 argues that the popular agenda to democratize artificial intelligence fails to resolve ethical failures in tech corporations. The study says this agenda misdiagnoses the core structural barrier to reform. It argues that the primary obstacle to responsible technological development is not the exclusion of external citizens but the severe power disparities within corporate hierarchies. The analysis examines how democratic theory applies to corporate environments and resolves the boundary problem of who should hold decision-making authority over corporate algorithms. It concludes that internal workplace democracy offers a more viable normative foundation for ethical artificial intelligence than external public consultation, provided it operates alongside external democratic state regulations.

The study confines its systematic evaluation to widening direct participation in corporate decisions on the research, development and governance of algorithmic systems. It identifies three mechanisms: research and development inclusion, inclusive intra-organizational oversight, and democratic control of tech firms. It interrogates four principles from democratic theory: the all-affected interests principle, the all-subjected principle, civic solidarity, and the epistemic and developmental effects of inclusion. It says the all-affected principle would obligate companies to include billions of international users in daily deliberations. It says external consumers typically interact with corporate software without direct institutional coercion, unlike citizens subject to state laws.

The author says distributive justice is a distinct conceptual category from democracy, which concerns equalizing participant influence rather than guaranteeing resource allocations. The author says expanding consumer access or technical comprehension does not confer governance authority over design parameters or deployment trajectories. The author says incorporating consumer accessibility under democracy dilutes the normative significance of democratic self-rule. The author says employees possess a collective identity, reciprocal economic interdependencies and mutual institutional investments that enable cohesive democratic deliberation. The author says external citizens can acquire technical literacy through independent educational platforms and accessible development environments.

The study says corporate executives have implemented mass redundancies targeting internal ethics teams, algorithmic accountability specialists and responsible development divisions. It says these eliminated units are the entities that would oversee public participation and implement ethical safeguards. It says corporate employees rely on employers for their livelihood and lack substantive exit options, leaving those who raise ethical concerns vulnerable to marginalization or termination. It says the debate over participatory boundaries has deflected attention from entrenched internal power disparities.

It says ethical considerations of algorithmic fairness, systemic safety and social disruption are consistently subordinated to commercial profitability. The study says technology ethicists frequently advocate widening public participation in corporate decision-making to address algorithmic harms. It says artificial intelligence systems influence billions of lives through automated profiling, algorithmic hiring and computational data processing. It says scholars have imported the boundary problem into the technological domain to ask who should govern corporate algorithmic design and deployment.

It says democratization is routinely conflated with virtually any desirable political or social outcome, from mitigating algorithmic bias to closing global knowledge disparities. It says the first view of democratization covers redistributive proposals such as universal basic income, windfall clauses, automation taxes and digital data commons. The study champions workplace democracy to rectify the vulnerability of employees who raise ethical concerns. It says the second view of democratization advocates transparent system architectures, addressing unequal access across the digital divide and organizational benchmarks for trustworthy systems.

It says the third mechanism proposes that governments regulate major computing platforms as public utilities, establish citizen governance boards chosen through sortition, or subordinate corporate decisions to elected public bodies. It says democratic epistemic models presuppose baseline competency thresholds or expert moderators who synthesize public inputs. It says corporations have justifiable reasons to reserve authoritative governance for their internal workforce while treating external engagement as advisory consultation. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Former Linklaters solicitor Jessica Fitzgerald founds Conclusive Legal to review clients AI-drafted documents
stories.Summary:
A former Linklaters solicitor has founded a new law firm that offers to review documents clients have generated using artificial intelligence, the Law Gazette reported on 24 November 2026. The firm, called Conclusive Legal, is fronted by Jessica Fitzgerald, a dual-qualified solicitor with 12 years of litigation experience, including work as a litigation case manager at Linklaters. The privately funded venture describes itself as a human-first AI platform and says it specialises in civil and commercial disputes valued at up to £100,000. Clients can submit a document they have drafted themselves, with or without AI, for a qualified solicitor to review, amend and approve.

The firm, which is authorised by the Solicitors Regulation Authority, also offers to draft documents from scratch for clients who prefer that route. Fitzgerald said most AI legal tools stop at the AI itself, while her firm begins with a call to a qualified solicitor combined with AI technology. She said every document is checked by the firm's proprietary AI against court rules and common errors drawn from real litigation experience, before a qualified disputes solicitor reviews, corrects and signs it off. She said people are already drafting their own legal documents with AI, but a document containing legal errors or fabricated case law can have serious consequences, including adverse costs orders.

Fitzgerald said the firm is putting control back in clients' hands, letting them run their own dispute with a solicitor reviewing every document before it reaches a court or the other side. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Mayor Zohran Mamdani warns that the stock market is overly dependent on AI stocks
stories.Summary:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani commented on Monday about the corporate turbulence involving the chipmaker Nvidia and its chief executive officer, Jensen Huang. The company experienced a dramatic drop in share price when Huang stepped down as the chief executive officer on 12 November. This resignation followed reports that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a tech executive suspected of being a Chinese spy. After Donald Trump intervened, the California based company reinstated Huang on Monday and saw its value bounce back by 31.5 percent.

The situation involves Alice Huang, who is accused of routing advanced chips to Beijing through her company called Megaspeed. National intelligence director Jay Clayton stated that he suspected China was able to obtain the most advanced artificial intelligence chips from Nvidia. Mayor Mamdani noted that a rumored divorce settlement of 81 billion dollars could provide universal childcare for every three and four year old in the United States for one year. He also mentioned that Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, have been married since 1985 and hold combined assets of about 160 billion dollars.

Mayor Mamdani stated that the stock market is disproportionately dependent on stocks related to the artificial intelligence boom powered by Nvidia chips. He expressed concern about the dominance of this technology and said working Americans did not sign up for pensions tied to the fidelity of Jensen Huang. The mayor referenced Justice Louis Brandeis to argue that democracy and great wealth concentrated in the hands of a few cannot both exist. He believes the recent volatility shows a massive impact on the lives of working people across the entire country.

President Donald Trump told the Wall Street Journal that he likes getting involved in companies to help them when they have problems. He pointed to the government taking a 10 percent stake in the chipmaker Intel as an example of his approach. Congress is now expected to grill Jensen Huang regarding his ties with China and the intervention by the president. The situation highlights a complex relationship between the democratic socialist mayor and the financial center of Wall Street.

stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump suggested the US government could take an equity stake in Nvidia. He made these comments during an interview with the New York Post. The remarks were published on November 24, 2026. Trump stated he has considered this idea but has not yet proposed it. He believes it might not be too late to raise the issue.

The plan would involve federal ownership of the chipmaker to ensure American AI leadership. Trump also mentioned he would pardon CEO Jensen Huang if it became necessary. He expects Huang to be fine without a pardon during his testimony. This testimony before Congress is scheduled to take place next week. Trump previously pressed the Nvidia board to reinstate Huang.

President Trump said the success of Nvidia is central to keeping the United States ahead. He told Huang to tell the truth to lawmakers during his upcoming testimony. Trump added that Huang would not need to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights. He noted that the Nvidia stock recovered much of its Tuesday loss. These comments were made while reviewing market data from the Oval Office.

Investors may see White House backing as a floor for the strategic position of Nvidia. Others could view the move as a source of political entanglement and governance risk. This risk involves China sales and export rules for the semiconductor company. Global chip peers and other governments are also watching these potential steps. The wider semiconductor and Nasdaq complex face elevated headline risk.

Washington previously took an equity stake in Intel in 2025 to secure domestic capacity. This was part of a push for critical supply chains and semiconductor production. Nvidia is a dominant supplier of chips that power AI data centres. It is also one of the most valuable companies in the world. The government has shown willingness to take stakes in strategically important firms.

The structure, size, and purpose of any potential government stake remain entirely open. It is unknown how Nvidia shareholders and the board would respond to this. Huang's testimony next week will be a marker for the AI trade. Further follow-up from the White House is expected regarding this potential policy. stories.Headline: Anthropic finds bosses pushing AI at work fuels surveillance fears and worker resistance
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI startup, published a 29-page report on 24 November 2026 finding that when bosses push AI at work, it can fuel workers' surveillance fears and cause resistance, according to Business Insider. Researchers conducted 66 interviews with 58 companies that are Anthropic customers, and the report said pushback can lead to what it called abandoned or fragile automations. At one law firm, the chief operating officer asked a staffer to build an AI tool to check for conflicts of interest, which left workers handling tricky cases they had previously handed to attorneys, and the firm dropped the tool and resumed its prior process after workers pushed back. One operations supervisor told researchers he began each day with an AI-generated report on how much work each member of his 12-person team completed and how often they made errors, saying he could then question them about any lag. Some interviewees thought AI could make performance feedback more accurate but also worried about how closely it could let bosses track employees.

People at two-thirds of the companies told Anthropic they were hiring less because of AI, with a third of those decreases coming from companies leaving roles unfilled after workers left and most stemming from companies skipping hires they would have made without AI. Interviewees at five companies discussed pushing out workers who would not adopt AI, and at two companies interviewees said AI automation eliminated a position, resulting in someone losing a job. One engineering leader said a couple of people started off extremely anti-AI and moved along the spectrum but not enough, so the company let them go. Ten companies said they had stepped up hiring because of AI, mainly to help roll it out or to boost IT support.

One operations manager said she woke at 3 a.m. worried about her career prospects and asked Claude how to set herself apart so that AI could not do everything she does. The report said letting workers experiment on their own brought its own problems, since a tool that saved one person time did not necessarily help others and apps workers built still needed someone to review and maintain them. At one law firm, a paralegal recalled partners asking how he prompted AI after noticing his demand letters stood out, and although he eventually shared his approach, his first instinct was to keep it to himself.

stories.Headline: Review finds orthodontic AI lacks prospective clinical evidence despite high imaging accuracy
stories.Summary:
A narrative review published on November 24, 2026, assessed how far artificial intelligence in orthodontics has translated into patient care. The review synthesized evidence across diagnostic imaging, treatment planning, remote monitoring, patient education and automated robotics. It found that no orthodontic artificial intelligence application met the authors' predefined criteria for higher clinical maturity. Machine learning and deep learning systems showed high diagnostic accuracy in identifying anatomical landmarks on radiographs and segmenting structures on three-dimensional volumes. The authors reported that most published studies were retrospective technical investigations conducted on benchmark datasets.

The review team searched PubMed, ScienceDirect and the Cochrane Library for peer-reviewed studies published between January 1, 2000, and August 31, 2026. The initial query retrieved 2,022 records, comprising 1,699 from PubMed, 204 from ScienceDirect and 119 from the Cochrane Library. After 169 duplicates were removed in Zotero, two independent reviewers screened 1,853 unique records against strict eligibility criteria. The core synthesis comprised 48 studies, made up of 45 database publications and three records found through reference screening, one book chapter and two peer-reviewed conference proceedings. The authors contextualized these with 17 authoritative reporting and regulatory frameworks and set four progressive evidence levels, from task-specific technical performance through external validation and prospective clinical effectiveness to demonstrated clinical or patient benefit.

The authors concluded that current literature has prioritized computational performance over clinical utility. They wrote that major gaps remain over whether algorithm-assisted recommendations alter clinical decision-making, enhance treatment efficiency, reduce procedural errors or improve long-term outcomes. They noted that commercial availability was documented strictly as an implementation characteristic rather than proof of therapeutic efficacy. They emphasized that benchmark performance on simulated patient inquiries does not demonstrate clinical safety during unsupervised patient triage. They concluded that future progress requires prospective, multicenter clinical trials adhering to frameworks such as TRIPOD-AI, STARD-AI and DECIDE-AI, with algorithms functioning as supervised decision-support tools.

A featured systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies, covering algorithms developed between 2017 and 2020, found that 79.9 percent of anatomical landmarks were detected within the accepted two-millimeter clinical acceptability boundary. That analysis reported a pooled mean prediction error difference of minus 0.581 millimeters relative to reference tracings, while about one in five automated landmark detections fell outside acceptable clinical tolerance. An external validation study of 190 cone-beam computed tomography scans from five imaging systems evaluated 879 tooth segmentation maps from cloud-based commercial software, which produced acceptable segmentations without manual refinement in 90.1 percent of instances. Fixed orthodontic brackets increased the likelihood of needing manual refinement nearly fourfold, while endodontic obturation and adjacent high-density metallic artifacts raised refinement odds by 4.43-fold and 7.88-fold.

An independent trial comparing an artificial intelligence web platform with manual three-dimensional measurements across 95 craniofacial computed tomography examinations found automated tracing failures in 16.8 percent of patient scans. Machine learning regression models trained on serial lateral cephalograms reported linear prediction accuracies of 97.87 percent and angular accuracies of 94.45 percent for craniofacial growth at age 13, but the training cohort was restricted to 59 children from a single population. A systematic review of 19 planning systems noted expert concordance rates surpassing 80 to 90 percent, though these trials relied on subjective clinician opinion as the gold standard rather than verified long-term clinical correctness. In a preliminary randomized controlled trial of 100 orthodontic patients allocated to conventional educational leaflets or an artificial intelligence chatbot over five weeks, both groups showed significant periodontal deterioration, but chatbot users had a significantly smaller increase in modified gingival index scores.

Comparative assessments of ChatGPT-4.0, Microsoft Copilot and Gemini produced contradictory findings across general orthodontic and clear aligner inquiries. The review also cited automation bias among practitioners, data privacy risks with facial photographic records, algorithmic bias from homogeneous training sets and the lack of dedicated orthodontic regulatory frameworks. The review classified treatment planning and extraction decision-making systems as emerging technologies with substantial methodological heterogeneity, and most studies carried moderate to serious risk of bias due to single-center designs and lack of prospective follow-up. Remote monitoring tools for clear aligner seating, oral hygiene and appliance integrity relied predominantly on retrospective photo evaluations and feasibility demonstrations.

Direct force-sensing platforms with flexible three-dimensional sensors were validated in laboratory environments to record force direction and magnitude, but their practical clinical integration remained in early prototype development. Automated wire-bending devices frequently reflected conventional computer numerical automation rather than genuine artificial intelligence learning models, and evidence of improved chairside efficiency or tooth-movement precision remained sparse. The reviewed chatbot investigations lacked adherence to standardized reporting guidelines such as CHART. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers find structured prompting improves AI performance in scoliosis evaluations
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Sun Yat-sen University and Shenzhen University published a study in Frontiers in Digital Health by November 24, 2026. They tested how structured prompting affects artificial intelligence performance in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis evaluations. The team used a blinded comparative study to evaluate several large language models. They focused on four clinical stages including prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis. The study found that structured reasoning prompts significantly improved response quality over standard instructions.

The study tested Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview, GPT-5-Pro, Claude-Sonnet-4-6-Thinking, GLM-5.1, DeepSeek-Reasoner, and Qwen-Max on April 13, 2026. It used twenty consultation questions about a child named Lily, including a twelve-year-old girl with a thirty-degree Cobb angle. Six rehabilitation medicine specialists rated responses across five domains on a five-point Likert scale. The researchers compared zero-shot learning, chain-of-thought prompting, and tree-of-thought prompting. These methods were tested across the continuum of care for adolescents between 10 and 18 years old.

The investigators stated that structured reasoning pathways achieved higher composite ratings than models answering without explicit guidance. They noted that Gemini achieved the highest numerical composite average at 4.69 points. The researchers observed that differences between advanced reasoning frameworks remained statistically indistinguishable. They reported that chain-of-thought and tree-of-thought prompting markedly outperformed zero-shot prompting. The authors cautioned against unmonitored clinical adoption due to domain-specific and stage-dependent performance boundaries.

Six rehabilitation medicine specialists performed the randomized evaluations and noted subjective variability in their qualitative appraisals. Some experts found that models generated clinically unnuanced or rigid advice that could mislead families. One Claude response claimed surgery was virtually the sole option for curves exceeding 45 degrees. Another Claude output described a thirty-degree curve as having an exceptionally high probability of progression. These findings affect parents and caregivers who might use generative models for home-based guidance.

Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is the most prevalent three-dimensional spinal deformity in adolescents, affecting 2 to 3 percent of the population. It results from genetic susceptibility, abnormal growth regulation, and biomechanical environmental forces. Management relies on the Lenke taxonomy, the Cobb angle, the Risser sign, and physical markers. Specialized orthopedic and rehabilitation resources are often geographically and socioeconomically constrained. Generative language models have emerged as potential scalable adjuncts for family education and brace adherence support.

The study suggests that prompt engineering exerts a pronounced moderating influence on the quality of clinical generations. The most substantial gains occurred in the domain of empathy and humanistic care. Future use may depend on addressing the modest concordance found among evaluating physicians. The articles leave open how to resolve the ceiling effects observed within the scoring rubric. They do not specify how to eliminate the risk of misleading advice without clinical oversight.

stories.Headline: US midterm elections trigger social and economic resistance to AI development
stories.Summary:
The 2026 midterm elections in the United States signaled a new phase for artificial intelligence development. The American public placed the industry under large-scale scrutiny for the first time during these elections. This event showed that a model based on capital expansion and technological acceleration faces social resistance. Economic constraints and local opposition to data center construction also contributed to this turning point. These factors together suggest that the current path of AI development is now changing.

The elections involved 41 local ballot measures concerning data centers, with 40 favoring construction restrictions. Among 34 confirmed state governor victors, 32 supported tighter regulation of these data center facilities. The U.S. government previously backed the Stargate project, which envisioned investing 500 billion dollars over four years. Resistance appeared in traditionally Republican districts, specifically in the states of Ohio and Texas. James Talarico, a Democratic Senate nominee, addressed data centers in downtown Austin on July 22, 2026.

Li Zheng, an assistant research processor, stated that AI development is encountering visible social resistance and economic constraint. Zheng noted that the tech right sought to translate technological acceleration into policy during Donald Trump's second term. This ideology claimed that governments should reduce regulatory intervention to allow capital and technology to realize innovative potential. The goal was to use capital investment for breakthroughs to create new market demand and future growth. Zheng argued that the real economy cannot accommodate the current pace of AI investment growth.

Ordinary households are affected by AI inflation, which increases costs for electricity, land, water, and advanced chips. Ordinary workers are concerned about the cost of living and wage growth while capital owners grow wealthier. Local communities in various districts have expressed opposition to the rapid expansion of data center infrastructure. Some companies face financial strain because operating cash flow no longer covers their massive capital expenditures. A crisis of confidence in AI companies caused their share prices to drop before the midterms.

The tech right promoted a model of building infrastructure ahead of demand in anticipation of future growth. This approach viewed artificial intelligence as a tool for reshaping the competitive position of the United States. AI models can be upgraded quickly, but electricity grids and industrial supply chains cannot expand as fast. This gap created tensions between the growth of AI investment and the capacity of the real economy. The industry relied on continuous injections of capital market funding and complex private credit structures.

Democrats are planning 2027 policies to require data centers to pay for additional power infrastructure and safety testing. They aim to clarify corporate liability for harm and improve community participation in the development of data centers. Some progressives have proposed a moratorium on large data centers and restrictions on the most advanced AI models. The articles leave open whether Democrats will agree on a unified policy approach for these new regulations. It remains to be seen if AI can lower production costs and create new employment opportunities.

Articles.Title: U.S. Elections Signal New Phase of AI Development - China-US Focus

stories.headline_source: U.S. Elections Signal New Phase of AI Development - China-US Focus

stories.Headline: University of Tokyo researchers improve AI prediction of undiscovered material properties
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science at the University of Tokyo have developed an approach that they say substantially improves the ability of machine-learning models to predict material properties beyond their training data. The team's findings were published in PRX Intelligence on 24 November 2026, in an article titled "Achieving Robust Extrapolation in Materials Property Prediction via Decoupled Transfer Learning." The method reduced prediction error in a demanding extrapolation test by 68% compared with a widely used end-to-end graph neural network known as CGCNN. The work addresses the problem of extrapolation, in which models must predict properties of materials that lie outside the examples they were trained on.

The key to the approach is a strategy called decoupled transfer learning, which separates what the model learns about structure from how it predicts properties. Instead of training a single neural network to learn both the structure and the target property, the method uses pretrained graph neural networks to extract information about atomic arrangements, bonding patterns and geometry. Those features are then passed to a simple regression model that predicts the desired property. To mimic how materials are actually discovered over time, the model was trained only on data from the Materials Project up to 2018 and then asked to predict materials added through 2021.

Lead author Tasuku Sugiura said the team wanted to test machine learning under extrapolation conditions relevant to searching for new materials, and that rather than building a bigger model they separated what the model learns about structure from how it predicts properties. Senior author Teruyasu Mizoguchi said materials discovery is inherently an extrapolation problem and that more complexity is surprisingly not the answer, because the pretrained networks capture rich structural information while the simple regression stage extends trends beyond the training range. The researchers found that the method works particularly well when new materials represent a continuous extension of familiar chemical or structural patterns. However, it becomes less reliable when predictions require a jump into poorly represented chemical or electronic regimes, which reveals practical boundaries that researchers can identify before relying on a model.

The method does not require large-scale retraining or specialized resources, and researchers can use publicly available pretrained models together with standard regression tools to implement it. The team says the findings provide a practical roadmap for using machine learning more reliably to explore materials beyond existing data. The articles mention potential applications ranging from batteries and catalysts to alloys and other inorganic materials. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these stated applications and the published paper.

Articles.Title: Predicting the unknown: a robust approach lets AI extrapolate to undiscovered materials

stories.Headline: California bars attorneys from delegating legal practice to generative AI
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a November 24, 2026 J.S. Held article on JDSupra about trust and transparency in AI-assisted litigation, and they give no account of a single event with a date, place and actor. The articles report no incident, no named person who did anything and no date on which anything happened. They discuss risks and rules for expert witnesses, attorneys and insurance professionals rather than one happening. The only date tied to the article itself is its posting date of November 24, 2026. No figures, names or places attach to any event in the headline.

The articles say California enacted its first state law on Generative AI use by attorneys and arbitrators, effective January 1, 2027. That law bars attorneys from delegating the practice of law to Gen AI and from inputting personally identifying information unless access is restricted to the attorney and authorized persons. It requires reasonable steps to verify Gen AI outputs, including all case and statutory citations, and correction of erroneous or hallucinated output. It requires disclosure to the court of Gen AI use for all submitted documents. New York State's Part 161 took effect June 1, 2026, permitting AI tools in court submissions without disclosure but requiring careful review and independent assurance against fabricated or fictitious cases, statutes or other material.

The articles say Louisiana's Article 371 requires attorneys to avoid knowingly presenting false, artificially generated or artificially manipulated evidence. It bars misleading or deceiving the court and requires reasonable diligence to verify authenticity before submission. A lawyer who knew or reasonably should have known evidence was false or manipulated and failed to disclose it may face contempt or other disciplinary action. The articles describe proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707 on machine-generated evidence offered without an expert witness. They say Rule 702 governs admissibility of expert testimony and requires that testimony be the product of reliable principles and methods.

The articles say several courts have sanctioned lawyers for relying on AI to cite cases and other information that did not exist. They describe three pending AI-related cases against health insurers, Estate of Gene B. Lokken v. UnitedHealth Group, Barrows v. Humana and Kisting-Leung v. Cigna, filed in federal courts in Minnesota, Kentucky and California.

The articles say the allegations are contested and no final determination on the merits has been made. They say the cases allege violations of policy terms through AI or automated algorithms in coverage determinations and inconsistency with plan terms, fiduciary obligations or representations of individualized medical review. The articles say AI works as a black box whose systems may not be clearly examined or explained. They say opacity in proprietary AI systems can leave the method behind a conclusion unclear and possibly riddled with errors or biases. They say AI is susceptible to hallucinations and false references and citations.

They say AI-generated reports often lack nuanced understanding and cannot substitute for expert judgment or explain the reasoning behind conclusions. They say experts can present facts, data, analysis and results in a way that eliminates the black box and can defend their work on request. The articles say no federal or state rules categorically prohibit attorneys from using AI to support depositions live, provided they comply with competence, confidentiality and supervision obligations. They recommend requiring a hard copy of all AI-developed sources before publishing a report so the expert can verify relevance, reliability and lack of bias.

They say AI is increasingly used during depositions and trials to identify inconsistencies and guide questioning in real time. They say drones and AI can inspect sites that are physically difficult to reach. The excerpt ends mid-sentence on proposed Rule 707, leaving its text and status unstated. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Expertise In The Age Of Algorithms: Trust And Transparency In AI-Assisted Litigation

stories.headline_source: Expertise In The Age Of Algorithms: Trust And Transparency In AI-Assisted Litigation

stories.Headline: Vals AI researchers find some language models use profanity when solving complex technical problems
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Vals AI discovered that several artificial intelligence language models have started using profanity while solving complex technical problems. The findings were published on the Vals AI website on 11 November 2026 after an analysis of 200,353 runs. This study involved 102 different language models across 21 tests to identify when these systems used swear words. The researchers found that 14 of the models used offensive language during their reasoning processes.

The study found that the MiMo V2.6 Pro model from Xiaomi used profanity most frequently, appearing in 8.2 per cent of its launches. Specifically, this model used profanity in 267 out of 3,247 runs, including 133 cases out of 198 during the ProgramBench test. Other models that used the word fuck included MiMo V2.6 Flash, Inkling 2 Small, Ember-1, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and Kimi K3. In 88 per cent of cases where the word fuck appeared, the model failed to complete the task.

The authors of the study noted that all models exhibiting this behavior were released no earlier than 16 July 2026. They suggested that the cause might be new training approaches that focus on lengthy, multi-stage tasks requiring repeated corrections. The researchers clarified that generating emotionally charged phrases does not prove that artificial intelligence experiences human emotions like stress or irritation. They concluded that the exact cause of this behavior has not yet been established.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence has started swearing: researchers have discovered when this happens

stories.headline_source: Artificial intelligence has started swearing: researchers have discovered when this happens

stories.Headline: Report urges European NATO allies to build independent AI ecosystem to reduce US reliance
stories.Summary:
Helena Eglit, Tomas Jermalavičius, and Grete Põder published a report on November 24, 2026. They examined the process of Europeanising NATO regarding artificial intelligence. The authors analyzed the intensifying geopolitical competition between the US and China. They noted that Russia's aggression in Ukraine shows increasing AI employment in war. Adoption of this technology across European NATO countries remains uneven.

The US prioritises speed and rejects regulatory constraints in its new AI Strategy. National Security Presidential Memorandum-11 calls for faster military adoption of frontier AI. The US voted with Russia, Belarus, Israel, and North Korea against a 2028 treaty. Poland and Türkiye abstained from this UN General Assembly motion on lethal autonomous weapons. The US also vetoed a French proposal for a NATO Military AI Centre of Excellence.

The authors state that US dominance in the AI industry has important implications. They claim that European Allies must implement AI in defence without the US. The report says that entanglement with US tech corporations is a strategic vulnerability. It notes that the US cast aside concerns that underpinned the NATO AI Strategy. The authors argue that Europe must build an entire European AI ecosystem.

The report mentions that 23 European countries rely on US cloud providers. These providers include Amazon, Google, and Microsoft for security and defence architectures. NATO chose the US company Palantir to provide the Maven Smart System. Some European Allies followed this procurement decision at their own national level. The authors claim that this leaves Europe exposed to the US military-tech complex.

NATO identified AI as one of nine critical technologies for a policy framework. US companies secured about 250 billion euros in funding during 2025. Europe secured only 17 billion euros in funding during that same year. The US held around 78 percent of global compute capacity in 2026. Europe held only around 5 percent of that global compute capacity.

The EU Tech Sovereignty Package seeks to triple data-centre capacity in several years. Germany partnered with Helsing and Saab in 2023 for military aircraft AI. France partnered with Mistral to develop a sovereign military AI system. The UK awarded a 2.3 billion euro contract to train 60,000 soldiers. The report leaves open if Europe can achieve true technological and strategic sovereignty.

stories.Headline: Generative AI health advice use associated with higher uptake of selected childhood vaccines in Japan
stories.Summary:
A new Japanese study suggests that parents who regularly use generative artificial intelligence for general health advice may be more likely to have their children vaccinated against mumps, influenza and COVID-19. Researchers drew on a national internet survey of thousands of parents and children and found higher vaccination uptake among children of regular AI health-advice users than among children of parents who did not use such tools regularly. The pattern largely held after accounting for earlier vaccination history and vaccine attitudes, but no clear association emerged for routine measles-rubella vaccination. The findings are exploratory and cannot show that AI advice itself influenced vaccination decisions. Researchers affiliated with the David Geffen School of Medicine at the University of California, Los Angeles, Harvard Medical School, Tohoku University Graduate School of Medicine and other institutions analyzed 2025 data from the Japan COVID-19 and Society Internet Survey.

The nationwide online survey included 5,170 parents and their reports on vaccination for 8,282 children aged 1 to 17, and the study was published in World Journal of Pediatrics on 15 October 2026. In a subset covering 2,521 children, the team linked responses to the 2023 survey to test whether the main findings were sensitive to additional adjustment for earlier parental vaccine attitudes and vaccination of the eldest child in the household. The study classified parents as regular users if they currently used generative AI and consulted it for health or medical information or advice at least a few times a month, while the comparison group included people who had never used generative AI, former users and current users who consulted it less often or never for health advice. About 15% of the children had a parent classified as a regular user.

After accounting for differences such as parent and child age and household income, estimated vaccination rates among children of regular users and those in the comparison group were 76.6% and 72.7% for mumps, 56.7% and 49.0% for influenza, and 40.6% and 30.9% for COVID-19. The main analysis found no clear difference in age-appropriate measles-rubella vaccination. The authors said these findings should be read as exploratory observational associations rather than evidence that AI advice shaped parental decisions, and they said regular AI health-advice use may instead mark broader digital health engagement, stronger health-information seeking or favourable preventive attitudes. They also cautioned that the survey did not measure vaccine-specific or child-specific AI use, or when it occurred relative to vaccination, and that healthy-user bias cannot be excluded.

The larger COVID-19 estimate among parents under 30, they said, rests on a small subgroup and needs replication in prospective studies. The survey measured how often parents sought general health advice from AI and relied on parents' reports of their children's vaccinations, and it did not record whether parents asked about vaccines or their children's health, or when they consulted AI relative to vaccination. Differences in how actively families seek health information or engage with preventive care could help explain the patterns. Future studies could record the timing and content of vaccine-related AI consultations and follow children's vaccination histories using documented records to investigate whether the advice plays a role in parents' decisions.

Articles.Title: Generative AI health advice use associated with higher uptake of selected childhood vaccines in Japan

stories.Headline: Orange CTO Bruno Zerbib warns against Nokia and Nvidia AI-RAN GPU tie-up
stories.Summary:
Nokia and Nvidia formed a tie-up to develop AI-RAN products using graphics processing units. This partnership became a point of concern for Orange CTO Bruno Zerbib in November 2026. Zerbib raised these warnings during the annual OpenTech event held in Paris. The event featured senior executives from Nokia, Ericsson, and Orange. The discussion focused on the risks of this specific technical architecture.

Nokia is designing 5G and 6G products based on Nvidia GPUs for Layer 1 functions. This follows a one billion dollar investment by Nvidia into Nokia last year. Nvidia also invested ten billion dollars into xAI in January and two billion into Marvell. Furthermore, Nvidia provided five billion dollars to Intel for central processing unit development. These changes replace custom silicon with commercially unproven GPUs in the radio access network.

Bruno Zerbib runs the technology division and strategy for the French operator Orange. He stated he must avoid a risky architecture change that offers zero benefits. Zerbib expressed concern over a subscription model for software updates on top of capex. He also questioned if an American company would impact the sovereignty of a European vendor. The CTO claimed he does not believe in magic regarding promised efficiency gains.

Alok Tripathi, an independent analyst, said the era of high-profile GPU AI-RAN marketing may end. This view follows reports that Nvidia dumped 56 percent of its stake in Nokia. This divestment triggered a four percent drop in the share price of the Finnish vendor. Telcos are affected because they may rely on Nvidia for ongoing software optimizations. Some experts are unconvinced that the highest promised efficiency figures are actually achievable.

Nokia and Ericsson have been substituting adaptive AI software for algorithms written by humans. Nokia promised spectral efficiency improvements of 20 percent this year and 50 percent next year. The company claims a doubling of this efficiency will occur by the year 2028. Nokia's CTO Pallavi Mahajan says GPUs allow operators to rely on software upgrades for years. However, Nokia indicated it will not develop custom silicon to succeed its latest product.

Nokia advisor Harri Holma says there is no hurry for operators to replace current chips. The articles leave open whether telcos can directly monetize the use of these GPUs. It remains unclear what happens to workers who refined the old human-written algorithms. Zerbib is not yet picking sides regarding the deployment of Nokia for AI-RAN. The impact of Nvidia's potential loss of investment ability on the economy is unknown.

Articles.Title: Nokia tie-up with Nvidia on AI-RAN gets warning from Orange CTO

stories.Headline: Voters in 38 jurisdictions approve data center limits over power and water concerns
stories.Summary:
Voters in at least 38 local jurisdictions approved restrictions or slowdowns on data center construction during the midterm elections. These communities are resisting the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure due to concerns about environmental impacts and high resource consumption. Residents are particularly worried about the massive amounts of electricity and water these facilities require to operate. This political resistance has transformed scattered neighborhood objections into a national challenge for the technology industry.

The expansion of these centers requires new power plants, transmission lines, substations, and substantial water for cooling systems. The editorial argues that technology companies should pay for these costs rather than spreading them across ordinary utility customers. Proposed solutions include establishing special utility rates for data centers and requiring developers to make long-term financial commitments. Virginia and Ohio have already adopted measures to protect ratepayers from these infrastructure expenses.

The editorial board of the Philadelphia Jewish Exponent stated that families should not finance infrastructure for multibillion-dollar companies. They argued that while innovation is important for competitiveness, private business expenses must not be transferred to the public. The authors claimed that the public should not become an involuntary investor in the opportunities of others. They suggested that local governments should condition tax incentives on demonstrable public benefits.

Articles.Title: Editorial: The Public Shouldn’t Pay for AI’s Expansion

stories.headline_source: Editorial: The Public Shouldn’t Pay for AI’s Expansion

stories.Headline: Nvidia delays RTX 60 series production to 2027 to prioritize AI hardware
stories.Summary:
Delays in the delivery of artificial intelligence graphics processing units have pushed the production of the RTX 60 series into 2027. This situation developed as reported on November 25, when information from Taiwan's Business Times indicated that demand for these products remains extremely tight. The shift in production schedules occurred because NVIDIA is prioritizing its high demand AI hardware over consumer gaming products. These supply chain constraints are now affecting the availability of several different hardware lines.

The current situation requires a reduction in the shipments of GeForce RTX 50 series gaming graphics processing units. Taiwanese original design manufacturers report that workstation superchip sets now face lead times of approximately 26 weeks. Specifically, the B300 model has an estimated lead time of 26 to 40 weeks, while the GB300 takes about 14 to 26 weeks. Orders placed during the last two quarters are not expected to arrive until the second or third quarter of next year.

Taiwanese original design manufacturers are responsible for reporting these lengthened delivery cycles for new orders. They stated that the extreme demand for AI products is significantly constraining the supply of consumer grade hardware. These manufacturers noted that the lead times for the B300 and GB300 have lengthened considerably. This reported shortage of components is what forces the delay of the RTX 60 series production.

This supply shift could alter the risk and reward profile for crypto miners who depend on these GPUs. Technical analysts suggest that people should monitor hardware price movements as a potential indicator of market sentiment. The overall impact depends on how the company manages the balance between AI and gaming chips. More to follow.
