stories.Headline: Podcast guests examine how AI politics and data centre protests shape South-east Asia growth
stories.Summary:
The Green Pulse podcast episode published on November 24, 2026, featured host Audrey Tan discussing with ST tech editor Irene Tham and Rajesh Sreenivasan, a partner at Rajah & Tann Singapore, how artificial intelligence has moved from a software issue into domestic politics and international relations. The episode examined what the global rise of AI and the data centres built to power it will mean for South-east Asia and its own plans to build more such facilities. It also looked at how the developing region will balance that growth against the environmental impact of data centres, which the episode said is driving protests globally. The discussion covered how AI evolved from a technology topic into a geopolitical one, and whether South-east Asia could see more protests against data centres. The episode asked whether the Nvidia controversy and United States efforts to clamp down on chip exports would act as a natural brake on the global expansion of data centres.

It also explored why Singapore chose to make environmental sustainability a key consideration for data centres alongside cyber security. The discussion covered what Singapore's digital infrastructure bill is about, and how data centres can contribute to the development of water and renewable energy infrastructure. The episode did not give further numbers, dates or names on these points. Sreenivasan is identified as a partner and the head of technology, media and telecommunications at the law firm Rajah & Tann Singapore, and Tham as ST's tech editor. The episode framed the spread of AI into politics and international relations as something that has dominated headlines globally.

It presented the protests against data centres and their environmental impact as a global phenomenon that the region will have to weigh against its growth plans. The podcast is hosted by Tan and produced and edited by Hadyu Rahim, with Ernest Luis and Zachary Lim as executive producers. The episode is part of Green Pulse, which is described as a podcast published every Tuesday to discuss how environmental issues intersect with business, politics and society. It was published on November 24, 2026, at 10:00 AM and updated at the same time. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the questions the episode raised.

stories.Headline: David Fincher faces suspicion of using generative AI in his new Netflix film
stories.Summary:
Early screenings of a new film by David Fincher have raised questions about generative AI. People suspect the director used this technology in the movie The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. These suspicions emerged after critic screenings took place last week. The film is a sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. It is scheduled to premiere on November 25th.

The story is set in 1977, about a decade after the first film. Brad Pitt stars as Cliff Booth, a fixer for Hollywood elites in this movie. Elizabeth Debicki plays Karen Crosby, and Scott Caan plays a TV actor named Charlie Peters. Carla Gugino also appears as the wife of the character played by Caan. The film is produced by Netflix, which recently bought InterPositive for 600 million dollars.

David Fincher spoke about AI in a recent interview with the Los Angeles Times. He stated that he is not a Luddite and does not fear the unknown. Fincher questioned why artists should stop iterating on their creative processes. He asked if people should not use tools that can change a person's eye color. He argued that the art form is only a hundred years old.

YouTuber Patrick Tomasso said on X that he felt completely gutted after his screening. Tomasso claimed the film featured some of the most blatant and egregious AI use. Other viewers wrote that the amount of AI in the movie is astounding to an absurd degree. Some critics disagreed and suggested the visuals were just bad CGI. These viewers are affected by what they call uncanny and inconsistent visuals.

The film follows Cliff Booth as he works as a projectionist and a bartender. One trailer shows people sitting backward in a horse-drawn carriage, which looks like generative AI. Netflix has used AI in its movies and series for some time now. The company acquired InterPositive to tweak lighting and remove unwanted background elements. These models are claimed to be well suited for replicating a director's signature style.

Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied whether AI was used to make the film. The company's recent investments in generative AI technology have left many people suspicious. The articles leave open whether the visuals are actually AI or just bad CGI. It remains unclear if Fincher used the InterPositive tools for this specific production. The public is waiting for the official premiere to see the final result.

stories.Headline: Anindo Saha leads a 22-country study finding AI matches radiologists on prostate cancer MRI
stories.Summary:
A study published on November 24 in the journal Radiology found that an artificial intelligence system detected prostate cancer on MRI with diagnostic performance comparable to expert radiologists across a diverse global population. The multinational SCARLET-1 study was led by Anindo Saha, PhD, of Radboud University Medical Center in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, and colleagues. The researchers analyzed 22,445 prostate MRI examinations from 21,252 men across 46 clinical sites in 22 countries, collected between January 2012 and October 2024. External validation spanned three datasets, the PRIME trial with 476 cases across 11 countries, STHLM3-MRI with 1,108 cases in Sweden, and IP1-PROSTAGRAM with 390 cases in the U.K. The primary outcome was agreement between AI assessments and standard-of-care diagnoses of Gleason grade group 2 or higher prostate cancer. The AI system's performance was comparable to radiology readings in all three external sets, with AUC values of 0.86 in PRIME, 0.89 in STHLM3-MRI, and 0.84 in IP1-PROSTAGRAM.

AI-to-standard-of-care agreement was 83% in PRIME, 87.9% in STHLM3-MRI, and 87.7% in IP1-PROSTAGRAM. Performance was consistent across age, ethnicity, cancer location, and risk subgroups, but varied substantially across 25 sites, with 28% showing an AUC below a stated threshold. The authors wrote that the study demonstrates AI achieved diagnostic performance comparable to standard-of-care radiology readings for detecting Gleason grade group 2 or higher prostate cancer across diverse populations and clinical settings. The researchers noted that prostate MRI is the international standard of care for men with suspected prostate cancer, but subspecialty urogenital radiology expertise is concentrated at a limited number of high-volume centers. They said the findings support a potential role for AI in extending prostate MRI interpretation, particularly where subspecialty expertise is limited.

The authors suggested that site-level performance variability signals the need for careful local implementation, because AI performance may be closely linked to patient and imaging characteristics. They added that shifts in case mix over time may affect results in ways that are not immediately apparent. The authors concluded that safe clinical use will require careful operating point selection, local testing, and longitudinal performance monitoring, along with prospective evaluation of clinical, equity, and cost outcomes. They stated that further large-scale trials are warranted to provide complementary evidence. In prior work, the group developed the AI system and demonstrated its noninferiority to radiologists in detecting Gleason grade group 2 disease or higher, though those studies were conducted in standardized Western settings.

stories.Headline: Solis tells Rio Grande Valley leaders that workers who know how to use AI will replace those who do not
stories.Summary:
South Texas College President Dr. Ricardo Solis told regional business, education and economic development leaders at the college's Annual Workforce Summit in McAllen that the Rio Grande Valley faces a rapidly evolving skills challenge driven by artificial intelligence and industrial expansion. He said the region is no longer facing a simple shortage of workers, and he described the area as sitting at the epicenter of global trade and nearshoring between Asia, Mexico and the United States. Solis said he is not convinced that AI will replace jobs, but he believes people who know how to use AI will have a significant advantage over those who do not. He repeated that AI is not going to replace workers, and that those who learn to manage and use AI are the ones who will replace those without AI knowledge.

The audience included Hidalgo County Judge Richard Cortez and representatives from RioPlex, according to the article. Solis reviewed economic trends he has highlighted at the summit over the past several years and how the college has adapted its curriculum to match shifting global dynamics. About four and a half years ago, the college rapidly scaled up commercial driver's license, automotive, transportation and manufacturing training to address post-pandemic supply chain bottlenecks, and North American regions later moved toward becoming more self-sustaining as supply chains reshored and consolidated. The college became the first community college in the nation to receive approval for registered nurse apprenticeships, a claim the article attributes to the college, alongside programs in manufacturing and business.

Having flagged AI as an emerging theme at the previous year's summit, Solis predicted the next major wave will be the convergence of superintelligence and employer-driven workforce development. He said the college's enrollment has surpassed 42,000 students across its six campuses when combining more than 30,000 academic and dual-credit students with its non-credit and continuing education programs. Solis said the college's primary service area covers Hidalgo and Starr counties, and that it is actively expanding its reach across the entire Rio Grande Valley to support major industrial growth at the Port of Brownsville, Eastern Cameron County and Boca Chica. To meet demand for high-paying, high-demand technical jobs, the college is ramping up capacity in welding, automotive, electronics, precision manufacturing and mechatronics, a specialized program combining electronics and advanced manufacturing that Solis noted is unique to the college in the region.

He added that the college is eyeing significant growth in its Mid-Valley and Starr County campuses to train workers centrally for port-related industries. Solis said no college can accomplish this alone and that employers need to be at the table telling the college what skills they need today and what they will need tomorrow. He also recognized Board of Trustees Chair Paul Rodriguez and Trustee Dr. Alejo Salinas, and said the future belongs to communities that can learn faster, reskill faster and adapt faster. Following his remarks, Solis introduced the summit's keynote speaker, Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board Commissioner Dr. Wynn Rosser, who traveled from Austin to discuss statewide strategies for aligning higher education with regional economic development.

stories.Headline: Chinese firms deploy adaptive robots to advance physical AI using massive manufacturing scale
stories.Summary:
Chinese firms have begun deploying and testing adaptive robots in production to enhance their physical artificial intelligence capabilities. This movement relies on a massive manufacturing base that installed 354,200 new industrial robots in 2025, which represented 59 per cent of the global total. These robots differ from conventional models because they can perceive their surroundings and adapt to changing conditions to perform complex tasks. Recent tests at an electric vehicle factory by Xiaomi showed that humanoid robot success rates rose from 90.2 to 98 per cent between March and July 2026.

Realizing this potential requires overcoming barriers to interoperability and the sharing of commercially sensitive information between enterprises. Beijing launched the Industrial Data Foundation Action in March 2026 to standardize industrial data, followed by the Model, Data Resonance Action in April 2026 to refine training datasets. In June 2026, the Special Action for Real-World Training of Humanoid Robots and Embodied AI directed 10 province-level jurisdictions and state-owned enterprises to open operating environments. Local initiatives in Shanghai and Wuxi are also establishing shared systems to standardize data from different robotic platforms and production lines.

The National Data Administration estimates that China produced approximately 27.4 per cent of global data in 2025, with over 30 per cent of industrial data coming from equipment. Engineers at Longcheer Technology stated that operational feedback from AI-enabled robots informed frequent model updates and improved robot movements. One developer of a fabric handling robot claimed a 97 per cent success rate and estimated an investment payback period of 18 months. These advancements aim to create a cycle where industrial deployment generates data that improves AI models, which then enables more capable robots.

This industrial scale could intensify pressure on Southeast Asian manufacturers by offsetting rising wages and retaining production in China. Such a shift might weaken the labor-cost advantage of the region and complicate its export-led industrialization. Other industrial economies, including Japan and South Korea, are developing their own testbeds and shared training datasets to remain competitive. These nations must improve coordination and harmonize technical standards across borders to compete with the scale of the Chinese manufacturing sector.

Articles.Title: China’s industrial scale could power its physical AI rise

stories.Headline: Deloitte says CFOs must embed AI in finance workflows to prove ROI as pilot window closes
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence in finance has moved from an experimental novelty to a board-level mandate, according to an article published by Deloitte on 24 November 2026, which says the window to prove value is closing. The article says pilots demonstrated digital potential, but chief financial officers now face the question of how to drive return on investment without eroding controllership. It says finance teams can rewire execution and elevate internal customer experience by embedding these capabilities into workflows. The article states that a stalled finance and accounting transformation often stems from ignoring data readiness, governance and security as strict prerequisites.

The article says one global beverage producer achieved 92% touchless invoice processing and reduced manual effort by more than 80% using AI in its finance operations. It says AI tools can draft variance explanations, suggest reconciliation steps and produce consistent management commentary when a reconciliation breaks or an unexpected variance occurs. For invoices with missing purchase order details, mismatches or duplicates, the article says trained tools can extract, interpret and supplement invoice content, flag issues for review and triage exceptions to the proper owner. It says AI can summarize account history, recommend next-best actions and standardize outreach when a dispute is opened or a customer inquiry comes in.

The article recommends that leaders pilot, learn quickly and scale gradually, with budget reserved for practical use cases and a plan to expand enterprisewide. It says not every problem needs AI, and that robotic process automation and other platforms may better serve rule-based scenarios, with AI more relevant when nuance is high. It says data readiness should be treated as a prerequisite rather than a phase-two task, because output quality ties directly to the underlying data and the organization's data maturity. It says investment decisions should align with a practical value roadmap assessed over short-term and long-term horizons, and that risk management and governance should be designed from day one, with Deloitte's Trustworthy AI framework named as one tool that can help design ethical safeguards.

The article says the highest-impact use cases are anchored to outcomes finance leaders already own, manage and report, such as cycle time, cost to serve, working capital and control effectiveness. It says the differentiator is workflow integration, with AI creating the most value when triggered at the moment of work rather than used as an after-the-fact summarizer. It says AI-based tools can draft and organize evidence narratives, map evidence to control requirements and flag gaps before they become findings, with typical measures including evidence collection cycle time and fewer documentation-driven findings. The article says moving from a promising pilot to an enterprise capability requires deliberate choices as CFOs seek tangible ROI and clarity on talent, platform direction, data risk and model governance.

A spokesperson for Apurva.ai said some problems do not need another solution but a different way of thinking.

Through the open call, participating organisations can submit one persistent challenge relating to programme implementation, impact measurement, knowledge management or organisational workflows. The exercise will examine existing processes, institutional knowledge and community experiences to identify alternative approaches, including opportunities where emerging technologies such as AI could contribute. The organisation cited the example of impact assessments that can take seven to ten months to complete, saying that by the time findings become available, community needs and priorities may have changed, limiting their usefulness in programme decisions. Apurva.ai currently works with over 50 organisations globally, using AI-powered products to connect community knowledge, research and institutional learning.

The articles do not say who is responsible for running the open call beyond Apurva.ai itself, and they give no closing date, selection process or further timeline for it. The only statement attributed to the organisation is the spokesperson's remark that some problems need a different way of thinking, along with the example of slow impact assessments. The articles do not say what happens after organisations submit their challenges or when results might be announced. More to follow.

Peter Boockvar of One Point BFG Wealth Partners said on CNBC's "Fast Money" that growth in AI capital spending is set to slow sharply in 2026, in a segment published on November 24, 2026. The segment ran about five minutes and eighteen seconds, and the page carrying it was dated the same day. The headline of the segment states his view that AI capex growth will slow sharply in 2026.

The segment framed the discussion around the recent volatility in the AI trade and whether it still stands on firm footing. The page gives no figures for expected spending, no forecast amounts and no dates beyond the 2026 year in the headline and the November 24, 2026 publication date. It names no companies in connection with his call and offers no detail on which areas of AI spending he expects to slow. Responsibility for the view rests with Boockvar, who gave it in the interview, and the page attributes the slowdown call to him and his firm. The page does not set out his reasoning, so what he said beyond the headline claim is not recorded there. It also does not say what he recommended or how he positioned for the slowdown he described. No one else is quoted on the call in the article text.

The context the page gives is a volatile few weeks in the AI trade, which the segment set out to examine. What happens next is not reported, and the page carries no follow-up on the forecast or on any response to it. stories.Headline: Experts debate whether AI supercomputing is an evolution or revolution at SC26 panel
stories.Summary:
Experts debated if AI supercomputing is an evolution or revolution during a panel at the SC26 conference. Joe Greenseid of Nvidia moderated the discussion between several industry and academic specialists. The panel included representatives from AMD, VAST Data, the University of Delaware, and ETH Zurich. They discussed whether machines built for AI differ from those used by scientists for decades. The group examined how AI has increased funding and the size of these machines.

Nicholas Malaya of AMD claimed that AI and traditional high performance computing can use the same hardware. He cited the Lux system at Oak Ridge National Laboratory as a design for both workloads. Malaya also pointed to the AMD MI430 chip as an example of a dual purpose design. Torsten Hoefler of ETH Zurich argued that AI chips use lower precision like FP4 and FP8. He noted that scientific simulations often require FP64 or double precision for accurate results.

Nicholas Malaya stated that AI training shares many commonalities with traditional high performance computing. He suggested that Slinky, which combines Slurm with Kubernetes, can support both types of workloads. Torsten Hoefler argued that inference systems must handle many requests with very little delay. He claimed that professionals who do not adapt to AI could become a lost generation. Joe Greenseid moderated these views on whether the two fields can move in one direction.

Glenn Lockwood of VAST Data doubted that a 200 million dollar supercomputer could serve both purposes. He claimed that AI developers do not need traditional tools like SSH, Slurm, or file systems. Lockwood also criticized AI theater, where organizations present traditional simulations as AI work. Sunita Chandrasekaran of the University of Delaware noted that scientists cannot easily switch between precision levels. She raised concerns about moving sensitive research data between computing centers due to restrictions.

The articles state that high performance computing has used fast memory and high speed networks for years. AI has pushed technology faster but brought new demands for software and machine usage. Malaya noted that AI coding agents helped him produce more software than in the previous six years. Chandrasekaran observed that students now prefer languages like Python, Triton, and JAX over Fortran. Researchers from other fields now bring data to these environments without much programming experience.

The panel did not settle whether the change is an evolution or a revolution. Hoefler suggested that AI agents might rewrite applications to weaken the CUDA advantage held by Nvidia. He noted that any converted code would still require checking for accuracy. The discussion left open whether AI and scientific computing can continue moving in the same direction. The experts remained divided on the necessity of compromises for dual purpose hardware systems.

stories.Headline: Dell posts $54.94 billion in quarterly revenue as AI server sales surge while HP misses PC market forecasts
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies Inc. and HP Inc. delivered strong earnings and revenue beats as they posted their latest financial results today, SiliconANGLE reported on Nov. 24, 2026. Dell reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $9.45 per share on revenue of $54.94 billion, the article said. HP reported fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of 83 cents per share on revenue of $16 billion, the article said. Dell's revenue more than doubled from a year earlier, the article said. The companies have very different prospects going forward as they try to come to terms with the diverging fortunes of the artificial intelligence server and personal computer markets they serve, the article said.

Dell's result blew past Wall Street's expectations of $6.59 per share in earnings and $49.32 billion in sales, the article said. Dell's Infrastructure Solutions Group delivered sales of $41.97 billion, far in excess of the Street's target of $35.27 billion, the article said. Around $22 billion came from direct AI-optimized server sales, and that segment was up 291% annually, the article said. Dell's Client Services Group generated revenue of $12.89 billion, below the Street's forecast of $14.33 billion, the article said. HP's profit surpassed the analyst consensus estimate of 75 cents per share, and its revenue was up 9% and above the Street's target of $15.4 billion, the article said.

Dell Vice Chairman and Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke said the company is now a different company, with the Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of its profit and growth. Clarke said Dell now has more than 7,500 customers buying its AI servers. Clarke told analysts the company has a significant competitive advantage over its rivals on the software side, which enables customers to get their servers up and running in data centers within hours of taking delivery. Clarke said that allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably. Clarke told analysts that every order is verified for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power.

Dell is raising its forecast for AI servers in the coming fiscal years and now sees sales rising to $78 billion, ahead of the Street's target of $74 billion, the article said. Dell has an order backlog of $132.3 billion for AI servers, the article said. Dell's stock rose more than 3% after hours, putting the brakes on an 11% decline earlier during the regular trading session, the article said. HP's stock briefly surged more than 17% after-hours before promptly surrendering all of those gains in under an hour, and it was down just under a percentage point at the time of writing, the article said. HP's stock is still up 25% in the year to date, the article said.

Last month, Gartner Inc. reported a 22% drop in global PC shipments in the third quarter, citing the increased costs of components such as memory chips, which have led to higher prices and compelled many people to hold onto their older laptops for longer, the article said. HP has been trying to mitigate the situation by raising its prices, but it couldn't stop its profit margins from declining in the quarter, the article said. HP has been without a CEO since PayPal Holdings Inc. swooped in to poach its former leader Enrique Lores in February, the article said. Broussard has held the fort for close to nine months, and the company named Walmsley, who formerly led the pharmaceutical giant GSK Plc, as his successor, the article said. Walmsley will assume the role full time on Jan. 4, when she's slated to take over from interim CEO Bruce Broussard, the article said.

The market was eagerly anticipating HP's guidance to try and get a lid on whether or not the PC market has any prospect of recovery in the near future, but the company disappointed by refusing to provide any, the article said. All HP would say is that it forecasts free cash flow in the current quarter to be $3 billion, plus or minus $100 million, while analysts are targeting free cash flow of $3.3 billion, the article said. The article said Walmsley will have her work cut out when she assumes the role. The article said Walmsley has a tough act to follow, for Broussard has done rather well in his efforts to cope with the PC market downturn and the higher component costs. The article did not say what Dell or HP expect in the PC market beyond the figures given.

Articles.Title: Dell and HP beat expectations, but their fortunes are diverging as AI dynamics crush the PC market

stories.Headline: Tiruchi colleges train faculty to teach AI and machine learning
stories.Summary:
Higher education institutions in Tiruchi have begun integrating emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and machine learning into their syllabi and into capacity building programmes for teachers and students in recent years, The Hindu reported on November 24, 2026. A growing number of institutes are opting for faculty development programmes that focus on how to integrate AI and ML in the pedagogy as well. The Tiruchi-based tech company Bodhi Multiverse UK has conducted six AI-related faculty development programmes for city colleges this year, according to its founder and director Anantha Ganesh. Capacity building programmes for educational institutions in Tiruchi typically cost upwards of ₹850 per person depending on the course and duration.

Many institutions offer degree programmes in emerging technologies, but there is a shortage of faculty qualified to teach them, the article said. Kevin Giftson, founder and CEO of Aske AI, a company that conducts tech learning modules for colleges, developers and healthcare professionals, said the syllabus has not been updated to cater to the new subjects, which has created problems for both students and teachers. He said it would be better for students to start industrial internships in the first year of their course so that they can get exposure to the technologies in real time. At National College, teachers are encouraged to complete at least two modules in emerging technologies every year through Massive Open Online Courses offered on government portals.

Ganesh said that though there is a buzz over the entry of AI into the classroom at present, it is not actually a new phenomenon, as it has existed in multiple forms before and is still developing newer versions. He said the best results are mainly down to prompting the machine, and that if one learns how to give an AI prompt one can create a product successfully and personalise it as well. He said the rapid increase in the number of AI tools and software can be frustrating for users and creators, but the company expects this to stabilise in the coming years. D. Prasanna Balaji, principal of National College, said that though AI and ML help to present lessons in an appealing manner, they cannot replace the teacher in making students actually understand what is being taught, and that the human factor is still important for the student's educational progress.

stories.Headline: OpenAI reports GPT-6 models design protein shapes and sequences using reasoning and code alone
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on November 24, 2026 that its GPT-6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. OpenAI published the claim in a preprint titled “GPT-6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models.” An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks, OpenAI said. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT-6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets, and redesigned antibodies also retained binding.

Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing, OpenAI said. OpenAI tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab, and 35 of them, or 10.9%, tested positive for binding to their intended target. OpenAI found 5 hits for PD-L1, 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. For three targets, OpenAI saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). Of 107 proteins made from GPT-6.2’s new sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes, 14 (13.1%) showed binding, and of 182 designs for six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind IL-4Rα, 128 (70%) showed signs of binding.

OpenAI said the models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. When designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, OpenAI said, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction. OpenAI said an internal model followed an instruction on how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs. OpenAI said the unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give strong evidence that GPT-6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. OpenAI said the results also suggest it could use GPT-6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence.

OpenAI said it compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT-6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while its latest internal models scored higher. OpenAI said the original RFdiffusion study reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. OpenAI said predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness. OpenAI said it used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design, and other specialized protein models helped select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target. OpenAI said it tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab, and of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) showed binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1.

OpenAI said proteins do much of the work in living cells, driving the chemical reactions that sustain life, carrying oxygen through the blood, and defending the body against infection. OpenAI said incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. OpenAI said proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids, and the order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does. OpenAI said scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do, and the challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. OpenAI said using and coordinating specialized biology models requires substantial expertise, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training.

OpenAI said it asked GPT-6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein, and when it already knew which two atoms formed a bond, it could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. OpenAI said it could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. OpenAI said it also asked its models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target. OpenAI said it gave GPT-6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where it wanted a minibinder to attach, and the model then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders without using specialized protein AI models. OpenAI said it gave GPT-6.2 three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose new ones.

Articles.Title: OpenAI says GPT-6 models can design new protein shapes and sequences using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate them (OpenAI)

stories.Headline: Bloomberg columnist warns US officials against aggressive AI chip restrictions on China
stories.Summary:
United States government officials recently closed a long-standing loophole that previously allowed Chinese artificial intelligence labs to access advanced American chips remotely. This policy change occurred around November 2026 and aimed to restrict the ability of China to develop its artificial intelligence capabilities. The move caused the Hang Seng Tech Index to drop 13 percent over two weeks, led by the e-commerce company Alibaba Group. Alibaba had been renting compute from Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based operator involved in an alleged espionage scandal with Nvidia.

These restrictions require American chipmakers to sever ties with Chinese entities and may change how companies report their global revenue. Nvidia changed its accounting policy in October 2025 to report revenue based on customer headquarters rather than billing locations. This change is significant because Singapore previously accounted for about 22 percent of total sales for Nvidia. Advanced Micro Devices also faces pressure as China represented 22 percent of its revenue in 2025. These companies must now navigate strict export controls while facing allegations that blacklisted Chinese firms still receive firmware updates.

National security hawks in Washington are responsible for these curbs and believe that squeezing China is necessary for security. However, Bloomberg columnist Shuli Ren suggests that officials should exercise caution because the global artificial intelligence value chain is deeply integrated. Ren argues that it is almost impossible to diversify risks away and that the United States will pay a hefty price. The author notes that any hit to chipmakers would reverberate far beyond Silicon Valley and hurt broader corporate profits.

The context of this situation involves a broader market concern that earnings for American chipmakers may have already peaked. Goldman Sachs warned that the S&P 500 could retreat to about 5,600 if earnings estimates revert to their 30-year trend. Investors are worried that companies like Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices cannot meet aggressive growth expectations. Future declines in artificial intelligence investments could also diminish orders for industrial companies like Caterpillar and GE Vernova. More to follow.

Articles.Title: US officials keen to squeeze China's AI dreams should exercise caution—here's why

stories.Headline: Driven Tech completes ADEX and TekBay acquisitions to expand enterprise AI expertise
stories.Summary:
Driven Tech, Inc. said in a press release issued through a wire service on November 24, 2026, that it had completed its acquisitions of ADEX and TekBay after receiving all required government and regulatory approvals. According to the release, the two deals significantly expand the company's expertise in enterprise AI, data engineering, agentic AI and cloud-native development across AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. The release said both teams will join Driven's Applied Intelligence Business Unit, which is led by Sanjeev Pant, and that the unit strengthens the company's three strategic platforms: Pervasive Security, Applied Intelligence and AI-Driven Digital Foundations. Driven said a key example of the collaboration is Lasius, its agentic AI orchestration and security platform, which the release says the ADEX engineering team developed based on Driven's strategic vision.

Vinu Thomas, President and Chief Operating Officer of Driven Tech, said in the release that the acquisitions represent a significant milestone in the company's evolution. According to the release, he said the company is bringing together exceptional AI engineering talent with its expertise in cybersecurity and infrastructure to help enterprises move beyond AI experimentation and securely operationalize AI at scale. The release said that with the acquisitions complete, Driven will focus on integrating its expanded engineering organization, accelerating innovation and bringing new AI-driven solutions to enterprise customers. Driven Tech describes itself in the release as a technology solutions and services company delivering integrated capabilities across Pervasive Security, Applied Intelligence and AI-Driven Digital Foundations.

The release was issued through WebWire, according to the press release, which directs readers to the wire service's website for more information. The release gives no financial terms for either acquisition and does not say how many employees the two teams bring to Driven. It also does not give a timeline for the integration work the company says it will now focus on. More to follow.

stories.Headline: India should prepare to reuse AI infrastructure after a market crash, Arindam Goswami argues
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence infrastructure boom has shifted from using cash to relying on debt, according to a report by Arindam Goswami. This transition occurred as large technology firms struggled to prove that the technology was boosting their earnings. American non-financial companies issued 940 billion dollars of investment-grade bonds in the first ten months of 2026, which was a third more than the previous year. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5 percent on 5 November, while Nvidia reported revenue growth of 103 percent twelve days later. These events indicate that companies now have less time to prove the worth of their massive investments.

Fitch Ratings warned on 17 November that borrowing by the largest technology firms will make bond markets more volatile next year. The agency says markets expect the five largest hyperscalers to spend over 1 trillion dollars in 2027, up from 772 billion dollars this year. Until 2024, firms like Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta paid for data centres using profits from software, cloud, and advertising. Now, these profits cover a shrinking share of the investment, forcing companies to borrow to finance the rest. An October stability report from the IMF counted 14 deals since 2023 where large firms put 300 billion dollars of equity and 650 billion dollars of debt into weaker AI companies.

Arindam Goswami, a research analyst at The Takshashila Institution, suggests that India should prepare to use the infrastructure left behind after a potential crash. He argues that India has little capital at stake and would barely feel a sharp correction in the market. He recommends that the IndiaAI Mission tilt its compute budget toward inference in hubs with existing power and fibre infrastructure. He also suggests that public funds adapt open-weight models to Indian languages, health data, court records, and farm advisories. Finally, he believes the government should set common standards for interfaces and liability, similar to what was done for UPI payments.

The current cycle faces political pushback, such as voters rejecting data-centre-friendly measures in the 3 November midterms. In the eastern US PJM grid region, data centres added 9.3 billion dollars to power capacity costs in a single year. OpenAI pledged on 5 November to pay the full cost of power at its own campuses following these political shifts. McKinsey's State of AI 2026 survey found that while almost nine in 10 firms use AI, only 37 percent see an effect on earnings. This suggests that the real constraint is the slow pace at which organisations redesign their workflows and legacy systems.

stories.Headline: Council of Europe trains 20 local authority teams in responsible AI governance
stories.Summary:
The Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe organised the first-ever Academy on responsible AI governance at local level, held in Paris from 17 to 19 November 2026. Twenty teams from local and regional authorities, selected in an open call, took part in the academy. The teams came from 18 municipalities and two counties, spanning the continent from Diyarbakır in Türkiye to Fingal in Ireland. The academy was organised by the Centre of expertise for multilevel governance (CEMG) at the Congress, in partnership with the Council of Europe's Steering Committee for new and emerging digital technologies (CDNET). It put into practice the Congress's call to strengthen local and regional authorities' capacity to use and manage AI.

Participants were provided with practical tools for responsible AI governance, based on the Council of Europe's HUDERIA methodology for assessing the impact of AI systems. Over three days, participants applied the methodology to a fictional AI-supported public consultation, identifying and analysing risks, mapping stakeholders and developing mitigation measures. The programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services on everyone they serve, from a human-rights, democracy and rule-of-law perspective. The participating authorities were Amaroussion (Greece), Bălți (Republic of Moldova), Bergen (Norway), Bitola (North Macedonia), City of Arezzo (Italy), City of Vigo (Spain), Diyarbakır (Türkiye), Fingal County (Ireland), Harghita County (Romania), Kutaisi (Georgia), London Borough of Camden (United Kingdom), Lviv (Ukraine), Nõo (Estonia), Resen (North Macedonia), Rivne (Ukraine), Shkodër (Albania), Szentendre (Hungary), Turnišče (Slovenia), Valongo (Portugal), and Ventspils Education Board (Latvia). The academy was also an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

Opening the discussions, Congress co-rapporteur on AI Annika Vaikla (Estonia, ILDG), Deputy Mayor of Viimsi, urged authorities to use AI to give public servants more time for people, while keeping people in control. She called for AI literacy among political leaders, staff and citizens. She also called for smaller municipalities to have access to shared expertise. Deputy Mayor Vaikla is co-rapporteur for the 2026 Congress report on strengthening the capacities of local and regional authorities in the use of artificial intelligence. The articles give no further remarks from her.

The articles state that local and regional authorities are on the frontline of the AI revolution in Europe's town halls. Faced with shrinking budgets, they see real potential in efficiency gains promised by AI. They also face hard questions such as planning applications for data centres and democratic accountability for decisions informed by AI. The articles say they lack capacity in understanding and governing AI technologies, particularly smaller municipalities.

The academy served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe and was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence. The articles give no further background beyond the academy's organisation and aims. They state that artificial intelligence is already in Europe's town halls. They describe the academy as the first-ever of its kind at local level.

They state that the twenty teams were selected in an open call. They state that the programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services. They give no further details on the Congress report or the Framework Convention. The articles state that the academy was an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

They state that it was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence. They state that it served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe. They give no further details on what follows the academy. They leave open what the participating authorities will do next and what the 2026 Congress report will contain.

stories.Headline: Perth and Kinross Council officials say AI-generated requests overwhelm staff and raise costs
stories.Summary:
Leaders at Perth and Kinross Council in Scotland said artificial intelligence is fuelling an “incredible” rise in the volume and complexity of correspondence from the public. Officers dealing with complaints, data compliance and freedom of information requests must wade through thousands of pages of AI-generated “gibberish” to work out which communications are genuine. Lisa Simpson, head of legal and governance at Perth and Kinross, told the council’s scrutiny and performance committee on 18 November that AI lets people produce 10, 11 or 12-page requests at the flick of a button. She said 80% of this material is “nonsensical”, so “an awful lot of time and resources” is taken up processing it. Jillian Walker, the council’s data protection officer, told councillors at the meeting that subject access requests had risen by 100% in the last two years, partly due to AI.

Subject access requests let people obtain the data an organisation holds on them by law. According to Scottish newspaper The Courier, Walker said compliance with subject access requests increased in 2025 despite the pressures. A report presented to councillors showed the 1,849 freedom of information requests received in 2025-26 was the highest number in figures going back seven years, and 21% more than in 2024-25. Walker said much of the increase in communications is also related to Scotland’s Redress Scheme, which provides survivors of historical child abuse in care homes with redress payments, emotional support and official apologies. She said staff dealing with these requests must process “thousands of pages of highly distressing records” and reply to those seeking redress in a compassionate, trauma-informed and sensitive way.

Walker praised her “highly conscientious” small team but said there is “just no way we can sustain the compliance rate we have achieved previously”. Asked whether the council could use its own AI tools to sift through AI-generated correspondence, she said that though it is “very low-tech”, staff had found the best way to decipher AI-generated text and requests was to print them off and go through them with highlighter pens. Simpson acknowledged that AI could be valuable but said there was a “time and a place” for its use. She said that in some cases the tools and technology are not being used responsibly and their purpose is to tie the council up in knots and almost grind things to a halt. She said this does not help when the council is trying to help people with genuine requests, genuine issues and genuine complaints.

According to the BBC, officials told councillors that Perth and Kinross Council is working with other local authorities to find out if the problem could be addressed at a national level. In a paper published in September, researchers from the UK-based Centre for the Governance of AI and from the Hertie School in Berlin identified 84 cases across 11 countries. In those cases public bodies or “credible observers” attributed surges in requests to public use of AI, including freedom of information requests, planning consultation responses and civil court claims. The report, “Characterizing agentic flooding of government services”, defines “agentic flooding” as a surge in the volume or complexity of requests to a service caused by AI use that substantially strains the body’s capacity.

The researchers warned that governments are likely to respond with fees or by blocking AI from accessing government websites rather than by building capacity. The report presented to councillors covered freedom of information requests received in 2025-26 and compared them with figures going back seven years. Walker linked part of the rise in communications to Scotland’s Redress Scheme for survivors of historical child abuse in care homes. Simpson and Walker both addressed the scrutiny and performance committee meeting on 18 November.

The Courier reported Walker’s statement that compliance with subject access requests increased in 2025. The BBC reported that officials said the council is working with other local authorities on whether the problem could be addressed at a national level. The September paper by the Centre for the Governance of AI and the Hertie School set out the 84 cases and the definition of agentic flooding. Officials told councillors that Perth and Kinross Council is working with other local authorities to find out if the problem could be addressed at a national level.

The researchers warned that governments are likely to respond with fees or by blocking AI from accessing government websites rather than by building capacity. The articles do not say what the council’s own next steps will be, or what the other local authorities have found. The articles do not say whether the council will adopt any new AI tools to handle the correspondence. The articles do not say what response, if any, the Scottish or UK government has given to the council’s concerns.

stories.Headline: History professor says GPT-6.2 Astra identifies the creator of an anonymous 1808 Yale sketchbook in 22 minutes
stories.Summary:
A history professor says GPT-6.2 Astra solved a historical mystery in 22 minutes by identifying the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale, according to Mark Humphries of Generative History. Humphries wrote that he tested OpenAI’s new model, GPT-6.2 Astra, before it was released. He said he gave the model access to images of the sketchbook and a throwaway prompt asking it to identify the artist. He said that 22 minutes and 1 second later, the model answered that Louis-Guy-Charles-Guillaume de Rohan-Chabot, vicomte de Chabot (1780, 1875), probably made the travel drawings. Humphries said he had never heard of Chabot and had not suspected him.

The sketchbook is held at Yale’s Beinecke Library, which bought it from an antiquarian bookseller in 2020 after it had been in private hands for decades. Humphries said the book has a mottled leather cover and 84 pages, 34 of which feature pencil and ink drawings or watercolours. He said most are labelled and only three are dated, and the handwriting is limited to short captions. He said the unknown artist began the book in March 1808, and it opens with the Newfoundland shoreline as seen from a passing ship. He said it includes Sir John Johnson’s house southeast of Montreal, the fortifications at Chambly, Chaudière Falls at modern-day Ottawa dated 8th June, the entrance of the Rivière Creuse dated 11 June, Fort St. Joseph on Lake Huron, Fort William on Lake Superior, islands in Lake Erie, and the mountains at Lake Champlain dated 16 August.

Humphries said the model suggested testing the hypothesis by ordering copies of a microfilmed diary of Chabot’s trip that it had found in an archival inventory held in the Special Collections of Cleveland State University. He said he ordered the journal and found there are two parts, one covering Chabot’s travels in Lower Canada and the other his journey to the Upper Country. He said the first is held in a private family archive in France and the second was microfilmed by the Library of Congress as part of its Lafayette papers. He said the model traced its finding to a single footnote in a 2014 PhD thesis on aristocratic refugee families fleeing the French Revolution, written by historian Juliette Reboul. He said that after some back and forth with both archives, all three documents arrived in his inbox, and the first thing he saw was handwriting with the same distinctive letter forms as the sketchbook.

Humphries said a quick bit of research revealed Chabot had been a minor French aristocrat and Irish landowner whose family was displaced by the French Revolution. He said Chabot became a British Army officer in exile and spent most of 1808 in Canada as Deputy Adjutant General. He said Chabot’s daughter eventually married the Marquis de Lafayette’s grandson and his papers were preserved in the family archive, lost until a descendant discovered them in 1984. He said the only scholarly reference he could find to Chabot’s 1808 trip to Canada was in fur trader George Nelson’s journals, published by Harry Duckworth as Friends, Foes, and Furs in 2019. He said Nelson mentioned hearing that a “Count de Chabot” had visited Fort William, and Duckworth provided a paragraph of context.

Humphries said he came across a reference to the anonymous sketchbook in 2022 while going through the Beinecke Library catalog for work on the authorship of Alexander Henry’s Travels and Adventures in Canada and the Indian Territories. He said the sketchbook depicts an 1808 journey from Montreal to Fort William and back, and is important because it uniquely depicts Great Lakes locations destroyed only a few years later. He said he spent many hours over the years trying to identify the artist with no luck. He said the chief problem is that the route was common, with hundreds of canoes and bateaux making the same journey every year, so the artist could be any one of several thousand people. He said only a tiny fraction of written sources survive, and those are handwritten, often un-indexed and mostly un-transcribed, scattered across dozens of archives.

Humphries said he included lines about Kendall and Berczy in his prompt, and that his “assistance” only led the model on a brief wild goose chase. He said he attached his article on Kendall and Henry for context and set the model to work on Ultra effort level in goal mode, which encourages it to work longer, but that he did not need goal mode. He said he initially felt the response was too improbable to be correct and suspected the journal would prove to be something else or would disprove the result. He said he ordered the journal anyway, and that how the model learned about it remains a bit unclear. He said neither Duckworth nor any of the other experts he has shared the finding with have given Chabot much thought, if they have even heard of him.

stories.Headline: Ray Dalio warns that great AI technology does not equal a good investment
stories.Summary:
Ray Dalio, the founder of Bridgewater Associates, warned in an interview on the "Sourcery" podcast that the market's habit of equating disruptive new technology with a high-quality asset is the core cause of every historical bubble. He cited the 1920s wave of technologies such as electricity, automobiles, airplanes, movies and radio, and said early investors may still lose money in the bubble first. He said the most dangerous aspect of this round of AI mania is the extreme concentration of the narrative. He said that once leveraged investors are forced to liquidate because of rising interest rates, maturing debt or tax pressure, selling pressure will feed on itself. He said that is where the bubble will burst.

Dalio argued that the real key mechanism is that people mistake a great new technology for a great investment. He said this mistake can still happen even when the technology truly does change the world. He said that even companies with good cash flow can go through a bubble. He said the key is not whether the technology is good, but whether the assets are concentrated in the hands of people who cannot withstand volatility and lack the capacity to hold. He said investors who borrow money to buy stocks must sell assets for cash once they face repayment pressure or a heavier interest burden, and falling prices trigger more selling.

Dalio said that when a company raises $50 million at a $1 billion valuation, a value of $1 billion immediately appears on the books, and holders may be called billionaires as a result. He said that until the assets are sold and converted into cash, that wealth can neither buy bread nor pay taxes. He said bubbles are often triggered when a large number of asset holders are forced to liquidate at the same time because of maturing liabilities, tax pressure or other reasons. He said selling pressure then spreads quickly, market sentiment turns from confidence to fear, and a negative cycle begins. He said that no matter how a company describes its social mission, where the money comes from is always the core question that cannot be avoided.

Dalio disclosed that he is building a system that writes his lifetime of investment judgment standards into rules and turns them into back-testable code. He said the system could keep operating across different market environments and even continue to work after he himself is no longer involved. He recalled that when he founded Bridgewater, his method was to write down investment judgment standards and hand them to computers to execute. He said relying on a single person to weigh various factors in his head and then make decisions in the traditional way is in fact already outdated. He said the future direction is for excellent human intelligence and excellent artificial intelligence to work together.

Dalio cautioned that AI will widen the cognitive divide. He said some people use it to understand causal mechanisms more deeply, while others outsource their thinking and simply wait for the system to give them answers. He said the most important thing is always to ask why, to understand cause and effect, rather than accept everything wholesale. He placed the current turmoil within the five major cyclical forces he distilled from his study of 500 years of history: debt and money, domestic political order, geopolitics, natural events, and technological change. He said these five forces interweave and usually form a grand cycle roughly the length of a human lifetime, and that the postwar world order established in 1945 is now in a phase of profound readjustment.

Dalio said the United States effectively has four political camps: the far left, the moderate left, the moderate right and the far right. He said no single extreme camp can completely suppress the other, and that only if the moderates form a force across party lines can structural problems such as the debt ceiling and fiscal consolidation be addressed. He said what has changed is the people handling the problems, not the problems themselves. He said debt, wealth disparity and the tearing of values remain, and whether pragmatic cross-party cooperation can be formed will largely determine where markets and the economy go next. He said that if the AI trade is to move from a bubble narrative back to a healthy cycle, it must first clear three hurdles: interest rates must not force debtors to dump assets at fire-sale prices, valuations must be supported by cash flow, and holders must be able to withstand price volatility.

stories.Headline: A study finds AI systems displace legal certainty, accountability and enforceability
stories.Summary:
A conceptual legal analysis published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance examines how artificial intelligence systems displace the core structural foundations that historically uphold legal legitimacy. The study conceptualizes these foundational conditions as the Tripod of Legal Legitimacy, consisting of legal certainty, accountability, and enforceability. Across public and private domains, the normative authority of law is increasingly challenged by opaque, adaptive, and privately administered algorithmic infrastructures. Rather than merely assisting human decision-makers, artificial intelligence technologies embed regulatory functions such as adjudication, classification, and enforcement directly into their computational architecture. These systems frequently operate outside the scope of democratic authorization, legislative scrutiny, or judicial review, raising fundamental questions about the capacity of legal orders to maintain normative authority.

The study defines normative legitimacy as the capacity of legal systems to justify authority through principled reasoning, procedural fairness, and democratic accountability. Legal institutions comprise public authorities such as legislatures, regulatory agencies, and courts charged with creating, interpreting, and enforcing rules. Legal certainty requires laws to be clear, general, prospective, and intelligible so that individuals and institutions can understand rules to comply or seek contestation. Accountability provides vertical oversight through public and electoral scrutiny, alongside horizontal checks via judicial review and inter-agency evaluation, ensuring decisions remain contestable and subject to justification or reversal. Enforceability ensures legal norms produce concrete behavioral effects through compliance mechanisms, coercion, or institutional alignment, preventing rules from decaying into symbolic declarations.

The author diagnoses how specific characteristics of artificial intelligence destabilize this legal tripod through institutional erosion, technical substitution, and infrastructural control. Modern machine learning models rely on statistical inference, automated optimization, and probabilistic classifications rather than human deliberation or causal deduction, creating an inherent black-box problem. The study distinguishes between two distinct layers of opacity: the internal architecture of deep neural networks that impedes legal explainability, and the institutional opacity of corporate structures that shields proprietary code and training data behind trade secrecy and platform terms of service. Accountability diffuses across fragmented supply chains of developers, deployers, and institutional adopters, producing a responsibility vacuum where fault-based liability falters. Enforceability erodes as transnationally deployed cloud platforms operate beyond the reach of domestic regulators, leaving state authorities with fragmented oversight.

In the Netherlands, the predictive algorithmic profiling system SyRI, deployed to detect social security fraud, operated with minimal transparency until the Hague District Court invalidated it for violating fair trial guarantees and European human rights transparency standards. European Union border operations examined by the EU Fundamental Rights Agency demonstrated that automated border management tools significantly constrain individuals' access to legal redress. Italian data protection authorities issued a moratorium on real-time facial recognition in public spaces, Spanish regulators suspended artificial intelligence systems in public schools over biometric profiling concerns, and Canadian provinces paused predictive policing programs due to discrimination risks and absent procedural safeguards. In the United States, police departments widely adopted facial recognition technologies within regulatory vacuums, demonstrating how technical systems hollow out legal protections in practice without explicitly repealing statutes. The study introduces a comparative process-based model that contrasts the recursive feedback cycles of traditional public law against artificial-intelligence-induced governance cycles.

Under the traditional legal-governance framework, legitimacy is maintained through four interlinked stages: norm formulation through deliberative processes such as legislative drafting and public hearings; institutional implementation by public bodies; behavioral adjustment alongside procedural contestation in administrative or judicial venues; and normative recalibration, wherein legal disputes and observed failures feed back into statutory reform. The European Union's Digital Services Act incorporated over 3,000 public submissions during drafting and established Digital Services Coordinators to oversee algorithmic risk management, while the AI Act mandates supervisory reviews and five-year revision cycles under Article 84. The artificial-intelligence-induced governance displacement framework traces how private infrastructures substitute code-based mechanisms for public law across five distinct stages. The cycle begins with design-based norm encoding, where private actors embed governance choices directly into technical system parameters, as seen in Meta's Community Standards or OpenAI's behavioral guidelines and prompt engineering. The second stage, infrastructural adoption, occurs when public institutions, educational bodies, and individual users integrate these unregulated models into everyday practice in the absence of statutory review.

Third, functional displacement emerges as platform-based systems simulate legal functions, such as adjudication and content moderation, exemplified by Meta's Oversight Board issuing non-binding rulings or OpenAI defining internal safety rules without judicial oversight. The fourth stage, epistemic dependency, manifests as public regulators face substantial technical knowledge gaps and increasingly rely on private developers for expertise, auditability, and regulatory guidance. During 2023 United States Senate hearings, lawmakers invited OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman alongside academic and civil society witnesses to suggest regulatory approaches, highlighting how technical elites increasingly influence public agenda-setting. Finally, legitimacy closure occurs when platform operators deploy internal ethics boards, transparency portals, system cards, and corporate audit reports to signal normative compliance.

In July 2025, major artificial intelligence developers including Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral signed the European Union's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI, pledging adherence to transparency, copyright, and traceability provisions, while Meta rejected the voluntary Code, publicly citing overregulation. The author notes that no major United States court, including the Supreme Court, has yet adjudicated cases regarding artificial-intelligence-generated pornography. The author outlines six structural policy priorities necessary to reconstruct legal authority rather than merely extending existing compliance checklists. First, legal frameworks must establish enforceable traceability through statutory algorithmic registries, mandatory version-update documentation, and publicly accessible audit trails to ensure administrative legibility.

Second, statutes must clarify liability across the entire artificial intelligence supply chain, establishing tiered liability models that apportion responsibility among system developers, practical deployers, and institutional adopters. Third, enforceability must be re-anchored in binding statutory entitlements, guaranteeing enforceable rights to explanation, mandatory justification protocols, and independent third-party appeals. Fourth, democratic jurisdictions must advance transnational coordination through interoperable regulatory standards and mutual recognition to prevent private jurisdictional arbitrage. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo open source AI cyber defense system
stories.Summary:
Cisco Systems and OpenAI announced Shirudo, a self-defending AI cybersecurity system for enterprises, in a release dated November 24, 2026. The system uses eBPF based agents that observe low level infrastructure activity and trigger real time automated threat responses. It watches Linux kernels and deploys cryptographically signed shields while regular patches catch up. The platform is released as open source software, and enterprise security teams and developers are invited to contribute and extend its capabilities.

The release gives Cisco a way to plug AI directly into low level defense, which the article says aligns closely with its existing security and networking stack. For enterprises already running Cisco gear, it turns the company's AI story into something operational rather than abstract, and it pushes AI Defense style capabilities deeper into infrastructure. The article says it sits alongside projects like Hypershield, Splunk integration and the US$9.3b in hyperscale AI orders that analysts already factor into growth and margin assumptions. The article describes Cisco as a US communications technology giant with a market value of about $381.6b that builds networking, security and data infrastructure many large enterprises already rely on, which it says gives the project a direct path into existing customer environments.

The article does not name individual executives or give direct statements from Cisco or OpenAI about the launch. It says the key tell will be whether Cisco starts to cite Shirudo usage and community contributions in earnings calls or product updates. Examples it gives are the number of enterprises running shields in production or tests contributed for new vulnerabilities. Concrete metrics around shields deployed, Linux hosts covered, or joint Cisco and OpenAI reference customers would show the project is turning into real world security adoption rather than just a high profile launch, according to the article.

The launch sits alongside broader shifts in Cisco's AI security positioning that recent research has highlighted, the article says. It says the current narrative hinges on Cisco extending AI focused networking and full stack security across hyperscalers, enterprises and governments while holding margins against hardware cost pressure. Shirudo fits that thesis by reinforcing the idea that security is integrated into the network rather than a bolt on product, the article says. It adds that the article was produced with the assistance of AI automation based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St, and that it is general in nature and not financial advice.

stories.Headline: Accenture survey finds 40% of shoppers want AI help finding holiday deals
stories.Summary:
Accenture’s holiday shopping survey found that 66% of shoppers plan to take part in Black Friday or Cyber Monday, even though retailers have been offering deals for weeks, according to a report published on November 24, 2026. Kelly Askew, Accenture’s global retail lead, said shoppers are still planning to participate, but many are doing more research before making a purchase. About one in five shoppers began holiday shopping during the summer, Askew said, and retailers have moved some promotions earlier, with deals appearing as far back as September. She said Black Friday used to be a day or two but is no longer that, and it is now becoming weeks.

Shoppers plan to spend about 12% more this year, according to the survey, but Askew said the increase is largely driven by higher prices. Consumers are buying a similar amount of merchandise as last year while shifting toward mass merchants and warehouse clubs, choosing lower-priced brands or using gift cards to manage costs. Accenture found that 40% of shoppers wanted AI’s help finding deals, while about one-third used it to compare options or decide where to buy. Askew described the technology as almost becoming a personal shopper, helping people narrow down gift choices.

The survey found that only 3% of shoppers plan to make an impulse purchase after seeing a deal. Askew said many consumers are deciding what they want to buy in advance and waiting for Black Friday or Cyber Monday to make their final purchase. In-store shopping remains part of the holiday season, with 44% of consumers planning to visit stores, according to Accenture. Askew said shoppers may go for inspiration, to try on clothes or test products, as well as to get into the holiday spirit.

stories.Headline: Review finds AI medical devices improve diagnosis and personalize care across specialties
stories.Summary:
A review published in the journal Biomedical Materials & Devices reports that artificial intelligence is being built into medical devices to improve diagnostic accuracy, customize treatment plans and raise patient outcomes across many clinical specialties, according to an account of the work published by bioengineer.org on November 25, 2026. The authors describe how adding intelligent algorithms to medical equipment creates opportunities to improve clinical performance while they weigh both the technological progress and the regulatory obstacles involved. The survey covers the growing role of these devices in dentistry, medical imaging, ophthalmology, mental health, autism spectrum disorder diagnosis, oncology and general medicine, and it reports consistent gains in diagnostic precision, tailored treatment planning and therapeutic results. The paper also says the algorithms help organize, classify, investigate and display complex healthcare data so that professionals can evaluate clinical information more effectively.

In oncology the review documents that artificial intelligence has been applied to identifying acute leukemia, breast cancer and pancreatic cancer, and that the systems can also estimate broader clinical parameters such as patient survival rates and the effectiveness of care plans. In dentistry the authors report that algorithmic tools are already widely used and spreading quickly for clinical diagnosis, patient charting, treatment planning, robotics and practitioner education, while also supporting general medical delivery. The review states that artificial intelligence-based medical devices must be formally approved or cleared by the United States Food and Drug Administration to verify their safety and clinical efficacy before widespread deployment, and it presents the regulatory guidance pathways established for such devices. The authors add that while regulatory compliance presents considerable challenges, the medical device industry has shown notable resilience and creativity in addressing hurdles to development and clearance.

The review is credited to Tettey-Engmann, Parupelli, Bauer, Bhattarai and Desai and was published in Biomedical Materials & Devices, volume 4, issue 2, pages 1767 to 1787, with the digital object identifier 10.1007/s44174-025-00379-1. The authors say that despite rapid clinical adoption, large-scale implementation faces substantial technical, ethical and practical obstacles that must be systematically resolved, and that the sector must remain flexible while keeping patient safety and verified clinical results at the center of innovation. They conclude that artificial intelligence will increasingly converge with complementary advanced disciplines to accelerate customized, patient-centered care, and they identify opportunities at the intersection of artificial intelligence, medical devices and internet-enabled systems, emphasizing integrations with the Internet of Things, biotechnology, nanotechnology and personalized therapeutics. The review says that combining artificial intelligence with targeted medicines tailored to individual patient needs promises to advance personalized healthcare delivery and offers insight into the future direction of collaborative, patient-centered medicine.
