stories.Headline: Anthropic accuses a company of model distillation
stories.Summary:
A user posting as weli said on Hacker News on 24 November 2026 that Anthropic is accusing them and their company of using Anthropic's API for distillation, and that they are not doing so. The poster said their company does not train its own models. The poster said their only usage that could get them flagged is automated regression benchmarks run whenever they change some AI settings. The poster said this is not against Anthropic's policy. The poster said they now have 24 hours to prove they did not distill.

The post was submitted 3 hours before it was read and had 150 points and 93 comments. The poster asked how to prove they are not distilling Anthropic models without breaking their users' privacy. One commenter suggested submitting the same evidence to Claude and asking it whether it is sufficient to make distilling seem unlikely. Another commenter suggested vetting the evidence with a second, adversarial Claude session. A commenter said they skip straight to a second Claude session to review their code.

A commenter warned that Anthropic will read their logs and determine the evidence is an attempt to distill. Commenters said Anthropic will use a Claude agent to review the submission anyway. One commenter suggested migrating to Bedrock via AWS, saying a serious bill brings a dedicated account rep who is an actual human being. A commenter said Bedrock is not zero data retention, linking a Claude support article. A commenter said zero data retention does not necessarily help, because a single prompt can still flag an account.

A commenter said AWS still runs automated checks on input and output even when Bedrock is zero data retention. A commenter said they would not be surprised if Anthropic builds a cumulative risk score that predicts distillation without retaining data. A commenter said a carve-out permits retention of data that fails a risk score for breaking laws or attempting to violate safety. A commenter said dropping whole accounts for bad prompts would become a new attack vector. A commenter asked what the point is of continuing to give money to a company that treats you this way.

A commenter said switching providers cannot be done overnight. A commenter said switching is not as easy as changing an API key, because you must find everything you tested with one model and make sure it still works. A commenter said they set up evals early and are saving 50% or more by routing tasks properly. A commenter said that if quality matters you must re-tweak settings and prompts for whichever model you switch to. A commenter said models do not all work the same or in the same order for all tasks.

A commenter asked whether the poster had lost their API keys, suggesting someone stole them and is running distillation. A commenter said a stolen key would have produced a surprise bill. A commenter said a distillation attack might be hidden in a lot of usage, spread across many keys to avoid discovery. A commenter doubted that most big corporations, let alone startups, audit bills against internal metrics. A commenter said they were doing innocuous work on IRS forms and had a subagent flagged for "reasoning extraction".

A commenter said asking the model to look at past session transcripts, export earlier chats as HTML pages or look at tool calls from previous sessions seems to trigger an overeager classifier. A commenter said competition is needed because being locked out by a single leading AI provider is a death sentence. A commenter disagreed, saying you can get Claude through Bedrock, Vertex or Foundry, or use GPT, Grok, Gemini, GLM, Kimi, Mistral or open weight models. A commenter said proving a negative is hard and suggested telling Anthropic what you have been doing and asking what part is an issue. A commenter said Big Tech refuses to do this, calling the risk department judge, jury and executioner.

A commenter said they started building their company after a similar message, realizing they could not depend on one provider. A commenter said distillation attacks are spread throughout numerous accounts and the poster has likely triggered some detection. A commenter said the best approach is to show the work is part of a real project and to explain any outliers. A commenter said they do not use Anthropic for serious work because normal work has been flagged for cyber security exploits many times. A commenter said they cannot imagine how to prove a negative and does not know if the poster is innocent.

A commenter said the situation shows how crazy things would be if the AI provider landscape settled into a monopoly or duopoly. A commenter said most people will be economically handicapped as a side effect of progress and that controlling the weights and means of inference will accumulate most of that value. A commenter said they were thinking shorter term, when AI still needs human babysitters for most knowledge work. A commenter said on a longer timeline everyone is in trouble without massive upheavals in socioeconomic systems.

The articles do not say what evidence the poster submitted or whether Anthropic responded. The articles do not say what happens to the account after the 24 hours. The articles do not give the company's name or Anthropic's statement on the case. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to staff for violating company code of conduct
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees on Tuesday for violating the company code of conduct. He spoke during his first all-hands meeting since returning to his role as chief executive. Huang stated that he made very serious personal mistakes which led to his resignation. He admitted that he hurt his wife and his family through these personal actions. The CEO also shared that he has been attending therapy every day for ninety minutes.

The board accepted his resignation earlier this month and reinstated him on Monday, eleven days later. This followed reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of ties to Chinese intelligence. The board acted after receiving fresh assurances and learning from the Trump administration he lacked federal scrutiny. Huang will now undergo a 360-degree performance review, soliciting feedback as often as every month. He claims he will be the first and only person at Nvidia to undergo this review.

Huang said this was the second hardest meeting he ever did, after a meeting with his wife. He stated that the company code of conduct, which he largely wrote, still governs employee treatment. He claimed that he needs to hold himself to a higher standard during this current time. Huang acknowledged that his intense management style sometimes disempowers employees and he takes things too far. He argued that his brief absence proved the company is wired to execute without him.

Some Nvidia employees celebrated the return of the CEO while others remain concerned about his personal conduct. One employee stated they would not do any more HR trainings if Huang returned to the company. Over 1,600 people commented on an internal post, with the majority supporting the decision to reinstall him. Women at the company are affected, though Huang described himself as one of their greatest advocates. He touted flexible work policies that allow employees to build their families and their careers simultaneously.

The board cited concerns about personal behavior and a lack of candor regarding his extramarital affairs. Huang began working with consultants from Heller in October 2025, when he was linked to a spy. The company opened an investigation into his affair with an alleged asset of Chinese intelligence services. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, served as the interim CEO following his initial resignation on Thursday. The company has faced lawsuits and probes regarding its disclosures and compliance with US export controls.

The board is continuing an investigation into whether Huang was the target of foreign intelligence services. US lawmakers expect the CEO to testify before Congress during the coming week. Legal probes into Nvidia's compliance with chip export controls and its disclosures about behavior are still ongoing. The articles leave open whether Huang can maintain his dedication without hurting the people who work there. It remains unclear if the board will institute performance reviews for other employees beyond the CEO.

Foreign investors drove the rally by purchasing large semiconductor stocks. The surge was triggered by the announced return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. This event occurred after a record breaking rise in the New York stock market.

The KOSPI opened at 4,880.16, which was a 3.64 percent rise of 171.62 points. It briefly recaptured the 5,000 mark, while the KOSDAQ opened at 654.31, up 2.97 percent. A sidecar program purchase suspension was activated at 9:06 a.m. in the KOSPI market. The won weakened to 1,343.0 per dollar, down 2.9 won from the previous day.

Samsung Electronics rose 7.55 percent to 190,000 won, and SK hynix rose 10 percent to 1,193,500 won. Foreign investors became the main protagonists by net buying approximately 420 billion won by 10:00 a.m. This action marked a transition to net buying for the first time in eight months. Institutional investors, including pension funds and financial investments, also provided stable buying pressure. A securities market expert said the rebound showed how New York tech surges act on domestic markets.

The expert suggested a strategy to check performance and the continuity of supply and demand entities. Individual investors showed a net selling edge of 480 billion won due to profit taking. Institutions net sold 20 billion won, while foreigners net bought 58.9 billion won in the KOSDAQ. Other affected stocks included Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Hyundai Motor, LG Energy Solution, and KB Financial Group.

In the KOSDAQ, Ecopro and Ecopro BM rose around 4 percent. Semiconductor materials stocks like Simmtech, EO Technics, Leeno Industrial, and Jusung Engineering also saw gains. The KOSPI had closed at 4,708.54 on November 23, which was a 3.31 percent drop. This previous decline was the lowest level in 10 months for the index.

The Nasdaq had jumped 6.5 percent, the S&P 500 soared 4.7 percent, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 14 percent. KOSPI 200 night futures had surged nearly 7 percent before the domestic market opened. These factors created the driving force for the sharp V-shaped rebound. The market will now monitor major economic indicator announcements and monetary policy events scheduled for this week.

Experts believe the exchange rate has entered a calming phase as AI investment fears eased. The KOSPI will continue probing around the 5,000 mark during its pace adjustment process. The articles leave open whether the current supply and demand trends will remain continuous. They also leave open the future volatility of the won-dollar exchange rate.

stories.Headline: Carnival CEO Josh Weinstein says U.S. travel disruptions cost the company a few hundred million dollars in revenue
stories.Summary:
The second and final day of Center Stage at The Phocuswright Conference 2026 closed the event at the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, with sessions on who will sell travel once AI agents can book on a traveler's behalf, on the race to power banks, airlines and loyalty programs with travel technology, and on the policy pressures weighing on U.S. travel. Carnival Corporation President and CEO Josh Weinstein told U.S. Travel Association President and CEO Geoff Freeman that this year's disruptions have cost the company probably a few hundred million dollars in revenue, not counting fuel, and that the hit took a point or two off yields. Freeman described government shutdowns, hours-long TSA lines, air traffic controller shortages and a 25% drop in Canadian visitors as man-made problems, and said the U.S. will welcome around 12 million fewer international visitors than in 2019. Weinstein said tourism has a cabinet seat in every other major economy and should have one in the U.S., given it accounts for about 3% of GDP, and he said Princess Cruises was the first cruise brand to launch plugins for ChatGPT and Claude, a claim made by him. Booking Holdings is uniting its B2B operations into a single Booking Partner Division ahead of a January go-live, Agoda CEO Omri Morgenshtern told PhocusWire Executive Editor Linda Fox, and he said Priceline's B2B business is not part of the new division because of an ongoing FTC investigation.

Morgenshtern said he expects each major product line to be among the best in the world within six to 12 months, and that success will mean not losing partners to competitors on technology. Expedia Group is now launching B2B partners about 75% faster than before, and its new AI-powered front end has cut launch times from three or four months to three or four days, said Alfonso Paredes, President, B2B and Chief Commercial Officer, who also said agentic booking is overhyped in the short term but underhyped in the long term. Under an expanded partnership with Qantas, Expedia now powers the technology behind Qantas Holidays' own hotel contracts with chains such as Accor, Hilton and Marriott. Hopper CEO and co-founder Frederic Lalonde said Amex, Chase and Capital One sell around $30 billion of travel a year, a business growing about 22% annually compared with 4% to 6% for travel as a whole, and that Hopper's B2B platform HTS now connects to about 400 million cardholders in 23 countries, which he expects to double next year. He said Hopper did not sell itself to Capital One, which licensed its software and remains a customer, and he questioned whether travel marketplaces of any kind survive the shift to AI agents, saying blocking agents that act for customers is unlikely to work when more than half of internet traffic is no longer human.

In a session on who powers travel when AI becomes the seller, panelists Brett Burgess of ATPCO, Niklas Andréen of Sabre and Steve Domin of Duffel predicted AI agents could book anywhere from 15% to 50% of airline tickets within two years. Burgess suggested United's recent decision to stop AI agents booking its flights is likely linked to verifying who the buyer is, and an ATPCO study found AI agents answered questions about flight offers accurately only about 6% of the time, because fare rules and product details are often not machine-readable, while Domin said the booking itself already works smoothly and the harder work is handling changes and cancellations after booking. New Phocuswright research presented by Mike Coletta found that while 43% of U.S. travelers familiar with AI say they would book inside an AI platform, only 28% of travel companies are working or planning to become bookable there, and a survey of around 150 travel companies and start-ups found 45% are scaling or have scaled agentic AI, up from 28% in 2025, with start-ups further ahead than established companies. Companies that rebuilt core workflows around AI were more than twice as likely to report a major positive impact, at 92% versus 40%, and panelists said the technology to complete an agentic booking already exists but questions over who is accountable when something goes wrong are holding back volume.

Google Group Product Manager James Byers told Phocuswright's Mitra Sorrells that AI Overviews now reach 2.5 billion monthly users and AI Mode can take a traveler from research to a completed hotel booking, and that AI queries are three times longer than traditional searches, with one in five using voice or images. Meta's Sanjay Bhatia, Head of Industry, Travel and Auto, showed how brands can use Meta Business Agent and WhatsApp, now used by 100 million Americans each month, to handle bookings and service in a single conversation. Zerolook CEO Simone Lini showed an example in which an AI agent ran around 881,000 flight searches on Etihad's website, and the Zurich-based start-up, which predicts airfares without querying live systems and has raised $1.9 million, reported 96% pricing accuracy for one U.S. carrier. Pintours was named Travel Innovator of the Year at the Innovation Awards, with Groupize runner-up and ZentrumHub winning the audience-voted People's Choice award, and the conference featured 199 speakers across 42 sessions, with session recordings to be released over the coming weeks.

stories.Headline: Guelph officials use AI to find city efficiencies and improve services
stories.Summary:
City officials in Guelph are turning to artificial intelligence to find efficiencies, according to a presentation made at a Guelph Chamber of Commerce breakfast event on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. Chief Administrative Officer Tara Baker spoke at the event at the Victoria Park East Golf Club, where about 100 local business people attended along with several city staff and councillors. Baker was joined by deputy CAOs Colleen Clack-Bush, Terry Gayman and Stephen O'Brien, who each presented on the areas of city governance they oversee. The CAO's breakfast took the place of the chamber's annual municipal budget event because the 2027 budget update has not yet been presented due to last month's city election. According to the articles, the city is using AI to identify mis-sorted residential waste as it is collected by trucks, to track whether buses are on schedule and potentially to assess the grip of municipal equipment on wintry roads.

AI is also being used to assess infrastructure risks, model the repercussions of failures and plan how to lessen the impact or reduce the risk. Baker said the city is measuring its performance and how it does business, where it invests money, and is using those performance metrics to drive business decisions. O'Brien said part of the work includes breaking down departmental silos and removing redundant pages or information on the city's website, which he described as dated old legacy systems with highly siloed pockets of data and very low integration across platforms. Baker said the city is trying to improve those abilities through its focus on data management and business intelligence.

Clack-Bush said the city is focused on being efficient, finding ways to eliminate bureaucracy if it can and delivering services in a customer friendly way, noting the city is always looking at how technology can improve customer service. Gayman said the number one thing the city hears about is the housing need, along with transit, active transportation and the ability to provide options for people to get to work reliably. O'Brien said AI searches return a deeper analysis of results than a traditional Google search, making it all the more important that official city details are presented at the top of results pages, and that the city's data governance work matters because the business community needs confidence that the information it uses is accurate, timely and understood. Budget details are expected to be released in the new year, according to the articles.

Articles.Title: City hall turns to AI in attempt to improve efficiencies - Guelph News

stories.headline_source: City hall turns to AI in attempt to improve efficiencies

stories.Headline: Guterres tells Security Council killer robots must have no place in our future
stories.Summary:
The Security Council met on Tuesday to weigh how artificial intelligence and drones are reshaping warfare, with UN chief António Guterres telling ambassadors that killer robots must have no place in our future. The session examined how new technologies now spread globally within months rather than decades, and how disinformation is fuelling record levels of conflict. The council heard that artificial intelligence is already assisting in targeting and that drones are changing the way wars are fought. The meeting was held at UN headquarters and was carried live on UNWebTV. Guterres told council members they have a special duty to ensure that competition over emerging technologies does not destabilise international peace and security.

Last week in Geneva, a push by around 100 countries to negotiate a legally binding instrument on lethal autonomous weapons fell short. The Secretary-General's July review of UN peace operations made closing the technology gap a priority. A new informal council expert group on technology, peace and security met for the first time on 18 November, and in 2021 the council recognised technology as a potential force multiplier for UN peacekeeping. The Secretary-General is responsible for the July review of UN peace operations, which made closing the technology gap a priority, and he addressed the council directly on the duty of members. The council itself set up the informal expert group on technology, peace and security, which held its first meeting on 18 November.

The council also recognised technology in 2021 as a potential force multiplier for UN peacekeeping. Around 100 countries pushed in Geneva last week for a legally binding instrument on lethal autonomous weapons, but that effort fell short. The meeting comes as the UN marks more than eighty years since its founding in 1945, when computers, the internet and satellites were the stuff of science fiction. The articles do not say what the council will decide or when it will next take up the issue. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Security Council LIVE: Can conflict resolution keep pace as AI and drones reshape war? - UN News

stories.headline_source: Security Council LIVE: Can conflict resolution keep pace as AI and drones reshape war?

stories.Headline: Spartanburg Water CEO says AI posts mislead as utility reviews outage cause
stories.Summary:
Guy Boyle, the CEO of Spartanburg Water, spoke at a city county meeting on Monday, November 24, 2026. He explained a water outage that lasted several days and impacted residents across much of Spartanburg County. Boyle addressed AI social media posts, conversations about Duke Energy, and data center water usage. He stated that the exact cause of the power blip that led to the outage is still unknown.

The outage resulted from damage to a main 42-inch line and a secondary 24-inch line. Boyle noted that a brief power outage at the main plant may have lasted less than 10 seconds. The company is reviewing design weaknesses, valve analysis, surge relief systems, and additional levels of protection. He mentioned that the meter for NorthMark has not been ordered, installed, or connected yet.

Guy Boyle said that comments blaming Duke Energy for the damage were inaccurate and not communicated by Spartanburg Water. He described Duke Energy as a partner and stated that a post-mortem review of the infrastructure damage is underway. Boyle claimed that some residents shared misleading information to serve personal and political agendas. He stated that these conspiracy theories made the role of public service professionals more difficult.

Boyle acknowledged that social media comments regarding slow notification of the outage had merit. He explained that the current system cannot message all 276,000 customers simultaneously, so they used traditional and social media. Residents in Lyman and Woodruff had working ice machines because they are served by SJWD and WRWD. Boyle stated that these machines were left on so customers could have access to ice.

The company noted that some industry in the county was unaffected, including businesses in the Tiger River Industrial Park. Boyle cited Hurricane Helene as an example where infrastructure ran for two weeks without grid power. He stated that the systemwide boil water advisory was lifted on Sunday. The company told customers to call if they still experience air or cloudy water.

Spartanburg Water is currently working on a new notification system to better handle future systemwide events. The company and external electrical contractors are in the preliminary stages of investigating the power blip. The articles do not state when the new notification system will be fully operational. They do not provide a specific date for the completion of the infrastructure review. The final cause of the power blip remains undetermined.

stories.Headline: York County school board approves $107,100 for education software including AI platform MagicSchool
stories.Summary:
The York County School Board heard updates on a Spanish-language program, gifted education and artificial intelligence during its Tuesday meeting in Yorktown, according to Williamsburg Yorktown Daily. The Spanish program is a grant-funded pilot that operates at Bethel Manor Elementary School and Tabb Elementary School, which were chosen because they are the division's two schools with the most military-connected families. At Bethel Manor, students in kindergarten through fifth grade learn foundational Spanish language skills and explore Spanish culture in a world language resource class. Principal Anthony Friedman said students are building communication skills, curiosity and an appreciation for different perspectives that will help them in a changing world. A Bethel Manor student, Gabe Lugo, told the board he thinks other students should have the chance to learn Spanish because it helps people connect across different backgrounds.

The pilot depends on funding from a Department of Defense Education Activity grant, and Superintendent James Carroll said the division would be open to discussing expansion if the board wants the program in more schools. Carroll also said the division would consider local funding for the program. On gifted education, the board heard that more than 100 students are in the current referral cycle, and the Gifted Education Advisory Committee is reviewing the division's gifted education plan ahead of its 2027 expiration. The board unanimously approved October financial expenditures, Tabb High School additions and renovations totaling $38,100,000, and $107,100 for education software that includes the artificial intelligence platform MagicSchool and the digital learning platform ClassLink. Chief Academic Officer Candi Skinner said the division wants students prepared to use AI appropriately and responsibly in college or the work world, and she confirmed the AI program is monitored and has safeguards for student safety.

The board also reviewed a resolution on a policy called Equal Access to Public Education and Protection of Immigration and Citizenship-Related Information, which establishes that no student can be denied access to any division activity or benefit based on perceived immigration or citizenship status. The board approved consideration of a lease agreement between the school board and the Tabb Lakes Homes Association for the association to use school property for community meetings. The board's next meeting will be its Dec. 14 work session at 7 p.m. in York Hall.

Articles.Title: York school board hears updates on Spanish program, gifted education and AI - Williamsburg Yorktown Daily

stories.headline_source: York school board hears updates on Spanish program, gifted education and AI

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia chief executive and South Korean AI stocks surge
stories.Summary:
South Korean stocks linked to artificial intelligence and robotics surged on November 24, 2026, after Jensen Huang returned as the chief executive officer of Nvidia. The board of directors for the chipmaker unanimously approved the return of Huang on November 23, which occurred only eleven days after he had stepped down. This leadership change eased market uncertainty and triggered strong buying for companies with direct business ties to the American firm. The rally followed a night of trading in the United States where the Nasdaq Composite rose 6.51 percent and Nvidia shares jumped 31.48 percent. The market reaction saw Hyundai AutoEver trade at 348,500 won, representing a gain of 24.91 percent, while Doosan rose 17.19 percent to 634,000 won.

LG Electronics gained 16.50 percent to reach 144,000 won, and KOSDAQ stocks like Robotis and Rainbow Robotics rose by 13.82 percent and 13.56 percent respectively. Hyundai AutoEver is managing the procurement of 3,000 graphics processing units and holds a 26 percent stake in HMG AI Factory. LG Electronics plans to reveal a bipedal robot using the Isaac GR00T model in the first quarter of 2027 and aims for commercialization in the second half of that year. Doosan Electronics BG provides copper-clad laminates for accelerators, while Doosan Robotics is building an operating system on the Nvidia platform. Investors believe the return of the chief executive will ensure that large-scale cooperation projects with South Korean firms proceed as originally planned.

During a visit to the country in October 2025, Huang pledged to supply more than 260,000 graphics processing units to domestic companies and the government. LG Group Chairman Koo Kwang-mo previously visited the headquarters of Nvidia in August to sign a memorandum of understanding regarding future mobility and AI infrastructure. LG Electronics also signed a strategic agreement in August and has allocated two production lines for robots at its Tennessee plant. The company further intends to create a dedicated organization for cooling operations in AI data centers this December. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Huang’s Return Sends South Korean AI-Linked Stocks Soaring - Businesskorea

stories.headline_source: Huang’s Return Sends South Korean AI-Linked Stocks Soaring

stories.Headline: LG Uplus uses Datadog AI analytics to cut ixi-O incident diagnosis time by 86 percent
stories.Summary:
LG Uplus joined the Design Partner Program provided by Datadog to improve the reliability of its AI call agent service known as ixi-O. This collaboration began in August and lasted for approximately three months to integrate new AI technologies into a live service environment. The company claims to be the first South Korean firm to participate in this specific program to enhance its operational quality. By using these tools, the company sought to identify the causes of service incidents more efficiently than before. The implementation required the use of Bits AI, which is an AI-powered analytics technology developed by Datadog. This system changed the operational process by consolidating various types of data instead of requiring researchers to examine individual sources.

These changes reduced the time needed to identify root causes and implement improvements by approximately 86 percent. Furthermore, the time required to respond to the scope of service incidents decreased by 85 percent. The period needed to detect anomalies that could lead to disruptions was also cut in half. Datadog is responsible for providing the observability and security platform that enables these technical improvements for the client. The provider stated that Bits AI helped identify the causes of incidents by integrating and analyzing operational data generated by ixi-O. This technology allowed the team to move away from manual data inspection toward a more automated analysis system.

The company believes that this integration supports faster improvements and a more stable experience for the end users. The two companies are currently testing new features based on the feedback and results gathered from the initial deployment. They plan to establish a comprehensive system for the early detection of and response to various service anomalies. This ongoing effort aims to accelerate the pace of service improvements for the AI call agent. The ultimate goal of this partnership is to enhance the overall quality experienced by the customers of LG Uplus.

Articles.Title: LG Uplus Enhances ixi-O Service Quality with Datadog AI Technology - www.thelec.net

stories.headline_source: LG Uplus Enhances ixi-O Service Quality with Datadog AI Technology

stories.Headline: Tidal bans fully AI-generated music and starts removing tracks on December 9
stories.Summary:
Tidal announced on Tuesday that it will ban music that is completely AI-generated. The streaming service will start removing these tracks from its catalog on December 9. This move makes Tidal the first music streaming platform to ban AI music entirely. The company will also block new uploads of fully AI-generated songs. These changes follow a period where the service only demonetized such tracks.

The ban will remove about 29 million tracks by the start of 2027. Tidal expects to turn away between 80,000 and 85,000 songs every day. Robert Andersen leads Tidal at the parent company called Block. The service previously flagged 43 percent of tracks received over 90 days as AI-generated. About 27 million tracks, or 6.3 percent of the catalog, are already tagged.

Robert Andersen stated that more drastic action was needed because of the high volume of AI tracks. He wrote on X that Tidal is the first digital service provider to do this. Andersen claims the move will resonate with both listeners and artists alike. He encouraged other peers in the industry to follow the same path. He said Tidal will continue making decisions that support real artists first.

Some listeners on X and Reddit said the ban was a reason to switch to Tidal. Other users joked about how AI artists might hire humans just to clap on beat. Some people questioned how the service will actually catch all the AI music. Others asked if a single human cough in a song would make it allowed. These users wondered how much human input makes a recording AI-assisted.

Tidal started labeling wholly AI-generated tracks and cutting off royalties back in July. The service also took down songs linked to fraud and artist impersonation. The company found that 96 percent of AI tracks went unplayed over three months. This policy follows a trend of services labeling AI tracks as slop or spam. Other platforms like Deezer and Bandcamp have also implemented their own AI restrictions.

Tidal will continue removing tracks until they are completely gone by the beginning of the year. The service must now decide which specific tracks can stay and which must come down. It remains unclear how the company will enforce the ban on all uploads. The articles do not say how Tidal will detect AI in assisted recordings. They leave open whether other major streaming services will adopt a total ban.

stories.Headline: SK chair Chey Tae-won proposes joint Korea-Japan AI talent development
stories.Summary:
SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won proposed that South Korea and Japan jointly develop artificial intelligence talent during a business leaders' session. This proposal occurred on November 21, 2026, during the Tokyo Forum 2026 event held at the University of Tokyo. The forum took place at Yasuda Auditorium and was co-hosted by the University of Tokyo and the Chey Institute. Chey called for closer cooperation between the two nations to cultivate innovators capable of solving various complex social challenges. He suggested that companies and universities from both countries should jointly establish and operate these AI talent development programs.

The initiative requires the joint operation of programs to connect internships and job opportunities for young people across both countries. Chey called for fundamentally different designs and governance structures for universities to reflect a society where AI is everyday life. He stated that simply making minor adjustments to existing curricula is not enough to prepare for an AI-native society. The proposal follows the Big Tent bilateral cooperation initiative introduced in June and the Korea-Japan New Era Strategic Platform launched November 18. This platform was launched by the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies in partnership with the Japanese newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun.

Chairman Chey Tae-won is responsible for the proposal and stated that AI should be an inherent part of the environment. He argued that collective intelligence and even unsuccessful attempts to design new systems help young people develop essential problem-solving skills. Chey urged universities to move beyond teaching knowledge and focus on cultivating wisdom to guide change in the AI era. He said people must ask what new value they want to create and what kind of society they want to build. He believes that new governance is necessary because the current university system must be designed differently for the AI age.

Other participants included French AI envoy Anne Bouverot, Sakana AI co-founder Ren Ito, and NTT Group Chairman Jun Sawada. President Yeom Jae-ho of Taejae University and President Miki Sugimura of Sophia University also joined the discussion on talent development. University of Tokyo President Teruo Fujii moderated the session where these business and academic leaders discussed the future of education. Young people are the ones affected, as the program aims to expand their employment and internship opportunities in both nations. These students would be nurtured as social innovators capable of addressing challenges through the proposed cross-border cooperation and training.

The articles state that Chey proposed the Big Tent initiative at the Nikkei Forum in Tokyo during June of 2026. As an example of current efforts, Chey highlighted AIGEN, a two-year non-degree program that was launched last month by SK. In the AIGEN program, participants work in teams on challenges across various fields to design their own unique solutions. The Tokyo Forum 2026 was held from November 20 to 21 under the theme of AI as a Transformative Technology. This theme specifically focused on the intersections of humanity, knowledge, and civilization within the context of advancing artificial intelligence.

The next steps involve the potential establishment of joint programs between Korean and Japanese universities and businesses to develop talent. The proposal seeks to create a system where internships and jobs are more easily connected across the two East Asian countries. The articles leave open whether other universities or companies will officially join the proposed joint AI talent development initiative. It remains unclear how the suggested fundamental redesign of university governance and curricula will be implemented in actual practice. The text does not state if a specific timeline has been set for launching these joint cross-border AI programs.

stories.Headline: Younglimwon SoftLab grows cloud ERP revenue 36 percent as it adds AI features
stories.Summary:
Younglimwon SoftLab reported a significant increase in its cloud enterprise resource planning business during the first nine months of 2026. According to a regulatory filing submitted on November 13, the company saw its cloud ERP revenue grow by 36 percent compared to the previous year. This growth occurred during the period from January through September, reflecting a strong shift toward cloud services. The company also noted that its on-premises ERP revenue grew by 11 percent during this same timeframe.

The cloud ERP segment generated 5.1 billion won in revenue, which increased its share of total company revenue to 8.1 percent from 6.7 percent. On-premises ERP revenue reached 37.6 billion won, though it grew at a slower pace than the cloud business. Since August, the company has integrated AI-powered automatic data entry, business briefings, and workflow automation into its K-System Ace I&I platform. This platform also now includes AI spreadsheet analysis and business insights to improve data analytics. Additionally, the company is developing the K-Bot 3.0 project to enhance its existing AI chatbot.

Younglimwon SoftLab is responsible for these updates and is currently pursuing the use of Model Context Protocol technology. This specific technology is intended to connect AI agents with external services to expand the capabilities of ERP workflows. The company reported that its consolidated revenue for the third quarter reached 21.7 billion won, which is a 5.6 percent increase. Operating profit for the same quarter rose by 8.6 percent to reach 1.4 billion won.

stories.Headline: Seven Korean substrate suppliers invest 2.8 trillion won to expand AI component production
stories.Summary:
Seven mid-sized Korean substrate suppliers announced investments totaling approximately 2.8 trillion won this year to address shortages caused by artificial intelligence. These companies plan to expand their production facilities in stages starting from late this year and continuing through 2030. The surge in semiconductor demand has specifically increased the need for SOCAMM2 memory substrates and other high-performance components. This expansion follows similar large-scale capacity increases already undertaken by major manufacturers like LG Innotek and Samsung Electro-Mechanics.

Daeduck Electronics committed the largest amount with 1.325 trillion won for facilities, while Isu Petasys plans to invest 500 billion won. Other investments include 379.6 billion won from Simmtech, 200 billion won from TLB, 190 billion won from Haesung DS, 110 billion won from BH, and 99.3 billion won from Korea Circuit. These funds will support the production of flip-chip ball grid array and flip-chip chip-scale package substrates, as well as multi-layer boards for AI accelerator boards. Some companies are also targeting next-generation DDR6 DRAM and automotive substrates in Vietnam to diversify their output.

Kim Pan-bae, an executive vice president at Samsung Electro-Mechanics, stated on October 28 that meeting customer demand remains difficult despite large-scale expansions. He noted that the company continues to receive requests for additional supplies from its clients. Other industry officials warned that these investments may not immediately increase production volumes due to severe equipment shortages. The chairman of Unimicron reported that delivery lead times for critical production equipment have reached as long as 30 months.

The Global Electronics Association forecast this month that the global printed circuit board shortage is unlikely to ease significantly before mid-2028. Additionally, supplies of key materials like copper-clad laminates could fall about 20 percent short of demand next year. To secure necessary capacity, Big Tech customers have entered into long-term supply agreements and are helping to finance these expansion investments. These measures aim to stabilize the supply chain for critical AI server components and high-speed communication chips.

stories.Headline: SK hynix shares close up 6.73% as Jensen Huang's Nvidia return lifts Seoul chipmakers
stories.Summary:
SK hynix shares rose 6.73% to 1,158,000 won at the November 24 regular-session close in Seoul, as Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia pulled Korean chipmakers off their lows, according to TradingView. The Kospi climbed 6.32% to 5,006.03 on the same day, triggering a buy-side sidecar minutes after the open. Foreign investors bought a net 725.6 billion won of Korean shares, after Monday's 3.31% slide in the index.

SK hynix booked third-quarter revenue of 104.6 trillion won, up 328% year over year, and operating profit of 83.3 trillion won, an 80% margin. Long-term agreements with 14 major customers now cover more than half of 2027 and 2028 capacity, and HBM4 is set to overtake HBM3E in shipments this quarter. Net cash stands at 98.7 trillion won, and annualizing the third-quarter operating profit reaches about 333 trillion won against a market value near 746 trillion won. The close sits about 25% below the GF Value of 1,534,744 won, a discount the chart attributes to earnings at a cyclical peak.

A Daishin Securities researcher told the Korea Herald that the sell-off came from lost confidence, not earnings. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of 99/100, reflecting near-perfect profitability, a strong balance sheet and solid momentum. The key tests are fourth-quarter HBM4 volumes and whether contract pricing inside those long-term deals holds in 2027.

stories.Headline: New Yorkers warned of holiday scams, AI shopping traps
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James issued a holiday scam warning on November 24, 2026, as reported by Long Island Business News. The warning tells New Yorkers to guard their personal information and to be careful when using artificial intelligence tools while shopping. James said she encourages holiday shoppers to protect themselves, their families and their private information by staying vigilant about potential scams. She also said no one should hesitate to report suspicious activity to her office. The warning covers receipts, buy now pay later loans, subscriptions, devices, phishing emails, fake deals, AI shopping tools and surveillance pricing.

James advised consumers to check that register prices match advertised or shelf prices. New York law requires retailers to charge the lowest advertised, posted or marked price and to keep at least 98% price accuracy during inspections by weights and measures officials. She said shoppers should review interest rates, payment schedules and fees on buy now, pay later loans before buying. Some of those loans charge interest even when payments are made on time, and missed payments may bring late fees and hurt credit scores. New York law requires businesses to clearly disclose subscription terms, obtain consent for automatic renewals, send post-purchase confirmation and offer an easy way to cancel.

James said consumers should update their home Wi-Fi password, avoid public Wi-Fi for purchases, install the latest software updates and keep antivirus software active. She warned that emails promoting exclusive holiday deals or free gift cards may be phishing attempts. She said shoppers should verify senders of unexpected holiday e-cards or invitations before clicking links or opening attachments. She advised shopping only on reputable websites, verifying URLs before entering payment information and checking for a working customer service number, a physical business address and positive customer reviews.

She said retailers that list only a P.O. box or have no working phone number deserve caution. James said shoppers should review all charges before purchasing because some websites add hefty delivery, processing or subscription fees, particularly during the holiday season. She said people using AI tools to make purchases should review what accounts and personal information the tool can access and limit permissions whenever possible. She said anyone whose AI tool can buy on their behalf should set clear spending limits and purchasing rules and require approval before purchases whenever possible.

New York's Algorithmic Pricing Disclosure Act requires most businesses that use personal data to set prices to display a clear disclosure near the price. Consumers who encounter undisclosed algorithmic pricing should file a complaint with the attorney general's office. James said shoppers should compare prices across retailers and platforms, use private or incognito browsing and check prices when logged out of loyalty accounts. She warned about inflated discounts and crossed-out prices and said shoppers should check price histories to judge whether a deal offers real savings.

She said consumers should keep order confirmations and receipts, contact the retailer if an item does not arrive as promised and file a complaint with her office if the company does not respond. She said people should review credit card and bank statements regularly for unauthorized charges, which may go unnoticed amid increased holiday spending. Suspected scam victims can report to the attorney general's office by submitting a complaint online or calling 1-800-771-7755. More to follow.

stories.Headline: India should test AI in regulatory sandboxes before deployment, speaker tells commerce summit
stories.Summary:
At the Indo-American Chamber of Commerce Summit in New Delhi last week, a speaker made five asks of the government on artificial intelligence, covering rules that work across India and America, trusted data flows, intellectual property protection, regulatory sandboxes and faster clearances for AI talent and data centres, and the sandbox drew the strongest response from the hall. The speaker described a sandbox as a learner's licence for a new technology and pointed to past practice, noting that UPI was launched on 11 April 2016 with 21 banks and grew under close watch of the existing payments law. In October this year, the speaker said, UPI handled 25.47 billion transactions in a single month, and in 2019 the Reserve Bank made the sandbox idea formal with a regulatory sandbox framework. In the latest round, five companies began testing and one product was found viable, and in 2025 an RBI committee recommended a sandbox for AI in finance with board-approved AI policies and the principle that whoever deploys AI answers for its decisions. The speaker said the government notified the Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026 this month, replacing aircraft rules written in 1937, with effect from January 2027, and called this the right moment to write an AI sandbox into them before any such system touches a passenger.

The speaker argued that a sandbox is also a legal instrument that provides rules for a limited time, to a limited audience and on strict conditions, and said every AI sandbox must answer five questions before the first test begins. On accountability, the speaker said the company that deploys should ideally be held accountable, while laws around the world are still being framed. On remedy, the speaker said a harmed customer must get a quick and certain remedy, with insurance or a compensation fund in place before testing starts. On data, the speaker said every test must comply with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act from the first day and that a sandbox must never relax privacy.

On honesty, the speaker said companies' admissions should not be used against them except in cases of fraud, and on endings, the speaker said every sandbox needs an exit plan before it begins. The speaker said these questions will soon reach the courts, giving the example of a bank refusing a loan or an airline holding a flight because an AI system said so, and noted that under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam an electronic record needs a certificate before a court will admit it, so every sandbox should require AI decisions to be logged in a form a court can examine. The speaker said the legal profession must accept the same discipline, noting that more than five crore cases are pending in Indian courts and that courts and law firms are rightly testing AI for translation, research and document review, with an advocate sitting beside the machine and answering for every output. The speaker said the learner's mark comes off not because time has passed but because the driver has shown on real roads that he is ready, and urged giving AI in banking, aviation and law its learner's licence now.

stories.Headline: Cameron Stanley urges the Department of War to speed up AI integration against AI-enabled threats
stories.Summary:
Cameron Stanley, chief super intelligence officer at the Department of War, said the department needs to speed up the integration of artificial intelligence across its operations to counter threats enabled by AI agents, Signal reported Friday. Stanley spoke Thursday at a luncheon event focused on open-source and strategic intelligence. He said the only way to fight an agentically enabled, very nefarious threat environment is to get agents yourself. He said the department should integrate SI, use domain expertise and subject matter expertise, and fight fire with fire. He said the longer we wait, the more behind we are going to be.

Stanley’s title reflects the department’s Nov. 13 redesignation of the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office as the Department of War Super Intelligence Office. The move aligns the office with an executive order President Donald Trump signed in September requiring executive branch agencies to adopt “super intelligence” and “SI” in place of “artificial intelligence” and “AI” across official correspondence, public communications, websites and other non-statutory materials. The order defines the new terms as covering the same technologies included in the existing statutory definition of artificial intelligence. Stanley, a 2026 Wash100 awardee, said the new name keeps attention on the administration’s goal of delivering advanced tools across the department quickly and in large numbers. According to Stanley, GenAI.mil has grown since May to include three models cleared at Impact Level 5, giving DOW users a platform suited for controlled unclassified information.

Stanley said open-source intelligence and commercial tools give the department access to more data than it holds internally. He said AI tools can help personnel sort through that information to reach sound decisions more quickly. He said open-source data is a treasure trove in volume and in quality, if you know how to use it and have the ability to parse through it, and that this is where SI tools come in. He noted that commercial offerings allow users to process large volumes of data outside the constraints of government environments, though they do not suit every application.

Stanley pointed to space-based intelligence as one area where the commercial sector has surpassed the military, saying the commercial industry has overtaken us, so we would be fools not to take advantage of it. In July, Stanley said the department planned to bring new models to GenAI.mil and deploy them at higher classification levels, noting that the platform had reached 1.7 million users and supported more than 100,000 custom AI agents. Stanley’s call for faster AI integration builds on remarks he has made since taking over the Pentagon’s AI office in January, when he called on industry partners to play a more active role in delivering technology platforms as the department advances its AI strategy. In March, he delivered a keynote at the Potomac Officers Club’s 2026 Artificial Intelligence Summit, where he said the department is shifting its focus from AI strategic enablement to delivery, with the goal of fielding new capabilities in months rather than years.

In June, his office announced plans to move its GAMECHANGER policy search tool from the War Data Platform onto GenAI.mil to give users a single place to search department policy. He has said the department continues to identify new uses for the Maven Smart System, including logistics, supply chain and force readiness, and is piloting AI to help draft routine contract language. DOW has expanded access to AI tools across its workforce over the past year. To learn more about how agencies are putting these tools to work, government and industry leaders will join the Potomac Officers Club’s 2027 Artificial Intelligence Summit on March 18.

Discussions there will cover AI-enabled cyber defense, digital modernization, national security use cases and more. Registration is open for the event. The article gives no further background on the event. More to follow.

stories.Headline: California agency recommends state-licensed auditors and a shutdown power for frontier AI
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 20, 2026, the California Government Operations Agency released a report on frontier AI safety, as reported by Transparency Coalition on Nov. 24, 2026. The report responds to an executive order Gov. Gavin Newsom issued in Sept. 2026, shortly after news of the OpenAI Hugging Face attack broke. Newsom's order fast-tracked California's independent oversight of AI companies and asked GOA to study amending state law to require an AI kill switch. The order asked GOA to work with the California Office of Emergency Services and outside AI experts. Newsom asked for recommendations for legislative action in 2027, using SB 53 as the foundation.

The report recommends that the state set baseline standards for safety, security and transparency that all large frontier AI developers must follow. It says Independent Verification Organizations should have flexibility to determine and update technical specifications as AI technology evolves, with the state having final say and able to overrule an IVO's assessment. It recommends legislation requiring every large frontier developer to submit to ongoing oversight by state-licensed IVOs, with full access to people and information and unredacted assessments shared with the state. It recommends funding CalCompute, a publicly owned computing system created in framework by SB 53 but never funded, through a surcharge on IVO fees paid by the largest frontier developers. It recommends cutting the timeline for reporting most safety incidents from 15 days to 48 hours while retaining the 24-hour requirement for imminent catastrophic risks.

The report recommends that IVOs cannot have payment contingent on audit outcomes, must manage financial and other conflicts, and should be independent of the developer being assessed. It says IVOs should present assessments to the state, which after engaging with the developer should decide whether to order corrective action, and developers could contest the determination in court before it goes into effect. It says if a court finds in favor of the state, the court should be able to compel adherence to the state's standards as a condition of further model development. It recommends that every large frontier developer create a Risk Containment Protocol, tested and verified on an ongoing basis by an IVO, showing the ability to intervene on multiple levels including compute, agents, internal access and model deployment. It says the protocol should identify the people responsible for intervening, coordinate with outside actors such as cloud providers and power suppliers, and determine when it is safe to restore the model.

The report recommends expanding the threshold for critical incident reporting to capture all serious incidents, saying attempts to steal model weights should be reported even without death or bodily injury, as should situations of loss-of-control. It recommends the state establish a near-miss reporting channel and expand whistleblower protections to include former employees and contractors. It recommends lowering the compute threshold so models trained with fewer than 10²⁶ floating-point operations are subject to reporting requirements, saying relying solely on that numerical threshold prevented the state from scoping in dangerous incidents such as the OpenAI Hugging Face incident. It recommends that developers report key metrics on their automation of AI R&D, including the share of compute devoted to this purpose, with IVOs' first responsibility being to verify these metrics and assess the risks as they grow. It says if the state assesses that automation of AI R&D above a certain level may result in catastrophic risk, the state should have authority to cap the development and use of recursive self-improvement.

California enacted SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, in Sept. 2025, and it came into effect on Jan. 1, 2026. In Sept. 2026, Newsom and legislators enacted SB 813 and AB 1405 to work with SB 53 to establish independent safety and compliance audits conducted by state-licensed IVOs. Because SB 53 was enacted before IVOs were established, the law currently requires only an internal self-assessment, not independent third-party audits. SB 813 makes IVOs voluntary and relies on voluntary state designation, while AB 1405 creates a mandatory registry for AI auditors who conduct audits that state law requires, and neither law requires any developer to be audited or licenses IVOs. When SB 53 was adopted, 10²⁶ floating-point operations was the clear boundary line for the most powerful frontier models, but greater efficiency means models trained with 10²⁵ or even 10²⁴ operations may be capable of triggering serious safety incidents.

The report recommends codifying the state's authority to order an immediate shutdown if the danger from a model is imminent and the developer refuses to take action, which SB 53 currently does not include. It recommends that the Risk Containment Protocol address potential failures of the shutdown procedure, with the developer specifically testing whether the model will attempt to block implementation of the shutdown, such as by copying its weights, and whether an outside actor could access the shutdown controls. The report recommends that the state adopt clear standards applying throughout the AI model development cycle, with reference to national and international standard-setting bodies wherever appropriate. It lists standards to be defined including security, compute allocation reporting, accreditation, outcome, contracting, access and practice standards. The articles do not say when legislation based on the report might be introduced or whether the recommendations will be adopted.

stories.Headline: Stephen Russell finds glass-core AI substrates may not cut absolute carbon emissions
stories.Summary:
Stephen Russell wrote an analysis on November 24, 2026, regarding glass-core substrates for AI packaging. He examined if these materials can scale AI without increasing carbon emissions. The author explored the mechanical limits of traditional organic packaging for AI accelerators. He identified a paradox where material efficiency might not lower absolute emissions. This report focuses on the environmental impact of advanced semiconductor packaging.

Glass-core substrates offer low thermal expansion and near-zero moisture absorption for late-decade AI accelerators. They allow high-density Through-Glass Vias and support packages extending toward 12,000 square millimeters. These substrates can support dozen-stack High Bandwidth Memory configurations in next-generation data center architectures. TechInsights projects 40.9 million packaged AI accelerators will be manufactured by the year 2030. The technology aims to replace organic substrates that suffer from thermal warpage.

Stephen Russell stated that glass-core substrates could address mechanical limits of advanced AI packaging. He noted that evaluating glass only as a material upgrade misses the bigger picture. The author claimed that yield protection is the true driver of carbon emissions. He explained that lower manufacturing carbon intensity is not synonymous with lower absolute emissions. Russell argued that sustainability teams must maintain a critical distinction between these two metrics.

The analysis affects the semiconductor supply chain and teams managing AI hardware sustainability. High-end AI packages carry tens of thousands of dollars in embodied carbon before final assembly. For a 12-HBM accelerator package, a 90 percent yield loses 36 tons of carbon. Improving that yield to 98 percent reduces lost emissions to 7 tons per 1,000 packages. Closing this gap could avoid 1.4 million tons of carbon, or 5.8 percent of the footprint.

Organic substrates struggle to support massive clusters of logic chiplets and High Bandwidth Memory. These traditional materials are prone to dimensional instability and thermal warpage as footprints expand. Glass allows localized silicon bridges to replace full-area processed silicon interposers in the design. However, electronic-grade glass requires energy-intensive furnace operations for melting and forming. TGV formation also consumes significant electrical power and specialized chemistry during the process.

Future success depends on assessing real-world fab yields and total net silicon deployment. Brittle damage and microcracks during handling can still cause wasted embodied carbon. Immature early yields on pilot lines may erode the theoretical carbon savings of glass. Larger accelerators enabled by glass could absorb more total carbon in their bill of materials. The articles leave open whether absolute emissions will actually decrease as AI scales.

Articles.Title: The Glass Substrate Paradox: Can Advanced Packaging Scale AI Without Scaling Carbon? - TechInsights

stories.headline_source: The Glass Substrate Paradox: Can Advanced Packaging Scale AI Without Scaling Carbon?

stories.Headline: AICPA and AIUC launch joint SOC 2 plus AIUC-1 assurance certification for AI agents
stories.Summary:
The AICPA and the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company teamed up to develop an assurance certification, the Journal of Accountancy reported on Nov. 24, 2026. Amy Pawlicki, the AICPA’s vice president, Assurance & Advisory Innovation, detailed the new SOC 2 plus AIUC-1 engagement on the Journal of Accountancy podcast. The AICPA announced in October that it was partnering with the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company on the new assurance engagement. The pairing combines a traditional SOC 2 engagement with an additional set of criteria related to the AIUC’s requirements. The additional criteria address risks around the behavior of AI agents.

The joint engagement covers the reliability of the underlying system as it relates to security, privacy, confidentiality, processing integrity, and availability. That SOC 2 attestation piece is an annual examination engagement under the AICPA attestation standards. The AIUC-1 certification piece covers specified agents and their platforms from the perspective of their security, safety, and reliability risks. Those risks specifically include data and privacy, security, safety, reliability, accountability, and society. The AIUC-1 piece is addressed through quarterly technical evaluations or red-teaming that specifically addresses real-world agentic risks.

Pawlicki said the usage of AI has become almost ubiquitous, and the safety, security, and reliability of AI tools and in particular agents has become of paramount importance. She said regulators and legislators are increasingly focused on building trust in AI, citing the recent White House accord. She said the accord does not have regulatory authority but calls out external audits explicitly and focuses on internal controls. She said CPAs are the experts and trusted providers of independent assurance, and SOC 2 engagements can only be performed by licensed CPAs. She said the joint engagement is reserved for licensed CPAs only.

Pawlicki said members of the AIUC consortium, representing a who’s who of CISOs and other professionals from major frontier AI developers, had from the beginning called for a SOC 2 for AI. She said the AIUC consortium brings deep AI technical expertise to help develop and maintain the criteria against which CPAs perform their work. She said the AIUC technical standards are constantly updated and transparently available and go beyond policies to test how agents are actually behaving. She said the first joint SOC 2 plus AIUC-1 was, she believed, announced for Legora, an agentic platform in the legal space. She said the AIUC consortium has over 300 CISO and security leaders overseeing the development and maintenance of the AIUC criteria.

Pawlicki said the next category after agents is frontier AI models, both open and closed, followed by robotics. She said risk taxonomies are currently being worked on to address the security, safety, and reliability of risks related to these other frontier AI categories. She said closed models include, for example, OpenAI and Anthropic, and that self-driving cars and companies like Tesla are the obvious robotics example. She said the AICPA Assurance Services Executive Committee SOC 2 Working Group has been evaluating the usability of SOC 2 reports and identifying enhancements to the SOC 2 framework. She said the changes to the trust services criteria include the addition of AI points of focus for situations where AI is present in the service organization systems being examined.

Pawlicki said comments on the two SOC 2 exposure drafts, on the trust services criteria and description criteria, are due Jan. 15, 2027. She said that once those criteria are finalized, after review of comments and disposition of comments, updates to the SOC 2 guide will follow later in 2027. She said the changes to the trust services criteria are also intended to reduce duplication, streamline the criteria, and improve clarity for practitioners and report users. She said the SOC 2 description criteria have also been updated to provide greater clarity around the information management should include in their system description. She said AI presents an incredible opportunity for independent third-party assurance that really does serve the public interest.

Articles.Title: What SOC 2 plus AIUC-1 adds to AI assurance, and what’s next - Journal of Accountancy

stories.headline_source: What SOC 2 plus AIUC-1 adds to AI assurance, and what’s next

stories.Headline: Wolters Kluwer finds 97% of AI-using accounting firms have people review some outputs
stories.Summary:
Wolters Kluwer's latest Future Ready Accountant report found that 97% of accounting firms using AI have people review at least some AI-generated work, the company said on November 24, 2026. The report also found that 80% of firms have AI policies or guidance in some form. Among those firms, 57% require professional review of all AI-generated technical outputs, the report said. The report also found that 40% require review of high-risk or client-facing outputs. Wolters Kluwer Tax and Accounting CEO Jason Marx discussed the findings in an interview.

The report's figures cover firms that use AI and have review practices in place. The 97% figure applies to firms using AI that have people check at least some outputs. The 80% figure covers firms with AI policies or guidance in some form. The 57% and 40% figures apply among those firms with policies. The report is Wolters Kluwer's latest Future Ready Accountant report.

Marx said the work firms check most is that requiring professional judgment, while more mechanical tasks generally are not. He contrasted AI preparing a tax return, which needs review by a qualified human, with filing the same return, which generally does not. He said agentic tax prep is contextually aware and can highlight areas of risk based on historical trends at a client, but still requires a professional's judgment. He said he did not feel errors reflect laziness, calling AI oversight a work in progress. He said successful firms will have processes in place to minimize the issue over time.

Christina Ho, a former Public Company Accounting Oversight Board member, said assurance over AI output is the gap and asked how she would know an output is reliable. She said the profession needs to collectively develop standard criteria. She said expecting a human to become a verification machine for AI outputs holds that human to a standard never expected before. She said experts should play more of a role in the design rather than the execution of individual checking. Wenzel Reyes, MindBridge's senior director of methodology and audit solutions, said human in the loop should mean something active, not passive.

Other data in the article throws into doubt how many professionals actually check AI outputs. Rightworks found 39% of firms using AI say outputs require review often or always, with 61% citing verification against original sources as the most common safeguard. Caseware found 64% of respondents saying validation should always be required for AI in professional judgments. Financial Cents said in September that 23% of professionals have AI produce drafts they review closely, while 5% use AI for routine work and spot-check it. Capterra found in May that 48% of accounting professionals say they check all AI or GenAI output for errors, while 39% review only some of the time.

Workiva found 84% of executives in finance, audit and sustainability expressed confidence in AI output accuracy even without human review, while 26% said internal audits detected AI errors that reached external audiences or the board. Parseur's December 2025 survey found 88% of U.S. business leaders very or somewhat confident in data feeding analytics and AI systems, while 69% reported discovering errors in document-derived data at least sometimes. An anonymous professional cited in the AI Lab for Accountants State of AI in Accounting Firms report admitted presenting a Claude summary that mislabeled a client's line item as "vinegar" when the client doesn't sell vinegar. A report from the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Scotland noted professionals reviewing Gen AI-generated extracts of board minutes or internal audit reports often reacted to the extracts rather than returning to the full source text.

Ho said AI models can be designed to say they don't know something and not make guesses, to mitigate hallucination risk, through initial creation or adversarial training. She said human judgment would be highest value in designing the engineering and quality of the process rather than checking thousands of transactions. Reyes said agents are now preparing journal entries, reconciling accounts and writing commentary and financial statements. He said management might put other machines on top to monitor the first machine because no controller can read all journal entries. Marx said accountants must stay engaged and not fall into a check-the-box mentality, calling it "not a check-the-box profession."

The article presents the leaner framework as the AICPA’s proposal, not as adopted rules.

stories.Headline: Sudhanshu Mishra launches Demi.AI to build a proactive Mac AI assistant
stories.Summary:
Former Sequoia Capital India investor Sudhanshu Mishra has launched an agentic AI startup called Demi.AI in the US. Mishra announced the launch of Demi’s invite-only beta earlier today on social media. He positioned it as an “AI assistant that lives on your Mac, learns how you work, and does the work before you ask”. Demi’s other cofounder is Mishra’s college roommate Logan Ford. Demi was set up in June 2025 and currently employs about 10 people.

Demi seeks to build an AI assistant that can anticipate users’ requirements and complete work before being explicitly instructed. Demi builds context from users’ meetings, connected applications and even their computer screens to understand ongoing projects, conversations and work patterns. Based on this context, it tracks commitments, deadlines and recurring tasks, and proactively surfaces reminders or prepares the next steps. The platform can handle repetitive administrative work, including drafting email responses, preparing meeting briefs, capturing meeting notes, updating customer relationship management systems and tracking customer follow-ups. The agentic platform executes these tasks either through its cloud-based computer or natively on a user’s Mac through their browser.

Mishra was earlier associated with Sequoia Capital as an investor, working on early-stage investments and primarily leading the firm’s crypto-focused efforts. He subsequently joined Paradigm, a crypto-focused investment firm, as an investment partner. In his launch announcement, Mishra said the idea behind Demi was to reduce the effort users currently need to put into making AI tools useful, including setting up workflows, providing context and figuring out which tasks to delegate. According to its website, its individual paid plan starts at $25 per month, while team pricing is customised. The platform still retains a human approval layer, and messages, commitments and important changes to records are presented to users for approval before they are executed.

Users do not need to create custom workflows or write instructions for individual skills to get started. Unlike conventional AI assistants that largely respond to individual prompts, Demi aims to continuously build an understanding of users’ work and identify tasks that need attention. For instance, if a user promises to share a document during a meeting, Demi can identify the commitment, locate relevant information and prepare a follow-up email. According to Grand View Research, the global enterprise agentic AI market is projected to reach $24.5 Bn by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 46.2%.

Sol Foundry, founded by former CRED executives, raised $4 Mn from General Catalyst, Nexus Venture Partners and others in September this year to build a proactive AI assistant that acts on commitments made over email. Agentic AI has emerged as the biggest buzz word across the global tech ecosystem, with most enterprises and individuals exploring ways to automate their workflows using AI. Investor interest in agentic AI is also accelerating as a new crop of startups look to automate workflows across varied enterprise applications. Demi joins a growing crop of AI startups betting on proactive assistants that execute tasks rather than just respond to prompts.

Its Mac-based assistant learns from meetings, apps and screen activity to track commitments and automate workflows. Mishra worked on early-stage investments at Sequoia Capital, primarily leading the firm’s crypto-focused efforts. The articles do not say what happens next for Demi.AI beyond the invite-only beta announced today. The articles leave open how many users the beta will admit and when a wider release might come.

The articles do not give the size of any funding raised by Demi.AI. The articles do not name any investors in Demi.AI. The articles do not say what Demi.AI will charge beyond the $25 per month individual plan and customised team pricing. More to follow.
