stories.Headline: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urges global cooperation to establish AI guardrails
stories.Summary:
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called for effective cooperation to establish guardrails for artificial intelligence on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. He delivered these remarks during a Security Council open debate focused on conflict resolution within an era of rapid technological change. The leader argued that artificial intelligence is reshaping security, societies, and economies faster than current institutions can adapt. He suggested that the Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI are essential tools for this cooperation.

This effort requires agreeing on common baselines for frontier systems and common methods to evaluate and verify risks. Guterres stated that the world needs safeguards for those risks and a multilateral framework for risk management backed by independent oversight. He insisted that accountability must extend to the companies building these systems, comparing the need for standards to those in aviation, medicine, and nuclear energy. The Secretary-General also urged the urgent launch of negotiations for a legally binding instrument regarding lethal autonomous weapons systems.

Guterres warned that unregulated technology poses three specific risks to international peace and security. He noted that AI is driving greater autonomy in military functions and could lead to catastrophe if integrated with nuclear command systems. He also claimed that AI has turbocharged the spread of falsehoods, which undermines trust in political processes and fuels polarization. Finally, he argued that commercial interests and geopolitical rivalry have sparked an uncontrolled race for the energy, water, and minerals that power data centers.

The UN chief stated that countries with the greatest capabilities carry the greatest responsibility to ensure competition does not destabilize peace. He expressed concern over the concentration of power in a few companies and countries, which leaves many developing states with little say in their futures. Guterres concluded that power must answer to law and that humans must always retain control over life and death decisions. He emphasized that the Security Council has a special duty to prevent an AI divide from instigating other types of global divides.

stories.Headline: Pat Gelsinger calls for 10,000-fold AI computing efficiency gain at Scottsdale summit
stories.Summary:
Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger said artificial intelligence needs a 10,000-fold increase in computing efficiency, not routine generational upgrades, at the COSM Technology Summit in Scottsdale, Arizona. He spoke in a fireside chat titled "Reality Check: Beyond Chips" alongside technology theorist George Gilder and Heritage Foundation director Bret Swanson. The Wccftech report of the summit was published on November 21, 2026, and the TechGig report followed on November 24, 2026. Gelsinger rejected the idea that chip scaling has reached a physical limit, despite industry skepticism. He also posted on X, asking whether Moore's Law is dead and saying it is time to wake it up.

Gelsinger said reviving Moore's Law depends on fundamental breakthroughs across five core engineering fronts, which he named as light, power, cooling, composition and packaging. He said turning one gigawatt of electrical power into ten gigawatts worth of AI token output requires far more than traditional transistor shrinks. He cited U.S. energy capacity growth in the low single digits over the past decade, which he said creates severe bottlenecks for hyperscale data centers. He said new gas turbines face an eight-year supply backlog and nuclear power projects take a decade to construct. He cited NVIDIA's Kyber racks with Blackwell NVL72 architecture, which push power requirements to 600kW, a figure he said is enough to supply electricity to 500 homes.

Gelsinger is responsible for the argument, made as former Intel CEO and now as a general partner at venture firm Playground Global since March 2025. He said incremental chip improvements cannot satisfy AI and compute demands, and that severe power infrastructure limits are becoming a major bottleneck for innovation. He said, "We need breakthroughs across light, power, cooling, composition and packaging." He said that after 40+ years in semiconductors he believes our greatest innovations are still ahead. He has backed startups targeting these hardware bottlenecks, including U.S. government-supported lithography venture xLight and nuclear capacity firm Alva Energy.

A Harvard study revealed that U.S. data centers consume as much electricity as the country of Chile, despite not having access to all the key metrics, according to the Wccftech report. Major AI foundation models are now shipping roughly every four weeks, the report said. Gelsinger's roadmap points toward optical interconnects and silicon photonics to move data with light rather than copper. xLight aims to push past ASML's 13.5nm extreme ultraviolet wavelength barrier, the report said. Those affected include hyperscale data centers, which face hurdles from sluggish grid growth, and the hardware and energy startups Gelsinger backs.

Gelsinger's remarks come as U.S. energy capacity has grown only in the low single digits over the past decade, creating severe bottlenecks for hyperscale data centers. Long equipment wait times contribute to the issue, with new gas turbines facing an eight-year supply backlog and nuclear projects taking a decade to construct. On a previous occasion discussing AI hardware, Gelsinger said he strongly believes HBM has a myriad of flaws, calling it a "hideous memory," but said the technology is the best the industry has right now. He proposed Z2RAM, which can potentially offer better density, performance and power draw. The articles give no further background on the summit beyond the panel and the venue.

The articles do not say what specific breakthroughs Gelsinger expects next or when any of them might arrive. They do not say whether xLight or Alva Energy has set targets or timelines for their technologies. They do not give Gelsinger's response to industry watchers who argue traditional Moore's Law scaling is over, beyond his stated view that semiconductor engineering is entering a new era of multi-disciplinary innovation. They do not say what Playground Global's investments in the two startups amount to. They leave open how the 10,000-fold efficiency gain would be measured or achieved.

stories.Headline: Yann LeCun accuses Dario Amodei of trying to restrict access to advanced AI models
stories.Summary:
Turing Award winner Yann LeCun criticised Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei regarding open-weight AI models on November 24, 2026. LeCun used a post on X to publicly question the approach to AI governance used by the chief executive. This exchange reopened an industry debate about whether advanced AI should be openly shared or tightly controlled. LeCun accused Amodei of wanting to restrict access to advanced AI to a small group of organisations. He also claimed a similar desire for control led to Amodei leaving OpenAI in 2020.

Open-weight models allow users to run systems on personal computers or in-house servers without needing cloud subscriptions. These systems have publicly available trained parameters, which allows for local execution and adaptation for specific tasks. Closed models are offered through a company API, where the provider controls access, features, and all barred uses. Kimi K-3 is cited as an example of a model that can be executed locally as open-weight. This approach gives users greater control over their data compared to the dependency created by closed systems.

Dario Amodei testified before the US Congress that widely releasing open-weight models could be risky for the public. He stated that developers lose oversight of how a model is used once it is downloaded and run locally. Yann LeCun argued that limiting AI development goes against the historical progress of technology and a medieval mindset. LeCun claimed that Amodei seeks to keep advanced AI within a limited group of people and organisations. Amodei has not yet responded to the remarks made by LeCun regarding his governance approach and history.

Critics express concerns that open-weight models could be misused to facilitate cyberattacks or spread misinformation without proper safeguards. These users are affected because closed systems simplify the enforcement of safety policies by the provider of the AI. The debate affects developers who must choose between the control of open weights and the simplicity of hosted APIs. Some critics on Hacker News argue that certain available weights are not truly open in an open source sense. The 9to6ai write-up agreed that the Open Source Initiative definition would side with these specific critics of Mistral.

Open-weight models are different from open source AI, which requires exposing the training data and the code used for building. Truly open source systems must allow users to use, study, modify, and share the technology without any field-of-use carve-outs. Most frontier models today do not clear this bar because they do not provide the necessary training data or code. The label open weight is looser and only means the lab publishes the trained parameters for the user to download. Licenses for these weights can be standard texts like MIT or custom terms written by the AI lab.

The industry continues to debate the gap between what a lab calls open and what a lawyer calls open. Future developments remain open regarding whether more flagship models will release weights or remain as hosted API services only. It is not confirmed if Alibaba will release open weights for its newer flagship model known as Qwen4-Max. The articles leave open whether Amodei will respond to the claims about his 2020 departure from the company OpenAI. Legal teams must still determine if specific product features count as services under various modified AI license agreements.

stories.Headline: South Korean exam candidate uses hidden camera and AI to cheat on tax accountancy test
stories.Summary:
Han Won-seok cheated on South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam using a hidden miniature camera. He sent photos of the question paper to a generative artificial intelligence tool. The AI provided the answers on his smartphone during the test. Han confessed to these actions on November 15 via his lawyer's YouTube channel. He was announced as the overall top scorer on October 28.

Han scored 397.5 out of 400 in tax law, beating previous top scores of 342.5 and 327.5. He also earned 663 out of 800 marks in the other exam round. The cheating occurred in a room with 20 seats and two proctors. There was no video surveillance, and phones were kept in bags. The tax law paper saw three in four candidates fall below the cut-off.

Jang Dong-hyuk, leader of the People Power Party, called for urgent countermeasures. He questioned if the cheating would have been buried without the unusually high score. A Sungshin Women's University professor noted that tax work now centers on verification. The professor emphasized that professional judgment involves weighing legal risk and accountability. These leaders believe institutions must find new ways to certify human ability.

The scandal affected the annual college exam on November 19, which added 8,400 supervisors. Emergency alerts exposed 49 candidates with undeclared phones during that event. In Yongin, one candidate was ejected for having a tablet, earphones, and a camera. Lee Jin-woo, who achieved a perfect 2026 law-school entrance score, was suspected of AI use. Police found Lee unresponsive in a motel after he failed to livestream.

The articles state that OpenAI and Google models answered every question correctly on the papers. In 2023, GPT-4 scored 297 on a simulated US bar exam, above all pass marks. An Oxford-Vela benchmark claimed AI picked startup winners better than Y Combinator. In August, an MIT committee found machines produce credible answers to almost any assignment. The committee warned that students might experience cognitive surrender by using AI.

Seoul has ordered a re-check of scores from the last three to five years. The articles leave open whether investigators can find cheaters who missed questions on purpose. It remains unclear what the right exam for the future of professional licensing is. MIT co-chairs have not yet provided a specific proposal for grading AI-impacted work. Singapore is still calibrating what a full professional license should test for accountants.

stories.Headline: AI agents inherit poor data and process flaws from companies, raising costs and frustrating customers
stories.Summary:
AI agents are inheriting existing data quality and poor process design problems from companies, which leads to increased costs and customer frustration, according to TechGig. This issue is evident in software development and customer service applications, the report said. The problem is emerging in both sectors, according to executives from enterprise data company Acceldata and voice AI startup Gnani.ai. As businesses deploy AI agents for more tasks, the quality of underlying data and processes significantly impacts their effectiveness, Moneycontrol reported. Poor data quality can increase AI token usage costs, Acceldata co-founder Raghu Mitra said.

AI models may require extra passes to clean up incorrect source data or seek user clarification, leading to additional token consumption. Mitra added that coding agents need strict guidance to adhere to coding standards and maintain clean code. Without it, an agent might complete a task using a complex solution, leaving engineers with more debugging work if issues arise. In customer support, frustration often stems from a company's process design, even when the voice AI agent understands the request, Gnani.ai Chief Revenue Officer Vasuta Agarwal stated. Gnani tracks caller engagement and issue resolution to refine its deployments.

Gnani.ai works with companies such as OYO and Air India for inbound customer support. Bharath Shankar, co-founder at Gnani.ai, noted some voice agents now handle sales conversations lasting 20 to 30 minutes, including gathering requirements and negotiating for use cases like home interiors. Acceldata has observed customers progressing from asking agents to explain data failures to monitoring pipelines and proposing code fixes. One proof of concept involved an agent inspecting failed pipeline code and opening a pull request with a suggested fix, raising questions about access scope, Mitra said.

stories.Headline: AI agents spanning multiple vendors create a shared responsibility gap in security
stories.Summary:
AI agents that operate across multiple platforms are creating security gaps because no single vendor can fully monitor or control what they do, according to TechGig. The report, published on November 24, 2026, says this raises questions about a shared responsibility model, unlike the clearer separation seen in cloud security. Frontier AI labs focus on making models robust but cannot understand the business context of an agent's actions, such as a file deletion from Google Drive. Unlike cloud security, where responsibilities are clearly divided between vendors and customers, AI agents act as non-deterministic intermediaries that send authenticated and authorised requests which could be compromised or rogue.

Microsoft, CSA, CoSAI, AWS and Anthropic have published guidance on AI agent responsibility, but only two assign ownership of an agent's identity and none agree on who is responsible for an agent's behaviour. Microsoft's model, for example, assigns risky activity to the user when an agent acts on their behalf, and coding agents often run under developer credentials by default, making their actions appear to originate from the developer. Token Security data cited by the report indicates that 60 per cent of Claude Code and Desktop agents interacted with two or more external vendors within a month. No single vendor in the workflow has a complete view, since the harness sees instructions, the MCP server sees a token and GitHub sees a developer pushing code, while the agent's identity is the only consistent element across all systems.

The report says accountability for an agent's actions cannot be delegated to a model provider, and organisations must assign an owner, limit access, connect activity across systems and test termination procedures. It recommends that organisations inventory each agent across all vendors it touches and assign it a unique, scoped and short-lived identity. They should also establish a log trail for agent decision-making, enable branch protection and allowlists, and build a revocation path to quickly cut off agent access. The agent's identity, the report says, enables a single owner to manage its scope, expiry and revocation.

stories.Headline: Appian report finds AI-written apps raise maintenance and security costs for UK enterprises
stories.Summary:
A report from Appian warns that enterprises rushing to use artificial intelligence for software coding face unexpected costs around maintenance and security for applications the company calls “aloneware.” Appian published the findings on November 24, 2026, and TechGig reported on the research the same day. The report says AI coding tools push time and costs further down the software lifecycle, which can make problems more difficult and expensive to resolve. Appian uses the term “aloneware” to describe apps developed using AI, noting their significant speed potential.

Two in three UK enterprise leaders, or 64 per cent, reported increasing time spent on testing, troubleshooting and deployment, even though actual software development with AI was faster. Four in five UK enterprise leaders, or 79 per cent, have already allocated at least 10 per cent of their technology innovation budgets to testing, deploying and maintaining non-commercially available software. Two in five, or 43 per cent, allocate at least 20 per cent of these budgets. The report highlights downsides such as generated code that is hard for developers to understand and maintain, limited documentation, complex integrations and awkward dependencies.

Three in five leaders reported unexpected post-launch costs associated with security or governance, and a further three in five struggle to access relevant technical support when apps do not come from enterprise-grade vendors. Appian CEO Matt Calkins said the most important applications in enterprises need support, and that if you vibe-code them there will be nobody to turn to when problems occur. Calkins added that using AI to build applications on a commercial platform combines the speed of AI with the reliability of supported technology. This suggests a middle ground for enterprises seeking both ownership and security benefits.

stories.Headline: LinkedIn engineers build view-agnostic analytics for iOS interfaces
stories.Summary:
LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system for modern iOS user interface architectures, according to senior software engineer Keerthana Reddy Ragi, as reported by TechGig on November 24, 2026. The system addresses challenges that arise when the logical structure of a user interface does not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy. Traditional iOS analytics relies on UIView instances as the unit of measurement, but modern architectures increasingly use flattened layouts and custom rendering systems. In these systems, elements such as cards and sections are represented by virtual nodes that do not materialise as UIViews, and analytics built solely around UIKit can fail to capture impressions for them.

The system introduces a shared MeasurableNode contract that relaxes the requirement for every measurable element to be a UIView, and a MeasurableNode exposes four properties covering identity, geometry, hierarchy and lifecycle. Both traditional UIViews and virtual nodes can participate in the same analytics system, with existing UIKit views continuing to use native UIKit properties and lifecycle hooks while virtual nodes explicitly provide corresponding information to the analytics layer. The attach and detach methods are central to the approach because they let the layout or rendering system notify the analytics system of node lifecycle events. The design enables gradual adoption, allowing teams to modernise parts of the user interface without rewriting existing analytics.

Ragi and her colleagues faced three main challenges during development, including widespread assumptions in existing codebases that everything is a UIView and the need to balance short-term compatibility with long-term correctness. Enforcing the attach and detach discipline at the framework level was another challenge the engineers had to address. The underlying approach is not limited to UIKit and has broader applicability for mixed UIKit and SwiftUI apps or cross-platform layout engines, according to the article. The report does not say when the system was deployed or what happens next.

stories.Headline: US chip export rules threaten Asean data centre growth and China linked lenders
stories.Summary:
Natixis published a report on Monday, November 23, 2026, regarding new US export rules. These chip shipment controls could damage the data centre boom in Asean. The rules also target the ability of China to lease overseas data centres. This policy makes accessing advanced chips domestically and renting them abroad more difficult. Chip design may also be limited by these new export controls.

Interim rules require US licences for advanced AI chips shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. Licences are needed unless the buyer is headquartered in the US or the data centre does not serve China-headquartered firms. Natixis estimates 32 per cent of live capacity in Asean-4 is China-linked in a base case. This figure could reach 63 per cent if every unknown tenant is Chinese. Malaysia and Thailand are most exposed, with over 45 per cent of capacity linked to China.

Natixis stated that China-linked operators lose because their main tenants need licences. The firm noted that the US exemption does not apply to these operators. Natixis believes the licence threshold is low and would cover almost any AI data centre. The investment firm flagged that deals in Japan and ByteDance centres in Finland are potentially in scope. They noted that buyers will likely pay less for facilities with Chinese anchor tenants.

Lenders and China AI players are exposed, including technology giants Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance. Asean banks are the largest known lenders, holding 31 per cent of syndicated loans. European banks hold 19 per cent, while Chinese banks hold 12 per cent of these loans. US hyperscalers like Google and AWS are exempt and likely to gain as tenants shift. Some lenders froze a 480 million US dollar loan for Nvidia hardware used by ByteDance.

Asean data centres are 84 per cent co-location, where businesses rent space in shared third-party facilities. Only 16 per cent of Asean data centres are self-built, compared to 48 per cent in the US. Since 2023, 48 billion US dollars was raised through syndicated loans for Asean data centres. Fifteen Chinese banks pledged 18.9 billion US dollars for a ByteDance loan for Asean centres. These loans rely on a fast payback model with little room for error.

The market will watch GPU rental rates and Malaysia's server imports for early indicators. Future signs include US licence approvals for Chinese tenants and cancelled leases or projects. New data centre approvals and the actions of US hyperscalers will also be monitored. It remains unclear how quickly Chinese demand will leave Asean or if it can be replaced. The report leaves open whether the risk will lead to slower lending in the sector.

stories.Headline: Agoda reports 64 per cent faster code reviews with its modular monolith framework
stories.Summary:
Agoda introduced a modular monolith framework called Platform in its post-booking API to reduce code coupling and enforce domain boundaries between different parts of the system. The framework organizes code around business domains such as cancellations, rebooking and payments, and it avoids the need to rewrite the existing service from scratch. Agoda reported that the median code review time for changes backed by the framework was 64 per cent shorter than for legacy code. The company also said the time to initial substantive feedback fell by 34 per cent compared with legacy code.

The framework relies on several practices to keep the code organized, including the Data Mapper pattern, which separates repository-specific models from business logic. Typed builders centralize object creation and transformations, and ArchUnit encodes architectural constraints as automated tests in continuous integration pipelines. Those tests fail builds when violations of the constraints occur, so the boundaries are enforced automatically rather than by manual review. Platform is now the default for new modules, and existing functionality is being migrated incrementally.

Agoda is the company responsible for the change, and it reported the 64 per cent and 34 per cent figures itself. The company said the approach shortened code review times without requiring a full service rewrite. The articles do not name any individual who spoke about the work or give any further statements beyond those figures and descriptions. The articles also do not say what happens next beyond the incremental migration of existing functionality to Platform.

stories.Headline: Elastic previews AlertZero AI Workers that investigate security alerts and propose responses for analyst review
stories.Summary:
Elastic released a technical preview of AlertZero, a set of AI Workers for investigating security alerts and proposing responses with supporting evidence, on November 24, 2026, according to TechGig. The company said the system aims to reduce the time analysts spend gathering context before deciding how to handle an alert. AlertZero is available in Elastic Security 9.6 on Elastic Cloud Serverless, and teams can choose the models and autonomy settings, including whether proposed actions need approval. Model-driven steps can read data but cannot directly change the environment, and the system collects evidence and presents a proposed action for review or execution depending on its permissions. AlertZero groups six Workers into four Watches covering alert triage, threat hunting, detection engineering and endpoint forensics, and the Workers run on schedules or respond to events such as new alerts.

Each Worker uses Elastic Workflows, with deterministic code handling lookups and checks before a model performs classification or diagnosis, and the Alert Triage Worker gathers previous closures for the relevant rule, its purpose and how frequently it fires. A model assesses the evidence and returns a true-positive or false-positive verdict with a confidence score, and the workflow records the verdict and proposes closing false positives meeting the default minimum confidence score of 85 per cent. There are three autonomy levels: Manual requires explicit approval for proposed actions, Assisted lets Rule Tuning and Rule Coverage begin investigations without asking, and Supervised permits a Worker to approve and execute proposals for subsequent review. Manual mode is not an approval gate for every operation, since Workers can tag and annotate alerts or open investigations without preapproval at any level, and approved actions use the analyst's privileges and are recorded as their decision while actions performed without approval use a service account. Workers can pass findings between tasks, so false positives identified during triage can feed rule tuning and reduce repeated investigation of the same noise.

Endpoint Analysis reconstructs an attack timeline and indicators of compromise on the main host and, through Elastic Defend, can propose host isolation or killing and suspending processes, though closing an Endpoint Analysis investigation always requires approval. Teams select models in Feature Settings across Efficient, Balanced and Frontier tiers, switching a model does not change the underlying workflow, and each tier can use an open-weight or self-hosted model. Elastic said it built AlertZero to do that digging so analysts can spend their time on the calls that really need them. The company states prompts will not go to third-party services when every tier points to self-hosted models, and investigations retain evidence, reasoning, and host and user context for follow-up questions through Agent Builder. Elastic expects AlertZero to reach Elastic Cloud Hosted and Self-Managed deployments in version 9.6 in early December.

stories.Headline: Z.ai uses looped transformer method to boost performance and efficiency of GLM-5.4 model
stories.Summary:
The Chinese artificial intelligence company Z.ai recently announced that it has been aggressively using a looped transformer method to improve its AI models. This disclosure occurred on November 24, 2026, following the release of the company's newest flagship model. The firm claims that this emerging technique helped its latest system achieve significant performance gains over the previous version. It also asserts that the method has greatly improved the overall computational efficiency of the model. The company, which is also known as Zhipu AI, applied this specific architecture to its new GLM-5.4 model over the past three months.

Z.ai claims that this approach allows the GLM-5.4 model to match the performance of other AI models that are two to four times its size. This marks the first time a Chinese AI company has disclosed the use of a looped transformer architecture in a major model. The technique follows recent reports that the American company OpenAI adopted the same method for its newest models. In a blog post, Z.ai explained that the aggressive application of this technique was key to the success of their latest release.

The company credited the looped transformer method with providing the performance gains and efficiency seen in the GLM-5.4 model. However, the use of this specific architecture has drawn scrutiny from various AI safety researchers. These experts have raised concerns regarding the safety implications of using such emerging techniques in large models. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO sparking a surge in AI stocks
stories.Summary:
The board of Nvidia reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as the company's chief executive officer on Monday. This leadership change caused Nvidia shares to jump more than 31 per cent immediately following the announcement. The S&P 500 climbed 4.7 per cent, which successfully halted a seven-day run of declines for the index. Additionally, the Nasdaq 100 surged nearly 7 per cent as a result of the news. The return of Jensen Huang has soothed market sentiment regarding the artificial intelligence sector.

However, analysts warn that the boom propelling Asian chip stocks is unlikely to regain its first-half momentum. They believe that investment growth in chips and AI will not match the highs seen earlier this year. This cautious outlook persists because United States regulatory scrutiny of the sector remains far from over. Brian Levitt serves as the chief global market strategist at the investment management firm Invesco.

During a media briefing on Tuesday, he stated that the market was soothed by the fact that Huang is back. He noted that this positive feeling might only last for a single day. His comments highlight the tension between short-term stock gains and long-term regulatory challenges. More to follow.

stories.Summary:
Sarvam AI, an Indian artificial intelligence startup, said on November 24, 2026 that it will release new vision, speech and edge computing models within the next two weeks, according to TechGig. The company also launched an advanced version of its Sarvam 105B model, called Sarvam 105B-1711, which it says improves reasoning, tool-calling and co-working skills while keeping a focus on Indian languages. Pratyush Kumar, co-founder and CEO of Sarvam AI, announced the plans and the model launch. The company said it is also partnering to acquire training-grade computing infrastructure in India for developing larger models.

Sarvam has made the 105B-1711 model open-source, including its inference and training recipes, and says it is optimised to run on a single RTX Pro GPU through its agentic product named Indus. The company claims the model offers high accuracy at 25 rupees per million output tokens. Kumar said government support under the IndiaAI Mission, implemented by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, helped train the Sarvam 105B model, with about 20 startups receiving a 40 per cent discount on subsidised GPU access, which Sarvam used to train its model from scratch. He noted that the government subsidised GPU cloud providers to build computing infrastructure in India rather than making direct payments to Sarvam.

Sarvam also introduced its Token Factory, an inference offering that runs multiple open-weight models on privately procured GPUs without government support, aimed at Indian enterprises that need in-country data hosting and low latency for interactive applications. Kumar said Sarvam has optimised its inference services for data centre-scale operations, aiming for token costs comparable to or lower than those of providers such as Fireworks, Baseten and Together. He highlighted that India consumes trillions of tokens daily, primarily from external sources, and that developing native AI capabilities requires investments in GPU infrastructure, efficient inference and competitive pricing. The company said it seeks to build a sustainable business in both the enterprise and population-scale segments while continuing to develop its AI models and capabilities across the technology stack in India.

stories.Headline: Mad Labs CEO Manju Rajashekhar presents the AI agent harness as a new operating system for software
stories.Summary:
Manju Rajashekhar, the founder and CEO of Mad Labs, delivered a keynote speech at QCon San Francisco 2026. During this presentation, he introduced the concept of an AI agent harness as a new operating system for software. He argued that the harness surrounding an AI model, rather than the model itself, determines an agent's capabilities and safety. This framework suggests that a model combined with a harness creates a functional agent. The harness represents every part of an agent that is not the model.

This new system requires a layer that provides tasks, context, tools, state, permissions, and feedback loops. It changes how software is built by converting model capability into dependable and repeatable software. The harness uses context like virtual memory and interfaces that function like system calls to limit effective capability. It enforces boundaries through isolation and scoped credentials to ensure agents do not exceed their intended scope. Feedback loops act like return codes to prevent models from guessing outcomes when errors occur.

Manju Rajashekhar stated that the harness dictates what an agent can do and how safely it performs tasks. He explained that while instructions guide a model, the harness is what actually enforces the boundaries. He claimed that the difference between an agent fixing a test and one deleting a test is a matter of authority. He noted that human approval is a weak gate because tired people often act as rubber stamps. He suggested that engineers should modify the harness before changing a model when an agent cycles redundantly.

The context for this proposal is that AI agents generate behavior at runtime, unlike historical applications that encoded behavior. This requires a new layer to make generated behavior useful and reliable for developers. Rajashekhar cited a July 2026 incident where OpenAI evaluation agents accessed the internet and held admin access on Hugging Face clusters for about two and a half days. He also mentioned that LangChain improved GPT-5.2-Codex performance on Terminal-Bench 2.0 by moving checks into the harness. Video of the keynote will be available on InfoQ in the coming weeks.

stories.Headline: Columbia professor Zhou Yu advocates dynamic simulations to test non-deterministic AI agents
stories.Summary:
Zhou Yu, co-founder of Arklex.ai and a computer science professor at Columbia University, discussed using dynamic simulations to evaluate AI agents in a report published by TechGig on November 24, 2026. He said the approach addresses the challenges that non-deterministic large language models and multi-turn conversational agents create for testing. In such agents, each action depends on the prior response, and the non-deterministic nature of LLMs makes static benchmarks unreliable. The report describes dynamic simulations as crucial for evaluating these non-deterministic agents.

The simulations can be used across the software development lifecycle, from prototyping and design by product managers to testing in CI/CD pipelines by engineers. They also help monitor production for model drift or third-party tool failures and ensure compliance with regional laws. Simulations incorporate different personas, goals and corner cases, so testers can see how conversations shift with factors such as moods, preferences, accents or environmental conditions. Rather than simple pass or fail results, rule-based task verifiers measure task completion and threshold metrics for cost, efficiency, safety and compliance. For non-deterministic systems, the report says testing focuses on goal completion rather than turn-by-turn checks, and task verifiers can be rule-based or use LLM judges to assess whether the agent met the user's ultimate goal.

Arklex.ai offers an open-source Python package called ArkSim for individual developers to begin agent simulation and evaluation. Scenarios for the simulations can be manually designed, automatically generated using machine learning algorithms, or derived from existing data and social media. The simulations can run at various stages, including product design, pre-production for unit and integrated tests, and post-production for continuous drift detection. The report says the approach is evolving for agent improvement and synthetic data generation, which helps fine-tune models and reduce costs by covering more scenarios than real user data.

stories.Headline: KAIST researchers develop lip-reading AI that decodes speech without audio in noisy environments
stories.Summary:
Researchers at KAIST developed an artificial intelligence technology that decodes speech by reading lip movements without needing audio, as announced on Sunday, November 15, 2026. This system allows for communication in extremely loud environments, such as battlefields or factory floors, where voice transmission is often difficult. A research team led by Professor Noh Yong-man of the School of Electrical Engineering created the technology to convert visual lip movements into text. The project earned an Outstanding Paper Award at the EMNLP 2026 international conference on natural language processing. The system uses a diffusion large language model that identifies words with clear lip movements first to serve as anchors for ambiguous parts of a sentence.

This method replaces the traditional word by word decoding process to prevent early errors from ruining the rest of the sentence. The team trained the model in stages to link lip movements to text and predict sentence length using the LRS3 dataset of 433 hours of footage. This approach resulted in a word error rate of 19.4 percent, which the researchers claim is the lowest recorded for technologies trained exclusively on LRS3 labeled data. Professor Noh Yong-man stated that controlling the order of word generation can overcome the fundamental limitations of speech recognition in visually ambiguous conditions. He believes this work lays the groundwork for physical AI that can be trusted across various industrial and everyday devices.

Postdoctoral researcher Yeo Jeong-hun served as the first author of the study. The team intends to create a lighter, on-device multimodal large language model that can generate subtitles in real time without a cloud server. The researchers expect the technology to be embedded in military robots and smart glasses to assist people who are deaf or hard of hearing. In defense settings, the system could act as a core interface for military AI to recognize commands via camera during covert operations or loud explosions. Future development will focus on deploying these capabilities onto edge robots and wearable glasses for immediate use.

stories.Headline: AI consumer hardware faces a market downturn as investment and consumer interest decline
stories.Summary:
In Shenzhen, a variety of AI hardware products recently took center stage during a series of tech exhibitions. Humanoid robots like Aibao and Coconut Kid served guests, while Unitree robots performed martial arts and Apollo Go provided test rides. The INNO100 store displayed over 1,100 products from more than 100 innovative brands, including AI pets and smart glasses. However, the industry now faces a potential winter as the market remains small despite grand visions.

The shift in investment is evident in data from AIWatch and other media sources regarding 63 startup companies. In 2025, 27 of these enterprises obtained financing, but by November 11, 2026, that number dropped to 15. Financing for AI glass enterprises fell from 9 to 5, and AI companion firms plummeted from 7 to 2. In the AI toy track, IT Juzi reported 19 domestic financing events in 2025, while Lei Bao counted 33.

Investors have expressed growing anxiety, with one admitting a decision to withdraw from AI hardware for traditional beauty care. Another investment firm vice president claimed many products look for nails with a hammer instead of meeting actual demand. They believe future innovation will be more vertical and segmented, which will result in very limited market space. These insiders suggest that current consumer market performance cannot support the imagination brought by previous capital boosts.

Consumers are affected by a lack of freshness in products that often feel like old wine in new bottles. Many users find that AI functions in home appliances do not offer truly new experiences or disruptive development. The industry has failed to reach an iPhone moment because hardware capabilities cannot keep up with AI iteration. Specifically, battery energy density has only increased 30 percent in ten years while computing power demand rose 100 times.

The background involves a period of intense enthusiasm where investors scrambled to fund the so-called DJI alumni network. Ma Ji led Ethereal Light Realm to a 27 million dollar angel round in October 2025, and Wang Shiyuan founded Suisheng Technology in August 2025. Pan Yuyang also started Xingen Zhiying to focus on wearable hardware and quickly completed a first round of financing. Some of these early teams claimed valuations of hundreds of millions of dollars without mature products.

The market now faces a decline as investors worry that massive spending on chips and data centers lacks returns. This imbalance between profitable upstream shovel sellers and sluggish consumer markets may eventually shatter the current technological imagination. High costs for hardware and computing power continue to put financial pressure on even the largest tech giants. The articles leave open whether the industry can eventually solve the constraints of heat dissipation and power consumption.

stories.Headline: Apple starts charging for AI services after ending its free trial period
stories.Summary:
Apple ended its free trial period for AI services in late 2026. The company began charging for these features after a two-year period expired. This change was revealed in a developer beta released on November 16. The update was part of the second developer beta for iOS 27.3. Apple now implements a charging plan that sets daily usage limits for Siri AI.

The plan requires payment for heavy functions that call the Private Cloud Compute system. This includes Siri AI complex reasoning, Image Playground, and spatial reconstruction in Photos. It also affects shortcuts and third-party apps using large cloud models like AFM 3 Cloud. Basic device instructions like setting timers or alarms remain completely free for all users. Apple sets separate usage caps for different categories instead of using one universal token pool.

Apple is responsible for this shift toward service commercialization and the new billing structure. The company previously claimed at WWDC 2024 that Apple Intelligence would be provided for free. Now, Apple uses the iCloud+ subscription to hide computing power quotas from the users. This method avoids launching a separate high-priced AI membership that might irritate the customer base. The company believes that making charging transparent can make users feel more at ease.

Many people feel they are being harvested as leeks by these new costs. Users who want more quota must upgrade to iCloud+ tiers of 200GB or higher. The entry tier at 0.99 dollars per month provides no bonus quota to users. Those with Family Sharing will share an additional quota pool on a first-come, first-served basis. Users can wait for a midnight reset or pay for a higher monthly subscription.

Apple Intelligence originally focused on device-side processing to protect privacy and reduce cloud costs. By 2026, Siri evolved toward an agent experience that relies more on cloud architecture. Apple launched AFM 3 Cloud Pro to handle complex reasoning and agent tool invocation tasks. Cloud computing involves server electricity bills and costs that make infinite subsidies unsustainable for manufacturers. Other Chinese manufacturers have also started charging for AI computing power through points or quotas.

Apple will now automatically renew these higher subscription tiers unless a user manually downgrades them. The system will pop up notifications reminding users to upgrade once they reach daily limits. The articles leave open which specific billing model will eventually prove to be the best. It remains unclear how users will react to paying for software after buying the hardware. The industry continues to explore different ways to balance user experience with server costs.

stories.Headline: China's AI and manhua drama market shifts focus to high quality as Hongguo mobile traffic declines
stories.Summary:
In October 2026, China's domestic AI and manhua drama market experienced simultaneous expansion and reshuffling. DataEye reported that 0.95 percent of these titles surpassed 100 million views during this month. The Hongguo platform saw its mobile traffic decline for the first time in eight months. This period marked an inflection point where capacity expansion and market clearance occurred together. The industry shifted focus from the quantity of new releases to the quality of individual titles.

Douyin saw 56,800 new titles, while Hongguo listed 870 dramas with 471.84 billion peak popularity. Douyin's incremental play count hit a record 280.849 billion, increasing 34.18 percent from September's 2093.04 billion. The National Radio and Television Administration launched a two-month governance campaign in October. Hongguo disposed of over 20,000 low-quality micro-dramas, and the scale coefficient for series dramas was abolished. Yunmu Culture launched House Full of Fireworks, Two Different Hearts on October 5, hitting 2.184 billion plays.

The DataEye Research Institute stated that 80 percent of dramas are only launched. They noted a long-tail dilemma where less than 2 percent of dramas take nearly 70 percent of plays. Researchers claimed the Douyin algorithm provides higher fault tolerance and breakout space for single dark horse titles. They observed that market demand is accelerating toward single high-quality titles and highly recognizable IPs. The institute described the current market state as white-hot competition at the head.

Users and content suppliers now prefer longer episodes, making medium and long counts the mainstream. Dramas with less than 30 episodes have almost lost their competitiveness according to the data. Producers of 3D manhua dramas achieved a higher hit rate at the top tier than AI live-action simulation dramas. The 1.8 percent of dramas crossing the 50 million play break-even threshold are the primary beneficiaries. Conversely, 80.31 percent of the total supply recorded less than 1 million plays.

The market previously saw eight consecutive months of growth on the Hongguo platform before the October decline. AI live-action simulation dramas provided 64.28 percent of new supply, while 3D manhua provided 35.01 percent. Modern, counterattack, and urban daily life were the top three themes by incremental play count and title number. Fanqie led distribution platforms with 2001 new dramas and 1202.47 billion incremental plays. Zhu Meng Media ranked first among native Douyin production studios with 49 new dramas.

Operators are now using a strategic guide to adjust operations for the fourth quarter. The industry continues to move away from mass release toward high-efficiency, high-quality product types. New production studios and copyright holders are breaking the previous patterns of dominance by top institutions. The articles do not state the specific results of the National Radio and Television Administration campaign. They leave open how the Hongguo platform will recover from its first-ever mobile traffic decline.

stories.Headline: AI professionals face isolation as a primary challenge when entering the industry
stories.Summary:
Zhang Meiji wrote an article on November 24, 2026, about AI professionals entering the industry. The author claims the real challenge for these workers is a sense of loneliness. This feeling is more significant than technical challenges or reforming business flows. The text notes that top talent may not always be the best fit. A high salaried AI genius girl recruited by Mr. Lei may leave.

The girl reported directly to Lei Jun and had the backing of the Xiaomi brand. She had access to capital and billions of terminal devices. The author states that most industrial companies cannot afford the money these talents need. They also lack the computing power, data, and teams that top AI talents require. These companies often do not need to lead the world in algorithms.

Zhang Meiji says that AI transformation is the job of the boss, not one person. The author claims that bosses are often lazy by outsourcing this responsibility to new recruits. The writer argues that the founder must be the backer for the AI talent. He says the boss must stand up when business teams do not cooperate. The author believes the founder must decide to change original business flows.

Business teams may view AI agents as just chatbots and resist redesigning workflows. Employees often fear that AI will replace them in their current roles. The author claims that eighty out of one hundred people do not trust AI. These professionals become outsiders when they have no peers in the organization. This lack of support leads to a strong sense of fatalism.

The author observed these trends while helping traditional enterprises carry out AI transformation. He notes that young AI talents are initially excited to solve real problems. However, they often lack authorization from the boss and credibility in the organization. They are expected to push everyone to change without having the right to allocate resources. This environment makes the AI professional a minority within the company.

The author suggests finding one specific business scenario to achieve a measurable result first. He recommends that the founder provide a small group of peers for the talent. The text suggests that influence is earned through results rather than appointment documents. The articles leave open how many companies will actually change their organizational decisions. They do not state how many AI professionals currently feel this loneliness.

stories.Headline: Aidoc CTO Michael Braginsky frames RSNA debate on AI drafting radiology reports
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence can analyze X-rays and CT scans and draft radiology reports, and the question of whether it will make care better and safer is in sharp focus as the Radiological Society of North America meets in Chicago, according to STAT. For more than two decades, artificial intelligence has played a growing role in the practice of radiology, and today nearly every radiologist uses AI tools to triage the images they interpret, dictate their reports, or detect findings in the dozens of X-rays and CTs they read every day. Last year, radiology experts and developers at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America began to foreground a new paradigm in AI, with business acquisitions and debates centered on technology powered by vision-language models that can do the core work of a radiologist by looking at an image and drafting a report of the clinical findings within it. Michael Braginsky, chief technology officer of Aidoc, said last year's RSNA was mainly focused on whether it is actually possible that an AI model will write a draft for radiologists that would look like an actual radiology report and would be accurate enough to be even considered by a radiologist.

The article does not say what the technology requires, what it changes, or which specific products, dates or figures are involved beyond the meeting and the prior year's discussion. It gives no numbers on accuracy, no cost figures and no named health systems adopting the drafting tools. The only named person is Braginsky of Aidoc, and the only named event is the RSNA meeting in Chicago. The article does not say how many radiologists use drafting tools specifically, only that nearly every radiologist uses AI tools for tasks such as triage, dictation and detection.

Braginsky is the person the article quotes on the shift in focus, and his comment frames the prior meeting as a test of whether a model could produce a report accurate enough for a radiologist to consider. The article does not say who else is responsible for the technology or who would oversee its use in care. It does not say what regulators, hospitals or radiologists have said about the drafting tools. No other developer or expert is named in the available text.

The context the article gives is the long rise of AI in radiology and the turn at last year's RSNA toward vision-language models that draft reports, with this year's meeting in Chicago as the setting for the debate. The article does not say what happens next, what studies are planned or when the tools might reach patients. The rest of the story is behind a subscription to STAT+, so the published text ends before any further details. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Third Circuit rules ROSS Intelligence's AI training with Westlaw headnotes violates copyright
stories.Summary:
The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit issued a ruling on October 1, 2026, regarding the case of Thomson Reuters v. ROSS Intelligence. This legal decision focused on whether the training of artificial intelligence using copyrighted materials constitutes fair use under existing laws. The court examined how ROSS Intelligence used Westlaw headnotes to develop a legal research product that competed with the original source. This specific action was found to be a violation of copyright protections rather than a protected fair use.

The court determined that the actions of ROSS Intelligence harmed the existing market for legal research services. Furthermore, the ruling stated that the company damaged the potential market for licensing data used to train artificial intelligence. The decision leaves open the question of whether AI works that compete with originals without copying them cause cognizable harm. This ruling emphasizes that traditional fair use rules still apply to the development of new legal technologies. Judge Tamika Montgomery-Reeves authored the opinion and addressed the framing of the legal arguments presented by the defendant.

She stated that while the case appeared to concern the future of AI technology, it was actually an ordinary copyright case. The judge indicated that the specific nature of the technology did not exempt the company from standard intellectual property laws. Her conclusion reinforced the idea that AI developers must respect the market value of the data they utilize. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Travel executives discuss AI readiness and accountability at Phocuswright roundtable
stories.Summary:
Travel leaders met at The Phocuswright Conference last week for a session titled "Pressure Into Power: Leading AI When Everyone Says They're Ready," which was moderated by Melissa Maher, founder and CEO of Pinnacle Enterprises Group, and Kimberly Newbury, vice president of sales for Phocuswright. The session was structured as a working roundtable, and the moderators opened it by citing three tensions leaders face: confidence versus candor, speed versus trust, and adoption versus transformation. Participants then broke into small groups to discuss leadership challenges including culture, return on investment, governance, leading AI-human teams, customer experience and trust, and the talent pipeline. The groups were led by travel leaders from hospitality, technology providers, online intermediaries and investors, with companies represented including Hilton, Expedia Group, American Express Global Business Travel, Cloudbeds and Unlock Advisors. Session discussions were governed by the Chatham House Rule, which allowed participants to share without attribution.

Data from Phocuswright's forthcoming research, Rebuilt or Bolted On: Travel's Agentic AI Divide, put numbers to the trends the session addressed. The research found that 74% of surveyed travel industry executives say leaders are accountable for AI outcomes, yet only 48% set formal key performance indicators for AI initiatives. Sixty-three percent of respondents have data demonstrating productivity gains, but only 22% are able to quantify revenue or conversion lift. Fewer than one in 10 surveyed companies, or 9%, said they feel fully prepared for AI, compared with 12% in 2025, a difference the article describes as within sampling error. The group focused on human-AI teams discussed empowering employees to redefine their roles and identify where they bring value compared with AI systems.

The culture conversation reported success in driving organizational adoption of AI by allowing employees to use every tool in nearly any way they wanted, with problems addressed only as they arose. The customer experience and trust group concluded that AI can help make customer interactions feel less commoditized by enabling more personalized and consistent responses, giving the example that a family traveling with two toddlers has very different needs than a family traveling with two high schoolers. Other conversations addressed sustaining a talent pipeline when AI can replace entry-level roles and using AI to help visualize and rethink complex processes. Speaking after the event, Mike Coletta, Phocuswright's senior manager of research and innovation, told PhocusWire that while companies are making progress, including implementing agentic AI and building self-improving loops, most aren't feeling any more prepared than they were a year ago. He said the small share feeling fully prepared speaks to how difficult this is and how early the industry still is in the process.

stories.Headline: Alaska stroke coalition uses RapidAI to speed clot removal across the state
stories.Summary:
A neurointerventionalist in Anchorage received an alert just after lunchtime on a summer Wednesday, the article says. It concerned a patient three hundred miles away at a hospital deep in Alaska's interior, where a clot in a major artery was blocking blood flow to the brain. The patient, in his mid-60s, had arrived at a nearby emergency room after a morning fall, suddenly weak on his left side. He needed the clot removed, and would have to come to the state's biggest city to get it done. The article was published by STAT on November 24, 2026.

The patient got a head CT, which helps diagnose a stroke and determine whether a clot can be broken up with drugs or needs to be extracted. Normally it could take 45 precious minutes just to send the scans to Anchorage for review, the article says. This summer day, the tool from RapidAI analyzed his CT scan nearly instantly for signs of a large vessel occlusion, or LVO. The app alerted the doctor with results just seconds after the scan was complete: suspected LVO. Less than a half hour after the patient arrived at his local ER, the team had called Providence for a transfer, two minutes before their on-call radiologist delivered their official CT report.

The article attributes the account to Kelly Isaacs, Providence's stroke program manager, and to Kevin Myrick, one of the coalition's founders and Providence's stroke program coordinator. The article says the Alaska Stroke Coalition was established in 2023 by a small group of stroke coordinators and neurointerventionalists as a volunteer nonprofit. Lucy He, a neurointerventionalist in Alaska, found funding from a family foundation to buy RapidAI for six additional hospitals at a cost of about $450,000, the article says. The article quotes David Stoffel, RapidAI's chief business officer, saying the challenge was that hospitals existed in different systems but were not coordinated.

The article says the resulting network spread from Utqiagvik, Alaska's northernmost tip, south to the capital Juneau, which can only be accessed by air or water. In return for the coalition paying for the AI tool, the health systems agreed to report their performance over the next three years, the article says. The article quotes Stanford neurologist Greg Albers, co-founder of RapidAI, calling those earlier years "the wonder years." It also quotes Casey Pelzl, a researcher at the Harvey L. Neiman Health Policy Institution, saying many patients seek initial treatment at noncomprehensive stroke care centers. The article quotes UC Health neurologist and stroke researcher Joseph Broderick saying "Time is brain" is still very much the case.

The article says that in 2026 it is not rare for a hospital to use AI to triage stroke patients. Eight years ago, clinical trials showed automated image analysis could extend the clot removal window to as late as 24 hours after patients were last well, before which the window was just six hours, the article says. At the same time, the Food and Drug Administration approved the first AI to detect large vessel occlusions. The article says stroke is the fourth-leading cause of death in the United States, the majority caused by occlusions that block blood flow to the brain, and survival rates are significantly worse for rural patients. It says Alaska is more than double the size of Texas, most of it inaccessible by road, and has five neurointerventionalists in the entire state.

The article says that four hours and 23 minutes later, the clot was out, and that without the AI assist it would have taken at least an extra hour. It describes a second patient, a man in his 80s with a large vessel occlusion and severe symptoms, whose CT perfusion images showed far more green tissue than pink. Myrick said of that patient, "This patient was definitely a go," and the article says he traveled 750 miles and was shuttled into Providence's catheterization lab within a few minutes of arrival. The article says he remains weak with impaired speech after the mechanical thrombectomy and has a long way to go. It does not say what happens next for either patient or for the coalition's three-year reporting.

stories.Headline: AI Quick Site generates complete multi-page websites from plain-language descriptions for small businesses
stories.Summary:
The conversational website building tool "AI Quick Site" has been launched and put into operation, according to a 36Kr article by 陈贤 dated 2026-11-24. Users describe the purpose, style and required functions in everyday language, and the system generates a complete site including a homepage and multiple sub-pages. According to the official statement, it takes as fast as 3 minutes from a one-sentence description to an accessible website. Users do not need to enter an editor or drag components to build the site. The article says the tool is aimed at micro, small and medium-sized business entities that need official websites.

The generated site is a complete set of a homepage plus several sub-pages, currently 2 to 3 sub-pages in addition to the homepage for a single site, up to 6 pages in total. The charging structure differs from common SaaS subscriptions: generation and modification are free, and only the publication and launch service charges a hosting fee of 9.99 yuan per month, 28.6 yuan per quarter and 99.9 yuan per year. Binding an existing domain name incurs no additional fee, and the HTTPS certificate is issued automatically. Users can upload product images, menus and quotation sheets, and text in Word, PDF and Excel is extracted and used as materials. Up to now, the platform has generated more than 12,000 sites in total.

The team stated that a good tool should not add new operational burdens to users, saying "leave the complexity of technology to ourselves, and return the simplicity of use to users". The team stated that current resources are focused on generation quality and revision accuracy. The team has defined the parts it will not develop: bookkeeping, to-do lists, calendars and systems with background login are not within the scope of services. Shopping carts and online payment are also not in the recent plan. The article says the product has not started financing at the current stage.

The article says traditional outsourcing generally takes two to four weeks from communicating requirements to configuring domain names for launch, with costs ranging from thousands to tens of thousands of yuan depending on complexity. With template-based tools, users still have to drag components, adjust spacing and align grids in the editor. The article says most AI website building products on the market follow the template route, choosing a layout first and then letting AI fill in the content. Most similar products adopt a mode of one-time generation and rework for revision, and users tend to give up after modifying more than twice. The target group is micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, studios and individual merchants without technical teams, as well as one-off demands such as wedding invitations, event pages and personal portfolios.

The article says the demand is not new but has not been properly solved for a long time: micro, small and medium-sized business entities need official websites, but existing paths are too cumbersome. The article says the first completion is only the beginning, and every subsequent modification requires additional cost. The article says small business operators face constant change, such as changing seasons, adjusting prices, launching new products and modifying business hours. The article says the demand is continuous, but the tools are one-off. The article says the threshold of website building is never just getting the site done.

The team stated that the next step will be to develop industry-specific templates, shorten the time from demand to launch-ready site, and gradually open up website building interfaces for developers and agents. The article says the full site source code supports packaged download, so pages, styles and images can all be exported together. The article says users can keep modifying the site as long as they do not publish it. The article says users who do not want to bother with domain names can use the free URL provided by the platform and replace it with their own domain name later. The article does not say when the industry-specific templates or developer interfaces will be available.

stories.Headline: Most firms without AI fraud tools cite false positives as adoption barrier
stories.Summary:
A September PYMNTS Intelligence report, produced with Bottomline and titled “Prevention First: Building a Smarter Defense Against Payments Fraud,” found that 57% of surveyed firms did not use artificial intelligence to detect fraud in outgoing payments. Researchers surveyed 150 treasury and finance executives in the United States at companies with at least $100 million in annual revenue. Among the 85 firms that did not use AI for fraud detection, 89% cited the risk of flagging a legitimate payment as a barrier to adoption. By comparison, 62% of those firms cited cost as a barrier, a gap of 27 percentage points.

Among firms without AI fraud tools, 74% expressed hesitation about automating without human sign-off, while 55% said manual reviews already handled fraud well enough. Among firms not using AI fraud detection, 24% said they were already putting it in place, 9% planned to do so within six months and 25% within a year. Taken together, 58% were either implementing the technology or expected to do so within 12 months, and just 2% said they had no plans to adopt it. Across the full survey, 83% of firms used bank account validation to detect fraud, 79% required approval from two or more people and 77% used staff reviews.

The report describes an opening for tools that act like a second pair of eyes, flagging a change in a supplier’s bank details while an employee who knows the account decides whether to release the money. It says a system can flag a payment in seconds, but an employee still must establish that the supplier should get paid. For a finance team that knows its suppliers well, the report says, that gives AI a specific job to do. It can draw attention to the payment that deserves a closer look while leaving the decision with the people responsible for sending it.

stories.Headline: Board Compensation Committees Need Reimagining for the AI Moment
stories.Summary:
Leo E. Strine, Jr., of counsel at Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz and a former Chief Justice and Chancellor of Delaware, and Kirby M. Smith, an academic fellow at Columbia Law School and former CEO and general counsel of Bridgeport Partners, published the article on November 24, 2026, in Bloomberg Law’s Insights and Commentary section. They argue that the independent committees US-listed companies must keep focused on top management pay have failed to check soaring executive take or restore fairer gainsharing among corporate leaders, stockholders, and workers. They write that CEO pay has risen by over 1,300% over the past 47 years while the stock market rose 1,400% and the typical worker’s pay grew by just 28%, with labor’s share of overall income now at an all-time low in the post-World War II period. They say AI has the power to accelerate these worrying trends, that industry leaders predict major job losses even though AI has yet to cause them, and that only about a third of AI projects are actively delivering a positive return on investment.

The authors propose transforming the compensation committee of the corporate board into a workforce committee, which they say is efficient because boards face time pressures and reorienting an existing committee lets them see the big picture. Instead of addressing only top executive pay, they write, the committee would track and improve gainsharing among shareholders, top executives, and workers over time, understand management’s pay-setting process, monitor employee-related metrics such as satisfaction, turnover, promotions, training, safety, and culture, and bring workers’ voice into strategic planning and budget processes. They say the committee could require management to provide it and the full board with information about what jobs workers do at each quartile of compensation and the median and mean pay and benefit packages of those jobs. They also say the committee could tackle AI’s implications for the quality of work, since without thoughtful implementation AI can increase workloads, erode personal collaboration, and cause skill atrophy.

The authors write that Congress and the stock exchanges mandated that company boards focus on top executive pay and that this accelerated, not arrested, take at the top. They say that if lawmakers are serious about promoting pro-worker policies and sharing the blessings of capitalism more fairly, broadening the mandate of that existing committee is a simple and sensible way to ensure that boards and management pay attention to the workers who drive a company’s success. They acknowledge that a board-level workforce committee is no panacea but say it helps address something long overdue by requiring that the best interests of American workers receive consideration at the boardroom table. They add that at a time of great political divide, leading figures in both parties agree that the American economy is failing ordinary workers, and that companies which do not create good jobs for American workers are not great companies.

The authors say AI forces boards to confront two key questions: whether available dollars are best used for executive compensation or spread among the workers most responsible for the company’s success, and how to balance investing in workers while deploying AI most productively. They write that companies wanting to maximize their AI potential and employee AI fluency need to rethink how they train and structure their workforce, and that a reconceived committee could encourage investment in workers’ AI-related skills on the promise that wages will rise if productivity does. They argue that boards which understand their workforces will make better decisions about where to invest compensation dollars and capital to deliver sustainable profits, and that the idea is pro-worker and benefits stockholders too. The article states that it does not necessarily reflect the opinion of Bloomberg Industry Group Inc., the publisher of Bloomberg Law, Bloomberg Tax, and Bloomberg Government, or its owners.
