stories.Headline: Heineken opens global GenAI lab in Singapore with AI Singapore
stories.Summary:
Heineken launched its first global generative artificial intelligence lab in Singapore on Wednesday 19 March 2025, in collaboration with AI Singapore, to enhance growth, productivity and customer engagement across its global operations. Kenneth Choo, Heineken’s Asia-Pacific managing director, said the lab serves as a global centre of expertise to boost AI innovation in Singapore as well as in the company’s global operations. He said that by harnessing Singapore’s exceptional AI ecosystem, skilled talent and supportive government policies, the company is excited to drive the development of innovative solutions that will transform the beverage industry for years to come. The lab will lead the development of scalable GenAI solutions across several areas, including systems that can autonomously solve complex problems such as automated marketing content creation and financial reporting.

By the end of 2025, the lab aims to assemble a core team including Heineken’s digital and technology specialists together with talent recruited from AI Singapore. The team will have access to AI Singapore’s talent pool to connect with AI professionals and learn the most innovative approaches in the field. Laurence Liew, AI Singapore’s AI Innovation director, said that by combining Heineken’s industry expertise with its AI capabilities and talent, the two are creating a powerful model for how businesses and research institutions can collaborate to create solutions with real-world impact. The Economic Development Board has welcomed the launch of the lab.

Chan Ih-Ming, EDB’s executive vice president, said the initiative will allow Heineken to unlock new business value from Singapore while concurrently serving as a valuable platform to level up on AI talent and capabilities. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the lab’s aim to assemble its core team by the end of 2025.

stories.Headline: Mercor researchers propose a six-test average that tracks OpenAI model perplexity rankings
stories.Summary:
Mercor researchers Jason Wei and Edward Hu published a November 24 research post saying an equal-weight average of six public multiple-choice tests closely tracks the perplexity measurements OpenAI published for its models. They compared the results with nine OpenAI models still available through OpenAI’s API. They used the lowest available reasoning setting, or none, to reduce the influence of post-training and extended reasoning. They report that the models’ rankings closely match their perplexity rankings, measured by Spearman correlation. Mercor also applied the six-test average to models from Anthropic and Google DeepMind.

The six datasets combine broad academic knowledge, scientific and medical reasoning, and factual recall. MMLU-Pro spans science, business, law, humanities and health, and its evaluation used a 2,000-question subset. GPQA-Diamond adds chemistry, physics and biology questions, while MedXpertQA-text and MedXpertQA-mm draw on medical questions filtered from exams and textbooks. BrowseComp-MCQ and SimpleQA-verified-MCQ test factual recall, and Mercor used GPT-OSS to generate nine incorrect options per question. Mercor estimates that testing up to 300 examples from each dataset with GPT-6.2 Astra costs $7, a figure covering only that limited run.

Mercor presents the six-dataset average as a starting point for a shared, open evaluation, not a permanent standard. The authors say other multiple-choice benchmarks may work too. They warn that optimizing for any chosen proxy can undermine its usefulness. They acknowledge that multiple-choice questions do not reflect real-world use cases. They argue that answer selection avoids judging how comprehensive or stylish a response is, while partial knowledge can still improve results through elimination and better guesses.

Mercor names Claude Fable 5.2, Gemini 4 Neon and GPT-6.2 Astra as the strongest performers. Corresponding perplexity figures for Anthropic and Google’s models were unavailable, so those scores do not provide the same check against perplexity that Mercor performed for OpenAI. OpenAI says perplexity does not directly measure a task people care about and misses capability gains from chain-of-thought reasoning. OpenAI also warns that developers’ different evaluation datasets and training mixtures make comparisons across labs difficult. Answers were graded by exact match, and when two post-trained OpenAI models shared the same published perplexity, Mercor tested both and averaged their benchmark scores.

OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki argued in a November 22 post, Perplexity and Intelligence, for using perplexity to compare progress across developers and help establish shared safety standards. Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token, a unit of text, on average, and lower perplexity means better predictions. OpenAI’s disclosed measurements use a fixed snapshot of its internal codebase, not a public test set that outside researchers can run. Mercor’s alternative gives each benchmark equal weight rather than weighting some subjects more heavily. The researchers argue that this mix exercises skills shared with general prediction: knowing about the world and reasoning about it.

The open question is whether researchers can build a shared public test that stays useful once models are trained against it. Mercor frames the measure as a possible starting point for shared evaluation, not a score for overall usefulness or a settled cross-lab standard. The tests have not been shown to track prediction scores across labs. A proxy for perplexity is therefore not a complete measure of what a finished AI system can do. The price claim is narrow: Mercor estimates that testing up to 300 examples from each dataset with GPT-6.2 Astra costs seven dollars, not the price of every experiment in the research.

Articles.Title: Mercor says six public tests closely track OpenAI’s AI prediction scores - Superpower Daily

stories.Headline: AI firms pay white-collar experts to train language models
stories.Summary:
AI companies are paying white-collar professionals to train large language models, a shift that gained traction throughout 2026 as firms realized textbook knowledge alone could not handle the nuances of professional work. Platforms such as Mercor, a Silicon Valley company valued at $10 billion that recently raised a $250 million Series D, are recruiting expert professionals for tasks like reviewing AI-generated work, demonstrating how they approach problems or evaluating LLM responses. Mercor has created 780,000 roles and pays out $4 million daily, according to the company, and current listings average $94 an hour. Heidi Hagberg, Mercor's head of communications and marketing, said the company is looking for people in pretty much any sector you can think of, including law, medicine and tech.

The work represents a new market for professional expertise that sits somewhere between consulting, contract work and training a potential future competitor. As with other forms of contract work, these assignments do not necessarily lead to permanent jobs, an ongoing role with the companies or ownership of the contributed IP, and some AI trainers have described the mental toll of an unreliable paycheck as soul-destroying. Anthropologist Mary L. Gray, who co-authored the 2019 book Ghost Work with Siddharth Suri, said the contract-based structure of that work can make it difficult to see the full impact on workers. Gray also wrote that the paradox of automation's last mile is the fallout of the effort to automate all of what technologists imagine people can do, and that no technology researcher she has met has ever been trained to study and understand the social dynamics and interactions that make us tick.

Besides the financial motivation, some professionals see the work as a way to contribute to something bigger, feeling a personal responsibility to help make sure that the AI systems people use are trustworthy, according to Hagberg. AI can take over some redundant, automatable tasks, but people will still be needed to handle gaps and bring human judgment, she said. A New York Magazine article from earlier this year featuring more than 30 experts on Mercor paints a pretty damning picture of the industry, and the way companies accumulate and use training data makes it hard to track how many jobs this work creates, eliminates or changes. The people teaching AI to perform professional work are themselves doing a kind of professional work that did not exist at this scale a few years ago.

stories.Headline: UNESCO and Thailand's judicial institute train 180 judges to use AI while keeping human judgement
stories.Summary:
UNESCO and the Judicial Training Institute of Thailand organized a training session in August 2026 for judicial personnel. Around 180 participants attended the event, including mid-career judges who are preparing for higher leadership roles. Many of these attendees are future regional chief judges who will lead courts across the country starting in April 2027. The session focused on how judges can use artificial intelligence without surrendering human judgement. The training required participants to study the UNESCO Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals.

It covered various complex topics such as the opacity of neural networks, agentic AI, and reasoning models. The curriculum also explored AI jurisprudence, emerging case law, and the future of legal education and apprenticeship. As a result of the session, the Judicial Training Institute decided to translate the UNESCO guidelines into the Thai language. Judge Kraiphol Aranyarat of the Office of the President of the Supreme Court stated that AI adoption must be guided by judicial values.

He emphasized that independence, impartiality, fairness, transparency, and accountability are fundamental to the process. Hironaka, the Regional Advisor and Chief of Communication and Information for UNESCO, noted a gap in formal AI training for judges. She argued that training is necessary to address data security and AI ethics within a human rights framework. The participants discussed how to maintain accountability and public trust while introducing innovation into the justice system.

Judge Patcharapa Intarakamhaeng reflected that human oversight and respect for the rule of law are especially significant for judges. Judge Suthawan Leelanapapat of the Judicial Training Institute observed a high level of involvement and interest from the attendees. The organizers believe that equipping judges for technological innovation will ensure that AI remains accountable to human rights. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Preparing Thailand's future judicial leaders for the age of AI - UNESCO

stories.Headline: DLA Piper lawyers find courts treat open AI input as waiving privilege
stories.Summary:
A year ago DLA Piper published an analysis of legal privilege and AI, when there was limited judicial or regulatory guidance and no case law on the issue. The firm took a first principles approach at that time. It has now revisited the topic with recent case law in key jurisdictions, judicial commentary and regulatory guidance. The update was published on 23 November 2026 by Phillip Kelly and Rachel Tookey. The analysis concentrates on legal advice privilege over litigation privilege, where the impact of AI may differ.

The update cites the Upper Tribunal decision in Munir in February 2026, which held that placing information into an open-source AI tool puts it in the public domain, breaching confidentiality and waiving privilege. It cites the US federal court decision in Heppner in February 2026, which held that open-source AI-generated documents prepared by a defendant and later shared with lawyers were not privileged. It cites Warner in February 2026 in the Eastern District of Michigan and Morgan in March 2026 in the District of Colorado. It cites Sir Colin Birss' April 2026 speech, the SRA's updated Effective supervision guidance of June 2026 and its August 2026 Warning Notice on Misuse of AI. It cites the Law Society Practice Note of 21 October 2026 and the Civil Justice Council's final report of 29 October 2026.

The SRA guidance requires AI output in legal work to be subject to appropriate human review, scrutiny and professional judgement. The SRA Notice confirms that using open AI tools can permanently waive privilege and reinforces supervision as a professional requirement. Sir Colin Birss said that on any view one cannot assume confidentiality is preserved with a public AI system, and that a lawyer using a secure system would be hard to see as affecting privilege. The Law Society note warns that inputting paid-for legal advice into AI systems without adequate data handling safeguards may undermine confidentiality and privilege. The Civil Justice Council report rejects any requirement for parties to obtain permission to use AI or declare it, except that witnesses of fact and experts should declare AI has not generated substantive content.

The articles state there is no standalone AI privilege, because AI is not a lawyer. In Heppner the court said documents generated by a client with an AI system are not privileged because the system is not an attorney. Warner commented that generative AI programmes are tools, not persons. Morgan commented that use of AI did not eliminate all expectations of privacy or automatically waive protections. The Law Society said questions remain over whether prompts, draft outputs and audit logs are lawyer's working papers attracting privilege.

The original article concluded that confidentiality, and therefore privilege, would almost certainly be lost if legal advice is uploaded into an open or public AI system. It noted a potential counter-argument from HT SRL v Wee Shuo Woon, which held that published confidential information may not lose its confidential character where it had not been accessed by the public at large. Warner and Morgan give some support to Woon, with Morgan saying routing information through a third-party system does not forfeit all privacy. Munir has not yet been tested by a higher court, and privilege was not in dispute between the parties in that case. The SRA Notice notes that in-house lawyers should be particularly careful as AI business tools may not be designed for legal work.

The articles state that whether a system is closed for privilege purposes depends on its terms and configuration, not on whether it is paid for. The Law Society recommends checking features such as processing, data transfer and safeguards. The articles say the safest course is not to put privileged material into public AI. They say future decisions may refine the position on open AI tools and address actual versus theoretical loss of confidentiality. They say it would be for Parliament to extend legal advice privilege beyond advice given by legal professionals.

Articles.Title: Is Legal Advice Developed By Or With An AI System Legally Privileged? | Reconsidered One Year On - Legal 500

stories.headline_source: Is Legal Advice Developed By Or With An AI System Legally Privileged? | Reconsidered One Year On

stories.Headline: Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna says AI now handles 90% of his work as engineers shift to system design and testing
stories.Summary:
Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s Executive Vice President of Copilot, Agents and Platform, gave an interview to Peter Yang, who worked at Microsoft over a decade ago, and the interview was published by Windows Latest on 23 November 2026. In it Lamanna said that about 90% of what he does has been replaced, comparing AI to what the cloud did to programmers in 1990. He said software engineers have gone through this before, once writing assembly by hand and then stopping when compilers arrived. He said that if you showed a software engineer in 1990 what Azure or AWS can do, they would say 90% of their work had been replaced. He said there are more software engineers now and they are more important.

Lamanna said his most AI-focused teams may not craft code line by line but now obsess over system design, verification, testing and safe rollouts. He said he feels he has never had to think harder than right now, calling it a different muscle. He said writing code no longer takes much time and that the time goes into coordination, which is why he writes a 20-page memo every six months and settles debates with A/B experiments. He said engineers are now solving higher order problems. He said Copilot Workspaces, which Microsoft announced at Ignite last week, suggests the right people and agents to add when preparing a customer proposal or handling a supply chain disruption.

Lamanna said it is probably inevitable that the main client of a lot of software and technology will be agents as we go forward. He said agents are very harsh customers who want the best performance and programmability, and that what an agent prefers is not always what a person prefers. He said an agent does not care and you can return a thousand results, where a person is given 10 links because nobody wants to read a thousand results. He said Microsoft’s APIs and user experiences will start to evolve and have modes that better support agents.

He said he already uses Copilot Cowork agents to review Microsoft’s GPU capacity and do budget planning. Lamanna said the industry has overfit to how software engineers work when applying AI to the rest of knowledge work. He said coding has always been a somewhat lonely profession, where you create a branch, work by yourself for days and submit a pull request, and that sales and finance do not work like that. He said a sales rep who spends days not talking to another person in single-player mode is probably not a very good salesperson.

He said he does not think Copilot will replace Office, because to move a text box eight pixels to the left he just wants to click and drag. He said that if you cannot be bothered to write 10 pages, you probably should not generate 10 pages and send it to 10 people, and that the right direction of travel is absolutely not generating more stuff for people to read. Lamanna pointed to GitHub.com, which saw a 14x increase in load, and said that is definitely not because the world just got 14 times more human developers. GitHub’s Octoverse 2026 report mentions agents starting more than 40% of pull requests in September, 110 million of them, up from 17% in March.

Lamanna made a similar prediction at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in September. Under Yang’s post on X, one person mentioned that agents will skip pricing pages that say contact sales, and another said an unhappy customer complains but stays, whereas an agent will just stop sending you orders. Someone in the reply said compilers never hallucinated a migration that drops prod, and Microsoft has admitted several times before that AI agents can hallucinate, which is why the tedious job of checking falls on engineers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cloudflare's Aaron McAllister warns federal agencies to secure AI agents and adopt post-quantum cryptography
stories.Summary:
Aaron McAllister of Cloudflare spoke about two emerging security challenges for federal agencies, according to FedScoop on November 23, 2026: managing the rapid growth of AI agents and preparing for post-quantum cryptography. He said agencies have made progress implementing zero-trust security, but traditional identity and authentication frameworks are struggling to keep pace with non-human identities. He pointed to AI-generated traffic surging as a particular strain on those frameworks. He emphasized the need for new security controls that can verify AI agents, limit their access to sensitive systems and provide visibility into their actions. On quantum readiness, McAllister warned that agencies cannot afford to delay adopting NIST’s finalized post-quantum cryptography standards.

He encouraged agencies to identify their most sensitive data and to use NIST guidance to build transition plans ahead of federal deadlines. He also encouraged them to engage executive leadership through tabletop exercises. The article gives no dates for the federal deadlines and no further numbers. McAllister is the person the article attributes these views to, and the article paraphrases what he said rather than quoting him at length. He framed the growth of AI agents and the move to post-quantum cryptography as the two emerging challenges federal agencies face.

He described zero-trust progress as real but outpaced by non-human identities and AI-generated traffic. He presented new controls for verifying and limiting AI agents, and NIST-guided transition planning, as what agencies need. The article places both warnings in the context of federal agencies’ security work, with zero-trust implementation as the backdrop for the AI agent problem. It does not say what agencies have done in response to either warning, and it gives no schedule beyond the federal deadlines it mentions without dates. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton
stories.Summary:
A tutorial published on November 24, 2026 by Oluwaseun Doherty, Oyindamola Omotuyi and Richard AntRi, all writing for NVIDIA, describes a workflow that adds local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. The authors say the walking policy from their first Microduck tutorial is reused with its weights unchanged, and that a separate avoidance controller is trained using time-of-flight sensing. In the described setup, a person chooses a direction with a gamepad, and the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy. The tutorial says NVIDIA Isaac Lab provides the robot-learning environment and Newton simulates physics and the sensor's depth measurements. The workflow requires a Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver, Git with Git LFS, the uv package manager, a configured Microduck, a supported time-of-flight sensor and a paired gamepad with a level test area.

The authors say the environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets from SimReady Central on Hugging Face, including a cardboard box, an office bin and a bedside cabinet alongside cones. The simulated sensor is said to model the VL53L5CX, which measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz, with a 45° field of view and a 0.12, 4 m range. Training is described as using PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 iterations, and the authors say they also trained the policy on NVIDIA DGX Spark in approximately 6 hours using 4,096 parallel environments for 3,000 PPO updates. The tutorial says the navigation policy's actor receives time-of-flight history and body and controller state available on the real robot, while its critic uses additional simulation state that is not needed for deployment. Rewards are described as encouraging progress toward the goal, safe arrivals and movement around obstacles, with penalties for fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions and falls.

The authors say training adds noise, delays and missing measurements, including near the grid's edges, to expose the policy to imperfect data. Forward speed is capped at 0.15 m/s by default, with an additional close-obstacle brake and stale-input stopping, and the authors advise starting in a clear area and verifying stopping before testing a course. The tutorial places the work in the context of the wider Microduck task collection, which it says includes velocity tracking on flat and rough terrain, stand-up recovery, sit, stand transitions, walking with fall recovery, ball kicking, ground picking, forward rolls and roller-skating motions. The authors direct readers to start with the first Microduck tutorial and then choose a task from the collection to build the next policy in Isaac Lab with Newton. They suggest exploring new behaviors by changing commands, rewards or environments.

Articles.Title: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton

stories.Headline: Clay uses OpenAI models and Codex and ChatGPT plugins to power sales research and go-to-market workflows
stories.Summary:
Clay, a startup in North America working in technology, offers a self-learning revenue engine that uses GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Sol and other OpenAI models to help sales teams build lists of companies and people, enrich those records with agents and turn the information into go-to-market plays, according to an OpenAI story published on November 24, 2026. Clay also offers plugins for Codex and ChatGPT, which the story says bring these capabilities to where customers already work, making it easier to create and run go-to-market workflows and to research accounts and deals. The Codex integration lets builders create and run go-to-market plays in Codex while giving sales reps access to data for researching an account or understanding a deal they are trying to close, and the ChatGPT plugin brings the same customer data into a tool reps already use so they can learn about prospects without leaving ChatGPT. OpenAI models power Claygent’s research, qualification, enrichment and signal detection, as well as the agent that helps users build workflows and coordinate other Clay agents.

Clay uses GPT-6 Sol as its primary model, with GPT-6 Astra for harder tasks and GPT-6 Luna for cost-sensitive work, which the story says supports background research and copywriting as well as agents that users work with directly. The Responses API lets Clay use different levels of intelligence and cost through the same interface, which Jeff Barg, Clay’s Head of AI, called super appealing across the different price points. Barg said GPT-6 Sol is a really great model for go-to-market plays, with good intuition and the ability to build long-horizon, outcome-based tasks, and he said GPT-6 Astra changed how he builds software because it closed the loop on the engineering process, letting him have Astra write code, add tests, run the tests, test the feature and upload the results in the pull request. Barg said Clay in ChatGPT gives sales reps a way to understand more about the customers they are trying to sell to by bringing rich context to the places they already work, and he said customers love using Codex for many different tasks in sales, with the best sales reps the most empowered by it.

Barg said Clay’s ChatGPT plugin has been a big success, and he described seeing reps combine information from their own systems and public datasets to work out how best to communicate a product’s value to a customer. Clay is working on inbound sales development features that would let an agent show a product or service to a prospect, and Barg sees GPT-Live-1 as a way to use Clay and Codex by voice to help prospects learn about a product. He also sees the Decisions API as another way to integrate models into Clay and open up new use cases. Clay’s stated ambition is to carry go-to-market workflows from start to finish with agents that improve as they learn from results, and Barg said the goal is to empower builders to bring the same shift that happened in software engineering to go-to-market.

stories.Headline: Legal study finds prohibitory injunctions protect better than damages against AI hallucinations
stories.Summary:
A legal analysis published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance found that court-ordered prohibitory injunctions protect better against generative artificial intelligence hallucinations than claims for financial compensation. The study was reported by Bioengineer.org on November 23, 2026. It examined European Union legislation and national civil frameworks. It assessed how existing European Union statutes and member state jurisprudence address reputational injury from large language models. The models output fabricated, defamatory factual claims about individuals.

The study assessed tort liability, product liability rules and personal data protections across jurisdictions including Spain, France and Germany. It evaluated damages, injunctive relief, data rectification and erasure when algorithmic systems produce false assertions without human communicative intent. It traced heightened risk of reputational injury to the convergence of web search technologies and large language models. Systems such as Microsoft Copilot and Google Search AI Mode embed large models to synthesize answers directly. Synthetic outputs are often presented with an authoritative tone that users struggle to distinguish from factual reporting.

The analysis established that generative artificial intelligence operators generally cannot shelter behind intermediary safe harbor provisions under Articles 4 through 6 of the Digital Services Act. It said these systems actively generate novel content rather than merely transmitting or hosting third-party data. The Court of Justice of the European Union has affirmed that safe harbor classifications cannot circumvent data protection duties. The study found that financial damage awards are almost universally modest due to narrow dissemination patterns characteristic of generative systems. It concluded that prohibitory injunctions represent a substantially more effective legal remedy than damage claims.

The analysis said defamation statutes in jurisdictions like Spain and France traditionally require an attribution of fact or an expression representing human intellectual reasoning. It said such conditions are difficult to establish against probabilistic algorithms operating mechanically without subjective intent. Under German civil doctrine, an entity facilitating dissemination of unlawful content may incur secondary liability as an interferer, or Störerhaftung. A 2024 ruling by the Landgericht Kiel involved automated business summaries that assigned false corporate insolvency statuses. The study highlighted Jeffery Battle's defamation claim against Microsoft after Copilot associated him with a convicted terrorist, and Mark Walters's lawsuit against OpenAI after ChatGPT fabricated an embezzlement complaint.

The revised European Union Product Liability Directive formally classifies software and artificial intelligence models as products regardless of delivery method. Compensable damages under Article 6 are strictly limited to death, personal injury including recognized psychological harm, property damage, and loss or corruption of non-professional data. Pure economic losses, privacy infringements and nonpecuniary personality injuries are expressly excluded from its scope. The General Data Protection Regulation's Article 5(1)(d) sets a principle of personal data accuracy, with associated rights to rectification and erasure. Under Article 82, individuals suffering material or nonmaterial damage from regulatory breaches may claim financial compensation, with fault presumed unless the controller demonstrates the damaging event was in no way attributable to its operations.

Exact machine unlearning requires retraining models across isolated data shards to expunge target data points. Approximate unlearning attempts to adjust network weights without full retraining, yet precisely localizing specific knowledge representations within billions of parameters remains technically difficult. Operators rely on output suppression filters to intercept and block fabricated text in real time. The European Commission is assessing whether ChatGPT's search feature qualifies as a very large online search engine under the Digital Services Act. The study concluded that regulatory protection must prioritize preventative structural interventions, emphasizing rigorous anonymization of training datasets and strict data governance during initial development phases.

Articles.Title: Injunctions Surpass Monetary Damages in Combating Artificial Intelligence Hallucinations, Legal Study Finds - Bioengineer.org

stories.Headline: Amateur astronomers use OpenAI tools to find potential exoplanets in public telescope data
stories.Summary:
Two amateur astronomers used OpenAI's Codex and Astra tools to search public telescope data for signs of planets, OpenAI said in a post dated November 24, 2026. Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope. Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, worked independently of Bond and used Astra to analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars. Both searches identified potential exoplanets, and the two men have turned to astronomers for an independent assessment of their results. Bond contacted an astronomer at the SETI Institute, who ran an independent search and found two of the same signals in the Kepler data.

Bond's search flagged more than 200 signals, including 10 from previously confirmed planets. The first star that stood out, KIC 5689121, is a relatively cool star about half the size of our sun in the constellation Lyra, and the Codex search found a dip in brightness every 13.8 days. If a planet is causing that dip, the amount of light it blocks suggests it could be about 2.4 times Earth's diameter. The second star, KIC 6691030, is faint and lies in the northern sky, and the Codex search found a dip in its brightness every 4.8 days, consistent with a planet smaller than Neptune. Byrd's first pass through the data turned up 49 candidates, and he sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on NASA's TESS mission, where it is awaiting further analysis, with two more candidates awaiting submission.

Vishal Gajjar, associate director for international SETI programs at the SETI Institute, said Kevin's work shows how citizen scientists equipped with AI can help astronomers explore the Kepler Bonus Catalog, a vast collection of stars beyond Kepler's original targets. Gajjar said Bond's pipeline has surfaced promising candidates in data traditional searches may have missed, and that the institute's initial checks are encouraging. OpenAI said Bond came to astronomy through his love of photographing the night sky, and that Byrd has always loved astronomy. OpenAI said Byrd tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data. OpenAI said Bond used Codex to compare published methods for picking out faint, recurring dips, combine them in a search program, and test whether changes to the code improved the search.

OpenAI said finding the 10 known planets gave Bond confidence that the program could pick out the kinds of signals he was looking for. OpenAI said confirming what caused the two signals could take months or years. OpenAI said Byrd used Astra to design two searches, one looking broadly for exoplanet candidates and the other focused on stars' habitable zones, the range of distances from a star where a planet with a suitable atmosphere could support liquid water on its surface. OpenAI said Byrd then asked Astra to review published methods, build the search software, and run initial checks on promising signals, drawing on observations from TESS, which NASA launched in 2018, and from other public telescope archives. OpenAI said Byrd's search is still running.

OpenAI said astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system since the first ones were announced in 1992. OpenAI said that in 2017 researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA's Kepler Space Telescope that astronomers had already examined, and that when the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90. OpenAI said the Kepler telescope was a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018, and that Kepler watched one field for four years. OpenAI said TESS surveyed both hemispheres in its first 26 sectors, from 2018 to 2020. OpenAI said astronomers can use statistics to show that an exoplanet is the most likely explanation for a series of dips, and can collect more observations, sometimes using a different method such as radial velocity.

OpenAI said that if a planet is passing in front of the star in Lyra every 13.8 days, astronomers can watch for the next crossing, and that further observations can help establish whether the dip repeats as expected. OpenAI said additional checks can help determine what is causing the dip. OpenAI said NASA's Exoplanet Watch lets people request data and learn to plot a light curve themselves, and that AAVSO's Exoplanet Observing Program can show people how to measure a dip in starlight and share observations with researchers. OpenAI said the Unistellar Network Investigating TESS Exoplanets coordinates volunteers around the world with a certain type of telescope to observe the same star. OpenAI said Bond and Byrd's searches are still open, and that it wants more people to have that opportunity in astronomy and across science.

Sarvam AI claims the updated model operates at a lower cost for businesses. The articles do not give further details on pricing, availability or how the model compares with earlier versions beyond these points.

Sarvam AI is the company responsible for the release, and it made the claims about improved instruction following, better digital tool use, enhanced Indian language support and lower cost. The articles do not name any individual at the company or give direct statements beyond these attributed claims. The model is aimed at businesses handling customer queries, phone calls and software tasks. No independent evaluation of the claims is reported in the articles.

The articles give little further context on what happens next, and they do not say when the model will be available to businesses or how it will be distributed. The update follows the original 105B model released in March, which the articles mention only as the earlier version. stories.Headline: JPMorganChase executive identifies six challenges of enterprise AI inference
stories.Summary:
Dio Rettori, who works at JPMorganChase, outlined six critical aspects of enterprise AI inferencing for large, globally distributed organisations, according to a TechGig report published on November 25, 2026. He described inference as a hard technical problem, an expensive problem and an ever-changing space, and he also identified it as a data sovereignty problem, a dependency problem and a regulatory problem. Inferencing is a real-time, user-facing workload that is latency-sensitive, stateful and bursty, and its core challenge lies in achieving response speed with stability against finite serving capacity. This differs significantly from training, which he compared to a large-scale high-performance computing workload focused on the core training stack and distributed frameworks.

Rettori said optimising GPU utilisation is crucial for managing significant expenses, and industry reports indicate GPU utilisation as low as 5 per cent, with hardware failure rates around 10 per cent. He shared that a system with 64 NVIDIA B200s has an estimated three-year total cost of ownership between $16 million and $20 million, including hardware, software licenses, spares, services, power and cooling. He said the AI inference landscape is constantly evolving, with new models and hardware emerging every three to 12 months, which requires intentional decision-making for adoption and planning. He stressed that every inference call to an external API constitutes a data transfer decision, raising data sovereignty concerns for global enterprises, and that self-hosted solutions can help maintain data perimeter control.

Rettori noted that enterprises often rely on small foundation model providers, which concentrates risk due to a lack of control over model changes, pricing, capacity and capability. He said emerging regulations like the EU AI Act require specific logging and proof of decision-making, necessitating robust governance and compliance mechanisms for inferencing. He also said deterministic inferencing is another significant challenge for transactional systems, and according to his demo, cloud-based multi-agent calls show a 41 per cent variation in processing time compared to 5.2 per cent on-premise. He highlighted the limitations of Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipelines, explaining that they have a mathematical ceiling, and that beyond 50,000 similar documents the vector space may not have enough dimensions to represent differences. He suggested that embedding business ontology into models through reinforcement learning with human feedback might be more effective.

stories.Headline: Richpanel uses OpenAI models to automate half of customer support within 30 days
stories.Summary:
Richpanel, a startup in the Asia-Pacific and Oceania technology sector, uses OpenAI models to set up the tools and procedures its AI support agents need and to handle customer conversations, according to an OpenAI customer story published on November 23, 2026. The company built an AI manager for agent setup, which customers began calling Boss AI, and it writes procedures and defines how Richpanel's frontline support agent, copilot and quality-assurance agent call the tools they need. Richpanel uses GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol for Boss AI, prioritizing accuracy when building the tools and procedures its other agents will follow, and it uses GPT-6 Luna and other OpenAI models for the frontline agent that handles hundreds of thousands of conversations. At the time of an October 2026 interview, CEO Amit RG said Richpanel had completed approximately 300 AI customer-support deployments over the previous six months.

Richpanel guarantees customers a 50% automation rate within the first 30 days or their money back, and Amit said the company met that commitment across all of those deployments. He added that in each of the cases the AI is beating human support agents when it comes to customer satisfaction. Amit said human support agents can use 20 or 30 tools to serve a customer, and the procedures they follow may never have been written down, which is the gap Richpanel addresses with OpenAI models. He said the intelligence is no longer the bottleneck and that everything around it is, and he described the balance the company seeks as one of cost and intelligence.

Amit said Richpanel's customers may already use low-cost outsourced support, so automating their operations has to make financial sense against that starting point. He credits OpenAI with making models available that can handle long context and longer tasks while remaining cost efficient, which lets Richpanel use deeper reasoning to prepare its support agents and more economical models to run the conversations that follow. He said OpenAI models can run these long-context, longer-horizon tasks while still being very cost efficient. The article does not say what happens next for Richpanel or its customers.

stories.Headline: Ai2 releases RoboTrack benchmark and two point tracking models for robotic manipulation
stories.Summary:
Ai2 released RoboTrack, a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation, on November 23, 2026. The Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) published the work on Hugging Face, with a tech report, data, code, project page and benchmark. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse. The videos show different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. Ai2 also released two new point tracking models, RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp.

RoboTrack-Bench holds 307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks in total. A subset of 33 video pairs was recorded simultaneously from two cameras, with the same physical points annotated in both views. RoboTrack-15M has 3,000 videos from 300 simulated homes with 5,000 tracks per video, for 15 million tracks in total. RoboTracker builds on AllTracker, a lightweight model with 17 million parameters, and RoboTracker-Warp builds on CoWTracker, a much larger model with about 1 billion parameters. RoboTracker-Warp's weights are for noncommercial use.

Ai2 said leading trackers score much lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on existing robotics benchmarks. The authors said they wanted to see whether current trackers' results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints and object interactions robots encounter in practice. They said every track in RoboTrack-Bench is annotated and verified by humans, with a second group of annotators checking every track frame by frame. They said their first attempt at synthetic data brought no gain on RoboTrack-Bench. They said RoboTracker-Warp achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of the five benchmarks they evaluated.

Every final tracker evaluated scored lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on RoboTAP, the only other real-video robotics benchmark, dropping by 3.0 to 6.6 AJ. CoWTracker, the strongest off-the-shelf tracker, dropped from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9 on RoboTrack-Bench. BootsTAPNext's extra real-world training raised its RoboTrack-Bench score by 5.1 AJ (55.1 to 60.2) but lowered its RGB-Stacking score by 9.5 AJ (75.0 to 65.5). CoWTracker leads CoTracker3 by 4.7 AJ on RoboTAP but by only 2.1 AJ on RoboTrack-Bench, and AllTracker's 2.7-point lead over CoTracker3 on RoboTAP shrinks to 0.8. BootsTAPNext, the strongest model on DAVIS, falls 3.7 AJ behind CoWTracker on RoboTrack-Bench and trails the Kubric-only AllTracker (60.2 vs 61.4 AJ).

The articles say many trackers train on synthetic videos generated with Kubric, which shows objects tossed into a scene. Ai2 extended MolmoSpaces, its robotic simulation environment, to generate dense point tracks on the robot and the objects it handles. In each episode a simulated robot arm picks up an everyday object such as a cup, a plate or a block, with two cameras recording, one on the wrist and one at the robot's base, rendered in MuJoCo. The pipeline calculates each point's position and visibility in every frame without human annotation and filters out static points on the background and the robot's fixed base. The articles say AllTracker scores differ slightly from the published ones because Ai2 fixed a scoring bug in its released evaluation code, and that RoboTAP and Kinetics were evaluated on all annotated points rather than following AllTracker's protocol.

Compared with the released AllTracker and CoWTracker models, RoboTracker improves RoboTrack-Bench by 0.8 AJ (62.6 to 63.4) and RoboTracker-Warp by 2.1 AJ (63.9 to 66.0), with gains of up to 1.2 AJ averaged across the three robotics benchmarks. On general video benchmarks both models perform on par with their base models, and RoboTracker-Warp has the highest AJ on four of the five benchmarks, with DAVIS the exception where BootsTAPNext and CoWTracker score slightly higher. RoboTracker-Warp improves on every source by roughly 1 to 3 AJ, including human footage from EgoVerse and Ego-Exo4D even though RoboTrack-15M contains only robot arms. Ai2 released both model checkpoints so other researchers can inspect and build on the work, and brought the pieces together on a real robot to help guide pipette handling in wet-lab tasks. The articles leave open the full evaluation protocols, which they say are in the paper.

stories.Headline: Authors adapt a Terminal-Bench task into raman-lab and show gpt-oss-120b fails all three rollouts
stories.Summary:
The article, published on Hugging Face on November 23, 2026, was written by Avijit Ghosh, Ben Burtenshaw and Irene Solaiman. It describes how to build and maintain an agentic evaluation, following one task through eight steps. The authors adapted Terminal-Bench's open raman-fitting task into a new evaluation called raman-lab. They ran the original task three times with the Terminus-2 harness and the gpt-oss-120b model. The article reports that gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts on the original task.

The Hugging Face hub hosts around 3500 eval leaderboards and saw about 16X growth in eval datasets in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. The authors say 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5, announced in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations, where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. In an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness, and accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points.

The authors argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. They say scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable. They state that privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and that withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. They say open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations. They say sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

The article says policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot. It says researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough. It says more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination, meaning questions or solutions entering training data so scores may reflect prior exposure. It says errors in tasks and graders are common, and the article looks at how they are found and corrected. It says AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent, and a glossary defines each term used.

The article says AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. It says question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. It says agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. It says research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. It says team and swarm evaluations are left outside the scope of the guide.

The article says the adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts on the eight adapted tasks, with three rollouts per task. It says the shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so the authors added checks on each fitted peak and the final verifier rejects it. It says in two of the three original rollouts gpt-oss-120b declared completion before observing relevant output, and in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas. It says the traces, not the score alone, could tell these failures apart from an incorrect fit. It says the eight tasks are a development set, and broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

stories.Headline: MarkTechPost publishes 27 cybersecurity terms covering AI model attacks, agentic risks and defenses
stories.Summary:
A reference article published by MarkTechPost on November 23, 2026 set out 27 cybersecurity terms intended to prepare readers for the age of artificial intelligence, grouping them into four parts covering attacks on models, agentic risks, AI-powered attacks on people and the defenses that answer them. The article reported that IBM's 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that one in four malicious breaches were AI-enabled, a rise of 56 percent year over year. It said those breaches cost an average of $6 million, which is about $1 million above the $4.99 million global average. The article stated that attackers now target the models themselves, the agents that act on their output and the people who trust what AI produces.

The article said the reference lists have moved quickly to keep up, noting that OWASP published its Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026 on August 4, 2026, and its first Top 10 for Agentic Applications in December 2025. It said MITRE ATLAS maps attacker tactics against AI systems in the way ATT&CK does for IT. It reported that NIST groups attacks on what a model reads, learns or reveals into evasion, poisoning, privacy and misuse in its Adversarial Machine Learning taxonomy, NIST AI 100-2e2025, published in March 2025. The article said prompt injection, which it described as input crafted to override a model's intended instructions, has ranked first on every edition of the OWASP LLM list, including the 2026 edition.

The article attributed several findings to named researchers and organizations, saying that Anthropic's many-shot jailbreaking research showed that stuffing a long prompt with up to 256 fake dialogues can override safety behavior. It said a joint study by Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute found that just 250 malicious documents could backdoor models from 600M to 13B parameters, with the number needed staying roughly constant regardless of model size. It said Anthropic's Sleeper Agents paper trained models to write secure code when the prompt said 2023 but insert exploitable code when it said 2024, and that standard safety training, including adversarial training, did not remove the behavior. It said Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported in February 2026 that distillation attacks were rising, with one campaign sending more than 100,000 prompts aimed at Gemini's reasoning.

The article described EchoLeak, tracked as CVE-2025-32711, as a zero-click flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot rated CVSS 9.3, and said Aim Security showed that one crafted email could make Copilot leak organizational data, which Microsoft fixed server-side in May 2025. It said Carlini et al. extracted hundreds of verbatim sequences from GPT-2, including personal contact details, using only query access, and found larger models more vulnerable. It said OWASP renamed and broadened System Prompt Leakage into an entry it called hidden context exposure, covering the leak of system prompts, tool definitions, retrieved documents or other context a user was not meant to see. The article did not say what happens next beyond the publication of the list itself.

stories.Headline: Pentagon renames its AI office the Super Intelligence Office and redesigns its website
stories.Summary:
The Pentagon’s office leading enterprise artificial intelligence deployments was renamed the Super Intelligence Office from the Chief Digital and AI Office, DefenseScoop reported on Nov. 24, 2026. The change followed a September executive order by President Donald Trump requiring federal agencies to call artificial intelligence “super intelligence” in official correspondence, websites, reports and job titles. The office’s public website moved from AI.mil to SI.mil and was redesigned. As of that week, the site’s “Leadership” page listed only Cameron Stanley, who oversees the office, and principal deputy Andy Mapes. Pentagon spokespersons declined to confirm the official serving as Maven Smart System program director or describe other high-level positions inside the hub.

The executive order requires all federal agencies to use the term “super intelligence” in official correspondence, websites, reports and job titles. The shift does not change existing U.S. regulations around AI without legislation from Congress, and it does not represent a new technological milestone. In academia and industry, “artificial superintelligence” typically refers to hypothetical future systems that exceed human-level general intelligence. Trump issued an executive order rebranding DOD as the DOW last year, though formally changing the agency’s name also requires an act of Congress. Stanley said the office’s existing operational programs, solicitations and partnerships will continue “uninterrupted under the new banner,” rolling out across digital systems, enterprise applications and component headquarters in the near term.

Stanley said the “redesignation is a clear signal of where the Department of War is going.” A War Department official, in a Monday email, said the organization routinely aligns personnel to meet operational requirements and does not comment on individual assignments below the Senior Executive Service level. Pentagon spokespersons did not directly respond to questions about who serves as the Super Intelligence Office’s program director for the Maven Smart System or confirm Army Col. Molly Solsbury’s current role. Spokespersons also did not provide updated information that week about the office’s current organizational setup and leadership lineup. A source who requested anonymity said Solsbury is no longer the Maven Smart System program director inside the SIO and suggested several other senior roles there are unfilled.

Savan Kong, CEO and co-founder of AI startup Your Roster and previously the DOD’s first chief experience officer, said reorganizing is normal but “who runs a program like Maven isn’t a minor detail.” Kong said being open about leadership during a transition builds trust and removing that information does the opposite. A former U.S. military official said transparency is a must given AI’s role in planning and executing military missions, and without it there is a real risk of AI being misused or misapplied. Virginia Burger, a senior defense policy analyst for the Project on Government Oversight’s Center for Defense Information, said the Maven platform is “a permanent, billion-dollar program” used by more than 100,000 defense and military personnel. Burger said the department’s own memo said making Maven a program of record would create clear lines of accountability, and if there has been a leadership change the Pentagon should say so.

Built by Palantir Technologies and anchored under the SIO, the Maven Smart System is considered the Pentagon’s flagship AI-enabled software platform for command-and-control, battlefield awareness and complex intelligence fusion. MSS adoption and investments have been surging across the military this year, largely influenced by a directive from DOD leadership to mature the platform into a formal program of record. The office has been iteratively changing the design and contents of its public-facing website. Unlike previous versions, the website no longer discloses any other positions or officials serving in the AI shop. Burger noted that experts’ calls for transparency are emerging as a new Congress prepares to ask hard questions about AI in targeting after a U.S. Tomahawk missile strike reportedly hit an elementary school in Iran during Operation Epic Fury.

Burger said the person in charge is the one who answers when something goes wrong, that this is the standard across the military, and that transparency is how Congress and taxpayers make sure these systems work as promised. Burger said if the department doesn’t want to put that face forward, she hopes senior leaders are willing to take the heat and answer the hard questions. Kong and others told DefenseScoop that industry partners, Congress and U.S. military personnel who depend on the office for algorithms and other in-demand frontier AI tools need to know who is accountable for their use inside the government. Sources urged DOD to share more information about the SIO’s workforce and priorities with the public, as the CDAO historically supplied. The articles do not say who currently runs the Maven Smart System program or what the office’s full leadership lineup is.

stories.Headline: Meta exposes warp-group GPU control in Triton for Nvidia and AMD chips
stories.Summary:
Meta published a detailed report on TLX, short for Triton Low-Level Extensions, which is the GPU compiler extension behind its production machine learning kernels, according to a MarkTechPost article dated November 23, 2026. TLX is an extension to Triton rather than a new language, and it exposes warp groups, barriers, TMA and clusters to Python kernels. It targets NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell plus AMD MI300 and MI350-series GPUs. The article says the message for kernel engineers is CUDA-level control without leaving Triton, and that a Blackwell GEMM takes roughly 200 lines of Python-level Triton.

The extension is MIT-licensed and runs on NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200, GB200) as well as AMD MI300 and MI350-series hardware. On six H100 FP16 GEMM shapes it lands within -0.9% to +3.7% of cuBLAS, and on 8192x8192x8192 it reaches 577.0 TFLOPS versus 582.3 for cuBLAS, per PyTorch. On MI350 GEMM it beats rocBLAS by 11.8% to 15.2% on square shapes from 256 to 2048. Meta reports a 4x speedup on an H100 linear compression kernel for ads inference, while dense LLM-style attention forward reaches about 87% of FlashAttention-4 on B200, per PyTorch.

The research team describes the model as MIMW, or Multi-Instruction, Multi-Warp, in which the warp group becomes the basic unit of orchestration. Triton still defines what runs, while TLX defines how it is orchestrated, and engineers write ordinary Triton and add TLX calls only where control matters. Warp groups get roles such as producer, consumer and epilogue, and they sync through hardware mbarriers while thread-level sync stays with the compiler. The API reads like Triton, with calls such as tlx.local_alloc, tlx.alloc_barriers, tlx.async_task, tlx.async_dot and tlx.barrier_wait.

In production at Meta, TLX delivered 20% to 25% end-to-end MFU on thousands of GPUs for Generative Ads Model training, and up to 2x forward speedup for Generalized Dot Product Attention. A warp-specialized linear compression kernel under In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization hit 4x speedup on H100, and FlashAttention under IKBO cut compute-intensive net latency by up to two-thirds. Distributed grouped GEMM fuses mixture-of-experts matmuls with communication for LLM pretraining on Blackwell, though Meta gives no speedup figure. The article notes that all numbers are self-reported with no independent benchmarks yet, and that TLX trails state-of-the-art attention most on the smallest causal-forward cases, with the gap narrowing as sequence length grows.

stories.Headline: Plural partner Sten Tamkivi closes €1bn fund in about six months
stories.Summary:
Plural, the London-based venture capital firm, has closed a new €1bn fund, according to an interview its partner Sten Tamkivi gave to Sifted on the sidelines of the Slush event in Helsinki. Tamkivi said the firm had raised the money in about six months, which he described as fast for a European fund of that size. Plural was founded in 2022 by Tamkivi and others including Taavet Hinrikus, and the firm has backed companies such as Helsing and Proxima Fusion. Tamkivi spoke about the fund, about defence technology and about why he believes Europe did not miss the wave of artificial intelligence.

The new fund is roughly double the size of Plural's previous vehicle, which the article puts at €400m. Tamkivi said the firm had not expected to raise so much so quickly, and he attributed the result to the team's record with founders. The article says Plural has backed Helsing, the defence technology company, and Proxima Fusion, a fusion startup, among other portfolio companies. It also names The Exploration Company among the businesses the firm has supported. The article gives no further figures for the fund beyond the €1bn total and the €400m earlier vehicle.

Tamkivi is responsible for the fund as a partner at Plural, and he made the case for defence technology as an investment area in the interview. He argued that Europe's founders have shown they can build serious companies in hardware and deep technology, not only in software. On artificial intelligence, he said the continent did not arrive late, and he pointed to the strength of its technical talent as the reason. The article paraphrases his view that European founders are enjoying record levels of entrepreneurship and surging investment, though it notes that the money is increasingly concentrated in fewer companies.

The interview took place at Slush in Helsinki, a startup event where investors and founders meet each autumn, and Sifted published it on 23 November 2026. The article presents Plural's €1bn fund as part of a wider rise in European venture activity, with more capital flowing to a smaller set of companies. It does not say what Plural plans to do with the money beyond the areas Tamkivi discussed, and it gives no timetable for the firm's next moves. More to follow.

stories.Headline: European AI startups reach large revenue with small teams so founders must build governance into products early
stories.Summary:
European AI startups are reaching revenue levels that once took a decade and a large workforce, according to Sifted, and this speed means founders must put governance in place much earlier than they used to. Lovable, based in Stockholm, passed $400 million in annual recurring revenue in February of this year with 146 full-time staff, while ElevenLabs reached $600 million in annual recurring revenue by September. The law firm Goodwin noted in May that the most sought-after companies can now insist on founder-controlled boards and narrower investor vetoes. Venture-backed companies have usually acquired governance as they grew, with senior hires bringing controls and each funding round bringing board seats and investor rights, but in many AI companies the teams handling security and risk stay small while board seats carry less weight.

In Europe, banks, hospitals and public bodies have to manage the security risks of the technology they buy and write that responsibility into their contracts with suppliers, so a European AI startup with a small team can find itself bound by a large bank's governance terms. Lovable's business customers include Klarna, which holds a Swedish banking licence and falls under the EU's digital resilience rules for financial firms, and since January 2025 these rules have required banks' contracts with technology providers to cover data security and provider support when an incident occurs. In February, a researcher reported that an app showcased on Lovable's platform had exposed more than 18,000 user records, and according to Lovable, acting on its security advice is up to the people who build the apps. At the time Lovable had fewer than 150 staff, and in July it advertised for a chief information security officer to build a security organisation from its first engineers and analysts and to win the certifications that enterprise customers require.

From December 2027, the EU AI Act will also set duties for organisations that use AI to assess people for credit, insurance, jobs or public benefits, requiring them to keep logs and assign human oversight, and their AI suppliers will have to make both possible. Professor Ioannis Ioannou of London Business School argues that founders should build the promises customers ask for into the product itself, since large customers usually ask whether their data will be used for training, where it is stored and how long it is kept. If the answers become product settings that apply to every customer, the company has little extra to track with each new contract, and founders should make sure their own suppliers have committed to at least as much as the startup offers its customers. The product should also record which model produced each output, what data it used and where a person stepped in, because customers will ask for those records in audits and investors will want them before the next funding round or a sale.

Founders should treat every model change as a release checked against the company's commitments before it goes live, and they should set out what each AI agent may do on its own and revisit those limits as the business grows. Many founders object that putting governance in place this early slows a startup down, but in practice many pay that cost later by hiring their first senior person for data, security or risk after a scare or when a large customer insists, and many write their governance down only when a buyer's questionnaire requires it, leaving a patchwork of terms written for different customers. A startup that builds its promises into its product and sets limits for its AI agents can keep those promises at any size, while founders who wait until a customer or regulator insists will end up with governance shaped by whoever asked first. Many of Europe's next large technology companies will reach the revenue of an established firm with a few hundred staff or fewer, and their risks will grow with that revenue, so governance will come late if they rely on senior hires and board seats to bring it.

stories.Headline: Nationwide's Assad Hussain leads Proj AI community to apply AI across project delivery
stories.Summary:
Assad Hussain, a programme manager at Nationwide Building Society, appeared on the Ctrl Alt Lead podcast to explain how a practitioner-led community is applying AI across the delivery lifecycle, in a conversation with Computing deputy editor Penny Horwood. He leads AI adoption for the project and programme practice in Nationwide's digital function, and he set up a community called Proj AI late last year. The group tests real delivery problems with tools such as Microsoft Copilot and Atlassian's Rovo, and an initial survey found plenty of enthusiasm but mostly basic use, such as summarising meetings and drafting emails. Hussain said the barrier was not willingness but confidence and consistency, according to the article.

The group mapped pain points across the delivery lifecycle and then held a promptathon judged by senior stakeholders and CIOs, teaching members the GCSE prompting framework of goal, context, source and expectation. Results so far include a solution intent document becoming a structured project plan, down to Jira tickets, within hours rather than days. Fortnightly demo sessions, a central library and a newsletter helped membership rise from 50 to around 250 by June. After the Virgin Money acquisition, Hussain can access about 500 delivery professionals, and the next step is an agent-a-thon to build AI agents that can act as a blueprint for other CIO areas.

Hussain insists the goal is less friction and better insight, with an accountable human owning every decision. He says AI will not make project leadership less important and will instead make the quality of that leadership more visible. The article describes him as pointing AI at project delivery rather than individual productivity, and it says most talk of AI productivity centres on chatbots, meeting summaries and code generation, which he thinks misses the bigger prize of speeding up how technology is delivered from requirements through to production. The full podcast can be watched as a video, played through the web player, or found on Spotify and Apple Podcasts, according to the article.

stories.Headline: UN negotiations on autonomous weapons end without breakthrough
stories.Summary:
Delegates from 128 countries met in Geneva for a United Nations conference on lethal autonomous weapons systems, and the talks ended early on Saturday without agreement on a legally binding ban. The meeting began on Monday and closed after several hours of overnight negotiations. The conference took place under the United Nations Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, a treaty involving 128 states that seeks to restrict weapons considered excessively harmful or indiscriminate. Campaigners had called for a binding treaty to prevent the development and use of machines that can make life-and-death decisions.

Despite the lack of a ban, the delegates agreed to begin developing an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems, with work expected to continue until 2028. Nearly 100 countries had backed calls for negotiations on a binding agreement, but major military powers and weapons-producing countries, including the US, Russia and Israel, opposed the proposed mandate. Lethal autonomous weapons systems use artificial intelligence and other technologies to identify, select and attack targets without requiring a human to make the final decision. Supporters of a ban want to prevent weapons from selecting and attacking targets in ways their operators cannot predict or control.

The Stop Killer Robots coalition, which represents more than 300 organisations, criticised the outcome as inadequate and said states had adopted a watered-down mandate that fails to chart a clear path towards a legally binding instrument. The group said that although more than 95 countries had expressed support for a treaty, a small number of states had weakened the final agreement during the closing hours of negotiations. Elizabeth Minor of Stop Killer Robots said machines should not make life and death decisions. Aurel Sari, an expert in international law at the University of Exeter, said autonomous weapons were already subject to existing international humanitarian law governing armed conflicts, but the challenge was agreeing on which types should be prohibited.

Campaigners warn that allowing machines to make life-and-death decisions could increase the risk of civilian casualties and make it harder to establish who is responsible when something goes wrong. Some countries rely on automated defensive systems that respond faster than humans can, including systems designed to intercept incoming missiles and protect warships. A ban broad enough to address concerns about unpredictable weapons could also cover these defensive technologies, while a narrower agreement might fail to restrict systems that campaigners consider particularly dangerous. Minor said she would not say it is too late to make rules and that this can be done at any point, adding that there is still time for a meaningful response that can prevent things going down an even worse path, but that depends on the international community acting now.

stories.Headline: VAST Data gains IMDA accreditation to support Singapore AI missions
stories.Summary:
VAST Data received accreditation from Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority, or IMDA, which recognises the company as a qualified technology provider for government agencies and large enterprise customers, according to a Telecompaper report dated 20 November 2026. The accreditation programme assesses innovative, high-growth infocomm and media companies and is intended to identify potential suppliers for public sector and enterprise projects. VAST Data's existing work in Singapore includes a collaboration with the Home Team Science and Technology Agency, known as HTX, to deliver a secure data platform supporting AI workloads for public safety. The company also works with NCS to build a unified, real-time data foundation for high-performance video analytics on the VAST AI Operating System across Singapore and the wider Asia-Pacific region. The accreditation follows VAST Data's launch of a regional centre of excellence in Singapore in partnership with EDBI, the arm of SG Growth Capital and the investment platform of Singapore's Economic Development Board and Enterprise Singapore.

The accreditation establishes VAST Data's credentials in Singapore and creates new opportunities for the company to deepen its engagement in the region, according to iTWire. Following the accreditation, VAST Data will look to further deepen its work with Singapore's government agencies and enterprises to bring more AI projects from proof-of-concept to real-world deployment. Sunil Chavan, Vice President for Asia Pacific and Japan at VAST Data, said the accreditation reflects the progress the company is already making as Singapore builds out the infrastructure needed for AI at scale. He said the company's work connects directly to Singapore's National AI Missions in Advanced Manufacturing, Financial Services, Connectivity, and Healthcare. Chavan said Singapore's National AI Strategy 2.0 is explicit about what it needs, namely sufficient compute, unlocked data, a trusted environment, and infrastructure that can scale with the country's AI ambitions, and he described these as the plumbing that determines whether a national AI mission ships or stalls.

Edwin Low, Director of Enterprise and Ecosystem Development at IMDA, said partnerships with technology companies such as VAST Data are important in strengthening the capabilities and infrastructure needed to support the deployment of AI at scale as Singapore advances its National AI Strategy 2.0. Low said VAST's accreditation follows a rigorous assessment of its technical, financial, and operational capabilities and recognises its ability to deliver trusted technology solutions, and he said the authority looks forward to its potential contributions to Singapore's digital and AI ecosystem. Chavan added that Singapore has set a high bar for what AI for the public good looks like, and that VAST Data intends to keep showing up as one of the partners helping it get there. The articles do not say what happens next beyond VAST Data's stated intention to deepen its work with government agencies and enterprises.
