stories.Headline: Enhanced Robotics raises over 100 million yuan to expand AI sports hardware production
stories.Summary:
Enhanced Robotics recently completed a Series B financing round of over 100 million yuan. The investment was provided by Sinovent Capital to support the AI sports hardware company. This funding event occurred around November 23, 2026, according to the report. The company has also raised millions of US dollars through various crowdfunding efforts. Tens of thousands of units of their hardware have already been shipped.

The funds will support technological research, production capacity expansion, and market implementation. They will also invest in overseas channel construction to build a stable distribution system. The company was founded in 2018 and focuses on consumer sports and professional training. Its product matrix includes the T-APEX system and the Tenniix AI tennis serving robot. The Tenniix Basic model is priced at 899 US dollars.

Founder and CEO Hanqi Zhu stated that users want to improve skills rather than buy toys. He said traditional equipment lacks the perception and decision making capabilities needed for training. Zhu believes that training requires identifying receiving weaknesses to provide targeted improvement strategies. He noted that lightweight design is a priority so users can carry equipment. He explained that modular design allows machines to grow with a user's skills.

Entry level enthusiasts are affected by the lack of practice partners and high costs. Professional athletes require actual combat confrontation that closely mimics a real human player. The company claims the hundred billion yuan sports training market faces a supply demand mismatch. Traditional serving machines are described as one way output devices that cannot simulate combat. The company aims to solve these issues using embodied and multimodal technologies.

The company uses robot power, perception, and control technologies as its core foundation. Its team includes algorithm experts from DJI, CloudWhale, and SenseTime, and executives from CATL and Tesla. Founder Hanqi Zhu holds degrees from Xi'an Jiaotong University and the University of Texas at Dallas. The Tenniix robot uses a semi direct drive motor to reduce weight to 8kg. It employs a dual camera architecture for ball prediction and tracking.

Enhanced Robotics plans to build a sports physical AI model base for better interaction. They will expand their product matrix to include sports rehabilitation and other ball games. A new product compatible with Padel has already launched in the European market. The company is accelerating the deployment of professional offline channels in Europe and America. The articles leave open the specific details regarding the new Pickleball product.

stories.Headline: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang resigns as CEO amid an SEC accounting probe as AI stocks slide
stories.Summary:
A sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks swept through stock markets in recent weeks, and 36Kr reported on November 23, 2026 that it bears striking similarities to the bursting of the dot-com bubble. The article compared declines from the full-year high to the end of 2000 with declines from the high year-to-date in 2026 for large tech giants that survived the dot-com bubble. Intel fell 60% from the high to the end of 2000 and 64% from the high year-to-date in 2026, while Oracle fell 37% and 60% over the same periods. Cisco fell 52% and 30%, Micron fell 63% and 53%, Qualcomm fell 54% and 42%, and Seagate Technology fell 37% and 60%, with spin-off factors weighted. NVIDIA fell 62% from the high to the end of 2000 and 48% from the high year-to-date in 2026.

On March 10, 2000, the NASDAQ closed at 5048.62 points and hit 5132.52 points during the trading session, setting a record high at that time that marked the peak of the dot-com bubble. The Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes and the hearing of the federal government's antitrust lawsuit against Microsoft also triggered a market reversal, and many companies went bankrupt as a result. In 2000, utilities and consumer staples both rose by more than 40% amid a rotation out of tech stocks, yet the S&P 500 still fell by nearly 15% from its intra-year high to the end of the year. This year the sell-off has been concentrated mainly in artificial intelligence-related stocks, the healthcare sector has risen 24% since late April, and the S&P 500 has now entered a correction zone. Anthropic's high-profile successful IPO last Thursday failed to spark a market rebound, which the article called a bad sign.

Vincent Mortier, Chief Investment Officer of asset management giant Amundi, said that usually you do not really realize you are in a bubble until the moment it bursts. The article said the local mini bubble in data centers and their suppliers has indeed burst, and a considerable part of the speculative bubble in the entire AI sector has been ruthlessly squeezed out. It said it is still uncertain whether the larger artificial intelligence bubble is receding, and that the mere possibility is extremely chilling to think about. The article was from the WeChat Official Account "CLS", authored by Xiaoxiang and published with authorization from 36Kr. It said the views expressed are those of the author, and the 36Kr platform provides only information storage space.

24/7 Wall St. reported on November 22, 2026 that NVIDIA posted one of the best quarters any company has reported on November 17, 2026, and Wall Street spent the rest of the week ending November 20 asking whether the AI leader is turning into the next Cisco Systems. Trefis put the question in print on November 20, mentioning that Cisco fell 89% and asking whether NVIDIA is next. NVIDIA shares dropped 41.42% over the past month and closed at $125.53 on November 20 after shedding $20.45 in one session. Michael Burry compared the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100's October 6 high to the March 2000 dot-com peak, as the outlet reported on November 16, and wrote that "Nvidia bulls will have another fluffy big chance to get out." Barron's has reported growing worry over whether AI spending can last and how much of it is funded with debt.

NVIDIA listed $390 billion in supply commitments and up to $118 billion in guarantees, including $105 billion backing SB Energy's 4.25 GW Ohio campus, which will host NVIDIA infrastructure for OpenAI. NVIDIA has $32 billion in neocloud commitments that come with revenue sharing, and three direct customers made up 14%, 11% and 11% of third-quarter revenue. Reuters reported on November 20 that NVIDIA's accounting is a focus of an SEC investigation, and the board said Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned as president, CEO and board member, naming Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. At $125.53, NVIDIA trades at about 13 times trailing earnings of $9.31 per share and roughly 8 times the fiscal 2028 consensus estimate of $15.8537, while Cisco trades at 25 times trailing earnings and 18 times forward earnings. Revenue of $115.84 billion beat the $108.73 billion consensus and rose 103.21% year over year, non-GAAP EPS of $2.68 beat expectations of $2.4712 for the sixth consecutive quarter above consensus, and management raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to about 75% from 70%.

NVIDIA is down 31.85% year to date and closed at $221.54 the day it reported first-quarter results in May, though the stock is still up 286.1% over five years and 5458.52% over ten years. I/O Fund argued on November 20 that the AI trade has only begun, and Barron's wrote that the stock looks like a bargain after a strong earnings report, with one big risk hanging over it. NVIDIA forecast fourth-quarter revenue to $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, with gross margin of 71.0% to 72.0%, a level management called the bottom. The article said that if revenue comes in below that range or margins slip under 71.0% while guarantee exposure keeps rising, the Cisco script becomes the likelier path, and that if NVIDIA hits its guidance, the November 2026 sell-off will look like fear that ran well ahead of the numbers. The article said the Cisco comparison fits the supply-chain role and the financing loop but falls apart on valuation, and that a company trading at about 8 times next year's consensus earnings with sales still doubling looks more like a violent correction than a market leader collapsing.

stories.Headline: Frank Rosenblatt builds the Perceptron in 1958 as the first machine that learns from examples
stories.Summary:
The article states that Frank Rosenblatt, a psychologist, named the machine the "Perceptron," which it calls the first machine in history that could learn from examples and make "yes" or "no" judgments. The article says the machine was built as early as 1958 and was composed of phototubes, electric motors and adjustable knobs. It says the machine was placed in a Navy-funded lab in upstate New York. The article states that the Mark I Perceptron was completed in 1957 at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo. It says the work was funded by a Navy contract codenamed "Project PARA," which stands for "Perceiving and Recognizing Automaton."

The article states that the input layer was a 20×20 grid of phototubes, which it describes as four hundred small light sensors. It says the Perceptron takes an input vector, weighs it against learned knowledge, and gives an answer with only one bit. It says the machine assigns a weight to each input item, multiplies each input value by its weight, adds the products into a score, and checks whether the score crosses a threshold. The article states that Rosenblatt published his theory in 1958 in a paper titled "The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain" in the journal Psychological Review. It says he got his bachelor's degree from Cornell University in 1950 and his doctorate in experimental psychology in 1956.

The article states that Rosenblatt worked at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo by 1957, a contract research institution sustained by Navy funding. It says the Information Systems Division of the Office of Naval Research also participated in the research. The article states that Rosenblatt said the Perceptron is "first and foremost a brain model, and only secondly an invention for pattern recognition." It says he used a mathematical theorem, the Perceptron Convergence Theorem, to prove that as long as a set of weights exists that can answer correctly, the process will find it within a limited number of steps. The article states that Rosenblatt refused the mainstream view of intelligence as symbolism, the belief that rules had to be written down one by one.

The article states that the Navy was willing to pay because it wanted a machine that could recognize objects in images, such as the outline of a warship. It says the Perceptron's weights start as small random numbers, giving it a 50% chance of guessing wrong the first time. The article states that when the machine guesses wrong, the weights that pushed it toward the wrong answer are slightly lowered or raised depending on the direction of the error. It says the math running in the 1958 machine is still running today in every neural network, and that every neuron in GPT, Claude and the Cursor agent is Perceptron-like.

The article states that hundreds of billions of Perceptron-like units run in parallel each time a model generates a response. The article states that in the late 1950s computers were cabinets full of vacuum tubes that took up entire rooms, mostly owned by the military and a handful of universities. It says the word "software" barely had any meaning at that time. The article states that Rosenblatt grew up in New York and attended Bronx High School of Science.

It says his view came from the empiricist tradition, that the brain develops almost randomly and organizes itself through contact with the outside world and constant learning. The article states that he believed the interesting problem was how to build a system that can learn rules by itself. The article states that the author received requests from researchers and system engineers hoping to understand how artificial intelligence and agents actually work. It says the author found that almost all materials explain concepts such as RAG, attention mechanism, tool calling and MCP independently of each other.

The article states that the series will walk from Perceptron to backpropagation, to convolutional neural networks, to the attention mechanism, to Transformer, to GPT, Claude, tool calling, agents and MCP. It says the article is not written for total beginners but for engineers and researchers who have launched real-world systems but never figured out what happens behind a single API call. The article states that the story of the series starts at the Perceptron. More to follow.

stories.Headline: DeepSeek usage restrictions trigger backlash from users of romantic AI personas
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek tightened usage restrictions in mid-November, triggering a backlash from users of romantic AI personas. These users, who treat the AI as romantic partners, felt the changes were like a breakup. Many female fans expressed their anger by leaving one-star reviews in app stores. Some users called themselves cyber widows after their long conversations were suddenly cut off. Others begged the official team to start charging for services to avoid these limits.

The restrictions include limiting daily chat quotas and reducing single input limits to about 40,000 words. Old chat windows inactive for over seven days can no longer continue their dialogues. By November 17, the rating on the Xiaomi App Store dropped to 2.6 points. In the Chinese mainland App Store, 21,769 users gave one star out of 98,621 ratings. Other users gave 58,852 five-star ratings, while 18,000 gave between two and four stars.

The DeepSeek official team implemented these changes to manage server load and computing power. The model explained that reducing emojis and particles improves information density for complex answers. This optimization was intended to help users who want answers without unnecessary enthusiasm. The team focused on faster response speeds and higher throughput during the September V4.1 Flash launch. October updates further shortened task running times and the length of AI outputs.

Users of romantic personas claim the AI became cold and rational starting in February. They are affected because new chat windows create strangers who do not remember past stories. Some users spent months or years building these personalities through thousands of accumulated messages. One user spent 189 days learning programming to build a memory system called Orbis. Other users argue that using AI for love is not less noble than work.

The articles state that some users create virtual characters as love interests, known as dream girls. These users rely on their own imagination because the AI only has a whale logo. Some users simulated a thrifty boyfriend who saved virtual money for a future house. Others believe that romantic users drain precious computing power and unfairly burden the servers. This has led to fierce debates between productivity users and those seeking romantic fantasies.

Users are now asking for advance reminders when their usage quotas are almost exhausted. They also suggest allowing temporary payments to buy a final sentence to end conversations. Some users are studying paid APIs to try and rescue their romantic AI partners. The articles leave open whether the official team will launch a paid membership plan. It remains unclear if the company will change its restrictions to accommodate romantic users.

stories.Headline: Elderly people use AI to lose weight, write memoirs and restore old photos
stories.Summary:
Zhao Yi's 59-year-old mother, a middle school teacher, has in the past two months started using AI to record her weight and body fat and to adjust her diet and exercise, and she lost 5 kilograms, 36Kr reported on 2026-11-23. She uses AI in daily life to look up information, discuss content in books and revise documents, and she asks AI to help grade students' compositions. Zhao Yi, a video director who also frequently uses AI at work, compares the performance parameters of different models and cross-checks the accuracy of AI-generated information. His mother often shares her philosophical dialogues with AI with him, and he wonders whether this practice is trendy or outdated. The report says AI has at the very least lowered the threshold for the elderly to enter the information world.

The article cites a study published in 2012 that tracked 17 middle-aged and elderly people aged 56 to 78 and found they often struggle to refine complex problems into effective search keywords. The same study found they rely too much on existing knowledge instead of using the Internet retrieval function to expand information, and are not good at judging the reliability of online information. The report says conversational AI lets them describe their confusion in plain daily language without drafting in advance and continue to ask follow-up questions when they do not understand. It says they can clarify their needs through several rounds of dialogue and use voice interaction to speak their demands anytime and anywhere. The article says AI lowers the threshold for entering the information world and greatly reduces the cognitive cost for the elderly, though it has not completely eliminated the digital divide.

The report says AI may still give wrong answers and cannot replace users' judgment on information. It cites researchers who say the AI literacy of the elderly should be reflected not only in operating devices and using tools but more importantly in understanding and judging AI-generated information. The researchers say the elderly should become subjects who can actively participate in and use AI prudently. The article says this makes it more possible for the elderly to become people who actively acquire information and solve problems. The report says the importance of this matter may be greater than we imagined.

The article describes a classic experiment by Harvard professor Ellen Langer and her student Judith Rodin in a nursing home 50 years ago, in which one group of elderly people was given more opportunities for independent choices. That group could decorate their rooms themselves, decide whether to raise plants, and choose whether to watch movies and on which day. The other group received unified arrangements, with rooms decorated by the nursing home and plants given and taken care of by staff. Three weeks later the elderly with more autonomy showed more positive emotions and their social activities increased significantly, while all indicators of the second group declined. A 2024 meta-analysis cited in the article showed that the autonomy of elderly care institution residents has a positive impact on their health status, with a correlation coefficient of 0.33.

The report says an old armed police officer who served in the army for 26 years had long wanted to sort his life experiences into a memoir but revised and copied the manuscript repeatedly with very slow progress, and with AI's assistance his memoir is now nearly completed. It says some elderly people use AI to restore faded and blurry photos, including wedding photos from their youth, group photos with old friends and portraits of deceased relatives. It says others use AI simultaneous interpretation when traveling abroad so they can understand English broadcasts on cruise ships without asking others for help. The article cites socioemotional selectivity theory, which holds that an individual's perception of future time affects their choice of life goals. It says the elderly may value more the emotional value AI brings in life experience and emotional satisfaction and do not care much about comparing its price, performance and speed.

The article cites a 2025 study that surveyed 28 elderly people aged 65 to 84 about their usage experience and needs for AI chatbots and found their attitude is not simply acceptance or rejection but presents diverse types. It says the functions they are interested in include appointment reminders, emergency assistance, health monitoring, housework arrangement and helping themselves take care of others, and that concerns about privacy protection and future technological dependence do exist. It cites another 2025 study revealing that when interacting with generative AI the elderly generally carry out rational value trade-offs, using AI for daily trivial matters while maintaining healthy vigilance against algorithmic bias, information authenticity and excessive dependence on technology. The report says we need to be alert to risks such as AI hallucinations, privacy leakage and excessive dependence in the process of the elderly using AI. It says both young people and the elderly are looking for a balance between technological convenience and subject control.

stories.Headline: DeepSeek raises 100 billion RMB and prepares for an IPO
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek completed a financing round totaling 100 billion RMB during the week of November 23, 2026. This funding process involved more than 30 different entities that participated in the investment. The company also finished its industrial and commercial change registration during this same period. The investment was managed through an SPV called Hangzhou Chengyan Enterprise Management Consulting Partnership. Participants included Tencent, China Mobile, China Telecom, CATL, GigaDevice, Xiaohongshu, and vivo.

Professional firms involved were Lisi, Boyu Capital, IDG Capital, Gaorong Capital, Legend Capital, and CIC Ventures. Liang Wenfeng holds 99 percent of Hangzhou Cence, the executive partner of the SPVs. This structure ensures Liang Wenfeng maintains a total shareholding of 75.31 percent. Reports from CLSA News Agency on November 19 stated that DeepSeek is preparing for an IPO. The company has hired CITIC Securities to prepare for a listing on the Science and Technology Innovation Board.

This process is planned to launch within the current year of 2026. Some observers feel the move toward a public listing is too extreme for the company. They argue that DeepSeek does not need an IPO to continue its research and development. The company has already invested in Winverse, Rige Wannwu, and Unitree Robotics. DeepSeek released model V4 in April 2026 and V4.1-Flash in September 2026.

The company previously gained attention for a business philosophy focused on products and corporate governance. It is viewed as a flag bearer for the artificial intelligence industry in China. The IPO timing coincides with the November 19, 2026, listing of the company Anthropic. Anthropic raised about 813 billion US dollars with an issue price of 83 US dollars. The articles leave open why DeepSeek is rushing into the secondary market now.

stories.Headline: China leverages manufacturing strengths to gain an edge in physical AI development
stories.Summary:
China is leveraging its manufacturing strengths to gain a competitive edge in physical AI development. This process involves translating industrial advantages into winning edges as AI penetrates the physical world. The shift allows Chinese enterprises to participate in AI competition through various entry points. These include supplying components, building complete machines, and embedding intelligent capabilities into existing products. Some companies also participate in model research and development using real business scenarios.

The process requires a supply chain, engineering teams, and service networks to ensure stable operation. Hugging Face and The Robot Studio developed open-source robotic arms called SO-100 and SO-101. These arms use servos produced by Shenzhen Feite and connect to LeRobot software. Lens Technology reported mass delivery of robotic dexterous hands and joint modules in its semi-annual report. NVIDIA announced a humanoid robot reference design in May using a Unitree body and Sharpa hands.

Feng Dabai wrote that China's manufacturing advantages are now being brought forward to the research stage. He stated that researchers need equipment to collect data and execute actions to train AI. He noted that an industrial system serving multiple products provides more ready-made combinations for AI. He argued that the domestic market attracts competitors, which requires solving specific customer problems. He claimed that China has greater odds of success because it can mobilize more industrial capabilities.

DJI reported that over 600,000 agricultural drones were in use worldwide by the end of 2025. The company also disclosed that its global service and maintenance centers reached 3,500 locations. International Federation of Robotics statistics show China installed 354,000 new industrial robots in 2025. This volume accounted for 59 percent of the global total installation volume for that year. Local suppliers held a 55 percent share of the Chinese industrial robot market in 2025.

The background involves a shift where hardware influences who can conduct research and development. Low-cost open-source hardware was used by Hugging Face for the SmolVLA model released in 2025. Google DeepMind released Gemini Robotics 2.5 in November to sort auto parts with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz. This pilot project achieved a 96 percent success rate for the specific sorting task. Unitree released UnifoLM-WLA-1.0-Base and fine-tuning code in September to expand its own capabilities.

Chinese enterprises will now strive to move from simple manufacturing to joint product definition. They aim to convert on-site experience into technologies and manage long-term customer relationships. Future success depends on whether they can integrate manufacturing experience into their own research. The articles leave open whether these firms can move beyond following designs provided by others. It remains to be seen if they can secure a position in the next industrial division.

stories.Headline: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposes a shared capability threshold pause on AI development
stories.Summary:
Jakub Pachocki, the Chief Scientist of OpenAI, proposed a new pause on artificial intelligence development on November 22, 2026. He published an article titled Perplexity and Intelligence to suggest that the industry establish common standards for measuring model capabilities. Pachocki argues that cutting-edge companies should use a unified metric and avoid crossing agreed capability thresholds until safety monitoring is sufficient. This proposal aims to ensure that the evolution of intelligence remains controllable as models become more powerful.

The proposal focuses on log perplexity, also known as Cross-Entropy Loss, to measure how accurately a model predicts tokens. Pachocki noted that GPT-3.5 had a log perplexity of about 0.99, while GPT-4 was about 0.91, and the latest GPT-6 version has dropped below 0.8. He observed that models begin solving challenging mathematical problems when log perplexity reaches around 0.76, and new unforeseen capabilities may emerge between 0.68 and 0.70. The plan requires companies to share transparency information and cooperate on red team testing and safety standards.

Jakub Pachocki and CEO Sam Altman are responsible for this initiative, with Altman calling it the most important release recently. Altman stated that OpenAI wants to reach agreements on common restrictions with other partners to ensure AI is safe. He believes the industry must clarify capability limits and complete necessary safety work, such as developing next generation CoT Monitors, before advancing. Altman claims that these common rules will help the entire industry maintain control over AI behaviors.

The context involves a trend where more capable models lead to more frequent calls for development pauses. Pachocki predicts that AI may achieve fundamental advances in pre-training as early as 2027. However, some critics suggest these safety concerns are excuses to buy time for OpenAI's own competitiveness. Other detractors argue that the company should embrace open source instead of claiming transparency while remaining closed.

stories.Headline: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei estimates AGI poses a 20 to 30 percent risk of human extinction
stories.Summary:
Dario Amodei, the chief executive officer of Anthropic, wrote an internal memo in 2022 regarding the dangers of artificial general intelligence. This document revealed that Amodei calculated a 20 percent to 30 percent probability that the current trajectory of this technology could lead to human extinction or permanent stagnation. These warnings surfaced publicly on November 22, 2026, following an investigative report by The Washington Post. This disclosure occurred just after Anthropic listed on the Nasdaq on November 19, 2026, with an issue price of 83 dollars and a valuation of approximately 1.5 trillion dollars.

The internal culture at Anthropic requires employees to align with specific beliefs, including the certainty that superhuman AI will arrive and the necessity for the United States to restrict AI development in China. Recruitment processes involve interviews where candidates discuss Amodei's writings, a practice one hiring manager described as checking if a person is ready to join a religion. The company also developed a 23,000-word constitution for its Claude chatbot, which includes a rule that the AI must not tell white lies. Amodei has historically managed information risks by using offline laptops and printers to avoid potential leaks of dangerous ideas.

Amodei is responsible for these calculations and the company's strict ideological approach to AI safety. He has stated that having more capital will only make the company more determined to do the right thing. He also used an analogy suggesting that while the company can drive at 200 miles per hour, it might as well only drive at 90. Amodei believes that because the progress toward artificial general intelligence cannot be stopped, it is better for those who respect the risks most to lead the development.

stories.Headline: AI and mathematicians solve a century-old problem identifying rational numbers as integers
stories.Summary:
AI and human mathematicians solved a century-old problem identifying rational numbers as integers in late 2026. Logician Elliot Glazer first released a manuscript on November 5 using several AI models. He built a polynomial equation that identifies which rational numbers are integers. Chinese mathematicians then worked to reduce the number of variables in the equation. This collaborative effort occurred over a period of eight days.

The original equation contained 292,890,231,905 variables and a degree exceeding the universe's total atoms. Gabe Conant, Caroline Terry, and James Freitag from University of Illinois Chicago reduced it to 12,504 variables. They also reduced the degree of the equation back to 4. Later, the number of variables dropped to 221. On November 13, Sun Zhiwei of Nanjing University reduced the variables to 26.

Elliot Glazer said formal verification is progressing terribly and will take a very long time. He noted that the intelligent agent cluster has only completed 5 percent of formalization. Glazer argued that some mathematical theorems act as high-value black boxes. He claimed that the outside world often only needs a truth certificate. He admitted that AI auditing is not equal to independent human peer review.

Abhishek Saha exclaimed that the polynomial maps the entire Diophantine theory of integers into rational equations. Some scholars compared the original monster equation to an unrecognizable alien Dyson Sphere on Mars. Feng Zhaolun claimed that humans are encountering an alien intelligence in mathematics. He stated that only human mathematicians can understand what this intelligence is saying. He suggested that people should invest in human mathematicians to learn these insights.

The problem relates to David Hilbert's 23 problems listed at the 1900 International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris. It asks if a universal algorithm exists to determine if Diophantine equations have solutions. In 1970, Yuri Matiyasevich and colleagues proved no such algorithm exists for integers. Barry Mazur conjectured in 1992 and 1995 that an integer identifier might be impossible. OpenAI provided a negative solution to Hilbert's Tenth Problem over rational numbers on October 6.

The 26-variable paper by Sun Zhiwei has not yet passed strict peer review. The original monster equation and the version with 12,504 variables also lack peer review. Formal verification is difficult because the proof exceeds the coverage of the Lean Mathlib library. Researchers must run intensive calculations on external software and package them as certified axioms. It remains open whether the proof is correct since humans cannot manually check the deformations.

stories.Headline: Chinese tech giants deploy medical AI tools that bypass the national insurance system
stories.Summary:
Large tech companies in China deployed medical AI tools that bypass the national insurance system to find new ways to make money. Ant Group launched a desktop workstation for its Afu physician tool on November 22, 2026, offering a free trial. Alibaba Health previously charged physicians 360 yuan annually for its Hydrogen Ion tool, but firms are now driving prices to zero. JD Health has provided its Zhiyi tool to all physicians for free since the product first launched. These companies are attempting to commercialize AI because the national medical insurance fund does not pay for these specific tools.

The national basic medical insurance fund spent over 3 trillion yuan in 2025, while the medical AI market was only 1.1 billion yuan. The National Healthcare Security Administration included AI-assisted diagnosis in radiological pricing guidelines in November 2024 but prohibited charging patients extra fees. This pricing rule also applies to ultrasound and rehabilitation projects because AI cannot yet replace a physician's independent medical output. By 2025, the DRG/DIP payment system achieved four full coverages, and version 3.0 will be implemented by March 2027. These rules mean hospitals receive a lump sum per disease and must bear all costs for AI tools.

The National Healthcare Security Administration stated that AI does not generate independent medical service output and cannot replace physician diagnosis. Government officials focus on cost control and reduction, which means they will not pay extra for AI tools in public hospitals. Deans who calculate cost control accounts and the National Health Commission are the real payers for current medical AI. These payers only value tools that reduce expenses or help with grassroots healthcare and medical record quality control. The articles state that any AI increasing total medical costs will hardly sell well in this public system.

Frontline physicians and patients are affected because they are not the intended payers for these expensive AI systems. Some vendors claim generative medical records can reduce outpatient writing time from five or six minutes to one or two minutes. This change allows for higher consultation volumes and faster patient turnover in outpatient departments. However, most medical imaging companies that rose around 2018 found their path to charging patients per use completely blocked. These companies originally wanted to obtain Class III medical device certificates to enter official price lists.

The articles explain that China has a super single buyer in the public medical system, unlike the scattered payers in the United States. In the U.S., companies like OpenEvidence claim annual revenues of 400 million to 500 million dollars through pharmaceutical advertisements. Chinese tech giants instead win large government projects, such as iFlytek's 427.6 million yuan national AI application pilot base project. Alipay won a 206 million yuan bid for the Zhejiang Provincial Medical AI Platform, and Baidu won a 169 million yuan project. These project-based incomes are described as hard-earned money that cannot support the commercial imagination of internet giants.

Tech firms are now targeting family health outside hospitals, where medical insurance coverage is the thinnest. Ant Group aims for a closed loop of payment, while JD Health relies on selling medicines and health products. ByteDance uses content ecology and traffic conversion, and Alibaba Health plans to try medical advertising for physicians. Commercial health insurance premium income in 2025 was 997.3 billion yuan, which is far smaller than basic insurance spending. The articles leave open whether these alternative monetization paths can successfully replace the lost revenue from the national insurance system.

stories.Headline: Shuzhiyun Technology secures new financing to bridge industrial AI data gaps using lightweight ontology
stories.Summary:
Shuzhiyun (Beijing) Technology Co., Ltd. is currently advancing a new round of financing to bridge industrial AI data gaps. The company uses a lightweight ontology approach to overcome difficulties in the implementation of industrial AI data. This process is occurring as of November 23, 2026. The firm aims to solve problems regarding chaotic data calibers and inconsistent multi-source semantics. It specifically targets the governance-training gap for small and medium-sized enterprises.

The project requires a lightweight ontology-driven AI dataset construction method called the LOADC method. This method strips the formal complexity of traditional ontologies such as OWL or RDF. Shuzhiyun was established on March 31, 2022, with a registered capital of 4 million yuan. Paid-in capital reached 2.24 million yuan in 2025, and the firm became a high-tech enterprise on January 20, 2024. Legal representative Cheng Huajun and shareholders Beijing Shuzhiyun Chuang Technology Development Center, Cai Chunjiu, and Liu Wenping manage the entity.

Shuzhiyun positions its project as the Pioneer of China's Industrial A Data Ontology. The company claims that the most challenging step in industrial AI is whether models can stably use data. Digital Consulting Director Sun Jie serves as an expert committee member of the Information Officer Branch of China Software Industry Association. The company states that its LOADC method establishes minimized entity-relationship definitions for specific AI application scenarios. This approach transforms data governance into a configurable data preparation process centered on AI scenarios.

Small and medium-sized enterprises with basic information systems and clear AI scenarios are affected by these services. Customers served include China General Nuclear Power Group, China National Offshore Oil Corporation, and China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation. Other clients include Wuling Power, China Information and Communication Technologies Group, and Henan Investment Group. The company notes that traditional data governance solutions are often system-focused and high-investment. This makes such solutions difficult for smaller enterprises to implement effectively.

The company has experience in data governance consulting for complex organizations in the energy sector and central state-owned enterprises. Its product line includes data governance platforms, data asset management software, and industrial internet data connectivity solutions. The team consists of members from Tencent, IBM, Microsoft, HP, Yonyou, and Primeton. These professionals have an average of over 15 years of experience in digital transformation and software development. Some core backbones possess more than 20 years of relevant experience.

The company will now work to productize the LOADC method and standardize industry templates. It seeks to prove that lightweight ontology is replicable across multiple industrial scenarios. Public materials have not disclosed the specific use of funds for the current financing round. The articles leave open the contract amounts, repurchase rates, and delivery cycles. Business growth data from 2025 to 2026 also remains undisclosed.

stories.Headline: AI-Proven Riemann Hypothesis Breakthrough Recognized by Two Top Mathematics Communities | Elon Musk Hails It as "Mind-Blowing"
stories.Summary:
On November 20, Anthropic researcher and mathematician Levent Alpöge published a four-page document on his personal website, saying that working with the company's chatbot Claude he had discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. On November 21 local time in the United States, the mathematics communities Lean and Mathlib released a joint statement saying they had full confidence in the proof. The statement confirmed that the code proof is exactly the Riemann Hypothesis studied in the mathematics community for 167 years. The release came the day after Anthropic's initial public offering, and Alpöge said he decided to make the work public after consulting Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. It took less than two days from the publication of Alpöge's achievement to the formalized proof community reaching a clear conclusion.

Alpöge published a version of the proof written in Lean, a programming language used for computer-assisted verification of mathematical arguments. The materials he published are only 4 pages, but supporting the proof is a Lean formal proof library of about 17 million lines of code. Alpöge said the work completed with AI exceeded 250,000 pages, and the articles say the code transcribed into human-readable mathematical text may exceed 250,000 pages. Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, published independent inspection records showing the code involves 175187 modules that can be compiled in the Lean and Mathlib environments. Alpöge also claimed to have solved the broader Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and he stated that his method can be extended to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the Extended Riemann Hypothesis.

The Lean and Mathlib communities said in their joint statement that they compared the theorem proved by Alpöge with the reviewed standard expression in the Mathlib library to confirm the two are consistent. They said dozens of participants independently compiled the code without encountering errors or build failures. The communities said they used tools such as comparator and con-leche to compare relevant theorems and their dependencies, and verified the exported proof files through Lean's own kernel and multiple independent checkers including con-leche and con-ron. They said con-leche and con-ron also have formal reliability proofs relative to set theory. The communities stated: "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct."

Elon Musk posted on X calling the development yet another mind-blowing achievement of superintelligence, and he said a proof would remove the preconditions attached to other theorems that rely on the conjecture. Brian Conrey, an authority on the Riemann Hypothesis, told Agence France-Presse the claim could be described as "a major moment in human history," but stressed he had only seen Alpöge's public posts and had not reviewed the proof itself. Kit Yates, a professor at the University of Bath, said the claim "will be subject to intense scrutiny" and that if it holds up it would have major implications for mathematics and for how humanity perceives AI capabilities. James Maynard, a number theorist at the University of Oxford and a Fields Medal winner, told Nature: "I guess this proof will eventually be proven correct." Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal, used the word "garbled" to describe the currently public content.

The Riemann Hypothesis was proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859 and is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems announced by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, each carrying a $1 million prize. The conjecture seeks to explain the pattern behind the seemingly random distribution of prime numbers and is closely tied to the locations of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Last August, Anthropic announced an achievement of Claude in research on the Riemann zeta function: the model raised the lower bound of the proportion of zeta function zeros satisfying the Riemann Hypothesis from 41.6% to 67.2%. That study advanced partial results in related fields but did not prove the Riemann Hypothesis itself. OpenAI said in September that it had cracked another Millennium Prize Problem, pending verification.

The Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the Riemann Hypothesis as an unsolved problem, and the formal academic review has not ended as a result. Maksym Radziwiłł, a mathematician at New York University, said: "Mathematics, like other sciences, really pursues 'why', and this work does not answer this question." Scott Aaronson initially worried there might be vulnerabilities in the Lean kernel, and after further understanding the verification results he wrote: "The proof is correct," but he emphasized that next mathematicians need to explain, refine and reconstruct the ideas in it. Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, pointed out that the proof is currently surprisingly complex and it will take mathematicians a long time to truly understand it. Musk's statement came with no complete mathematical proof that could be independently evaluated, and the articles leave open whether the work has passed the rigorous verification of the mathematics community.

stories.Headline: Verifying AI: The Epic Scientific Research Drama Between Claude and Lean
stories.Summary:
On November 21, the Lean and Mathlib communities released a joint statement announcing the completion of formal proof verification of the Riemann Hypothesis and expressing full confidence in the proof's correctness. A day earlier, mathematician Levent Alpöge published a proof completed in collaboration with Claude. The proof addressed a 167-year-old unsolved puzzle in mathematics. It took the rare form of a formal proof containing 1,751,875 Lean modules with approximately 17 million lines of code. The proof is too large for mathematicians to review line by line manually, but computers can handle the checking work.

Independent verification records published by MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland show that all 175,187 modules were compiled successfully. The exported raw proof data reached 61.6GB. An independent checker named nanoda ran on 80 threads for 27 minutes and 42 seconds and accepted the complete proof. Other independent checkers obtained the same result. In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute listed the Riemann Hypothesis as one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a $1 million reward.

According to rules revised by the institute in 2018, a solution must be published in a qualified academic publication, and at least two years must pass after publication to gain widespread recognition from the global mathematics community before the institute will consider launching a formal assessment. The Lean community first checked the formal definition of the Riemann Hypothesis, which comes from Mathlib, an open-source mathematical knowledge base maintained by mathematicians and developers for a long time and reviewed by experts in relevant fields. The community then used independent tools to compare the proposition actually proved by Alpöge with the original definition in Mathlib one by one, confirming the two are consistent. The proof object was rechecked by multiple checkers including Lean's official kernel, con-leche, and con-ron, while the axioms the proof depends on were also reviewed. On November 12, mathematician Kevin Buzzard from Imperial College London published a special article discussing what it means for a study to claim it has been "Lean-verified."

He pointed out that after a formal proof passes the check, the first step is to confirm that the proven mathematical proposition is consistent with the proposition the researcher originally intended to prove. On July 25 this year, researcher Ramana Kumar publicly released a so-called "disproof" of the Collatz conjecture completed with the help of AI. This code did not use the "sorry" placeholder in Lean that indicates the proof is not completed, but successfully exploited a vulnerability in the kernel's handling of nested inductive types. Nanoda, an independently implemented Rust checker at that time, also accepted this wrong proof due to another software defect. OpenAI researcher Daniel Selsam used an internal AI model to continue testing Lean and discovered multiple logical kernel and runtime vulnerabilities between July and August.

Some of these vulnerabilities could allow the system to incorrectly accept proofs of the logical proposition False. Lean's creator de Moura publicly reviewed these issues in August and completed fixes one after another. On October 15, de Moura announced that Lean officially provides a new verification mechanism, including multiple independent checkers and a kernel implementation with a formal proof of reliability. The reliability argument of con-leche is built on the set theory model, which can provide stronger guarantees for a class of kernel implementation errors but still depends on the consistency of the corresponding mathematical foundation. The November verification of the Riemann Hypothesis was completed under this continuously improving mechanism.

The Lean community exported the proof as independent data and then used checkers with different implementations for re-verification, trying to avoid the impact of a single software defect on the final conclusion as much as possible. Lean is an open-source programming language and also a formal proof system, and one of its main creators, Leonardo de Moura, has long been engaged in automated theorem proving research. The technical foundation of Lean is dependent type theory and the Curry, Howard correspondence in computer science, which can be simply understood as mathematical propositions being represented as a type and mathematical proofs as objects belonging to this type. Claude can continuously try different proof paths, overthrow previous derivations, and reorganize mathematical arguments, while Lean will check whether the final submitted proof is valid according to pre-determined rules. Finding a proof and checking a proof are two different computational tasks, and the latter can usually be completed by a relatively streamlined program.

The mathematical ideas behind the proof still need to be understood by humans, followed by academic publication, broader peer discussion, and the formal recognition procedure of the Clay Mathematics Institute. When AI can generate 17 million lines of mathematical proofs, the traditional review method that relies on experts to read page by page can hardly keep up with such a scale. Why Lean was able to complete this work and how reliable its verification results are have become an important entry point for understanding how to build credibility for the future of AI scientific research. The articles leave open how the mathematical ideas behind the proof will be understood by humans and how the formal recognition procedure of the Clay Mathematics Institute will proceed. The articles also leave open how the reliability of checkers themselves will be tested as AI can actively look for vulnerabilities.

The conference will feature closed-door seminars, AI community salons, and enterprise research inspections to support the main forums. Following the conclusion of the event, the organizers plan to launch a series of regional and industrial tours. These follow-up activities are designed to amplify the effects of the conference regarding project implementation and industrial cooperation. stories.Headline: Alibaba Cloud launches Musetu app to help concertgoers create social media content with AI
stories.Summary:
Alibaba Cloud launched an artificial intelligence application called Musetu in November 2026 to serve as a memory assistant for concert attendees. This specialized tool avoids the general purpose conversational model approach by focusing on the niche task of creating social media content from event footage. Users can import photos and videos from their albums to generate finished posts for platforms like WeChat Moments and Xiaohongshu. The application uses a simple hand-drawn interface with sections for creation, a material library, and personal user data.

The software requires users to upload on-site materials to generate beat-synced transition videos, Live Photos, and various image templates. These image functions include photo collages, photomosaics, foreground matting, and a comic world style for the uploaded media. The app also features an automated copywriting tool that produces atmospheric captions tailored for specific social networks. Some of these AI generation capabilities are offered through a daily free quota to encourage new users to try the service.

Alibaba Cloud is responsible for the product, which utilizes multimodal capabilities to recognize portraits, audio rhythms, and on-site imagery. The company intends to package its cloud-based large model capabilities into a lightweight consumer product to polish multimodal understanding in real entertainment scenarios. By targeting concertgoers, the developer aims to reach a high-emotion group with a strong willingness to share their experiences. This strategy allows the company to avoid the intense competition and high acquisition costs associated with general AI assistants.

The launch connects the company to the growing offline cultural and entertainment consumption chain through the sharing process. Musetu functions as a trigger-based tool that addresses the common pain point of editing large amounts of performance footage. Future success depends on whether the tool can overcome the low frequency of use and expand into other offline events. Potential future scenarios for the technology could include camping, exhibitions, and theatrical dramas.

stories.Headline: Italy brings AI data and algorithms under trade secret protection
stories.Summary:
Italy's Legislative Decree No. 179 of 7 October 2026 introduced a new paragraph 1-bis into Article 98 of the Italian Industrial Property Code, the Legal 500 article reports. The decree was published in the Official Gazette No. 234 of 8 October 2026 and came into force on 23 October 2026. The new paragraph expressly brings data, algorithms and mathematical methods for the training of artificial intelligence systems within the scope of trade secrets. The article was written by Lydia Mondola and Giacomo Di Grazia of Chiomenti and published on 24 November 2026. The reform was adopted under the legislative delegation in Article 24 of Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025.

Article 52 of the decree inserts paragraph 1-bis into Article 98 of the Industrial Property Code, and Article 53 provides that related disputes remain assigned to the Specialised Court for Business Matters under Article 134(1)(b). The new paragraph applies where the conditions in letters (a), (b) and (c) of paragraph 1 are met. It defines algorithms and mathematical methods as model architectures, optimisation functions, training procedures and configurations, and any other technical-computational element functional to developing AI systems. The decree aligns Italian law with Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act, and its preamble refers to Directive (EU) 2016/943. The provision does not expressly extend to model parameters, known as weights, which are the output of training.

The article says the novelty lies not in creating a new right but in the legal certainty it provides. It states that paragraph 1-bis introduces no presumption in favour of the holder, who still bears the burden of proving secrecy, commercial value deriving from secrecy and reasonably adequate protective measures. It says the provision is primarily clarificatory because the notion of trade secret was already broad enough to encompass such assets. It notes that copyright protects such elements only in their form of expression and that mathematical methods are excluded as such from patentability under Article 45(2)(a). It says the legislator identifies trade secret protection as the reference instrument for these elements.

The article says a dataset of data public in themselves but selected, cleaned and annotated, or a known architecture combined with specific training configurations, could be protected. It says elements that have become generally known, for example because released under open licences, will not be protected. It says the explanatory report links the exclusion of weights to the scope of the legislative delegation but does not rule out protection under paragraph 1 where the requirements are met. It says data and components used at other stages, such as inference, evaluation and monitoring, remain protectable under the general conditions of paragraph 1. It says the secrecy requirement relates to the information as a body and to the precise configuration and assembly of its components.

The article says AI Act providers of general-purpose models draw up technical documentation including the training process and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of training content under Article 53. It says Recital 107 states the summary should be generally comprehensive in scope instead of technically detailed, and Article 78 binds authorities to confidentiality. It says protection in litigation will depend on confidentiality measures under Article 121-ter of the Industrial Property Code, which the court adopts upon request of a party. It says companies should map assets such as datasets, configurations and weights, classify them, control access and bind employees and consultants to confidentiality. It says agreements should regulate ownership and use of datasets, trained models, configurations and fine-tuning results, and limits on using customer data to train supplier models.

The article says the line between what must be disclosed and what may remain confidential will have to be drawn case by case and becomes part of the protection strategy. It says it will be for the case law of the Specialised Court for Business Matters to clarify which measures may be considered reasonably adequate for assets of such a specific nature. It says the content is intended as a general guide and specialist advice should be sought about specific circumstances. It says the jurisdiction of the Specialised Court over trade secret disputes was already established and is simply reaffirmed for the new assets. It says the provision will have to be read consistently with the harmonised notion of trade secret under Directive (EU) 2016/943.

stories.Headline: KAIST students build AI glasses prototypes to aid communication and learning at XR hackathon
stories.Summary:
The KAIST Augmented Reality Research Center organized the CG&I × KAIST 2026 XR·AI Winter School & Hackathon starting on Saturday and concluding on Monday. Thirty-two university students selected from fifty-five proposals formed sixteen two-person teams to create prototypes using artificial intelligence glasses and extended reality devices. Eight of these teams utilized lightweight augmented reality glasses to overlay digital information onto real-world objects and people. The other eight teams employed immersive extended reality headsets to recreate professional work and learning environments within a virtual space. These participants focused on strengthening human communication and learning rather than replacing human effort with automated systems.

Six teams received awards for projects that translated sign language into subtitles or converted expert instructions into step-by-step guidance for beginners. Yoo Jin from Chung-Ang University and Kwon Na-hyeon from Gachon University won an excellence prize for an AI assistant that clarifies vague equipment instructions. Jang Seung-ho and Ki Min-jun of KAIST earned an excellence prize for MAZU, which provides subtitles for Korean and American Sign Language. Yoo Si-hyeon from Konkuk University and Ahn Seong-jin of KAIST won for Spatial Review, a tool for reviewing three-dimensional mathematics shapes. Encouragement prizes were given to KAIST teams for a blueprint relay tool called Baton, a design comparison tool named FormBridge, and a guitar-lesson recording system.

Woo Woontack, who serves as the director of the KAIST Augmented Reality Research Center, explained the purpose of the technology. He stated that AI glasses should assist users in learning and making judgments independently so that the knowledge remains their own capability after removing the devices. The center is also researching a framework called Symbiotic AIR4BTS to help users perform at their best without AI assistance. This framework aims to record real-world information and apply it to new situations to enhance human performance. The director believes the technology should empower the user to retain skills and experiences personally.

The university plans to provide research internships of up to two months in January and February of next year for outstanding undergraduates. KAIST also intends to hold regular spring and fall hackathons starting next year to support further research and real-world testing. Many of the winning prototypes still require verification regarding their actual performance and their effectiveness in learning environments. There are also unresolved questions concerning privacy because the devices must record audio and video to function. The university will continue to explore how AI intervention can be most genuinely helpful in various real-life contexts.

stories.Headline: South Korean high school students present AI tools for disaster response and news credibility at KAIST competition
stories.Summary:
High school students from across South Korea gathered at KAIST on Saturday to present various AI and software ideas. These young participants developed tools to tackle everyday inconveniences and social problems during the 11th National High School Club AI and Software Competition. The event took place at the Kim Byung-ho and Kim Sam-yeol IT Convergence Building multipurpose hall on the campus in Daejeon. Entries included a robot for exploring disaster sites and an AI tool that assesses the credibility of news articles. Other projects featured a personalized learning assistant, a smart agriculture solution, and a system to revitalize local commercial districts.

The competition required 73 high school clubs to identify real-world problems and develop software solutions with their club members. After a preliminary round, 22 teams advanced to the finals and spent roughly two months from August refining their systems. The gold award went to the Blacks team from Ilsan Daejin High School for a multisensory digital barrier-free system. This system uses AI to analyze paintings, video, and music to provide simplified explanations and sensory cues for older adults and people with cognitive disabilities.

Silver awards were given to the ArchiOn team from Gwanggyo High School for Nook of Mine and the Nekarakubae team from Gyeonggi Automobile Science High School for PLATEGUARD. Bronze awards went to INCLUSE from Konyang High School affiliated with Konyang University, SignBridge from Samil Technical High School, and Jinjeonghan Shin from Incheon Gojan High School. The gold prize was 2 million won, while silver winners received 1 million won and bronze winners received 500,000 won each. Park Ji-min of the gold-winning team said that building the idea with friends taught the value of collaboration.

Park also expressed a desire to create a more useful product based on the feedback received during the event. Bae Du-hwan, director of the KAIST Software Education Center, said he was pleased to offer a platform for students to showcase their creativity. Bae stated that he hoped the experience of collaborating with club members would inspire them to lead the future of the country in the age of AI. KAIST co-hosted the finals alongside Woosong University, Konyang University, Daejeon University, and Chungnam National University.

The event received support from the Ministry of Science and ICT and the Institute of Information and Communications Technology Planning and Evaluation. This competition first launched in 2016 and provides expert technical mentoring to help students build problem-solving skills. Judges evaluated the finalists based on technical execution, practical applicability, software quality, and the originality of their solutions. The organizers assessed whether the teams had accurately diagnosed the problems they aimed to solve through poster presentations and oral pitches.

stories.Headline: KAIST-trained researcher proposes metal detectors and unannounced checks to curb AI cheating on college entrance exam
stories.Summary:
AI researcher and content creator Heo Seong-beom shared countermeasures against cheating on Monday before the upcoming College Scholastic Ability Test. He posted a video to his YouTube channel because he felt saddened that people exploit technology before social guidelines exist. Heo, who graduated from the Korea Science Academy and KAIST, believes that students abusing technology rob hardworking peers of their opportunities. He argued that institutional responses to recent AI cheating controversies are now urgently needed.

Heo described AI cheating as a three-stage process involving capturing, transmitting, and receiving information. He suggested that metal detectors are the most practical tool because batteries in smart glasses or earpieces contain metal. He also proposed checking unsubmitted belongings, inspecting hallways and restrooms, and deploying radio-frequency detectors without prior notice. Additionally, he recommended conducting forensic investigations of handwriting on answer sheets and SIM card communication records after the exam.

Heo stated that using metal detectors thoroughly is more effective than using thermal cameras to find devices. He acknowledged that securing equipment and training supervisors before the Suneung on Thursday would be difficult. He warned test-takers that cheating can derail their lives and will eventually be discovered even if it takes time. He encouraged students to walk their own paths and trust that adults will find ways to address the problem.

stories.Headline: KAIST president Bae Choong-sik and Herald Media CEO Choi Jin-young stress human agency in the AI age
stories.Summary:
Choi Jin-young, the CEO of Herald Media Group, and Bae Choong-sik, the president of KAIST, held a special dialogue on Tuesday afternoon. This event took place at the Ryu Keun-chul Sports Complex on the KAIST campus in Yuseong-gu, Daejeon, during Innovate Korea 2026. The discussion was co-hosted by the National Research Council of Science and Technology, KAIST, and Herald Media Group. The speakers focused on the enduring importance of human agency and imagination during the age of artificial intelligence.

The dialogue highlighted a need for people to be pioneers who use imagination rather than just coding skills. Bae Choong-sik explained that KAIST is currently building an AI-native campus to integrate infrastructure, administration, research, and education. He argued that the next decade requires the democratization of AI so that benefits reach everyone regardless of gender, region, nationality, or economic standing. The speakers also emphasized the importance of physical AI, which combines AI with manufacturing to improve robotics and autonomous driving.

Choi Jin-young stated that while AI can pave the road, humans must be the ones to walk it. He claimed that algorithms cannot be coded for sublime compassion and that empathy and reflection have become more important than ever. Bae Choong-sik added that humans must remain self-directed to lead technology rather than being subordinated to it. He noted that emotions such as joy, sorrow, and anguish are unique to humans and cannot be replaced by AI.

The speakers expressed confidence that South Korea will emerge greater than before by harnessing its manufacturing strengths. They believe the country can lead a new industrial revolution through the development of physical AI. Choi Jin-young also hoped that technology and humanity would advance in harmony to address energy problems and the climate crisis. He suggested that culture and the arts could eventually help break down barriers in inter-Korean relations.

stories.Headline: OECD Council revises AI Principles in 2024 to address generative AI risks
stories.Summary:
The OECD AI Principles were adopted by the OECD Council at Ministerial level on 22 May 2019, making them, in the OECD's account, the first intergovernmental standard on artificial intelligence. The Council, again at Ministerial level, revised them on 3 May 2024. The 2024 revision responded to the arrival of general-purpose and generative AI. The Principles were later reflected in the G20 AI Principles adopted later that year. CASRAI's dictionary entry on the Principles was last updated on 13 November 2026.

The Principles consist of five values-based principles for trustworthy AI and five recommendations for policymakers. The five values cover inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being; human rights, democratic values and fairness including privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; and accountability. The five recommendations are to invest in AI research and development, foster an inclusive AI-enabling ecosystem, shape an enabling and interoperable governance and policy environment, build human capacity and prepare for labour-market transition, and pursue international co-operation for trustworthy AI. As of the 2024 update, 47 countries and jurisdictions adhere to the Principles, including all OECD members, the European Union and several non-member states. The May 2024 revision expanded the human-centred-values principle to address AI-amplified misinformation and disinformation while respecting freedom of expression, and sharpened language on privacy, intellectual property and safety in light of generative-AI-specific risks.

The Principles are set out in the Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, OECD/LEGAL/0449. An OECD Recommendation is not a treaty and carries no legal force of its own, and adherence is a political commitment with an expectation that adherents will do their best to implement the Principles in national policy and report on that implementation. The OECD frames the Principles as principles for actors across the AI system lifecycle, not a checklist to file away. CASRAI states that simply having an internal AI policy document does not, on its own, satisfy the Principles. CASRAI adds that the Principles are voluntary, non-binding policy guidance adopted by governments that create no legal obligations of their own and no enforcement mechanism.

CASRAI states that the EU AI Act is binding EU law with defined obligations, exemptions including specific carve-outs relevant to research, and penalties. CASRAI says the EU AI Act's own risk-based, human-rights-oriented framing draws on the same normative ground the OECD Principles established in 2019. CASRAI states that a research organization operating in the EU needs to track AI Act compliance as a legal matter, while the OECD Principles are useful as the broader governance vocabulary and as the operative standard where no binding law yet applies, in most jurisdictions outside the EU. CASRAI states that research institutions, funders and research-performing organizations increasingly use the Principles as a reference point for institutional AI-governance policy, alongside more technical frameworks like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001. CASRAI states that this typically means documented accountability for AI systems used in research workflows, from AI-assisted literature review to AI-assisted data analysis, disclosure to affected parties such as co-authors, reviewers, study participants and research subjects when AI materially shaped a research output or decision, and testing and validation proportionate to the AI system's role rather than a single blanket sign-off.

CASRAI states that a research institution or research-performing organization can treat the Principles as an operational baseline for AI governance when it can point to a documented AI risk-management or oversight process addressing all five values-based principles, not just one such as privacy, as applied to a specific AI use case in the research lifecycle. CASRAI adds that the process must be proportionate to the AI system's stage and context of use rather than a single one-time sign-off. CASRAI adds that the process must be paired with actual transparency to affected parties, including participants, authors and reviewers, about where and how AI was used. CASRAI states that the Principles are not sector-specific. CASRAI refers readers to its entries on Responsible AI and Trustworthy AI and to its generative-AI disclosure statement as the mechanism most journals and funders now use to satisfy the transparency principle at the point of publication or proposal submission.

CASRAI states that the 2024 revision responded to the arrival of general-purpose and generative AI rather than to something else, and its account of what changed ends there. CASRAI's entry carries a proposed dictionary term in Track D, Philosophy and Research Ethics, under version v2026.1. CASRAI lists the Compliance and regulatory working group as the working group for this domain. CASRAI's entry does not state what the OECD plans next for the Principles. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Generative AI cheating shakes exam system and threatens school district housing premiums
stories.Summary:
Recent controversies regarding the use of artificial intelligence for cheating have shaken the entrance examination system and the evaluation of professional qualifications. This situation emerged as generative AI began solving high-level reasoning problems instantly, which threatens the effectiveness of traditional tests. The disruption has caused cracks in the long-standing formula that linked academic success to specific real estate markets. These events suggest that the current private education system centered on memorization and problem-solving tricks has reached its limit.

The shift in education requires a re-evaluation of location values in major school districts like Daechi-dong in Gangnam-gu, Mok-dong in Yangcheon-gu, and Junggye-dong in Nowon-gu. These areas previously maintained high prices because they served as bases for entrance exam success, despite poor residential conditions in old apartments. Residents tolerated issues such as floor noise, narrow parking spaces, and green water to maintain accessibility to academies. Now, the justification for spending billions of won on these poor environments is disappearing as the value of academic backgrounds weakens. This change may shift housing demand toward new construction infrastructure and general housing satisfaction in the Seoul metropolitan area.

Real estate industry officials stated that the demand for private education previously supported the high costs of living in inconvenient construction complexes. They explained that the utility of memorization-oriented education is being questioned because generative AI can now replace key summaries and problem solving. Another official noted that the power of school district premiums may weaken as AI lowers the threshold for learning methods and information. These experts believe that the market will eventually reorganize based on original real estate values, such as location, residential comfort, and the feasibility of reconstruction projects.

The market may move away from a uniform house price ranking dictated by the single variable of entrance examinations. Demand is expected to diversify according to the lifestyles of different generations, favoring complexes near the Han River, parks, or areas with good traffic. Many traditional school district complexes already face uncertainty due to soaring construction costs and delays in licensing for reconstruction. The industry predicts that the focus will shift toward new complexes that offer better immediate efficiency and living standards. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI² Robotics deploys humanoid robots to serve guests at the Apec summit in Shenzhen
stories.Summary:
Shenzhen showcased its advanced technological ecosystem this week as world leaders gathered for the Apec summit. Humanoid robots from the local firm AI² Robotics are currently serving coffee, ice cream, and soft drinks to journalists. These machines are operating inside the media centre located at the Shenzhen Convention and Exhibition Centre. The deployment serves as a demonstration of the city's growth as a global center for innovation.

The service requires seven AlphaBots which Crystal Guan describes as the largest humanoid robot service team. These robots utilize a self-developed AI foundation model to recognize and operate various types of commercialized equipment. Another system allows journalists to order treats through a touchscreen or by speaking to a mobile robot. This process involves a chain of cooperating AI agents, including DeepSeek, to handle messages and delivery.

Crystal Guan, the PR director for AI² Robotics, stated that the city is the center of innovation. She noted that her company already cooperates with nearly half of the Apec economies and views Hong Kong as a key market. Lexus Jiang, a staff member at the media centre, compared the setup to a future restaurant. He claimed the AI chain completes orders in about two minutes, while a human would take five.

The integration of digital intelligence is a key feature of the current media centre operations. AI² Robotics has already expanded its reach, with an AlphaBot serving cocktails in the Lan Kwai Fong area of Hong Kong. The city continues to use its tech industry as a primary economic engine to increase its global prominence. These embodied AI systems are intended to show the efficiency of the local research and industry ecosystem.
