Responsibility for the framework rests with the initiative she founded, according to the article, and the episode presented the pillars as its subject. No other person or organization is named in connection with the framework.

The article comes from the All About AI series on KY3, and this episode was published on November 23, 2026, with an update posted about half an hour later. stories.Headline: Nurse leader urges nurses to define clinical outcomes and govern AI across its lifecycle
stories.Summary:
Elizabeth Anderson, a registered nurse and director at Rauland, wrote the MedCity News piece published on November 23, 2026. She argued that AI is entering clinical workflows faster than many expected. She asked whether nurses are part of the decisions about how it gets used. She said AI may reduce administrative burden and help nurses find clinically relevant information faster. She said AI may support earlier recognition of patient needs and give nurses more time for professional judgment.

Anderson wrote that nursing leaders should ask what they are attempting to improve for patients and nurses. She said nurses should help identify the problems AI is meant to address and define desired clinical outcomes. She said nurses should take part in solution development and evaluate whether implementation produces meaningful improvement. She cited the American Nurses Association's position that nurses should have a leading voice in the design, implementation, evaluation, and governance of AI in nursing practice. She said nursing participation should extend across the AI lifecycle, from problem identification through testing, implementation, governance and outcomes evaluation.

Anderson said nursing leadership has an obligation to shape the direction of AI. She said nurse executives should set expectations for nursing participation in AI governance. She said they should create mechanisms for frontline nurses and nursing informatics experts to influence solution development. She said they should advocate for appropriate clinical validation and ensure implementation measures extend beyond efficiency. She said they should also take part in decisions about how capacity created through AI will be reinvested.

Anderson said AI may reduce one task while inadvertently creating another. She said AI may improve access to information while increasing notifications or adding steps to workflows. She said the National Academy of Medicine's Health Care Artificial Intelligence Code of Conduct emphasizes a human-centered approach. She said it identifies safety, effectiveness, equity, transparency, accountability and engagement as important principles. She said nurses must participate in determining whether an AI application produces the outcomes for which it was introduced.

Anderson said documentation, information retrieval, communication requirements and fragmented technology take time away from patient care. She said saving minutes on a task is an incomplete measure of success. She said organizations should define what they intend to accomplish with the capacity AI creates. She said that capacity could include time for assessment, patient and family education, mobility, symptom management, discharge preparation, care coordination and surveillance. She said time returned to nursing requires appropriate boundaries.

Anderson said efficiency gains could instead contribute to greater workload, expanded patient assignments or new responsibilities. She said organizations should examine whether AI lets nurses complete important interventions more consistently and coordinate care more effectively. She said success requires measures beyond productivity, including documentation burden, cognitive workload, missed nursing care, nurse satisfaction and patient experience. She said AI intended to affect nursing practice should be developed with an understanding of clinical context, workflow variability, patient safety and unintended consequences. She said the more important question is whether nursing will meaningfully influence AI.

Articles.Title: The Future of AI in Nursing Must Begin with the Outcomes We Intend to Achieve

stories.headline_source: The Future of AI in Nursing Must Begin with the Outcomes We Intend to Achieve

stories.Headline: Researchers develop a statistical tool that tests whether synthetic data can stand in for patients in clinical trials
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Virginia Tech, the University of Maryland Baltimore County, Texas Tech University and Princeton University jointly developed a statistical tool that tests whether AI-generated synthetic data can accurately stand in for patient data in clinical trials, and the model was published Nov. 23 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The work responds to a push by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to explore synthetic data alternatives that could compress trial timelines from years to a matter of months. Yulia R. Gel, a Virginia Tech professor of statistics, said the problem is that you have to verify the synthetic data is true to life, and that the goal is for trials using synthetic data to reach the same conclusions as trials with real people. The tool bridges computational topology and statistics to measure and compare complex image data, and the team tested it by comparing synthetic mammograms against real patient data while tracking how breast cancer responds to different radiation doses.

The proposed method let the researchers assess how faithfully the synthetic images could replace human data in trial evaluations, and the team is already in conversation with the FDA to customize the model for streamlined pre- and post-market evaluations. The researchers have also applied the model in materials science to verify synthetic representations of wood, fabric and metal. Jaidev Goel, a statistics graduate student and one of the leading authors on the paper, said AI is being used to generate new protein structures and new compounds in drug discovery, and that a materials scientist may want to make something with the properties of cotton, which the tool can check for density or texture. Down the road, the articles say, the model could verify synthetic data for power grids and 3D objects or help spot false assertions and restrict behavior in large language models.

Gel is quoted as saying the team wants clinical trials with synthetic data to reach the same conclusions they would get with real people, and Goel said we should not blindly buy into the hype of AI, adding that humans have always come up with ways to stress-test new tools and that statistics plays a crucial role in that history. The other researchers listed are Ansu Chatterjee of the University of Maryland Baltimore County, Asim Dey of Texas Tech University and Vincent Poor of Princeton University. The work was supported by the FDA Center for Devices and Radiological Health, the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health through the NSF-NIH-FDA Foundations for Digital Twins as Catalyzers of Biomedical Technological Innovation program. The articles say the research will not stop with publication, given the ongoing talks with the FDA.

Articles.Title: Can AI expedite medical imaging? Yes — if we can trust the picture

stories.Headline: Rob Baker argues AI literacy can help young Black men navigate banks and institutions
stories.Summary:
Dr. Rob "Biko" Baker wrote an op-ed published by civicmedia.us on Nov 23, 2026, at 10:00 AM CT, titled The New Gatekeepers: Black Men, Literacy, and the Age of AI. In it he describes a young Milwaukee entrepreneur who contacted him after his bank placed a hold on a check. For nearly three days the man had been getting the runaround, and eventually he asked Baker to get on the phone. Baker suggested asking for the branch manager, who was more polished but equally unhelpful and offered information that ultimately proved inaccurate.

The article cites the 2024 National Assessment of Educational Progress, under which only 8% of Black eighth graders in Milwaukee scored at or above the NAEP Proficient level in reading. Across all racial groups, just 11% of Milwaukee's eighth-grade boys reached that benchmark, figures the article says are not measures of basic literacy. According to Wisconsin's Department of Public Instruction, 62.7% of Black Milwaukee Public Schools students graduated within four years in 2024, compared with 79.2% of white students. The district's overall graduation rate improved to 72% for the class of 2025, though substantial disparities remain. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the national unemployment rate for Black men ages 20 to 24 was 9.1% in the third quarter of 2026, compared with 6.8% for white men in the same age group.

Baker writes that he has spent much of his life as an advocate but is no expert at navigating bureaucracies, and still struggles with obstacles built into schools, healthcare systems, banks and government agencies. He says his fear of systems extended his time in grad school, with hours in the financial aid office trying to get a refund check processed. He says things were much easier at UWM, where he knew who to talk to solve his problems. He says he has learned which questions to ask, when to request a supervisor, and how to recognize when someone is giving him the runaround. He writes that many young Black men who seek his help lack the same experience or access to people who understand these systems.

Baker describes the young man as polite and professional throughout the encounter, wearing a Green Bay Packers hat and sweater with long braids, not yelling or behaving inappropriately. After leaving the bank, the man called Baker again, frustrated, and sitting in his car noticed what he believed were police officers moving through the parking lot. He wondered whether they had been called because of him, and Baker says he could not confirm his suspicions but understood why the possibility crossed his mind. Eventually they resolved the issue, and Baker talked with him about navigating such encounters, including that wearing more conventionally respectable clothing might influence how he is received when handling large financial transactions. Baker writes that he was uncomfortable giving that advice, because the man had done absolutely nothing wrong.

Baker writes that as artificial intelligence becomes integrated into banking, education, healthcare and employment, the ability to navigate institutions may depend even more on literacy, communication and understanding complicated systems. He asks what happens to young Black men already facing educational and employment barriers when artificial intelligence becomes another gatekeeper. He recalls loving books as a child, traveling the world through encyclopedias, novels, biographies and historical accounts, and calls the library his pathway to the middle class. He attended private Lutheran schools where he was challenged academically and developed reading, writing and critical-thinking skills that continue to serve him as an educator and advocate. He writes that reading taught him to ask questions, recognize patterns, understand unfamiliar language and challenge information that did not make sense.

Baker writes that schools must prioritize reading comprehension, writing, critical thinking and practical AI literacy, and that community organizations must teach young men how to navigate financial institutions, employment systems and public services. He writes that institutions adopting AI must remain accountable for the barriers their technology creates. He says artificial intelligence could democratize knowledge and help young Black men overcome obstacles that once required professional assistance, but that future isn't guaranteed. He writes that he does not want the next generation spending their lives looking for someone like him to get a banker, administrator or automated system to listen. He wants them to have the skills, knowledge and confidence to advocate for themselves.

Articles.Title: The New Gatekeepers: Black Men, Literacy, and the Age of AI

stories.Headline: Schneider Electric doubles CDU manufacturing capacity at its Conselve site to meet European AI cooling demand
stories.Summary:
Schneider Electric is doubling manufacturing capacity for cooling distribution units at its facility in Conselve, Italy, the company said on November 25, 2026. The company said AI and high-density deployments are increasing demand for liquid cooling across Europe's data centre market. The additional CDU production capacity is expected to be available from January 2027. Chiller manufacturing capacity at the site will rise by 50% by the end of 2026. A new cooling test laboratory due for completion in December 2027 will triple Conselve's existing testing capacity.

CDU manufacturing capacity at Conselve will increase by 100%, with expanded production expected from January 2027. The planned laboratory will validate chillers rated at up to 4MW, Motivair by Schneider Electric CDUs rated at up to 5MW, and CRAH and fan wall systems rated at up to 800kW. Conselve, in the Veneto region of north-east Italy, is Schneider Electric's principal cooling manufacturing facility in Europe. The site also serves as a centre for research and development, engineering and technical training. Conselve's workforce has nearly doubled over the past five years.

Damien Dhellemmes, Senior Vice President of the Secure Power and Data Center Business in Europe at Schneider Electric, said Europe's ability to compete in the global AI economy will depend on its capacity to manufacture and deploy critical infrastructure. He said access to advanced liquid cooling technologies, resilient supply chains and specialist engineering expertise will be fundamental as rack densities increase. He said the Conselve investment reflects a long-term commitment to strengthening Europe's industrial capabilities and accelerating cooling innovation. He said the company is strengthening its ability to deploy resilient, scalable and energy-efficient AI infrastructure. He said AI is fundamentally transforming the way customers design and operate data centers.

Schneider Electric said the expansion industrialises its advanced cooling manufacturing capabilities and moves engineering and technical expertise closer to European customers. The company said AI workloads are driving higher rack densities and more complex thermal requirements, and it describes liquid cooling as becoming essential to the next generation of data centre infrastructure. The company said the investment will help it meet those demands through added manufacturing capacity, greater supply chain resilience and closer collaboration with customers in Europe. CDUs manage the transfer of heat between a facility's water system and the secondary coolant loop serving liquid-cooled IT equipment, such as direct-to-chip cold plates. The ratings cover heat rejection through chillers, liquid distribution through CDUs and air handling in the white space through CRAH and fan wall units.

The investment follows Schneider Electric's acquisition of a controlling stake in liquid cooling specialist Motivair, which completed in February 2025, further to an agreement signed in October 2024. Under the terms of the deal, Schneider Electric acquired an initial 75% of the Buffalo, New York-based company for US$850m and expects to buy the remaining 25% in 2028. Motivair's CDUs are now sold as Motivair by Schneider Electric and will be validated in the new Conselve laboratory. In May, the company agreed to operate a facility integrating data centre power modules within an industrial cluster that SoftBank Group is developing at the Port of Dunkirk in northern France. Conselve is one of several European manufacturing commitments Schneider Electric has made in 2026.

The expanded CDU production is expected from January 2027, and the chiller capacity increase is due by the end of 2026. The new cooling test laboratory is due for completion in December 2027. Schneider Electric expects to buy the remaining 25% of Motivair in 2028. The articles do not say how much the Conselve investment will cost.

stories.Headline: Abits Group signs nonbinding letter of intent to acquire Soter Technologies for AI-enabled data center monitoring
stories.Summary:
Abits Group Inc, a U.S.-focused digital infrastructure company listed on Nasdaq under ABTS, announced on November 23, 2026 that it had signed a nonbinding letter of intent to acquire Soter Technologies, Inc. The announcement came in a press release dated November 23, 2026, issued from Duff, Tennessee. Soter Technologies is a provider of environmental sensing technology and AI-enabled monitoring software. The proposed acquisition would support Abits' strategy to develop integrated digital infrastructure capabilities. Abits management believes the added technology could help data center operators predict and identify early warning signs of potential equipment and infrastructure problems.

The letter of intent is nonbinding except for specified provisions. The proposed transaction remains subject to satisfactory due diligence, negotiation and execution of definitive agreements, required financing and approvals and other closing conditions. Soter is headquartered in Ronkonkoma, New York, and develops and markets its FlySense environmental sensing platform and cloud-based monitoring software. Soter reports more than 30,000 active FlySense devices and approximately 3,000 paying customers subscribing to its monitoring and software services. Soter's FlySense sensors are manufactured in the United States.

Stephen Faucetta, Chairman and CEO of Abits Group, said reliable operations are essential to data centers, particularly as increasing computing demands place greater pressure on uptime and availability. He said Abits believes Soter's combination of advanced sensors and AI-enabled monitoring software could give operators additional insight into environmental changes that may indicate, even predict, developing problems before they lead to equipment failures or service interruptions. He said Abits' strategy is to build a digital infrastructure platform combining the facilities, power and technology needed to support increasingly demanding computing applications. He said Abits believes Soter's technology could complement its existing infrastructure. He said Abits intends to evaluate how Soter's sensing and monitoring capabilities can be adapted for AI and high-performance computing environments.

Abits and Soter believe Soter's capabilities could be adapted to detect certain irregularities in data center environments. Abits and Soter will work together developing applications of the technology for data center infrastructure monitoring. These capabilities remain subject to further development, technical validation and integration with existing facility management systems. Soter's FlySense platform incorporates sensors that monitor changes in air quality, airborne particles, sound patterns and other environmental conditions, and its cloud-based monitoring software analyzes sensor data and delivers automated alerts when unusual conditions are detected. Soter has worked with more than 3,000 school districts, and its technology is used in institutional and commercial environments to monitor air quality, vaping, unusual sound patterns and device tampering.

According to Soter management, the company is generating positive EBITDA, although its financial results remain subject to verification through Abits' due diligence. Soter generates revenue through hardware sales and paid monitoring and software subscriptions, providing a recurring revenue stream. If the acquisition is completed, Abits intends to operate Soter as a standalone business serving third-party customers while supporting the expansion of its existing product portfolio, recurring software services and customer base. Abits also sees opportunities to extend Soter's sensing and monitoring capabilities into additional markets, including manufacturing, industrial facilities, utilities and other environments where equipment reliability and continuous operations are important. Abits intends to retain Soter's existing senior management team, subject to mutually acceptable agreements, and support the continued development and commercialization of its technology.

If the acquisition is completed, Abits intends to evaluate deploying Soter's technology at its existing facilities and incorporating its capabilities into future AI and high-performance computing infrastructure projects. There can be no assurance that definitive agreements will be executed, that the acquisition will be completed or that the anticipated operating and strategic benefits will be realized. The press release states that forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. These include the possibility that definitive agreements may not be executed or the proposed acquisition may not be completed. The release also cites the accuracy of preliminary and unaudited financial and operating information provided by Soter management and the Company's ability to obtain required financing, consents and other approvals.

stories.Headline: Atlas Signal begins coverage of DataMeds AI with highly speculative rating
stories.Summary:
Atlas Signal Inc. published an initiation equity report on DataMeds AI, Inc. (Nasdaq:MEDS) on November 23, 2026, the company announced that day. Atlas Signal is a publisher of investor-facing equity reports covering publicly traded companies. DataMeds AI, formerly Wellgistics Health, is a Tampa, Florida-based pharmacy, pharmaceutical distribution, health-technology and diagnostics company. The report is titled "MEDS: AI-Enabled Physical Pharmacy, Laboratory and Telehealth Infrastructure - One Digital Platform." The report initiates Atlas Signal's coverage of DataMeds AI and reviews the company's 2026 pharmacy rebuilding effort centered around the GLP-1 patient.

The report reviews third-quarter 2026 revenue of $2,668,980, up 50.0% from $1,779,860 in the quarter ended June 30, 2026, led by Corexa Pharmacy retail sales of $2,393,191. Gross margin widened to 16.2% from 10.2%, and the first $144,755 of technology and platform revenue came from KareHub patient-access services. Corexa Pharmacy is licensed in 34 states and the District of Columbia, and its retail sales reached $5,117,974 in the first nine months of 2026, compared with $865,695 for all of 2025. The September 11, 2026 settlement with the former owners of Wellgistics, LLC extinguished $17.5 million of seller-note principal and $1.7 million of accrued interest for $450,000. Positive total stockholders' equity of $171,695 on September 30, 2026 compared with a deficit of $12.4 million at December 31, 2025.

The November 3, 2026 termination of the non-binding letter of intent with Datavault AI, EOS, Scilex, HealthBridge Advisors and REBOOT would have issued shares targeting approximately 89.5% of the company to those parties. The exclusive REBOOT GLP-1 license and the Datavault PharmacyChain license remained in force. The Health Lives Here app, marketed with NFL Alumni Health, brings GLP-1 patients to Corexa Pharmacy, together with the exclusive U.S. license to REBOOT Health AI's patented GLP-1 patient-management platform. The November launch of compounded peptides and a non-binding memorandum of understanding with a Florida HMO to offer the Health Lives Here app to its more than 25,000 members were also reviewed. The September 11, 2026 acquisition of Helomics, a CLIA-certified Pittsburgh laboratory offering the ChemoFx chemotherapy-selection assay, was covered under Humana's South Carolina Medicaid policy according to the company, and Helomics holds a biobank of more than 70,000 tumor samples.

The November peptide-discovery partnership with DiaGen AI and an agreement, subject to court approval, to acquire the TBIA cancer blood-test platform from the estate of Todos Medical were reviewed. The demand backdrop included U.S. spending on medicines of $435 billion in 2023, according to IQVIA as cited by the company, and KFF's November 2025 finding that 18% of U.S. adults had taken a GLP-1 drug. Atlas Signal describes DataMeds as a Delaware holding company headquartered in Tampa, Florida, that owns Corexa Pharmacy, a dispensing pharmacy; Wellgistics, LLC, a 50-state FDA-licensed and NABP-accredited pharmaceutical wholesaler; the DelivMeds prescription-hub application; the Helomics laboratory; and a 51% interest in Healthstar Technologies, which runs the KareHub patient-access platform. The report also examines how EinsteinRx and PharmacyChain fit alongside its existing pharmacy. EinsteinRx supports pharmacy workflow and patient services, while PharmacyChain is designed to provide blockchain-enabled, smart contracts and auditable transactions between manufacturers and patients.

The REBOOT agreement adds a separate layer of licensed GLP-1 patient-management technology intended for integration into the Health Lives Here app. The report notes that, unlike telehealth companies that hand fulfillment to third parties, DataMeds owns the pharmacy, the wholesaler and the laboratory behind its application. At the November 20, 2026 closing price of $1.34, DataMeds had a market capitalization of approximately $7.7 million, against revenue of $7.7 million over the twelve months to September 30, 2026. Atlas Signal rates DataMeds Highly Speculative, and the report sets out the risks investors should weigh, including the company's financing needs and potential dilution. Atlas Signal prepared the report using publicly available information, including DataMeds's filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, official exchange information and company announcements.

The report identifies several potential catalysts for investors to monitor, including definitive agreements with the Florida HMO, which the company expects in the fourth quarter, and the first user, prescription and revenue figures from the Health Lives Here app. Nasdaq confirmed on October 19, 2026 that DataMeds had regained compliance with its stockholders' equity rule. Management said it expects continued growth from medical foods, diagnostic testing and compounded peptides. Financing on acceptable terms includes the at-the-market facility with Dawson James Securities and further advances under a third-party lender promissory note. Atlas Signal has received or is entitled to receive $25,000 from DataMeds AI, Inc. for twelve months of equity reports, consisting of an initiating report and three updated reports.

stories.Headline: Review finds no validated AI model predicts ischemic stroke cell therapy potency
stories.Summary:
A narrative review by Jun Wu, Haotian Xu, Kewei Li and Chao Cheng of Wuxi People's Hospital Affiliated to Nanjing Medical University was published in Frontiers in Neuroscience on 25 November 2026. The review states that the literature lacks an externally validated computational model able to predict therapeutic product potency or treatment-attributable clinical benefit. It says artificial intelligence and multiomics are powerful tools for profiling postischemic cerebral tissue. The authors evaluated the translational bottleneck facing cell and extracellular vesicle therapies for ischemic stroke. The review says molecular signatures hold value only when guiding defined manufacturing, host-targeting or patient treatment decisions.

The review cites the Global Burden of Disease 2021 study estimate of 11.9 million incident strokes and 93.8 million people living with stroke worldwide. It covers literature searches of publications from January 2020 through November 2026. It notes the randomized phase two MASTERS trial and the phase two-slash-three TREASURE trial of allogeneic multipotent adult progenitor cells, both of which failed to achieve primary clinical recovery endpoints. It describes four hierarchical levels of evidence, from baseline molecular descriptions to controlled clinical trials showing patient benefit. It says current stroke studies are restricted to molecular descriptions and isolated assay validations.

The authors argue that restoring blood flow through endovascular recanalization for acute large-vessel occlusion cannot reconstruct neural tissue and complex circuitry destroyed during an ischemic event. They say biological plausibility and descriptive omics data cannot substitute for proven functional efficacy. They state that an intravenous therapy designed to alter systemic splenic immune responses cannot be evaluated against endpoints established for local cortical circuit reconstruction. They introduce an evidence-to-decision framework built on three practical questions about reproducible biological activity, host conditions and clinical improvement attributable to therapy. They say computational imputation provides statistical estimates rather than physical measurements.

The review states that preclinical studies initially showed intravenous bone marrow stromal cells improved behavioral outcomes in rat stroke models. It says candidate therapies include mesenchymal stromal cells, multipotent adult progenitor cells, neural stem and progenitor grafts and cell-derived extracellular vesicles, which act through different mechanisms. It reports that Scott and colleagues found lesion-proximal astrocytes in ischemic mice showed lipid-processing programs including Apoe and Fabp5 enrichment. It says Wu and colleagues profiled 55,520 cells after middle cerebral artery occlusion and intranasal mesenchymal stromal cell treatment, with one biological sample per condition. It says O'Shea and colleagues used graft-specific RiboTag profiling to show ischemic injury diverted transplanted neural progenitors toward wound-repair astroglial fates.

The review says weighted nearest-neighbor methods lack generative likelihoods and require fully matched multimodal cells. It says totalVI cannot integrate independent single-modality cohorts, and GLUE can produce false biological alignments from erroneous graph assumptions or nonoverlapping cell states. It says MultiVI uses paired anchor cells to regularize shared latent representations and impute missing assays for mosaic datasets. It says Cell2location risks assigning uncharacterized postischemic reactive states to standard healthy cell types. It says NicheNet and CellChat neither measure protein secretion, active receptor binding nor downstream physiological signaling directly.

The review says CellRank 2 and moscot infer state transitions across multi-timepoint profiles, but apparent trajectories in an evolving infarct can reflect cell death, immune extravasation or sampling disparities. It says Geneformer, scGPT, scFoundation and Universal Cell Embeddings were not trained on poststroke therapeutic potency labels. It says benchmarks by Ahlmann-Eltze and colleagues found foundation models failed to exceed simple baselines for perturbation prediction, and Miller and colleagues found apparent superiority depended on calibrated, perturbation-sensitive metrics. It says the multi-scale virtual-cell framework of Jiang and colleagues is a design agenda, not an operational digital twin for neural grafts. It says MIF2GO predicts general functional annotations rather than extracellular vesicle cargo delivery.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: PwC India opens Gurugram AI lab with over 90 industry solutions for enterprise testing
stories.Summary:
PwC India opened its Future AI Experience Lab in Gurugram on Monday, according to Livemint, and the facility houses more than 90 industry-specific AI solutions and assets that let business leaders simulate operations, test emerging technologies and develop prototypes against their own organisational challenges. The lab brings together solutions spanning agentic AI, robotics and Physical AI, with applications across manufacturing, infrastructure, pharmaceuticals, healthcare, telecommunications and banking, financial services and insurance. PwC said the solutions have been built, tested and validated in live business scenarios, and the lab draws on the firm's experience from more than 500 client workshops and over 200 accelerators. The engagements are designed around specific business challenges, with the aim of helping clients identify applications that can deliver measurable outcomes in productivity, revenue growth, risk reduction and customer service. The initiative follows similar investments by other consulting firms, with EY Global Delivery Services having launched its 40,000 sq.

ft. ey.ai Center for Reimagination in Bengaluru in June 2026, a centre that combines agentic AI, robotics, digital twins and conversational AI to help organisations simulate business scenarios and test ideas in controlled environments. Deloitte announced investments of $5-10 million in March 2025 in its Global AI Simulation Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru, and in June 2026 Deloitte India and SAP launched a dedicated AI-led delivery centre in Bengaluru supported by a talent ecosystem of more than 1,000 professionals, with plans to add 300-500 specialised AI professionals over the following 12 to 24 months. KPMG is working with enterprises on industry-specific AI implementations, including a partnership with Bangalore International Airport Limited to develop a generative AI platform tailored to airport operations.

The article says these developments point to a shift in the consulting industry, with firms seeking to move beyond technology advisory towards hands-on experimentation, solution development and implementation. Manpreet Singh Ahuja, chief clients and industries leader at PwC India, said everything in the lab is designed to be experienced rather than just observed, and that leaders can run their own scenarios, test their ideas and see the outcomes for themselves. Janet Truncale, global chair and chief executive of EY, said at the launch of the ey.ai center that it is where strategy meets execution and a space where leaders can test ideas responsibly and define a clear path to scale. Sudeepta Veerapaneni, partner and chief innovation officer at Deloitte India, told Mint that no single firm, however large, can build deep, cutting-edge capability across every emerging technology domain internally, and that collaborations with specialist startups allow consulting firms to bring innovation into enterprise-grade delivery, governance and scale.

George Fanthome, chief digital and information officer at BIAL, said the partnership would help enhance real-time decision-making and predictive analytics while keeping data privacy, responsible AI and cybersecurity central to the platform. The article says the proliferation of AI labs and experimentation platforms does not automatically translate into enterprise-wide adoption, because companies still need to address data readiness, integration with legacy systems, security, governance and the availability of skilled talent before taking successful prototypes into production. For consulting firms, the opportunity increasingly lies in helping enterprises navigate this entire journey, from identifying use cases and validating technology to building, integrating and scaling solutions. For CIOs, the article says, the more important measure of these initiatives will be whether they translate experimentation into sustained business value.

stories.Headline: Pixxel and IIT Kanpur sign MoU to research hyperspectral imaging and AI
stories.Summary:
Pixxel, a space technology company based in Bengaluru, signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur to advance research and development in hyperspectral imaging, artificial intelligence and geospatial applications, according to a report published by The Hindu on November 23, 2026. The report said the partnership will combine Pixxel's commercial satellite imaging capabilities with the institute's scientific expertise to develop and validate advanced remote sensing models. The two sides also aim to enhance the interpretation of Earth observation data and to translate academic research into practical geospatial solutions, according to a media statement cited in the report. The report described the initiative as one that aims to strengthen environmental monitoring and analysis through advanced multi-sensor data fusion and next-generation remote sensing applications.

The collaboration will focus on three areas, the report said, with the first being the development and validation of machine learning models, computer vision algorithms and automated feature extraction techniques for high-resolution hyperspectral imagery. The second area is the use of satellite data to study Earth surface dynamics, river basin processes, river health and land-use changes, according to the report. The third area is the integration of hyperspectral, multispectral, Synthetic Aperture Radar and thermal imagery with ground-based observations, the report said. The report did not give a duration for the agreement or a value for any investment in it.

Awais Ahmed, the Founder and CEO of Pixxel, said India has an incredible depth of scientific and engineering talent and that there is a real opportunity to bring more of that expertise into the country's growing commercial space ecosystem. He said that as the company builds increasingly sophisticated capabilities in space, it also needs to invest in the knowledge, talent and partnerships that will help it make the most of them. He added that collaborations with institutions such as IIT Kanpur were an important part of that journey, according to the report. The report did not name any official from IIT Kanpur or give any statement from the institute.

The report placed the agreement in the context of Pixxel's work as a commercial satellite imaging company and IIT Kanpur's role as a scientific institution, saying the partnership is meant to connect the two. It said the collaboration is expected to help develop and validate remote sensing models and to turn academic research into practical geospatial solutions. The report did not say what happens next, such as when work under the agreement would begin or what specific projects the two sides would take up first. It also did not give any date beyond the publication and update times of November 23, 2026.

stories.Headline: Ten companies lead on ethical AI by publishing principles and building safeguards
stories.Summary:
The article is a list of ten companies that Sustainability Magazine describes as leading in ethical AI, published on November 25, 2026, and written by Lucy Potter. It names DataRobot, Accenture, NVIDIA, Amazon Web Services, Salesforce, IBM, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Microsoft. The piece says these companies treat responsible AI as a core business priority rather than an afterthought. It says they publish principles, set up dedicated governance teams and build safeguards into their products. It says their efforts span bias detection, transparency, safety research and human oversight.

The article says DataRobot offers an enterprise AI platform that automates building, deployment and management of machine learning models. It says DataRobot's governance layer tracks every model and flags bias, drift and anomalies before deployment. It says Accenture's Responsible AI framework governs how AI systems are designed, deployed and monitored across client work. It says IBM's Principles for Trust and Transparency were first set out in 2018. It says Microsoft's principles were first published in 2018 and updated since, covering fairness, reliability, privacy, inclusiveness, transparency and accountability.

The article quotes Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft, speaking at VivaTech in Paris in 2018. It reports that he said the future people invent is a choice they make, not something that just happens. It says Microsoft enforces its principles through responsible AI teams, internal review boards, Azure AI Content Safety and the Purview data-governance suite. It says Microsoft funds AI for Good programmes and opened centres in Seattle and London to develop AI governance tools. It says Microsoft supports the EU's AI Act.

The article says Accenture's Centre for Responsible AI brings together researchers and practitioners to develop tools for fairness, explainability and transparency. It says NVIDIA's stewardship centres on NVIDIA AI Assurance, a portfolio of tools and services for evaluating models for bias, hallucinations and robustness before deployment. It says Amazon Web Services offers Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, which filter harmful content and block prompt-injection attacks in generative AI applications. It says Salesforce launched a voluntary AI Code of Conduct committing signatories to transparency and avoiding harmful use of AI. It says IBM has publicly paused facial-recognition work.

The article says Anthropic's safety research focuses on interpretability and on constitutional AI, where models are trained to follow a written set of principles rather than ad hoc human feedback. It says Anthropic has shown a willingness to have third parties evaluate its models before release. It says OpenAI has a dedicated Preparedness team that stress-tests models for dangerous capabilities. It says Google offers SynthID to watermark AI-generated content. It says Google publishes model and system cards that document capabilities and limitations.

The article does not say what happens next for any of the ten companies. It does not give dates for the governance teams, the review boards or the centres in Seattle and London. It does not say when Salesforce launched its AI Code of Conduct or when IBM paused its facial-recognition work. It does not name the third parties Anthropic would allow to evaluate its models. It does not say what the EU AI Act requires of the companies it lists.

stories.Headline: Markets question AI economics as investors demand evidence of sustainable revenues
stories.Summary:
Financial markets are beginning to question the economics, reliability and sustainability of the artificial intelligence revolution, according to The Hindu, and the AI trade is facing what the paper calls its most significant reality check yet. The article, published on November 23, 2026, and written by Arathi E.A., describes how artificial intelligence had been Wall Street's defining investment story. The proposition was straightforward, the article says: AI would transform the global economy, companies would spend unprecedented sums building the infrastructure to support it, and businesses supplying the essential technology would reap extraordinary rewards. At the centre of this investment narrative stood Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, with the semiconductor giant becoming the indispensable supplier of the computing power driving the AI revolution.

The article reports that Microsoft, Amazon and Google committed enormous sums to data centres, while OpenAI and Anthropic emerged as leading contenders in the race to develop increasingly sophisticated AI models. Markets are moving away from rewarding companies simply for their AI ambitions and increasingly demanding evidence of sustainable revenues, cash flows and returns on capital, according to the article. The piece does not give specific figures, dates or named events behind the shift beyond this general description of changing market sentiment. It presents the change as a broad reassessment rather than a single incident, and it names no individual as responsible for it.

The article does not say what happens next, and it gives no further details on the leadership turmoil or IPO jitters mentioned in its headline. It offers no statements from Nvidia, Jensen Huang, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, OpenAI or Anthropic about the shift it describes. No timeline is provided for how the reality check will unfold or what it will mean for the companies involved. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI reality check: Leadership turmoil, IPO jitters and the fragility of big tech

stories.headline_source: AI reality check: Leadership turmoil, IPO jitters and the fragility of big tech

stories.Headline: Albert P’Rayan asks whether AI-made books deserve dismissal in an essay on libraries and reading
stories.Summary:
The Hindu published an opinion article by Albert P’Rayan on November 23, 2026, asking what defines a good or high-quality book and whether books translated or generated by artificial intelligence should be dismissed outright. The piece appeared in the paper’s Education Plus section and was updated the same morning after first being published at 09:30. It is an essay about libraries, reading and the value of books rather than a report of a single event, and it names no institution, project or decision behind the questions it raises. The article describes a library as a sanctuary for intellectuals and writers and as a world of ideas, imagination and intellectual discovery.

The essay says that until a few decades ago libraries both large and small attracted readers who enjoyed exploring books of their own choosing. It argues that even now, in an age dominated by information technology and social media, people who value knowledge and wisdom still visit libraries and protest against their closure. P’Rayan writes that human beings do not live by bread alone and need intellectual and spiritual nourishment, which he says great books provide. Borrowing a thought from the Bible, he compares words nourishing the mind and spirit to bread sustaining the body, and he cites Jane Austen’s line that she would be miserable without an excellent library.

Responsibility for the views rests with the author, Albert P’Rayan, who wrote the piece in his own voice and framed the questions about quality and about AI-made books as open ones. He states his own belief that millions of readers find intellectual nourishment and fulfilment in books, and he treats a library as far more than a building filled with shelves. The article does not answer its own questions about AI-translated or AI-generated books and does not name anyone who decides which books count as good. No publisher, library body or technology company is named in connection with the questions raised.

The context the article gives is the continued pull of libraries for readers despite the dominance of information technology and social media, and the willingness of such readers to protest when libraries are closed. It places the debate over AI and books inside that wider attachment to libraries as places of ideas and discovery rather than as storage for printed volumes. The piece offers no dates, numbers or plans for what happens next, and it does not say how the question of AI-translated or AI-generated books might be settled. It ends by leaving the definition of a high-quality book and the standing of AI-made books as questions for readers to weigh.

Articles.Title: Libraries, books, and the question of AI

stories.Headline: Education ministry says teachers decide when and how students use AI in schools
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Education responded in a forum letter published on November 23, 2026, to a commentary by Tiffany Ong Rou Ying that had appeared on November 8 and argued that artificial intelligence in schools must preserve the human elements of learning. The letter was written by Lee Lin Yee, the ministry's Divisional Director for Educational Technology, and it agreed with the writer that AI use must not weaken human connection in the classroom. The ministry also said it was mindful of the pitfalls and limitations of AI, including the risk that students come to rely on it too heavily. The letter set out the ministry's position that AI use in schools should be judicious so as to preserve human agency, independent thinking and the individual voice.

Under the ministry's approach, teachers exercise their professional judgment on when to withhold or use AI and on how it should be used, so that students can develop qualities such as personal voice and creativity while strengthening their subject mastery. The ministry provides guidelines to ensure AI is introduced gradually and in ways that are developmentally appropriate and age-appropriate for students. The letter said AI can expedite the analysis of students' responses at both individual and class levels, identify common misconceptions and generate suggestions for teachers to consider. Teachers then draw on their professional knowledge, judgment and understanding of student learning needs to review and finalise the personalised feedback given to students, which helps them track progress, adjust their teaching and respond more closely to learning needs. The letter stated that all assessment scripts will be reviewed by teachers, and that AI supports rather than replaces teachers' professional judgment, with teachers remaining responsible for assessing students' learning.

The letter said students learn to use AI safely, responsibly and effectively through cyberwellness lessons and programmes such as Code for Fun, and that they also develop these skills when using AI across their subjects. The ministry acknowledged that students may have different experiences with AI use in schools and encouraged them to share feedback with their teachers. It said it would continue to enhance AI literacy development efforts so students can use the technology purposefully while understanding its limitations and risks. The letter also welcomed the writer's suggestion to give students opportunities to share their views on AI implementation, and said the ministry will work with schools to gather perspectives from teachers, students and parents as it continues to review and adjust its approach to AI in education and to AI literacy development.

Articles.Title: Forum: Teachers remain central to assessing and guiding students’ learning, even with AI

stories.headline_source: Forum: Teachers remain central to assessing and guiding students’ learning, even with AI

stories.Headline: AI concerns trigger volatility in US stock futures
stories.Summary:
U.S. stock futures traded lower on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, following a period of volatile equity market movements. These declines occurred as investors reacted to artificial intelligence jitters and awaited key inflation data. Nasdaq 100 futures fell by 491 points, or 1.9 percent, by 03:05 ET. S&P 500 futures dropped 72 points, or 1.0 percent, while Dow futures decreased by 251 points, or 0.5 percent.

The market is awaiting the October personal consumption expenditures price index, which economists expect to rise 0.3 percent month-on-month. Truflation estimates the annualized metric increased by 3.8 percent, nearly double the 2 percent target of the Federal Reserve. Dell Technologies increased its fiscal year revenue projection ending in January to around 202 billion dollars from 192 billion dollars. Dell expects 78 billion dollars of those sales to come from AI servers. The Trump administration is reportedly preparing new tariffs on dozens of countries, including China and the European Union.

Analysts at Deutsche Bank stated in a research note that the current market environment is pretty wild. Vital Knowledge analysts noted that investors decided to fade the tech squeeze induced by Jensen Huang on Monday. They claimed the sector's problems reflect a range of questions and concerns rather than a single incident. Mizuho analysts described Dell as the overall server leader with leading OEM AI server share. Dell Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke reported a record AI backlog of 132.3 billion dollars and 60.2 billion dollars in orders.

Investors in the artificial intelligence trade are affected by mood swings and worries regarding the sustainability of the technology. Shareholders of Anthropic saw an initial 34 percent pop in a first-time share sale wiped out. Nvidia shares erased gains that followed the reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang. Traders are also grappling with reports of new tariffs based on a 1974 rule regarding unfair trade practices. The Federal Reserve may be affected as some investors argue market ructions could pause an aggressive tightening cycle.

The Federal Reserve lifted interest rates in October for the first time since 2023 to combat stubbornly elevated inflation. This inflation has been driven in part by an energy shock resulting from the ongoing Iran war. Dell had previously increased its financial outlook in May and September of the current year. The U.S. Trade Representative is investigating excess manufacturing capacity to justify the potential new tariffs. Previous sweeping levies were struck down by the Supreme Court, leading to the current planning of replacements.

The Federal Reserve is widely tipped to raise interest rates again at its next meeting in December. The market will react to the official release of the October inflation gauge to determine future policy. It remains open whether the AI-related stock market volatility will actually give policymakers pause before further tightening. The articles leave open the final outcome of negotiations between Washington and Tehran regarding sanctions and frozen assets. It is unclear if the U.S. will target senior leadership in Iran following recent regional hostilities.

Articles.Title: AI jitters spark "wild" stock moves; PCE data ahead - what’s moving markets

stories.Headline: American scholar Ruha Benjamin on seeding a new reality with AI, ‘abundant imagination’
stories.Summary:
American transdisciplinary scholar Ruha Benjamin gave a keynote address titled Ctrl + Alt + Rethink at the Singapore Writers Festival 2026, speaking to a full house at the Victoria Theatre on Nov 22. Benjamin, who is the Alexander Stewart 1886 Professor of African American Studies at Princeton University, drew on her family's move to the Marshall Islands when she was 15, where she saw the contrast between the Kwajalein Atoll and Ebeye. She linked that experience, and the impact of atomic testing on local communities, to wider questions about race, justice and technology. The talk was reported by The Straits Times on Nov 23.

In the lecture, Benjamin said technology often hides bias behind a veneer of impersonal objectivity, citing the UK's use of a predictive algorithm to grade students during the Covid-19 pandemic after they could not sit their A levels. She said students from working-class and more diverse schools were graded lower than wealthier, whiter counterparts, and argued that such systems reflect and reproduce existing inequities. She called on people to unlearn seven long-held assumptions, including that innovation equals social progress and that technology is self-propelled rather than human-driven. She proposed what she called abundant imagination, urging people to unplug from false notions of hierarchy and scarcity while protecting imagination, and to seed a different reality.

Benjamin said the limiting narratives of techno-dystopia and techno-utopia are pushed by a small group with vested interests, and that it serves their interests for people to believe AI has a will of its own. She warned that without actively rethinking and reimagining, people will remain trapped inside what she called a deeply racist, colonialist and eugenic imagination. She advocated starting in education, to equip younger generations with the muscle to exercise imagination. Asked how to hold on to hope, she described a personal practice of historical imagination, time-travelling to prior eras when an overriding regime seemed impossible to bring down, and channelling the stubborn insistence of people in every era who said this is not right.

Articles.Title: American scholar Ruha Benjamin on seeding a new reality with AI, ‘abundant imagination’

stories.Headline: Humanoid robot speed records inspire new startups to enter the field
stories.Summary:
Humanoid robotics have evolved significantly since the 1970s, when the first bipedal robot took 30 seconds to take one step. Over the following decades, companies like Honda developed machines capable of dancing and navigating stairs. Recent advancements have pushed these capabilities even further, with robots now surpassing human athletic limits.

At a sporting event in China this August, a humanoid robot ran 100 meters in 8.64 seconds. This performance beat the world record of 9.58 seconds held by Usain Bolt. These rapid technological leaps are now motivating new startups to enter the field.

Articles.Title: Visions of Japan overrun by humanoid robot imports inspire startups

stories.Headline: Korean stocks fall 3.31 percent as AI sell-off deepens and government readies stabilization fund
stories.Summary:
Korean stocks fell 3.31 percent in Seoul on Monday, November 23, 2026, as a deepening sell-off in artificial intelligence shares drove the KOSPI to its lowest close since January 13. The benchmark index closed at 4,708.54 after falling as much as 5 percent intraday and briefly slipping to 4,586.8, which triggered a sell-side sidecar at 11:33 a.m. Samsung Electronics dropped 3.06 percent to 177,500 won, while SK hynix fell 2.52 percent to close at 1,085,000 won. The tech-heavy Kosdaq also shed 1.58 percent to finish at 635.45, which was its lowest level in two years.

The government announced preparations on Sunday to activate a stock market stabilization fund and ease restrictions on share buybacks. Authorities also plan to intensify enforcement against illegal short selling for a period of three months to support the market. David Chung estimated that combined buying from the stabilization fund, the National Pension Service, and SK hynix could total between 31 trillion and 35 trillion won. However, he noted that none of this spending is guaranteed and may not offset foreign selling.

David Chung stated that foreign selling must ease before the KOSPI can turn around, as foreign investors have sold a net 55 trillion won since September. Anna Wu suggested that the recovery of the KOSPI depends on whether United States chip stocks find a floor. Citi economist Kim Jin-wook estimated that household losses could reach 563 trillion won in the second half of the year. He further claimed that these losses could reduce overall consumption by 8.4 trillion won.

The market rout follows a sharp sell-off on Wall Street that affected major semiconductor companies and the broader AI supply chain. This decline puts pressure on the Lee Jae Myung administration, which had previously highlighted the KOSPI rally as a major achievement. Retail investors are now demanding a blanket ban on short selling, with over 10,000 people signing a petition for the Kosdaq. Analysts warn that domestic buying capacity may be insufficient to counter the current trend of foreign divestment.

Articles.Title: Seoul stocks lose 3.3% as AI rout tests gov't rescue plans

stories.Headline: President Lee Jae Myung calls for swift overhaul of Korea's national testing system to counter AI cheating
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung called on Friday for a swift overhaul of Korea's national testing system, pushing forward proposals to move the College Scholastic Ability Test beyond multiple-choice questions, according to The Korea Times. The National Education Commission presented Lee with a plan in August to consider absolute grading and written-response and essay questions, and it has since sought public input through discussions with its citizen participation committee. In October, weeks before the CSAT, students were caught using AI-powered smart glasses during essay-based entrance exams at Yonsei University and the University of Seoul. The scrutiny comes as Korea's decades-old testing system faces growing fears of cheating powered by artificial intelligence.

The proposed changes face practical hurdles and offer no guarantee of stopping increasingly sophisticated AI-driven cheating, the article says. Moon Hyung-nam, a professor at Sookmyung Women's University and president of the Korea AI Education Association, said generative AI can select answers, explain its reasoning and write essays, so simply switching to written-response questions would not prevent AI-assisted cheating. Song Ki-chang, chancellor of Sungsan Hyo University, argued that manual grading of written responses would be virtually impossible given the number of CSAT test-takers, while relying on AI could reward conventional answers over creativity and critical thinking. Park Joo-ho, president of Daelim University, said reform should clarify whether the CSAT is meant to assess mastery of the school curriculum or determine university admission.

One alternative gaining attention is turning the CSAT into a basic qualification exam and giving universities greater freedom to select their own students, with Song saying greater weight could go to university-administered entrance exams. Kim Won-jung, head of admissions strategy at Daesung Academy, said universities would welcome such a shift and that it may be the most realistic way to tackle AI-related problems, though he acknowledged it would likely create new demand for private tutoring. Song said concerns over private tutoring would inevitably resurface if university-administered exams gained greater weight, and he argued that rather than seeking a perfect system, the focus should be on minimizing its shortcomings. The article says such a shift could intensify competition for admission and drive up demand for private tutoring, reigniting long-standing concerns over Korea's highly competitive education system.

Articles.Title: AI cheating puts Korea's decades-old exam system under scrutiny

stories.Headline: Virginia Tech-led team publishes statistical test for AI medical imaging
stories.Summary:
A Virginia Tech-led team published a new statistical test for AI medical imaging on Nov. 23, 2026, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team includes researchers from the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Texas Tech University and Princeton University. Virginia Tech News reported the work the same day in an article by Kelly Izlar. The tool combines computational topology and statistics to compare complex image data. The researchers tested it on synthetic mammograms compared with real patient data.

The method's job is to decide whether AI-generated medical images are faithful enough to stand in for real patient data in clinical trials. The team tracked how breast cancer responds to different radiation doses. The National Science Foundation funded the research through a joint partnership with the National Institutes of Health and the Food and Drug Administration. The announcement gives no sample sizes, error rates or number of synthetic images used. The paper's exact title as it appears in PNAS and any product name for the method are not established in the sources.

Yulia R. Gel, a professor of statistics at Virginia Tech, said the goal is that clinical trials with synthetic data reach the same conclusions as with real people. Statistics graduate student Jaidev Goel, one of the paper's leading authors, told Virginia Tech News that statistics has always supplied the stress tests for new tools. Goel also said people should not buy into AI hype blindly. Virginia Tech says the tool bridges computational topology and statistics to measure and compare complex image data. The announcement does not spell out which topological features the team extracted or how the statistical test is built.

Virginia Tech explains that deploying a more powerful, more precise MRI in a hospital requires FDA approval. The university adds that the FDA is exploring AI-generated synthetic data alternatives that could compress trial timelines to months. The team is in talks with FDA on pre- and post-market use, confirmed as talks only. A systematic literature review and meta-analysis in npj Digital Medicine examines how AI implementation affects efficiency in medical imaging. Approval for routine clinical use is not confirmed, and no evidence was found for it.

Generative adversarial networks, introduced in 2014, showed that neural networks could produce convincing images. Medical researchers soon tried them on scans, mostly to augment small datasets. Computational topology studies the shape of data and summarizes structure such as connected regions, loops and gaps. Statistics turns a comparison into a decision by asking whether two collections of images differ by more than chance would explain. The announcement does not give cost or an implementation date.

The research is real and published, while the commercial and regulatory consequences remain forecasts. Independent replication on other modalities will tell us far more than the first paper can. The method exists to say no when a synthetic set falls short. A pass on one generator, one organ and one dose range tells us little about another generator. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Jongno District deploys AI crosswalk system that extends crossing time for slower pedestrians
stories.Summary:
Jongno District in central Seoul will begin operating pavement-level pedestrian signals and voice guidance devices at 123 locations from Dec. 1, the district office said, and an AI system will extend crossing time at a crosswalk near Jogye Temple by up to 10 seconds. The installations are intended to help pedestrians, especially children and older adults, cross streets more safely. The district completed construction of the pavement-level signals and voice guidance devices in October after developing and testing the equipment through August. The district plans to finish final inspections by the end of November. The pavement-level pedestrian signals illuminate the tactile pavers at crosswalks so people can detect when it is safe to cross, while the voice guidance devices use infrared sensors to detect pedestrians and issue audible warnings when they attempt to cross against the signal.

The installations target roads with at least four lanes, prioritizing areas with heavy pedestrian traffic and a history of accidents. The AI video recognition system is scheduled for installation by Dec. 31 at a crosswalk in front of Seonjae Daycare Center, within a child protection zone near Jogye Temple. It detects when pedestrians are still crossing as the signal approaches its end and automatically adds up to 10 seconds only when additional time is needed, balancing pedestrian safety with vehicle traffic. The technology was previously introduced at two crossings near Tapgol Park and Unhyeon and Gyodong elementary schools, where it automatically extended pedestrian signals 6,147 times during a two-week monitoring period in June.

At Tapgol Park, extensions occurred 4,289 times, accounting for 44.2 percent of signal cycles, while the two school-area crossings recorded 1,858 extensions, or 19.1 percent. The district said the results showed the system could help older residents and other pedestrians who need more time to cross. Jongno District Mayor Yoo Chan-jong said the district would expand smart traffic infrastructure tailored to residents' needs and pursue transportation policies aimed at improving daily safety. The district is considering expanding the time-extension technology to areas with significant child and senior pedestrian populations, according to the article.

Articles.Title: Jongno District deploys AI crosswalks to give slower pedestrians more time

stories.Headline: Dell raises fiscal 2027 revenue forecast to $202B as AI server backlog reaches $132.3B
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies raised its full-year forecasts on November 24, 2026, after a record fiscal third quarter driven by AI servers. The company now expects $202.0 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue, up from $192.0 billion, and adjusted earnings of $29.68 per share, up from $25.50. Quarterly revenue hit $54.9 billion, and the AI-server order book swelled to $132.3 billion. The quarter ended October 30, 2026, and Dell reported revenue of $54.9 billion, a record. Dell had told investors in September to expect about $49.0 billion, so the company beat its own forecast by $5.9 billion.

Dell lifted three full-year targets at once, with revenue guidance rising by $10 billion to $202.0 billion. Adjusted EPS guidance rose by $4.18 to $29.68, and AI-server revenue guidance rose by $4 billion to $78.0 billion. The backlog opened the quarter at $95.0 billion, gained $60.2 billion of new orders, lost $22.0 billion to AI-server sales, shed another $0.9 billion, and closed at $132.3 billion. Dell booked $60.2 billion of new AI-server orders in a single quarter while shipping $22.0 billion of them. The fourth-quarter AI-server forecast of about $23.5 billion equals roughly 18% of the backlog.

Founder and CEO Michael Dell said in a public post on X that it was another record quarter 42 years after starting Dell in his dorm room. He cited record revenue of $54.9 billion, record AI servers revenue of $22 billion and a record AI backlog of $132.3 billion. He said the world's demand for intelligence is accelerating and Dell is building the infrastructure to power it. Vice Chairman and COO Jeff Clarke said on the earnings call that the company will have added nearly $58 billion of ISG revenue. He said $28 billion of that was in AI servers and $30 billion in core servers or traditional servers, networking and storage.

CNBC reported that Jeff Clarke said every AI order is checked for customer quality, access to capital, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power. Dell said more than 7,500 customers are now deploying Dell AI Factories. The Infrastructure Solutions Group posted $41.97 billion in sales, beating an LSEG estimate of $35.27 billion and accounting for about 85% of Dell's total revenue. Client Solutions Group PC sales were $12.89 billion against a $14.33 billion expectation. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $9.45 against $6.59 expected by analysts polled by LSEG.

Stock Titan's tally shows Dell beat its own revenue forecast in each of the first three quarters of fiscal 2027. In the first quarter it guided to $35.2 billion and reported $43.8 billion, and in the second it guided to $44.5 billion and reported $47.0 billion. The backlog stood at $43.0 billion on January 30, 2026, at $51.3 billion on May 1, 2026, and at $95.0 billion on July 31, 2026. The SEC filing records $22.0 billion of AI-Optimized Servers revenue, up 291% year over year. Reports put the prior consensus for fiscal 2027 revenue at roughly $194.48 billion.

Dell guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $56.3 billion against an LSEG consensus of $53.61 billion, and adjusted EPS to $8.40 against $7.50. Dell's shares fell sharply during the regular session before the release, then turned higher in extended trading once the numbers came out. Micron slipped 6.4% to $662 as Dell earnings loomed. Dell has not said when the rest of the backlog ships. If no new orders arrived at all, the backlog would still sit near $108.8 billion after the fourth quarter, by simple subtraction.

Articles.Title: Dell Lifts Forecast to $202B as AI Backlog Hits $132.3B
