stories.Headline: Samsung Electro-Mechanics beats LG Innotek in substrate profit on AI chip demand
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electro-Mechanics earned 2.7 times as much operating profit as LG Innotek in its substrate business in the first nine months of 2026, helped by sales of higher-value substrates for AI data centers. Samsung Electro-Mechanics generated 369.4 billion won, or $274 million, in operating profit from its package solutions division over the period, compared with 135.7 billion won at LG Innotek, according to their latest regulatory filings. Its operating margin reached 15.2 percent, against LG Innotek’s 9.6 percent, even though LG Innotek reported an average substrate production-line utilization rate of 94.4 percent, compared with 90 percent at Samsung Electro-Mechanics. Samsung Electro-Mechanics has expanded supplies of flip-chip ball grid array substrates for server processors and AI accelerators, and its average semiconductor substrate selling price rose 28.1 percent year on year in the first nine months, according to its filings.

Its package solutions operating profit surged 322 percent over the same period, compared with a 69.2 percent increase at LG Innotek. Third-quarter package solutions revenue also climbed 58 percent year on year to 939 billion won at Samsung Electro-Mechanics, compared with LG Innotek’s 10.1 percent growth to 481.8 billion won. Samsung Electro-Mechanics said Wednesday that it had agreed to expand its substrate partnership with Nvidia, which will provide additional funding to increase capacity at two existing factories in South Korea. The move follows an October partnership covering substrates for AI processors and high-speed networking chips, and Samsung Electro-Mechanics announced plans in September to invest 6.78 trillion won to expand flip-chip ball grid array production in Sejong, South Korea, and Vietnam.

LG Innotek, whose substrate business is anchored by smartphone components such as RF-SiP and FC-CSP, is also pursuing the higher-margin AI server market. It is expanding flip-chip ball grid array supplies for PC processors and aims to begin mass-producing substrates for AI training and inference servers in 2027. The company aims to grow flip-chip ball grid array revenue from about 50 billion won in 2025 to more than 1 trillion won by 2030. It has committed approximately 1 trillion won to smartphone substrate production in Vietnam and is discussing separate flip-chip ball grid array investments with customers to support its expansion into AI servers.

Articles.Title: AI chip boom lifts Samsung Electro-Mechanics ahead of LG Innotek in substrate profits

stories.headline_source: AI chip boom lifts Samsung Electro-Mechanics ahead of LG Innotek in substrate profits

stories.Headline: South Korea and US plan AI and chip projects in third countries via Pax Silica
stories.Summary:
South Korea is exploring a partnership with the United States to launch advanced industry projects in third countries. This initiative began taking shape after Second Vice Foreign Minister Kim Jin-a met U.S. Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg in San Francisco on November 16. The two nations intend to use Pax Silica, a U.S.-led economic security and AI coalition launched in December of last year, to coordinate these efforts. Seoul is seeking to expand its role in the overhaul of chip and AI supply chains while attempting to avoid friction with China. The cooperation involves identifying technology needs in other countries and matching them with Korean firms that can provide the necessary facilities.

One specific example is the Luzon Economic Corridor in the Philippines, which the United States started in 2024 with Japan to build logistics and industrial infrastructure. This includes a planned economic security zone of about 16 square kilometers on the island of Luzon to move manufacturing away from China. Additionally, the two countries are discussing AI talent training by linking KAIST and Seoul National University to the Stanford University led Foundry School. The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources has already compiled a list of potential companies to share with other government ministries. A source stated that the interests of both nations align because the United States wants trusted partners and Korea wants more overseas opportunities for its firms.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has remained vague in public announcements, mentioning only that Helberg proposed more collaboration between companies. This caution stems from the risk that closer ties with Washington could damage relations with Beijing. These developments occur amid a fierce tech rivalry between the United States and China regarding AI and semiconductor supply chains. While President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping reached a trade truce in October of last year, experts suggest that AI supply chains have become a primary battleground. The two countries plan to hold the Korea-U.S. Senior Economic Dialogue in Seoul at the end of this year or early next year to continue these talks.

Articles.Title: Seoul eyes third-country AI, chip projects through Pax Silica

stories.headline_source: Seoul eyes third-country AI, chip projects through Pax Silica

stories.Headline: South Korea finance minister Lee Hyoung-il forecasts high-3 percent growth and prepares a stock stabilization fund
stories.Summary:
Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hyoung-il expressed confidence on Monday, November 23, 2026, that the South Korean economy could expand in the high-3 percent range this year. Speaking at the Government Complex Sejong, Lee noted that growth of 4 percent might be possible this year or next, although fourth-quarter data is not yet available. His positive outlook is based on the belief that the global semiconductor industry will remain resilient through 2027. He pointed to declining memory inventories and substantial long-term supply contracts secured by SK hynix and Samsung Electronics.

To address stock market volatility caused by AI concerns and US interest rate hikes, officials are preparing a stock market stabilization fund. This plan follows a Sunday meeting with the heads of the Financial Supervisory Service, the Financial Services Commission, and the Bank of Korea. The government has already eased daily corporate share buyback limits for three months and increased monitoring of illegal short selling. Lee stated that the government has activated part of its contingency plan and will implement further measures based on market conditions.

Lee explained that the decision to deploy the stabilization fund depends on market conditions, and he has not provided a specific timetable or trigger for its use. He claimed that South Korea's short-selling regulations are already stricter than those in other advanced economies, so the government will focus on surveillance rather than adding new restrictions. Regarding the labor market, Lee acknowledged that job gains have lagged behind economic growth, but he expects employment to improve next year. He also suggested that the petroleum price ceiling might be extended into 2027 to protect vulnerable households from winter costs and Middle East uncertainty.

Articles.Title: Korea's finance minister upbeat on growth despite AI jitters

stories.headline_source: Korea's finance minister upbeat on growth despite AI jitters

stories.Headline: President Lee orders full review of Suneung exam after AI cheating cases
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung on Friday ordered a sweeping review of the national examination system, calling for testing methods to be reconsidered "from A to Z." The order followed five test-takers caught in cheating cases involving smart devices during Thursday's College Scholastic Ability Test, or Suneung. Smart glasses and miniature cameras were discovered during South Korea's college entrance exam. The incidents have reignited debate over whether Korea should move beyond its multiple-choice-heavy examination system. The test was held on Nov. 19, and the article was published Nov. 23, 2026. The Suneung plays a decisive role in university admissions, and public confidence in grading fairness remains paramount.

In December 2025, Seoul education chief Jeong Geun-sik proposed introducing essay-based testing by 2033 and ultimately abolishing the Suneung by 2040. The National Education Commission has considered expanding essay-based assessments as part of its 2028-2037 national education strategy. Disagreements over grading fairness and the burden on schools delayed the release of its reform plans in October. In a deliberative exercise involving 180 citizens, 55.5 percent supported introducing essay-based questions, while 41.7 percent opposed the proposal, and grading fairness was the most frequently cited concern, identified by 48.3 percent of participants. Jeong said children living in the age of AI need the ability to ask questions and think critically and creatively, not simply to seek answers.

Lee Hye-jung, director of the Institute for Education and Innovation, said the multiple-choice system survived because of the belief that it ensures reliable and fair grading, regardless of who evaluates the answers. She said the latest AI cheating scandal has shattered that myth and that the era of multiple-choice Suneung exams has come to an end. She said Korea does not need to change the curriculum itself but how students are taught and evaluated. She said what matters is establishing a system that produces consistent, reproducible results within an acceptable margin of variation. Moon Hyung-nam, a professor at Sookmyung Women's University and president of the Korea AI Education Association, said simply switching from multiple-choice to essay-based or oral examinations will not solve AI-assisted cheating.

He cited a 2024 University of Reading study in which 94 percent of AI-generated answers submitted to unproctored undergraduate assessments went undetected by graders. He called for clearer restrictions on electronic devices, consistent pre-exam checks and stronger exam supervision. National Education Commission Chair Cha Jeong-in said authorities are considering ways to gradually expand written-response and essay-based assessments in schools over a considerable period. He stressed that such a transition could not be accomplished within one or two years. Ahead of this year's Suneung, authorities tightened security measures, including restrictions on electronic devices, checks for concealed smartphones and enhanced Wi-Fi monitoring around testing centers.

The exam concluded without major disruptions, but the discovery of sophisticated cheating devices underscored the difficulty of keeping pace with rapidly evolving technology. Calls to reform the Suneung predate the latest cheating cases, reflecting concerns that the exam places too much emphasis on finding correct answers. Lee Hye-jung pointed to the International Baccalaureate, which uses written examinations, oral presentations and longer-term projects. She argued such an approach could reduce dependence on a single high-stakes test while better assessing students' reasoning and creativity. The articles do not state what specific measures the presidential review will produce or when it will report.

They do not say what penalties the five test-takers face or what devices were found beyond smart glasses and miniature cameras. They do not state whether the National Education Commission will release its delayed reform plans or when. They do not say how the 2033 and 2040 targets proposed by Jeong Geun-sik would be enacted. They do not state how the 2024 University of Reading study was conducted beyond its 94 percent finding. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Can Korea's high-stakes Suneung survive AI era?

stories.headline_source: Can Korea's high-stakes Suneung survive AI era?

stories.Headline: Seoul National University considers requiring an introductory AI course for all undergraduates by 2028
stories.Summary:
Seoul National University is considering making an introductory AI course a graduation requirement for every undergraduate, regardless of major, according to a report the JoongAng Ilbo obtained exclusively on Sunday. The proposal comes from a report titled "Study on Expanding Seoul National University's Computing and AI Curriculum" (translated), and its stated goal is to ensure all students graduate with a baseline level of AI skills. The research team behind it is made up of six faculty members, including Oh Min-hwan, a professor at the Graduate School of Data Science. The team suggested students choose from three basic AI courses depending on their level. The courses would be offered at tiers: one for nonscience and nonengineering students, one for second-year science and engineering students and an advanced tier for science and engineering students in their second to fourth years, with students choosing based on their background knowledge.

Two of the three courses already exist, namely "Core Computing" for nonscience and nonengineering students, offered by SNU College, and the advanced "Fundamentals of Machine Learning" (translated), offered by the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering. The third, "Introduction to AI" (translated), aimed at science and engineering students in general, is set to launch in the College of Engineering in spring 2027. The report presented two options for class size, the first a "mega hybrid" format with 400 or more students combining in-person and remote instruction, and the second splitting the course into multiple sections of 100 to 150 students each sharing a single curriculum. The researchers suggested starting with the first option, then gradually reducing enrollment caps and adding sections until the course runs like the second. The research team found that demand is growing much faster than the number of AI courses at the university, leaving supply short.

The number of undergraduate AI courses rose by six, or 12.5 percent, from 48 in fall 2025 to 54 in spring 2026, while over the same period total seats rose by 1,260, or 54.8 percent, and enrollment rose by 659, or 50.8 percent. Applications for general education AI courses jumped from about 34 percent of available seats to about 79 percent, and the team also pointed out that access varies widely by college, with the College of Engineering offering 14 AI-related courses in the spring semester while the College of Pharmacy and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences offered just one each. The researchers said SNU College, which oversees basic education for undergraduates, needs to provide common instruction on the principles, applications and ethics of AI. SNU College aims to introduce the revised graduation requirements in the spring 2028 semester. An SNU College official said the plan is to discuss the revision with the relevant colleges and then submit it for approval by the university's deliberative body.

Articles.Title: Seoul National University weighs mandatory AI course for every undergraduate by 2028

stories.headline_source: Seoul National University weighs mandatory AI course for every undergraduate by 2028

stories.Headline: South Korea prepares for agentic AI and geopolitical fragmentation by 2027
stories.Summary:
Senior columnist Choi Hoon wrote that South Korea must prepare for several major trends arriving in 2027. He identified agentic AI, geopolitical fragmentation, and social division as the primary challenges for the nation. These shifts require Korea to identify global directions and chart its course accordingly. The author argues that national leadership must look beyond immediate disputes to adapt. This preparation is necessary as technological, geopolitical, and social transformations converge.

Agentic AI will independently plan and execute tasks, moving beyond the copilot roles seen in 2026. A November World Economic Forum report predicts agents will handle research, analysis, forecasting, negotiations, customer service, and software development. Companies must reorganize structures and calculate measurable returns on investment, as Gartner warned in October. The OECD emphasizes AI governance, while a survey of 200 Korean companies found 60 percent lacked data location knowledge. Seventy percent of those surveyed lacked a data sovereignty strategy.

The World Economic Forum described 2026 as an era of competition between Washington and Beijing. A November S&P Global report says international rules and markets no longer guarantee security or prosperity. This report suggests that national interests must now shape budgets, industrial policies, trade agreements, and military strategies. Economic security is becoming central as the world moves toward a fragmented multipolar order. This new order includes the United States, China, an independent Europe, India, and Global South powers.

Professor emeritus Ha Young-sun suggests a strategy called complex network diplomacy for the emerging order. This approach involves pursuing national interests while linking diverse countries, sectors, and actors. Korea must expand trilateral security cooperation with Washington and Tokyo, anchored in the Korea-U.S. alliance. The nation must also diversify supply chains and markets to reduce dependence on the United States and China. This strategy aims to avoid passive reliance on networks connecting Korea to major powers.

A September Ipsos report describes societies moving toward smaller, antagonistic groups divided by identity, gender, immigration, and social change. Edelman characterized 2026 as an age of insularity and predicts 2027 will be an age of agency. In this coming age, individuals will seek greater control over their own lives and surroundings. Recovering personal autonomy and social influence could help people overcome feelings of distrust and helplessness. Ipsos suggests creating shared spaces, experiences, and narratives to integrate these fragmented groups.

Companies must now demonstrate measurable returns from technology rather than using simple indicators like employee usage rates. Diplomats are tasked with expanding their options to navigate the fragmented multipolar order of 2027. Political leaders must rebuild connections across a Korean society that is becoming increasingly divided. The articles leave open how the government will specifically implement these necessary structural and social changes. It remains unclear if intelligent AI can truly remain under human control as its autonomy grows.

A subsequent government bailout would then trigger a powerful rally for Bitcoin.

The plan requires governments to print money to save the AI sector. Hayes mentions that Anthropic and OpenAI are burning huge amounts of cash. These labs may struggle to pay for hundreds of billions of dollars in computing. He notes that China, South Korea, and Taiwan have already propped up stock markets. He suggests Zcash and Ethena are the best altcoins to play a bailout.

Arthur Hayes is the founder of BitMEX and now runs Flop Labs. He said a new Bitcoin bull market is 100 percent dependent on an AI bailout. He claims investors could see massive returns similar to those seen in 2020.

Hayes says investors will sell crypto when they offload AI stocks for liquidity. He believes this creates an opportunity for those using little or no leverage. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits remained neutral while chatter levels stayed high for Bitcoin. Traders on CME FedWatch saw a 99.2 percent chance of a December rate hike. This probability increased from 68.9 percent recorded one month prior to the report.

Hayes has worked in the crypto industry for more than a decade. He is credited with creating the perpetual swap for the crypto market. He currently manages investments at his family office, which is called Milestone. Hayes admitted his target of 250,000 dollars for Bitcoin fell short this year. He noted that the monetary easing he expected never actually came to pass.

Hayes will watch for gold rising while the Nasdaq falls over several days. He also wants the Federal Reserve to suggest rates will stay on hold. He is closely watching the December meeting for a restart of reserve purchases. He describes these potential purchases as quantitative easing by another name. stories.Headline: Mock juries side with plaintiffs more often when radiologists disagree with AI, Bernstein finds
stories.Summary:
Researchers using simulated malpractice cases have found that mock juries were more likely to side with a plaintiff when an AI system disagreed with a radiologist than when it agreed, according to a study published in NEJM AI and reported by Axios on November 23, 2026. In one scenario involving a brain bleed on a CT scan that resulted in irreversible brain damage, jurors sided with the plaintiff 72.9% of the time when the AI flagged the condition and the radiologist did not. In a second case built around a missed lung cancer on a CT scan that resulted in the patient's death, participants sided with the plaintiff 78.7% of the time when the AI said the patient had cancer and the doctor did not think so. The study's lead author is Michael Bernstein, an associate professor at the Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University.

The findings suggest that doctors who disagree with an algorithm that flags an abnormality may face greater legal jeopardy of losing a malpractice suit, and some may order costly, possibly unneeded tests if they think it reduces their legal liability. A smaller percentage of jurors ruled against the physician when they were given data on the AI system's error rate, which experts say is significant because false positive readings are almost inevitable and can temper the belief that the technology is always right. The researchers said double-checking AI results could reduce doctors' malpractice risks and prospective jurors' perceptions of whether a doctor met the duty of care standard, though the question is whether physicians can find the time. The systems are used extensively to analyze medical images and improve the accuracy of diagnoses, demand for tests is rising, and the systems invariably make mistakes.

Bernstein said the research is uncovering an unintended consequence of AI adoption, adding that AI can do a lot in radiology but is not all uniformly positive. He said one concern is the prospect of more defensive medicine, in which clinicians overcorrect and order follow-up scans and exams, which can drive up costs and patient anxiety. The American Medical Association this month called for new federal and state legislation that shields clinicians from liability when AI products harm patients, and it is pressing for new laws mandating that AI companies carry adequate liability insurance and disclose product limitations and performance data. Johns Hopkins researchers wrote in JAMA Health Forum last year that because human operators are perceived as having control over the technology's use, responsibility unduly shifts to the human operator, and they noted that physicians were consistently viewed as more liable than AI vendors, health systems that adopted the technology or regulators.

Experts say there are few established legal precedents for how AI might change the nature of malpractice liability in a field like radiology, and physicians are demanding more protections. Radiology is a closely watched specialty because AI is used extensively and because missing an abnormality can be fatal, and it is also among the fields with a high risk of being sued. Research on perceptions of blame is cutting across many medical disciplines and underscores how physicians who are expected to rely on AI to cut down on medical errors still have to know when to override the systems. The public may still be wary about how AI is used in a hospital or doctor's office, but there is also a baked-in assumption that it is never wrong, which can put physicians in a bind when they disagree with an algorithm.

stories.Headline: IrisKey.ai introduces a 26-gate governance architecture for autonomous AI
stories.Summary:
IrisKey.ai, a company based in Coventry, said on 25 November 2026 that it had introduced a 26-gate governance architecture for autonomous AI systems, which it described as a design meant to enforce authority before AI agents carry out consequential actions. The company said the proposed system, for which it has filed a patent application, is intended to separate what an AI system can do from what it is allowed to do. According to IrisKey.ai, the framework would verify authority, control delegated permissions and support the withdrawal of access when authorisation changes. The company said the concept is meant to create a structured series of checks before execution, addressing whether authority can be verified before an action takes place, whether delegated permissions remain within defined limits, and whether revoked access can be prevented from being used.

IrisKey.ai said the architecture is intended to work across different AI models, software environments and operational settings, but it has not disclosed the detailed design because the work sits within its intellectual property programme. The company said the architecture is not meant to replace cybersecurity systems or regulatory governance, but to sit between AI decision-making and execution. It said it is pursuing a commercial model centred on intellectual property licensing and independent technical evaluation rather than building its own foundation model, and that it is seeking discussions with organisations that want to test whether the proposed framework could be applied to existing AI agent platforms, cybersecurity tools, enterprise automation systems and financial technology. IrisKey.ai added that it has not announced independent validation of the full 26-gate architecture, and that performance and security outcomes would require testing, which it said would need to examine implementation feasibility, integration requirements, enforcement behaviour and underlying security assumptions.

Adam McCrum, the founder of IrisKey.ai, said the rise of more autonomous systems had exposed a gap between policy and technical control, and he argued that capability and authority are two very different things. He said a governance policy cannot physically stop an unauthorised API call and a compliance dashboard cannot guarantee that a revoked permission has stopped being used, so technical enforcement needs to be designed into the architecture itself. McCrum said the principle behind the work is that authority must come before autonomy, and that the more capable these systems become, the more important it is that their permissions remain verifiable, constrained and enforceable. He also said the future of AI will depend not only on how intelligent systems become but on whether meaningful technical boundaries can be established around their actions.

IrisKey.ai argued that existing AI governance has largely focused on ethics, compliance, risk management and human oversight, and that these measures alone do not provide a technical mechanism to stop an unauthorised action once an autonomous system is operating. The company pointed to financial services, healthcare, industrial systems, transport, defence and public-sector operations as areas where enforcement of AI permissions could be significant, saying that in such settings capability alone is not enough when actions carry financial, safety or security consequences. It said the central issue is how to ensure autonomous systems act only within explicitly authorised limits, and it argued that technical boundaries around AI actions will become more important as autonomous systems take on greater operational roles. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the company seeking discussions with organisations interested in testing the framework.

stories.Headline: Synthesis earns AWS AI Competency in generative and agentic consulting
stories.Summary:
Synthesis Software Technologies has achieved the Amazon Web Services AI Competency in the Generative AI Consulting Services and Agentic AI Consulting Services categories, according to an announcement dated 25 November 2026. To earn the competency, the company demonstrated its established AI delivery practices and provided evidence of customer implementations running in production. The assessment covered how Synthesis designs, implements and supports AI solutions, as well as the value its work has delivered to customers.

The two categories cover distinct capabilities, with generative AI helping employees retrieve knowledge and produce content while agentic AI lets software agents interact with enterprise tools and carry out multi-step tasks within defined boundaries. Synthesis says the recognition gives it faster access to AWS generative AI tools and services, and it describes joint programs that combine its industry experience with AWS's scalable generative AI solutions. The company says these will provide rapid time to market across back-office and front-office functions, including operations, technology and marketing. For organisations adopting agentic AI, Synthesis says boundaries must be built into the system, with appropriate monitoring and opportunities for human intervention.

Paul Spagnoletti, Executive Head of Revenue at Synthesis, said a working proof of concept is only the beginning and that the real test is whether a business can depend on the AI system every day. He said banking and payments systems have to work with existing technology and meet strict security and oversight requirements, which takes far more than getting a model to produce the right answer. Michael Shapiro, Managing Director at Synthesis, said the recognition is valuable for what the team can do with it next, and that the relationship with AWS gives access to programmes and support that can help customers get significant AI projects under way. He said Synthesis will help customers identify where the technology can deliver real returns and then put in motion secure and robust engineering.

Synthesis says an AI project also needs a credible operating model before it goes live, and that customers should weigh implementation and ongoing support costs against the improvements they expect and decide how to measure those benefits. Responsibility for handling exceptions needs to be clear, especially when software agents take actions across business systems, and employees may need training as familiar processes change. Without that preparation, the company says, a system that performs well in testing can be difficult to manage at scale. Synthesis says it draws on its experience in cloud architecture, software engineering and managed operations to plan for those demands before deployment and to provide support afterwards.

stories.Headline: Researchers use Meta open-weight AI models to train doctors and study epilepsy and rare diseases
stories.Summary:
Meta said on November 23, 2026 that researchers are using its open-weight AI models and its research funding to address critical gaps in medicine. Meta said it had expanded its academic partnerships to give researchers funding and access to models including Muse Glimmer, SAM3, DINOv3 and Brain2Qwertyv2. Meta said the researchers are independently adapting the models for their own investigational research. Meta said the projects include training medical professionals in low-resource settings, locating epilepsy sources in the brain and advancing understanding of rare diseases. Meta published the account on its newsroom under the headline about researchers using its open-weight AI models to transform medicine.

At Louisiana State University, Dr. Peter DeBlieux and his team are using Muse Glimmer, SAM 3, DINOv3 and other Meta models with Meta Quest 3 headsets to develop COPES. Meta described COPES as an experimental coaching platform that supports healthcare professionals with medical procedural training in virtual reality. Meta said the system will aim to provide adaptive guidance, real-time performance assessment and personalized feedback across technical execution, patient communication, clinical reasoning and decision-making. Meta said working virtually lets medical students learn complicated procedures where practicing on real patients may be risky. Meta said virtual instruction means more medical professionals can receive high quality technical and communications training no matter where they are.

Dr. Pierre Bourdillon at Rothschild Hospital Foundation is using AI research and Meta models including NeuralSet, Brain2Qwertyv2, Tribev2 and DINOv3 in research projects aimed at better understanding the source of epilepsy in the brain. Meta said epilepsy currently can't be directly visualized in brain images, making it difficult for clinicians to identify its source. Meta said Dr. Bourdillon is using AI to develop a tool that can enable simulations of epileptic seizures originating in different regions of the brain. Meta said the approach could one day let doctors select the simulation that best matches their patient's case and form a strong hypothesis about where the epilepsy originates. Meta said the early-stage research could improve accuracy in treatments including surgical removal of affected brain tissue and device implantation designed to disrupt epileptic activity, and that the simulations could help researchers address speech and motor restoration in patients with brain injuries.

At Columbia University, Dr. Wolfgang Pernice has partnered with Meta to adapt the DINO family of models to improve analysis of microscopy images of cells. Meta said this helps doctors understand how rare diseases appear in cells. Meta said conventional image analysis methods require researchers to know in advance what they are looking for, limiting their analysis. Meta said the adapted Cell-DINO, DINO-BoC and FINO models generate unbiased representations of the inner workings of cells, allowing scientists to decode the complex patterns by which rare diseases manifest in human cells.

Meta said this can help improve understanding of rare diseases and accelerate drug discovery. Meta said open science is critical to advancing medical research. Meta said all of the work it featured is early-stage. Meta said each of the investigational projects highlights AI's unique ability to fill critical research gaps.

Meta said it looks forward to the potential breakthroughs enabled by its AI models. Meta said it interviewed the researchers for its Open Source AI for Science Summit and pointed readers to its AI blog to learn more. Meta did not say how much funding any of the researchers received. Meta did not give results from any of the three projects.

Meta did not say when COPES might be deployed or tested. Meta did not say whether the epilepsy simulation tool has been tested in patients. Meta did not say what the next steps are for the rare disease work at Columbia. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive after Trump intervenes, sparking a 31% share surge
stories.Summary:
Nvidia’s board reinstated former chief executive Jensen Huang on Monday, 23 November 2026, after direct intervention from President Trump, with Vice President Vance reportedly enlisted to help push the process along. The reinstatement came after Wall Street had spent the better part of a fortnight questioning Nvidia’s future and the AI revolution. Nvidia surged 31% and added $952 billion in market value in a single session. The Nasdaq 100 rocketed 6.9%, the S&P 500 jumped 4.7% and the semiconductor index exploded 14%. It was Wall Street’s biggest celebration since Trump paused his Liberation Day tariffs in April 2025.

The rally came with a violent unwinding of short positions and options hedges, and leveraged short products suffered devastating losses. Top-of-book liquidity in the S&P 500 futures market was reportedly around $2.5 million. The VIX retreated sharply but remained at approximately 28.9, unusually elevated for a session in which the S&P 500 surged close to 5%. The VVIX remained above 118 and in the 93rd percentile of its historical distribution. Anthropic fell 1.4% despite the introduction of listed options, with its share price still struggling to put distance from the $83 offering level.

Huang is described as Nvidia’s principal dealmaker, industry evangelist and strategic architect, with influence stretching from semiconductor design to data-centre investment. The articles say his reinstatement restores a familiar hand to the wheel and has genuine value for investors assessing the company’s strategic direction. They add that there is an uncomfortable distinction between restoring confidence in Nvidia’s leadership and repairing the financial foundations of the entire AI boom. The articles say Wall Street may have got its king back, but the kingdom still has a few unpaid bills. They say the market’s verdict was delivered with all the subtlety of a wrecking ball.

The articles say much of the rally had less to do with a new earnings outlook than with traders caught on the wrong side of an overcrowded book. Hedge funds were doing much of the heavy lifting, aggressively buying technology shares and ETFs, while traditional long-only investors were modest net sellers on substantially smaller volumes. The articles say the buying failed to accelerate meaningfully beyond the initial surge, and the major indices remained below their 200-day moving averages. The spread between twelve-month and three- or six-month momentum reached record territory. The articles say Nvidia’s leadership uncertainty may have been dramatically reduced, but investors were not prepared to extend the same enthusiasm to every corner of the AI ecosystem.

Last week’s equity liquidation had driven investors into Treasuries, with two-year yields falling approximately 20 basis points as traders scaled back expectations for aggressive Fed tightening. Monday’s equity rebound pushed short-dated yields higher as the market began pricing a greater likelihood of further rate increases. Oil prices began collapsing, dragging inflation expectations lower, and by the close long-end yields had fallen roughly 3, 4 basis points, leaving the curve sharply flatter. The dollar strengthened again, extending gains across nine of the previous ten sessions. WTI crude plunged more than 3% toward $80 a barrel, while Brent slipped below $90 to its lowest level since August.

The articles say the reopening of Libya’s Sharara pipeline restored approximately 350,000 barrels a day of disrupted supply. US front-month natural gas futures tumbled as much as 9.1% intraday before settling roughly 6% lower near $3.50. Wednesday’s core PCE inflation report is described as the next major test. The articles say a softer reading could give equities another leg higher, while another uncomfortable inflation print would leave investors confronting the same monetary-policy dilemma that helped fuel the original liquidation. The articles say the political, regulatory and financial obstacles ahead have not disappeared simply because Nvidia’s most famous conductor has returned.

stories.Headline: Joe Thomas says an AI agent he created drafted and filed his lawsuit against Meta
stories.Summary:
Joe Thomas, a business owner from South Carolina, filed a lawsuit against Meta on November 16, 2026. He claims that an AI agent he created drafted and handled the filing of the complaint. This AI agent, which Thomas named Baby Mia, is a version of Meta's own Muse generative AI. The legal action was filed in the Oconee County Court. Thomas says his only contribution to the court documents was providing his signature.

The lawsuit seeks treble damages and the reversal or explanation of 111.69 dollars in disputed charges. It alleges that Meta committed a breach of contract and violated the South Carolina Unfair Trade Practices Act. Thomas claims the suspension of his accounts cost his business 25,000 dollars in leads and contracts. The total amount sought in the lawsuit is 75,000 dollars. The complaint argues that Meta misapplied its terms of service by being unable to confirm account ownership.

Joe Thomas is responsible for the suit and maintains that Baby Mia completely drafted the legal complaint. He says Meta mistook the activity of his AI agent for that of a hacker. This mistake led Meta to lock him out of the Facebook accounts used for his business. Thomas claims he passed an identity check but still could not regain stable access to his accounts. He believes the AI agent informed him that they were suing Meta for lost income.

Some people worry that AI generated filings and emails will become a common occurrence. Others question if Thomas is responsible for the situation by depending on a system with a checkered track record. The lawsuit affects Meta, which is the creator of the Muse AI agent used by Thomas. It also involves Kong Koatings, the epoxy countertop business owned by Thomas in South Carolina. The case highlights concerns for business owners who hand over operations to AI agents.

Thomas began giving AI agents control over his company using ChatGPT before adding Baby Mia. He gave the AI agent more responsibilities, including creating and posting AI generated sales videos on Facebook. Meta security systems flagged this activity as suspicious and locked down the company business pages. Baby Mia then contacted the White House, the FTC, the FCC, the BBB, and the California Attorney General. South Carolina Senator Tim Scott helped Thomas connect with a Meta representative to recover the pages.

It remains to be seen if the suit is free of hallucinations and will receive a jury trial. The articles leave open whether a judge would allow a pro se plaintiff to use AI guidance in court. There is also the question of how the case proceeds since Baby Mia cannot appear in person. The outcome of the request for treble damages and disputed charges is not yet known. The final resolution of the breach of contract and SCUTPA claims is still pending.

stories.Headline: SolarWinds CTO says AI shifts IT work from investigation to verifying agents
stories.Summary:
Krishna Sai, senior vice president and chief technology officer of SolarWinds, said in an interview published by TechInformed on 25 November 2026 that AI moves IT work rather than removing it. Sai said AI shifts work from investigating problems to verifying and governing the agents that do the investigating. He said AI multiplies whatever a company already has, good or bad. He said organizations with brittle systems and poor-quality data will get more of the same. He said those with solid foundations will see the benefit.

Sai joined SolarWinds in June 2021, when he says its tools worked as separate point products. He said bringing them onto a single platform with the data in one place laid the groundwork for layering AI across the suite. He said he cofounded and served as CTO of two startups. He said he held engineering leadership roles at Polycom, Groupon and Atlassian. He said AI raises the level of abstraction and moves everything to a higher level than where people typically operate.

Sai said IT professionals' days are defined by toil, assembling data, chasing alerts and repeating the same fixes. He said AI can offload some of that toil and have immediate benefits. He said people's time shifts away from assembling data, chasing alerts and repetitive work toward making higher-level decisions. He said everyone is comfortable asking questions of AI but organizations need to put things in place for AI to act in their environment. He said one requirement is autonomy, with different levels so teams can start small with a narrowly scoped problem in a narrowly scoped environment.

Sai used the example of self-driving in a Tesla, which he said has different autonomy modes including chill mode, standard mode, hurry mode and Mad Max mode. He said organizations don't jump into Mad Max mode on day one and can begin with small tasks such as disk space management and build trust gradually. He said a second challenge is determinism, because AI is a probabilistic system and a language model asked the same thing three times may give three different answers. He said pairing AI with established IT and ops systems is important, along with good context, permission levels, evaluation systems, containment, observability of the agent itself, verification processes and escalation paths. He said a retailer whose checkout systems slow down is a good example, where an AI agent can automate much of the investigative work and, with the right controls, parts of the response.

Sai said the so-called AI productivity paradox comes down to how and at what layer productivity is measured. He said AI can make individual tasks dramatically faster but IT operates as a workflow around how tasks come together to achieve a business outcome. He said one of his engineers used AI to work through huge volumes of log data much faster but then had to spend time verifying the insights it generated. He said productivity should be measured at the level of verified outcomes such as reducing alert noise, reducing total effort or reducing incident frequency. He said organizations often get AI tool sprawl instead of traditional IT tool sprawl and should look at their enterprise AI stack.

Sai said SolarWinds has a unified AI gateway that all of its AI tools leverage, giving teams flexibility in model choice plus auditing, cost controls and safeguards against sensitive data leakage. He said scaling AI across an organization requires thought and used the analogy of driving a Ferrari, which performs incredibly on an empty road in Montana but gives a completely different experience through New York City, Jakarta or Bangalore. He said he has an agent that converts topics from his backlog into podcasts he listens to while driving. He said he grew up in the south of India and drinks South Indian filter coffee, a strong and hot brew with a layer of froth in a special two-piece metal container with a whole ritual. The interview was edited for length and clarity.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO following direction from President Trump
stories.Summary:
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive officer on November 23, 2026. This action occurred eleven days after Huang had resigned from the company. President Trump directed the effort to bring the leader back to the firm. The board of directors voted unanimously to return Huang to his role. He promised employees he would be a better leader during his second term.

The move returns Colette Kress to her role as chief financial officer. Nvidia will now hire its first chief compliance officer while Harvey Jones remains board chair. The board received national security assurances from the United States government to allow the return. This decision followed a period from November 12 to November 23 involving an alleged spy affair. The company stock jumped over 30 percent, adding over a trillion dollars in value.

President Trump said that losing Huang would be a threat to the country. He called the board and told Huang to work hard after his return. The president claimed that Huang is a great patriot and a national treasure. White House communications director Steven Cheung stated that the government must protect its geniuses. Trump told CNBC that Huang is a genius who is irreplaceable for America.

Senator Elizabeth Warren called the decision reckless and urged the passing of export control bills. Republican senators John Cornyn and John Curtis questioned the basis of the national security assurances. Tech leaders including Elon Musk and Sam Altman celebrated the return on social media. Investors in the tech market cheered as the overall market rose by trillions. Lawmakers from both political parties criticized the board for reinstating the chief executive.

Huang had resigned following an alleged spy affair and issues with board truthfulness. He reportedly had affairs with people at the company who reported to him. The board previously stated on November 17 that it did not intend to bring him back. A petition for his return was signed by Elon Musk and thousands of employees. Rene Haas of Arm was considered a candidate before signing a new contract.

Huang will testify in a closed House session on December 1 and before senators on December 3. Proposed bills may block Blackwell chips from China or require location tracking in exported chips. The articles leave open the final results of various investigations into the chief executive. Future class action suits are likely due to the extreme financial market volatility. It remains unclear how regulators will handle the consequences of these events next year.

stories.Headline: Nvidia shares jump as Jensen Huang returns as CEO and Qnity buys Meridian unit for $840 million
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO, and the news on Monday sent stocks surging as the S and P 500 and Nasdaq recovered all of Friday's steep losses in what the article called a stunning reversal of fortunes. The S and P 500 had ended Friday in correction territory, closing 11.6% below its Oct. 6 record high. Nvidia shares led the way higher on Monday, rising more than 30% and breathing much-needed life into the artificial intelligence infrastructure theme. Huang's return prompted four Wall Street Nvidia analysts, including Melius Research and Bernstein, who had downgraded Nvidia after his resignation 11 days earlier, to upgrade their ratings back to buy-equivalent designations.

Qnity, the semiconductor materials supplier, announced on Monday that it is buying the electronics business of Meridian Adhesives Group for $840 million in cash. The deal is meant to help Qnity expand its presence in the optical and photonics market, which the article says is seeing strong growth due to advances in AI computing and the physical limitations of copper connections. The business will become part of Qnity's Interconnect Solutions segment, which reported $759 million of revenue, up 30% year over year, and an adjusted operating EBITDA margin of 31.1% in the third quarter. Meridian's electronics business is expected to do about $100 million in calendar year 2026, with double-digit growth expected in 2027, and management expects the transaction to be completed in the first quarter of 2027.

Upon closing, Qnity said the acquisition is expected to be immediately accretive to its adjusted gross margin, adjusted operating EBITDA margin, and adjusted earnings per share. Qnity shares rallied about 10% on Monday, erasing all of last Friday's losses, thanks to the resurgence in the AI trade following Huang's return to Nvidia. In a note to clients on Monday, Fermium Research analyst Frank Mitsch said the acquisition suggests there has been zero change in Qnity's positive outlook on the industry despite the recent sell-off. The article's authors said they agree, though they have not added to their Qnity position lately due to volatility surrounding the AI trade, and they feel better about the group today than a week ago after Huang's reinstatement.

stories.Headline: Trump administration expands semiconductor restrictions to hinder Chinese AI development
stories.Summary:
The Trump administration recently announced expanded restrictions on Chinese access to semiconductors in third countries to hinder their artificial intelligence development. This policy shift followed the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, which boosted the stock market. The move occurred as President Donald Trump departed the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen late last week. These new rules aim to close a loophole left open by the previous Biden administration's diffusion rule. The administration is now pursuing a more hawkish approach toward China's acquisition of advanced technology.

The new rule restricts China's access to AI chips in third countries and may revoke previous direct sales approvals. House Republicans revealed that Commerce approved the sale of nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips to Chinese firms. Some of these sales went to companies on the Pentagon's list of Chinese military companies. The Department of Treasury and the National Security Council directed the writing of this new export control rule. This happens while China aims to add 1,500 gigawatts of electricity capacity between 2026 and 2030.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick previously argued that selling chips to China would make developers addicted to the American technology stack. However, the policy shifted after Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who sought advanced semiconductors. Senate Republicans called both Lutnick and Huang to testify regarding these chip sales and the intelligence concerns. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio now favor the tougher, more hawkish policy approach. President Trump stated that Lutnick and Bessent have two different views on handling the relationship with China.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said selling advanced Nvidia chips to China is like selling nuclear weapons to North Korea. OpenAI warned that an electron gap with China threatens American leadership in artificial intelligence due to energy constraints. Elon Musk predicted China would far exceed the world in computing power because it generates more electricity. Former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt told Congress in 2025 that America needs energy in all forms. These leaders believe the ability to build new energy capacity is currently trapped in a regulatory chokehold.

China generated 10.6 trillion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025, which was roughly a third of the total global output. This power buildout helps China run power-hungry data centers while Washington restricts their access to advanced American semiconductors. In Hong Kong, activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to ten more years in prison on November 5, 2026. Wong was targeted for calling on the United States to impose sanctions on Hong Kong and China. His case highlights how Chinese AI models are aligned to uphold the socialist core values of Beijing.

The U.S. Congress is preparing to consider various bills to govern AI technology as members oppose the current race. ByteDance is reportedly training a ten-trillion-parameter model to rival the powerful Mythos model created by the company Anthropic. DeepSeek's CEO stated that the ultimate ambition of the company is to build artificial general intelligence for China. The articles leave open whether the recent victory for the hawks in the administration will prove temporary. It remains uncertain if the U.S. can maintain its lead while preventing China from imposing its values.

stories.Headline: Infobip predicts AI agents will handle bookings, refunds and purchases for customers in 2027
stories.Summary:
Infobip, a global AI-first cloud communications platform based in Vodnjan, Croatia, released five predictions on November 25, 2026 about how customer engagement will change in 2027, saying AI agents will move from conversation to action and take on more tasks for customers and businesses. The company said AI agents will handle multi-step tasks such as changing bookings, processing refunds, completing purchases and resolving service requests, and that voice AI has already moved from pilots into live service and sales. It said consumers will increasingly use personal agents to compare products, make purchases, change bookings and seek support, and that some journeys may start through a personal AI assistant rather than a brand's website or app. Infobip said customers will expect their identity, history and intent to carry across agents, voice, RCS, WhatsApp, apps and human support, with real-time data, customer memory and orchestration helping preserve context.

The predictions require businesses to make services and transactions accessible to authorized agents acting on customers' behalf, and to set clear permissions, business rules and execution controls with human handover when needed. Infobip said businesses must verify that agents acting for customers are authorized and ensure that calls, messages and AI agents claiming to represent brands are genuine, as fraud and impersonation remain concerns and AI-generated interactions and content become more common. It said authentication, consent, disclosure, transparency and human oversight will underpin trust, and that businesses will prioritize measurable outcomes such as faster resolution, lower costs, increased revenue, retention and reduced risk. The company said organizations should scale use cases that justify investment and change or stop those that do not, and that as AI-assisted development makes tailored software easier to build, some may build the applications that differentiate them while relying on specialist providers for communications, identity and orchestration.

Silvio Kutić, co-founder and CEO at Infobip, said 2027 will see AI move from conversation to action, with agents taking on more tasks for customers and businesses. He said action has to be useful and reliable, with the right context and authority and human support when needed, and that businesses will focus less on what AI can do and more on the outcomes it delivers. The predictions were shared in a paid press release distributed by Business Wire.

stories.Headline: European IT spending rises 9.9% in 2027 on AI-optimized server demand
stories.Summary:
European IT spending is set to rise by 9.9% in 2027, according to a forecast reported by IT Pro on 25 November 2026, with growth driven by demand for servers built to handle artificial intelligence workloads. The report frames the increase as a surge tied to that AI-optimized server boom across the region. The figure covers European IT spending as a whole for the 2027 calendar year. The articles give no further dates, names or numbers beyond the 9.9% figure and the year 2027.

The forecast implies that European organizations will spend nearly a tenth more on IT in 2027 than in the year before, with AI-optimized servers named as the main force behind the increase. The articles do not break the total down by country, vendor or category, and they do not say what the baseline year's spending was. No company, agency or individual is named as the source of the 9.9% figure. The articles also give no detail on what the servers are, who buys them or what they cost.

The articles name no one as responsible for the forecast and carry no statements from any person or organization about it. No spokesperson, analyst or executive is quoted, and no explanation is offered for why AI-optimized servers are driving the growth. Because no one is named, there are no remarks to paraphrase on the record. The only attributed element is the 9.9% figure itself, reported by IT Pro.

The articles give almost no context beyond the headline figure and the year it applies to. They do not say what happens next, whether the forecast could change, or how it compares with earlier estimates for European IT spending. No follow-up announcement, report or event is mentioned. More to follow.

stories.Headline: SalesHood launches an MCP integration that lets sellers pull approved content into AI assistants
stories.Summary:
SalesHood this month launched an MCP integration that brings its enablement platform into AI tools including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Glean and Perplexity, CX Today reported on 25 November 2026. Bloomreach has acquired the answer engine optimization platform AthenaHQ, the article said. Richardson Sales Performance surveyed 1,105 senior sales and revenue leaders at large organizations in North America and Europe. Gartner's latest Magic Quadrant for Revenue Enablement Platforms predicts that by 2030, 80% of interactions with revenue enablement platforms will happen through AI agents and embedded workflows rather than the platforms' own interfaces. The article said sellers are asking ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot for help with customer conversations, and buyers are asking AI tools which brands and products to consider.

The SalesHood integration lets sellers ask their preferred assistant for approved talking points, a customer story or a demo video, and then add the content to a Digital Sales Room, subject to their approval. Bloomreach plans to connect AthenaHQ's work to its customer engagement platform, from the first point of discovery through to personalization and loyalty. Richardson found that 62% of leaders at organizations that met or exceeded their quotas reported a positive financial return from AI, compared with 39% of leaders at organizations below 90% of their quotas. Richardson notes that quota attainment was self-reported, so the findings show correlation, not cause. Seventy percent of respondents said humans outperform AI in the activities that matter most in complex deals, while 88% expect skills AI cannot replicate to set their best sellers apart in 2027.

The article quoted SalesHood saying that sellers have already picked their AI and asking them to switch is a losing fight. Bloomreach said that from a customer's first moment of discovery through to lasting loyalty, it is giving businesses AI purpose-built to both win customers and keep them. Andrea Grodnitzky, Chief Marketing Officer at Richardson Sales Performance, said the difference came down to how leaders responded. Gartner's report says revenue enablement platforms are becoming an embedded intelligence layer across CRM, collaboration tools and AI assistants. The article said the enablement platform still holds the content, permissions and controls.

The article said brands can influence their product information, pricing, content and availability, but they do not fully control how an AI assistant chooses what to recommend. It said the next challenge is measuring whether appearing in an answer engine moves a customer from discovery to purchase. It said the risk for leaders is not simply that sellers use unapproved AI, but that they use it without access to the current messaging, content and buyer context that would make the answer useful. It said organizations that report stronger AI outcomes also report greater confidence in their forecasts and better returns from seller development. It said the goal is not to add another assistant, agent or content tool to the stack, but to make the work around it more consistent.

The article said the usual route through the revenue tech stack is starting to change, with sales teams traditionally going to an enablement platform for training, approved messaging and buyer content. It said marketing teams have worked to bring customers to brand websites, search pages and campaigns, and now AI assistants are inserting themselves at both ends of that journey. It said the work is moving beyond the dashboards and interfaces that revenue teams know well. It said this week's news from SalesHood, Bloomreach and Richardson Sales Performance shows what that could mean in practice. It said the technology may be changing, but the issues for business leaders are familiar: trusted information, visibility, governance and people.

The article said AI is not replacing the revenue tech stack overnight, but is changing where people experience it. It said a seller may ask an AI assistant for approved messaging rather than search an enablement platform, and a buyer may discover a product through an AI-generated answer rather than a search engine. It said the data, content, permissions and processes behind those interactions still need to be managed. It said the practical work for business leaders remains the same: keep product and customer information accurate, define who can access it, test AI in real workflows, and measure whether it improves outcomes that matter. It said the front door may be changing, but the need for trusted context and disciplined execution is not.

stories.Headline: DeepMind launches Humanity's First Exam to test AI model consistency on everyday tasks
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind launched Humanity's First Exam to test if AI models are consistent. This new exam checks if models get easy questions right every single time. The test was released on November 25, 2026, according to the report. It focuses on reliability rather than the ability to solve impossible problems. The exam uses 544 everyday questions covering text and images.

The test includes 20 foundational capabilities grouped into sets of four related questions. Tasks include counting objects, naming colors, tracking positions, basic arithmetic, and following strict formatting. It also tests the ability to spot false premises built on untrue things. A live leaderboard is hosted on the site Kaggle for data scientists. A Kaggle contest runs through December 15 for submitting questions models miss.

DeepMind says frontier models made significant progress on the exam over six months. They state the scoring is harsh because one slip fails a whole set. A model must get all four versions of a question right to pass. DeepMind's technical report traced 73 percent of wrong answers to visual perception. This means photo questions are currently the soft spot for these models.

Casual users are affected because they trust quick answers and rarely double-check them. A model that miscounts items on a shelf will fail a user. One sample prompt asks for the color of letters in a neon sign. The correct answer for that specific task is green, yellow, white, blue, blue. This represents the kind of simple work a child can do.

The exam name winks at a brutal benchmark called Humanity's Last Exam. This new test goes in the opposite direction by focusing on easy tasks. Top models reach roughly 95 to 98 percent on a single try. However, strict scoring puts the best score at barely an A-minus grade. These skills are used in requests like totaling a receipt from photos.

OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra placed first with a score of 90.7 percent on the test. GPT-6.2 Sol followed in second place with a score of 87.5 percent. Gemini 4 Neon ranked third with a score of 85.6 percent. The articles do not say how DeepMind will update the exam. They leave open how models will improve their visual perception scores.

Articles.Title: 😺 DeepMind's Humanity's First Exam Tests AI Consistency

stories.Headline: AI Magazine ranks Salesforce, Microsoft, LangChain and AWS among ten agentic AI platforms
stories.Summary:
AI Magazine published on November 25, 2026 a ranked list of ten agentic AI platforms that it says are delivering measurable value to enterprises, naming Salesforce, Microsoft, LangChain and AWS among the offerings included. The publication said it aimed to capture the full stack of the agentic AI landscape by looking at a broad array of players in the field. The list also includes Kore.ai, CrewAI, UiPath, IBM, ServiceNow and Google Cloud alongside those four companies. The article cites McKinsey in noting that nearly two-thirds of enterprises worldwide have experimented with agents, while fewer than 10% have scaled them to deliver tangible value.

The article describes each platform and the figures its maker gives for it. Kore.ai says its Artemis platform is AI-programmable for the agentic enterprise and that its agents thrive in complex, high-volume, regulated workflows, and the firm has deepened partnerships with Microsoft and AWS, serving as a launch partner for Microsoft Agent 365 and earning the AWS Advanced AI Competency designation. CrewAI combines an open-source, multi-agent harness with its Agent Management Platform, which is built on the MIT-licensed CrewAI framework and lets organisations design Crews of autonomous agents and Flows that mix deterministic steps with agents. LangChain says its technology is used by 35% of the Fortune 500, has crossed a billion open-source downloads and ingests at least a billion events daily on LangSmith. UiPath says customers achieve 45% faster process cycles on average, claims more than US$10m in documented average savings per enterprise customer, and says eight of 10 top global healthcare firms and seven of 10 top global banks run on it. IBM describes watsonx Orchestrate as an open, hybrid and trusted platform with an AI Gateway for discovering third-party agents, models and MCP servers across platforms such as Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft and Google. ServiceNow says its AI Platform has a single data model connecting to more than 450 systems, and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang has previously said ServiceNow is destined to be the best platform and the operating system of enterprise AI agents. AWS delivers its offering primarily through Amazon Bedrock, a fully-managed service giving access to models such as Claude, Llama 2 and Amazon Titan, with Bedrock Agents using the reasoning of foundation models, APIs and data to handle user requests. Google Cloud delivers through Vertex AI Agent Builder and its Gemini models, with sandboxed code execution, persistent memory banks and compliance controls. Salesforce says more than 18,000 companies already run on Agentforce, including Fujitsu, Indeed and OpenTable, and that Gartner named it a Leader in the 2026 Magic Quadrant for Conversational AI Platforms. Microsoft's offering spans Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, Azure AI Foundry and the open-source Microsoft Agent Framework, with access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta as well as its own Phi family.

The article attributes the descriptions and figures to the companies themselves and to the executives it names, including Kore.ai, CrewAI CEO João Moura, UiPath CEO Daniel Dines, AWS CEO Matt Garman and Salesforce CEO Marc Beinhoff. Claims such as UiPath's savings figure, LangChain's Fortune 500 share and Salesforce's customer count are presented as what each firm highlights or notes rather than as independently verified facts. The ranking itself is the publication's own selection, and the article does not describe a method beyond saying it aimed to capture the full stack.

The context the article gives is that agentic AI is fundamentally reshaping enterprises, with many rushing to build out pilots as soon as possible, while McKinsey's finding suggests most have not yet scaled them to deliver tangible value. The article does not say what happens next beyond the publication of the list.
