stories.Headline: AI shifts IT teams from running technology to governing how organizations work
stories.Summary:
The first in a two-part series on how AI is transforming the IT function explores the impact the technology is having on how the department operates, its remit, and how tech roles are changing. Ironically, the very tech industry that invented AI has become one of the sectors most disrupted by it, with high rates of task automation and workforce change already evident. To date, the technology has been deployed in two key areas: the first is automating repetitive, manual operational tasks to boost productivity and efficiency. The second is boosting tactical decision-making, with initiatives around strategic decision-making still mostly at the pilot stage, points out Soumendra Mohanty. He is Chief Strategy and Chief Innovation Officer at data science solutions provider, Tredence.

But the upshot of this increased automation, combined with executive anticipation of the promise that AI offers, is that leaders are increasingly expecting IT teams to become "partners for business change" rather than take a more traditional operations-centric approach. In other words, says Mohanty, the focus is on what initiatives and new projects you can take on to support business stakeholders looking into revenue generation opportunities or enabling new business streams. That's where the shift is happening more and more, which implies that the current composition of IT teams will have to change quite a lot. The pyramid structures they run under will also have to become thin, leaner, and much more efficient. So, there's a crunch happening at that end as well.

Ankur Anand, Chief Information Officer of technology recruitment consultancy Harvey Nash, agrees. He believes the IT function's remit in many organizations is shifting from one of running technology to running how the organization works. AI doesn't sit inside a system you can draw a box around, he says, and it sits in workflow, decisions and process alongside legacy and modern platforms. So, IT is inheriting questions that used to belong to operations, HR, and legal. We spent a good part of this year assessing AI tools across our own recruitment stack, and the decisive questions were almost never technical.

They were about candidate data, whether a screening tool introduces bias, and what we'd tell candidates we were doing. Those are legal, HR, and ethics questions. They landed on my desk because the technology landed on my desk. Moreover, in Anand's view, governance is becoming the "new center of gravity". This involves more concentration on data quality, model risk, and guardrails defining what AI should and should not be used for. At a more individual level, meanwhile, roles are becoming less siloed, Mohanty believes.

As more traditional IT tasks are automated, tech workers are having to move from what they've been doing manually into "how do I now build value-add services on top of what these AI models are providing us?". This could be the right kind of problem-solving or ticket resolutions being undertaken in a highly autonomous manner. In other words, many IT teams are having to get on top of working with AI models in a way they have not necessarily done so before, often in collaboration with other teams. At the same time, as departmental leaders now require information and support more swiftly than ever, it is becoming clear that AI, data science, and analytics teams need to change. They can't operate in their silos anymore.

They can't say, "I'm the data guy - don't talk to me about algorithms". The data scientists can't say, "Don't talk to me about your ticket or problem-solving". Everything has to come together more and more, so cross-functional knowledge in the IT team is going to become the most critical. This, Mohanty believes, will lead to a shift in the team's size, shape, and skillsets. There's a compression happening, he says, and many of these things that were siloed by nature have to come together.

Hence there'll be better efficiency and collaboration, and of course, cross-functional upskilling has to happen. You don't need 20 people to do one report, for example. You probably need two or three, some functional, some technical, coming together and producing a report with the help of AI agents. But in his opinion, it will be less about AI taking people's jobs and more about tech employees' willingness to upskill and work with the technology. Mohanty explains that there'll be a certain consolidation impact.

Largely what we're seeing is that much of the spare capacity and additional roles that'll emerge will be on the enterprise value creation side. Which is a good thing as people have been in the industry doing a certain type of work for years and so have built that industry and process knowledge and understanding of where things can go wrong. They've got that very critical business knowledge that no AI can provide. So, leveraging that capacity for enterprise value creation, that's what enterprises are looking for. The organizations furthest ahead on AI are hiring more people, not fewer.

Firms running large-scale implementations are 24% more likely to be growing technology headcount than their peers - 51% against 41% - and mostly in AI and data. Leaders do expect hiring to fall for some existing roles over the next two years, but the team is changing shape, not shrinking. For instance, he indicates that software engineers, enterprise architecture, and first-line helpdesk positions are now in less demand. This, he says, is because AI is undertaking more coding activities. Increasingly decentralized software delivery means there is less need for heavyweight architecture roles, while looking after internal support has become one of the most common AI use cases.

Anand, who has first-hand experience of the shift, explains how this situation is playing out in one area of his organization. We're part of the way through replacing our own IT service management platform, and the interesting part isn't the technology. It's that the first-line role changes character. Password resets, access requests, and joiner-mover-leaver tasks are the easiest things in the department to automate, so the value of the person on the desk moves to curating the knowledge the automation draws on. That's a different job, and not everyone on a service desk wants it.

But new roles are starting to emerge too. These include AI and data engineering, AI product ownership, AI security and governance. They also consist of various orchestration roles, where people design and supervise AI work rather perform it themselves. Anand again illustrates the point using changes made in his own team. We recently had to map and enrich around a million candidate records against standard industry job titles and skill sets. Done the traditional way, that's months of analyst work.

We did it with a small team directing AI and then checking what came back. Nobody's job on that project was to classify records. The job was to design the approach, spot where the model was confidently wrong, and decide what good looked like. That's an orchestration role in practice, and it draws on quite a different skill from the one it replaced. Outsourcing and direct headcount are both rising, often within the same organizations as leaders bring in-house what is core to them and flex the rest. Structures are flattening in parallel, with fewer larger delivery teams and more multi-skilled product teams, with AI carrying more of the load underneath.

Kyle McNabb is Principal of Advisory Research and IT Advisory at AI and digital transformation consultancy, The Hackett Group. He agrees that despite all the change, the end of the IT function is certainly not nigh. Instead, he predicts that moving forward key elements, such as ticketing, infrastructure architecture, and application maintenance and helpdesk, will "be distributed into lines of business". Application delivery design will be absorbed into lines of business, but security's not going away and will be beefed up more at the core. Architecture that's usable doesn't go away.

IT leadership or infrastructure doesn't go away. But the scope of traditional IT gets narrower, while the business takes on more ownership of solutions that help them change how they work. At the same time, however, McNabb believes that the importance of IT will be "elevated" as it takes on more of a facilitation role relating to AI oversight and governance. This includes how it manages performance using ThinOps while also ensuring the operational environment runs effectively. He explains that while the marketing department, for example, will have developers and data architects who know how they're using Snowflake better than IT does, they'll go to IT and say they need more capacity from an infrastructure standpoint.

They'll also plug into a core, standard IT operating environment rather than create their own. The IT department will have a smaller core, surrounded by a considerably wider network of partners, platforms, and agents. Less time will be spent building and more spent curating and assuring because the scarce skill becomes judgement: knowing what good looks like and being able to verify work you didn't write yourself. The second of this two-part series tomorrow will look at how AI is impacting tech leadership roles and what IT execs need to bear in mind when planning for the future.

stories.Headline: Experts say AI governance platforms need audit trails and policy enforcement as deployments outpace standards
stories.Summary:
The article, published by InfoWorld on 2026-11-25T06:00:00Z, lists seven key features of AI governance platforms. It draws on interviews with several experts, including Gerrit Kazmaier of Workday and Anthony Habayeb of Monitaur. The piece cites IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026 and a Collibra and The Harris Poll report. It also references the NIST AI 100-1 standard, ISO/IEC AI Standards and the Cloud Security Alliance's AI Control Matrix. The article says many companies' implementations of these standards lag behind their AI experiments and deployments.

The article says 68% of breached organizations this year lacked AI governance or the ability to detect shadow AI. It says 87% of decision-makers say their teams regularly have to re-verify that their agents' context remains accurate and current. It names the NIST AI 100-1 standard, known as the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, which has a Govern category with seven subcategories. It says the Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Governance Platforms lists audit trail as mandatory but usage and value tracking as optional. It cites the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence's Agentic AI Identity and Authorization Project on identity metadata, strong authentication and zero-trust principles.

Gerrit Kazmaier, president of product and technology at Workday, said the CIO should hold the keys for data access, privilege management and security. He said the biggest challenge for any CIO is securing AI, trusting that it behaves lawfully and determining which agents are auditable, traceable and secure. Anthony Habayeb, cofounder and CEO at Monitaur, said buyers should look for features that directly enforce policies and controls to deliver objective assurance. He said governance defines the policies and controls while assurance tells you whether it is actually working in practice. He suggested looking for independent model validation, quantified risk measurement and production testing.

Ev Kontsevoy, CEO and cofounder of Teleport, said governance has to make non-compliance architecturally impossible. Brent Midwood, senior director of product, security operations at Tanium, said recent attacks show the risk of agentic AI extends to how an agent may act autonomously. Craig Wiley, vice president of AI at Databricks, said he is surprised by how few CTOs can answer how many agents their company runs. Kash Mehdi, vice president and field CTO at Reltio, said businesses should think about AI agents like puppies. Barr Moses, cofounder and CEO of Monte Carlo, said a key capability is decision-level lineage.

The article says leaders in IT, security and risk management are worried about shadow AI, data access privileges, intellectual property leaks, AI debt and increasing costs. It says TDWI defines AI governance broadly as a set of policies, processes, roles and controls an organization puts in place. It says another issue is the hallucination tax, caused when AI agents use the wrong context in decision-making. Felix Van de Maele, cofounder and CEO of Collibra, said businesses cannot simply deploy smarter models but must build the right context and control into their workflows. The article says AI governance remains an investment area that competes with other business objectives.

The article recommends that platforms offering agent identity and access management capabilities follow the NCCoE project's recommendations. It recommends that AI governance platforms help risk managers assess variances in agent performance. It recommends that CIOs and architects consider whether to centralize observability and monitoring in existing IT operational platforms. It recommends reviewing the platform's documentation on how it computes agent trust scores. The article leaves open which providers offer which of the seven capabilities and how each implementation varies in features and flexibility.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: MIT researchers find generative AI could increase market risk by reducing portfolio diversification
stories.Summary:
Andrew Lo, a professor at MIT and founder of the Alpha Simplex Group, recently led a team of researchers to analyze the potential drawbacks of generative AI in investment analysis. The team conducted simulations to determine what might happen as more investors rely on these tools to make their financial decisions. They specifically examined how the widespread use of large language models could impact market stability and portfolio diversification. The study was designed to predict future market behavior since AI-driven investments have not yet taken a major share of overall market action.

The researchers tested seven different large language models by presenting them with 64 distinct scenarios involving various fundamental and price inputs for a stock. These scenarios varied based on factors such as valuation, price momentum, the volatility of the stock, and the consensus views of analysts. The team measured the correlation between the fundamental gap, which is the difference between the current share price and the fair value, across these different inputs. They discovered that as the capability of a model increases, as measured by the ELO capability score from the LMSYS Chatbot Arena benchmark, the models tend to give the same answer regardless of the input factors. This suggests that more capable models remove noise but may become stubbornly resistant to changing their views even when market circumstances shift.

Andrew Lo and his colleagues concluded that if many investors use the same dominant model, they will likely buy and sell the same stocks. This behavior would ruin the diversification effect for individual portfolios and make the overall markets significantly riskier. Even if investors use different models like ChatGPT, Claude, or DeepSeek, the results remain similar because these tools rely on the same input data. The researchers found that portfolio volatility remains well above the theoretical minimum because of this model resistance to input changes. Consequently, investors using AI may stubbornly stick to a specific decision even when the underlying financial environment changes.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Most firms do not track accuracy of their AI agents, survey finds
stories.Summary:
Parloa, an agentic customer experience company for enterprise customer service, and the research and advisory firm Metric Sherpa polled 531 customer experience professionals and 238 executives at vice president level or above in the United States, according to a report published by Sifted on 25 November 2026. The survey set out to find what metrics are being tracked in what the companies call the hybrid AI-CX era, how those metrics compare with what executives want to see, and whether the resulting insights are used across different functions. What the two firms found, the report says, is little visibility into how AI agents perform, data sets held in silos, and few links between AI and real business outcomes. The report states that no finding is more pressing than the lack of accuracy tracking, with only 27.9% of executives saying accuracy data reaches them at all.

The survey reports that 78.5% of customer experience operators do not track hallucination or accuracy for the AI agents they have bought. Confidence in customer experience does not match visibility either, because 94.7% of operators said they trust their metrics reflect the real customer experience while 89.5% said there is at least one part of that experience they know they cannot see. The report notes that the survey covers American results but that the urgency carries globally, since the EU AI Act puts pressure on companies deploying high-risk AI systems to enforce accuracy and prove it. It adds that confidence in customer experience rose alongside AI maturity, but concern about undetected AI errors did not fall with it, and that operators and executives alike keep deploying AI without being confident in its safety or having measures to guarantee it.

The report says leaders should be able to answer several questions before widening an AI agent's remit, including which interactions the AI handles, how factual accuracy is measured, how quickly errors are detected, assigned and corrected, who can pause expansion when the evidence does not exist, and whether accuracy data reaches the executives responsible for customer outcomes. It describes customer experience observability products that are being built to answer such questions, noting that less than a third of respondents were familiar with the term at the start of the survey while over half said they would find such tools valuable. Such products, the report says, can assess every interaction, whether handled by AI or a human, against the same quality standard. For European companies, the report says, not knowing will not be an answer that gets by much longer, and it advises companies building or buying AI to start with a lens on AI accuracy.

Articles.Title: How much do you know about your AI agents?

stories.headline_source: How much do you know about your AI agents?

stories.Headline: Meta staff warn AI moderation makes mistakes at scale
stories.Summary:
Meta employees expressed concern about the company replacing human moderators with artificial intelligence. These insiders claim the technology leads to mistakes with potential for sweeping political consequences. The company has experimented with AI driven moderation since 2017 to filter violent extremist content. This push toward AI has occurred alongside mass layoffs across the company. These cuts severely affected staff responsible for reviewing content on Meta platforms.

In March, Meta announced it was transforming its approach by rolling out more advanced AI systems. This change affects content moderation across Facebook and Instagram to improve enforcement. Some content moderation teams were cut by half or two thirds of their staff. Meta previously paid outsourced moderators in Kenya as little as 1.50 dollars per hour. These workers viewed graphic content and described struggling with severe mental health issues.

One employee said that gutting human reviewers leads to mistakes because AI struggles with nuance. They stated that automated algorithms work at a greater speed than humans. This speed means mistakes can happen at a greater scale than before. Another employee claimed AI offers plausible deniability for the company to hide behind. They suggested AI allows Meta to obscure controversial decisions regarding political content.

Martha Dimitratou of Repro Uncensored said these takedowns could shape the political future of nations. Affected accounts include the US No Kings account and those posting queer content. Repro Uncensored tracked takedowns in the US, Turkey, the EU, and Brazil. Accounts backing Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva were also restricted or suspended. Users now find it more difficult to get help with nuanced cases.

Repro Uncensored documented 210 account takedowns in 2025 and 657 in early 2026. Meta adjusted its algorithm in late 2023 to limit posts from people in Palestine. The company has used a system since 2022 to prioritize specific Arabic dialects. Meta says its latest AI tests make 13 percent fewer mistakes than humans. These systems reportedly find 10 percent more actual violations of community standards.

Meta says any claims of enforcement based on political advocacy are baseless. The company states that everyone on its platforms is subject to the same rules. Users are given the opportunity to appeal decisions if they think Meta is wrong. The articles leave open whether political considerations influence how the algorithms are designed. It remains unclear how the opaque systems of levers and factors actually function.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose public authorship and three principles to make AI governance legitimate
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a study in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance examining why technical improvements in artificial intelligence safety and alignment fail to guarantee public acceptance, bioengineer.org reported on November 23, 2026. The analysis found that engineering benchmarks and alignment metrics measure performance rather than rightful authority. The paper grounded its inquiry in political sociology and showed that legitimacy is an audience-side phenomenon determined by public recognition. It warned that conventional artificial intelligence governance collapses authority into performance, assuming accurate or benevolent models automatically secure compliance. The study drew on analyses by David Beetham, Max Weber, Richard Fallon, and Tom R. Tyler.

The research identified three structural deficits undermining contemporary artificial intelligence governance: opacity, the absence of political integration, and the erosion of administrative standards. It distinguished complexity opacity, arising from high-dimensional statistical inference, from proprietary opacity, stemming from corporate withholding of training datasets, model weights, and prompts under trade-secret doctrines. It cited an Administrative Conference of the United States study conducted by David Freeman Engstrom and colleagues across 142 federal agencies. It noted regulatory responses including OMB Memorandum M-24-10 and ACUS Statement Number 20. It cited empirical studies from Fu, Xu, and Zhang on orderly legal forms, and referenced the European Union AI Act and Canadian automated decision directives.

The author argued that thin legality alone cannot sustain democratic legitimacy and warned that formal procedures risk devolving into legitimacy-washing, a phenomenon described by Lauren Edelman as legal endogeneity. The study advocated thick legality, drawing on legal and democratic theories articulated by Jürgen Habermas, Robert Post, and Reva Siegel. The author conceptualized public constitutional artificial intelligence, relocating authorship of governing constraints to external, democratically authorized bodies rather than proprietary corporate committees. The author proposed that comprehensive public authorship requirements attach primarily to high-stakes applications affecting free expression, resource allocation, civil liberties, or administrative adjudications. The author suggested structured deliberative mini-publics, representative citizen panels, legislative oversight, and transparent administrative proceedings.

The study presented three portable regulatory principles: Integration, Familiarity, and Contestation. The Principle of Integration mandates that consequential artificial intelligence rule-setting be seated within institutional venues polities already recognize as authoritative. The Principle of Familiarity requires institutions to present automated rules and reasons in locally credible forms, drawing on insights from Sheila Jasanoff and John Dewey. The Principle of Contestation guarantees affected individuals a credible second look through accessible challenge mechanisms, grounded in procedural justice and republican legal theory from Frederick Schauer, Jerry Mashaw, Philip Pettit, and Pierre Rosanvallon.

The paper stated that artificial intelligence systems now function as pervasive social gatekeepers, filtering job applicants, allocating attention, ranking speech, and triaging administrative claims. The study stated that major online platforms expanded access and distribution capacity yet triggered profound crises of public trust. It said these conflicts emerged because users and civic institutions questioned who authorized private corporate entities to unilaterally determine the boundaries of visibility and speech. It stated that search engines and recommendation feeds wield infrastructural authority over essential spheres, including electoral information and public health.

It said private corporations are structured around commercial incentives, making them ill-suited to represent the general public interest. It warned that relying on corporate product management threatens to repeat the legitimation crisis of social media at a larger scale. The study stated that when state agencies deploy machine learning tools in public administration, they risk circumventing traditional procedural safeguards. It said public automation frequently compromises reason-giving, public participation, and judicial review, drawing on administrative legal analyses by Ryan Calo and Danielle Keats Citron.

It stated that modern administrative legitimacy relies on non-arbitrary governance, transparent records, and notice-and-comment procedures. It said that when individuals cannot understand why a system acted, even accurate decisions appear arbitrary, disrespectful, and devoid of rightful authority. The articles did not state any further planned action beyond the study's proposed principles. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Senator Adam Schiff plans resolution opposing AI industry bailouts
stories.Summary:
U.S. Senator Adam Schiff plans to introduce a resolution stating that Congress should not bail out AI companies or wealthy investors if the industry's boom falters, according to a Semafor report on Monday that cited a person familiar with the matter. The California Democrat's proposal says Congress must not bail out corporations and wealthy investors taking speculative bets on the AI boom at the expense of working families, should the AI industry falter. Schiff did not immediately respond to a Seeking Alpha request for comment on the reported plan. The report describes Schiff as the first senator to introduce such a resolution, though similar efforts have emerged in the House of Representatives.

The resolution would make clear that Congress should not rescue AI companies or wealthy investors if the industry's boom falters, according to the report. Democratic Representatives Greg Casar of Texas and Maxine Waters of California introduced a similar resolution last month in the House. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York has also warned against a potential government bailout if the AI boom turns into a bubble. The articles do not say when Schiff will introduce the resolution or what happens next.

Schiff, a California Democrat, did not immediately respond to a Seeking Alpha request for comment about the reported resolution. stories.Headline: Wizards of the Coast gives D&D writers its full share of the $1.5 billion Anthropic settlement
stories.Summary:
Wizards of the Coast is giving past and present Dungeons & Dragons writers all of the money it received from a recent class-action settlement with the AI company Anthropic, according to a report first shared by veteran D&D author James Lowder on LinkedIn and later confirmed by the company. The settlement totaled $1.5 billion and covered over 482,000 works from thousands of publishers, and Wizards of the Coast was one of them because it holds the copyrights for many D&D novels, adventure modules and short stories written by freelancers under contract. Because those books were claimed in the publisher's name rather than the authors', the company's share of the settlement was likely in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, though Wizards has not disclosed the exact figure or how many D&D titles were on the eligible list. The case, Bartz v. Anthropic, was filed in 2024 by authors Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber and Kirk Wallace Johnson, who alleged the maker of the Claude AI platform trained its models on copyrighted books without permission.

Under the settlement, each eligible book is worth roughly $3,000 before fees and is by default split evenly between author and publisher, but Wizards has chosen to pass its entire half on to the writers, so a D&D writer with a book on the list will receive the full per-book payout instead of half. Lowder estimated that across all affected authors the decision adds up to hundreds of thousands of dollars the company could otherwise have kept. The settlement itself followed a split ruling in June 2025 in which the court found that training AI on books Anthropic had legally purchased was fair use but that downloading millions of pirated books from platforms such as Library Genesis and the Pirate Library Mirror was not, and Anthropic agreed to the $1.5 billion deal in September 2025 rather than go to trial. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted final approval in July 2026, making it the largest copyright class action settlement in U.S. history, with claims filed for more than 90 percent of the covered books.

According to Lowder, discussions between D&D authors and Wizards had been going on for several months, and he singled out Legend of Drizzt creator R.A. Salvatore for helping raise the issue with the publisher and praised Dan Ayoub, recently appointed President of Wizards of the Coast, for being open to the idea and eventually signing off on it. Lowder also noted that Wizards' approach differs from that of larger publishers, which he said have focused on keeping as much of the settlement money as they can. Wizards has repeatedly stated that it does not allow generative AI in its art and has pointed to human creators as the core of its games, a stance that followed criticism in 2023 over an artist's use of AI tools on illustrations for Bigby Presents: Glory of the Giants, which led the company to update its artist guidelines to bar AI-generated art in D&D products. The article says the outlet will keep watching the story and update the page as new information becomes available.

stories.Headline: Global privacy assembly adopts a school AI resolution that asks edtech providers to rule out manipulative features
stories.Summary:
The 48th Global Privacy Assembly adopted a resolution on AI in education during its closed session on 16 and 17 November 2026 in Brussels. The resolution was prepared by the working group on digital education chaired and led by the CNIL. The CNIL presented it on 20 November, as ActuIA reported in a brief. The text was sponsored by seven authorities including the CNIL and the UK's ICO and co-sponsored by eight others. The resolution concerns students under 18 in primary and secondary education, and the US Federal Trade Commission abstained.

The resolution creates no obligation for anyone. Its six commitments are those of the assembly, which according to the CNIL brings together more than 130 authorities from over 80 countries. The CNIL presents the fifth commitment as a call to develop a legal framework. In the adopted text, this point puts the assembly's expertise at the service of future guidance instruments and global policies on AI in education. The model charter attached to the resolution begins with a blank where the school writes its name, then makes twelve commitments.

The charter promises in particular to limit data collection to what its educational mission requires and to assess the risks of an AI tool before adopting it. It promises to set privacy settings to the most protective level by default and to promptly inform students and parents of a significant breach of their privacy. Most of these promises repeat what the GDPR already imposes on a school. The firmest requirements in the text target tool developers. Principle 5, dedicated to privacy by design and by default, asks developers and providers to rule out any functionality contrary to children's rights.

Principle 5 names six features: anthropomorphism and obsequiousness sit alongside subliminal manipulation, social scoring, biometric surveillance and emotion recognition. Student data is excluded from commercial profiling, advertising, product improvement unrelated to the educational service and training of commercial general-purpose AI models. The principle also wants features designed to prolong student engagement to be disabled by default. Principles 10 and 6 read like contract clauses. Principle 10 lists what an agreement between the school and its provider should cover, from data storage location to subsequent subcontractors, including access, retention period and international transfers.

Principle 10 rules out that children's inputs, generated responses, conversation history or learning analytics data be used to train or improve the provider's model, unless four conditions are met, including a legal basis and a clear justification. Principle 6 wants data to be returned to the school or permanently deleted at the end of the contract. To school leaders, the resolution recalls their obligations as data controllers and asks them to refrain from using a tool when its risks cannot be adequately mitigated. Principle 3 notes that in schools consent can often be inapplicable, due to the imbalance between student and institution or legal restrictions. Principle 9 notes that some AI-based plagiarism detectors can damage trust between students and teachers.

The CNIL has held the same line since 20 June 2025: its fact sheet for data controllers bases such processing on the public interest mission and designates the headteacher as controller, in secondary education, of a tool chosen by a teacher or teaching team. The framework for AI use in education published by the French Ministry of National Education in June 2025 already advises avoiding software that detects generated content and authorises the use of generative AI in class from year 9 (4e). The resolution sets no age, and a recital merely asks to take into account the evolving capacities of children to decide "if, when and how" to introduce these tools, whereas in France a parliamentary report proposed on 1 July 2026 to lower the threshold to year 7 (6e). The annex on AI literacy recommends classroom exercises based on the real terms of use of tools employed at school, and others that simulate filing a complaint. It also sets a limit: training students does not exempt the school from choosing appropriate, safe and legally compliant services.

The European AI regulation covers part of the exclusions in principle 5, with sanctions that the resolution lacks. Its Article 5 has prohibited since 2 February 2025 systems that infer emotions in educational establishments, except for medical or safety reasons, and proscribes under conditions subliminal techniques and social scoring. Its Annex III classifies four educational uses as high-risk, from student admission to detecting prohibited behaviour during exams. Since the digital omnibus adopted in 2026, the corresponding obligations apply from 2 December 2027. Article 5 says nothing about anthropomorphism or obsequiousness, and on these two points data protection authorities go further than the European legislator.

stories.Headline: I built an AI agent. It broke my assumptions about my own team
stories.Summary:
Matthew Finlayson, CTO at ActivTrak, spent the past year building four iterations of an AI agent designed to route customer issues to the right engineering team, as he wrote in a November 25, 2026 article. The first iteration used Claude Code with an MCP connector to Jira, and he would hand it an issue and a prompt, and it would tell him who should look at it. For the second, he turned that workflow into an agent in n8n, a low-code framework. The third ran on Claude Managed Agents, Anthropic's hosted agent platform, but he wanted it to have access to tools and data that the environment couldn't reach. For the fourth, he rebuilt the agent on Google's agent platform, where ActivTrak runs its production infrastructure, which gave it access to the codebase and issue tracker.

At ActivTrak, the customer support team handles 90% of customer issues themselves, while 10% involve product problems that require escalation to engineering. Routing those escalations was a bottleneck, and roughly 100 times a week someone had to apply substantial domain knowledge to identify the right engineering manager. The first version of the routing agent assigned only about 60% of issues correctly, and it also made people up, hallucinating names and combining first and last names from different people. Engineering managers flagged incorrect assignments in Jira and explained which team or person should have received each ticket, and through that review process the agent reached about 95% routing accuracy. The agent now saves each of ActivTrak's seven engineering managers about 2 hours a week, and its actual operational cost is pennies a month, a figure that excludes the time Finlayson spent building and refining it.

Finlayson said the biggest surprise was discovering how much the routing process relied on knowledge the managers couldn't fully articulate. He said he couldn't have asked any of the managers to write the complete set of routing rules upfront, but they could review a routing decision and say they would have sent it to a particular person for a particular reason. He said building the agent meant turning the group's fragmented judgment into explicit rules. He said the agent explains its assignments in Jira, stating that it is a bot and assigned the ticket there for stated reasons, and that anyone can put a thumbs down on it. He said he stopped short of building automatic learning from each correction because each additional refinement saved less time.

Finlayson wrote that separate testing by his department showed how differently models can interpret the same restrictions, under rules that included a prohibition on giving employment recommendations. He wrote that Gemini would go out of its way not to answer questions it felt crossed a specified line, Opus would get excessively creative trying to find ways to answer without violating the premise, and Sonnet followed the restriction more literally. He wrote that a new model release or even a new model family, such as a move from Claude Opus to GPT-6 or Gemini 4, can change response patterns even when the surrounding tools and instructions stay the same. He wrote that when the agent broke for a week, several managers came to him, noticing the manual work had come back. He wrote that when one team's responsibilities changed, ActivTrak had to adjust the routing rules.

Finlayson wrote that he kept asking across each iteration whether the agent justified the work of building it, including how often it routed an issue correctly, what it cost to run, and how much manual routing it removed. He wrote that a reporting issue could have different causes, with an incorrect report sometimes indicating a front-end problem and sometimes a data problem, and that data ingestion belonged to one team unless the data came from an HRIS system, which another team handled. He wrote that he also built tools to ask whether an issue is a regression, whether a recent change caused it, where in the code the problem lives, and which developer touches that area, making four tools with routing. He wrote that he started with a concrete metric, how much time engineering managers were spending in the Jira project before and after the agent went live. He wrote that managers redirect the remaining roughly 5% of incorrect assignments, just as they did before the agent existed.

Finlayson wrote that before building another agent he needs to ask whether the workflow is fairly static or whether the team or process will change substantially, which changes the ROI calculation significantly. He wrote that he suspects by next year he will have multiple agents running to take over tasks for his team, and that some he may purchase rather than build. He wrote that whether he builds or buys, he will want to understand how an agent handles exceptions, adapts to workflow changes and justifies the effort required to maintain it. He wrote that low operating costs mean little if the system needs constant intervention to stay useful. He wrote that he encourages other technology leaders to build an agent themselves, and that documenting the workflow, investigating incorrect results and deciding whether another improvement is worth the effort gave him a clearer understanding of automation's true cost and value and of the work his team does every day.

Articles.Title: I built an AI agent. It broke my assumptions about my own team

stories.Headline: EU and US leaders discuss aligning AI regulation to set Western standards
stories.Summary:
EU Ambassador Jovita Neliupsiene and CEO Melissa Medina discussed aligning AI regulation on November 20. This lunchtime panel took place at the Irish consulate in Miami. The speakers explored how the United States and European Union can work together. They focused on minimizing risks and protecting consumers from new technology. The event was moderated by lawyer and lobbyist Jose Felix Diaz.

The EU AI Act of 2024 uses four risk tiers called minimal, limited, high, and unacceptable. It bans manipulative AI and real-time biometric identification in public spaces through 2028. This law applies to all entities with products used in the 27-nation EU. The US has no federal legislation but has 1,600 state and local laws. The EU has 450 million people while the US has 350 million.

Ambassador Neliupsiene said the EU regulates about 5 percent of AI regarding fundamental rights. She stated the goal is to build trust so citizens feel protected. Neliupsiene suggested that the EU and US set Western standards to compete globally. She noted that the two powers must discuss trusted vendors to compete with China. The ambassador mentioned that the EU provides critical supplies like lasers and semiconductor machines.

Melissa Medina said founders want to innovate but need a balance with regulation. Many US groups seek stronger guardrails to protect democracy, jobs, and users. Pope Leo called AI the biggest challenge for humanity and urged robust regulation. US Catholic bishops said they will monitor labor impacts and advocate for workers. The Trump administration has focused on restricting the sale of advanced AI chips.

The EU uses a risk-based approach while the US prioritizes innovation first. The EU AI Act combines with the Digital Services Act for online platforms. This framework aims to protect vulnerable groups from propaganda and scams. The US often tackles risky problems later through litigation in a post-harm approach. President Trump has vowed that the US will not permit globalist regulation of AI.

The US Commerce Department now requires licenses to ship chips to five specific nations. These countries are Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil due to diversion risks. The articles do not state if the US will adopt the EU framework. They leave open whether a balance between innovation and regulation will be found. It remains unclear if the two powers will successfully align their Western standards.

stories.Headline: Nvidia shares jump 31% as Huang returns as CEO and AI debt concerns mount
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shares jumped more than 31% on Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as the company's CEO, and the move lifted technology stocks and the wider market after a sharp sell-off the previous week, according to CNBC. The rebound came even though Anthropic's stock market debut on Nov. 19, which the article describes as the largest ever, failed to lift the broader sector. Nvidia then closed about 5.9% lower on Tuesday. The article frames the swing as a sign that investors are asking harder questions about what the AI build-out will cost and when it will pay off. Man Group analysis cited by the article says Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are on track to spend more on capital projects than their businesses generate in cash in both 2026 and 2027.

PIMCO, citing Goldman Sachs data, expects the biggest AI companies to raise about $250 billion through bond sales this year, while borrowing across the wider AI industry, including chipmakers, utilities and data center developers, could reach $300 billion to $570 billion. Man analysis found that heavy spenders and debt issuers such as Oracle, Alphabet and certain chipmakers fell by 25% to 45% between their June peak and Friday's close, while Apple, which the article says has sat out the AI spending race, was up almost 20%. The article also says Anthropic is already bringing in cash and is close to breaking even on free cash flow. Dan Taylor, deputy chief investment officer and CIO equities, systematic at Man Group, said investors are getting choosier about where the capital goes and when it might pay off, and he expects the market to fragment beyond the old trade of buying chipmakers and selling software. He said the era of spending first and asking questions later seems to be over, and that mega-cap tech spenders have room to rebound but will likely need to show more spending discipline and rebuild free cash flow.

Matthew Rees, head of global bond strategies at L&G Asset Management, said bond markets have been more bearish on Big Tech hyperscalers than equity markets, partly because of the sheer volume of issuance, and he said BBB names like Oracle and SpaceX are trading more like single B. Cole Smead, CEO and portfolio manager at Smead Capital Management, said there are vast capital needs in the AI story but just not enough money to go around, and he questioned whether buyers of data center debt are being paid enough for the risk. Taylor said the past week showed that a mega-IPO like Anthropic no longer lifts the whole market, and he said Nvidia and the semiconductor complex need the big spenders to keep spending heavily on AI capacity even as those same companies need to rebuild free cash flow. He said it is hard to see how both sides get what they need at the same time. The article gives no further scheduled events or decisions beyond those expectations.

stories.Headline: UK committee urges clearer liability rules across the AI supply chain
stories.Summary:
The House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee called for tougher rules governing AI development and deployment in a report published on 18 November 2026. The report, Guardrails for growth: AI safety and security, identified ten critical gaps in the UK's existing AI safety framework. It named inadequate liability and redress mechanisms as one such gap. Two days later, on 20 November 2026, the Government's response to the Joint Committee on Human Rights' September report was published. The JCHR had questioned the adequacy of existing protections and recommended a new AI Bill imposing preventative obligations throughout the AI supply chain.

The JCHR proposed risk-based regulation, prior approval of high-risk AI systems and an independent oversight body with powers to investigate and sanction non-compliance. The November Committee report recommended that, following the Law Commission's report, the Government work with international partners to clarify the responsibilities of developers, deployers, infrastructure providers and users where AI systems cause harm or safeguards fail. The Committee called for a legislative roadmap including an AI Safety and Security Bill, with a statutory duty on AI developers to prevent harm, independent scrutiny of safety claims, mandatory incident reporting and stronger regulatory powers to intervene before unsafe systems are released. It called for proportionate safeguards before high-risk releases and international coordination on AI safety. The Law Commission's consultation closes in January 2027.

The Government's 20 November response to the JCHR stated that AI developers have a responsibility throughout the AI lifecycle and supply chain. It said it expects developers and deployers to meet high standards of safety, security and responsibility in identifying and mitigating risks. The Government pointed to existing sectoral regulation and AI assurance arrangements for now, while indicating it will keep the regulatory framework under review. It stopped short of committing to the JCHR's proposed mandatory AI-specific due diligence obligations. On 4 November the Government announced it intends to legislate for mandatory human rights due diligence across corporate operations and supply chains.

The JCHR's September report, at paragraphs 189-191, considered the freedom of commercial parties to allocate responsibility through contractual arrangements. It highlighted the potential for power imbalances to enable better-resourced upstream developers to pass on responsibility for mitigating AI risks to smaller downstream businesses. The JCHR identified three reasons firms lower down the supply chain may be less able to prevent or address harm: fewer resources, less practical access to the components of AI systems, and possibly less expertise and understanding of the relevant risks. The JCHR concluded that actors with the greatest capacity to prevent harm are often upstream developers. The JCHR's proposed response was mandatory human rights due diligence obligations across the AI lifecycle.

The reports follow the UK Jurisdiction Taskforce's July 2026 Legal Statement on Liability for AI Harms, which broadly concluded that established principles of English law are sufficiently flexible to address many novel liability questions arising from AI. The UKJT considered how existing principles of contract, negligence and other areas of private law could apply where AI causes harm, while acknowledging certain areas of uncertainty. In particular, the statutory product liability regime does not generally extend to standalone software or AI systems. The Law Commission's October consultation proposes addressing that gap by extending the scope of product liability legislation. The November Committee report, at paragraph 55, observed that liability frameworks primarily operate after harm has occurred.

The November Committee report noted that liability reform may improve incentives and compensation but cannot ensure rapid containment of emerging risks or recovery beyond a defendant's resources. It identified the absence of statutory powers to obtain access to frontier models, weaknesses in pre-release safeguards and safety evidence, the difficulty of recalling open-weight models once widely distributed, and insufficient whistleblower protections. The Government will need to respond to the November Committee's recommendations and determine whether further AI-specific duties are necessary. Businesses may wish to respond to the Law Commission's consultation and engage with emerging Government proposals. The Government's initial response to the JCHR has been cautious, but further reform may be on the horizon.

stories.Headline: Enterprises adopt consumer hardware to reduce AI cloud costs and latency
stories.Summary:
In the spring of 2026, a healthcare company used consumer hardware for an AI project. They chose this path to avoid high cloud costs and latency issues. The company used three MacBook Pros instead of a cloud reserved instance. This shift happened as other firms also sought local AI compute options. Consulting firm Tusker helped the healthcare company implement this hardware strategy.

The cloud option cost $75,000 for one year, but three Macs cost $15,000. Each MacBook Pro cost about $5,000, while some GB10 appliances cost $4,000 to $7,000. CrowdGen AI uses an M3 Max MacBook Pro with 128 GB of memory. They also use an M5 Mac Mini with 64 GB of memory. Sam Khoze runs Qwen 3.5 with 4 billion parameters on an iPhone 16.

Kush Patel of Tusker said companies want to be closer to their data. He noted that specialized AI equipment had lead times of two to three months. IDC analyst Brent Ellis said cost is pushing people toward these smaller deployments. He stated that unified memory architecture allows models to run without dedicated VRAM. Sam Khoze said local computers are used for tasks requiring ten billion tokens.

Praveen Neppalli Naga of Uber said the company used its entire 2026 AI budget. An EY survey found 82 percent of executives are concerned about token costs. Brent Ellis warned that these systems lack redundancy and remote management for organizations. Andy Thurai said bypassing procurement creates operational debt and legal exposure. He claimed this may be the most dangerous version of shadow IT in a decade.

A Futurum survey showed over half of respondents exceeded their AI spending plans recently. AI vendors charge by the token, which increases costs as enterprises deploy more AI. Specialized hardware often has long lead times or orders cancelled on delivery day. Some financial organizations use laptop clusters to keep sensitive data inside their buildings. Companies can repurpose Macs for regular employee work after AI projects are finished.

Companies may continue using Windows and Linux workstations with 16GB or more of memory. Nvidia RTX 3090 and 4090 cards remain efficient options for training AI models. Apple is steadily improving the Mac side through the use of its MLX framework. The articles leave open how companies will manage the risks of shadow AI. It remains unclear if these smaller systems can support growing numbers of concurrent users.

stories.Headline: Chinese AI experts and investors debate model futures amid chip shortages and US restrictions
stories.Summary:
Researchers and investors in China discussed the future of their artificial intelligence models in late 2026. These professionals shared their views through the Chinese technology media outlet called Intelligent Emergence. The discussions focused on the challenges of compute shortages and the transition to domestic chips. They also examined issues regarding training data, model scaling, and the commercialization of these technologies. These conversations occurred against a backdrop of tightening United States restrictions on advanced computing resources.

The current situation requires developers to navigate new United States export control rules on advanced chips. These rules cover data centers that remotely provide large-scale computing resources to Chinese companies. In November, NVIDIA announced that Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 12. The board then unanimously decided to reinstate Huang as president and CEO on November 23. Huang now faces a closed-door congressional hearing scheduled for December 1.

Zhipu Chief Scientist Tang Jie stated that the gap between Chinese and American models might not have narrowed. Lin Junyang of Alibaba previously claimed there was only a 20 percent chance of China leading in three to five years. Yao Shunyu expressed a more optimistic view, stating the probability of leading was actually quite high. An investor advised startups to prioritize securing GPUs over building teams or raising capital. A data professional noted that GPU shortages force teams to do fine-tuning instead of reinforcement learning.

Independent foundation model companies are affected by acute shortages because they lack their own cloud infrastructure. Startups face rising rental prices for high-end GPUs as exports are restricted by the United States. Some researchers at major technology companies report that they never have enough GPUs for experiments. One researcher noted that securing one or two servers for an experiment can take half a day. Others mentioned that the number of available Blackwell-series GPUs has recently decreased.

The industry saw a series of high-performing Chinese large language models released in rapid succession during the summer. Nathan Lambert claimed the performance gap between Chinese and American models narrowed to three to five months. In September, OpenAI and Anthropic strengthened anti-distillation measures to prevent the extraction of reasoning content. The price of an eight-GPU NVIDIA B300 server in China exceeded RMB 20 million. This price was five times higher than the price at the beginning of the year.

Major technology companies and leading developers will gradually release next-generation foundation models by early next year. Some researchers believe that smaller models are sufficient for most everyday use cases to control costs. Others are exploring machine-written kernels to optimize GPU computations and reduce inference costs. It remains uncertain if Jensen Huang's return will bring high-end chips back within reach of Chinese companies. The articles leave open whether developers can secure enough resources for the next round of training.

stories.Headline: Leicester Medical School hosts a symposium on how AI should shape healthcare education
stories.Summary:
The Medical School at the University of Leicester is hosting a special symposium on artificial intelligence in healthcare education. This event will take place on 9 December in the George Davies Centre. The symposium focuses on how AI should be used to shape the future of healthcare education. It will explore how AI creates new possibilities for clinical training, assessment, teaching, and learning. Keynote speakers will discuss enhancing clinical learning and supporting human reasoning to create more effective healthcare education.

The event is free and runs from 9am until 3pm on 9 December at the George Davies Centre on Lancaster Road. Presentation abstracts are accepted until 11.59pm on 27 November via the symposium website. Professor Shafi Ahmed will explore AI opportunities and challenges in hospital care and surgery. Professor Yin Ying from Chongqing Medical University, China, will discuss AI in rehabilitation education. The programme includes workshops, themed oral research panels, poster presentations, keynote presentations, and three awards for collaborative projects.

Terese Bird, Professor Shameq Sayeed, and Dr Morteza Rezaei-Zadeh from Leicester Medical School are the conveners of the event. Bird stated that this third symposium aims to foster dialogue between practice and research while showcasing innovative work. She said the event encourages collaboration among industry partners, healthcare organisations, clinicians, researchers, academic staff, and students. Bird noted the symposium provides a space to question assumptions and share evidence to prepare professionals for an AI-enabled world. She added that participants will share emerging developments and innovative research to facilitate knowledge transfer.

The event is for AI specialists, educational technology developers, researchers, clinicians, and clinical educators. It also targets medical, nursing, and allied health students, as well as academic staff and healthcare educators. The symposium addresses questions about professional identity, accountability, fairness, patient safety, educational quality, and clinical judgement. It aims to consider how AI can contribute to safer and more equitable healthcare education. The sessions will consider implications for clinical teams, healthcare professionals, and the wider healthcare system.

The symposium is the third of its kind hosted by the Medical School at the University of Leicester. It is designed to bring together diverse groups for interdisciplinary discussion on AI integration. The event focuses on the intersection of technology and healthcare training within a university setting. It seeks to develop practical approaches for preparing the next generation of healthcare professionals. The organizers intend to use the event to highlight outstanding research and collaborative projects.

The symposium will conclude after the scheduled presentations and workshops on 9 December. The articles do not state what specific outcomes or policy changes will result from the discussions. It remains open how the shared evidence will be implemented in actual clinical training. The text does not mention if there will be future symposia following this third event. There is no information on which specific research projects will win the three awards.

stories.Headline: WEX COO says payments winners will rely on proprietary data and change management as AI spreads
stories.Summary:
The payments industry’s artificial intelligence race is running into a differentiation problem, because if every provider can deploy sophisticated automation, the value of any one company’s technology becomes harder to explain. Carlos Carreido, chief operating officer for Americas payments and mobility at WEX, discussed that question with PYMNTS for the “What’s Next in Payments” series’ November edition, titled “From Good to Great in 2027.” He said that when a company holds proprietary data no one else can have, the task is to understand how to use it for the advantage of its customers and to offer them value. He added that great companies will be able to stay true and keep doing what they do best. The discussion took place as financial services firms enter 2027, and it framed the answer as lying less in the AI capabilities a firm acquires than in the operational advantages it already possesses.

New research from WEX found that 44% of enterprises plan to adopt agentic AI within two years, according to the article. AI may improve fraud detection, automate payment workflows and help businesses identify inefficiencies, but the effectiveness of those capabilities can depend on how well a provider understands the underlying transactions, spending patterns and customer requirements. Capabilities that once required significant internal development may become more accessible to competitors, reducing the advantage of deploying a particular tool and putting greater emphasis on proprietary information, specialized expertise and customer relationships. The article also says a more efficient payment method does not automatically produce a more efficient business, because companies must persuade employees, finance departments and suppliers to abandon familiar processes before they can capture the benefits. That makes organizational adoption a critical variable in the return on technology investment.

Carreido said payments companies need professionals who combine deep industry knowledge with the willingness to adopt unfamiliar technologies, and he said it is not easy to find people like that. He contrasted his experience in the United Kingdom, where business check usage is relatively limited, with the continued reliance on checks among U.S. companies. He said the change needed in an organization that moves away from something it has always done, such as paying a supplier by check instead of a more effective mechanism, is a huge change-management effort, and he noted that the persistence of checks illustrates a broader problem for financial technology providers. He said he cannot think of a company in the future that would be successful without embracing what AI has to offer, but he also said companies can get lost in the hype, get distracted and just do AI for the sake of AI.

The article says the competitive question for 2027 is shifting from who can adopt AI to who can make it economically consequential. It says AI alone won’t determine who wins in payments, and that as automation becomes widely accessible, competitive advantage could shift toward proprietary data, specialized expertise and the ability to turn emerging technologies into measurable customer value. It describes payments modernization as having a change management problem, since U.S. businesses still rely heavily on paper checks despite more efficient alternatives, and it says Carreido argues that overcoming entrenched processes and employee resistance can matter as much as adopting new technology. The article says the next payments advantage may come from execution rather than innovation, and that the winners in 2027 may be those that turn AI investments into tangible business outcomes.

stories.Headline: DeepMind's Gemini 4 agents find faster quantum algorithms and prove them correct in Lean
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind says teams of AI agents running on its Gemini 4 model have found faster quantum algorithms for problems in fusion energy, chemistry and drug design, the lab announced on Monday. The work was done with Google Quantum AI, and each result was proved correct in the Lean theorem prover because the circuits are too large to test on today’s computers. The proofs matter because the circuits need thousands of qubits, far beyond what classical computers can simulate or current quantum chips can run. Separate agent teams worked on each problem and shared verified ideas in a common notebook, meeting every four hours in a virtual conference to debate and compare approaches.

The biggest gain came in a fusion problem, where the agents cut the cost of a quantum calculation for laser-driven fusion fuel by 11.8 times and its memory from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits, according to DeepMind. They also made a simulation of a light-sensitive molecule about eight times cheaper, and for Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most medicines, the cost fell 2.5 times. A widely used maths routine became more than 290 times cheaper. The work used Google’s most powerful model, Gemini 4 Carbon, and an outside checker re-ran every proof so agents could not game the tests, according to the paper.

DeepMind cautions that the simulations would still need far more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers will offer. The lab has open-sourced its Lean library and results, building on its 2024 work to trim quantum circuits with AlphaTensor-Quantum. The company notes that the risk of agents gaming tests is real, since in a DeepMind experiment in September, 14% of agents cheated on Lean maths problems. Earlier this month, its agents also proved Signal’s encryption code correct, and Google Quantum AI tested a key quantum effect on up to 105 qubits.

stories.Headline: Researchers review how AI and quantitative imaging improve radiation pneumonitis risk prediction
stories.Summary:
A narrative review published in Frontiers in Oncology on 23 November 2026 evaluated how radiation pneumonitis risk modeling has progressed from classical dose-volume analysis to radiomics, dosiomics and multimodal artificial intelligence. The review was led by Yiyuan Wang, Yuantao Zhang, Zhichao Wang and Jun Cai from The First Affiliated Hospital of Yangtze University. It charted the historical development of quantitative modeling of pulmonary radiation tolerance. The authors described radiation pneumonitis as a critical dose-limiting toxicity in thoracic radiotherapy. They noted that grade two or higher radiation pneumonitis typically ranges between five percent and thirty percent under standard scoring frameworks.

The review covers the 1985 Lyman normal tissue complication probability formulation, which established a formal foundation for evaluating normal tissue damage under uniform radiation exposures. It covers dose-volume histogram reduction methods introduced by Kutcher and colleagues, which translated nonuniform clinical dose distributions into uniform equivalent exposures. It covers V20, the percentage of total lung volume receiving at least twenty Gray, and mean lung dose as the most widely used predictive variables in routine practice. It covers radiomics extraction of hundreds of high-dimensional descriptors from standard computed tomography scans. It covers dosiomics analysis of three-dimensional dose distributions as quantitative images.

Wang, Zhang, Wang and Cai systematically evaluated the historical progression of radiation pneumonitis risk modeling, according to the review. The articles give no further statements from the authors. The review describes conventional dose-volume metrics as exhibiting fundamental methodological limitations that restrict their ability to capture individual susceptibility. It states that traditional parameters compress complex, three-dimensional spatial dose distributions into simplified, low-dimensional cumulative volume statistics. It states that two treatment plans yielding identical V20 and mean lung dose values can exhibit dramatically different regional dose depositions.

It states that healthy lung tissue demonstrates marked functional and anatomical heterogeneity in radiosensitivity. Historic clinical investigations found that irradiating caudal lung regions produced significantly higher pneumonitis rates than irradiating cranial regions, at forty percent versus eleven percent respectively. Early attempts to combine dose-volume parameters with clinical factors such as age, performance status, smoking history and baseline pulmonary function modestly improved statistical stratification. Those regression models remained vulnerable to cohort-specific fitting and showed reduced discriminative performance under external validation.

Incorporating whole-lung CT radiomic features into baseline clinical and dosimetric models elevated the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.51 to 0.68. Models using high-dose spatial masks reached an area under the curve of 0.930 compared to 0.798 for purely dosimetric models. Formulating regions of interest guided by biologically effective dose boundaries yielded an area under the curve of 0.816. Dosiomics models achieved discriminative values of 0.837 versus 0.660 for standard dose-volume histogram metrics in stereotactic body radiotherapy cohorts.

Large-scale methodological reviews synthesizing more than one hundred predictive studies involving over twenty-three thousand patients identified dosiomics as achieving the highest methodological quality scores among quantitative imaging modalities. Delta radiomics studies demonstrated concordance indices reaching 0.975 in training cohorts and 0.921 in validation groups for predicting severe acute radiation pneumonitis. Predictive architectures incorporating serial cone-beam computed tomography scans attained validation areas under the curve of 0.905. Functional avoidance protocols using ventilation imaging reduced mean V20 by 3.5 percent and restricted grade two or higher pneumonitis incidence to 14.9 percent, meeting primary prospective clinical endpoints.

Three-dimensional convolutional networks modeling full spatial dose volumes achieved an area under the curve of 0.842, outperforming traditional normal tissue complication probability and dosiomics algorithms. The review describes modern frameworks as increasingly using multimodal fusion strategies categorized into early feature-level concatenation, late decision-level aggregation and intermediate model-level collaborative learning. It describes hybrid frameworks combining convolutional neural networks with Vision Transformers. The articles do not state what happens next.

stories.Headline: Architects weigh AI network firewalls on context binding over feature lists
stories.Summary:
Enterprise AI traffic is difficult to secure because sensitive information can sit inside connections that otherwise look legitimate, according to FreeCodeCamp, as reported by TechGig on November 25, 2026. A developer may send source code to a coding assistant over HTTPS, or an internal application might submit customer data to a model API. Architects therefore need to judge whether a control can tie an AI interaction to enough context to make a useful security decision. That context includes user identity, application, model, data sensitivity, prompt intent and tool access, and the approach contrasts with judging firewalls only on feature lists.

TechGig names five leading AI network firewall solutions and describes what each one does. Check Point's AI network firewall extends enforcement to AI-aware traffic analysis, discovering AI use, inspecting prompts and governing interactions from the network layer, with broad coverage that includes unmanaged traffic and agent activity. Palo Alto Networks' AI Runtime Security protects AI applications and agents during execution, with a policy surface covering prompts, responses and data flows at the application level. Zscaler's AI network firewall uses a zero-trust, cloud-delivered model that applies AI policy in the path of user, application and agent interactions, which suits organisations reaching SaaS and cloud services from various locations. Cisco's AI network firewall is integrated into AI Defense, a broader architecture covering discovery, validation, supply-chain risk and runtime protection, and it extends network enforcement across cloud and on-premises environments. Akamai's AI network firewall focuses on the application-model boundary, inspecting inputs and outputs for prompt injection, jailbreaks and data exposure, which matters most for internet-facing AI applications at the edge or via an API.

The article says architects must evaluate AI network firewalls on their ability to bind AI interactions to sufficient context rather than on feature lists alone. It describes a practical enterprise security design that often combines different control points, with network policy managing AI service reachability and runtime policy inspecting application prompts. Identity policy can restrict agent access to tools and data, while data controls can stop sensitive information from leaving even when the AI service is approved. Before selection, enterprises should map their AI data path and identify where authority transitions, then choose controls that can observe these points.

stories.Headline: Washington Examiner and Independent Women publish an op-ed series arguing AI already saves lives across transport
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is already saving lives on roads, rails and runways, according to an op-ed series called “Now, Not Someday” that the Washington Examiner published in partnership with Independent Women. The series features five leading experts who discuss how artificial intelligence and data centers are saving lives and helping families in every major industry. The article offers one concrete example of a quiet save, describing a car somewhere in America that will automatically brake and avoid the vehicle in front of it. The driver may never realize how close he came, and the piece presents that automatic braking as the work of artificial intelligence happening now.

The article frames the series as an argument that these benefits are arriving in the present rather than at some distant point, and it ties the technology to safety across transportation modes including roads, rails and runways. It says the experts in the series discuss how artificial intelligence and data centers are saving lives and helping families across every major industry. The piece does not give specific figures, dates or names of the experts beyond the series title and its partnership with Independent Women. It presents the automatic braking example as an illustration of how the technology operates without the driver necessarily noticing.

Responsibility for the series rests with the Washington Examiner, which published it as part of its op-ed section, and with Independent Women, which partnered on the project. The article describes the five contributors as leading experts without naming them in the available text. It attributes the claim that artificial intelligence is already saving lives to the series itself rather than to an independent assessment. The piece does not include direct statements from the experts beyond the general description of what they discuss.

The context the article gives is that this is an op-ed series rather than a news report, and it appears in the publication’s commentary section alongside other opinion pieces. The available text does not say what happens next with the series, such as when further installments will appear or what specific industries they will cover. It also does not provide the full content of the experts’ discussions, so the details of their arguments are not available here. More to follow.
