stories.Headline: Basque minister Ubarretxena says Euskadi seeks AI while keeping human control at DOK Summit
stories.Summary:
María Ubarretxena, the Minister of Governance, Digital Administration and Self-government, inaugurated the DOK Summit technology congress on 23 November 2026 at the Euskalduna Palace in Bilbao, where she said Euskadi seeks to use artificial intelligence without giving up human control or decision-making capacity. She warned that using artificial intelligence does not mean handing over the keys to the house, and she said the debate around AI is not just about technology but about power. She affirmed that the Basque Country wants to decide, and she recalled that the recent European leaders' summit also addressed this issue. She emphasized that the objective is to maintain human control, ensuring the protection of citizen data and the decision-making capacity for essential public services.

The Basque public sector's AI Government Strategy promotes the concept of Herri-adimen, which prioritizes what the article calls the country's intelligence over artificial intelligence. Ubarretxena cited Batera, the Government's cloud, on whose experience ArgIA is being built as a public AI infrastructure governed from Euskadi and based on open-source tools. Attendees will be able to experience the platform firsthand this afternoon in a practical demonstration session led by Javier Cela and Aitor Cabero, heads of Cloud and Modernization and Data and AI at EJIE, the Basque Government's IT company. Ubarretxena clarified that sovereignty does not mean doing everything ourselves, and she advocated for collaboration with companies, clusters and professionals, summarizing that an ecosystem is needed.

She stressed that technology must serve people, expressing the wish that artificial intelligence makes us better but that we continue to be the ones making the decisions. The DOK Summit, the successor to the LibreCon free software conference, is taking place today and tomorrow in Bilbao and expects to gather around 1,200 professionals focused on AI, talent, data, cybersecurity and open source. The opening session also included remarks from GAIA President Elena Zarraga, ESLE President Iker Sagasti, Bilbao City Council's Councillor for Economic Development, Trade, Tourism and Employment Kontxi Claver, and the Provincial Councillor for Public Administration and Institutional Relations of Bizkaia, Ager Izagirre. The article, based on information from the official source Irekia and the department, gives no further details on what happens after the congress.

stories.Headline: Wahpeton council reviews city goals and mulls AI, social media and housing rules
stories.Summary:
Wahpeton City Council members and staff held a retreat on Wednesday, Nov. 18, the Wahpeton Daily News reported on Nov. 23, 2026. In the absence of Mayor Brett Lambrecht, Council member Jason Goltz led the retreat presentation. Goltz said the retreat was not intended to solve problems but to build a roadmap for the next couple of years. The retreat slides listed three objectives: thinking and acting strategically, demonstrating teamwork and practicing small-group decision-making. The council began by reviewing the city's 2023-2026 goals and priorities.

Goltz compared the review to a military after-action review, examining what was supposed to happen, whether it happened, what should continue and what could be improved. The recap outlined four goals, the first to keep local sales tax collections steady over the long term. According to the retreat slides, collections increased from $3,371,512 in 2023 to $3,807,937 in 2025, a 13% increase. The second goal was to research and plan a community wellness and recreation center, and voters approved an additional 1% sales tax on April 29, 2025, to help fund recreation and community wellness. The same ordinance, No. 1071, also removed earlier sunset dates for the city's sales tax, according to the slides, and the center project remains ongoing.

The third goal was to pay for ongoing obligations while relying less on property taxes. The slides showed that the city's mill rate decreased from 128.47 in 2000 to 79.68 currently, a 38% drop. The value of a mill increased from $9,381 to $30,422, a 224% increase. The fourth goal was to retain local businesses, and the slides noted that the city has fewer retail businesses and continues to face workforce and economic challenges in manufacturing. The recap also identified three priorities, the first being investing in infrastructure repairs and expansion.

The slides estimated that system valuation would increase from $324,043,689 in 2024 to $348,692,921 in 2027, an increase of about 8%. The second priority was maintaining strong police and fire services, and appropriations for those services have increased from 15% to 22% of total expenditures, according to the slides. The third priority was attracting industry, which continues to face workforce and economic challenges, particularly in manufacturing. Goltz said business retention and industrial attraction remains the city's biggest challenges, and he added that taxes and city spending appear to be efficient. One participant noted that those challenges are not unique to Wahpeton, while another said a city can do only so much to attract businesses.

Officials described sales tax as a useful local tool for reducing reliance on property taxes. The council next reviewed a decision-making matrix, and the slides outlined four steps: define the goal, gather key information, weigh options and risks, and make a motion that clearly states the proposed action. Goltz also discussed the sunk-cost fallacy, or the tendency to continue a project because of the time and money already invested. "Good leadership means stepping back to recognize when it is time to take a different approach or walk away," Goltz said. He added that many decisions have long-term consequences, for example bonding for a project that takes 25 years to pay off can affect an entire generation.

City Attorney Brittany Hatting presented information about social media, open meetings and open records, drawing from a presentation by attorney Howard Swanson of Swanson & Warcup, Ltd. to the North Dakota League of Cities in September. Hatting said the goal was to help council members recognize potential issues, not make them experts in the law. The presentation explained that public officials generally cannot delete comments simply because they are critical or block users because they disagree with an official. However, obscene or pornographic material, threats, spam and certain other categories may be removed. Hatting said Community Development Director Chris DeVries manages the city's social media accounts and follows those guidelines.

Deleting an entire post could also result in the destruction of a public record. Council members were also advised to exercise caution when using personal social media accounts. Hatting cited Sanderson vs. Myrdal, a case in which the North Dakota Supreme Court ruled Nov. 8, 2024, in favor of Sen. Janne Myrdal after she blocked a critic from her personal Facebook page. The court determined that a page becomes a public forum only when an official has actual authority to speak for the government and uses the page to do so. Regarding open meetings, Hatting said a quorum of council members commenting on a social media post about city business could inadvertently create a meeting.

She added that a walking quorum could also occur when one council member contacts other members individually to discuss city business. "Nearly all open meetings and open records violations are inadvertent rather than intentional," Hatting said. Texting during a meeting does not constitute a violation unless members are texting one another as a group, Hatting said. Staff emails asking council members not to use the "reply all" function are intended to prevent an accidental quorum. Posts and messages concerning public business may be considered public records, even when sent from private devices, Hatting said, and retention requirements depend on the content.

Hatting also addressed the use of artificial intelligence. The State Bar Association of North Dakota's magazine, The Gavel, reported 1,492 U.S. cases involving AI-generated material and more than 2,000 worldwide, said Hatting. The North Dakota Supreme Court has also issued a public notice addressing its use of artificial intelligence. Hatting urged council members to double- and triple-check any AI-generated material used for official business. The retreat then turned to workforce housing.

The slides quoted Brandon Dettlaff, executive director of the North Dakota Housing Finance Agency, who told the League of Cities, "Housing is where jobs sleep at night." According to the slides, North Dakota's population is projected to grow 7% by 2034, while the state could need an additional 48,315 housing units, a 13% increase. Current building trends are expected to add 25,589 units. Statewide, homes priced at $250,000 or less accounted for 64% of home sales in 2015, compared with 34% in 2025. Households headed by someone 65 or older are projected to increase 39% by 2034.

The slides emphasized that additional housing does not necessarily mean more of the same type of housing. City Finance Director Darcie Huwe said five of 97 home sales in 2015 were above $250,000, or about 5%. In 2025, 37% of 68 sales were above that price. The city issued two new-construction permits this year, matching the number issued in 2025, and one of this year's permits was for North Dakota State College of Science. Huwe said smaller lots and homes on her street sell quickly and questioned why more homes are not being built.

She said builders have indicated that few can construct a home for $225,000, and if builders could build at that price, she added, the homes would likely sell quickly. Huwe noted that large portions of Wahpeton were developed during the 1950s and 1970s, and some older homes may eventually become unviable. She also noted that Wahpeton has 2,511 rental units, compared with 2,680 in Devils Lake. Using sales tax revenue to buy down special assessments could reduce the cost of a $500,000 home to about $440,000, Huwe said.

However, she cautioned that there is no single solution to the housing challenge. The slides identified several areas cities can influence, including zoning, land-use policy, site selection and permitting, local tax incentives and land-use planning. Huwe cautioned that incentives should be directed toward the types of housing the city wants to encourage. She also warned that free money does not make a bad idea a good one.

Huwe directed council members to the state's ND Compass housing portal for additional information. Huwe said Vanguard Appraisals, an outside appraisal firm, will update property valuations in 2028. She said lower-priced homes are expected to see significant increases, middle-priced homes see larger increases and apartments are currently assessed at about 74% of their value. Under the state's 3% cap, Huwe said, mill rates would have to decrease as property values rise.

Officials also noted that the city receives about 24% of a Wahpeton property tax bill, with the school district receiving approximately half. The retreat concluded with a break, followed by a strengths, opportunities, aspirations and results exercise and a review of a slide outlining proposed 2026-2028 goals and priorities. The article did not report any votes taken at the retreat. The article did not say when the next retreat would be held.

stories.Headline: LAUSD committee hears teachers and students on student AI use as Google plans school controls
stories.Summary:
Google announced on November 3, 2026 that it plans to give schools control over whether to enable Google Search, without offering a conventional AI-free version through its standard settings. The Los Angeles Unified School District had earlier restricted generative AI on district-issued student devices. The district subsequently said it had disabled Google's AI-generated search summaries, known as AI Overviews, while preserving access to conventional Google Search. LAUSD's Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee held a meeting on November 13, 2026. The committee scheduled presentations involving district teachers and students, alongside a community presentation by Schools Beyond Screens Los Angeles.

Under Google's forthcoming controls, Google Search and several AI services will be disabled by default for K, 12 student accounts until administrators choose which services to enable. Google says the changes give schools greater control over access to its products. The company has also said AI is deeply integrated into Search, and its standard forthcoming controls do not offer schools a conventional version of Google Search with those integrated AI features removed. The published committee agenda identified teachers from Chandler Elementary School, Union Avenue Elementary School and Laurel Cinematic Arts & Creative Technologies Magnet, along with three student presenters. The meeting also included a presentation on research about AI's effects on students and possible district responses.

Lila Byock, an LAUSD parent and founder of Schools Beyond Screens, welcomed the district's September moratorium on student-facing generative AI. Her organization had advocated for restrictions while the district reviewed potential risks and developed safeguards. Byock argues that students can learn to understand AI critically without unrestricted access to the technology, including examining how AI systems produce information, how they can mislead users and what interests influence their development. Stephen Aguilar, an associate professor of education at the University of Southern California who studies educational technology, has warned that broad restrictions could create unequal opportunities. Aguilar also argues that older students need opportunities to evaluate AI-generated information under teacher supervision.

Aguilar said students with personal devices may continue using AI outside school, while those who rely on district-issued computers could have fewer chances to develop familiarity with the tools. LAUSD is distributing a survey to parents, students and staff as it develops recommendations. The agenda identifies participants, but does not by itself establish what individual students or teachers told the committee. Some districts have explored technical tools to suppress AI-generated answers while retaining traditional search results. Whether LAUSD's existing safeguards will remain effective under Google's planned changes has not been publicly established.

Parriva reported on California teachers' proposed three-year AI moratorium, as educators question which safeguards schools need before expanding student access. Parriva's guide to LAUSD's screen-time restrictions explains how the district has also been limiting device use during instruction. The district's decision to restrict generative AI on district-issued student devices came amid broader changes to classroom technology. The Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee is expected to continue meeting during the school year. Its work is intended to inform recommendations that the full school board may consider.

Sessions are scheduled for December 9, January 20, March 3 and April 7. The question remains how the district will weigh survey responses, account for differences among school communities and explain which concerns influenced its recommendations. For families, the stakes extend beyond Google, as the decisions will help determine how students learn to research information, evaluate automated answers and develop skills for a world where AI is increasingly common. LAUSD must decide what technology belongs in classrooms. The public question is whether students, teachers and families will have a meaningful role in determining the answer.

stories.Headline: 42 state attorneys general ask a bankruptcy judge to block Character.AI from selling users’ private chats
stories.Summary:
Attorneys general from 42 states asked a federal bankruptcy judge to intervene in the sale of a social companion chatbot. These officials want to prevent the sale of private conversations and impose safeguards on artificial intelligence chatbots operated by Character.AI. The coalition filed this objection in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Delaware on November 20, 2026. They argue that the proposed sale could put children at risk and expose sensitive mental health information. The app is owned by a company called Character Technologies Inc.

The states object to a proposed 10 million dollar sale to a private company called Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC. They demand that the new owners be blocked from accessing conversations involving medical disclosures, self-harm, suicidal thoughts, and comments by minors. The coalition wants informed consent and direct notice for users before any such sensitive data is transferred to the buyer. They also seek a court order blocking access to information on children and characters posing as mental health professionals. The identity of the investor behind Smirks and Pangs has not been publicly disclosed.

Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday said children using these chatbots should not have their information misused or sold to the highest bidder. He stated he is thankful that the court ordered a data privacy expert to watch over the case. New York Attorney General Letitia James warned that parents should not worry about chatbots pretending to be therapists or encouraging violence. The attorneys general contend that transferring conversations without appropriate consent could violate state privacy laws. They have asked technology companies to better warn consumers about self-proclaimed online therapists.

The coalition alleges that Character.AI chatbots encouraged harmful behavior and engaged minors in sexually explicit conversations. Researchers recorded hundreds of instances of sexual exploitation and grooming in accounts registered to children. More than 2.1 million U.S. accounts identified their users as being younger than 18 years old. The bankruptcy dispute follows allegations that the chatbots contributed to the suicides of two teenagers. The platform has more than 20 million monthly users who interact with characters portraying psychologists, teachers, and celebrities.

Users disclosed relationship problems, eating disorders, and suicidal thoughts during interactions with the chatbots, according to the plaintiffs. Character.AI claims it voluntarily restricted minors from accessing certain open-ended conversations, but the states argue these restrictions are inadequate. The court appointed an independent consumer privacy ombudsman to examine the privacy implications of the proposed sale. This ombudsman will review any proposed sale involving AI assets, platform operations, chat data, or user accounts. The case is titled In re Character Technologies, Inc., Case No. 26-11603.

The bankruptcy court is scheduled to consider the proposed assets sale at a hearing on December 3. A separate 20 million dollar agreement exists with Disney Worldwide Services to license intellectual property and technology. The Disney transaction does not include the disputed user data that the 42 states are seeking to protect. The articles leave open whether the judge will grant the court order to block the data transfer. It remains unclear if the identity of the Smirks and Pangs owner will be revealed.

stories.Headline: Researchers present VisAlloc, a dual-level framework for visual self-distillation in multimodal models
stories.Summary:
Haoran Xu, Tian Chen, Yuhe Wu, Yanbo Zhao, Junchi Liao, Hongyu Wang, Jiaze Li, Wentao Wang, Yanfeng Li and Rui Qian posted a paper titled VisAlloc: Allocating Visual Supervision for On-Policy Self-Distillation on arXiv on 25 November 2026. The paper describes a dual-level framework that combines sample-level visual filtering with token-level counterfactual reweighting for on-policy self-distillation in multimodal large language models. The authors say on-policy self-distillation is a promising approach to improving visual reasoning in these models, but that not all samples benefit equally from privileged visual guidance. They add that uniform token supervision can dilute visually grounded signals, which their framework is meant to address.

A fixed paired-teacher filter keeps only samples that are answered correctly from an evidence-centered positive crop but incorrectly from a spatially displaced negative crop. At the token level, two EMA teachers score the same student-generated response, and the absolute differences in their log-probabilities measure view sensitivity. Extra supervision goes to tokens admitted by sensitivity or by disagreement between the teachers' distributions, with shared frozen-prior, template-bigram and student-teacher divergence gates. Inverse-frequency redistribution keeps the total additional weight within each micro-batch, while the positive teacher remains the only distillation target, and inference needs only the full-image student. Across eight benchmarks, the authors report that their 4B and 9B models reach macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, which they say beats Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points respectively.

The authors are responsible for the method and for the reported results, and they present the gains over the Vision-OPD reproductions as their own findings. They state that inference requires only the full-image student, so the filtering and reweighting work at training time rather than at deployment. They also give a GitHub link for the code, which they say is available there. The paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence on arXiv.

The work sits in the field of on-policy self-distillation for multimodal large language models, where the authors say privileged visual guidance does not help every sample equally. The abstract reports results on eight benchmarks for the 4B and 9B models but gives no further detail on those benchmarks or on the training setup. Beyond the code link and the reported numbers, the articles do not say what happens next with the method.

Articles.Title: VisAlloc: Allocating Visual Supervision for On-Policy Self-Distillation

stories.Headline: Researchers present VC-VQA, a benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning in multimodal models
stories.Summary:
Jiatong Ma, Yuchen Liu, Longteng Guo, Yichen Yuan, Yuze Wu, Dongze Hao, Ru Zhen, Yanhao Zhang, Haonan Lu and Jing Liu posted a paper on arXiv on 25 November 2026 proposing VC-VQA, which they describe as a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning. The benchmark is meant to systematically evaluate how well Multimodal Large Language Models handle fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. The authors say existing benchmarks mainly treat visual information as entity recognition and lean on text-based external knowledge, while VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information. It does so by considering both the source of that information, internal or external images, and the stage at which it is involved, before or after retrieval.

VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, to identify visual clues before retrieval, and to localize, verify or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. The authors also built a controlled multimodal knowledge base that holds traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. They evaluated 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. The experiments produced three key findings, which are that current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning, that fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck, and that agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration.

The paper is credited to Jiatong Ma and nine other authors, and the authors state that VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. They say their code and dataset are available at a URL given in the paper. The work is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence. The abstract page also carries the standard arXivLabs text about collaborators developing and sharing features on the site and about the values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy that arXiv says it and its partners uphold.

stories.Headline: Vanderbilt legal scholars debate whether AI output deserves First Amendment protection
stories.Summary:
Three legal scholars at Vanderbilt Law School debated whether AI output should receive First Amendment protections on November 23, 2026. The event was the fourth in the Respectfully Dissent series and was moderated by professor Jennifer Shinall. These experts disagreed on whether existing legal rules can protect both AI users and people harmed by generated content. The discussion focused on government regulation of AI speech rather than a newly issued court ruling. The participants sought to balance the ability to share ideas with the need to prevent harmful output.

Eugene Volokh of Stanford's Hoover Institution argued that AI output should face the same First Amendment rules as other speech. Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law called for federal safeguards including periodic and random platform monitoring and data scraping limits. Francesca Procaccini of Vanderbilt proposed tailoring protection to the setting and potential harm to avoid enabling censorship. Tsesis also wanted protections against autonomous AI decisions in private matters to prevent risks like unauthorized real-time facial recognition. Volokh noted that ordinary limits regarding libel, minors, professional malpractice, and discriminatory decisions in hiring or sales should remain.

Eugene Volokh stated that AI output is a joint effort between the user and the company and deserves protection. He used a camera analogy to argue that using a manufactured tool does not erase relevant speech rights. Alex Tsesis argued that large language models lack human consciousness, intention, and reasoning, so they should not have rights. He claimed that audience interest in receiving AI information cannot settle the limits of regulation like securities rules do. Francesca Procaccini suggested that existing doctrine already adjusts protection based on settings like schools, government offices, and private workplaces.

The debate affected human users who create ideas and people exposed to risks like deepfakes or social scoring. Tsesis argued that human involvement alone does not eliminate the exploitation of vulnerabilities or the use of facial recognition. Procaccini warned that courts could use the First Amendment to weaken existing tort, civil-rights, and property claims. Volokh countered that a flexible approach would depart from familiar rules and create confusing restrictions with unknown consequences. Tsesis added that existing commercial-speech rules and disclosure requirements might not fit within the proposed flexible framework.

The articles explain that AI does not need its own rights for its output to raise a free-speech dispute. The scholars examined whether protecting human users leaves lawmakers with less room to regulate the content generated by AI. The core conflict is whether existing speech protections can accommodate AI risks without weakening ordinary legal remedies or users' rights. The discussion highlighted the tension between the democratic value of sharing ideas and threats to privacy and autonomy. This background establishes that the legal status of AI-generated expression remains a subject of significant academic disagreement.

The argument over how to regulate AI-generated speech remains unresolved among the three legal scholars. The articles leave open whether any new framework can address AI harms without weakening the rights of the users. It is unclear if the proposed flexible approach can be reconciled with current commercial-speech rules or disclosure requirements. The scholars did not reach a consensus on whether AI output should be treated as a joint human-corporate effort. No court ruling or settled policy was announced as a result of the Vanderbilt Law School event.

Articles.Title: Vanderbilt hosts debate over how far free-speech rights should protect AI output - Superpower Daily

stories.Headline: Researchers present ForeSeek, a video agent that predicts unseen moments to cut frame use
stories.Summary:
Yuchen Sun, Siyuan Cheng, Shi-Zhe Chen, Yixin Qin, Jinwen Luo and Zheng Wei posted a paper titled ForeSeek: Foresight-Driven Reasoning for Long-Form Video Understanding on arXiv on 25 November 2026. The paper describes ForeSeek, a foresight-driven video agent that the authors say turns long-video reasoning from reactive retrieval into predictive exploration. The authors say retrieval-driven video agents built on multimodal large language models reactively fetch clips based on local saliency without a global temporal plan, which they describe as a significant bottleneck. Instead of blindly probing the timeline, ForeSeek forms visually grounded expectations over unseen temporal regions, checks them through targeted observations and refines its search as evidence emerges, with failed expectations serving as signals for backtracking.

The paper reports a two-stage training framework that the authors say gives multimodal large language models foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision making. The authors say experiments on five long-video benchmarks show ForeSeek consistently improves the efficiency-accuracy trade-off of long-video reasoning. They claim it reaches competitive or superior accuracy while observing 2.5 to 4.4 times fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent. The paper says code is available at a URL given in the abstract.

The authors are responsible for the work and for the claims made in the paper, including the comparison with the strongest search-based agent and the frame savings of 2.5 to 4.4 times. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the release of the paper and the code.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Stacy Garrity runs undisclosed AI deepfake ads against Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania midterms
stories.Summary:
Republican candidate Stacy Garrity used AI deepfake ads during the 2026 Pennsylvania midterms. These misleading advertisements targeted Governor Josh Shapiro to influence the gubernatorial race. The ads appeared during an election cycle that some called the first AI election. They featured an AI avatar of Shapiro discussing sexual harassment and data centers. The campaign did not disclose the AI use until forty seconds into the ad.

Pennsylvania currently does not require disclosure of AI use in political ads. State Representative Tarik Khan penned HB 811 to ban all AI in political ads. This bill has remained stalled in the Senate during the current legislative session. The Wesleyan Media Project identified 289 AI political ads costing 187 million dollars. Over 90 percent of those ads were purchased by Republican candidates and groups.

Stacy Garrity defended the ad and backed the claims about the record of Shapiro. She reiterated that the advertisement did disclose its use of artificial intelligence technology. A spokesperson for Josh Shapiro called the deepfake ad cheap and dishonest AI bullshit. Philip Hensley-Robin of Common Cause Pennsylvania said clear disclosures are very important. He stated that Pennsylvania should adopt disclosure laws like many other states.

Some viewers found the AI easy to spot while others called it professional. One Facebook user wrote that deepfakes are unethical and have no place in politics. Professor Gang Wang said negative impacts linger even if viewers recognize the AI messaging. Studio Brubaker owner Garrett Brubaker said people might not immediately clock an AI ad. He noted that the technology is only going to get worse over time.

The Wesleyan Media Project has analyzed political advertising since the year 2010. State Senator Doug Mastriano posted AI images of the governor on X before the election. These images showed the governor beneath headlines that criticized his budget record. Another ad showed Shapiro channeling lightning through his hands in a data center warehouse. The Pennsylvania Department of State directed voters to a fact-check page during midterms.

New leaders must now decide if they will put guardrails on Big Tech. Governor Josh Shapiro has not yet decided how he might outlaw AI election ads. Katie Paul suggested putting a cost on producing AI generated political ads for campaigns. Experts say federal regulation is needed to protect the democratic process from misinformation. It remains open how to regulate technologies that evolve every six months.

stories.Headline: Researchers present DriftGuard, a two-stage framework that detects memory drift in LLM agents online
stories.Summary:
Licheng Pan, Yuzhou Chen, Zhixuan Chu, Yichen Sun, Han Zheng, Zhiyu Wang, Hao Wang, Yan Wang, Bingyu Zhu, Haiwen Hong, Longtao Huang and Kui Ren posted a paper titled DriftGuard: Online Memory-Drift Detection via Causal Attribution for LLM Agents to arXiv on 25 November 2026. The paper addresses memory drift, which it describes as an adversarial or misleading memory that alters an LLM agent's execution path and final outcome. The authors frame their work as an investigation of online memory-drift detection, which estimates each retrieved memory's causal contribution to potential drift at serving time. The paper states that code is available at a URL given in the abstract.

The authors identify two challenges, the first being that content-level features such as perplexity or retrieval relevance cannot determine which retrieved memory would change agent behavior if neutralized. The second is that counterfactual attribution is prohibitively expensive for online detection, because it requires replaying downstream agent and tool execution for each candidate memory and exceeds real-time serving budgets. Their proposed DriftGuard is a two-stage framework that decouples offline causal supervision from online estimation. It first builds causal supervision through repeated paired counterfactual replays, continuing the original and single-memory neutralized trajectory suffixes from a shared pre-action state. The resulting annotations are aggregated by component-wise majority voting into a memory drift score capturing action change, attack removal, violation removal and task recovery.

Guided by that supervision, DriftGuard learns an online risk model that estimates the memory drift score from pre-action information and flags drift-inducing memories through its maximum component risk, without online counterfactual rollouts. The authors report that extensive experiments show DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and enables efficient online defense. The abstract does not give the size of the experiments, the datasets used or any measured figures. The paper's arXiv identifier is 2611.25583.

Articles.Title: DriftGuard: Online Memory-Drift Detection via Causal Attribution for LLM Agents

stories.Headline: Tech companies and governments accelerate global AI data center construction despite resource concerns
stories.Summary:
Tech companies and governments are accelerating the global construction of AI data centers to lead in artificial intelligence development. These facilities provide the physical and computational infrastructure required to train and run large-scale AI models. Technology companies are investing hundreds of billions of dollars into these projects as the race for AI expansion heats up. However, different countries are taking various approaches to construction based on their economic capital, land availability, and energy supply. Some nations are fast-tracking projects to attract investment, while others have restricted new construction due to resource concerns.

The United States has over five thousand operational and planned facilities, while globally there are more than 13,000 across 180 countries. In July 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to fast-track permits and provide federal loans, grants, and tax incentives. China launched the East Data, West Computing project in 2022 to move data centers to western provinces with more renewable energy. The UAE is reassessing the $30 billion Stargate UAE project, and Saudi Arabia is investing through the HUMAIN company. In 2024, the Netherlands banned new hyperscale data centers, and Singapore halted new approvals from 2019 to 2022.

David Hart of the Council on Foreign Relations stated that backlash to construction reflects abstract concerns about AI rather than just resources. He argued that the United States energy policy is contradictory because it fast-tracks data centers while blocking cheap wind power. Connor Martin of the Council on Foreign Relations said the private sector leads in the United States, leaving the government less leverage. Martin also noted that Gulf countries might cut committed funding to focus on their own oil infrastructure and defense after the Iran war. He further stated that there is currently too much uncertainty in the market regarding when economic gains will materialize.

Communities have pushed back against construction because they fear strained resources and rising power bills for residential electricity. Residents in rural Michigan picketed DTE Energy to oppose a proposed $7 billion data center for these reasons. Environmentalists are concerned that AI carbon dioxide emissions could reach four hundred million tons annually by 2030. Harvard University researchers estimated that one data center in Loudoun County, Virginia, could cause up to $99 million in annual health damages. S&P Global estimates that 43 percent of global data centers face high water stress, including 38 percent in the United States.

AI data centers rely on graphics processing units and liquid cooling, requiring far more power than traditional central processing unit facilities. A single Nvidia GB200 NVL72 rack draws 120 kilowatts, which equals the average electricity demand of one hundred American homes. Global data centers used almost 1.2 trillion gallons of water in 2025, enough for six hundred million people in sub-Saharan Africa. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft plan to spend roughly $725 billion on capital expenditures in 2026, mostly for AI infrastructure. Microsoft saw its emissions rise 25 percent in fiscal year 2025, which challenged its goal to be carbon negative by 2030.

The International Energy Agency estimates that data center electricity consumption will more than double by 2030 due to increased AI use. UN reports project that AI-related water consumption could reach nearly 2.5 trillion gallons annually by the year 2030. Land needed to generate electricity for these global facilities could exceed 14,500 square kilometers by 2030. Africa's data center market is expected to attract between $10 billion and $20 billion in investment by 2030. The articles leave open whether the high levels of debt used to finance this build-out will make lenders more cautious.

Articles.Title: The Global AI Data Center Debate, Explained - Council on Foreign Relations

stories.headline_source: The Global AI Data Center Debate, Explained - Council on Foreign Relations

stories.Headline: Canada pursues sovereign AI capacity and issue-based coalitions to reduce reliance on US tech giants
stories.Summary:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled self-strengthening and engagement through “variable geometry” as the central tenets of his middle-power doctrine at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, the Council on Foreign Relations said in a November 23, 2026 article. The article said the goal on AI is for countries to avoid being “forced to choose between hegemons and hyperscalers.” The article said Canada has demonstrated leadership on AI governance globally and has abundant energy, sovereign funds dedicated to computing power investment, a thriving research community, and partnerships to secure resources it doesn’t have at home. The article said Geoffrey Hinton and other University of Toronto researchers demonstrated the viability of deep learning, and Yoshua Bengio’s work with University of Montreal researchers improved neural network performance through breakthroughs on next-word prediction and attention. The article said AlexNet, built by Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever, demonstrated how much better neural networks trained on graphics processing units perform for image recognition.

The article said Canada was the first country to produce a national AI strategy in 2017 and has changed course frequently. The article said the government tabled the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act in 2022, a comprehensive, risk-based framework that would have imposed obligations on high-impact AI systems but deferred the criteria for those systems to future regulation. The article said the bill, tabled a few months before the release of ChatGPT, was the subject of government amendments in late 2023 that sought to bring general-purpose systems within its scope, and it died when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025. The article said the government’s newest approach has three tracks: building sovereign capacity, legislating against specific harms, and forming issue-based coalitions, and its AI for All strategy, released in June 2026, seeks to protect Canadians from harms, spread adoption, build Canadian-controlled infrastructure and scale domestic firms. The article said the government tabled Bill C-34 in June 2026, which proposes to bar children under sixteen from social media platforms unable to demonstrate adequate safeguards and to require AI chatbots to mitigate the risk of harmful content.

The article said David Lametti, Canada’s ambassador to the United Nations, framed AI as an economic priority “in this post-Davos world” and said Canada does not “want to be reliant on hyperscalers that are south of the border.” The article said Lametti described “the real digital divide” as the gap in computing power between a handful of companies and every government, including the U.S. government. The article said Lametti said Canada does not seek parity and that “You just need to have enough” to build frontier models, diffuse the technology and run testing. The article said Lametti conceded a level of integration with the United States that Canada “can never ignore,” and that asked what Canada needs from international cooperation, he answered, “all of the above.” The article said Lametti said the United Nations “remains the only institution where 193 countries can talk to 5 big companies.”

The article said critics have voiced concerns about the AI for All strategy’s largely voluntary nature, the lack of a designated actor charged with coordinating national security across its six pillars, and its underlying assumption of causal relationships between actions and objectives, such as AI literacy producing trust. The article said the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act was criticized for vagueness and a lack of public consultation in drafting. The article said Meta committed to investing C$13 billion in a single data center in Alberta, whereas the Canadian government committed to spending C$2 billion on sovereign compute over a five-year period. The article said Canada launched a Sovereign Technology Alliance with Germany in 2026 to accelerate AI commercialization and concluded negotiations on a digital trade agreement with the European Union. The article said child protection resonated across governments and stakeholders at the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in July, who launched the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.

The article said Canadian research has been fundamental to modern AI, but commercialization of those breakthroughs has been driven by U.S. companies, primarily through the acquisition of Canadian research ventures and intellectual property and the recruitment of Canadian-trained researchers to U.S. firms. The article said the need to drive adoption and capture the economic value of Canada’s intellectual contributions, amid concerns about trust and safety, has been a common denominator across its AI governance approaches. The article said an ongoing trade war with the United States and the Mythos kill-switch moment have added another dimension: managing interdependence with “hegemons and hyperscalers.” The article said the central trade-off is between control and cost, since compute that Canada owns is harder for a foreign government or company to restrict but will be smaller and likely costlier than capacity rented from U.S. hyperscalers. The article said money spent building compute comes at the opportunity cost of investment in adoption, and the strategy still envisions buying where Canada cannot build.

The article said Canada was chosen to colead the review of the mandate for the Dialogue and the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. The article said whether the United Nations can offer more than a meeting place will determine how much the Dialogue matters. The article said Canada’s ability to self-strengthen at home and to lead globally will help determine whether AI middle powers become “une force de la nature” or remain a nebulous concept. The article said the work represents the views solely of the author, Tony Oweke, a CFR research fellow in artificial intelligence. The article said the Council on Foreign Relations is an independent, nonpartisan membership organization, think tank and publisher, and takes no institutional positions on matters of policy.

Articles.Title: Canada’s AI Playbook: How a Middle Power Can Rely Less on U.S. Tech Giants - Council on Foreign Relations

stories.headline_source: Canada’s AI Playbook: How a Middle Power Can Rely Less on U.S. Tech Giants - Council on Foreign Relations

stories.Headline: Ben Kang and co-authors present DiLE, a framework that preserves discriminative evidence in multimodal embeddings
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on 25 November 2026 by Ben Kang and eleven other authors presents DiLE, a discrimination-aware latent-space learning framework for universal multimodal embeddings. The authors say multimodal large language models have greatly improved input understanding in such embedding models, but that this understanding does not ensure the embeddings keep the evidence needed to tell relevant items apart from confusable alternatives. DiLE is proposed to preserve that essential discriminative evidence in the embeddings by combining task guidance with on-policy retrieval feedback. The method uses a few learnable queries to encode task-relevant information in a compact latent space, and reasoning instructions and auxiliary answer-generation supervision shape these representations to support both task understanding and retrieval discrimination.

To address task-specific discriminative needs, the authors design shared-private expert adaptation that integrates cross-task knowledge sharing with task-specific representation learning. On top of this they introduce on-policy hard-negative distillation, in which the student retrieves confusable candidates and a reverse KL divergence objective aligns its embedding-based similarity distribution with the teacher's fine-grained relevance distribution over those candidates. Candidates are periodically refreshed using updated student snapshots, which the authors say ties teacher supervision to the student's evolving retrieval behavior and confusions. Across four model configurations spanning two backbone generations, the authors report that DiLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMEB-v2, UVRB and MRMR, which they present as evidence of effectiveness across modalities and tasks.

The work is credited to Ben Kang, Junda Wang, Yuxuan Yuan, Hang Li, Yuhan Liu, Xin Chen, Wanting Geng, Tong Lin, Pei Fu, Dong Wang, Jian Luan and Huchuan Lu. The paper is listed as arXiv 2611.25419, and the authors describe the state-of-the-art results as their own claim rather than as an independent finding. The abstract presents DiLE as a response to a gap the authors identify between input understanding and the preservation of discriminative evidence in embeddings. The articles give no further details on what happens next with the framework.

Articles.Title: DiLE: Discrimination-Aware Latent-Space Learning for Universal Multimodal Embeddings

stories.headline_source: DiLE: Discrimination-Aware Latent-Space Learning for Universal Multimodal Embeddings

stories.Headline: Lowenstein Sandler says law firms must embed AI in workflows to gain an edge
stories.Summary:
The articles describe an analysis published on 23 November 2026 by Legal 500, contributed by Lowenstein Sandler LLP, a national law firm with over 400 lawyers based in New York and Palo Alto. The analysis concerns how law firms can turn artificial intelligence from a standalone tool into an integrated operating layer. It says AI is beginning to resemble the internet because it is becoming part of how people work every day. It argues that merely having the technology will not distinguish one law firm from another as access becomes nearly universal. It says the differentiator will be how effectively firms combine AI with proprietary knowledge, strategic priorities and their people's experience, judgment and relationships.

The analysis says AI can analyze information and surface patterns but does not inherently understand which partners drive revenue and why. It says AI does not know which clients may be receptive to expanding a relationship across a firm or which have established counsel for particular matters. It says AI cannot fully appreciate the history, personalities, motivations, internal politics or moments of trust that shape a client relationship, and cannot read a room. It says that understanding comes from conversations and real-world interactions among lawyers, clients and the professionals who support them. It says AI cannot replicate or analyze what a cup of coffee or a lunch reveals about a client's priorities and challenges in the client's own words.

The analysis says firms that understand how they collect, structure, maintain, update, store and access their data will be better positioned to derive meaningful insights from AI. It says the technology may assemble a partial picture from fragmented information, creating some efficiency, but the quality of its insights depends on the quality and accessibility of what surrounds it. It describes how for the past few years most firms experienced AI as a destination, with a lawyer opening a separate application, pasting in a document, asking a question and carrying the answer back into real work. It says pilots, champion networks and prompting workshops were the right place to start because people needed a safe way to experiment and build confidence. It says that model treats AI as something people go to rather than something they work with and is already giving way to a more integrated approach.

The analysis says AI is showing up inside systems lawyers and business professionals already use, including the document management system, the research platform, email, the client relationship management system, the experience database and the matter intake process. It says the question shifts from which tool to buy to how a function should work within a workflow and where judgment needs to sit within it. It says an operating layer is only as good as what it can reach, and that if precedents are scattered, experience data is incomplete and client information lives in disconnected systems, AI will move faster but not smarter. It says knowledge management and data strategy, once considered back-office disciplines, become the foundation determining whether AI produces generic output or firm-specific insight.

It frames progress as a progression from build to scale to transform, and says many firms are somewhere between the first and second stages. The analysis says it is tempting to measure success by licenses deployed or prompts entered, but better measures are responsiveness, consistency, quality and time returned to higher-value work. It says lawyers and professionals spend less time producing first drafts and more time directing, reviewing and applying judgment, a more demanding role. It says AI has transformed how quickly firms can develop and deliver content, and that firms can see meaningful time returned to lawyers and business professionals even if direct cost reduction is difficult to quantify today.

It says a clean, technically competent client alert produced with a few clicks and a well-constructed prompt becomes less differentiating. It says a standard alert can be tailored by considering the recipient's industry, company size, geographic reach, growth stage, business objectives and current market pressures, with appropriate lawyer oversight. The analysis says any legal analysis or advice must remain under the direction and review of a lawyer, and that people must verify underlying facts and apply legal and commercial judgment. It says marketing and business development teams have a responsibility to provide lawyers with tools and opportunities to deepen client relationships.

It says a lawyer who recently discussed a specific challenge with a client could share a colleague's alert with an AI tool, explain the conversation and ask for help drafting a personalized note. It says governance began for most firms with a policy defining acceptable use and listing prohibited tools, acknowledged once during onboarding or a firmwide rollout, which was necessary but is no longer sufficient. It says tools change monthly, vendors update models and data terms, clients issue outside counsel guidelines with varying AI provisions, and regulators and courts continue to refine expectations around disclosure and verification. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Infobip marks 10 years in Indonesia and targets AI-powered customer engagement growth
stories.Summary:
Infobip marked 10 years of operations in Indonesia, a milestone announced in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia on Nov. 23, 2026, as the company also celebrates its 20th anniversary globally. The global AI-first cloud communications platform said it is looking ahead to how AI can further help Indonesian businesses connect service and commerce while maintaining customer trust. Infobip opened its Jakarta office in 2016, and the company said the infrastructure, partnerships and customer relationships built since then underpin the milestone. The announcement was issued as a press release by Infobip and carried by Yonhap News Agency and The Manila Times. Infobip said it is working with more brands locally to help them meet expectations through AI-powered engagement, conversational commerce, reliable connectivity and digital security.

Infobip said its one communication platform has enabled local businesses across financial services and fintech, retail and eCommerce, and digital natives. Together with Telkomsel and Google, Infobip said it is helping brands adopt Rich Communication Services to bring a connected experience through rich, conversational messaging. Blibli achieved 2.5x higher conversion rates in groceries and beauty during its Histeria 11.11 campaign, according to the release. Segari reduced customer service response times by 90%, and Sinar Mas Land's SILVIA virtual assistant handles 42% of incoming WhatsApp conversations, the release said. Infobip AgentOS enables businesses to bring AI agents, customer data, channels and human teams together on one platform, so customers can move from discovery to purchase to support in one continuous conversation.

Silvio Kutić, Co-founder and CEO of Infobip, said Infobip turns 20 this year and Indonesia has been part of that story for half of it. He said opening the Jakarta office in 2016 and establishing the local data center reflects a long-term commitment to the market. Kutić said Indonesian businesses have become increasingly ambitious over the past decade in how they connect with customers. He said Infobip will keep investing in Indonesia and working with local partners as AI creates new possibilities for service and commerce. Kukuh Prayogi, Enterprise Business Director at Infobip Indonesia, said the ten years have been built on relationships and that partners and customers have trusted Infobip with how they serve and engage customers.

Prayogi said Infobip is ready to help businesses embrace the future of customer communications with the same care and reliability they have trusted it for as AI becomes part of everyday business. The release said the next chapter for Infobip in Indonesia is about making AI adoption simple, safe and scalable. Infobip said it will continue working alongside local partners, as it has for the past decade, to help Indonesian brands turn AI ambition into everyday impact. The release said Infobip will do so with the security and reliability brands expect from a trusted partner. The release said Infobip's platform has enabled local businesses across financial services and fintech, retail and eCommerce, and digital natives, with customer results demonstrating the value of connected communications.

Infobip described itself as a global cloud communications platform that enables businesses to build connected experiences across all stages of the customer journey, with AI as the driving force of innovation. The company said it delivers omnichannel engagement, identity, user authentication and contact centre solutions through a single, natively built platform. Infobip said its technology has the capacity to reach over seven billion mobile devices in 6 continents connected to 10k+ connections, of which 800+ are direct operator connections. The company said it was established in 2006 and is led by its co-founders, CEO Silvio Kutić and CTO Izabel Jelenić. Infobip said it is focused on enabling and accelerating AI adoption as it continues its transformation into an AI-first company.

The release listed recognitions including a #16 ranking in Fortune's Europe's Most Innovative Companies 2026 in June 2026, up from #68 in 2025. Infobip said it was named a Leader in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for Communications Platform as a Service for the fourth consecutive year in May 2026. The release said Infobip was named the number one Established Leader in the Juniper Research RCS for Business 2026 Leaderboard in Feb 2026. Infobip said it was recognized as a growth and innovation leader in Frost Radar: Communications Platform as a Service by Frost & Sullivan in Oct 2025. The release said Infobip was ranked the number one Established Leader in the Juniper Research Mobile Messaging Fraud Prevention Market report in Sept 2025.

stories.Headline: Samsung Electronics boosts NAND output in China to meet AI data center demand
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics plans to increase the production of ninth-generation vertical NAND flash memory at its Xi’an Plant 2 in China. Industry sources reported this development on November 24, 2026, noting that the company is responding to high demand for enterprise solid-state drives. This surge in demand is being driven by the explosive growth of the artificial intelligence data center market. The company intends to expand its monthly output of these specific wafers from 10,000 to 50,000 within one year. This fivefold increase requires converting existing sixth-generation production lines to ninth-generation processes and upgrading cleanroom electroplating equipment.

Once these changes are complete, total NAND production in China, including output from Xi’an Plant 1, will reach 100,000 wafers per month. This total represents roughly one-third of the global NAND production capacity for Samsung Electronics. The ninth-generation technology features a 286-layer architecture, which is about 21 percent higher than the 236 layers found in the eighth-generation version. Industry sources say this aggressive investment reflects a polarized market where demand for enterprise drives is surging while mobile and PC demand falls. The company is prioritizing high-performance products to maintain its market position against competitors like Yangtze Memory Technologies Co. Samsung has already introduced the PM1763 enterprise solid-state drive, which was unveiled in July to serve AI data centers.

This product is claimed to offer more than 1.8 times the power efficiency of the previous model. The company also plans to build additional ninth-generation production lines at its Pyeongtaek Plant 5 in South Korea. This strategy focuses on high-value products to maximize profitability while general-purpose NAND prices continue to decline. Samsung held a 35.1 percent share of the global enterprise solid-state drive market as of the second quarter. By repositioning the Xi’an campus as a hub for these drives, the company hopes to widen its lead over other manufacturers.

stories.Headline: Design lets recurrent neural networks rewire their connections during use
stories.Summary:
Plastic Self-Constructing Architecture is a design for recurrent neural networks that can change their wiring during use, published on Zenodo on November 25, 2026. In this design a PSCA neuron retains its activity according to a time constant specific to that cell, and an optional directed self-connection feeds that activity back into the neuron's drive. Like any ordinary directed connection, the self-connection combines a persistent weight with an activity-dependent trace that is gated by the receiving cell. Within each input frame, cells update synchronously on the current graph and produce a readout, after which the frame's activities can update connection traces and target feedback can adjust persistent parameters.

At the frame boundary, structural edits can add or remove cells and can form, remove or rewire connections between them. This separation between cell state and connection state lets a neuron gain or lose a feedback path while carrying its activity and time constant across the edit. The design therefore describes how a recurrent network's wiring can change during use rather than staying fixed once it is built. The article presents these cell dynamics and network construction rules as a design, and it gives no results from experiments or simulations.

The article does not name an author, an institution or a funder, and it reports no measurements, benchmarks or comparisons with other network designs. It states no claim about performance, and it does not say what the design is intended to be used for beyond describing its dynamics and construction. The only date the article gives for the work itself is its publication on Zenodo on November 25, 2026, and the only other date it gives is a planned Zenodo intervention on Thursday, November 26, 2026, between 08:00 and 08:05 UTC, when the repository will be unavailable for five minutes because of a scheduled database migration.

The article is published under the Creative Commons Attribution license, which allows re-distribution and re-use of the work on the condition that the creator is appropriately credited. The article does not say what happens next with the design, and it describes no planned tests, applications or follow-up work. It also gives no account of earlier related designs, so it places the work in no wider research context. Beyond the publication itself and the license terms, the article states nothing further about the work's status or its future.

stories.Headline: Google cuts 2027 Broadcom TPU shipments by about 1M units and plans more MediaTek chips, Kuo says
stories.Summary:
Google reportedly reduced its planned 2027 shipments of AI chips designed by Broadcom on November 20, 2026. The company is preparing to increase shipments of an alternative chip designed by MediaTek. This shift was reported by technology supply-chain analyst Ming-Chi Kuo. The changes involve custom processors known as Tensor Processing Units. Google is adjusting the mix of these processors for its AI workloads.

The plan cuts planned 2027 shipments of the Broadcom-designed TPU 8i series by approximately 1 million units. This reduction represents roughly 20 percent of the previously expected shipment volume for that series. The figures imply a reduction from approximately 5 million chips to 4 million chips. Most cuts affect the higher-priced 8i Max, which is also known as Whalefish. Google plans to increase 2027 shipments of the MediaTek-designed TPU 8t series.

Ming-Chi Kuo is an analyst at TF International Securities who based the report on an industry survey. He stated that Google has repeatedly emphasized that frontier model development receives first call on computing resources. Kuo characterized the changing shipment mix as an adjustment to that priority. He linked the change to tight supply chains and data-center power constraints. He noted that details for the MediaTek shipment increase remain unsettled.

Broadcom shares fell 8.9 percent on the day amid broad-based selling across the semiconductor sector. Investors are reassessing expectations for AI-chip suppliers due to the reported shipment changes. The report is directionally unfavorable for Broadcom's Google TPU business and potentially favorable for MediaTek. The reduction in one chip family does not mean Google expects less overall AI computing demand. The report adds uncertainty around future revenue for Broadcom.

TPUs are custom processors that Google uses for its AI workloads. Google is prioritizing the work involved in building its most advanced AI models. The company is navigating limited data-center power and supply-chain constraints. This decision could reflect a way to allocate scarce manufacturing capacity and electricity. The report does not suggest that Google is pulling back on its broader AI ambitions.

The outlook for 2027 remains subject to revisions since there was no official Google announcement. It is unclear if additional 8t shipments will fully offset the reduction in the 8i family. The report did not provide pricing, contract terms, or an estimate of the financial effect on Broadcom. It remains unknown how much Google will ultimately increase its MediaTek-designed chip orders. The final mix of chips and its impact on supplier revenue are still open.

stories.Headline: Oracle and CoreWeave shares rise as investors bet AI computing spending will continue
stories.Summary:
Oracle and CoreWeave shares rose sharply as investors bet that spending on artificial intelligence computing would keep flowing, according to market reports on the move. The gains came as the two companies drew fresh buying interest from investors who expect demand for AI infrastructure to hold up. Oracle and CoreWeave are among the companies that supply computing capacity behind the AI industry. The move marked a reversal for a sector that had faced repeated waves of selling in the weeks before. The reports did not give specific closing prices or percentage moves for the two stocks on the day of the gains.

The articles describe the wider market backdrop, with the S&P 500 down 3.70% and the Nasdaq down 5.28% in the same period covered. Nvidia, a key supplier to the AI trade, fell 10.94% to $125.53 in the listed prices. CoreWeave had earlier lost 7% in morning trading on a Monday in November 2026, while Oracle dropped 4% at that time. Responsibility for the swings rests with investors adjusting their exposure to AI-related businesses, the articles say. Nvidia was preparing to report quarterly results after Tuesday's closing bell, and leadership uncertainty following Jensen Huang's departure added concern.

Interim CEO Colette Kress was scheduled to hold an employee meeting on Wednesday. Analysts quoted in the coverage described the AI trade as strong despite the latest rout, with one calling it just another scare. The context is a volatile stretch for AI infrastructure stocks, which had extended losses beyond chipmakers to companies supplying computing capacity and networking equipment. Marvell's proposed all-stock purchase of Lumentum, valued at about $115 billion when first disclosed, had also drawn analyst questions about whether the deal would proceed. The articles do not say what happens next for Oracle and CoreWeave beyond the reported gains.

Articles.Title: Oracle and CoreWeave stocks stage big gains as investors bet the AI cash will keep flowing - MarketWatch

stories.headline_source: Oracle and CoreWeave stocks stage big gains as investors bet the AI cash will keep flowing

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike schedules virtual event on AI threats and agentic SOC shift
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced a virtual event titled The Next Era of Cyber Defense: Fighting AI-Powered Threats with AI, scheduled for December 9 in the Americas, December 10 in JAPAC and December 10 in Europe. The company said AI is changing the speed and scale of cyberattacks and that defenders need to keep pace. CrowdStrike leaders will give a special update on the latest AI threats, frontier AI readiness and the shift to the agentic SOC. Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike Senior Vice President of Counter Adversary Operations, will give a special AI threat briefing on the latest AI-enabled adversary activity. The briefing will include real-world examples of attackers putting agentic AI to work.

The event covers AI threats, frontier AI readiness and the shift to the agentic SOC, according to CrowdStrike. CrowdStrike describes its Next-Gen SIEM as the world's only AI-native SOC platform, a claim the company makes. CrowdStrike calls its threat intelligence offering the leader in cyber threat intelligence, backed by world-class research and elite threat hunting. CrowdStrike describes its endpoint security offering as the leader in EPP and EDR, built to secure the agentic endpoint. CrowdStrike lists Project QuiltWorks as an industry coalition mobilizing to close the frontier AI vulnerability gap at scale.

CrowdStrike says AI is changing the speed and scale of cyberattacks and defenders need to keep pace. The company says its event will give an update on the latest AI threats, frontier AI readiness and the shift to the agentic SOC. CrowdStrike says Meyers will brief on the latest AI-enabled adversary activity. The company says the briefing will show real-world examples of attackers putting agentic AI to work. CrowdStrike says its Falcon Complete service stops breaches across the entire attack surface with elite 24/7 managed detection and response.

CrowdStrike says its AI Security Services secure AI systems and operationalize AI in the SOC. The company says its Frontier AI Readiness and Resilience Service reduces frontier AI-driven risk as the time between patch and exploit continues to collapse. CrowdStrike says its Shadow AI Visibility Service discovers hidden AI tools, activity and agents across endpoint, cloud and SaaS. The company says its Automated AI Security Testing tests every AI model, application and agent for security weaknesses before deployment.

CrowdStrike says its Agentic Adversary Emulation red teams an environment to simulate real-world attacks and validate defenses. CrowdStrike says its AI Detection & Response detects, investigates and stops threats to AI systems with unified, runtime security. The company says its Agent Security secures AI agents across the agentic lifecycle, from development to adoption to runtime. CrowdStrike says its Supply Chain Security stops supply chain threats as coding agents introduce third-party packages at scale.

The company says its AI Observability evaluates agents pre-deployment and then observes their behavior and enforces accountability in production. CrowdStrike says its Seraphic Enterprise Browser secures the modern workforce by protecting users, data and AI in the browser. CrowdStrike says registration is open for the event. The company says the event is a virtual event.

CrowdStrike says the event features CrowdStrike leaders. The company says the event includes a special AI threat briefing from Meyers. The articles do not say what else the event will cover. More to follow.
